Puna tassa sikkhanakiccaṃ natthīti asekkhā. Iti satta ariyā sikkhantīti sekkhā. Khīṇāsavā aññassa santike sīlādīnaṃ sikkhitattā sikkhitaasekkhā nāma. Buddhapaccekabuddhā sayambhūtatāya asikkhitaasekkhā nāma. Sesapuggalā neva sikkhanti na sikkhitāti nevasekkhānāsekkhā.

19. In the explanation of "trainee" (sekkha) — those endowed with the path at the moment of the path, and those endowed with the fruit at the moment of the fruit, are trainees because they are still training in all three trainings of higher virtue, etc. But for the Arahant, at the moment of the fruit of arahantship, the threefold training has been fully trained. Since there is no further training to be done, they are "beyond training" (asekkha). Thus, the seven noble ones are called trainees (sekkhā) because they are still training. Those with destroyed taints are called "trained beyond training" (sikkhitaasekkhā) because they have trained in virtue, etc., under another. The Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas are called "untrained beyond training" (asikkhitaasekkhā) because they are self-enlightened. The remaining individuals neither train nor are trained, thus called "neither-trainee-nor-beyond-training" (nevasekkhānāsekkhā).

20. Tevijjaniddese – paṭhamaṃ pubbenivāsadibbacakkhuñāṇāni nibbattetvā pacchā arahattaṃ pattopi, paṭhamaṃ arahattaṃ [P 0.0189] patvā pacchā pubbenivāsadibbacakkhuñāṇanibbattakopi tevijjoyeva nāma. Suttantakathā pana pariyāyadesanā abhidhammakathā nippariyāyadesanāti imasmiṃ ṭhāne āgamanīyameva dhuraṃ. Tasmā paṭhamaṃ dve vijjā nibbattetvā pacchā arahattaṃ pattova idha adhippeto. Chaḷabhiññepi eseva nayo.

20. In the exposition of the Three Knowledges—one who first develops the knowledge of past lives and the divine eye, and afterwards attains arahantship; or one who first attains arahantship and afterwards develops the knowledge of past lives and the divine eye—is still called one with the Three Knowledges. However, Suttanta discourse is teaching by way of implication, while Abhidhamma discourse is teaching directly. In this connection, the authoritative tradition is what must be followed. Therefore, in this context, the intended meaning is one who first develops the two knowledges and afterwards attains arahantship. The same principle applies to one with the six superknowledges.

22. Sammāsambuddhaniddese [M 0.0040] – pubbe ananussutesūti pacchimabhave saccappaṭivedhato pubbe aññassa [V 0.0040] kassaci santike assutapubbesu. Tato purimapurimesu pana bhavesu sabbaññubodhisattā buddhasāsane pabbajitvā tīṇi piṭakāni uggahetvā gatapaccāgatavattaṃ āruyha kammaṭṭhānaṃ anulomaṃ gotrabhuṃ āhacca ṭhapenti. Tasmā pacchimabhavasmiṃyeva anācariyakabhāvaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tadā hi tathāgato pūritapāramittā aññassa santike sāmaṃ ananussutesu saṅkhatāsaṅkhatadhammesu “idaṃ dukkhaṃ…pe… ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā”ti attapaccakkhena ñāṇena cattāri saccāni abhisambujjhati.

22. In the exposition of the Perfectly Enlightened One—"previously unheard of" means that in the final existence, prior to the penetration of the truths, they were not previously heard from anyone else. However, in previous existences, the Bodhisattas aspiring to omniscience, having gone forth in the dispensation of a Buddha, learned the three Piṭakas, undertook the practice of coming and going, cultivated meditation subjects in forward order, and having reached the change-of-lineage, established it. Therefore, this statement refers only to the final existence, intending the state of having no teacher. For then, the Tathāgata, by virtue of having fulfilled the perfections, by himself with direct personal knowledge in regard to conditioned and unconditioned phenomena previously unheard of from anyone else, awakens to the four truths: "This is suffering... This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering."

Tattha cāti tasmiñca catusaccasambodhisaṅkhāte arahattamagge. Sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇāti balesu ca vasībhāvanti sabbaññutaññāṇañceva balesu ca ciṇṇavasībhāvaṃ pāpuṇāti. Buddhānañhi sabbaññutaññāṇassa ceva dasabalañāṇassa ca adhigamanato paṭṭhāya aññaṃ kātabbaṃ nāma natthi. Yathā pana ubhatosujātassa khattiyakumārassa abhisekappattito paṭṭhāya ‘idaṃ nāma issariyaṃ anāgata’nti na vattabbaṃ, sabbaṃ āgatameva hoti. Evameva buddhānaṃ arahattamaggassa āgamanato paṭṭhāya ‘ayaṃ nāma guṇo na āgato, na paṭividdho, na paccakkho’ti na vattabbo, sabbepi sabbaññuguṇā āgatā paṭividdhā paccakkhakatāva honti. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evaṃ pāramīpūraṇasiddhānubhāvena ariyamaggena paṭividdhasabbaññuguṇo puggalo sammāsambuddhoti vuccati.

Here, "and there" refers to the path of arahantship, which is the full enlightenment of the four truths. He attains omniscience and mastery over the powers—that is, he attains both the knowledge of omniscience and mastery over the powers perfected through long practice. For Buddhas, from the attainment of the knowledge of omniscience and the ten powers onward, there is nothing further to be done. Just as for a well-born khattiya prince, from the time of his consecration, it cannot be said, "This sovereignty is yet to come," for all has already come—so too for Buddhas, from the attainment of the path of arahantship onward, it cannot be said, "This quality has not yet come, been penetrated, or been directly experienced," for all the qualities of omniscience have come, been penetrated, and been made directly present. This is called—this very person, whose qualities of omniscience have been penetrated by the noble path through the power of the accomplishment of the perfections, is called a Perfectly Enlightened One.

23. Paccekabuddhaniddesepi [P 0.0190] – pubbe ananussutesūti pade pubbe vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Paccekabuddhopi hi pacchimabhave anācariyako attukkaṃsikañāṇeneva paṭividdhasacco sabbaññutaññāṇañceva balesu ca ciṇṇavasībhāvaṃ na pāpuṇāti.

23. In the exposition of the Paccekabuddha as well—in the phrase "previously unheard of," the meaning should be understood in the same way as previously explained. For a Paccekabuddha, in his final existence, without a teacher, realizes the truth through his own superior knowledge, but does not attain the knowledge of omniscience or mastery of the powers perfected through long practice.

24. Ubhatobhāgavimuttaniddese – aṭṭha vimokkhe kāyena phusitvā viharatīti aṭṭha samāpattiyo sahajātanāmakāyena paṭilabhitvā viharati. Paññāya cassa disvāti vipassanāpaññāya saṅkhāragataṃ, maggapaññāya cattāri saccāni passitvā cattāropi āsavā khīṇā honti. Ayaṃ vuccatīti [M 0.0041] ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo ubhatobhāgavimutto nāmāti vuccati. Ayañhi dvīhi bhāgehi dve vāre vimuttoti ubhatobhāgavimutto. Tatrāyaṃ theravādo – tipiṭakacūḷanāgatthero tāva āha – “samāpattiyā vikkhambhanavimokkhena, maggena samucchedavimokkhena [V 0.0041] vimuttoti ubhatobhāgehi dve vāre vimutto”ti. Tipiṭakamahādhammarakkhitatthero “nāmanissitako eso”ti vatvā –

24. In the exposition of one liberated in both ways—"He dwells having touched the eight liberations with the body" means he attains and dwells in the eight attainments along with the co-arisen mental body. "And having seen with wisdom" means that having seen the conditioned formations with insight wisdom, and the four truths with path wisdom, his four taints are destroyed. This is called—such a person is called one liberated in both ways. For he is liberated by two parts, on two occasions, thus he is 'liberated in both ways.' Herein, this is the Theravāda view—first, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga said: "He is liberated by the suppression-liberation through the attainment and by the cutting-off-liberation through the path, thus liberated by both parts, on two occasions." The Elder Tipiṭaka Mahādhammarakkhita, saying "This is dependent on name," and then—

“Accī yathā vātavegena khittā, (upasīvāti bhagavā;)

Atthaṃ paleti na upeti saṅkhaṃ;

Evaṃ munī nāmakāyā vimutto,

Atthaṃ paleti na upeti saṅkha”nti. (su. ni. 1080);

"Just as a flame, struck by the force of the wind, (Upasīva," said the Blessed One,) Goes to its end and cannot be reckoned; So too the sage, freed from the mental body, Goes to his end and cannot be reckoned." (Snp 1074)

Vatvā suttaṃ āharitvā “nāmakāyato ca rūpakāyato ca suvimuttattā ubhatobhāgavimutto”ti āha. Tipiṭakacūḷābhayatthero panāha – “samāpattiyā vikkhambhanavimokkhena ekavāraṃ vimutto maggena samucchedavimokkhena ekavāraṃ vimuttoti ubhatobhāgavimutto”ti. Ime pana tayopi therā paṇḍitā, ‘tiṇṇampi vāde kāraṇaṃ dissatī’ti tiṇṇampi [P 0.0191] vādaṃ tantiṃ katvā ṭhapayiṃsu.

Having recited the sutta, he said, "Because of being well-liberated from the mental body and the form body, he is liberated in both ways." The Elder Tipiṭakacūḷābhaya, however, said, "Liberated once through liberation by suppression with attainment, and liberated once through liberation by cutting off with the path—thus, he is liberated in both ways." These three elders were wise, and seeing reason in all three statements, they established all three views as the teaching.

Saṅkhepato pana arūpasamāpattiyā rūpakāyato vimutto, maggena nāmakāyato vimuttoti ubhohi bhāgehi vimuttattā ubhatobhāgavimutto. So catunnaṃ arūpasamāpattīnaṃ ekekato vuṭṭhāya saṅkhāre sammasitvā arahattaṃ pattānaṃ catunnaṃ, nirodhā vuṭṭhāya arahattaṃ pattassa anāgāmino ca vasena pañcavidho hoti. Tattha purimā cattāro samāpattisīsaṃ nirodhaṃ na samāpajjantīti pariyāyena ubhatobhāgavimuttā nāma. Aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī anāgāmī taṃ samāpajjitvā tato vuṭṭhāya vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pattoti nippariyāyena ubhatobhāgavimuttaseṭṭho nāma. Nanu ca arūpāvacarajjhānampi upekkhācittekaggatāhi duvaṅgikaṃ rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānampi, tasmā tampi padaṭṭhānaṃ katvā arahattaṃ pattena ubhatobhāgavimuttena bhavitabbanti? Na bhavitabbaṃ. Kasmā? Rūpakāyato avimuttattā. Tañhi kilesakāyatova vimuttaṃ, na rūpakāyato; tasmā tato vuṭṭhāya arahattaṃ patto ubhatobhāgavimutto nāma na hoti[M 0.0042]. Arūpāvacaraṃ pana nāmakāyato ca vimuttaṃ rūpakāyato cāti tadeva pādakaṃ katvā arahattaṃ patto ubhatobhāgavimutto hotīti veditabbo.

In brief, one is liberated from the form body through the formless attainments and liberated from the mental body through the path; thus, being liberated in both aspects, one is called 'liberated in both ways.' He is of five types: the four who attain arahantship by emerging from each of the four formless attainments and contemplating the formations, and the non-returner who attains arahantship by emerging from cessation. Herein, the first four, since they do not enter cessation, which is the peak of attainments, are called 'liberated in both ways' in a figurative sense. A non-returner who masters the eight attainments, enters cessation, emerges from it, develops insight, and attains arahantship is called the foremost 'liberated in both ways' in a literal sense. But is not the formless sphere jhāna also twofold, consisting of equanimity and one-pointedness, like the fourth jhāna of the form sphere? Therefore, should not one who attains arahantship based on that also be considered 'liberated in both ways'? No, it should not be so. Why? Because one is not liberated from the form body. That arahant is liberated from the body of defilements, not from the form body; thus, one who emerges from that and attains arahantship is not called 'liberated in both ways.' However, since the formless attainment entails liberation from the mental body and the form body, one who attains arahantship having made that very attainment the basis is to be understood as 'liberated in both ways'.

25. Paññāvimuttaniddese – paññāya vimuttoti paññāvimutto. So sukkhavipassako catūhi [V 0.0042] jhānehi vuṭṭhāya arahattaṃ pattā cattāro cāti pañcavidho hoti. Etesu hi ekopi aṭṭhavimokkhalābhī na hoti. Teneva na heva kho aṭṭha vimokkhetiādimāha. Arūpāvacarajjhānesu pana ekasmiṃ sati ubhatobhāgavimuttoyeva nāma hotīti.

25. In the exposition of one liberated by wisdom – one liberated by wisdom is called 'wisdom-liberated.' He is of five types: the dry-insight practitioner, and the four who attain arahantship having emerged from the four jhānas. Among these, not even one is a master of the eight liberations. Therefore, it is said, "not indeed the eight liberations," and so on. However, when one of the formless jhānas is present, he is simply called 'liberated in both ways'.

26. Kāyasakkhiniddese – ekacce āsavāti heṭṭhimamaggattayavajjhā. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo kāyasakkhīti vuccati. So hi phuṭṭhantaṃ sacchikarotīti kāyasakkhī. Jhānaphassaṃ paṭhamaṃ phusati, pacchā nirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikarotītipi kāyasakkhī. So sotāpattiphalaṭṭhaṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva arahattamaggaṭṭhā chabbidho hoti.

26. In the exposition of the bodily witness: 'Some taints' refers to those abandoned by the three lower paths. 'This is called' means that such a person is called a bodily witness. For he directly experiences the tangible; thus, a bodily witness. He first touches the contact of jhāna, and later realizes cessation, Nibbāna; thus, he is also a bodily witness. He is of six kinds, beginning from the one standing in the fruit of stream-entry up to the one standing in the path of arahantship.

27. Diṭṭhippattaniddese [P 0.0192] – idaṃ dukkhanti idaṃ dukkhaṃ, ettakaṃ dukkhaṃ, na ito uddhaṃ dukkhaṃ. Dukkhasamudayādīsupi eseva nayo. Yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti ṭhapetvā taṇhaṃ pañcupādānakkhandhe ‘dukkhasacca’nti yāthāvasarasato pajānāti. Taṇhā pana dukkhaṃ janeti nibbatteti, pabhāveti, tato taṃ dukkhaṃ samudeti; tasmā naṃ ayaṃ ‘dukkhasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Yasmā pana idaṃ dukkhañca samudayo ca nibbānaṃ patvā nirujjhanti vūpasammanti appavattiṃ gacchanti; tasmā naṃ ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Ariyo pana aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, taṃ dukkhanirodhaṃ gacchati; tena taṃ ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Ettāvatā nānākkhaṇe saccavavatthānaṃ dassitaṃ. Idāni ekakkhaṇe dassetuṃ tathāgatappaveditātiādimāha. Tattha tathāgatappaveditāti mahābodhimaṇḍe nisīdatvā tathāgatena paṭividdhā viditā pākaṭīkatā. Dhammāti catusaccadhammā. Vodiṭṭhā hontīti sudiṭṭhā honti. Vocaritāti sucaritā. Tesu anena paññā suṭṭhu carāpitā hotīti attho. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo diṭṭhippattoti vuccati. Ayañhi diṭṭhantaṃ patto. “Dukkhā saṅkhārā, sukho nirodho”ti ñāṇaṃ hoti[M 0.0043]. Diṭṭhaṃ viditaṃ sacchikataṃ passitaṃ paññāyāti diṭṭhappatto. Ayampi kāyasakkhī viya chabbidhova hoti.

27. In the exposition of the one attained to view: 'This is suffering' means this is suffering, this much is suffering, there is no suffering beyond this. The same principle applies to the origin of suffering, and so forth. 'He understands as it actually is' means that, setting aside craving, he understands the five aggregates of clinging as the 'truth of suffering' according to their true nature. But craving generates suffering, produces it, brings it into being; from that, suffering originates. Therefore, he understands this as the 'origin of suffering' as it actually is. But because this suffering and its origin cease, subside, and come to non-occurrence upon attaining Nibbāna, he therefore understands this as the 'cessation of suffering' as it actually is. And the Noble Eightfold Path leads to that cessation of suffering; by this, he understands it as the 'path leading to the cessation of suffering' as it actually is. So far, the determination of the truths at different moments has been shown. Now, to show it at a single moment, it is said, 'proclaimed by the Tathāgata,' and so forth. Here, 'proclaimed by the Tathāgata' means penetrated, known, and made manifest by the Tathāgata while seated at the great Bodhi-maṇḍala. 'Dhammas' refers to the dhammas of the four truths. 'Clearly seen' means well-seen. 'Well practiced' means well-practiced. The meaning is that wisdom is made to function excellently in them by him. 'This is called' means that such a person is called one attained to view. For he has attained what is seen. The knowledge arises: 'Conditioned things are suffering, cessation is happiness.' He is one attained to view because he has attained that which is seen, known, realized, and perceived by wisdom. This one, like the bodily witness, is also of six kinds.

28. Saddhāvimuttaniddese – no ca kho yathā diṭṭhippattassāti yathā diṭṭhippattassa āsavā parikkhīṇā, na evaṃ saddhāvimuttassāti attho. Kiṃ pana nesaṃ kilesappahāne nānattaṃ atthīti? Natthi. Atha kasmā saddhāvimutto diṭṭhippattaṃ na pāpuṇātīti? Āgamanīyanānattena. Diṭṭhippato hi āgamanamhi kilese vikkhambhento appadukkhena appakasirena akilamantova [V 0.0043] vikkhambhetuṃ sakkoti. Saddhāvimutto [P 0.0193] pana dukkhena kasirena kilamanto hutvā vikkhambhetuṃ sakkoti, tasmā diṭṭhippattaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Apica nesaṃ paññāyapi nānattaṃ atthiyeva. Diṭṭhippattassa hi upari tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ tikkhaṃ sūraṃ pasannaṃ hutvā vahati. Saddhāvimuttassa vipassanāñāṇaṃ no tikkhaṃ sūraṃ pasannaṃ hutvā vahati, tasmāpi so diṭṭhippattaṃ na pāpuṇāti.

28. In the exposition of the faith-liberated: 'But not as for one attained to view' means that the taints of the faith-liberated are not destroyed in the same way as those of one attained to view. Is there, then, a difference in the abandoning of their defilements? There is not. Why then does the faith-liberated not reach the level of one attained to view? Due to a difference in the way of progress. For one attained to view, while suppressing defilements in the course of progress, is able to suppress them with little pain, little effort, and without fatigue. The faith-liberated, however, is able to suppress them only with pain, effort, and fatigue; thus, he does not reach the level of one attained to view. Moreover, there is indeed a difference in their wisdom. For one attained to view, the insight-knowledge for the three higher paths flows sharply, heroically, and clearly. The insight-knowledge of the faith-liberated does not flow sharply, heroically, or clearly; for that reason also, he does not reach the level of one attained to view.

Yathā hi dvīsu taruṇesu sippaṃ dassentesu ekassa hatthe tikhiṇo asi, ekassa kuṇṭho. Tikhiṇena asinā kadalī chijjamānā saddaṃ na karoti. Kuṇṭhena asinā chijjamānā ‘kaṭakaṭā’ti saddaṃ karoti. Tattha tikhiṇena asinā saddaṃ akarontiyā eva kadaliyā chedanaṃ viya diṭṭhippattassa tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ vipassanāñāṇassa tikhiṇasūravippasannabhāvo. Kuṇṭhena asinā saddaṃ karontiyāpi kadaliyā chedanaṃ viya saddhāvimuttassa tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ vipassanāñāṇassa atikhiṇaasūraappasannabhāvo veditabbo. Imaṃ pana nayaṃ ‘no’ti paṭikkhipitvā, āgamanīyanānatteneva saddhāvimutto diṭṭhippattaṃ na pāpuṇātīti sanniṭṭhānaṃ kataṃ.

Just as when two young men are demonstrating their skill, one has a sharp sword in his hand, the other a blunt one. A banana tree being cut by the sharp sword makes no sound. The one being cut by the blunt sword makes a 'kaṭakaṭā' sound. Therein, the cutting of the banana tree by the sharp sword, which makes no sound, is like the sharp, heroic, and clear nature of the insight-knowledge of the three paths for one attained to view. The cutting of the banana tree by the blunt sword, which makes a sound, should be understood as being like the not-sharp, not-heroic, and not-clear nature of the insight-knowledge of the three paths for one liberated by faith. However, having rejected this reasoning with 'no,' the conclusion is made that the faith-liberated does not reach the one attained to view solely due to the difference in their way of progress.

Āgamaṭṭhakathāsu pana vuttaṃ – “etesu hi saddhāvimuttassa pubbabhāgamaggakkhaṇe saddahantassa viya okappentassa viya adhimuccantassa viya ca kilesakkhayo hoti. Diṭṭhippattassa pubbabhāgamaggakkhaṇe kilesacchedakañāṇaṃ adandhaṃ tikhiṇaṃ sūraṃ hutvā vahati. Tasmā yathā nāma atikhiṇena asinā kadaliṃ chindantassa chinnaṭṭhānaṃ na maṭṭhaṃ hoti, asi na sīghaṃ vahati, saddo suyyati, balavataro vāyāmo kātabbo hoti[M 0.0044]; evarūpā saddhāvimuttassa pubbabhāgamaggabhāvanā. Yathā pana sunisiteneva asinā kadaliṃ chindantassa chinnaṭṭhānaṃ maṭṭhaṃ hoti, asi sīghaṃ vahati, saddo na suyyati, balavavāyāmakiccaṃ na hoti; evarūpā [P 0.0194] diṭṭhippattassa pubbabhāgamaggabhāvanā veditabbā”ti. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo saddhāvimuttoti vuccati. Ayañhi saddahanto vimuttoti saddhāvimutto. Ayampi kāyasakkhī viya chabbidhova hoti.

But in the commentaries on the Āgamas, it is said: 'Among these, for one liberated by faith, at the moment of the preliminary path, the destruction of defilements occurs as if believing, as if approving, and as if resolving. For one attained to view, at the moment of the preliminary path, the knowledge that cuts off defilements proceeds unhesitatingly, sharply, and heroically. Therefore, just as when one cuts a banana tree with a blunt sword, the cut is not smooth, the sword does not move quickly, a sound is heard, and a stronger effort must be made—such is the development of the preliminary path for one liberated by faith. But just as when one cuts a banana tree with a well-sharpened sword, the cut is smooth, the sword moves swiftly, no sound is heard, and there is no need for strong effort—such should the development of the preliminary path for one attained to view be understood.' 'This is called' means that such a person is called one liberated by faith. For he is liberated while believing; thus, he is faith-liberated. This one, like the bodily witness, is also of six kinds.

29. Dhammānusārīniddese – paṭipannassāti iminā sotāpattimaggaṭṭho dassito. Adhimattanti balavaṃ. Paññaṃ vāhetīti paññāvāhī. Paññā imaṃ puggalaṃ vahatīti paññāvāhītipi [V 0.0044] vuttaṃ hoti. Paññāpubbaṅgamanti paññaṃ purecārikaṃ katvā. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo dhammānusārīti vuccati. So hi paññāsaṅkhātena dhammena sarati anussaratīti dhammānusārī. Sotāpattimaggaṭṭhassevetaṃ nāmaṃ. Phale pana patte diṭṭhippatto nāma hoti.

29. In the exposition of the Dhamma-follower: 'For one practicing' indicates one standing in the stream-entry path. 'Intense' means strong. 'He carries wisdom' means he is wisdom-led. It is also said that wisdom carries this person; thus, he is wisdom-led. 'With wisdom as the forerunner' means having made wisdom the precedent. 'This is called' means that such a person is called a Dhamma-follower. For he follows along with, recollects, the Dhamma, which is characterized by wisdom; thus, he is a Dhamma-follower. This is the name for one standing in the stream-entry path. But upon attaining the fruit, he is called one attained to view.

30. Saddhānusārīniddesepi – saddhaṃ vāhetīti saddhāvāhī. Saddhā imaṃ puggalaṃ vahatīti saddhāvāhītipi vuttameva. Saddhāpubbaṅgamanti saddhaṃ purecārikaṃ katvā. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo saddhānusārīti vuccati. So hi saddhāya sarati. Anussaratīti saddhānusārī. Sotāpattimaggaṭṭhassevetaṃ nāmaṃ. Phale pana patte saddhāvimutto nāma hoti. Lokuttaradhammañhi nibbattentānaṃ dve dhurāni nāma, dve abhinivesā nāma, dve sīsāni nāma. Tattha saddhādhuraṃ paññādhuranti – dve dhurāni nāma. Eko pana bhikkhu samathābhinivesena abhinivisati, eko vipassanābhinivesenāti – ime dve abhinivesā nāma. Eko ca matthakaṃ pāpuṇanto ubhatobhāgavimutto hoti, eko paññāvimuttoti – imāni dve sīsāni nāma. Ye keci hi lokuttaradhammaṃ nibbattenti, sabbe te ime dve dhamme dhuraṃ katvā imesu dvīsu ṭhānesu abhinivisitvā imehi dvīhi ṭhānehi vimuccanti. Tesu yo bhikkhu aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī paññaṃ dhuraṃ katvā samathavasena abhiniviṭṭho aññataraṃ arūpasamāpattiṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, so sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe dhammānusārī nāma. Parato pana chasu ṭhānesu kāyasakkhī nāma. Arahattaphale patte ubhatobhāgavimutto nāma.

30. In the exposition of the faith-follower: 'He carries faith' means he is faith-led. It is also said that faith carries this person; thus, he is faith-led. 'With faith as the forerunner' means having made faith the precedent. 'This is called' means that such a person is called a faith-follower. For he follows by faith, recollects; thus, he is a faith-follower. This is the name for one standing in the stream-entry path. But upon attaining the fruit, he is called one liberated by faith. For those who bring about the supramundane Dhamma, there are what are called two leading principles, two resolutions, and two summits. Herein, the leading principle of faith and the leading principle of wisdom—these are the two leading principles. One monk resolves upon serenity, another resolves upon insight—these are the two resolutions. And one reaching the summit becomes liberated in both ways, and one becomes liberated by wisdom—these are the two summits. Indeed, all who bring about the supramundane Dhamma, having made these two qualities their leading principle and having resolved upon these two standpoints, are liberated by these two standpoints. Among them, that monk who is a gainer of the eight attainments, having taken wisdom as his leading principle, being resolved by way of serenity, having made one of the immaterial attainments the basis, establishes insight and attains arahantship—he is called a Dhamma-follower at the moment of the stream-entry path. But subsequently, in the six instances, he is called a bodily witness. Upon attaining the fruit of arahantship, he is called one liberated in both ways.

Aparo [M 0.0045] paññameva [P 0.0195] dhuraṃ katvā vipassanāvasena abhiniviṭṭho suddhasaṅkhāre vā rūpāvacarajjhānesu vā aññataraṃ sammasitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, ayampi sotāpattimaggakkhaṇeyeva dhammānusārī nāma. Parato pana chasu ṭhānesu diṭṭhippatto nāma. Arahatte patte paññāvimutto nāma. Idha dve nāmāni apubbāni, tāni purimehi saddhiṃ pañca honti. Aparo aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī saddhaṃ dhuraṃ katvā samādhivasena abhiniviṭṭho aññataraṃ arūpasamāpattiṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti – ayaṃ sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe saddhānusārī nāma. Parato chasu ṭhānesu kāyasakkhīyeva nāma. Arahatte patte ubhatobhāgavimuttoyeva nāma. Idha ekameva nāmaṃ apubbaṃ. Tena saddhiṃ purimāni pañca cha honti. Aparo saddhameva dhuraṃ katvā vipassanāvasena abhiniviṭṭho suddhasaṅkhāre vā rūpāvacarajjhānesu vā aññataraṃ sammasitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Ayampi sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe saddhānusārī [V 0.0045] nāma. Parato chasu ṭhānesu saddhāvimutto nāma. Arahatte patte paññāvimutto nāma. Idhāpi ekameva nāmaṃ apubbaṃ. Tena saddhiṃ purimāni cha satta honti. Ime satta puggalā loke aggadakkhiṇeyyā nāmāti.

Another, making wisdom his leading principle and devoting himself to insight, having contemplated either the bare formations or one of the form-realm jhānas, attains Arahantship. At the moment of the path of stream-entry, he is called a "Dhamma-follower." Subsequently, in the six stages, he is called "one attained to view." Upon attaining Arahantship, he is called "one liberated by wisdom." Here, two names are new, making five in total with the preceding ones. Another, who has gained the eight attainments, making faith his leading principle and devoting himself to concentration, making one of the formless attainments his basis, establishes insight and attains Arahantship. At the moment of the path of stream-entry, he is called a "faith-follower." Subsequently, in the six stages, he is called "a body-witness." Upon attaining Arahantship, he is called "one liberated in both ways." Here, only one name is new, making six in total with the preceding ones. Another, making faith his leading principle and devoting himself to insight, having contemplated either the bare formations or one of the form-realm jhānas, attains Arahantship. At the moment of the path of stream-entry, he is called a "faith-follower." Subsequently, in the six stages, he is called "one liberated by faith." Upon attaining Arahantship, he is called "one liberated by wisdom." Here too, only one name is new, making seven in total with the preceding ones. These seven persons are called the foremost of those worthy of offerings in the world.

31. Sattakkhattuparamaniddese – sattakkhattunti sattavāre. Sattakkhattuparamā bhavūpapatti attabhāvaggahaṇaṃ assa, tato paraṃ aṭṭhamaṃ bhavaṃ nādiyatīti sattakkhattuparamo. Sotāpanno hotīti ettha sototi ariyamaggo, tena samannāgato sotāpanno nāma. Yathāha –

31. In the exposition of 'one with a maximum of seven existences': 'Seven times' means seven occasions. For him, the taking up of existence, the grasping of individuality, is at most seven times; thereafter he does not take up an eighth existence. Thus, he is called 'one with a maximum of seven existences.' 'He is a stream-enterer'—here, 'stream' means the noble path; one endowed with that is called a stream-enterer. As it is said:

“Soto sototi hidaṃ, sāriputta, vuccati. Katamo nu kho, sāriputta, sototi? Ayameva hi, bhante, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo soto, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhīti. Sotāpanno sotāpannoti, hidaṃ, sāriputta, vuccati. Katamo nu kho, sāriputta, sotāpannoti? Yo hi, bhante, iminā ariyena aṭṭhaṅgikena maggena samannāgato ayaṃ vuccati sotāpanno, svāyaṃ āyasmā evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto iti vā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1001).

“‘Stream, stream,’ it is said, Sāriputta. What, Sāriputta, is the stream?” “Indeed, venerable sir, this Noble Eightfold Path is the stream, namely: right view … right concentration.” “‘Stream-enterer, stream-enterer,’ it is said, Sāriputta. What, Sāriputta, is a stream-enterer?” “Whoever, venerable sir, is endowed with this Noble Eightfold Path is called a stream-enterer, such as this venerable one of such a name and such a clan.”

Evaṃ [M 0.0046] maggakkhaṇepi sotāpanno nāma hoti. Idha [P 0.0196] pana maggena phalassa nāmaṃ dinnanti phalakkhaṇe sotāpanno adhippeto.

Thus, even at the moment of the path, one is called a stream-enterer. Here, however, since the name for the fruit is given by way of the path, a stream-enterer at the moment of fruition is intended.

Avinipātadhammoti vinipātasaṅkhātaṃ apāyaṃ upapattivasena anāgamanasabhāvo. Niyatoti magganiyāmena niyato. Sambodhiparāyaṇoti bujjhanakabhāvaparāyaṇo. So hi paṭiladdhamaggena bujjhatīti sambodhiparāyaṇo. Upari tīhi maggehi avassaṃ bujjhissatīti sambodhiparāyaṇo. Deve ca manusse cāti devalokañca manussalokañca. Sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvāti paṭisandhivasena aparāparaṃ gantvā. Dukkhassantaṃ karotīti vaṭṭadukkhassa pariyantaṃ parivaṭumaṃ karoti. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo sattakkhattuparamo nāma vuccati. Ayaṃ pana kālena devalokassa kālena manussalokassa vasena missakabhavena kathitoti veditabbo.

“Not subject to falling away” means one whose nature it is not to return to the states of woe, called the lower realms, by way of rebirth. “Destined” means fixed by the certainty of the path. “Bound for enlightenment” means having awakening as his final goal. For he is to awaken by means of the path he has attained; thus he is bound for enlightenment. He is bound for enlightenment because he will certainly awaken by means of the three higher paths. “Among gods and humans” means in the divine realm and the human realm. “Wandering on and transmigrating” means going again and again by way of re-linking. “Makes an end of suffering” means he makes an end, a complete cessation, of the suffering of the round. “This is called” means this kind of person is called 'one with a maximum of seven existences.' It should be understood, however, that this is spoken of in terms of a mixed existence, at one time in the divine realm and at another time in the human realm.

32. Kolaṃkolaniddese – kulato kulaṃ gacchatīti kolaṃkolo. Sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyato hi paṭṭhāya nīce kule upapatti nāma natthi, mahābhogakulesuyeva nibbattatīti [V 0.0046] attho. Dve vā tīṇi vā kulānīti devamanussavasena dve vā tayo vā bhave. Iti ayampi missakabhaveneva kathito. Desanāmattameva cetaṃ – ‘dve vā tīṇi vā’ti. Yāva chaṭṭhabhavā saṃsarantopi pana kolaṃkolova hoti.

32. In the exposition of ‘kolaṅkola’—one who goes from family to family is called ‘kolaṅkola.’ From the realization of the fruit of stream-entry onwards, there is no rebirth in a low family; one is reborn only in wealthy families—this is the meaning. “Two or three families” means two or three existences, as gods or humans. Thus, this too is spoken of in terms of mixed existences. This is merely a designation—‘two or three.’ Even if one wanders until the sixth existence, one is still a ‘kolaṅkola.’

33. Ekabījiniddese – khandhabījaṃ nāma kathitaṃ. Yassa hi sotāpannassa ekaṃyeva khandhabījaṃ atthi, ekaṃ attabhāvaggahaṇaṃ, so ekabījī nāma. Mānusakaṃ bhavanti idaṃ panettha desanāmattameva. Devabhavaṃ nibbattetītipi pana vattuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Bhagavatā gahitanāmavaseneva cetāni etesaṃ nāmāni. Ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ gato sattakkhattuparamo nāma hoti, ettakaṃ kolaṃkolo, ettakaṃ ekabījīti bhagavatā etesaṃ nāmaṃ gahitaṃ. Niyamato pana ayaṃ sattakkhattuparamo, ayaṃ kolaṃkolo, ayaṃ ekabījīti natthi.

33. In the exposition of ‘one-seeder’—the seed of the aggregates is spoken of. For a stream-enterer who has only one seed of the aggregates, one more grasping of individuality, is called a ‘one-seeder’. “Human existence” is merely a designation here. It is also proper to say that one produces rebirth in a divine existence. These names are simply terms taken by the Blessed One. The Blessed One took these names for them: one who has gone this far is called 'one with a maximum of seven existences,' this far 'a kolaṅkola,' this far 'a one-seeder'. But there is no fixed rule that this one is 'one with a maximum of seven existences,' this one is 'a kolaṅkola,' this one is 'a one-seeder'.

Ko [M 0.0047] pana tesaṃ etaṃ pabhedaṃ niyametīti? Keci tāva therā ‘pubbahetu niyametī’ti vadanti, keci ‘paṭhamamaggo’, keci ‘upari tayo maggā’, keci ‘tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ vipassanā’ti. Tattha ‘pubbahetu niyametī’ti vāde ‘paṭhamamaggassa upanissayo kato nāma hoti, upari tayo maggā nirupanissayā uppannā’ti vacanaṃ āpajjati. ‘Paṭhamamaggo niyametī’ti [P 0.0197] vāde upari tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ niratthakatā āpajjati. ‘Upari tayo maggā niyamentī’ti vāde ‘aṭṭhamamagge anuppanneyeva upari tayo maggā uppannā’ti āpajjati. ‘Tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ vipassanā niyametī’ti vādo pana yujjati. Sace hi upari tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ vipassanā balavatī hoti, ekabījī nāma hoti; tato mandatarāya kolaṃkolo; tato mandatarāya sattakkhattuparamoti.

But who determines this distinction among them? Some elders say, “A prior cause determines it.” Some say, “The first path.” Others say, “The three higher paths.” And some say, “The insight into the three paths.” In the view that “a prior cause determines it,” the implication arises that “the first path has a supporting condition, while the three higher paths arise without a supporting condition.” In the view that “the first path determines,” the three higher paths become pointless. In the view that “the three higher paths determine,” it follows that “the three higher paths have arisen even before the eighth path has arisen.” However, the view that “the insight into the three paths determines” is reasonable. For if the insight into the three higher paths is strong, one is called a ‘one-seeder’; if somewhat weaker, a ‘kolaṅkola’; and if still weaker, 'one with a maximum of seven existences'.

Ekacco hi sotāpanno vaṭṭajjhāsayo hoti, vaṭṭābhirato, punappunaṃ vaṭṭasmiṃyeva vicarati sandissati. Anāthapiṇḍiko seṭṭhi, visākhā upāsikā, cūḷarathamahārathā devaputtā, anekavaṇṇo devaputto, sakko devarājā, nāgadatto devaputtoti ime hi ettakā janā vaṭṭajjhāsayā vaṭṭābhiratā ādito paṭṭhāya cha devaloke sodhetvā akaniṭṭhe ṭhatvā parinibbāyissanti, ime idha na gahitā. Na kevalañcime; yopi manussesuyeva sattakkhattuṃ saṃsaritvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, yopi devaloke nibbatto devesuyeva sattakkhattuṃ aparāparaṃ saṃsaritvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, imepi idha na gahitā. Missakabhavavaseneva panettha sattakkhattuparamakolaṃkolā [V 0.0047] mānusakabhavanibbattakoyeva ca ekabījī gahitoti veditabbo. Tattha ekeko dukkhāpaṭipadādivasena catubbidhabhāvaṃ āpajjati. Saddhādhureneva cattāro sattakkhattuparamā, cattāro kolaṃkolā, cattāro ekabījinoti dvādasa honti. Sace paññāya sakkā nibbattetuṃ, ‘ahaṃ lokuttaraṃ dhammaṃ nibbattessāmī’ti evaṃ paññaṃ dhuraṃ katvā sattakkhattuparamādibhāvaṃ pattāpi paṭipadāvasena dvādasevāti ime catuvīsati sotāpannā ihaṭṭhakanijjhānikavaseneva imasmiṃ ṭhāne kathitāti veditabbā.

For a certain stream-enterer has a tendency toward the round of existence, delights in the round, and repeatedly wanders and lingers in the round itself. The merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, the laywoman Visākhā, the devaputtas Cūḷaratha and Mahāratha, the devaputta Anekavaṇṇa, Sakka, king of the devas, and the devaputta Nāgadatta—these many people, inclined toward the round and delighting in it, will, after purifying the six deva worlds from the start, establish themselves in the Akaniṭṭha heaven and attain final Nibbāna. These are not included here. Not only these, but also one who, having wandered among humans seven times, attains Arahantship, or one who, having been reborn in the divine worlds, wanders among the devas again and again for seven existences and attains Arahantship—these too are not included here. It should be understood that here, by way of mixed existences, are included the 'one with a maximum of seven existences,' the 'kolaṅkola,' and only that 'one-seeder' who is reborn in the human realm. Among them, each attains a fourfold state by means of painful practice and so forth. With faith as their leading principle, there are four 'ones with a maximum of seven existences,' four 'kolaṅkolas,' and four 'one-seeders'—thus making twelve. And if, by making wisdom their leading principle with the thought, 'I will bring about the supramundane Dhamma,' they attain the state of 'one with a maximum of seven existences' and so forth, these too, by way of practice, are twelve. Thus, it should be understood that these twenty-four stream-enterers are discussed in this section by way of the classification of those who abide here.

34. Sakadāgāminiddese – paṭisandhivasena sakiṃ āgacchatīti sakadāgāmī. Sakidevāti ekavāraṃyeva. Imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvāti iminā pañcasu [M 0.0048] sakadāgāmīsu cattāro vajjetvā ekova gahito. Ekacco hi idha sakadāgāmiphalaṃ patvā idheva parinibbāyati, ekacco idha patvā devaloke parinibbāyati, ekacco devaloke patvā tattheva parinibbāyati, ekacco devaloke [P 0.0198] patvā idhūpapajjitvā parinibbāyati – ime cattāropi idha na gahitā. Yo pana idha patvā devaloke yāvatāyukaṃ vasitvā puna idhūpapajjitvā parinibbāyati – ayaṃ ekova idha gahitoti veditabbo. Sesamettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā taṃ sabbaṃ heṭṭhā dhammasaṅgahaṭṭhakathāyaṃ lokuttarakusalaniddese vuttameva. Imassa pana sakadāgāmino ekabījinā saddhiṃ kiṃ nānākaraṇanti? Ekabījissa ekāva paṭisandhi, sakadāgāmissa dve paṭisandhiyo – idaṃ nesaṃ nānākaraṇanti.

34. In the explanation of the Once-Returner—'He comes back once by way of rebirth,' thus he is called a once-returner. 'Only once' means just one time. 'Having come to this world'—by this, among the five kinds of once-returners, four are excluded, and only one is included here. For some, having attained the fruit of a once-returner here, attain final Nibbāna right here. Some, having attained it here, attain final Nibbāna in the deva world. Some, having attained it in the deva world, attain final Nibbāna right there. Some, having attained it in the deva world, are reborn here and then attain final Nibbāna—these four are not included here. But the one who, having attained it here, lives out their lifespan in the deva world and is then reborn here before attaining final Nibbāna—this one alone is included here. Whatever else should be said here has all been said below in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī commentary in the section on supramundane wholesome states. Now, what is the difference between this once-returner and the one-seeder? The one-seeder has only one rebirth, while the once-returner has two rebirths—this is their difference.

35. Anāgāminiddese – orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānanti oraṃ vuccati kāmadhātu. Yassa imāni pañca bandhanāni appahīnāni honti, so bhavagge nibbattopi gilitabaḷiso maccho viya dīghasuttakena pāde baddhakāko viya tehi bandhanehi ākaḍḍhiyamāno kāmadhātuyaṃyeva pavattatīti pañca bandhanāni orambhāgiyānīti vuccanti. Heṭṭhābhāgiyāni heṭṭhākoṭṭhāsikānīti attho. Parikkhayāti tesaṃ bandhanānaṃ parikkhayena. Opapātikoti upapātayoniko. Imināssa gabbhaseyyā paṭikkhittā. Tattha parinibbāyīti tattha suddhāvāsaloke parinibbāyitā. Anāvattidhammo tasmā lokāti paṭisandhiggahaṇavasena tasmā lokā idha anāvattanasabhāvo. Buddhadassanatheradassanadhammassavanānaṃ panatthāyassa āgamanaṃ anivāritaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evaṃvidho puggalo paṭisandhivasena puna anāgamanato anāgāmī nāma vuccati.

35. In the explanation of the Non-Returner: Regarding 'the lower fetters,' 'ora' is said to be the sense-sphere realm. For one who has not abandoned these five bonds, even if reborn in the highest existence, he is dragged back by those bonds—like a fish that has swallowed a baited hook or a crow with its foot tied by a long string—and continues in the sense-sphere realm. Thus, these five bonds are called 'the lower fetters.' This means they belong to the lower part, that is, they are of the lower portion. 'By the destruction' means by the destruction of those bonds. 'Spontaneously born' means born of spontaneous birth; by this, womb-birth is rejected for him. 'Attains final Nibbāna there' means he is one who attains final Nibbāna in that Pure Abode world. 'One whose nature is not to return from that world' means his nature is not to return here from that world by way of taking rebirth. However, his coming for the sake of seeing the Buddha, the elders, or hearing the Dhamma is not prevented. 'This is called' means this kind of person, on account of not coming again by way of rebirth, is called a 'Non-Returner'.

36. Antarāparinibbāyiniddese [V 0.0048] – upapannaṃ vā samanantarāti upapannasamanantarā vā hutvā. Appattaṃ vā vemajjhaṃ āyuppamāṇanti āyuppamāṇaṃ vemajjhaṃ appattaṃ vā hutvā ariyamaggaṃ sañjanetīti attho. Vāsaddavikappato pana vemajjhaṃ pattantipi attho veditabbo. Evaṃ tayo antarāparinibbāyino siddhā honti. Upariṭṭhimānaṃ saṃyojanānanti upari pañcannaṃ uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanānaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ vā kilesānaṃ. Pahānāyāti etesaṃ pajahanatthāya [M 0.0049] maggaṃ sañjaneti. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo āyuvemajjhassa antarāyeva parinibbāyanato antarāparinibbāyīti vuccati.

36. In the explanation of the One Who Attains Final Nibbāna in the Interval: 'Having been reborn or immediately after' means having been reborn or immediately thereafter. 'Before reaching the midpoint of the lifespan' means that he generates the noble path before having reached the midpoint of the lifespan. However, from the alternative indicated by the word 'or,' it should be understood that it can also mean having reached the midpoint. Thus, three types of those who attain final Nibbāna in the interval are established. Regarding 'the higher fetters,' this means the five higher fetters or the eight defilements above. 'For abandoning' means he generates the path for the sake of abandoning these. 'This is called' means this kind of person, because he attains final Nibbāna in the interval of the lifespan, is called an 'antarāparinibbāyī'.

37. Upahaccaparinibbāyiniddese [P 0.0199] – atikkamitvā vemajjhaṃ āyuppamāṇanti āyuppamāṇaṃ vemajjhaṃ atikkamitvā. Upahacca vā kālakiriyanti upagantvā kālakiriyaṃ. Āyukkhayassa āsanne ṭhatvāti attho. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo avihesu tāva kappasahassappamāṇassa āyuno pañcakappasatasaṅkhātaṃ vemajjhaṃ atikkamitvā chaṭṭhe vā kappasate sattamaṭṭhamanavamānaṃ vā aññatarasmiṃ dasameyeva vā kappasate ṭhatvā arahattaṃ patvā kilesaparinibbānena parinibbāyanato upahaccaparinibbāyīti vuccati.

37. In the explanation of the One Who Attains Final Nibbāna Upon Approach: 'Having surpassed the midpoint of the lifespan' means having surpassed the midpoint of the lifespan's measure. 'Or upon approaching death' means having come near to death. The meaning is standing near the exhaustion of the lifespan. 'This is called' means this kind of person—in the Aviha realm, for instance, having surpassed the midpoint, reckoned as five hundred eons, of a lifespan measuring a thousand eons, and then, while in the sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, or even the tenth hundred eons, having attained Arahantship—is called an 'upahaccaparinibbāyī' because he attains final Nibbāna by extinguishing the defilements.

38. Asaṅkhārasasaṅkhāraparinibbāyiniddesesu – asaṅkhārena appadukkhena adhimattapayogaṃ akatvāva kilesaparinibbānena parinibbānadhammoti asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī. Sasaṅkhārena dukkhena kasirena adhimattapayogaṃ katvāva kilesaparinibbānena parinibbāyanadhammoti sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī.

38. In the explanations of the asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī and sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī—one whose nature is to attain final Nibbāna through the extinction of defilements without effort, without suffering, and without making excessive exertion, is called an asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī. One whose nature is to attain final Nibbāna through the extinction of defilements with effort, with difficulty, and only after making excessive exertion, is called a sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī.

40. Uddhaṃsotaniddese – uddhaṃ vāhibhāvena uddhamassa taṇhāsotaṃ vaṭṭasotaṃ vāti uddhaṃsoto. Uddhaṃ vā gantvā paṭilabhitabbato uddhamassa maggasotanti uddhaṃsoto. Akaniṭṭhaṃ gacchatīti akaniṭṭhagāmī. Avihā cuto atappaṃ gacchatītiādīsu avihe kappasahassaṃ vasanto arahattaṃ pattuṃ asakkuṇitvā atappaṃ gacchati. Tatrāpi dve kappasahassāni vasanto arahattaṃ pattuṃ asakkuṇitvā sudassaṃ gacchati. Tatrāpi cattāri kappasahassāni vasanto arahattaṃ pattuṃ asakkuṇitvā sudassiṃ gacchati. Tatrāpi aṭṭha kappasahassāni vasanto arahattaṃ pattuṃ asakkuṇitvā akaniṭṭhaṃ gacchati. Tattha vasanto ariyamaggaṃ sañjanetīti attho.

40. In the explanation of the Upward-Streamer (uddhaṃsota): He is an 'uddhaṃsota' because his stream of craving, the stream of the cycle of existence, flows upwards. Or, he is an 'uddhaṃsota' because his path-stream is upwards, as it is to be attained by going upwards. 'Going to Akaniṭṭha' is why one is called an 'akaniṭṭhagāmī.' For example, a being dwelling in Avihā for a thousand eons and being unable to attain Arahantship goes to Atappa. There too, dwelling for two thousand eons and being unable to attain Arahantship, he goes to Sudassa. There too, dwelling for four thousand eons and being unable to attain Arahantship, he goes to Sudassī. There too, dwelling for eight thousand eons and being unable to attain Arahantship, he goes to Akaniṭṭha. The meaning is that, dwelling there, he generates the noble path.

Imesaṃ [V 0.0049] pana anāgāmīnaṃ pabhedajānanatthaṃ uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmīcatukkaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tattha yo avihato paṭṭhāya cattāro devaloke sodhetvā akaniṭṭhaṃ gantvā parinibbāyati ayaṃ uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī nāma. Yo pana heṭṭhā tayo devaloke sodhetvā sudassīdevaloke ṭhatvā parinibbāyati – ayaṃ uddhaṃsoto, na akaniṭṭhagāmī nāma[M 0.0050]. Yo pana ito akaniṭṭhameva gantvā parinibbāyati, ayaṃ na uddhaṃsoto, akaniṭṭhagāmī nāma[P 0.0200]. Yo pana heṭṭhā catūsu devalokesu tattha tattheva parinibbāyati, ayaṃ na uddhaṃsoto, na akaniṭṭhagāmī nāmāti. Evamete aṭṭhacattālīsa anāgāmino honti.

Now, to understand the distinctions among these Non-Returners, the fourfold classification of the Upward-Streamer (uddhaṃsota) and the One Who Goes to Akaniṭṭha (akaniṭṭhagāmī) should be understood. Among them, one who, beginning from Avihā, traverses the four deva-worlds and goes to Akaniṭṭha to attain final Nibbāna is called an 'uddhaṃsota akaniṭṭhagāmī.' One who traverses the three lower deva-worlds and, staying in the Sudassī deva-world, attains final Nibbāna is called an 'uddhaṃsota,' but not an 'akaniṭṭhagāmī.' One who goes from here directly to Akaniṭṭha and attains final Nibbāna is not an 'uddhaṃsota,' but is called an 'akaniṭṭhagāmī.' One who attains final Nibbāna right there in each of the four lower deva-worlds is neither an 'uddhaṃsota' nor an 'akaniṭṭhagāmī.' Thus, there are forty-eight types of Non-Returners.

Kathaṃ? Avihe tāva tayo antarāparinibbāyino, eko upahaccaparinibbāyī, eko uddhaṃsoto te asaṅkhāraparinibbāyino pañca, sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyino pañcāti dasa honti. Tathā atappāsudassāsudassīsūti cattāro dasakā cattālīsaṃ. Akaniṭṭhe pana uddhaṃsoto natthi. Tayo pana antarāparinibbāyino, eko upahaccaparinibbāyī. Te asaṅkhāraparinibbāyino cattāro, sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyino cattāroti aṭṭha. Evaṃ aṭṭhacattālīsaṃ honti.

How? In Avīha, there are three antarāparinibbāyīs, one upahaccaparinibbāyī, and one uddhaṃsota; these are five asaṅkhāraparinibbāyīs and five sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyīs, making ten. Similarly, in Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī, there are four sets of ten, totaling forty. In Akaniṭṭha, however, there is no uddhaṃsota. There are three antarāparinibbāyīs and one upahaccaparinibbāyī. These are four asaṅkhāraparinibbāyīs and four sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyīs, making eight. Thus, there are forty-eight in total.

Te sabbepi papaṭikopamāya dīpitā – divasaṃ santattānampi hi ārakaṇṭakavipphalikanakhacchedanānaṃ ayomukhe haññamāne papaṭikā uppajjitvāva nibbāyati – evarūpo paṭhamo antarāparinibbāyī veditabbo. Kasmā? Uppannasamanantarāva kilesaparinibbānena parinibbāyanato. Tato mahantatare ayomukhe haññamāne papaṭikā ākāsaṃ ullaṅghitvā nibbāyati – evarūpo dutiyo antarāparinibbāyī daṭṭhabbo. Kasmā? Vemajjhaṃ appatvā parinibbāyanato. Tato mahantatare ayomukhe haññamāne papaṭikā ākāsaṃ ullaṅghitvā nivattamānā pathaviyaṃ anupahaccatalā hutvā parinibbāyati – evarūpo tatiyo antarāparinibbāyī daṭṭhabbo. Kasmā? Vemajjhaṃ patvā anupahacca parinibbāyanato. Tato mahantatare ayomukhe haññamāne papaṭikā ākāsaṃ ullaṅghitvā pathaviyaṃ patitvā upahaccatalā hutvā nibbāyati – evarūpo upahaccaparinibbāyī veditabbo. Kasmā? Kālakiriyaṃ upagantvā āyugatiṃ khepetvā parinibbāyanato. Tato mahantatare ayomukhe haññamāne papaṭikā paritte tiṇakaṭṭhe patitvā taṃ parittaṃ tiṇakaṭṭhaṃ jhāpetvā nibbāyati – evarūpo asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī veditabbo. Kasmā? Appayogena lahusāya gatiyā parinibbāyanato. Tato mahantatare ayomukhe haññamāne papaṭikā vipule tiṇakaṭṭhapuñje [P 0.0201] patitvā taṃ vipulaṃ tiṇakaṭṭhapuñjaṃ [V 0.0050] jhāpetvā nibbāyati – evarūpo sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī veditabbo. Kasmā? Sappayogena alahusāya [M 0.0051] gatiyā parinibbāyanato. Aparā mahantesu tiṇakaṭṭhapuñjesu patati, tattha mahantesu tiṇakaṭṭhapuñjesu jhāyamānesu vītaccitaṅgāro vā jālā vā uppatitvā kammārasālaṃ jhāpetvā gāmanigamanagararaṭṭhaṃ jhāpetvā samuddantaṃ patvā nibbāyati – evarūpo uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī daṭṭhabbo. Kasmā? Anekabhavabījavipphāraṃ phussa phussa byantīkatvā parinibbāyanato. Yasmā pana ārakaṇṭakādibhedaṃ khuddakampi mahantampi ayokapālameva, tasmā sutte sabbavāresu ayokapālantveva vuttaṃ (a. ni. 7.55). Yathāha –

All these are illustrated by the simile of sparks. For even when struck from an iron pan that has been heated all day, a spark arises and is immediately extinguished—such is to be understood as the first antarāparinibbāyī. Why? Because they attain Nibbāna by the extinction of defilements immediately upon arising. Then, when struck from a larger iron pan, a spark leaps into the air and is extinguished—such is to be seen as the second antarāparinibbāyī. Why? Because they attain Nibbāna without reaching the midpoint of their lifespan. Then, when struck from an even larger iron pan, a spark leaps into the air, turns back, and is extinguished without striking the ground—such is to be seen as the third antarāparinibbāyī. Why? Because they attain Nibbāna having reached the midpoint but without striking the ground. Then, when struck from a still larger iron pan, a spark leaps into the air, falls to the ground, strikes the ground, and then is extinguished—such is to be understood as the upahaccaparinibbāyī. Why? Because they attain Nibbāna having reached the time of death and exhausted their lifespan. Then, when struck from an even larger iron pan, a spark falls onto a small pile of grass or sticks, burns that small pile, and then is extinguished—such is to be understood as the asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī. Why? Because they attain Nibbāna with little exertion and swift progress. Then, when struck from a still larger iron pan, a spark falls onto a large pile of grass or sticks, burns that large pile, and then is extinguished—such is to be understood as the sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī. Why? Because they attain Nibbāna with exertion and slow progress. Another spark falls onto even larger piles of grass or sticks, and while those great piles are burning, a glowing ember or flame leaps up, burns the blacksmith’s workshop, burns villages, towns, cities, and districts, reaches the ocean’s edge, and then is extinguished—such is to be seen as the uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī. Why? Because they attain Nibbāna having exhausted the proliferation of seeds of many existences, one by one. Since the various kinds of iron objects, whether small or large, are essentially an iron pan, therefore in the Sutta, in all instances, it is simply called an 'iron pan' (A. Ni. 7.55). As it is said—

“Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ paṭipanno hoti – ‘no cassa, no ca me siyā, na bhavissati, na me bhavissati, yadatthi yaṃ bhūtaṃ, taṃ pajahāmī’”ti upekkhaṃ paṭilabhati. So bhave na rajjati, sambhave na rajjati, atthuttari padaṃ santaṃ sammappaññāya passati. Tañca khvassa padaṃ na sabbena sabbaṃ sacchikataṃ hoti. Tassa na sabbena sabbaṃ mānānusayo pahīno hoti, na sabbena sabbaṃ bhavarāgānusayo pahīno hoti, na sabbena sabbaṃ avijjānusayo pahīno hoti. So pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā antarāparinibbāyī hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, divasaṃ santatte ayokapāle haññamāne papaṭikā nibbattitvā nibbāyeyya; evameva kho[V 0.0051], bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ paṭipanno hoti – no cassa…pe… antarāparinibbāyī hoti.

Here, monks, a monk practices thus: 'May it not be, may it not be mine; it will not be, it will not be mine; what exists, what has come to be, that I abandon.' Thus he attains equanimity. He does not delight in being, he does not delight in becoming. He sees with right wisdom the supreme peaceful state, yet that state is not fully realized by him in every respect. Not all of his underlying tendency to conceit is abandoned in every respect, not all of his underlying tendency to craving for being is abandoned in every respect, not all of his underlying tendency to ignorance is abandoned in every respect. With the destruction of the five lower fetters, he is an antarāparinibbāyī. Just as, monks, when a red-hot iron pan is struck during the day, a spark arises and is extinguished; in the same way, monks, a monk practices thus: 'May it not be...' and is an antarāparinibbāyī.

“Idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ paṭipanno hoti – no cassa…pe… antarāparinibbāyī hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, divasaṃ santatte ayokapāle haññamāne papaṭikā nibbattitvā uppatitvā nibbāyeyya; evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ paṭipanno hoti – no cassa…pe… antarāparinibbāyī hoti.

Here, monks, a monk practices thus: 'May it not be...' and is an antarāparinibbāyī. Just as, monks, when a red-hot iron pan is struck during the day, a spark arises, flies up, and is extinguished; in the same way, monks, a monk practices thus: 'May it not be...' and is an antarāparinibbāyī.

“Idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ paṭipanno hoti – no cassa…pe… antarāparinibbāyī [P 0.0202] hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, divasaṃ santatte ayokapāle haññamāne papaṭikā nibbattitvā uppatitvā anupahacca [M 0.0052] talaṃ nibbāyeyya; evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ paṭipanno hoti – no cassa…pe… antarāparinibbāyī hoti.

Here, monks, a monk practices thus: 'May it not be...' and is an antarāparinibbāyī. Just as, monks, when a red-hot iron pan is struck during the day, a spark arises, flies up, and is extinguished without striking the ground; in the same way, monks, a monk practices thus: 'May it not be...' and is an antarāparinibbāyī.

“Idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ paṭipanno hoti – no cassa…pe… upahaccaparinibbāyī hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, divasaṃ santatte ayokapāle haññamāne papaṭikā nibbattitvā uppatitvā upahacca talaṃ nibbāyeyya; evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ paṭipanno hoti – no cassa…pe… upahaccaparinibbāyī hoti.

Here, monks, a monk practices thus: 'May it not be...' and is an upahaccaparinibbāyī. Just as, monks, when a red-hot iron pan is struck during the day, a spark arises, flies up, strikes the ground, and is extinguished; in the same way, monks, a monk practices thus: 'May it not be...' and is an upahaccaparinibbāyī.

“Idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ paṭipanno hoti – no cassa…pe… parikkhayā asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, divasaṃ santatte ayokapāle haññamāne papaṭikā nibbattitvā uppatitvā paritte tiṇapuñje vā kaṭṭhapuñje vā nipateyya, sā tattha aggimpi janeyya, dhūmampi janeyya, aggimpi janetvā dhūmampi janetvā tameva parittaṃ tiṇapuñjaṃ vā [V 0.0052] kaṭṭhapuñjaṃ vā pariyādiyitvā anāhārā nibbāyeyya; evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ paṭipanno hoti – no cassa…pe… parikkhayā asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī hoti.

Here, monks, a monk practices thus: 'May it not be...' and, with the destruction of the fetters, is an asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī. Just as, monks, when a red-hot iron pan is struck during the day, a spark arises, flies up, and lands on a small heap of grass or wood. There, it may produce fire and smoke, and after producing fire and smoke, it consumes that small heap of grass or wood, and, being without fuel, is extinguished; in the same way, monks, a monk practices thus: 'May it not be...' and, with the destruction of the fetters, is an asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī.

“Idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ paṭipanno hoti – no cassa…pe… sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, divasaṃ santatte ayokapāle haññamāne papaṭikā nibbattitvā uppatitvā vipule tiṇapuñje vā kaṭṭhapuñje vā nipateyya, sā tattha aggimpi janeyya…pe… tameva vipulaṃ tiṇapuñjaṃ vā kaṭṭhapuñjaṃ vā pariyādiyitvā anāhārā nibbāyeyya; evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ paṭipanno hoti – no cassa…pe… sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī hoti.

Here, monks, a monk practices thus: 'May it not be...' and is one who attains final Nibbāna with exertion. Just as, monks, when a red-hot iron pan is struck during the day, a spark arises, flies up, and falls on a large heap of grass or wood, it might produce fire there... and after consuming that large heap of grass or wood, being without fuel, it would be extinguished; in the same way, monks, a monk practices thus: 'May it not be...' and is one who attains final Nibbāna with exertion.

“Idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ paṭipanno hoti – no cassa…pe… parikkhayā uddhaṃsoto hoti akaniṭṭhagāmī. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, divasaṃ santatte ayokapāle haññamāne papaṭikā nibbattitvā uppatitvā mahante tiṇapuñje vā kaṭṭhapuñje vā nipateyya, sā tattha aggimpi janeyya…pe… tameva mahantaṃ tiṇapuñjaṃ vā kaṭṭhapuñjaṃ vā pariyādiyitvā gacchampi daheyya, dāyampi daheyya[M 0.0053], gacchampi dahitvā dāyampi [P 0.0203] dahitvā haritantaṃ vā pathantaṃ vā selantaṃ vā udakantaṃ vā ramaṇīyaṃ vā bhūmibhāgaṃ āgamma anāhārā nibbāyeyya; evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ paṭipanno hoti – no cassa…pe… parikkhayā uddhaṃsoto hoti akaniṭṭhagāmī”ti (a. ni. 7.55).

Here, monks, a monk practices thus: 'May it not be...' and, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, is an upstream-bound one, going to the Akaniṭṭha realm. Just as, monks, when a red-hot iron pan is struck during the day, a spark arises, flies up, and lands on a great heap of grass or wood. There, it may produce fire... and after consuming that great heap of grass or wood, it may burn up the undergrowth or the forest. Having burned up the undergrowth or the forest, it may reach the edge of a green area, a road, a rocky place, a watery place, or a delightful stretch of land, and there, being without fuel, it would be extinguished; in the same way, monks, a monk practices thus: 'May it not be...' and, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, is an upstream-bound one, going to the Akaniṭṭha realm.

41-44. Sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipannādiniddesā uttānatthāva. Ayaṃ vuccati puggalo arahāti ettha pana dvādasa arahanto veditabbā. Kathaṃ? Tayo hi vimokkhā – suññato, animitto, appaṇihitoti. Tattha suññatavimokkhena vimuttakhīṇāsavo paṭipadāvasena catubbidho hoti; tathā animittaappaṇihitavimokkhehīti – evaṃ dvādasa arahanto veditabbā. Iti ime dvādasa arahanto viya dvādaseva sakadāgāmino, catuvīsati sotāpannā, aṭṭhacattālīsa anāgāminoti ettakā puggalā ito muccitvā bahiddhā nuppajjanti, imasmiññeva sabbaññubuddhasāsane uppajjantīti.

41-44. The exposition of those practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry and so forth is clear in meaning. But concerning "this person is called an arahant," here twelve arahants should be understood. How? There are three liberations: liberation through emptiness, liberation through signlessness, and liberation through wishlessness. Among these, a taint-destroyed one liberated through the liberation of emptiness is fourfold according to the mode of practice; similarly for the liberations of signlessness and wishlessness—thus twelve arahants should be understood. Thus, just as there are these twelve arahants, so too there are twelve once-returners, twenty-four stream-enterers, and forty-eight non-returners. So many persons, having been freed from here, are not produced elsewhere but are produced only in this dispensation of the Omniscient Buddha.

Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Exposition of Singles.

2. Dukaniddesavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Exposition of Pairs.

45. Dukaniddese kodhanoti kujjhanasīlo mahākodho. Evaṃ puggalaṃ pucchitvāpi dhammena puggalaṃ dassetuṃ tattha katamo kodhotiādimāha. Upanāhīniddesādīsupi eseva nayo. Kodho kujjhanātiādīni heṭṭhā vuttatthāneva. Tathā upanāhīniddesādīsu pubbakālaṃ kodhotiādīni. Ayaṃ kodho appahīnoti ayaṃ ettako kodho vikkhambhanappahānena vā tadaṅgappahānena vā samucchedappahānena vā appahīno. Parato upanāhādīsupi eseva nayo.

45. In the exposition of the pairs, "one who is angry" means one of a wrathful nature, greatly angry. Thus, even when asked about such a person, to show the person in terms of the Dhamma, it is said, "Here, what is anger?" and so on. The same method applies in the expositions on resentment and so forth. "Anger, wrath," and so on have the meanings stated previously. Likewise, in the expositions on resentment and so on, "formerly, anger" and so forth. "This anger is not abandoned" means this much anger has not been abandoned by abandonment through suppression, by abandonment by substitution, or by abandonment through eradication. The same method applies to resentment and so on that follow.

53. Ahirikaniddesādīsu – iminā ahirikenāti iminā evaṃpakārena ahirikadhammena samannāgato. Iminā anottappenātiādīsupi eseva nayo.

53. In the expositions on shamelessness and so forth, "with this shamelessness" means endowed with such a quality of shamelessness. The same principle applies to "with this lack of moral dread" and so on.

63. Ajjhattasaṃyojanoti [M 0.0054][V 0.0053] ajjhattabandhano. Bahiddhāsaṃyojanoti bahiddhābandhano. Te ubhopi vacchakasālūpamāya dīpetabbā. Vacchakasālāya hi anto baddho antoyeva [P 0.0204] sayitavacchako viya idhaṭṭhakasotāpannasakadāgāmino. Tesañhi bandhanampi idheva, sayampi idheva. Anto baddho pana bahi sayitavacchako viya rūpārūpabhave sotāpannasakadāgāmino. Tesañhi bandhanameva idha, sayaṃ pana brahmaloke ṭhitā. Bahi baddho bahi sayitavacchako viya rūpārūpabhave anāgāmī. Tassa hi bandhanampi bahiddhā, sayampi bahiddhāva. Bahi baddho pana antosayitavacchako viya idhaṭṭhakaanāgāmī. Tassa hi bandhanaṃ rūpārūpabhavesu, sayaṃ pana idha ṭhito.

63. "Internal fetter" means internal bondage. "External fetter" means external bondage. Both should be illustrated by the simile of the calf pen. Just as a calf tied inside the pen lies inside, so too with stream-enterers and once-returners established here. For them, the bondage is here, and they themselves are here. But one tied inside yet lying down outside is like stream-enterers and once-returners in the realms of form and the formless realms. For them, bondage is here, but they themselves are in the Brahma realms. One tied outside yet lying down outside is like non-returners in the realms of form and the formless realms. For them, bondage is external, and they themselves are external. One tied outside yet lying down inside is like non-returners established here. For them, bondage is in the realms of form and the formless realms, but they themselves are here.

65. Akkodhananiddesādīsu – pahīnoti vikkhambhanappahānena vā, tadaṅgappahānena vā, samucchedappahānena vā pahīno.

65. In the expositions on non-anger and so forth, "abandoned" means abandoned by suppression, by abandonment by substitution, or by eradication.

83. Dullabhaniddese – dullabhāti na sulabhā. Pubbakārīti paṭhamameva kārako. Katavedīti kataṃ vedeti, viditaṃ pākaṭaṃ karoti. Te agāriyānagāriyehi dīpetabbā. Agāriyesu hi mātāpitaro pubbakārino nāma. Puttadhītaro pana mātāpitaro paṭijaggantā abhivādanādīni tesaṃ kurumānā katavedino nāma. Anagāriyesu ācariyupajjhāyā pubbakārino nāma. Antevāsikasaddhivihārikā ācariyupajjhāye paṭijaggantā abhivādanādīni tesaṃ kurumānā katavedino nāma. Tesaṃ āvibhāvatthāya upajjhāyaposakasoṇattherādīnaṃ vatthūni kathetabbāni.

83. In the exposition on the hard to find, "hard to find" means not easy to find. "One who does good first" means one who is the first to act. "One who is grateful" means one who makes known what has been done, making it evident. These should be illustrated with reference to householders and the homeless. Among householders, parents are called those who do good first. Sons and daughters who attend to their parents, performing acts of reverence and so forth for them, are called grateful ones. Among the homeless, teachers and preceptors are called those who do good first. Resident disciples and co-residents who attend to their teachers and preceptors, performing acts of reverence and so forth for them, are called grateful ones. To make this clear, stories should be told, such as those of Elder Soṇa who supported his preceptor.

Aparo nayo – parena akateyeva upakāre attani kataṃ upakāraṃ anapekkhitvā kārako pubbakārī, seyyathāpi mātāpitaro ceva ācariyupajjhāyā ca. So dullabho; sattānaṃ taṇhābhibhūtattā. Parena katassa upakārassa anurūpappavattiṃ attani kataṃ upakāraṃ upakārato jānanto, vediyanto, kataññukatavedī. Seyyathāpi mātāpituācariyupajjhāyesu sammā paṭipanno. Sopi dullabho; sattānaṃ avijjābhibhūtattā.

Another way: one who acts first is a doer who helps without expecting a service done to oneself, even when no service has been done by another, just as parents, teachers, and preceptors. Such a person is rare, because beings are overwhelmed by craving. A grateful and thankful person is one who knows and acknowledges a service done to them as a service, and whose conduct is in accordance with the service done by another. Just as one who conducts oneself properly towards parents, teachers, and preceptors. That person too is rare, because beings are overwhelmed by ignorance.

Apica – akāraṇavacchalo pubbakārī, sakāraṇavacchalo kataññukatavedī. ‘Karissati me’ti evamādikāraṇanirapekkhakiriyo [V 0.0054] pubbakārī. ‘Karissati [M 0.0055] me’ti evamādikāraṇasāpekkhakiriyo kataññukatavedī. Tamojotiparāyaṇo pubbakārī, jotijotiparāyaṇo kataññukatavedī. Desetā pubbakārī, paṭipajjitā kataññukatavedī. Sadevake loke arahaṃ sammāsambuddho [P 0.0205] pubbakārī, ariyasāvako kataññukatavedīti. Dukanipātaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.2.120) pana – “‘pubbakārī’ti paṭhamaṃ upakārassa kārako, ‘kataññukatavedī’ti tena kataṃ ñatvā pacchā kārako. Tesu pubbakārī iṇaṃ demīti saññaṃ karoti, pacchākārako ‘iṇaṃ jīrāpemī’ti saññaṃ karotī”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ.

Moreover, one who is affectionate without a reason is a benefactor, while one who is affectionate with a reason is grateful and thankful. The benefactor is one whose action is independent of such reasons as, 'They will do something for me.' The grateful and thankful one is one whose action is dependent on such reasons as, 'They will do something for me.' The benefactor is one whose destination is light from darkness, while the grateful and thankful one is one whose destination is light from light. The benefactor is the teacher, while the practitioner is grateful and thankful. In the world with its gods, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, is the benefactor, while the noble disciple is grateful and thankful. But in the commentary to the Book of Twos (Aṅguttara Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 2.2.120) it is said: “'A benefactor' is one who first performs a helpful act; 'one who is grateful and thankful' is one who, knowing what was done, acts afterwards. Among them, the benefactor has the perception, 'I am giving a loan,' while the one who acts afterwards has the perception, 'I am paying off the loan.'” Only this much is said.

84. Duttappayaniddese – duttappayāti atappayā, na sakkā kenaci tappetuṃ. Yo hi upaṭṭhākakulaṃ vā ñātikulaṃ vā nissāya vasamāno cīvare jiṇṇe tehi dinnaṃ cīvaraṃ nikkhipati, na paribhuñjati. Punappunaṃ dinnampi gahetvā nikkhipateva. Yo ca teneva nayena laddhaṃ laddhaṃ vissajjeti parassa deti. Punappunaṃ laddhampi tatheva karoti. Ime dve puggalā sakaṭehipi paccaye upanentena tappetuṃ na sakkāti duttappayā nāma.

84. In the explanation of 'Hard to Satisfy': 'Hard to satisfy' means insatiable; they cannot be satisfied by anyone. For instance, there is one who, living in dependence on a supporter's family or a relative's family, when his robe is worn out, puts aside the robe given by them and does not use it. Even when given it repeatedly, he takes it and just puts it aside. And there is another who, in the same way, gives away whatever he has received, offering it to others. Even when receiving things repeatedly, he does the same. These two persons, even when requisites are brought to them by the cartload, cannot be satisfied—thus they are called 'hard to satisfy.'

85. Sutappayaniddese – na vissajjetīti attano akatvā parassa na deti. Atireke pana sati na nikkhipati parassa deti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yo pana bhikkhu upaṭṭhākakulā vā ñātikulā vā jiṇṇacīvaro sāṭakaṃ labhitvā cīvaraṃ katvā paribhuñjati, na nikkhipati; aggaḷaṃ datvā pārupantopi puna diyyamāne sahasā na paṭiggaṇhāti. Yo ca laddhaṃ laddhaṃ attanā paribhuñjati, paresaṃ na deti. Ime dvepi sukhena sakkā tappetunti sutappayā nāmāti.

85. In the explanation of 'easy to satisfy': 'He does not give it away' means he does not give to another what he has not made for his own use. But when there is an excess, he does not put it aside; he gives it to another. This is what is said: There is a monk whose robe is worn out who, having received a cloth from a supporter's family or a relative's family, makes it into a robe and uses it; he does not put it aside. Even while wearing it fastened, if another is offered, he does not accept it hastily. And there is another person who uses for himself whatever he receives and does not give it to others. These two persons can be satisfied with ease, thus they are called 'easy to satisfy'.

86. Āsavāti kilesā. Na kukkuccāyitabbaṃ kukkuccāyatīti na kukkuccāyitabbayuttakaṃ kukkuccāyati. Sūkaramaṃsaṃ labhitvā acchamaṃsanti kukkuccāyati, migamaṃsaṃ, labhitvā dīpimaṃsanti kukkuccāyati. Kāle santeyeva ‘kālo natthī’ti, appavāretvāva ‘pavāritosmī’ti, patte rajasmiṃ apatiteyeva ‘patita’nti, attānaṃ uddissa macchamaṃse akateyeva ‘maṃ uddissa kata’nti kukkuccāyati. Kukkuccāyitabbaṃ na kukkuccāyatīti kukkuccāyitabbayuttakaṃ na kukkuccāyati. Acchamaṃsaṃ labhitvā sūkaramaṃsanti na [M 0.0056] kukkuccāyati…pe… attānaṃ uddissa macchamaṃse kate ‘maṃ uddissa kata’nti na kukkuccāyati[V 0.0055]. Aṅguttaraṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana – “‘na kukkuccāyitabba’nti saṅghabhogassa apaṭṭhapanaṃ avicāraṇaṃ na kukkuccāyitabbaṃ [P 0.0206] nāma, taṃ kukkuccāyati. ‘Kukkuccāyitabba’nti tasseva paṭṭhapanaṃ vicāraṇaṃ, taṃ na kukkuccāyatī”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ. Imesanti imesaṃ dvinnaṃ puggalānaṃ subhūmiyaṃ tiṇalatādīni viya rattimpi divāpi āsavā vaḍḍhantiyeva. Sukkapakkhe kappiyamaṃsaṃ labhitvā kappiyamaṃsantveva gaṇhanto na kukkuccāyitabbaṃ na kukkuccāyati nāmāti iminā nayena attho veditabbo.

86. `Āsavas` means defilements. 'He feels remorse where one should not feel remorse' means he feels remorse about something that is not a matter for remorse. Having received pork, he feels remorse, thinking it is bear meat; having received deer meat, he feels remorse, thinking it is leopard meat. When it is the proper time, he thinks, 'It is not the proper time.' Without having been invited to take more, he thinks, 'I have been invited.' When dust has not fallen into his bowl, he thinks, 'It has fallen.' When fish and meat have not been prepared specifically for him, he feels remorse, thinking, 'It was prepared for me.' 'He does not feel remorse where one should feel remorse' means he does not feel remorse about something that is a matter for remorse. Having received bear meat, he does not feel remorse, thinking it is pork... and so on... When fish and meat have been prepared specifically for him, he does not feel remorse, thinking, 'It was prepared for me.' But in the commentary to the Aṅguttara Nikāya it is said: “'What one should not be remorseful about' refers to not setting up or not investigating the Saṅgha's property; this is something one should not be remorseful about, but he feels remorse. 'What one should be remorseful about' refers to the very act of setting it up and investigating it; this is something one should be remorseful about, but he does not feel remorse.” Only this much is said. For these two persons, the āsavas grow day and night, like grass and vines in fertile soil. The meaning should be understood by this method: for instance, one who, having received allowable meat during the bright fortnight, takes it as just allowable meat, is called 'one who is not remorseful about what is not a matter for remorse'.

88. Hīnādhimuttoti hīnajjhāsayo. Dussīloti nissīlo. Pāpadhammoti lāmakadhammo.

88. One with a low inclination means one with a base disposition. An immoral one means one without morality. One of evil qualities means one of base qualities.

89. Paṇītādhimuttoti paṇītajjhāsayo. Kalyāṇadhammoti bhaddakadhammo, sucidhammo, sundaradhammo.

89. One with a refined inclination means one with a refined disposition. One of wholesome qualities means one of auspicious qualities, pure qualities, and beautiful qualities.

90. Tittoti suhito pariyosito. Tappetāti aññesampi tittikaro. Paccekasambuddhā ye ca tathāgatasāvakāti ettha paccekabuddhā navahi lokuttaradhammehi sayaṃ tittā paripuṇṇā. Aññe pana tappetuṃ na sakkonti. Tesañhi dhammakathāya abhisamayo na hoti. Sāvakānaṃ pana dhammakathāya aparimāṇānampi devamanussānaṃ abhisamayo hoti. Evaṃ santepi yasmā pana te dhammaṃ desentā na attano vacanaṃ katvā kathenti, buddhānaṃ vacanaṃ katvā kathenti. Sotuṃ nisinnaparisāpi ‘ayaṃ bhikkhu na attanā paṭividdhadhammaṃ katheti, buddhehi paṭividdhadhammaṃ kathetī’ti cittīkāraṃ karoti. Iti so cittīkāro buddhānaṃyeva hoti. Evaṃ tattha sammāsambuddhova tappetā nāma. Yathā hi ‘asukassa nāma idañcidañca dethā’ti raññā āṇattā kiñcāpi ānetvā denti, atha kho rājāva tattha dāyako. Yehipi laddhaṃ hoti, te ‘raññā amhākaṃ ṭhānantaraṃ dinnaṃ, issariyavibhavo dinno’tveva gaṇhanti, na rājapurisehīti. Evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

90. `Titto` means satisfied, fulfilled. `Tappetā` means one who satisfies others. Regarding 'Paccekabuddhas and the Tathāgata's disciples,' here the Paccekabuddhas are themselves satisfied and complete with the nine supramundane qualities, but they cannot satisfy others. For through their teaching of the Dhamma, there is no realization. However, through the teaching of the Dhamma by the disciples, there is realization for countless gods and humans. Even so, when they teach the Dhamma, they do not speak it as their own words, but speak it as the words of the Buddhas. The assembly seated to listen also pays respect, thinking: 'This monk does not speak a Dhamma he has himself penetrated, but speaks the Dhamma penetrated by the Buddhas.' Thus, that respect belongs solely to the Buddhas. Therefore, in this context, only the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One is called the satisfier. It is like when a king commands, 'Give this and that to so-and-so'; even though others bring and give it, the king alone is the giver there. Those who have received it consider, 'The king has given us this position, the king has granted us power and wealth,' not that the king’s men have. This matter should be understood in this way. The rest is clear in meaning everywhere.

Dukaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Niddesa on Pairs.

3. Tikaniddesavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Niddesa on Triads.

91. Tikaniddese [M 0.0057][V 0.0056] – dussīloti nissīlo. Pāpadhammoti lāmakadhammo. Sīlavipattiyā vā dussīlo, diṭṭhivipattiyā pāpadhammo[P 0.0207]. Kāyavacīsaṃvarabhedena dussīlo, sesasaṃvarabhedena pāpadhammo. Asuddhapayogatāya dussīlo, asuddhāsayatāya pāpadhammo. Kusalasīlavirahena dussīlo; akusalasīlasamannāgamena pāpadhammo. Asucīti asucīhi kāyakammādīhi samannāgato. Saṅkassarasamācāroti saṅkāya parehi saritabbasamācāro. Kiñcideva asāruppaṃ disvā ‘idaṃ iminā kataṃ bhavissatī’ti evaṃ parehi āsaṅkanīyasamācāro, attanoyeva vā saṅkāya saritabbasamācāro – sāsaṅkasamācāroti attho. Tassa hi divāṭṭhānādīsu sannipatitvā kiñcideva mantayante bhikkhū disvā ‘ime ekato hutvā mantenti, kacci nu kho mayā katakammaṃ jānitvā mantentī’ti evaṃ sāsaṅkasamācāro hoti.

91. In the Tikaniddesa – 'Dussīla' means one who is without virtue. 'Pāpadhamma' means one of evil qualities. 'Dussīla' is due to a failure in virtue, while 'pāpadhamma' is due to a failure in view. 'Dussīla' is due to the breaking of bodily and verbal restraint, while 'pāpadhamma' is due to the breaking of other restraints. 'Dussīla' is due to impure application, while 'pāpadhamma' is due to impure intention. 'Dussīla' is due to the absence of wholesome virtue; 'pāpadhamma' is due to being endowed with unwholesome virtue. 'Asuci' means endowed with impure bodily actions and so forth. 'Saṅkassara-samācāra' means behavior that is to be recalled with suspicion by others. Seeing something improper, others may think, 'This must have been done by him'—such is behavior to be suspected by others, or it is behavior to be recalled with suspicion by oneself. This is the meaning of 'sāsaṅka-samācāra' (behavior arousing suspicion). For when he sees monks gathered in their day-quarters and discussing something, he thinks, 'They are gathered together discussing—could it be that they are discussing something they have learned about what I have done?' Thus his behavior is 'sāsaṅka-samācāra'.

Paṭicchannakammantoti paṭicchādetabbayuttakena pāpakammena samannāgato. Assamaṇo samaṇapaṭiññoti assamaṇo hutvāva samaṇapatirūpakatāya ‘samaṇo aha’nti evaṃ paṭiñño. Abrahmacārī brahmacāripaṭiññoti aññe brahmacārino sunivatthe supārute sumbhakapattadhare gāmanigamajanapadarājadhānīsu piṇḍāya caritvā jīvikaṃ kappente disvā sayampi tādisena ākārena tathā paṭipajjanato ‘ahaṃ brahmacārī’ti paṭiññaṃ dento viya hoti. ‘Ahaṃ bhikkhū’ti vatvā uposathaggādīni pavisanto pana brahmacāripaṭiñño hotiyeva, tathā saṅghikaṃ lābhaṃ gaṇhanto. Antopūtīti pūtinā kammena anto anupaviṭṭho, nigguṇatāya vā guṇasāravirahitattā antopūti. Avassutoti rāgādīhi tinto. Kasambujātoti sañjātarāgādikacavaro. Atha vā kasambu vuccati tintakuṇapagataṃ kasaṭaudakaṃ. Imasmiñca sāsane dussīlo nāma jigucchanīyattā tintakuṇapakasaṭaudakasadiso. Tasmā kasambu viya jātoti kasambujāto.

'Paṭicchanna-kammanta' means one who is endowed with evil deeds that ought to be concealed. 'Assamaṇo samaṇa-paṭiñña' means one who, being a non-ascetic, claims 'I am an ascetic' because he resembles an ascetic. 'Abrahmacārī brahmacārī-paṭiñña' means that when he sees other celibates who are well-dressed, well-robed, carrying a polished bowl, and making a living by wandering for alms in villages, towns, districts, and royal cities, he too behaves in a similar manner, as if making the claim, 'I am a celibate.' Furthermore, by saying 'I am a bhikkhu' and entering the Uposatha hall and so forth, he is indeed one who claims to be a celibate, and likewise when he receives a share of the Sangha's gains.
