'Antopūti' means inwardly penetrated by putrid deeds, or he is rotten inside due to being without virtue, being devoid of the essence of virtue. 'Avassuta' means stained by lust and so forth. 'Kasambujāta' means one in whom the rubbish of lust and so forth has arisen. Or, 'kasambu' is said to be the foul water from a putrid corpse. And in this dispensation, an immoral person, due to being repulsive, is like the foul water from a putrid corpse. Therefore, he is 'kasambujāta' because he is born like 'kasambu'.

Tassa na evaṃ hotīti kasmā na hoti? Yattha patiṭṭhitena sakkā bhaveyya arahattaṃ laddhuṃ, tassā patiṭṭhāya bhinnattā. Yathā hi caṇḍālakumārakassa [M 0.0058] ‘asuko nāma khattiyakumāro [P 0.0208] rajje abhisitto’ti sutvāpi, yasmiṃ kule paccājātā abhisekaṃ pāpuṇanti, tasmiṃ kule apaccājātattā na evaṃ hoti – ‘kudāssu nāmāhampi so khattiyakumāro viya abhisekaṃ [V 0.0057] pāpuṇeyya’nti; evameva dussīlassa ‘asuko nāma bhikkhu arahattaṃ patto’ti sutvāpi, yasmiṃ sīle patiṭṭhitena arahattaṃ pattabbaṃ, tassa abhāvato ‘kudāssu nāmāhampi so sīlavā viya arahattaṃ pāpuṇeya’nti na evaṃ hoti. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo arahattāsāya abhāvā nirāsoti vuccati.

For him, it is not so. Why is that? Because the foundation upon which one could attain arahantship is broken. Just as when a young outcaste hears, 'So-and-so, a noble youth, has been anointed king,' but since he was not born in a family where coronation is attained, he does not think, 'When will I too attain anointment like that noble youth?' Even so, when an immoral one hears, 'So-and-so, a monk, has attained arahantship,' but since the virtue upon which one must be established to attain arahantship is lacking, he does not think, 'When will I too attain arahantship like that virtuous one?' This is called: such a person, due to the absence of aspiration for arahantship, is said to be 'nirāsa' (without hope).

92. Tassa evaṃ hotīti kasmā hoti? Yasmiṃ patiṭṭhitena sakkā bhaveyya arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ, tassā patiṭṭhāya thirattā. Yathā hi sujātassa khattiyakumārassa ‘asuko nāma khattiyakumāro rajje abhisitto’ti sutvāva yasmiṃ kule paccājātā abhisekaṃ pāpuṇanti, tasmiṃ paccājātassa evaṃ hoti – ‘kudāssu nāmāhampi, so kumāro viya abhisekaṃ pāpuṇeyya’nti evameva sīlavato ‘asuko nāma bhikkhu arahattaṃ patto’ti sutvāva yasmiṃ sīle patiṭṭhitena arahattaṃ pattabbaṃ, tassā patiṭṭhāya thirattā – ‘kudāssu nāmāhampi so bhikkhu viya arahattaṃ pāpuṇeyya’nti evaṃ hoti. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo āsaṃso nāma vuccati. So hi arahattaṃ āsaṃsati patthetīti āsaṃso.

92. Why is that so for him? Because the foundation upon which one could attain arahantship is firm. Just as when a well-born noble youth hears, 'So-and-so, a noble youth, has been anointed king,' since he was born in a family where coronation is attained, he thinks, 'When will I too attain anointment like that noble youth?' Even so, when a virtuous one hears, 'So-and-so, a monk, has attained arahantship,' since the virtue upon which arahantship is to be attained is firm, he thinks, 'When will I too attain arahantship like that monk?' This is called: such a person is called 'āsaṃsa' (one with aspiration). For he aspires to arahantship, he desires it, therefore he is 'āsaṃsa'.

93. Yā hissa pubbe avimuttassāti yā tassa khīṇāsavassa pubbe arahattavimuttiyā avimuttassa vimuttāsā ahosi, sā paṭippassaddhā, tasmā na evaṃ hoti. Yathā hi abhisittassa khattiyassa ‘asuko nāma khattiyakumāro rajje abhisitto’ti sutvā ekassa rañño dvinnaṃ rajjābhisekānaṃ dvinnaṃ setacchattānaṃ abhāvā na evaṃ hoti – “kudāssu nāmāhampi so kumāro viya abhisekaṃ pāpuṇeyya”nti; evameva khīṇāsavassa ‘asuko nāma bhikkhu arahattaṃ patto’ti sutvā, dvinnaṃ arahattānaṃ abhāvā – ‘kudāssu nāmāhampi so bhikkhu viya arahattaṃ pāpuṇeyya’nti [M 0.0059] na evaṃ hoti. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo arahattāsāya vigatattā vigatāsoti vuccati.

93. 'Yā hissa pubbe avimuttassā' means: whatever hope for liberation existed for that one whose taints are destroyed, back when he was not yet liberated by the liberation of arahantship, that hope has now subsided; therefore, it is not so for him. Just as when an anointed king hears, 'So-and-so, a noble youth, has been anointed king,' because there cannot be two coronations or two white parasols for one king, he does not think, 'When will I too attain anointment like that noble youth?' Even so, when one whose taints are destroyed hears, 'So-and-so, a monk, has attained arahantship,' because there cannot be two arahantships, he does not think, 'When will I too attain arahantship like that monk?' This is called: such a person is called 'vigatāsa' (one who is free from aspiration), because his aspiration for arahantship has departed.

94. Gilānūpamaniddese – yāya upamāya te gilānūpamāti vuccanti, taṃ tāva upamaṃ dassetuṃ tayo gilānātiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sappāyānīti hitāni vuddhikarāni. Patirūpanti [P 0.0209] anucchavikaṃ. Neva vuṭṭhāti tamhā ābādhāti iminā atekicchena vātāpamārādinā rogena samannāgato niṭṭhappatto gilāno kathito. Vuṭṭhāti tamhā ābādhāti iminā khipitakacchutiṇapupphakajarādippabhedo appamattakābādho kathito.

94. In the Exposition on the Simile of the Sick, to illustrate the simile by which they are called 'like the sick,' the passage beginning 'three sick persons' is stated. Therein, 'sappāyāni' means beneficial and conducive to growth. 'Patirūpa' means suitable. By 'he does not recover from that illness,' a critically ill person is meant, one afflicted by an incurable disease such as a severe wind disorder. By 'he recovers from that illness,' one with a minor ailment is meant, of a type such as sneezing, itching, or hay fever.

Labhanto [V 0.0058] sappāyāni bhojanāni no alabhantoti iminā pana yesaṃ paṭijagganena phāsukaṃ hoti, sabbepi te ābādhā kathitā. Ettha ca patirūpo upaṭṭhāko nāma gilānupaṭṭhākaaṅgehi samannāgato paṇḍito dakkho analaso veditabbo.

'Obtaining suitable food or not obtaining it' refers to all those illnesses for which comfort is achieved through tending to them. Here, a suitable attendant should be understood as one endowed with the qualities of a sick-nurse: wise, skillful, and not lazy.

Gilānupaṭṭhāko anuññātoti ‘bhikkhusaṅghena dātabbo’ti anuññāto. Tasmiñhi gilāne attano dhammatāya yāpetuṃ asakkonte bhikkhusaṅghena tassa bhikkhuno ‘eko bhikkhu ca sāmaṇero ca imaṃ paṭijaggathā’ti apaloketvā dātabbā. Yāva pana te taṃ paṭijagganti, tāva gilānassa ca tesañca dvinnaṃ yenattho sabbaṃ bhikkhusaṅghasseva bhāro. Aññepi gilānā upaṭṭhātabbāti itarepi dve gilānā upaṭṭhātabbā. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Yopi hi niṭṭhappattagilāno, so anupaṭṭhiyamāno ‘sace maṃ paṭijaggeyyuṃ, phāsukaṃ me bhaveyya, na kho pana maṃ paṭijaggantī’ti manopadosaṃ katvā apāye nibbatteyya. Paṭijaggiyamānassa pana evaṃ hoti – ‘bhikkhusaṅghena yaṃ kattabbaṃ taṃ sabbaṃ kataṃ, mayhaṃ pana kammavipāko īdiso’ti so bhikkhusaṅghe mettaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā sagge nibbattati. Yo pana appamattakena byādhinā samannāgato labhantopi alabhantopi vuṭṭhātiyeva, tassa vināpi bhesajjena vūpasamanakabyādhi bhesajje kate khippataraṃ vūpasammati. Tato so buddhavacanaṃ [M 0.0060] vā uggaṇhituṃ samaṇadhammaṃ vā kātuṃ sakkhissati. Iminā kāraṇena aññepi gilānā upaṭṭhātabbāti vuttaṃ.

The attendant to the sick is permitted—this means 'permitted to be assigned by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.' For when a sick bhikkhu is unable to sustain himself due to his condition, the Saṅgha should assign to that bhikkhu, having announced, 'One bhikkhu and a novice, attend to him.' As long as they are caring for him, all the needs of the sick bhikkhu and those two are the responsibility of the Saṅgha. 'Other sick bhikkhus should also be attended to'—this means the other two types of sick bhikkhus should be cared for. Why is that? Even one who is terminally ill, if not attended to, might develop resentment, thinking, 'If they had cared for me, I would have been comfortable, but they do not attend to me,' and thus be reborn in a lower realm. But if he is cared for, he thinks, 'The Saṅgha has done all that should be done; this is the result of my own kamma,' and with loving-kindness toward the Saṅgha, he is reborn in a heavenly realm. As for one afflicted with a minor illness, whether he receives treatment or not, he will recover. Even without medicine, his illness, which would subside on its own, will subside more quickly if medicine is administered. Then he will be able to learn the Buddha’s teachings or practice the ascetic duties. For this reason, it is said that other sick bhikkhus should also be attended to.

Neva okkamatīti neva pavisati. Niyāmaṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammattanti kusalesu dhammesu magganiyāmasaṅkhātaṃ sammattaṃ. Iminā padaparamo puggalo kathito. Dutiyavārena ugghaṭitaññū gahito sāsane nāḷakattherasadiso[P 0.0210]. Buddhantare ekavāraṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ santike ovādaṃ labhitvā paṭividdhapaccekabodhiñāṇo ca. Tatiyavārena vipañcitaññū puggalo kathito. Neyyo pana tannissitova hoti.

'Does not enter' means does not go in. 'Fixedness in wholesome qualities' means rightness, designated as the fixed course of the path in wholesome qualities. With this, the person limited to words is described. In the second instance, the one who understands upon a brief utterance is referred to, like the Elder Nāḷaka in the Dispensation. And in an interval between Buddhas, having received advice once from the Paccekabuddhas, he penetrated the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha. In the third instance, the person who understands through elaboration is described. The one to be guided, however, is dependent on that.

Dhammadesanā anuññātāti māsassa aṭṭha vāre dhammakathā anuññātā. Aññesampi dhammo desetabboti itaresampi dhammo kathetabbo. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Padaparamassa hi imasmiṃ attabhāve dhammaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ asakkontassāpi anāgate paccayo bhavissati. Yo pana tathāgatassa rūpadassanaṃ labhantopi alabhantopi dhammavinayañca savanāya labhantopi alabhantopi dhammaṃ abhisameti; so alabhanto na tāva abhisameti, labhanto pana khippameva abhisamessatīti iminā [V 0.0059] kāraṇena tesaṃ dhammo desetabbo. Tatiyassa pana punappunaṃ desetabbova. Kāyasakkhidiṭṭhappattasaddhāvimuttā heṭṭhā kathitāyeva.

'The teaching of the Dhamma is permitted'—this means that a Dhamma talk is permitted eight times a month. 'The Dhamma should also be taught to others'—this means the Dhamma should be spoken to others. Why is that? For one limited to words, even if unable to penetrate the Dhamma in this very existence, it will become a condition for the future. But as for one who, whether or not they gain the sight of the Tathāgata’s form, and whether or not they gain the opportunity to hear the Dhamma and Vinaya, comprehends the Dhamma—if they do not gain it, they do not yet comprehend it, but if they gain it, they will quickly comprehend it. For this reason, the Dhamma should be taught to them. For the third type, however, it should be taught repeatedly. The body-witness, the view-attainer, and the faith-liberated have already been described earlier.

98. Gūthabhāṇīādīsu – sabhaggatoti sabhāyaṃ ṭhito. Parisaggatoti gāmaparisāya ṭhito. Ñātimajjhagatoti dāyādānaṃ majjhe ṭhito. Pūgamajjhagatoti seṇīnaṃ majjhe ṭhito. Rājakulamajjhagatoti rājakulassa majjhe mahāvinicchaye ṭhito. Abhinītoti pucchanatthāya nīto. Sakkhipuṭṭhoti sakkhiṃ katvā pucchito. Ehambho purisāti ālapanametaṃ. Attahetu vā parahetu vāti attano vā parassa vā hatthapādādihetu vā dhanahetu vā. Āmisakiñcikkhahetu vāti ettha āmisanti lābho adhippeto. Kiñcikkhanti yaṃ vā taṃ vā appamattakaṃ. Antamaso tittiravaṭṭakasappipiṇḍanavanītapiṇḍādiappamattakassāpi lañjassa hetūti attho. Sampajānamusā bhāsitā hotīti jānantoyeva musāvādaṃ kattā hoti. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo gūthasadisavacanattā gūthabhāṇīti vuccati. Yathā hi gūthaṃ nāma mahājanassa aniṭṭhaṃ [M 0.0061] hoti akantaṃ; evameva imassa puggalassa vacanaṃ devamanussānaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ hoti akantaṃ.

98. In the case of 'filth-speaker' and so on—'gone to an assembly' means standing in an assembly hall. 'Gone to a company' means standing in a village assembly. 'Gone among relatives' means standing among heirs. 'Gone amidst a guild' means standing among a guild. 'Gone into the royal court' means standing in the midst of the royal family during a great inquiry. 'Brought forward' means brought forth for questioning. 'Questioned as a witness' means questioned after being made a witness. 'Come now, good man' is an address. 'For one's own sake or another's sake' means either for one's own or another's sake, whether for the sake of limbs like hands and feet, or for wealth. 'For the sake of some trifling material thing' means here, by 'material thing' gain is intended. 'Some trifle' means any small thing whatsoever. The meaning is, even for the sake of a small bribe, such as a lump of ghee from a partridge or quail, or a lump of fresh butter. 'Knowingly speaks falsely' means one knowingly tells a lie. 'This one is called' means such a person is called a 'filth-speaker' because their speech is like filth. Just as filth is disagreeable and unpleasant to the populace, so too is this person's speech disagreeable and unpleasant to gods and humans.

99. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo pupphasadisavacanattā pupphabhāṇīti vuccati. Yathā hi phullāni vassikāni vā adhimuttakāni vā mahājanassa iṭṭhāni kantāni honti; evameva imassa puggalassa vacanaṃ devamanussānaṃ iṭṭhaṃ [P 0.0211] hoti kantaṃ.

99. 'This one is called' means such a person is called a 'flower-speaker' because their speech is like flowers. Just as blooming jasmine or adhimuttaka flowers are desirable and pleasing to the populace, so too is this person's speech desirable and pleasing to gods and humans.

100. Nelāti elaṃ vuccati doso. Nāssā elanti nelā. Niddosāti attho, “nelaṅgo setapacchādo”ti (udā. 65) ettha vuttanelaṃ viya. Kaṇṇasukhāti byañjanamadhuratāya kaṇṇānaṃ sukhā. Sūcivijjhanaṃ viya kaṇṇasūlaṃ na janeti. Atthamadhuratāya sakalasarīre kopaṃ ajanetvā pemaṃ janetīti pemanīyā. Hadayaṃ gacchati appaṭihaññamānā sukhena cittaṃ pavisatīti hadayaṅgamā. Guṇaparipuṇṇatāya pure bhavāti porī. Pure saṃvaḍḍhanārī viya sukumārātipi porī. Purassa esātipi porī. Nagaravāsīnaṃ kathāti attho. Nagaravāsino hi yuttakathā honti. Pitimattaṃ pitāti, mātimattaṃ mātāti, bhātimattaṃ bhātāti vadanti. Evarūpī kathā bahuno janassa kantā hotīti bahujanakantā. Bahujanassa kantabhāveneva bahuno janassa manāpā cittavuddhikarāti bahujanamanāpā. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo madhubhāṇīti [V 0.0060] vuccati. Mudubhāṇītipi pāṭho. Ubhayatthāpi madhuravacanoti attho. Yathā hi catumadhuraṃ nāma madhuraṃ paṇītaṃ; evameva imassa puggalassa vacanaṃ devamanussānaṃ madhuraṃ hoti.

100. ‘Nela’—‘ela’ is said to mean fault. ‘Without ela’ means ‘nela,’ faultless—this is the meaning, as in the ‘nela’ mentioned in the phrase ‘nelaṅgo setapacchādo’ (Udāna 65). ‘Pleasing to the ear’ means sweet in expression, delightful to the ears. It does not cause an earache like a needle's prick. Because the meaning is sweet, it does not provoke anger but instead generates affection throughout the body—thus, it is endearing. ‘Heart-reaching’ means it enters the mind without obstruction, effortlessly entering the heart. ‘Porī’—this means it is foremost due to its fullness of qualities. It is also ‘porī’ because it is delicate like a woman brought up in the city. It is also ‘porī’ because it belongs to the city. This means it is the speech of city-dwellers. For city-dwellers’ speech is fitting. They speak of one who is like a father as ‘father,’ of one who is like a mother as ‘mother,’ of one who is like a brother as ‘brother.’ Such speech is pleasing to many—thus, it is ‘beloved by many.’ Because it is beloved by many, it is delightful to many and causes the mind to grow—thus, it is ‘delightful to many.’ ‘This is called’—such a person is called a ‘honeyed speaker.’ There is also a variant reading, ‘gentle speaker.’ In both cases, the meaning is sweet speech. Just as the ‘fourfold honey’ is sweet and excellent, so too is this person's speech sweet to gods and humans.

101. Arukūpamacittādīsu – abhisajjatīti laggati. Kuppatīti kopavasena kuppati. Byāpajjatīti pakatibhāvaṃ pajahati, pūtiko hoti. Patitthīyatīti thinabhāvaṃ thaddhabhāvañca āpajjati. Kopanti dubbalakodhaṃ. Dosanti dussanavasena tato balavataraṃ. Appaccayanti atuṭṭhākāraṃ domanassaṃ. Duṭṭhārukoti purāṇavaṇo. Kaṭṭhenāti daṇḍakakoṭiyā. Kaṭhalāyāti kapālena. Āsavaṃ detīti aparāparaṃ savati. Purāṇavaṇo hi attano dhammatāya eva pubbaṃ lohitaṃ yūsanti imāni tīṇi savati[M 0.0062], ghaṭṭito pana tāni adhikataraṃ savati. Evamevaṃ khoti ettha idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ, duṭṭhāruko viya hi kodhano puggalo. Tassa attano dhammatāya savanaṃ viya kodhanassapi attano dhammatāya uddhumātakassa viya caṇḍikatassa caraṇaṃ. Kaṭṭhena vā kaṭhalāya vā ghaṭṭanaṃ viya appamattakampi [P 0.0212] vacanaṃ bhiyyoso mattāya savanaṃ viya ‘mādisaṃ nāma esa evaṃ vadatī’ti bhiyyoso mattāya uddhumāyanabhāvo daṭṭhabbo. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo arukūpamacittoti vuccati. Purāṇavaṇasadisacittoti attho.

101. In the simile of the mind like a festering sore, etc.—‘abhisajjati’ means it adheres or clings. ‘Kuppati’ means it becomes agitated due to anger. ‘Byāpajjati’ means it abandons its natural state and becomes putrid. ‘Patitthīyati’ means it becomes stiff and rigid. ‘Kopa’ refers to weak anger. ‘Dosa’ refers to stronger anger arising from resentment. ‘Appaccaya’ refers to discontentment, displeasure. ‘Duṭṭhāruko’ means an old sore. ‘Kaṭṭhena’ means with the tip of a stick. ‘Kaṭhalāya’ means with a potsherd. ‘Āsavaṃ deti’ means it oozes repeatedly. An old sore, by its own nature, oozes pus, blood, and serum, but when struck, it oozes even more. So too, here, is the application of the simile: an angry person is like a festering sore. The sore’s natural oozing is like the angry person's naturally fierce conduct, like one puffed up with rage. Being struck with a stick or potsherd is like being provoked by even a slight word; the sore oozing all the more is like the anger swelling all the more, as one thinks, ‘How dare someone like this speak to me like that!’ This is called a person with a mind like a festering sore. The meaning is that their mind resembles an old sore.

102. Rattandhakāratimisāyāti rattiṃ cakkhuviññāṇuppattinivāraṇena andhabhāvakaraṇe bahalatame. Vijjantarikāyāti vijjuppattikkhaṇe. Idhāpi idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – cakkhumā puriso viya hi yogāvacaro daṭṭhabbo. Andhakāraṃ viya sotāpattimaggavajjhā kilesā. Vijjusañcaraṇaṃ viya sotāpattimaggañāṇassa uppattikālo. Vijjantarikāya cakkhumato purisassa sāmantā rūpadassanaṃ viya sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe nibbānadassanaṃ. Puna andhakārāvattharaṇaṃ viya sakadāgāmimaggavajjhā kilesā. Puna vijjusañcaraṇaṃ viya sakadāgāmimaggañāṇassa uppādo. Vijjantarikāya cakkhumato purisassa sāmantā rūpadassanaṃ viya sakadāgāmimaggakkhaṇe nibbānadassanaṃ. Puna andhakārāvattharaṇaṃ viya anāgāmimaggavajjhā kilesā. Puna vijjusañcaraṇaṃ viya anāgāmimaggañāṇassa uppādo. Vijjantarikāya cakkhumato purisassa sāmantā rūpadassanaṃ viya anāgāmimaggakkhaṇe nibbānadassanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo vijjūpamacittoti vuccati. Ittarakālobhāsena vijjusadisacittoti attho.

102. ‘Rattandhakāratimisāya’ refers to the thickest darkness of night, which prevents the arising of eye-consciousness and causes blindness. ‘Vijjantarikāya’ means at the moment when lightning arises. Here too, this simile should be understood: the meditator should be regarded as a person with eyesight. The darkness is like the defilements to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry. The flash of lightning is like the time of the arising of the knowledge of the path of stream-entry. Just as a person with eyesight sees forms all around in the interval of the lightning, so too is the seeing of Nibbāna in the moment of the path of stream-entry. Again, the darkness covering over is like the defilements to be abandoned by the path of once-returning. Again, the flash of lightning is like the arising of the knowledge of the path of once-returning. Just as a person with eyesight sees forms all around in the interval of the lightning, so too is the seeing of Nibbāna in the moment of the path of once-returning. Again, the darkness covering over is like the defilements to be abandoned by the path of non-returning. Again, the flash of lightning is like the arising of the knowledge of the path of non-returning. Just as a person with eyesight sees forms all around in the interval of the lightning, so too should the seeing of Nibbāna in the moment of the path of non-returning be understood. ‘This is called’—this means that such a person is called ‘one whose mind is like lightning.’ The meaning is that his mind is like lightning due to its brief illumination.

103. Vajirūpamacittatāyapi [V 0.0061] idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – vajiraṃ viya hi arahattamaggañāṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Maṇigaṇṭhipāsāṇagaṇṭhi viya arahattamaggavajjhā kilesā. Vajirassa maṇigaṇṭhiṃ vā pāsāṇagaṇṭhiṃ vā vinivijjhitvā agamanabhāvassa natthibhāvo viya arahattamaggañāṇena acchejjānaṃ kilesānaṃ natthibhāvo. Vajirena nibbiddhavedhassa puna apaṭipūraṇaṃ viya arahattamaggena chinnānaṃ kilesānaṃ puna anuppādo daṭṭhabbo. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo [M 0.0063] vajirūpamacittoti vuccati. Kilesānaṃ mūlaghātakaraṇasamatthatāya vajirena sadisacittoti attho.

103. In the simile of the diamond-like mind, this comparison should be understood: the knowledge of the path of arahantship should be regarded as the diamond. The defilements to be abandoned by the path of arahantship are like knots of jewels or knots of stones. Just as a diamond, having pierced a jewel-knot or stone-knot, invariably passes through, so too there is no defilement that is not cut by the knowledge of the path of arahantship. Just as a hole pierced by a diamond cannot be filled again, so too, the defilements cut off by the path of arahantship should be understood as not arising again. ‘This is called’—this means that such a person is called ‘one whose mind is like a diamond.’ The meaning is that his mind is similar to a diamond in its ability to strike at the root of the defilements.

104. Andhādīsu tathārūpaṃ cakkhu na hotīti tathājātikaṃ tathāsabhāvaṃ [P 0.0213] paññācakkhu na hoti. Phātiṃ kareyyāti phītaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ kareyya. Sāvajjānavajjeti sadosaniddose. Hīnappaṇīteti adhamuttame. Kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgeti kaṇhasukkāyeva aññamaññapaṭibāhanato paṭipakkhavasena sappaṭibhāgāti vuccanti. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo – kusale dhamme ‘kusalā dhammā’ti yena paññācakkhunā jāneyya, akusale dhamme ‘akusalā dhammā’ti, sāvajjādīsupi eseva nayo. Kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgesu pana kaṇhadhamme ‘sukkasuppaṭibhāgā’ti, sukkadhamme ‘kaṇhasappaṭibhāgā’ti yena paññācakkhunā jāneyya. Tathārūpampissa cakkhu na hotīti iminā nayena sesaṭṭhānesupi attho veditabbo. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo diṭṭhadhammikabhogasaṃharaṇapaññācakkhuno ca samparāyikatthasodhanapaññācakkhuno ca abhāvā andhoti vuccati. Dutiyo diṭṭhadhammikabhogasaṃharaṇapaññācakkhuno bhāvā, samparāyikatthasodhanapaññācakkhuno pana abhāvā ekacakkhūti vuccati. Tatiyo dvinnampi bhāvā dvicakkhūti vuccati.

104. In 'blind' and so on, 'there is no such eye' means there is no wisdom-eye of such a kind, of such a nature. 'May he make it abundant' means may he make it plentiful, developed. 'Faulty and faultless' means with fault and without fault. 'Inferior and superior' means base and excellent. 'Having dark and bright counterparts' means that dark and bright qualities are called 'counterparts' because of their mutual opposition, by way of being opposites. Here, this is the summary: by which wisdom-eye one would know wholesome states as 'wholesome states', unwholesome states as 'unwholesome states'—and this is the method for 'faulty' and so on as well. But regarding 'having dark and bright counterparts', it is by which wisdom-eye one would know dark states as 'having bright counterparts' and bright states as 'having dark counterparts'. The meaning of 'there is no such eye for him' should be understood by this method in the remaining instances as well. 'This is called' means: such a person is called 'blind' due to the absence of both the wisdom-eye for acquiring wealth in the present life and the wisdom-eye for purifying the goal for the future life. The second person is called 'one-eyed' due to the presence of the wisdom-eye for acquiring wealth in the present life, but the absence of the wisdom-eye for purifying the goal for the future life. The third is called 'two-eyed' due to the presence of both.

107. Avakujjapaññādīsu dhammaṃ desentīti upāsako dhammassavanatthāya āgatoti attano kammaṃ pahāya dhammaṃ desenti. Ādikalyāṇanti ādimhi kalyāṇaṃ bhaddakaṃ anavajjaṃ niddosaṃ katvā desenti. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Ettha pana ādīti pubbapaṭṭhapanā. Majjhanti kathāvemajjhaṃ. Pariyosānanti sanniṭṭhānaṃ. Itissa dhammaṃ kathentā pubbapaṭṭhapanepi kalyāṇaṃ bhaddakaṃ anavajjameva katvā kathenti, vemajjhepi, pariyosānepi. Ettha ca atthi desanāya ādimajjhapariyosānāni, atthi sāsanassa. Tattha desanāya tāva – catuppadikagāthāya paṭhamapadaṃ ādi, dve padāni majjhaṃ, avasānapadaṃ pariyosānaṃ. Ekānusandhikasuttassa – nidānaṃ ādi, anusandhi majjhaṃ, idamavocāti appanā pariyosānaṃ. Anekānusandhikassa – paṭhamo anusandhi ādi[V 0.0062], tato paraṃ eko vā anekā vā majjhaṃ, pacchimo pariyosānaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva desanāya nayo.

107. In 'one with wisdom bent down' and so on, 'they teach the Dhamma' means that when a lay follower comes to listen to the Dhamma, they set aside their own work and teach the Dhamma. 'Good in the beginning' means they teach it, making it good, auspicious, faultless, and blameless in the beginning. This is the method in the remaining phrases as well. Here, 'beginning' refers to the initial establishment. 'Middle' refers to the heart of the talk. 'End' refers to the conclusion. Thus, those who teach the Dhamma teach it, making it good, auspicious, and blameless in the initial establishment, in the middle, and in the conclusion. Here, there are beginnings, middles, and ends of a teaching, and there are also of the Dispensation. Therein, regarding a teaching: for a four-line verse, the first line is the beginning, the two middle lines are the middle, and the final line is the end. For a sutta with a single connection, the introduction is the beginning, the connection is the middle, and the concluding statement 'Thus he spoke' is the end. For one with multiple connections, the first connection is the beginning, one or many subsequent connections are the middle, and the last is the end. This, for a start, is the method regarding a teaching.

Sāsanassa [M 0.0064] pana sīlaṃ ādi, samādhi majjhaṃ, vipassanā pariyosānaṃ. Samādhi vā ādi, vipassanā majjhaṃ, maggo pariyosānaṃ. Vipassanā vā ādi, maggo majjhaṃ, phalaṃ pariyosānaṃ. Maggo vā ādi, phalaṃ majjhaṃ, nibbānaṃ pariyosānaṃ[P 0.0214]. Dve dve vā kariyamāne sīlasamādhayo ādi, vipassanāmaggā majjhaṃ, phalanibbānāni pariyosānaṃ. Sātthanti sātthakaṃ katvā desenti. Sabyañjananti akkharapāripūriṃ katvā desenti. Kevalaparipuṇṇanti sakalaparipuṇṇaṃ anūnaṃ katvā desenti. Parisuddhanti parisuddhaṃ nijjaṭaṃ niggaṇṭhiṃ katvā desenti. Brahmacariyaṃ pakāsentīti evaṃ desentā ca seṭṭhacariyabhūtaṃ sikkhattayasaṅgahitaṃ ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ pakāsenti. Neva ādiṃ manasi karotīti neva pubbapaṭṭhapanaṃ manasi karoti. Kumbhoti ghaṭo. Nikkujjoti adhomukho ṭhapito. Evamevanti ettha kumbho nikkujjo viya avakujjapañño puggalo daṭṭhabbo. Udakāsiñcanakālo viya dhammadesanāya laddhakālo. Udakassa vivaṭṭanakālo viya tasmiṃ āsane nisinnassa uggahetuṃ asamatthakālo. Udakassa asaṇṭhānakālo viya uṭṭhahitvā asallakkhaṇakālo veditabbo. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo avakujjapaññoti vuccati. Adhomukhapaññoti attho.

For the Dispensation, however, virtue is the beginning, concentration is the middle, and insight is the end. Or, concentration is the beginning, insight is the middle, and the path is the end. Or, insight is the beginning, the path is the middle, and the fruit is the end. Or, the path is the beginning, the fruit is the middle, and Nibbāna is the end. Or, when taken two by two, virtue and concentration are the beginning, insight and the path are the middle, and the fruit and Nibbāna are the end. 'With meaning' means they teach it, making it meaningful. 'With phrasing' means they teach it, making the letters complete. 'Wholly complete' means they teach it, making it entirely complete and without deficiency. 'Purified' means they teach it, making it pure, untangled, and without knots. 'They make manifest the holy life' means: thus teaching, they make manifest the noble eightfold path, which is the supreme conduct, included in the threefold training. 'He does not attend to the beginning' means he does not attend to the initial establishment. 'Pot' means a water jar. 'Overturned' means placed face-down. 'Just so' means: here, a person with wisdom bent down should be seen as like an overturned pot. Like the time of pouring water is the time when the Dhamma teaching is received. Like the time of the water flowing away is the time when one sitting in that seat is unable to grasp it. Like the time of the water not settling is to be understood as the time when, having stood up, one does not comprehend it. 'This is called' means: such a person is called 'one with wisdom bent down'. The meaning is 'one with downward-facing wisdom'.

108. Ākiṇṇānīti pakkhittāni. Satisammosā pakireyyāti muṭṭhassatitāya vikireyya. Evamevanti ettha ucchaṅgo viya ucchaṅgapañño puggalo daṭṭhabbo. Nānākhajjakāni viya nānappakāraṃ buddhavacanaṃ. Ucchaṅge nānākhajjakāni khādantassa nisinnakālo viya tasmiṃ āsane nisinnassa uggahaṇakālo. Vuṭṭhahantassa satisammosā vikiraṇakālo viya tasmā āsanā vuṭṭhāya gacchantassa asallakkhaṇakālo veditabbo. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo ucchaṅgapaññoti vuccati. Ucchaṅgasadisapaññoti attho.

108. 'Filled' (ākiṇṇāni) means 'put in'. 'He would scatter them through confusion of mindfulness' (satisammosā pakireyya) means he would spill them due to lapsed mindfulness. 'Just so' means: here, a person with lap-wisdom should be seen as like a lap. The diverse word of the Buddha is like various snacks. The time of grasping while sitting in that seat is like the time of sitting and eating various snacks from one's lap. The time of not comprehending when getting up from that seat and leaving is to be understood as like the time of spilling them through confusion of mindfulness when standing up. 'This is called' means: such a person is called 'one with lap-wisdom'. The meaning is 'one with wisdom like a lap'.

109. Ukkujjoti uparimukho ṭhapito. Saṇṭhātīti patiṭṭhahati. Evameva khoti ettha uparimukho ṭhapito kumbho viya puthupañño puggalo daṭṭhabbo. Udakassa āsittakālo viya desanāya laddhakālo. Udakassa saṇṭhānakālo viya tattha nisinnassa uggahaṇakālo. No vivaṭṭanakālo [M 0.0065][V 0.0063] viya uṭṭhāya gacchantassa sallakkhaṇakālo veditabbo. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo puthupaññoti vuccati. Vitthārikapaññoti attho.

109. 'Set upright' means placed with the opening upward. 'It settles' means it becomes established. 'Just so indeed' means: here, a person with broad wisdom should be seen as like a pot placed with its opening upward. Like the time of pouring in water is the time when the teaching is received. Like the time of the water settling is the time of grasping while seated there. The time of comprehending when one rises to leave is to be understood as like the time of the water not flowing away. 'This is called' means: such a person is called 'one with broad wisdom'. The meaning is 'one with extensive wisdom'.

110. Avītarāgādīsu – yathā sotāpannasakadāgāmino, evaṃ puthujjanopi [P 0.0215] pañcasu kāmaguṇesu, tīsu ca bhavesu avītarāgo. Adabbatāya pana na gahito. Yathā hi cheko vaḍḍhakī dabbasambhāratthaṃ vanaṃ paviṭṭho na ādito paṭṭhāya sampattasampattarukkhe chindati, ye panassa dabbasambhārūpagā honti, teyeva chindati; evamidhāpi bhagavatā dabbajātikā ariyāva gahitā, puthujjanā pana adabbatāya na gahitāti veditabbā. Kāmesu vītarāgoti pañcasu kāmaguṇesu vītarāgo. Bhavesu avītarāgoti rūpārūpabhavesu avītarāgo.

110. Regarding those not free from lust, etc.: Just as the stream-enterer and once-returner, so too the ordinary person is not free from lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure and the three realms of existence. However, they are not included because they are unsuitable material. For example, a skilled carpenter entering a forest to gather timber does not, from the start, cut down every tree he comes across, but only those that are suitable for his timber needs. Similarly, here the Blessed One has included only the noble ones, who are of the nature of suitable material, while ordinary persons are to be understood as not included because they are unsuitable material. 'Free from lust for sensual pleasures' means free from lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Not free from lust for the realms of existence' means not free from lust for the realms of form and formless existence.

113. Pāsāṇalekhūpamādīsu – anusetīti appahīnatāya anuseti. Na khippaṃ lujjatīti na antarā nassati, kappuṭṭhāneneva nassati. Evamevanti evaṃ tassāpi puggalassa kodho na antarā punadivase vā aparadivase vā nibbāti, addhaniyo pana hoti. Maraṇeneva nibbātīti attho. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo pāsāṇalekhā viya kujjhanabhāvena ciraṭṭhitikato pāsāṇalekhūpamoti vuccati.

113. In the simile of a line on a rock, etc.: 'It persists' (anuseti) means it persists because it has not been relinquished. 'It does not quickly disappear' (na khippaṃ lujjati) means it does not vanish in between; it disappears only when the eon ends. 'In the same way,' the anger of such a person does not subside in between, not on the next day or the day after, but lasts a long time. The meaning is that it subsides only with death. 'This is called'—such a person, because of the enduring nature of their anger like a line on a rock, is called 'one comparable to a line on a rock.'

114. So ca khvassa kodhoti so appamattakepi kāraṇe sahasā kuddhassa kodho. Na ciranti aciraṃ appahīnatāya nānuseti. Yathā pana pathaviyaṃ ākaḍḍhitvā katalekhā vātādīhi khippaṃ nassati, evamassa sahasā uppannopi kodho khippameva nibbātīti attho. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo pathaviyaṃ lekhā viya kujjhanabhāvena aciraṭṭhitikato pathavīlekhūpamoti vuccati.

114. 'And indeed, their anger' (so ca khvassa kodho)—this refers to the anger of one who suddenly becomes angry even for a trivial reason. 'Not long' (na ciraṃ) means it does not persist for long because it is not abandoned. Just as a line drawn on the ground quickly disappears due to wind and such, so too does their suddenly arisen anger quickly subside—this is the meaning. 'This is called'—such a person, due to the short-lived nature of their anger, being comparable to a line on the ground, is called 'one comparable to a line on the ground.'

115. Āgāḷhenāti atigāḷhena mammacchedakena thaddhavacanena. Pharusenāti na sotasukhena. Amanāpenāti na cittasukhena. Saṃsandatīti ekībhavati. Sandhiyatīti ghaṭayati. Sammodatīti nirantaro hoti. Atha vā – saṃsandatīti cittakiriyādīsu cittena samodhānaṃ gacchati. Khīrodakaṃ viya ekībhāvaṃ upetīti attho. Sandhiyatīti ṭhānagamanādīsu kāyakiriyādīsu [M 0.0066] kāyena samodhānaṃ gacchati. Tilataṇḍulā viya missībhāvaṃ upetīti attho. Sammodatīti uddesaparipucchādīsu vacīkiriyāsu vācāya samodhānaṃ gacchati. Vippavāsagatopi [V 0.0064] piyasahāyako viya piyatarabhāvaṃ upetīti attho. Apica – kiccakaraṇīyesu tehi saddhiṃ āditova ekakiriyabhāvaṃ upagacchanto saṃsandati. Yāva majjhā pavattanto sandhiyati, yāva pariyosānā anivattanto sammodatītipi veditabbo. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo udakalekhā [P 0.0216] viya khippaṃ saṃsandanato udakalekhūpamoti vuccati.

115. 'Harshly' (āgāḷhena) means with excessively harsh, cutting, and stiff words. 'Roughly' (pharusena) means not pleasant to hear. 'Disagreeable' (amanāpena) means not pleasing to the mind. 'Merges' (saṃsandati) means becomes one. 'Bonds' (sandhiyati) means connects. 'Reconciles' (sammodati) means becomes continuous. Alternatively: 'Merges' means the mind comes into harmony in mental activities and so forth, attaining unity like milk and water—this is the meaning. 'Bonds' means the body comes into harmony in bodily activities like standing and going and so forth, attaining a state of mixture like sesame seeds and rice—this is the meaning. 'Reconciles' means speech comes into harmony in verbal activities like recitation and questioning and so forth, attaining a state of even greater affection like a beloved friend after separation—this is the meaning. Furthermore: by undertaking shared activities with them from the very beginning and attaining a state of unified action, one 'merges.' By continuing through the middle, one 'bonds.' By not turning back until the end, one 'reconciles'—this should also be understood. 'This is called'—such a person, because of quickly merging like a line drawn on water, is called 'one comparable to a line on water.'

116. Potthakūpamesu – yāya upamāya te potthakūpamāti vuccanti, taṃ tāva upamaṃ dassetuṃ tayo potthakātiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha navoti navavāyimo. Potthakoti sāṇavākasāṭako. Dubbaṇṇoti vivaṇṇo. Dukkhasamphassoti kharasamphasso. Appagghoti atibahuṃ agghanto kahāpaṇagghanako hoti. Majjhimoti paribhogamajjhimo. So hi navabhāvaṃ atikkamitvā jiṇṇabhāvaṃ appatto majjhe paribhogakālepi dubbaṇṇo ca dukkhasamphasso ca appagghoyeva ca hoti. Atibahuṃ agghanto aḍḍhaṃ agghati. Jiṇṇakāle pana aḍḍhamāsakaṃ vā kākaṇikaṃ vā agghati. Ukkhaliparimajjananti kāḷukkhaliparipuñchanaṃ.

116. In the similes of coarse cloth: First, to show the simile by which they are called 'like coarse cloth,' 'three types of coarse cloth' and so forth are mentioned. There, 'new' (nava) means newly woven. 'Coarse cloth' (potthaka) means a hempen or bark-fiber cloth. 'Of poor color' (dubbaṇṇa) means discolored. 'Unpleasant to the touch' (dukkhasamphassa) means rough to the touch. 'Of little value' (appaggha) means that, when valued at the very most, it is worth a kahāpaṇa. 'Middle' (majjhima) means in the middle of its use. For having passed its new state but not yet reached its worn-out state, even in the middle of its use, it is of poor color, rough to the touch, and still of little value. When valued at the very most, it is worth half (a kahāpaṇa). But in its worn-out state, it is worth only half a māsaka or a kākaṇika. 'Mortar-wiping' (ukkhaliparimajjana) means wiping the black mortar.

Navoti upasampadāya pañcavassakālato heṭṭhā jātiyā saṭṭhivassopi navoyeva. Dubbaṇṇatāyāti sarīravaṇṇenapi guṇavaṇṇenapi dubbaṇṇatāya. Dussīlassa hi parisamajjhe nisinnassa nittejatāya sarīravaṇṇopi na sampajjati, guṇavaṇṇe vattabbameva natthi. Ye kho panassāti ye kho pana tassa upaṭṭhākā vā ñātimittādayo vā etaṃ puggalaṃ sevanti. Tesaṃ tanti tesaṃ puggalānaṃ cha satthāre sevantānaṃ micchādiṭṭhikānaṃ viya, devadattaṃ sevantānaṃ kokālikādīnaṃ viya ca taṃ sevanaṃ dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya hoti. Majjhimoti pañcavassakālato paṭṭhāya yāva navavassakālā majjhimo nāma. Theroti dasavassakālato paṭṭhāya thero nāma. Evamāhaṃsūti evaṃ vadanti. Kiṃ nu kho tuyhanti tuyhaṃ bālassa bhaṇitena ko atthoti vuttaṃ hoti. Tathārūpanti tathājātikaṃ tathāsabhāvaṃ ukkhepanīyakammassa kāraṇabhūtaṃ.

'New' (nava) means one who has been ordained for less than five years, even if one is sixty years old by birth. 'Due to poor appearance' (dubbaṇṇatāya) means due to poor appearance in both physical complexion and virtuous qualities. For an immoral person sitting in an assembly, their physical complexion does not shine due to their lack of luster, and there is nothing to be said of their virtuous qualities. 'But those who associate with him' (ye kho panassa) means those attendants, relatives, or friends and so forth who associate with that person. 'For them, that' (tesaṃ taṃ) means that for those persons, that association leads to their long-term harm and suffering, just as for those with wrong views who follow the six teachers, or like Kokālika and others who followed Devadatta. 'Middle' (majjhima) refers to one from five years up to nine years after ordination. 'Elder' (thera) refers to one from ten years onward. 'Thus they spoke' (evamāhaṃsu) means thus they say. 'What is it to you?' (kiṃ nu kho tuyhaṃ) means 'What use is the talk of a fool like you?' 'Of such a kind' (tathārūpa) means one of such a kind, of such a nature, being a cause for an act of suspension.

117. Kāsikavatthūpamesu [M 0.0067] – kāsikavatthaṃ nāma tayo kappāsaṃsū gahetvā kantitasuttena vāyitaṃ sukhumavatthaṃ. Taṃ navavāyimaṃ anagghaṃ hoti. Paribhogamajjhimaṃ vīsampi tiṃsampi sahassāni agghati. Jiṇṇakāle pana aṭṭhapi dasapi sahassāni agghati.

117. In the similes of Kāsī cloth: Kāsī cloth is a fine fabric woven with thread spun from three cotton fibers. When newly woven, it is priceless. In its prime for use, it is worth twenty or thirty thousand. But when worn out, it is worth eight or ten thousand.

Tesaṃ [V 0.0065] taṃ hotīti tesaṃ sammāsambuddhādayo sevantānaṃ viya taṃ sevanaṃ dīgharattaṃ [P 0.0217] hitāya sukhāya hoti. Sammāsambuddhañhi ekaṃ nissāya yāvajjakālā muccanakasattānaṃ pamāṇaṃ natthi. Tathā sāriputtattheramahāmoggallānatthere avasese ca asītimahāsāvake nissāya saggaṃ gatasattānaṃ pamāṇaṃ natthi. Yāvajjakālā tesaṃ diṭṭhānugatiṃ paṭipannasattānampi pamāṇaṃ natthiyeva. Ādheyyaṃ gacchatīti tassa mahātherassa taṃ atthanissitaṃ vacanaṃ yathā gandhakaraṇḍake kāsikavatthaṃ ādhātabbataṃ ṭhapetabbataṃ gacchati, evaṃ uttamaṅge sirasmiṃ hadaye ca ādhātabbataṃ ṭhapetabbatampi gacchati. Sesamettha heṭṭhā vuttānusāreneva veditabbaṃ.

“For them, that occurs” (tesaṃ taṃ hoti) means that for those who attend upon the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones and so forth, that association is for their long-term welfare and happiness. For there is no measure of beings who, relying on just one Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, are liberated up to the present day. Similarly, there is no measure of beings who have gone to heaven relying on the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and the remaining eighty great disciples. Indeed, there is no measure even of beings who undertake their way of seeing up to the present day. “It goes to a place of deposit” (ādheyyaṃ gacchati) means that this statement of the great elder, being rooted in meaning, becomes fit to be deposited and kept, like Kāsī cloth in a scent-box; so too, it becomes fit to be deposited and kept on the crown of the head and in the heart. The rest here should be understood in accordance with what has been stated below.

118. Suppameyyādīsu – sukhena pametabboti suppameyyo. Idhāti imasmiṃ sattaloke. Uddhatoti uddhaccena samannāgato. Unnaḷoti uggatanaḷo; tucchamānaṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitoti attho. Capaloti pattamaṇḍanādinā cāpallena samannāgato. Mukharoti mukhakharo. Vikiṇṇavācoti asaṃyatavacano. Asamāhitoti cittekaggatārahito. Vibbhantacittoti bhantacitto, bhantagāvībhantamigīsappaṭibhāgo. Pākaṭindriyoti vivaṭindriyo. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo ‘suppameyyo’ti vuccati. Yathā hi parittassa udakassa sukhena pamāṇaṃ gayhati; evameva imehi aguṇaṅgehi samannāgatassa sukhena pamāṇaṃ gayhati. Tenesa ‘suppameyyo’ti vutto.

118. Regarding 'suppameyya' and so forth: one who is easily measured is 'suppameyya'. 'Here' (idha) means in this world of beings. 'Uddhato' means endowed with agitation. 'Unnaḷo' means one whose pride is uplifted; the meaning is one who stands having raised up empty conceit. 'Capalo' means endowed with frivolity, such as adorning bowls and so forth. 'Mukharo' means harsh-mouthed. 'Vikiṇṇavāco' means one with unrestrained speech. 'Asamāhito' means lacking concentration. 'Vibbhantacitto' means one whose mind is bewildered, like a bewildered cow, a frightened deer, or a snake. 'Pākaṭindriyo' means one whose faculties are manifest. This is called: such a person is called 'suppameyya'. Just as a small amount of water is easily measured, so too is the measure of one endowed with these unwholesome qualities easily taken. Therefore, he is called 'suppameyya'.

119. Dukkhena pametabboti duppameyyo. Anuddhatādīni vuttapaṭipakkhavasena veditabbāni. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo ‘duppameyyo’ti vuccati. Yathā hi mahāsamuddassa dukkhena pamāṇaṃ gayhati; evameva imehi guṇaṅgehi samannāgatassa dukkhena pamāṇaṃ gayhati. Tādiso ‘anāgāmī nu kho, khīṇāsavo nu kho’ti vattabbataṃ gacchati, tenesa ‘duppameyyo’ti vutto.

119. 'Duppameyyo' means difficult to measure. Unagitated and so forth should be understood in terms of the opposites of what was stated before. This is called: such a person is called 'duppameyyo'. Just as it is difficult to gauge the measure of the great ocean, so too is it difficult to gauge the measure of one endowed with these qualities. Such a one becomes a subject for speculation: 'Is he a non-returner? Is he one whose taints are destroyed?' Therefore, he is called 'duppameyyo'.

120. Na [M 0.0068] sakkā pametunti appameyyo. Yathā hi ākāsassa na sakkā pamāṇaṃ gahetuṃ, evaṃ khīṇāsavassa. Tenesa ‘appameyyo’ti vutto.

120. 'Appameyyo' means that which cannot be measured. Just as it is impossible to take the measure of space, so too is it impossible to take the measure of one whose taints are destroyed. Therefore, he is called 'appameyyo'.

121. Na sevitabbādīsu – na sevitabboti na upasaṅkamitabbo. Na bhajitabboti na allīyitabbo. Na payirupāsitabboti na santike nisīdanavasena punappunaṃ upāsitabbo. Hīno [V 0.0066] hoti sīlenātiādīsu upādāyupādāya hīnatā veditabbā[P 0.0218]. Yo hi pañca sīlāni rakkhati, so dasa sīlāni rakkhantena na sevitabbo. Yo pana dasa sīlāni rakkhati, so catupārisuddhisīlaṃ rakkhantena na sevitabbo. Aññatra anuddayā aññatra anukampāti ṭhapetvā anuddayañca anukampañca. Attano atthāya eva hi evarūpo puggalo na sevitabbo. Anuddayānukampāvasena pana taṃ upasaṅkamituṃ vaṭṭati.

121. Regarding 'should not be associated with' and so forth: 'Na sevitabbo' means one should not approach. 'Na bhajitabbo' means one should not become attached. 'Na payirupāsitabbo' means one should not repeatedly attend upon him by sitting near. 'Inferior in virtue' and so forth should be understood as indicating inferiority in one aspect after another. For one who observes the ten precepts should not associate with one who observes the five precepts. Likewise, one who observes the fourfold purified virtue should not associate with one who observes the ten precepts—except out of pity and compassion. For one’s own sake, such a person should not be associated with. However, it is permissible to approach him out of pity and compassion.

122. Sadiso hotīti samāno hoti. Sīlasāmaññagatānaṃ satanti sīlena samānabhāvaṃ gatānaṃ santānaṃ. Sīlakathā ca no bhavissatīti evaṃ samānasīlānaṃ amhākaṃ sīlameva ārabbha kathā bhavissati. Sā ca no phāsu bhavissatīti sā ca sīlakathā amhākaṃ phāsuvihāro sukhavihāro bhavissati. Sā ca no pavattinī bhavissatīti sā ca amhākaṃ kathā divasampi kathentānaṃ pavattinī bhavissati, na paṭihaññissati. Dvīsu hi sīlavantesu ekena sīlassa vaṇṇe kathite itaro anumodati; tena tesaṃ kathā phāsu ceva hoti, pavattinī ca. Ekasmiṃ pana dussīle sati dussīlassa sīlakathā dukkathāti neva sīlakathā hoti, na phāsu hoti, na pavattinī. Samādhipaññākathāsupi eseva nayo. Dve hi samādhilābhino samādhikathaṃ, sappaññā ca paññākathaṃ kathentā, rattiṃ vā divasaṃ vā atikkantampi na jānanti.

122. 'Sadiso hoti' means he is equal. 'Among those equal in virtue' (sīlasāmaññagatānaṃ sataṃ) means among good people who have attained similarity in virtue. 'There will be talk of virtue among us' (sīlakathā ca no bhavissati) means that for us who are equal in virtue, talk will arise concerning virtue itself. 'And it will be comfortable for us' (sā ca no phāsu bhavissati) means that talk about virtue will be a comfortable and happy abiding for us. 'And it will be continuous for us' (sā ca no pavattinī bhavissati) means that our talk, even if we speak for a whole day, will be continuous and not obstructed. For when among two virtuous people, one speaks in praise of virtue, the other approves; thus, their talk is both comfortable and continuous. But if there is one unvirtuous person, talk of virtue is bad talk for the unvirtuous, so there is no talk of virtue, no comfort, and no continuity. The same method applies to talk about concentration and wisdom. For two who have gained concentration, talking about concentration, or those with wisdom, talking about wisdom, do not know even that the night or day has passed.

123. Sakkatvā garuṃ katvāti sakkārañceva garukārañca karitvā. Adhiko hotīti atireko hoti. Sīlakkhandhanti sīlarāsiṃ. Paripūressāmīti taṃ atirekasīlaṃ puggalaṃ nissāya attano aparipūraṃ sīlarāsiṃ paripūraṃ karissāmi. Tattha tattha paññāya anuggahessāmīti ettha sīlassa [M 0.0069] asappāye anupakāradhamme vajjetvā sappāye upakāradhamme sevanto tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne sīlakkhandhaṃ paññāya anuggaṇhāti nāma. Samādhipaññākkhandhesupi eseva nayo.

123. 'Having honored and respected' (sakkatvā garuṃ katvā) means having shown both honor and reverence. 'Adhiko hoti' means he is superior. 'The aggregate of virtue' (sīlakkhandhaṃ) refers to the mass of virtue. 'I will fulfill it' (paripūressāmi) means, relying on that person of superior virtue, I will complete my own incomplete mass of virtue. 'Therein, I will support it with wisdom' (tattha tattha paññāya anuggahessāmi) means that by avoiding things unsuitable and unhelpful for virtue and cultivating things suitable and helpful, one supports the aggregate of virtue with wisdom in each and every instance. The same method applies to the aggregates of concentration and wisdom as well.

124. Jigucchitabbādīsu – jigucchitabboti gūthaṃ viya jigucchitabbo. Atha kho nanti atha kho assa. Kittisaddoti kathāsaddo. Evamevanti ettha gūthakūpo viya dussīlyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Gūthakūpe patitvā ṭhito dhamanīahi viya dussīlapuggalo. Guthakūpato uddhariyamānena tena ahinā purisassa sarīraṃ āruḷhenāpi adaṭṭhabhāvo viya dussīlaṃ sevamānassāpi [P 0.0219] tassa kiriyāya [V 0.0067] kāraṇabhāvo sarīraṃ gūthena makkhetvā ahino gatakālo viya dussīlaṃ sevamānassa pāpakittisaddassa abbhuggamanakālo veditabbo.

124. Regarding 'to be disgusted by' and so forth: 'Jigucchitabbo' means one should be disgusted as with feces. 'Atha kho naṃ' means 'but for him'. 'Sound of reputation' (kittisaddo) means spoken word. 'In the same way' (evamevaṃ): here, unvirtuousness should be regarded as like a cesspit. An immoral person is like one who has fallen into a cesspit and is standing among dhamanī creepers. Just as there is the state of not being bitten by a snake even when it is pulled out of a cesspit and has climbed onto a person's body, so for one associating with an immoral person the causal nature of that action is not immediately apparent. And just as the time when the snake departs, having smeared the body with feces, so should the time when the sound of a bad reputation arises for one associating with an immoral person be understood.

125. Tindukālātanti tindukarukkhaalātaṃ. Bhiyyoso mattāya cicciṭāyatīti tañhi jhāyamānaṃ pakatiyāpi papaṭikāyo muñcantaṃ cicciṭāyati ciṭiciṭāti saddaṃ karoti. Ghaṭṭitaṃ pana adhimattaṃ karotīti attho. Evamevanti evamevaṃ kodhano attano dhammatāyapi uddhato caṇḍikato hutvā carati. Appamattakaṃ pana vacanaṃ vuttakāle ‘mādisaṃ nāma evaṃ vadatī’ti atirekataraṃ uddhato caṇḍikato hutvā carati. Gūthakūpoti gūthapuṇṇakūpo, gūtharāsiyeva vā. Opammasaṃsandanaṃ panettha purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Tasmā evarūpo puggalo ajjhupekkhitabbo, na sevitabboti yasmā kodhano atiseviyamānopi atiupasaṅkamiyamānopi kujjhatiyeva, ‘kiṃ iminā’ti paṭikkamantopi kujjhatiyeva, tasmā palālaggi viya ajjhupekkhitabbo, na sevitabbo. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yo hi palālaggiṃ atiupasaṅkamitvā tappati, tassa sarīraṃ jhāyati. Yo atipaṭikkamitvā tappati, tassa sītaṃ na vūpasammati. Anupasaṅkamitvā apaṭikkamitvā pana majjhattabhāvena tappentassa sītaṃ vūpasammati, kāyopi na ḍayhati. Tasmā palālaggi viya kodhano puggalo majjhattabhāvena ajjhupekkhitabbo, na sevitabbo, na bhajitabbo, na payirupāsitabbo.

125. 'Tindukālātaṃ' means a firebrand from a tinduka tree. 'Bhiyyoso mattāya cicciṭāyati' means it crackles with even greater intensity. For when burning, it naturally emits sparks and makes a crackling, 'ciṭiciṭā,' sound. When struck, it makes an even louder noise; this is the meaning. 'In the same way' (evamevaṃ): similarly, an angry person, by their very nature, behaves in an agitated and fierce manner. But when even a slight word is spoken, thinking, 'How dare they speak to someone like me thus,' they become even more agitated and fierce. 'Cesspit' (gūthakūpo) means a pit full of feces or simply a heap of feces. The connection of the simile here should be understood in the same way as before. Therefore, such a person should be regarded with equanimity, not associated with. Because an angry person gets angry even when served excessively or approached excessively, and gets angry even when one withdraws thinking, 'What is the use of this?'; therefore, like a fire of straw, they should be regarded with equanimity, not associated with. What is meant by this? For one who warms themselves by approaching a fire of straw too closely, their body is scorched. One who warms themselves by staying too far away does not have their cold allayed. But for one who warms themselves with a neutral attitude, neither approaching nor withdrawing, their cold is allayed and their body is not burned. Therefore, like a fire of straw, an angry person should be regarded with equanimity—not associated with, not befriended, not attended upon.

126. Kalyāṇamittoti sucimitto. Kalyāṇasahāyoti sucisahāyo. Sahāyoti sahagāmī saddhiṃcaro. Kalyāṇasampavaṅkoti kalyāṇesu [M 0.0070] sucipuggalesu sampavaṅko, tanninnatappoṇatappabbhāramānasoti attho.

126. 'Kalyāṇamitto' means a virtuous friend. 'Kalyāṇasahāyo' means a virtuous companion. 'Sahāyo' means one who travels together, one who fares along with. 'Kalyāṇasampavaṅko' means one who is inclined towards virtuous, pure individuals—that is, one whose mind is inclined, disposed, and leans towards them; this is the meaning.

127. Sīlesu paripūrakārītiādīsu – sīlesu paripūrakārinoti ete ariyasāvakā yāni tāni maggabrahmacariyassa ādibhūtāni, ādibrahmacariyakāni, pārājikasaṅkhātāni cattāri mahāsīlasikkhāpadāni, tesaṃ avītikkamanato yāni khuddānukhuddakāni āpajjanti, tehi ca vuṭṭhānato sīlesu yaṃ kattabbaṃ, taṃ paripūraṃ samattaṃ karontīti ‘sīlesu paripūrakārino’ti vuccanti. Samādhipāribandhakānaṃ pana kāmarāgabyāpādānaṃ, paññāpāribandhakassa ca saccapaṭicchādakassa mohassa [P 0.0220] asamūhatattā, samādhiṃ paññañca bhāventāpi samādhipaññāsu yaṃ [V 0.0068] kattabbaṃ taṃ mattaso pamāṇena padesamattameva karontīti samādhismiṃ paññāya ca mattaso kārinoti vuccanti. Iminā upāyena itaresupi dvīsu nayesu attho veditabbo.

127. Regarding 'one who fulfills virtuous conduct' and so forth: 'Sīlesu paripūrakārino' means that these noble disciples, regarding the four great training rules known as the pārājikas, which are fundamental to the holy life, pertaining to the beginning of the holy life, do not transgress them. Even if they commit minor and lesser offenses, they recover from them. Thus, they fully and completely accomplish what should be done in terms of virtue; hence, they are called 'fulfillers of virtuous conduct'. But because sensual desire and ill-will, which hinder concentration, and delusion which conceals the truth and hinders wisdom, have not been eradicated, even though they develop concentration and wisdom, they only partially accomplish what should be done in terms of concentration and wisdom; hence, they are called 'partial doers in concentration and wisdom'. In this way, the meaning in the other two cases should also be understood.

Tatrāyaṃ aparopi suttantanayo –

Herein is also another method according to the suttas:

“Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sīlesu paripūrakārī hoti, samādhismiṃ mattaso kārī, paññāya mattaso kārī. So yāni tāni khuddānukhuddakāni sikkhāpadāni tāni āpajjatipi, vuṭṭhātipi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Na hi mettha, bhikkhave, abhabbatā vuttā. Yāni ca kho tāni sikkhāpadāni ādibrahmacariyakāni brahmacariyasāruppāni, tattha dhuvasīlo ca hoti, ṭhitasīlo ca, samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesu. So tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā sotāpanno hoti, avinipātadhammo niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo. Idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sīlesu…pe… so tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā, rāgadosamohānaṃ tanuttā, sakadāgāmī hoti; sakideva imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvā dukkhassantaṃ karoti. Idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sīlesu paripūrakārī hoti, samādhismiṃ paripūrakārī, paññāya mattaso kārī. So yāni tāni…pe… sikkhati sikkhāpadesu. So pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ…pe… anāvattidhammo tasmā lokā. Idha pana, bhikkhave[M 0.0071], bhikkhu sīlesu paripūrakārī, samādhismiṃ paripūrakārī, paññāya paripūrakārī. So yāni tāni khuddānukhuddakāni…pe… sikkhati sikkhāpadesu. So āsavānaṃ khayā…pe… upasampajja viharatī”ti (a. ni. 3.87).

“Here, monks, a monk is accomplished in virtue, one who practices moderately in concentration, and one who practices moderately in wisdom. He falls into and rises out of minor and subsidiary training rules. Why is that? Because, monks, no inability has been declared here. But as for those training rules that are fundamental to the holy life, suitable for the holy life—there he is constant in virtue, firm in virtue, and having undertaken them, he trains in the training rules. With the destruction of the three fetters, he is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to downfall, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. Here, monks, a monk is accomplished in virtue… With the destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of greed, hatred, and delusion, he becomes a once-returner; having come back to this world just once, he makes an end of suffering. Here, monks, a monk is accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, and one who practices moderately in wisdom. He falls into and rises out of minor and subsidiary training rules… but as for those training rules that are fundamental to the holy life, suitable for the holy life—there he is constant in virtue, firm in virtue, and having undertaken them, he trains in the training rules. With the destruction of the five lower fetters… he is a non-returner, not liable to return from that world. Here, monks, a monk is accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, and accomplished in wisdom. He falls into and rises out of minor and subsidiary training rules… but as for those training rules that are fundamental to the holy life, suitable for the holy life—there he is constant in virtue, firm in virtue, and having undertaken them, he trains in the training rules. With the destruction of the taints… he enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge.”

130. Satthāraniddese – pariññaṃ paññapetīti pahānaṃ samatikkamaṃ paññapeti. Tatrāti tesu tīsu janesu. Tena daṭṭhabboti tena paññāpanena so satthā rūpāvacarasamāpattiyā lābhīti daṭṭhabboti attho. Dutiyavārepi eseva nayo. Sammāsambuddho satthā tena daṭṭhabboti tena titthiyehi asādhāraṇena paññāpanena ayaṃ tatiyo satthā sabbaññubuddho daṭṭhabbo. Titthiyā hi kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapentā rūpabhavaṃ vakkhanti. Rūpānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapentā [P 0.0221] arūpabhavaṃ vakkhanti. Vedanānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapentā asaññabhavaṃ vakkhanti. Sammā paññapentā ‘evaṃ paññapeyyuṃ’, no ca sammā paññapetuṃ sakkonti. Sammāsambuddho pana kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ pahānaṃ anāgāmimaggena paññapeti[V 0.0069]. Rūpavedanānaṃ pariññaṃ pahānaṃ arahattamaggena paññapeti. Ime tayo satthāroti ime dve janā bāhirakā, eko sammāsambuddhoti – imasmiṃ loke tayo satthāro nāma.

130. In the Explanation of Teachers: 'He declares full understanding' means he declares abandonment and overcoming. 'Therein' means among those three kinds of people. 'By that, it should be seen' means: by that declaration, that teacher should be seen as one who has attained the form-sphere meditative attainments; this is the meaning. The same applies to the second instance. The Perfectly Self-Enlightened One is the Teacher; 'by that, it should be seen': by that declaration, which is not common to sectarians, this third teacher should be seen as the All-Knowing Buddha. For sectarians, while declaring the full understanding of sensual pleasures, will speak of form existence. While declaring the full understanding of forms, they will speak of formless existence. While declaring the full understanding of feelings, they will speak of perceptionless existence. If they were to declare correctly, they would declare thus, but they are not able to declare correctly. However, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One declares the full understanding of sensual pleasures as abandonment by means of the path of non-returning. He declares the full understanding of forms and feelings as abandonment by means of the path of arahantship. 'These three teachers' means: these two persons are outsiders, and one is the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Thus, in this world, there are these three called 'teachers'.

131. Dutiye satthāraniddese – diṭṭhe ceva dhammeti imasmiṃ attabhāve. Attānaṃ saccato thetato paññapetīti “attā nāmeko atthi nicco dhuvo sassato”ti bhūtato thirato paññapeti. Abhisamparāyañcāti aparasmiṃ attabhāve evameva paññapeti. Sesamettha vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

131. In the second exposition on the Teacher – 'In this very life' means in this present existence. He declares the self as true and substantial, saying: 'There is indeed a self that is permanent, stable, everlasting,' thus declaring it as real and firm. 'And in the next life' means he similarly proclaims it in a future existence. The rest should be understood in the same way as previously explained.

Tikaniddesavaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Exposition of the Triad.

4. Catukkaniddesavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Exposition of the Tetrad.

132. Catukkaniddese – asappurisoti lāmakapuriso. Pāṇaṃ atipātetīti pāṇātipātī. Adinnaṃ ādiyatīti adinnādāyī. Kāmesu micchā caratīti kāmesumicchācārī. Musā vadatīti musāvādī. Surāmerayamajjapamāde tiṭṭhatīti surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhāyī.

132. In the exposition of the tetrad – 'asappuriso' means an inferior person. 'Pāṇaṃ atipātetīti' means 'he destroys life'; thus he is a 'destroyer of life' (pāṇātipātī). 'Adinnaṃ ādiyatīti' means 'he takes what is not given'; thus he is a 'taker of what is not given' (adinnādāyī). 'Kāmesu micchā caratīti' means 'he engages in misconduct in sensual pleasures'; thus he is 'one who engages in misconduct in sensual pleasures' (kāmesumicchācārī). 'Musā vadatīti' means 'he speaks falsely'; thus he is a 'speaker of falsehood' (musāvādī). 'Surāmerayamajjapamāde tiṭṭhatīti' means 'he abides in heedlessness due to distilled and fermented intoxicants'; thus he is 'one who abides in heedlessness due to distilled and fermented intoxicants' (surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhāyī).

133. Pāṇātipāte [M 0.0072] samādapetīti yathā pāṇaṃ atipāteti, tathā naṃ tattha gahaṇaṃ gaṇhāpeti. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo yasmā sayaṃ katena ca dussīlyena samannāgato yañca samādapitena kataṃ, tato upaḍḍhassa dāyādo, tasmā asappurisena asappurisataroti vuccati. Sappurisoti uttamapuriso.

133. 'He instigates the destruction of life' means that just as he himself destroys life, so he causes another to undertake it. The same method applies to the rest. 'This is said' means this kind of person, because he is endowed with immorality through what he has done himself and through what was done by his instigation, is an heir to half of that. Therefore, he is called 'worse than an inferior person' (asappurisena asappurisataro). 'Sappuriso' means a superior person.

135. Sappurisena sappurisataroti attanā katena susīlyena samannāgatattā yañca samādapito karoti. Tato upaḍḍhassa dāyādattā uttamapurisena uttamapurisataro.

135. 'Better than a good person' means that because he is endowed with morality through what he has done himself and through what one he has instigated does, and is thus an heir to half of that, he is 'more superior than a superior person' (uttamapurisena uttamapurisataro).

136. Pāpoti akusalakammapathasaṅkhātena dasavidhena pāpena samannāgato.

136. 'Pāpo' means one who is endowed with the ten kinds of evil, reckoned as the paths of unwholesome action.

138. Kalyāṇoti [V 0.0070] kusalakammapathasaṅkhātena dasavidhena kalyāṇadhammena samannāgato suddhako [P 0.0222] bhadrako. Sesamettha heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthameva.

138. 'Kalyāṇo' means one who is endowed with the ten kinds of virtuous qualities, reckoned as the paths of wholesome action—pure and excellent. The rest here is of obvious meaning, because it follows the method stated below.

140. Pāpadhammādīsu – pāpo dhammo assāti pāpadhammo. Kalyāṇo dhammo assāti kalyāṇadhammo. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

140. Regarding 'one with evil qualities' and so on—'pāpo dhammo assāti' means 'his qualities are evil'; thus he is 'one with evil qualities' (pāpadhammo). 'Kalyāṇo dhammo assāti' means 'his qualities are good'; thus he is 'one with good qualities' (kalyāṇadhammo). The rest here is of obvious meaning.

144. Sāvajjādīsu – sāvajjoti sadoso. Sāvajjena kāyakammenāti sadosena pāṇātipātādinā kāyakammena. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo tīhi dvārehi āyūhanakammassa sadosattā, gūthakuṇapādibharito padeso viya sāvajjoti vuccati.

144. Regarding 'blameworthy' and so on—'sāvajjoti' means 'blameworthy', that is, 'with fault' (sadoso). 'Sāvajjena kāyakammenāti' means 'by blameworthy bodily action', that is, 'by bodily action with fault, such as the destruction of life and so on'. The same method applies to the others. 'This is said' means this kind of person is called 'blameworthy' (sāvajjo), because his accumulating action through the three doors is faulty, like a place filled with dung, carcasses, and so on.

145. Sāvajjena bahulanti yassa sāvajjameva kāyakammaṃ bahu hoti, appaṃ anavajjaṃ; so sāvajjena bahulaṃ kāyakammena samannāgato, appaṃ anavajjenāti vuccati. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Ko pana evarūpo hotīti? Yo gāmadhammatāya vā nigamadhammatāya vā kadāci karahaci uposathaṃ samādiyati, sīlāni pūreti. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo [M 0.0073] tīhi dvārehi āyūhanakammesu sāvajjasseva bahulatāya anavajjassa appatāya vajjabahuloti vuccati.

145. 'Sāvajjena bahulanti' means one for whom blameworthy bodily action is abundant, and blameless action is scarce; he is called 'one endowed with bodily action that is mostly blameworthy and little that is blameless'. The same method applies to the others. But who is such a person? One who, due to village custom or town custom, occasionally undertakes the Uposatha and fulfills the precepts. 'This is said' means this kind of person, because among the accumulating actions through the three doors, the blameworthy are abundant and the blameless are scarce, is called 'one for whom faults are abundant' (vajjabahulo).

Yathā hi ekasmiṃ padese dubbaṇṇāni duggandhāni pupphāni rāsikatānassu, tesaṃ upari tahaṃ tahaṃ atimuttakavassikapāṭalāni patitāni bhaveyyuṃ. Evarūpo ayaṃ puggalo veditabbo. Yathā pana ekasmiṃ padese atimuttakavassikapāṭalāni rāsikatānassu, tesaṃ upari tahaṃ tahaṃ dubbaṇṇaduggandhāni badarapupphādīni patitāni bhaveyyuṃ. Evarūpo tatiyo puggalo veditabbo. Catuttho pana tīhipi dvārehi āyūhanakammassa niddosattā, catumadhurabharitasuvaṇṇapāti viya daṭṭhabbo. Tesu paṭhamo andhabālaputhujjano. Dutiyo antarantarā kusalassa kārako lokiyaputhujjano. Tatiyo sotāpanno sakadāgāmianāgāminopi eteneva saṅgahitā. Catuttho khīṇāsavo. So hi ekantena anavajjoyeva. Ayaṃ aṅguttaraṭṭhakathāyo.

For example, in one place there might be a heap of ill-colored, foul-smelling flowers, and on top of them, here and there, atimuttaka, vassika, and pāṭalā flowers might have fallen. This kind of person should be understood thus. Or, just as in one place there might be a heap of atimuttaka, vassika, and pāṭalā flowers, and on top of them, here and there, ill-colored, foul-smelling flowers like jujube blossoms and so on might have fallen. The third kind of person should be understood thus. The fourth, however, because his accumulating action through the three doors is faultless, should be seen as like a golden bowl filled with the four sweet things. Among these, the first is a blind, foolish ordinary person. The second is a worldly ordinary person who performs wholesome deeds from time to time. The third is a stream-enterer; once-returners and non-returners are also included by this. The fourth is one whose taints are destroyed. He is indeed entirely blameless. This is from the Aṅguttara commentary.

148. Ugghaṭitaññūādīsu – ugghaṭitaññūti ettha ugghaṭitaṃ nāma [P 0.0223] ñāṇugghāṭanaṃ, ñāṇe ugghaṭitamatteyeva [V 0.0071] jānātīti attho. Saha udāhaṭavelāyāti udāhāre udāhaṭamatteyeva. Dhammābhisamayoti catusaccadhammassa ñāṇena saddhiṃ abhisamayo. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ ‘cattāro satipaṭṭhānā’tiādinā nayena saṃkhittena mātikāya ṭhapiyamānāya desanānusārena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhituṃ samattho puggalo ugghaṭitaññūti vuccati.

148. Among those like 'one who understands upon utterance' and so on—here, 'ugghaṭita' means the opening of knowledge; the meaning is that one understands as soon as knowledge is opened. 'Saha udāhaṭavelāyāti' means 'at the very moment of utterance', that is, as soon as it is uttered. 'Dhammābhisamayo' means the realization of the Dhamma of the Four Truths together with knowledge. 'This is said' means this person, who is capable of attaining arahantship by directing knowledge according to the teaching when a brief matrix is laid out in the manner of 'the four foundations of mindfulness' and so forth, is called 'one who understands upon utterance' (ugghaṭitaññū).

149. Vipañcitaṃ vitthāritameva atthaṃ jānātīti vipañcitaññū. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ saṅkhittena mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā vitthārena atthe bhājiyamāne arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ samattho puggalo vipañcitaññūti vuccati.

149. 'Vipañcitaṃ vitthāritameva atthaṃ jānātīti' means 'one who understands the meaning only when it is made clear and elaborated'; thus he is 'one who understands by elaboration' (vipañcitaññū). 'This is said' means this person who, when a matrix is set forth briefly and then the meaning is analyzed in detail, is capable of attaining arahantship, is called 'one who understands by elaboration' (vipañcitaññū).

150. Uddesādīhi netabboti neyyo. Anupubbena dhammābhisamayo hotīti anukkamena arahattappatti.

150. 'Uddesādīhi netabboti' means 'to be guided by instruction and so on'; thus he is 'one who is to be guided' (neyyo). 'Anupubbena dhammābhisamayo hotīti' means 'there is a gradual realization of the Dhamma', that is, the gradual attainment of arahantship.

151. Byañjanapadameva [M 0.0074] paramaṃ assāti padaparamo. Na tāya jātiyā dhammābhisamayo hotīti na tena attabhāvena jhānaṃ vā vipassanaṃ vā maggaṃ vā phalaṃ vā nibbattetuṃ sakkotīti attho.

151. 'Byañjanapadameva paramaṃ assāti' means 'for whom the mere letter of the text is supreme'; thus he is 'one for whom the letter is supreme' (padaparamo). 'Na tāya jātiyā dhammābhisamayo hotīti' means 'there is no realization of the Dhamma in that birth'; the meaning is that with that existence one is incapable of producing jhāna, insight, path, or fruition.

152. Yuttapaṭibhānādīsu – paṭibhānaṃ vuccati ñāṇampi, ñāṇassa upaṭṭhitavacanampi. Taṃ idha adhippetaṃ. Atthayuttaṃ kāraṇayuttañca paṭibhānamassāti yuttappaṭibhāno. Pucchitānantarameva sīghaṃ byākātuṃ asamatthatāya no muttaṃ paṭibhānamassāti no muttappaṭibhāno. Iminā nayena sesā veditabbā. Ettha pana paṭhamo – kiñci kālaṃ vīmaṃsitvā yuttameva pekkhati, tipiṭakacūḷanāgatthero viya. So kira pañhaṃ puṭṭho pariggahetvā yuttapayuttakāraṇameva katheti.

152. Among those like 'one with fitting readiness of mind' and so on—'paṭibhāna' is said to be both knowledge and speech that is ready because of knowledge. The latter is intended here. 'Atthayuttaṃ kāraṇayuttañca paṭibhānamassāti' means 'whose readiness of mind is connected with meaning and reason'; thus he is 'one with fitting readiness of mind' (yuttappaṭibhāno). 'Pucchitānantarameva sīghaṃ byākātuṃ asamatthatāya no muttaṃ paṭibhānamassāti' means 'whose readiness of mind is not quick, due to being incapable of answering swiftly immediately after being questioned'; thus he is 'one whose readiness of mind is not quick' (no muttappaṭibhāno). The rest should be understood in this way. Here, the first—after reflecting for some time, considers only what is fitting, like the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga. It is said that when asked a question, he would grasp it and speak only of what was reasonable and fitting.

Dutiyo – pucchānantarameva yena vā tena vā vacanena paṭibāhati, vīmaṃsitvāpi ca yuttaṃ na pekkhati catunikāyikapaṇḍitatissatthero viya. So kira pañhaṃ puṭṭho pañhapariyosānampi nāgameti, yaṃ vā taṃ vā kathetiyeva. Vacanatthaṃ panassa vīmaṃsiyamānaṃ katthaci na laggati.

The second—immediately after being questioned, rebuts with some speech or another, and even upon reflection does not see what is fitting, like the Elder Catunikāyika Paṇḍita Tissa. It is said that when asked a question, he would not even wait for the question to be finished, and would just say whatever. However, when the meaning of his words was examined, it did not apply anywhere.

Tatiyo – pucchāsamakālameva yuttaṃ pekkhati, taṅkhaṇaññeva vacanaṃ byākaroti tipiṭakacūḷābhayatthero [V 0.0072] viya. So kira pañhaṃ puṭṭho sīghameva katheti, yuttapayuttakāraṇo ca hoti.

The third—at the very moment of being questioned, sees what is fitting and answers immediately, like the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya. It is said that when asked a question, he would speak quickly, and his explanation would be fitting and reasoned.

Catuttho – puṭṭho samāno neva yuttaṃ pekkhati[P 0.0224], na yena vā tena vā paṭibāhituṃ sakkoti tibbandhakāranimuggo viya hoti lāḷudāyitthero viya.

The fourth—when questioned, neither sees what is fitting nor is able to retort in any way; he is like one submerged in dense darkness, like the Elder Lāḷudāyi.

156. Dhammakathikesu – appañca bhāsatīti sampattaparisāya thokameva katheti. Asahitañcāti kathento ca pana na atthayuttaṃ kāraṇayuttaṃ katheti. Parisā cassa na kusalā hotīti sotuṃ nisinnaparisā cassa yuttāyuttaṃ kāraṇākāraṇaṃ siliṭṭhāsiliṭṭhaṃ na jānātīti attho. Evarūpoti ayaṃ evaṃjātiko bāladhammakathiko. Evaṃjātikāya bālaparisāya dhammakathikotveva nāmaṃ labhati. Iminā nayena sabbattha attho veditabbo. Ettha ca dveyeva janā sabhāvadhammakathikā, itare pana dhammakathikānaṃ antare paviṭṭhattā evaṃ vuttā.

156. Among Dhamma speakers—"he speaks little" means he speaks only a little to the assembled company. "And it is disconnected" means that while speaking, he does not speak what is connected with meaning and reason. "And his assembly is not skilled" means the assembly sitting to listen does not know what is fitting or unfitting, reasonable or unreasonable, elegant or inelegant—that is the meaning. "Such a one" means this kind of foolish Dhamma speaker. For such a foolish assembly, he gains merely the name of 'Dhamma speaker'. The meaning should be understood in this way in all cases. Here, only two persons are Dhamma speakers by nature; the others, however, are described thus because they are included among Dhamma speakers.

157. Valāhakūpamesu [M 0.0075] valāhakāti meghā. Gajjitāti thanitā. Tattha gajjitvā no vassanabhāvo nāma pāpako. Manussā hi yathā devo gajjati ‘suvuṭṭhikā bhavissatī’ti bījāni nīharitvā vapanti. Atha deve avassante khette bījāni khetteyeva nassanti, gehe bījāni geheyeva nassantīti dubbhikkhaṃ hoti. No gajjitvā vassanabhāvopi pāpakova. Manussā hi ‘imasmiṃ kāle dubbuṭṭhikā bhavissatī’ti ninnaṭṭhānesuyeva vappaṃ karonti. Atha devo vassitvā sabbabījāni mahāsamuddaṃ pāpeti, dubbhikkhameva hoti. Gajjitvā vassanabhāvo pana bhaddako. Tadā hi subhikkhaṃ hoti. No gajjitvā no vassanabhāvo ekantapāpakova.

157. In the similes of clouds, "valāhakā" means clouds. "Gajjitā" means thunderers. There, the state of thundering without raining is indeed bad. For when the sky thunders, people, thinking, "There will be good rain," bring out seeds and sow them. But if the sky does not rain, the seeds in the field perish right there in the field, and the seeds in the house perish right there in the house; thus, a famine occurs. The state of raining without thundering is also bad. For people, thinking, "There will be poor rain this season," sow only in low-lying areas. Then, when the sky rains, it carries all the seeds to the great ocean, and a famine occurs. But the state of thundering and then raining is good, for then there is abundance. The state of neither thundering nor raining is utterly bad.

Bhāsitā hoti no kattāti ‘idāni ganthadhuraṃ pūressāmi, vāsadhuraṃ pūressāmī’ti kathetiyeva, na pana uddesaṃ gaṇhāti, na kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāveti.

One who is a speaker but not a doer: he only says, "Now I will fulfill the burden of study, I will fulfill the burden of dwelling," but he does not take up the lesson, nor does he cultivate the meditation subject.

Kattā hoti no bhāsitāti ‘ganthadhuraṃ vā pūressāmi vāsadhuraṃ vā’ti na bhāsati. Sampatte pana kāle tamatthaṃ sampādeti. Iminā nayena itarepi veditabbā. Sabbaṃ panetaṃ paccayadāyakeneva kathitaṃ. Eko hi ‘asukadivase nāma dānaṃ dassāmī’ti saṅghaṃ nimanteti, sampattakāle no karoti. Ayaṃ puggalo puññena parihāyati, bhikkhusaṅghopi lābhena parihāyati[V 0.0073]. Aparo saṅghaṃ animantetvāva sakkāraṃ katvā ‘bhikkhū ānessāmī’ti na labhati, sabbe aññattha nimantitā honti. Ayampi puññena parihāyati[P 0.0225], saṅghopi tena lābhena parihāyati. Aparo paṭhamaṃ saṅghaṃ nimantetvā, pacchā sakkāraṃ katvā dānaṃ deti, ayaṃ kiccakārī hoti. Aparo neva saṅghaṃ nimanteti, na dānaṃ deti, ayaṃ ‘pāpapuggalo’ti veditabbo.

One who is a doer but not a speaker: he does not say, "I will fulfill the burden of study or the burden of dwelling." Yet when the time comes, he accomplishes that purpose. The others should also be understood in this way. All this, however, has been said with reference to the giver of requisites. For one person invites the Saṅgha, saying, "On such and such a day, I will give a donation," but when the time arrives, he does not do it. This person declines in merit, and the Bhikkhu Saṅgha also declines in gain. Another, without inviting the Saṅgha, having prepared an offering, does not succeed in bringing the monks, for all have been invited elsewhere. This one also declines in merit, and the Saṅgha also declines in that gain. Another first invites the Saṅgha, and afterward, having prepared an offering, gives a donation; this one is a doer of what is to be done. Yet another neither invites the Saṅgha nor gives a donation; this one should be known as "a wicked person."

158. Mūsikūpamesu – gādhaṃ kattā no vasitāti attano āsayaṃ bilaṃ kūpaṃ khaṇati, no tattha vasati, kismiñcideva ṭhāne vasati, evaṃ biḷārādiamittavasaṃ gacchati. Khattātipi pāṭho. Vasitā no gādhaṃ kattāti sayaṃ na khaṇati, parena khate bile vasati, evaṃ jīvitaṃ rakkhati. Tatiyā dvepi karontī, jīvitaṃ rakkhati. Catutthā dvepi akarontī amittavasaṃ gacchati. Imāya pana upamāya upamitesu puggalesu [M 0.0076] paṭhamo yathā sā mūsikā gādhaṃ khaṇati, evaṃ navaṅgaṃ satthusāsanaṃ uggaṇhāti. Yathā pana sā tattha na vasati, kismiñcideva ṭhāne vasantī, amittavasaṃ gacchati; tathā ayampi pariyattivasena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā catusaccadhammaṃ na paṭivijjhati, lokāmisaṭṭhānesuyeva caranto maccumārakilesamāradevaputtamārasaṅkhātānaṃ amittānaṃ vasaṃ gacchati. Dutiyo yathā sā mūsikā gādhaṃ na khaṇati, evaṃ navaṅgaṃ satthusāsanaṃ na uggaṇhāti. Yathā pana parena khatabile vasantī jīvitaṃ rakkhati; evaṃ parassa kathaṃ sutvā catusaccadhammaṃ paṭivijjhitvā tiṇṇaṃ mārānaṃ vasaṃ atikkamati. Iminā nayena tatiyacatutthesupi opammasaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

158. In the similes of mice—one who digs deep but does not dwell there: a mouse digs a burrow, a pit, for its own shelter, but does not live there, instead dwelling in some other place; thus it falls under the power of enemies like cats and others.
