There is also the reading 'khattā'. One who dwells but does not dig deep: it does not dig itself, but lives in a burrow dug by another; thus it preserves its life. The third does both, and preserves its life. The fourth does neither, and falls under the power of enemies. However, among the individuals compared by this simile, the first, just as that mouse digs deep, so too does this person learn the ninefold teaching of the Teacher. But just as that mouse does not dwell there, instead living in some other place and falling under the power of enemies, so too does this person, having sent forth knowledge through study, fail to penetrate the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. Wandering in the realm of worldly gains, they fall under the power of enemies known as Death-Māra, Defilement-Māra, and Devaputta-Māra. The second, just as that mouse does not dig deep, so too does this person not learn the ninefold teaching of the Teacher. But just as that mouse lives in a burrow dug by another and preserves its life, so too does this person, hearing the words of another, penetrate the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths and transcend the power of the three Māras. In this way, the connection of the simile should be understood for the third and fourth types as well.

159. Ambūpamesu – āmaṃ pakkavaṇṇīti anto āmaṃ bahi pakkasadisaṃ. Pakkaṃ āmavaṇṇīti anto pakkaṃ bahi āmasadisaṃ. Sesadvayesupi eseva nayo. Tattha yathā ambe apakkabhāvo āmatā hoti, evaṃ puggalepi puthujjanabhāvo āmatā, ariyabhāvo pakkatā. Yathā ca tattha pakkasadisatā pakkavaṇṇitā; evaṃ puggalepi ariyānaṃ abhikkamanādisadisatā pakkavaṇṇitāti – iminā nayena upamitapuggalesu opammasaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

159. In the similes of mangoes—'unripe with the appearance of ripe' means unripe inside but resembling the ripe on the outside. 'Ripe with the appearance of unripe' means ripe inside but resembling the unripe on the outside. The same principle applies to the remaining two cases as well. Here, just as the state of unripeness in a mango is its rawness, so too in a person, the state of an ordinary person is rawness, while the state of a noble one is ripeness. And just as the resemblance to ripeness there is called 'the appearance of ripe,' so too in a person, resemblance to the noble ones in their deportment and so on is called 'the appearance of ripe.' In this way, the connection between the simile and the individuals being compared should be understood.

160. Kumbhūpamesu [P 0.0226] – kumbhoti ghaṭo. Tucchoti anto ritto. Pihitoti pidahitvā ṭhapito. Puroti anto puṇṇo. Vivaṭoti vivaritvā ṭhapito. Upamitapuggalesu panettha anto guṇasāravirahito [V 0.0074] tuccho bāhirasobhanatāya pihito puggalo veditabbo. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

160. Among the examples of pots—'pot' means a jar. 'Hollow' means empty inside. 'Covered' means closed and set aside. 'Full' means filled inside. 'Open' means opened and set aside. Here, among the individuals being compared, a person who is hollow, being devoid of the essence of virtue within, and covered by outward beauty, is to be understood. The same principle applies to the remaining cases as well.

161. Udakarahadūpamesu – udakarahado tāva jaṇṇumattepi udake sati paṇṇarasasambhinnavaṇṇattā vā bahalattā vā udakassa apaññāyamānatalo uttāno gambhīrobhāso nāma hoti. Tiporisa catuporisepi pana udake sati acchattā udakassa paññāyamānatalo gambhīro uttānobhāso nāma hoti. Ubhayakāraṇasambhāvato pana itare dve veditabbā. Puggalopi kilesussadabhāvato guṇagambhīratāya ca abhāvato guṇagambhīrānaṃ sadisehi abhikkamādīhi yutto uttāno gambhīrobhāso nāma. Iminā nayena sesāpi veditabbā.

161. Among the examples of water pools—first, a water pool: even with water only up to the knee, because its bottom is not seen due to the mingling of colors or the thickness of the water, it is shallow but has the appearance of being deep; this is called 'shallow appearing deep.' But with water reaching the height of three or four men, because its bottom is seen due to the clarity of the water, it is deep but has the appearance of being shallow; this is called 'deep appearing shallow.' The other two, however, are to be understood from the combination of both these causes. Similarly, a person who, due to an abundance of defilements and an absence of depth in virtue, is endowed with conduct such as deportment that resembles those with depth in virtue, is called 'shallow appearing deep.' In this way, the rest are also to be understood.

162. Balībaddūpamesu [M 0.0077] – balībaddo tāva yo attano gogaṇaṃ ghaṭṭeti ubbejeti, paragogaṇe pana sorato sukhasīlo hoti – ayaṃ sakagavacaṇḍo no paragavacaṇḍo nāma. Puggalopi attano parisaṃ ghaṭṭento vijjhanto pharusena samudācaranto, paraparisāya pana soraccaṃ nivātavuttitaṃ āpajjanto sakagavacaṇḍo hoti no paragavacaṇḍo nāmāti. Iminā nayena sesāpi veditabbā. Niddesavāre panettha ubbejitā hotīti ghaṭṭetvā vijjhitvā ubbegappattaṃ karoticceva attho.

162. Among the examples of bulls—first, the bull who disturbs and agitates his own herd, but is docile and of pleasant behavior among other herds, is called 'fierce with his own, not with others.' Similarly, a person who harasses, afflicts, and behaves harshly towards their own group, but adopts docility and humble conduct towards other groups, is called 'fierce with his own, not with others.' In this way, the rest should also be understood. Here, in the section on explanation, 'agitates' means to disturb, afflict, and cause to reach a state of agitation—this is the meaning.

163. Āsīvisūpamesu – āsīviso tāva yassa visaṃ āsuṃ āgacchati sīghaṃ pharati; ghoraṃ pana na hoti, cirakālaṃ na pīḷeti – ayaṃ āgataviso no ghoraviso. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Puggalavibhājanaṃ pana uttānatthameva.

163. Among the examples of snakes—first, a snake: one whose venom comes quickly and spreads swiftly, but is not severe and does not torment for long; this is called 'quick-venomed, not deadly.' The same principle applies to the remaining instances as well. The classification of individuals, however, is straightforward in meaning.

164. Ananuvicca apariyogāhetvā avaṇṇārahassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsitā hotītiādīsu ananuviccāti atulayitvā, apariggaṇhitvā. Apariyogāhetvāti paññāya guṇe anogāhetvā.

164. In the phrases 'praising one undeserving of praise without examination or scrutiny,' and so forth, 'without examination' means without weighing or without estimating. 'Without scrutiny' means without plunging into the qualities by wisdom.

166. Bhūtaṃ tacchanti vijjamānato bhūtaṃ, aviparītato tacchaṃ. Kālenāti yuttapayuttakālena. Tatra kālaññū hotīti yamidaṃ [P 0.0227] kālenāti vuttaṃ. Tatra yo puggalo kālaññū hoti, kālaṃ jānāti, tassa pañhassa veyyākaraṇatthāya “imasmiṃ kāle pucchitenāpi mayā [V 0.0075] na kathetabbā, imasmiṃ kāle kathetabbā”ti – ayaṃ kālena bhaṇati nāma. Upekkhako viharatīti majjhattabhūtāya upekkhāya ṭhito hutvā viharati. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthameva.

166. ‘Actual’ (bhūtaṃ) is so because it exists; ‘true’ (tacchaṃ) is so because it is not contrary to fact. 'In due time' means at the fitting and proper time. In this context, 'one is a knower of time' refers to what was stated as 'in due time.' There, the person who knows the time, who understands the time, for the purpose of answering a question, thinks: 'At this time, even if asked, I should not speak; at this time, I should speak'—this one is called 'one who speaks in due time.' 'Dwells equanimous' means one dwells established in impartial equanimity. The rest is straightforward in meaning everywhere.

167. Uṭṭhānaphalūpajīvītiādīsu – yo uṭṭhānavīriyeneva divasaṃ vītināmetvā tassa nissandaphalamattaṃ kiñcideva labhitvā jīvikaṃ kappeti, taṃ pana uṭṭhānaṃ āgamma kiñci puññaphalaṃ na paṭilabhati, taṃ sandhāya yassa puggalassa uṭṭhahatotiādi vuttaṃ. Tatūpari devāti tato upari brahmakāyikādayo devā. Tesañhi uṭṭhānavīriyena kiccaṃ nāma natthi. Puññaphalameva upajīvanti. Puññavato cāti idaṃ puññavante khattiyabrāhmaṇādayo ceva bhummadeve ādiṃ katvā nimmānaratipariyosāne deve ca sandhāya [M 0.0078] vuttaṃ. Sabbepi hete vāyāmaphalañceva puññaphalañca anubhavanti. Nerayikā pana neva uṭṭhānena ājīvaṃ uppādetuṃ sakkonti, nāpi nesaṃ puññaphalena koci ājīvo uppajjati.

167. Regarding 'one who lives by the fruits of exertion' and so on: This refers to one who spends the day solely by exertion and energy, sustaining a livelihood by obtaining only a little, a mere residue of the results of that exertion. However, relying on that exertion, they do not receive any fruit of merit. It is with reference to such a person that the statement beginning, 'of the person who exerts,' was made. Regarding 'devas above that': This refers to the Brahmā-realm devas and others above them. For them, there is no need for exertion or energy; they live solely by the fruits of merit. Regarding 'the meritorious': This was stated with reference to meritorious individuals such as nobles, brahmins, and so on, as well as devas, beginning with the terrestrial devas and extending up to the Nimmānarati devas. All of these experience both the fruit of exertion and the fruit of merit. However, hell-beings can neither produce a livelihood through exertion, nor does any livelihood arise for them through the fruit of merit.

168. Tamādīsu – “nīce kule paccājāto”tiādikena tamena yuttoti tamo. Kāyaduccaritādīhi puna nirayatamūpagamanato tamaparāyaṇo. Nesādakuleti migaluddakādīnaṃ kule. Venakuleti vilīvakārakule. Rathakārakuleti cammakārakule. Pukkusakuleti pupphachaḍḍakakule. Kasiravuttiketi dukkhavuttike. Dubbaṇṇoti paṃsupisācako viya jhāmakhāṇuvaṇṇo. Duddasikoti vijātamātuyāpi amanāpadassano. Okoṭimakoti lakuṇḍako. Kāṇoti ekakkhikāṇo vā ubhayakkhikāṇo vā. Kuṇīti ekahatthakuṇī vā ubhayahatthakuṇī vā. Khañjoti ekapādakhañjo vā ubhayapādakhañjo vā. Pakkhahatoti hatapakkho pīṭhasappī. Padīpeyyassāti telakapallakādino padīpūpakaraṇassa. Evaṃ puggalo tamo hoti tamaparāyaṇoti ettha eko puggalo bahiddhā ālokaṃ adisvā mātukucchismiññeva kālaṃ katvā apāyesu nibbattanto sakalepi kappe saṃsarati. Sopi tamo tamaparāyaṇova. So pana kuhakapuggalo bhaveyya. Kuhakassa hi evarūpā nibbatti hotīti vuttaṃ.

168. Regarding 'darkness' and so on: 'Darkness' (tamo) means one who is endowed with darkness, as in 'born in a low family' and so on. Again, one is 'destined for darkness' (tamaparāyaṇo) due to misconduct of body and so on, leading to falling into the darkness of hell. 'Nesāda family' refers to the families of deer hunters and the like. 'Vena family' refers to the families of basket weavers. 'Rathakāra family' refers to the families of leather workers. 'Pukkusa family' refers to the families of flower scavengers. 'Kasiravuttika' means one who lives with difficulty. 'Dubbaṇṇa' means one with a repulsive color, like a dust-demon or a charred stump. 'Duddasika' means one whose appearance is displeasing even to his own mother. 'Okoṭimaka' means a hunchback. 'Kāṇa' means one-eyed or blind in both eyes. 'Kuṇī' means one with a crippled hand or both hands. 'Khañja' means one with a crippled foot or both feet. 'Pakkhahata' means paralyzed on one side, one who crawls on his buttocks. 'Padīpeyya' refers to lamp equipment, such as oil lamps and so on. Thus, a person is darkness and destined for darkness. Here, a person, not seeing the light outside, dies while still in the mother's womb and is reborn in the lower realms, wandering through entire aeons. Even he is darkness and destined for darkness. But that person might be a deceitful person. For a deceitful person, such a rebirth is said to occur.

Ettha ca nīce kule paccājāto [P 0.0228] hoti caṇḍālakule vātiādīhi āgamanavipatti ceva pubbuppannapaccayavipatti ca dassitā. Daliddetiādīhi pavattipaccayavipatti. Kasiravuttiketiādīhi ājīvupāyavipatti. Dubbaṇṇotiādīhi rūpavipatti. Bahvābādhotiādīhi dukkhakāraṇasamāyogo. Na lābhītiādīhi sukhakāraṇavipatti ceva upabhogavipatti [V 0.0076] ca. Kāyena duccaritantiādīhi tamaparāyaṇabhāvassa kāraṇasamāyogo. Kāyassa bhedātiādīhi samparāyikatamūpagamo. Sukkapakkho vuttapaṭipakkhanayena veditabbo.

Here, being reborn in a low family, such as a caṇḍāla family, shows both the misfortune of birth and the misfortune of previously arisen conditions. Being poor, etc., shows the misfortune of conditions for continuance. Having a difficult livelihood, etc., shows the misfortune of the means of livelihood. Being ugly, etc., shows the misfortune of appearance. Being frequently ill, etc., shows association with the causes of suffering. Not gaining, etc., shows both the misfortune of the causes of happiness and the misfortune of enjoyment. Misconduct by body, etc., shows association with the cause of being destined for darkness. Upon the breakup of the body, etc., shows going to darkness in the next world. The bright side should be understood by the method of the opposite of what has been stated.

Apicettha tividhāya kulasampattiyā paccājātiādikena jotinā yuttato joti, ālokabhūtoti vuttaṃ hoti. Kāyasucaritādīhi pana saggūpapattijotibhāvūpagamanato jotiparāyaṇo. Khattiyamahāsālakule vātiādīsu khattiyamahāsālāti khattiyā mahāsārā [M 0.0079] mahāsārappattā khattiyā. Yesañhi khattiyānaṃ heṭṭhimantena koṭisataṃ nidhānagataṃ hoti, tayo kahāpaṇakumbhā vaḷañjanatthāya gehamajjhe rāsiṃ katvā ṭhapitā honti, te khattiyamahāsālā nāma. Yesaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ asītikoṭidhanaṃ nihitaṃ hoti, diyaḍḍho kahāpaṇakumbho vaḷañjanatthāya gehamajjhe rāsiṃ katvā ṭhapito hoti, te brāhmaṇamahāsālā nāma. Yesaṃ gahapatīnaṃ cattālīsakoṭidhanaṃ nihitaṃ hoti, kahāpaṇakumbho vaḷañjatthāya gehamajjhe rāsiṃ katvā ṭhapito hoti, te gahapatimahāsālā nāma. Tesaṃ kuleti attho. Aḍḍheti issare. Nidhānagatadhanassa mahantatāya mahaddhane. Suvaṇṇarajatabhājanādīnaṃ upabhogabhaṇḍānaṃ mahantatāya mahābhoge. Nidhānagatassa jātarūparajatassa pahūtatāya pahūtajātarūparajate. Vittūpakaraṇassa tuṭṭhikaraṇassa pahūtatāya pahūtavittūpakaraṇe. Godhanādīnañca sattavidhadhaññānañca pahūtatāya pahūtadhanadhaññe. Abhirūpoti sundararūpo. Dassanīyoti aññaṃ kammaṃ pahāya divasampi passitabbayutto. Pāsādikoti dassaneneva cittapasādāvaho. Paramāyāti uttamāya. Vaṇṇapokkharatāyāti pokkharavaṇṇatāya. Pokkharaṃ vuccati sarīraṃ. Tassa vaṇṇasampattiyāti attho. Samannāgatoti upeto.

Furthermore, here, 'light' (joti) is said because one is endowed with light through the threefold family prosperity, rebirth, and so on, meaning one is light-like. Moreover, one is 'destined for light' (jotiparāyaṇo) because one attains the state of light of rebirth in heaven through bodily good conduct and the like. In the phrases 'either in a noble great-family' and so on, 'noble great-family' refers to nobles who are greatly prosperous, having attained great essence. For among those nobles, those who have at least one hundred crores of buried treasures, and three pots of coins are heaped up in the middle of the house for daily use—these are called 'noble great-families.' Among brahmins, those who have eighty crores in buried wealth, with one and a half pots of coins heaped up in the middle of the house for daily use, are called 'brahmin great-families.' Among householders, those who have forty crores in buried wealth, with a pot of coins heaped up in the middle of the house for daily use, are called 'householder great-families.' This is the meaning of 'of such a family.' 'Wealthy' means powerful. 'With great riches' means having great wealth, due to the greatness of buried wealth. 'With great possessions' means having great enjoyments, due to the greatness of gold, silver vessels, and other goods for enjoyment. 'With abundant gold and silver' means having abundant gold and silver, due to the abundance of buried gold and silver. 'With abundant wealth and means' means having abundant wealth and means, due to the abundance of wealth and means that cause contentment. 'With abundant wealth and grain' means having abundant wealth and grain, due to the abundance of cattle and so on, and the seven kinds of grain. 'Handsome' means having a beautiful form. 'Pleasing to behold' means one is worthy of being looked at even for a day, abandoning other work. 'Inspiring confidence' means one brings serenity to the mind merely by being seen. 'Of the highest' means supreme. 'With lotus-like complexion' means having a lotus-like hue. 'Pokkhara' is said to be the body, so the meaning is the accomplishment of its complexion. 'Endowed' means possessed.

169. Oṇatoṇatādīsu [P 0.0229] – diṭṭhadhammikāya vā samparāyikāya vā sampattiyā virahito oṇato. Nīco, lāmakoti attho. Tabbipakkhato uṇṇato. Ucco, uggatoti attho. Sesamettha tamādīsu vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Apica – oṇatoṇatoti idāni nīco, āyatimpi nīcova bhavissati. Oṇatuṇṇatoti idāni nīco, āyatiṃ ucco bhavissati. Uṇṇatoṇatoti idāni ucco, āyatiṃ nīco bhavissati. Uṇṇatuṇṇatoti idāni ucco, āyatimpi uccova bhavissatīti.

169. Regarding the terms 'low and low' and so on: one who is deprived of attainment in this life or the next is called 'low' (oṇato). It means inferior, base. In contrast, one is called 'high' (uṇṇato). It means lofty, elevated. The rest here should be understood by the method stated in the section on 'darkness' and so on. Furthermore: 'low and low' means one is presently low and will remain low in the future. 'Low and high' means one is presently low but will become high in the future. 'High and low' means one is presently high but will become low in the future. 'High and high' means one is presently high and will remain high in the future.

170. Rukkhūpamesu – rukkho tāva pheggusāraparivāroti vanajeṭṭhakarukkho sayaṃ pheggu hoti[V 0.0077], parivārarukkhā panassa sārā honti. Iminā nayena sesā veditabbā. Puggalesu pana sīlasāravirahato pheggutā, sīlācārasamannāgamena ca sāratā veditabbā.

170. Regarding the tree similes: a tree, for instance, is 'sapwood with a retinue of heartwood' (pheggusāraparivāro), meaning the chief tree of the forest is itself sapwood, while its surrounding trees are heartwood. The rest should be understood in this way. Among individuals, however, being sapwood should be understood as arising from the absence of virtue as heartwood, and being heartwood as arising from being endowed with virtuous conduct.

171. Rūpappamāṇādīsu [M 0.0080] – sampattiyuttaṃ rūpaṃ pamāṇaṃ karotīti rūpappamāṇo. Tattha pasādaṃ janetīti rūpappasanno. Kittisaddabhūtaṃ ghosaṃ pamāṇaṃ karotīti ghosappamāṇo. Ārohaṃ vātiādīsu pana – ārohanti uccattanaṃ. Pariṇāhanti kisathūlabhāvāpagataṃ parikkhepasampattiṃ. Saṇṭhānanti aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ dīgharassavaṭṭatādiyuttaṭṭhānesu tathābhāvaṃ. Pāripūrinti yathāvuttappakārānaṃ anūnataṃ, lakkhaṇaparipuṇṇabhāvaṃ vā. Paravaṇṇanāyāti parehi parammukhā nicchāritāya guṇavaṇṇanāya. Parathomanāyāti parehi thutivasena gāthādiupanibandhanena vuttāya thomanāya. Parapasaṃsanāyāti parehi sammukhā vuttāya pasaṃsāya. Paravaṇṇahārikāyāti paramparathutivasena parehi pavattitāya vaṇṇaharaṇāya.

171. Regarding 'measuring by form' and so on: 'one who measures by form' (rūpappamāṇo) means one who makes form endowed with attainment the measure. 'One who is pleased by form' (rūpappasanno) means one who generates pleasure therein. 'One who measures by sound' (ghosappamāṇo) means one who makes sound, which is fame or reputation, the measure. As for 'height' and so on: 'height' (āroha) means elevation. 'Proportion' (pariṇāha) means perfect proportion, free from thinness or thickness. 'Figure' (saṇṭhāna) refers to the state of limbs and features being long, short, round, etc., in their respective appropriate positions. 'Completeness' (pāripūri) means the completeness of the aforementioned aspects, or the perfection of characteristics. 'Praise by others' (paravaṇṇanā) means praise of virtues uttered by others behind one's back. 'Eulogy by others' (parathomanā) means praise spoken by others in the form of eulogy, composed in verses and so on. 'Commendation by others' (parapasaṃsanā) means praise spoken by others directly to one's face. 'Carrying of praise by others' (paravaṇṇahārikā) means the carrying of praise, transmitted by others through successive eulogies.

172. Cīvaralūkhanti cīvarassa dubbaṇṇādibhāvena lūkhataṃ. Pattalūkhanti bhājanassa vaṇṇasaṇṭhānavatthūhi lūkhataṃ. Senāsanalūkhanti nāṭakādisampattivirahena senāsanassa lūkhataṃ. Vividhanti acelakādibhāvena anekappakāraṃ. Dukkarakārikanti sarīratāpanaṃ.

172. ‘Roughness of robes’ (cīvaralūkha) means the roughness of robes due to their poor colour, etc. ‘Roughness of the bowl’ (pattalūkha) means the roughness of the bowl due to its colour, shape, or material. ‘Roughness of the lodging’ (senāsanalūkha) means the roughness of the lodging due to the absence of such amenities as theatrical performances. ‘Various’ (vividha) means of many kinds, such as being naked. ‘Performing what is hard to do’ (dukkarakārika) means the mortification of the body.

Aparo nayo – imesu hi catūsu puggalesu rūpe pamāṇaṃ gahetvā pasanno rūpappamāṇo nāma. Rūpappasannoti tasseva atthavacanaṃ. Ghose pamāṇaṃ gahetvā pasanno ghosappamāṇo [P 0.0230] nāma. Cīvaralūkhapattalūkhesu pamāṇaṃ gahetvā pasanno lūkhappamāṇo nāma. Dhamme pamāṇaṃ gahetvā pasanno dhammappamāṇo nāma. Itarāni tesaṃyeva atthavacanāni. Sabbasatte ca tayo koṭṭhāse katvā dve koṭṭhāsā rūpappamāṇā, eko na rūpappamāṇo. Pañca koṭṭhāse katvā cattāro koṭṭhāsā ghosappamāṇā, eko na ghosappamāṇo. Dasa koṭṭhāse katvā nava koṭṭhāsā lūkhappamāṇā, eko na lūkhappamāṇo. Satasahassaṃ koṭṭhāse katvā pana eko koṭṭhāsova dhammappamāṇo, sesā na dhammappamāṇā. Evamayaṃ catuppamāṇo lokasannivāso.

Another method: among these four types of individuals, one who is pleased by taking form as a standard is called ‘one who measures by form’ (rūpappamāṇo). ‘Pleased by form’ (rūpappasanno) is another expression for the same meaning. One who is pleased by taking sound as a standard is called ‘one who measures by sound’ (ghosappamāṇo). One who is pleased by taking rough robes and bowls as a standard is called ‘one who measures by roughness’ (lūkhappamāṇo). One who is pleased by taking the Dhamma as a standard is called ‘one who measures by Dhamma’ (dhammappamāṇo). The other terms are just expressions for the same meaning. Moreover, having divided all beings into three parts, two parts are those who measure by form, and one is not one who measures by form. Having divided them into five parts, four parts are those who measure by sound, and one is not one who measures by sound. Having divided them into ten parts, nine parts are those who measure by roughness, and one is not one who measures by roughness. But having divided them into a hundred thousand parts, only one part is one who measures by Dhamma; the rest are not ones who measure by Dhamma. Thus, this population of the world has four standards of measurement.

Etasmiṃ catuppamāṇe lokasannivāse buddhesu appasannā mandā, pasannāva bahukā. Rūpappamāṇassa hi buddharūpato uttari pasādāvahaṃ rūpaṃ nāma natthi. Ghosappamāṇassa buddhānaṃ kittighosato uttari pasādāvaho ghoso nāma natthi. Lūkhappamāṇassa kāsikāni vatthāni mahārahāni [V 0.0078][M 0.0081] kañcanabhājanāni tiṇṇaṃ utūnaṃ anucchavike sabbasampattiyutte pāsādavare pahāya paṃsukūlacīvaraselamayapattarukkhamūlādisenāsanasevino buddhassa bhagavato lūkhato uttari pasādāvahaṃ aññaṃ lūkhaṃ nāma natthi. Dhammappamāṇassa sadevake loke asādhāraṇasīlādiguṇassa tathāgatassa sīlādiguṇato uttari pasādāvaho añño sīlādiguṇo nāma natthi. Iti bhagavā imaṃ catuppamāṇikaṃ lokasannivāsaṃ muṭṭhinā gahetvā viya ṭhitoti.

In this world-assembly with its four standards, those who are not pleased with the Buddhas are few, while those who are pleased are many. For one who measures by form, there is no form more inspiring of confidence than the Buddha’s form. For one who measures by sound, there is no sound more inspiring of confidence than the Buddhas’ voice of fame. For one who measures by roughness, having relinquished priceless Kāsika garments, golden vessels, and a splendid mansion furnished with all luxuries suitable for the three seasons, the Blessed One dwells wearing rag-robes, using a stone bowl, and frequenting lodgings such as the foot of a tree—there is no austerity more inspiring of confidence than that of the Blessed One. For one who measures by Dhamma, there is no virtue or quality more inspiring of confidence than the virtues and qualities of the Tathāgata, which are unique in the world with its gods. Thus, the Blessed One stands as if holding this world-assembly with its four standards in his fist.

173. Attahitāya paṭipannādīsu – sīlasampannoti sīlena sampanno samannāgato. Samādhisampannotiādīsupi eseva nayo. Ettha ca sīlaṃ lokiyalokuttaraṃ kathitaṃ. Tathā samādhipaññā ca. Vimutti arahattaphalavimuttiyeva. Ñāṇadassanaṃ ekūnavīsatividhaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ. No parantiādīsu – parapuggalaṃ “tayāpi sīlasampannena bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā yathā sīlaṃ samādiyati, evaṃ na samādapeti, na gaṇhāpeti. Eseva nayo sabbattha. Etesu pana catūsu paṭhamo vakkalittherasadiso hoti. Dutiyo upanandasakyaputtasadiso[P 0.0231]. Tatiyo sāriputtamoggallānattherasadiso. Catuttho devadattasadisoti veditabbo.

173. In the passage beginning ‘practicing for one’s own welfare’ (attahitāya paṭipanna), ‘endowed with virtue’ (sīlasampanno) means one who is accomplished and possessed of virtue. The same principle applies to ‘endowed with concentration’ (samādhisampanno), etc. Here, virtue is spoken of as both mundane and supramundane. Likewise, concentration and wisdom. Liberation refers specifically to the liberation of the fruit of arahantship. Knowledge and vision refer to the nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge. In the passage beginning ‘not for others’ (no para), one does not encourage or persuade another person to undertake virtue by saying, “You too should become endowed with virtue,” so that they do so. The same principle applies in all cases. Among these four, the first is like the Elder Vakkali. The second is like Upananda the Sakyan. The third is like the Elders Sāriputta and Moggallāna. The fourth should be understood as like Devadatta.

174. Attantapādīsu – attānaṃ tapati dukkhāpetīti attantapo. Attano paritāpanānuyogaṃ attaparitāpanānuyogaṃ. Acelakoti niccelo, naggo. Muttācāroti visaṭṭhācāro. Uccārakammādīsu lokiyakulaputtācārena virahito ṭhitakova uccāraṃ karoti, passāvaṃ karoti, khādati, bhuñjati ca. Hatthāpalekhanoti hatthe piṇḍamhi niṭṭhite jivhāya hatthaṃ apalekhati. Uccāraṃ vā katvā hatthasmiññeva daṇḍakasaññī hutvā hatthena apalekhatīti dasseti. Te kira daṇḍakaṃ sattoti paññapenti. Tasmā tesaṃ paṭipadaṃ pūrento evaṃ karoti. Bhikkhāgahaṇatthaṃ ‘ehi bhaddante’ti vutto, na etīti naehibhaddantiko. Tena hi ‘tiṭṭha bhaddante’ti vuttopi na tiṭṭhatīti natiṭṭhabhaddantiko. Tadubhayampi hetaṃ titthiyā “etassa vacanaṃ kataṃ bhavissatī”ti na karonti. Abhihaṭanti puretaraṃ gahetvā āhaṭaṃ bhikkhaṃ. Uddissakatanti “imaṃ tumhe uddissa kata”nti evaṃ ārocitabhikkhaṃ. Na nimantananti “asukaṃ nāma kulaṃ vā vīthiṃ vā gāmaṃ vā paviseyyāthā”ti evaṃ nimantitabhikkhampi na sādiyati, na gaṇhāti.

174. In the passage beginning ‘self-mortifiers’ (attantapa), ‘self-mortifier’ (attantapo) means one who torments and afflicts oneself. ‘The practice of self-torment’ (attaparitāpanānuyoga) is the pursuit of self-affliction. ‘Naked ascetic’ (acelako) means without clothes, nude. ‘Unrestrained in conduct’ (muttācāro) means unrestrained in behaviour. In the passage beginning ‘defecating’ (uccārakamma), he performs bodily functions like defecating, urinating, eating, and drinking while standing, devoid of the manners of ordinary sons of good family. ‘Licking the hands’ (hatthāpalekhano) means licking the hand with the tongue after the food in the hand is finished. Or, after defecating, he licks his hand, perceiving it as a stick—this illustrates his practice. They declare that a stick is a sentient being. Therefore, one who fulfills their practice does this. For alms collection, if told, “Come, venerable,” he does not come—hence, ‘not one who comes when told “Come, venerable”’ (naehibhaddantiko). Similarly, if told, “Stay, venerable,” he does not stay—hence, ‘not one who stays when told “Stay, venerable”’ (natiṭṭhabhaddantiko). Indeed, sectarians do not do both of these, thinking, “His word will have been followed.” ‘Pre-offered food’ (abhihaṭaṃ) refers to alms brought, having been taken previously. ‘Specially prepared food’ (uddissakataṃ) means alms announced as, “This was prepared especially for you.” ‘Not accepting invitations’ (na nimantanaṃ) means not accepting alms even when invited with, “You should enter such-and-such family, street, or village.”

Na [M 0.0082] kumbhimukhāti kumbhito uddharitvā diyyamānaṃ bhikkhaṃ na gaṇhāti. Na kaḷopimukhāti [V 0.0079] kaḷopīti ukkhali, pacchi vā. Tatopi na gaṇhāti. Kasmā? Kumbhī kaḷopiyo kaṭacchunā pahāraṃ labhantīti. Na eḷakamantaranti ummāraṃ antaraṃ katvā diyyamānaṃ na gaṇhāti. Kasmā? Ayaṃ maṃ nissāya antarakaraṇaṃ labhatīti. Daṇḍamusalesupi eseva nayo. Dvinnanti dvīsu bhuñjamānesu ekasmiṃ uṭṭhāya dente na gaṇhati. Kasmā? Kabaḷantarāyo hotīti. Na gabbhiniyātiādīsu pana gabbhiniyā kucchiyaṃ dārako kilamati. Pāyantiyā dārakassa khīrantarāyo hoti. Purisantaragatāya ratiantarāyo hotīti na gaṇhāti na saṅkittīsūti saṅkittetvā katabhattesu. Dubbhikkhasamaye kira acelakasāvakā acelakānaṃ atthāya tato tato taṇḍulādīni samādapetvā [P 0.0232] bhattaṃ pacanti, ukkaṭṭhācelako tato na paṭiggaṇhāti. Na yattha sāti yattha sunakho ‘piṇḍaṃ labhissāmī’ti upaṭṭhito hoti, tattha tassa adatvā āhaṭaṃ na gaṇhāti. Kasmā? Etassa piṇḍantarāyo hotīti.

‘Not from a pot’s mouth’ (na kumbhimukhā) means he does not accept almsfood taken from a pot and given to him. ‘Not from a mortar’s mouth’ (na kaḷopimukhā) means he does not accept from a kaḷopī, which is a cooking pot or a basket. Why? Because pots and kaḷopīs receive blows from a ladle. ‘Not across an intermediary’ (na eḷakamantaraṃ) means he does not accept almsfood given across a threshold. Why? Because he thinks, “On my account, this is being made an intermediary.” The same applies to sticks and pestles. ‘Not from two’ (dvīnaṃ) means when two are eating, he does not accept almsfood given by one who stands up. Why? Because it would interrupt their meal. In the passage beginning ‘not from a pregnant woman’ (na gabbhiniyā), he does not accept from them because the child in a pregnant woman’s womb may be afflicted; a nursing woman’s child’s milk may be interrupted; and the pleasure of a woman who is with a man may be interrupted. ‘Not from collected food’ (na saṅkittīsu) means from meals prepared by collection. In times of famine, the disciples of naked ascetics gather rice and other provisions from here and there to cook meals for the ascetics, but the strict naked ascetic does not accept from them. ‘Not where a dog is present’ (na yattha sā) means where a dog is present, expecting to get a morsel, he does not accept almsfood brought from there without giving to the dog. Why? Because it would be an obstacle to its morsel.

Saṇḍasaṇḍacārinīti samūhasamūhacārinī. Sace hi acelakaṃ disvā ‘imassa bhikkhaṃ dassāmā’ti mānussakā bhattagehaṃ pavisanti, tesu ca pavisantesu kaḷopimukhādīsu nilīnā makkhikā uppatitvā saṇḍasaṇḍā caranti, tato āhaṭaṃ bhikkhaṃ na gaṇhāti. Kasmā? Maṃ nissāya makkhikānaṃ gocarantarāyo jātoti. Thusodakanti sabbasassasambhārehi kataṃ sovīrakaṃ. Ettha ca surāpānameva sāvajjaṃ. Ayaṃ pana etasmimpi sāvajjasaññī. Ekāgārikoti yo ekasmiṃyeva gehe bhikkhaṃ labhitvā nivattati. Ekālopikoti yo ekeneva ālopena yāpeti. Dvāgārikādīsupi eseva nayo. Ekissāpi dattiyāti ekāya dattiyā. Datti nāma ekā khuddakapāti hoti, yattha aggabhikkhaṃ pakkhipitvā ṭhapenti.

‘Where flies swarm in groups’ (saṇḍasaṇḍacārinī) means moving in group after group. For instance, if people see a naked ascetic and think, “We will give alms to him,” they enter a refectory. As they enter, flies hiding in places like the rim of a pot fly up and move about in swarms. He does not accept the alms brought from there. Why? Because he thinks, “On my account, the flies’ feeding has been obstructed.” ‘Chaff-water’ (thusodakaṃ) refers to a sour gruel made from all kinds of grain, called sovīraka. In this context, only the drinking of liquor is blameworthy, but this one perceives even this as blameworthy. ‘One-house-goer’ (ekāgāriko) refers to one who obtains alms at just one house and then returns. ‘One-morsel-eater’ (ekālopiko) refers to one who sustains himself with just a single morsel. The same principle applies to ‘two-house-goer’ (dvāgāriko) and so on. ‘From a single serving’ (ekissāpi dattiyā) means from a single serving. A ‘serving’ (datti) here refers to a small bowl in which the choicest alms are placed and kept.

Ekāhikanti ekadivasantarikaṃ. Aḍḍhamāsikanti aḍḍhamāsantarikaṃ. Pariyāyabhattabhojananti vārabhattabhojanaṃ. Ekāhavārena dvīhavārena sattāhavārena aḍḍhamāsavārenāti – evaṃ divasavārena ābhatabhattabhojanaṃ. Sākabhakkhoti allasākabhakkho. Sāmākabhakkhoti sāmākataṇḍulabhakkho. Nīvārādīsu – nīvārā nāma tāva araññe sayaṃ jātā vīhijāti. Daddulanti cammakārehi cammaṃ vilikhitvā chaḍḍitakasaṭaṃ. Haṭaṃ vuccati [M 0.0083] silesopi, sevālopi kaṇikārādirukkhaniyyāsopi. Kaṇanti kuṇḍakaṃ. Ācāmoti bhattaukkhalikāya laggo jhāmodano. Taṃ chaḍḍitaṭṭhāne gahetvā khādati. “Odanakañjiya”ntipi vadanti. Piññākādayo pākaṭā eva. Pavattaphalabhojīti patitaphalabhojī.

‘Eating once a day’ (ekāhika) means eating on alternate days. ‘Eating every half-month’ (aḍḍhamāsika) means eating on alternate half-months. ‘Eating by turns for alms’ (pariyāyabhattabhojana) means eating almsfood by rotation: by a one-day rotation, a two-day rotation, a seven-day rotation, or a half-month rotation—thus, eating almsfood brought according to a rotation of days. ‘Eating only greens’ (sākabhakkha) means consuming fresh greens. ‘Eating millet’ (sāmākabhakkha) means consuming millet grains. Among ‘wild rice’ (nīvāra), etc., nīvāra refers to a type of rice that grows naturally in the forest. ‘Daddula’ refers to the scraps or refuse discarded by leatherworkers after scraping hides. ‘Haṭa’ is said to mean phlegm, moss, or the sap of trees like the kaṇikāra. ‘Kaṇa’ refers to rice bran. ‘Ācāma’ is scorched rice adhering to the cooking pot. It is taken from where it has been discarded and eaten. Some also call it ‘rice gruel’ (odanakañjiya). Things like ‘oilcake’ (piññāka) are well-known. ‘Eating fallen fruits’ (pavattaphalabhojī) means consuming fruits that have dropped naturally.

Sāṇānīti [V 0.0080] sāṇavākacelāni. Masāṇānīti missakacelāni. Chavadussānīti matasarīrato chaḍḍitavatthāni. Erakatiṇādīni vā ganthetvā katanivāsanāni. Paṃsukūlānīti pathaviyaṃ chaḍḍitanantakāni. Tirīṭānīti rukkhattacavatthāni. Ajinanti [P 0.0233] ajinamigacammaṃ. Ajinakkhipanti tadeva majjhe phālitaṃ. Sakhurakantipi vadanti. Kusacīranti kusatiṇāni ganthetvā katacīrakaṃ. Vākacīraphalakacīresupi eseva nayo. Kesakambalanti manussakesehi katakambalaṃ. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, yāni kānici tantāvutānaṃ vatthānaṃ kesakambalo tesaṃ patikuṭṭho akkhāyatī”ti (a. ni. 3.138). Vāḷakambalanti assavāḷādīhi katakambalaṃ. Ulūkapakkhanti ulūkapattāni ganthetvā katanivāsanaṃ. Ubbhaṭṭhakoti uddhaṃ ṭhitako.

‘Hemp cloth’ (sāṇa) means garments made of hemp fiber. ‘Mixed cloth’ (masāṇa) means garments made of mixed fibers. ‘Discarded cloth’ (chavadussa) means clothes discarded from a corpse, or lower garments made by stringing together eraka grass and so on. ‘Rag-robes’ (paṃsukūla) refer to cloths discarded on the ground without an owner. ‘Tree bark cloth’ (tirīṭa) means garments made from the bark of trees. ‘Hide’ (ajina) means the skin of an antelope. ‘A hide cloak’ (ajinakkhipa) is the same, split in the middle. Some also call it ‘with hoofs’ (sakhuraka). ‘A grass garment’ (kusacīra) is a garment made by stringing together kusa grass. The same method applies to bark garments (vākacīra) and leaf garments (phalakacīra). ‘A hair blanket’ (kesakambala) is a blanket made from human hair. Regarding this, it is said: “Just as, bhikkhus, among all woven fabrics, a hair blanket is considered the worst” (AN 3.138). ‘A horsehair blanket’ (vāḷakambala) is a blanket made from the hair of horses, etc. ‘An owl’s wing garment’ (ulūkapakkha) is a lower garment made by stringing together owl feathers. ‘Standing upright’ (ubbhaṭṭhaka) means standing erect.

Ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyuttoti ukkuṭikavīriyaṃ anuyutto. Gacchantopi ukkuṭikova hutvā uppatitvā uppatitvā gacchati. Kaṇṭakāpassayikoti ayakaṇṭake vā pakatikaṇṭake vā bhūmiyaṃ koṭṭetvā tattha cammaṃ attharitvā ṭhānacaṅkamādīni karoti. Seyyanti sayantopi tattheva seyyaṃ kappeti. Sāyaṃ tatiyamassāti sāyatatiyakaṃ. “Pāto, majjhanhike, sāyanti divasassa tikkhattuṃ pāpaṃ pavāhessāmī”ti udakorohanānuyogaṃ anuyutto viharati.

‘Devoted to the practice of squatting’ (ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyutta) means devoted to the exertion of squatting. Even while walking, he goes by squatting, jumping up and jumping up. ‘A thorn-bed ascetic’ (kaṇṭakāpassayika) means one who, having fixed iron thorns or natural thorns into the ground, spreads a hide there and performs standing and walking meditation, etc. As for ‘lying down’ (seyya): even when lying down, he arranges his lying down right there. ‘The practice with the evening as the third’ (sāyatatiyakaṃ) means that the evening is his third time. Thinking, “In the morning, at midday, and in the evening, I will wash away evil three times a day,” he dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water.

175. Paraṃ tapatīti parantapo. Paresaṃ paritāpanānuyogaṃ paraparitāpanānuyogaṃ. Orabbhikādīsu – urabbhā vuccanti eḷakā. Urabbhe hanatīti orabbhiko. Sūkarikādīsupi – eseva nayo. Luddoti dāruṇo kakkhaḷo. Macchaghātakoti macchabandho kevaṭṭo. Bandhanāgārikoti bandhanāgāragopako. Kurūrakammantāti dāruṇakammantā.

175. ‘One who torments others’ (parantapa) means one who torments others. ‘The practice of tormenting others’ (paraparitāpanānuyoga) means engagement in tormenting others. Among ‘sheep-butchers’ (orabbhika) and the like: urabbhā are called sheep. One who kills sheep is an orabbhika. The same method applies to pig-butchers (sūkarika) and the like. ‘A cruel one’ (ludda) means fierce and rough. ‘A fish-killer’ (macchaghātaka) means a fisherman (macchabandha), a kevaṭṭa. ‘A prison-keeper’ (bandhanāgārika) means a prison guard (bandhanāgāragopaka). ‘Kurūrakammanta’ refers to cruel actions.

176. Muddhāvasittoti khattiyābhisekena muddhani abhisitto. Puratthimena nagarassāti nagarato puratthimadisāya. Sandhāgāranti yaññasālaṃ[M 0.0084]. Kharājinaṃ nivāsetvāti sakhuraṃ ajinacammaṃ nivāsetvā. Sappitelenāti sappinā ca telena ca. Ṭhapetvā hi sappiṃ avaseso yo koci sneho telanti vuccati. Kaṇḍuvamānoti nakhānaṃ chinnattā kaṇḍuvitabbakāle tena kaṇḍuvamāno. Anantarahitāyāti asanthatāya. Sarūpavacchāyāti sadisavacchāya. Sace gāvī setā hoti, vacchopi setakova sace kabarā vā, rattā vā, vacchopi tādisovāti – evaṃ sarūpavacchāya. So evamāhāti [P 0.0234] so rājā evaṃ vadeti. Vacchatarāti taruṇavacchakabhāvaṃ atikkantā [V 0.0081] balavavacchā. Vacchatarīsupi eseva nayo. Barihisatthāyāti parikkhepakaraṇatthāya ceva yaññabhūmiyaṃ attharaṇatthāya ca.

176. ‘One anointed on the head’ (muddhāvasitta) means one whose head is anointed with the royal anointment of a warrior. ‘To the east of the city’ (puratthimena nagarassa) means in the eastern direction from the city. ‘The assembly hall’ (sandhāgāra) means the sacrificial hall. ‘Wearing a rough hide’ (kharājinaṃ nivāsetvā) means wearing an animal skin with the hoofs attached. ‘With ghee and oil’ (sappitela) means with clarified butter and oil. Indeed, setting aside ghee, any other fat is called oil. ‘Scratching’ (kaṇḍuvamāna) means scratching with it when it is time to scratch, because the nails are cut. ‘Without a gap’ (anantarahita) means not spread out. ‘With a calf of similar appearance’ (sarūpavacchā) means with a similar calf. If the cow is white, the calf is also white; if speckled or red, the calf is likewise. Thus, with a calf of similar appearance. ‘He speaks thus’ (so evamāha) means the king says this. ‘Young bullocks’ (vacchatarā) are strong young calves that have passed beyond the state of being a young calf. The same principle applies to young heifers (vacchatarī). ‘For spreading grass’ (barhisatthāya) means both for the purpose of making a boundary and for spreading on the sacrificial ground.

177. Diṭṭheva dhammeti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve. Nicchātoti chātaṃ vuccati taṇhā, sā assa natthīti nicchāto. Sabbakilesānaṃ nibbutattā nibbuto. Anto tāpanakilesānaṃ abhāvā sītalo jātoti sītībhūto. Jhānamaggaphalanibbānasukhāni paṭisaṃvedetīti sukhappaṭisaṃvedī. Brahmabhūtena attanāti seṭṭhabhūtena attanā.

177. ‘In this very life’ (diṭṭheva dhamme) means in this present existence. ‘Free from craving’ (nicchāta) means that craving is called thirst, and he has none of it, thus he is free from craving. ‘Extinguished’ (nibbuta) means extinguished because all defilements are extinguished. ‘Cool’ (sītībhūta) means become cool due to the absence of defilements that cause burning within. ‘Experiencing bliss’ (sukhappaṭisaṃvedī) means experiencing the bliss of jhana, path, fruition, and Nibbāna. ‘With a self become Brahma’ (brahmabhūtena attanā) means with a self become supreme.

Imaṃ pana puggalaṃ buddhuppādato paṭṭhāya dassetuṃ – idha tathāgatotiādimāha. Tattha tathāgatoti aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi bhagavā tathāgato – tathā āgatoti tathāgato, tathā gatoti tathāgato, tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgatoti tathāgato, tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddhoti tathāgato, tathadassitāya tathāgato, tathāvāditāya tathāgato, tathākāritāya tathāgato, abhibhavanaṭṭhena tathāgatoti. Arahaṃ sammāsambuddhotiādīni visuddhimagge vitthāritāneva. Taṃ dhammanti taṃ vuttappakārasampadaṃ dhammaṃ. Suṇāti gahapati vāti kasmā paṭhamaṃ gahapatiṃ niddisati? Nihatamānattā ussannattā ca. Yebhuyyena hi khattiyakulato pabbajitā jātiṃ nissāya mānaṃ karonti. Brāhmaṇakulā pabbajitā mante nissāya mānaṃ karonti. Hīnajaccakulā pabbajitā attano vijātitāya patiṭṭhātuṃ na sakkonti. Gahapatidārakā pana kacchehi sedaṃ muñcantehi piṭṭhiyā loṇaṃ pupphamānāya bhūmiṃ kasitvā tādisassa mānassa abhāvato nihatamānadappā honti. Te pabbajitvā mānaṃ vā dappaṃ vā akatvā yathābalaṃ buddhavacanaṃ [M 0.0085] uggahetvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karontā sakkonti arahatte patiṭṭhātuṃ. Itarehi ca kulehi nikkhamitvā pabbajitā nāma na bahukā, gahapatikāva bahukā. Iti nihatamānattā ussannattā ca paṭhamaṃ gahapatiṃ niddisatīti.

To explain this person from the arising of the Buddha onwards, it begins with ‘Here, the Tathāgata…’. Herein, the Blessed One is called ‘Tathāgata’ for eight reasons: because he has come thus (tathā āgato); because he has gone thus (tathā gato); because he has arrived at the true characteristic (tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgato); because he has fully awakened to the true dhammas as they are (tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddho); because he sees what is true (tathadassitāya); because he speaks what is true (tathāvāditāya); because he does what is true (tathākāritāya); and because of overcoming (abhibhavanaṭṭhena). ‘Arahant, perfectly enlightened’ (arahaṃ sammāsambuddha), etc., are explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. ‘That Dhamma’ (taṃ dhamma) refers to the Dhamma endowed with the qualities as described. ‘A householder… hears’ (suṇāti gahapati vā): Why is the householder mentioned first? Because of their subdued pride and their abundance. For, generally, those gone forth from warrior families take pride in their birth. Those gone forth from brahmin families take pride in their mantras. Those gone forth from low-born families cannot establish themselves because of their inferior lineage. But the sons of householders, sweating from their armpits, with salt blossoming on their backs, plow the fields, and thus, due to the absence of such pride, they are free from pride and arrogance. Having gone forth, without pride or arrogance, they grasp the Buddha’s word according to their ability, practice insight, and are able to be established in arahantship. Moreover, those who have gone forth from other families are not many, while those from householder families are many. Thus, because of their subdued pride and their abundance, the householder is mentioned first.

Aññatarasmiṃ vāti itaresaṃ vā kulānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ. Paccājātoti patijāto. Tathāgate saddhaṃ paṭilabhatīti parisuddhaṃ [P 0.0235] dhammaṃ sutvā dhammassāmimhi tathāgate “sammāsambuddho vata so bhagavā”ti saddhaṃ paṭilabhati. Iti paṭisañcikkhatīti evaṃ paccavekkhati. Sambādho gharāvāsoti sacepi saṭṭhihatthe ghare yojanasatantarepi vā dve jāyampatikā vasanti, tathāpi nesaṃ sakiñcanasapalibodhaṭṭhena gharāvāso sambādhoyeva. Rajopathoti rāgarajādīnaṃ uṭṭhānaṭṭhānanti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ [V 0.0082] vuttaṃ. Āgamanapathotipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Alagganaṭṭhena abbhokāso viyāti abbhokāso. Pabbajito hi kūṭāgāraratanapāsāde ca devavimānādīsu ca supihitadvāravātapānesu paṭicchannesu vasantopi neva laggati, na sajjati, na bajjhati. Tena vuttaṃ – “abbhokāso pabbajjā”ti.

‘In one or another family’ (aññatarasmiṃ) means in one or another of the other families. ‘Reborn’ (paccājāta) means born. ‘He gains faith in the Tathāgata’ (tathāgate saddhaṃ paṭilabhati) means after hearing the purified Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata, the master of the Dhamma, thinking, “Indeed, that Blessed One is perfectly enlightened.” ‘Thus reflecting’ (iti paṭisañcikkhati) means considering in this way. ‘Living in a house is crowded’ (sambādho gharāvāso): even if two people, husband and wife, live in a house sixty cubits wide or a hundred yojanas apart, still, because of their possessions and attachments, living in a house is indeed crowded. ‘The path of dust’ (rajopatha) means the place of arising of the dust of passion and so on, as stated in the Great Commentary. It can also be called ‘the path of coming’ (āgamanapatha). ‘Open space’ (abbhokāsa) means like the sky in the sense of non-attachment. For one gone forth, even dwelling in a peaked house, a jeweled palace, or divine mansions with well-sealed doors and windows shut, he does not cling, is not attached, is not bound. Therefore, it is said: “Going forth is open space” (abbhokāso pabbajjā).

Apica – sambādho gharāvāso kusalakiriyāya okāsābhāvato. Rajopatho asaṃvutasaṅkāraṭṭhānaṃ viya rajānaṃ kilesarajānaṃ sannipātaṭṭhānato. Abbhokāso pabbajjā kusalakiriyāya yathāsukhaṃ okāsasambhāvato. Nayidaṃ sukaraṃ…pe… pabbajeyyanti ettha ayaṃ saṅkhepakathā – yadetaṃ sikkhattayabrahmacariyaṃ ekampi divasaṃ akhaṇḍaṃ katvā carimakacittaṃ pāpetabbatāya ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ. Ekadivasampi ca kilesamalena amalinaṃ katvā carimakacittaṃ pāpetabbatāya ekantaparisuddhaṃ. Saṅkhalikhitaṃ likhitasaṅkhasadisaṃ dhotasaṅkhasappaṭibhāgaṃ caritabbaṃ. Idaṃ na sukaraṃ agāraṃ ajjhāvasatā agāramajjhe vasantena ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ…pe… carituṃ – “yaṃnūnāhaṃ kese ca massuñca ohāretvā kasāyarasapītatāya kāsāyāni brahmacariyaṃ carantānaṃ anucchavikāni vatthāni acchādetvā paridahitvā agārasmā nikkhamitvā anagāriyaṃ pabbajeyya”nti. Ettha ca yasmā agārassa hitaṃ kasivāṇijjādikammaṃ “agāriya”nti vuccati, tañca pabbajjāya natthi, tasmā pabbajjā “anagāriya”nti ñātabbā. Taṃ anagāriyaṃ. Pabbajeyyanti [M 0.0086] paṭipajjeyyaṃ. Appaṃ vāti sahassato heṭṭhā bhogakkhandho appo nāma hoti, sahassato paṭṭhāya [P 0.0236] mahā. Abandhanaṭṭhena ñātiyeva ñātiparivaṭṭo. Sopi vīsatiyā heṭṭhā appo hoti, vīsatiyā paṭṭhāya mahā.

Moreover, the household life is crowded, there being no opportunity for wholesome deeds. ‘The path of dust’ is so called because, like an unrestrained refuse heap, it is a gathering place for the dust of defilements. The homeless life is an open space, there being ample opportunity for wholesome deeds as one pleases. Concerning the passage, ‘This is not easy… I should go forth,’ here is the summary: that threefold training and holy life, even for a single day, should be practiced unbroken, to be brought to the final thought, making it utterly complete. Even for a single day, it should be made unstained by the stain of defilements, to be brought to the final thought, making it utterly pure. It should be practiced like a polished conch, resembling a washed conch. This is not easy for one dwelling in a house, living amidst household life, to practice it as utterly complete… “Why don’t I shave off my hair and beard, put on the saffron robes dyed with astringent flavors, suitable for those living the holy life, and, leaving home, go forth into the homeless life?” Here, because work beneficial to the house, such as farming and trade, is called ‘of the household,’ and this does not exist in the homeless life, therefore the going forth should be understood as ‘the homeless life.’ That is the homeless life. ‘I should go forth’ means ‘I should undertake it.’ ‘Little’ means a heap of possessions below a thousand; from a thousand upwards it is much. In the sense of a bond, the circle of relatives consists of one's kin. Even that, below twenty, is little; from twenty upwards it is much.

178. Bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpannoti yā bhikkhūnaṃ adhisīlasaṅkhātā sikkhā, tañca. Yattha cete saha jīvanti, ekajīvikā sabhāgavuttino honti, taṃ bhagavatā paññattasikkhāpadasaṅkhātaṃ sājīvañca. Tattha sikkhanabhāvena samāpannoti bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno. Samāpannoti sikkhaṃ paripūrento sājīvañca avītikkamanto hutvā tadubhayaṃ upagatoti attho. Pāṇātipātaṃ pahāyātiādīsu pāṇātipātādikathā heṭṭhā vitthāritā eva. Pahāyāti imaṃ pāṇātipātacetanāsaṅkhātaṃ dussīlyaṃ pajahitvā. Paṭivirato hotīti pahīnakālato paṭṭhāya tato dussīlyato orato viratova hoti. Nihitadaṇḍo nihitasatthoti parūpaghātatthāya daṇḍaṃ vā satthaṃ vā ādāya avattanato nikkhittadaṇḍo ceva nikkhittasattho cāti [V 0.0083] attho. Ettha ca ṭhapetvā daṇḍaṃ, sabbampi avasesaṃ upakaraṇaṃ sattānaṃ vināsanabhāvato ‘sattha’nti veditabbaṃ. Yaṃ pana bhikkhū kattaradaṇḍaṃ vā dantakaṭṭhavāsiṃ vā pipphalikaṃ vā gahetvā vicaranti, na taṃ parūpaghātatthāya. Tasmā nihitadaṇḍā nihitasatthātveva saṅkhaṃ gacchanti. Lajjīti pāpajigucchanalakkhaṇāya lajjāya samannāgato. Dayāpannoti dayaṃ mettacittataṃ āpanno. Sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampīti sabbe pāṇabhūte hitena anukampako. Tāya dayāpannatāya sabbesaṃ pāṇabhūtānaṃ hitacittakoti attho. Viharatīti iriyati, pāleti.

178. Bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno (one who has entered upon the training and livelihood of the bhikkhus) means the training of the bhikkhus, which is called higher virtue, and that livelihood. And wherever they live together, having a single way of life, having a similar mode of conduct, that is the livelihood, which is called the training rules laid down by the Blessed One. There, 'entered upon the training and livelihood of the bhikkhus' means one who has entered upon it by way of training. Samāpanno (entered upon) means one who, fulfilling the training and not transgressing the livelihood, has thus attained both. In phrases such as 'having abandoned the destruction of life,' the discussion on the destruction of life and so on has already been elaborated below. Pahāya (having abandoned) means having given up this unwholesome conduct, which is the intention to destroy life. Paṭivirato hoti (abstains) means that from the time of abandoning onwards, one is indeed restrained, withdrawn from that unwholesome conduct. Nihitadaṇḍo nihitasattho (laying down the rod, laying down the knife) means one who does not wield a rod or a knife for harming others, that is, one who has discarded both rod and knife. Here, apart from the rod, all other implements that destroy beings should be understood as 'knife.' However, when bhikkhus carry a knife for cutting robes, a small adze for tooth-wood, or a fan, it is not for harming others. Therefore, they are still reckoned as having laid down the rod and the knife. Lajjī (conscientious) means endowed with shame, which has the characteristic of disgust at evil. Dayāpanno (compassionate) means one who has attained compassion, a mind of loving-kindness. Sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampī (sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings) means one who is compassionate toward all living beings with a mind directed towards welfare. The meaning is that through that compassion, one has a mind of welfare for all living beings. Viharati (dwells) means one lives, maintains.

Dinnameva ādiyatīti dinnādāyī. Cittenapi dinnameva paṭikaṅkhatīti dinnapāṭikaṅkhī. Thenetīti theno. Na thenena athenena. Athenattāyeva sucibhūtena. Attanāti attabhāvena. Athenaṃ sucibhūtaṃ attabhāvaṃ katvā viharatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Dinnameva ādiyatīti dinnādāyī (he takes only what is given, thus he is one who takes only what is given). Cittenapi dinnameva paṭikaṅkhatīti dinnapāṭikaṅkhī (even in his mind, he anticipates only what is given, thus he is one who anticipates only what is given). Thenetīti theno (he steals, thus he is a thief). Na thenena athenena (not by thieving, but by non-thieving). Athenattāyeva sucibhūtena (by the very fact of not stealing, he has become pure). Attanāti attabhāvena (attanā means by one's own being). Athenaṃ sucibhūtaṃ attabhāvaṃ katvā viharatīti vuttaṃ hoti (it is said that he dwells having made his own being non-thieving and pure).

Abrahmacariyanti [M 0.0087] aseṭṭhacariyaṃ. Brahmaṃ seṭṭhaṃ ācāraṃ caratīti brahmacārī. Ārācārīti abrahmacariyato dūracārī. Methunāti rāgapariyuṭṭhānavasena sadisattā methunakāti laddhavohārehi paṭisevitabbato methunāti saṅkhaṃ gatā asaddhammā. Gāmadhammāti gāmavāsīnaṃ dhammā.

Abrahmacariyanti aseṭṭhacariyaṃ (abrahmacariya means inferior conduct). Brahmaṃ seṭṭhaṃ ācāraṃ caratīti brahmacārī (one who practices the supreme conduct, the Brahma-conduct, is called a brahmacārī). Ārācārīti abrahmacariyato dūracārī (ārācārī means one who keeps far from non-celibacy). Methunāti rāgapariyuṭṭhānavasena sadisattā methunakāti laddhavohārehi paṭisevitabbato methunāti saṅkhaṃ gatā asaddhammā (methuna refers to unwholesome practices which, because they are practiced by those who have received the designation 'methunaka' due to being similar in nature and being overwhelmed by lust, have thus gained the designation 'methuna'). Gāmadhammāti gāmavāsīnaṃ dhammā (gāmadhammā means the practices of village dwellers).

Saccaṃ [P 0.0237] vadatīti saccavādī. Saccena saccaṃ sandahati ghaṭetīti saccasandho. Na antarantarā musā vadatīti attho. Yo hi puriso kadāci musā vadati, kadāci saccaṃ, tassa musāvādena antaritattā saccaṃ saccena na ghaṭīyati, tasmā na so saccasandho. Ayaṃ pana na tādiso. Jīvitahetupi musā avatvā saccena saccaṃ sandahatiyevāti saccasandho. Thetoti thiro, thirakathoti attho. Eko hi puggalo haliddirāgo viya, thusarāsimhi nikhātakhāṇuko viya, assapiṭṭhe ṭhapitakumbhaṇḍamiva ca, na thirakatho hoti. Eko pāsāṇalekhā viya, indakhīlo viya ca thirakatho hoti. Asinā sīse chindantepi dve kathā na katheti. Ayaṃ vuccati theto. Paccayikoti pattiyāyitabbako, saddhāyikoti attho. Ekacco hi puggalo na paccayiko hoti. ‘Idaṃ kena vuttaṃ? Asukenā’ti vutte ‘mā tassa vacanaṃ saddahathā’ti vattabbataṃ āpajjati. Eko paccayiko hoti. ‘Idaṃ kena vuttaṃ? Asukenā’ti vutte ‘yadi tena vuttaṃ, idameva pamāṇaṃ, idāni upaparikkhitabbaṃ natthi, evameva ida’nti vattabbataṃ āpajjati. Ayaṃ vuccati paccayiko. Avisaṃvādako lokassāti tāya saccavāditāya lokaṃ na visaṃvādetīti attho.

Saccaṃ vadatīti saccavādī (he speaks truth, thus he is a truth-speaker). Saccena saccaṃ sandahati ghaṭetīti saccasandho (he connects truth with truth, binds truth with truth, thus he is a truth-binder). The meaning is that he does not speak falsehood intermittently. Indeed, a person who sometimes speaks falsehood and sometimes truth, for him, truth is not bound with truth due to being interrupted by falsehood; therefore, he is not a truth-binder. But this one is not like that. Even for the sake of his life, he does not speak falsehood, but indeed binds truth with truth; thus he is a truth-binder. Thetoti thiro, thirakathoti attho (theto means firm, resolute in speech). Indeed, one person is like turmeric dye, like a post sunk in a heap of chaff, and like a gourd placed on a horse's back—he is not resolute in speech. Another is like an inscription on stone, and like an Inda pillar—he is resolute in speech. Even if his head is cut off with a sword, he does not speak two different things. Such a one is called theto. Paccayikoti pattiyāyitabbako, saddhāyikoti attho (paccayiko means one who is to be trusted, reliable). Indeed, some people are not trustworthy. When it is said, 'Who said this? So-and-so,' they become subject to the statement, 'Do not believe his words.' Another is trustworthy. When it is said, 'Who said this? So-and-so,' they become subject to the statement, 'If he said it, this is the proof; now there is no need for further investigation; it is indeed so.' Such a one is called paccayiko. Avisaṃvādako lokassāti tāya saccavāditāya lokaṃ na visaṃvādetīti attho (avisaṃvādako lokassa means that by his truthfulness, he does not deceive the world).

Imesaṃ [V 0.0084] bhedāyāti yesaṃ ito sutvāti vuttānaṃ santike sutaṃ, tesaṃ bhedāya. Bhinnānaṃ vā sandhātāti dvinnaṃ mittānaṃ vā samānupajjhāyakādīnaṃ vā kenacideva kāraṇena bhinnānaṃ ekamekaṃ upasaṅkamitvā – ‘tumhākaṃ īdise kule jātānaṃ, evaṃ bahussutānaṃ idaṃ na yutta’ntiādīni vatvā sandhānaṃ kattā. Anuppadātāti sandhānānuppadātā. Dve jane samagge disvā – ‘tumhākaṃ evarūpe kule jātānaṃ, evarūpehi guṇehi samannāgatānaṃ [M 0.0088] anucchavikameta’ntiādīni vatvā daḷhīkammaṃ kattāti attho. Samaggo ārāmo assāti samaggārāmo. Yattha samaggā natthi, tattha vasitumpi na icchatīti attho. Samaggarāmotipi pāḷi. Ayameva attho. Samaggaratoti samaggesu rato. Te pahāya aññatra gantumpi na icchatīti attho. Samagge disvāpi sutvāpi nandatīti samagganandī. Samaggakaraṇiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitāti yā vācā satte samaggeyeva karoti, taṃ sāmaggīguṇaparidīpakameva [P 0.0238] vācaṃ bhāsati, na itaranti.

Imesaṃ bhedāyāti yesaṃ ito sutvāti vuttānaṃ santike sutaṃ, tesaṃ bhedāya ('for the division of these' means for the division of those from whom he has heard, who are indicated by the phrase 'having heard from here'). Bhinnānaṃ vā sandhātāti dvinnaṃ mittānaṃ vā samānupajjhāyakādīnaṃ vā kenacideva kāraṇena bhinnānaṃ ekamekaṃ upasaṅkamitvā – ‘tumhākaṃ īdise kule jātānaṃ, evaṃ bahussutānaṃ idaṃ na yutta’ntiādīni vatvā sandhānaṃ kattā (or a reconciler of the divided means one who, when two friends or fellow disciples and so on are divided for some reason, approaches each individually and says, 'For you, born in such a family, so learned, this is not fitting,' and so brings about reconciliation). Anuppadātāti sandhānānuppadātā (anuppadātā means one who promotes reconciliation). Dve jane samagge disvā – ‘tumhākaṃ evarūpe kule jātānaṃ, evarūpehi guṇehi samannāgatānaṃ anucchavikameta’ntiādīni vatvā daḷhīkammaṃ kattāti attho (seeing two people in harmony, he strengthens their bond by saying, 'For you, born in such a family, endowed with such virtues, this is fitting,' and so on—this is the meaning). Samaggo ārāmo assāti samaggārāmo (samaggārāmo means one for whom harmony is his pleasure-garden). Yattha samaggā natthi, tattha vasitumpi na icchatīti attho (the meaning is that he does not even wish to live where there is no harmony). Samaggarāmotipi pāḷi. Ayameva attho (Samaggarāmo is also a reading. The meaning is the same). Samaggaratoti samaggesu rato (samaggarato means delighting in those who are harmonious). Te pahāya aññatra gantumpi na icchatīti attho (the meaning is that he does not even wish to leave them and go elsewhere). Samagge disvāpi sutvāpi nandatīti samagganandī (samagganandī means he rejoices upon seeing or hearing of harmony). Samaggakaraṇiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitāti yā vācā satte samaggeyeva karoti, taṃ sāmaggīguṇaparidīpakameva vācaṃ bhāsati, na itaranti (he speaks words that promote harmony means he speaks only words that illuminate the virtue of harmony, words that make beings harmonious, not otherwise).

Kālena vadatīti kālavādī. Vattabbayuttakālaṃ sallakkhetvā vadatīti attho. Bhūtaṃ tathaṃ tacchaṃ sabhāvameva vadatīti bhūtavādī. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikatthasannissitameva katvā vadatīti atthavādī. Navalokuttaradhammasannissitaṃ katvā vadatīti dhammavādī. Saṃvaravinayapahānavinayasannissitaṃ katvā vadatīti vinayavādī. Nidhānaṃ vuccati ṭhapanokāso. Nidhānamassa atthīti nidhānavatī. Hadaye nidhātabbayuttakaṃ vācaṃ bhāsitāti attho. Kālenāti evarūpiṃ bhāsamānopi ca “ahaṃ nidhānavatiṃ vācaṃ bhāsissāmī”ti na akālena bhāsati. Yuttakālaṃ pana sallakkhetvāva bhāsatīti attho. Sāpadesanti saupamaṃ, sakāraṇanti attho. Pariyantavatinti paricchedaṃ dassetvā. Yathāssā paricchedo paññāyati, evaṃ bhāsatīti attho. Atthasaṃhitanti anekehipi nayehi vibhajantena pariyādātuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya atthasampannaṃ bhāsati. Yaṃ vā so atthavādī atthaṃ vadati, tena atthena saṃhitattā atthasaṃhitaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati. Na aññaṃ nikkhipitvā aññaṃ bhāsatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

He speaks at the proper time, thus he is a speaker in season. The meaning is that he speaks after considering the appropriate time to speak. He speaks what is factual, true, and in accordance with reality, thus he is a speaker of fact. He speaks after basing his words on the benefit connected with this life and the next, thus he is a speaker of benefit. He speaks after basing his words on the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, thus he is a speaker of the Dhamma. He speaks after basing his words on the discipline of restraint and the discipline of abandonment, thus he is a speaker of the Discipline. A treasure is called a place for storing. It has a treasure, thus it is speech with a treasure. The meaning is that he speaks words that should be stored in the heart. 'At the proper time'—even while speaking such speech, he does not speak out of season, thinking, 'I will speak words worth storing.' Rather, he speaks only after considering the appropriate time. 'With an illustration' means with a simile, with a reason. 'With a limit' means showing a boundary. He speaks in such a way that its limit is discernible. 'Connected with the benefit'—he speaks what is endowed with benefit, because it is impossible for one analyzing it in many ways to exhaust it. Alternatively, since that speaker of benefit speaks the benefit, his speech is connected with that benefit. This means it is said that he does not set aside one thing and speak of another.

179. Bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhāti mūlabījaṃ, khandhabījaṃ, phaḷubījaṃ, aggabījaṃ bījabījanti pañcavidhassa bījagāmassa ceva yassa kassaci nīlatiṇarukkhādikassa bhūtagāmassa ca samārambhā. Chedanabhedanapacanādibhāvena vikopanā paṭiviratoti attho. Ekabhattikoti pātarāsabhattaṃ, sāyamāsabhattanti dve bhattāni. Tesu pātarāsabhattaṃ antomajjhanhikena paricchinnaṃ. Itaraṃ majjhanhikato uddhaṃ antoaruṇena. Tasmā antomajjhanhike [V 0.0085] dasakkhattuṃ [M 0.0089] bhuñjamānopi ekabhattikova hoti. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – ekabhattikoti. Rattiyā bhojanaṃ ratti, tato uparatoti rattūparato. Atikkante majjhanhike yāva sūriyasatthaṅgamanā bhojanaṃ vikālabhojanaṃ nāma, tato viratattā virato vikālabhojanā. Sāsanassa ananulomattā visūkaṃ paṭāṇībhūtaṃ dassananti visūkadassanaṃ. Attanā naccananaccāpanādivasena naccā ca gītā ca vāditā ca antamaso mayūranaccanāpanādivasenapi pavattānaṃ naccādīnaṃ visūkabhūtā dassanā cāti naccagītavāditavisūkadassanā. Naccādīni [P 0.0239] hi attanā payojetuṃ vā parehi payojāpetuṃ vā yuttāni passituṃ vā neva bhikkhūnaṃ na bhikkhunīnaṃ vaṭṭanti. Mālādīsu – mālāti yaṃkiñci pupphaṃ. Gandhanti yaṃkiñci gandhajātaṃ. Vilepananti chavirāgakaraṇaṃ. Tattha piḷandhanto dhāreti nāma. Ūnaṭṭhānaṃ pūrento maṇḍeti nāma. Gandhavasena chavirāgavasena ca sādiyanto vibhūseti nāma. Ṭhānaṃ vuccati kāraṇaṃ. Tasmā yāya dussīlyacetanāya tāni mālādhāraṇādīni mahājano karoti, tato paṭiviratoti attho. Uccāsayanaṃ vuccati pamāṇātikkantaṃ. Mahāsayanaṃ akappiyasanthataṃ, tato paṭiviratoti attho. Jātarūpanti suvaṇṇaṃ. Rajatanti kahāpaṇo, lohamāsako, jatumāsako, dārumāsakoti ye vohāraṃ gacchanti. Tassa ubhayassāpi paṭiggahaṇā paṭivirato, neva naṃ uggaṇhāti, na uggaṇhāpeti, na upanikkhittaṃ sādiyatīti attho.

179. Abstaining from the destruction of seed and plant life—this refers to the destruction of the five kinds of seeds: root seeds, stem seeds, joint seeds, bud seeds, and seed seeds; and any plant life such as green grass, trees, etc. The meaning is refraining from causing their destruction by cutting, breaking, cooking, and so forth. One who eats a single meal—there are two meals: the morning meal and the evening meal. Of these, the morning meal is defined as ending by midday. The other is from midday until dawn. Therefore, even if one eats ten times before midday, they are still considered to be one who eats a single meal. This is what is meant by 'one who eats a single meal.' Refraining from eating at night—eating at night is 'ratti'; one who has ceased from that is 'rattūparato'. Food eaten after midday until sunset is called untimely food; because one abstains from it, one is called 'one who abstains from untimely food.' Avoiding shows—this refers to seeing performances that are contrary to the teachings. Dancing, singing, and music—whether performed by oneself or arranged by others, even displays like peacock dances—are considered inappropriate spectacles. Indeed, it is not proper for monks or nuns to engage in, arrange, or watch such performances. Regarding garlands, perfumes, and cosmetics—'garland' refers to any kind of flower. 'Perfume' means any fragrant substance. 'Cosmetics' are substances that color the skin. In this context, wearing them is called 'adorning,' applying them to fill in deficiencies is called 'embellishing,' and enjoying them for their fragrance or skin-coloring properties is called 'decorating.' 'Occasion' means reason. Therefore, the meaning is to refrain from wearing garlands and so on, which ordinary people do with immoral volition. High and luxurious beds—this refers to beds that exceed the proper measure or are spread with unallowable coverings. The meaning is to refrain from such beds. Gold and silver—'gold' is suvaṇṇa. 'Silver' refers to kahāpaṇas, copper māsakas, lac māsakas, and wooden māsakas that are in circulation. The meaning is to refrain from accepting both—one neither takes them oneself, nor has others take them, nor consents to them being set aside for one’s use.

Āmakadhaññapaṭiggahaṇāti sālivīhiyavagodhumakaṅguvarakakudrūsakasaṅkhātassa sattavidhassāpi āmakadhaññassa paṭiggahaṇā. Na kevalañca etesaṃ paṭiggahaṇameva, āmasanampi bhikkhūnaṃ na vaṭṭatiyeva. Āmakamaṃsapaṭiggahaṇāti ettha aññatra odissa anuññātā āmakamacchamaṃsānaṃ paṭiggahaṇameva bhikkhūnaṃ na vaṭṭati, no āmasanaṃ. Itthikumārikapaṭiggahaṇāti ettha itthīti purisantaragatā. Itarā kumārikā nāma. Tāsaṃ paṭiggahaṇampi āmasanampi akappiyameva. Dāsidāsapaṭiggahaṇāti ettha dāsidāsavaseneva tesaṃ paṭiggahaṇaṃ na vaṭṭati. ‘Kappiyakārakaṃ dammi’, ‘ārāmikaṃ dammī’ti evaṃ vutte pana vaṭṭati. Ajeḷakādīsupi khettavatthupariyosānesu kappiyākappiyanayo vinayavasena upaparikkhitabbo. Tattha khettaṃ nāma yasmiṃ pubbaṇṇaṃ ruhati. Vatthu nāma yasmiṃ aparaṇṇaṃ ruhati. Yattha vā ubhayampi [M 0.0090] ruhati taṃ khettaṃ. Tadatthāya akatabhūmibhāgo vatthu. Khettavatthusīsena cettha vāpitaḷākādīnipi saṅgahitāneva.

Accepting raw grain—this refers to receiving any of the seven kinds of raw grain: rice, paddy, barley, wheat, millet, beans, and kodo millet. Not only is the acceptance of these prohibited for monks, but even touching them is not allowed. Accepting raw meat—here, except for what is specifically allowed, the acceptance of raw fish and meat is not permitted for monks, but touching them is not prohibited. Accepting women and girls—here, 'women' refers to those who have gone to another man. Others are called 'girls.' Both accepting them and touching them is improper. Accepting male and female slaves—here, the acceptance of them as male and female slaves is not allowed. However, if it is said, 'I give you an allowable attendant,' or 'I give you a monastery attendant,' then it is permissible. Regarding goats, sheep, etc., up to fields and properties—the permissibility or impermissibility should be examined according to the Vinaya rules. Here, a 'field' refers to land where early-season crops grow. 'Property' refers to land where late-season crops grow. Or, where both grow, that is a field. Land unprepared for that purpose is considered property. In this context, even things like sown fields and reservoirs are included under the terms 'field' and 'property.'

Dūteyyaṃ vuccati dūtakammaṃ. Gihīnaṃ pahitaṃ paṇṇaṃ vā sāsanaṃ vā gahetvā tattha tattha gamanaṃ[V 0.0086]. Pahīṇagamanaṃ vuccati paragharaṃ pesitassa khuddakagamanaṃ. Anuyogo nāma tadubhayakaraṇaṃ. Tasmā dūteyyapahīṇagamanānaṃ anugoti [P 0.0240] evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Kayavikkayāti kayā ca vikkayā ca. Tulākūṭādīsu – kūṭanti vañcanaṃ. Tattha tulākūṭaṃ nāma rūpakūṭaṃ, aṅgakūṭaṃ gahaṇakūṭaṃ, paṭicchannakūṭanti catubbidhaṃ hoti. Tattha rūpakūṭaṃ nāma dve tulā samarūpā katvā gaṇhanto mahatiyā gaṇhāti, dadanto khuddikāya deti. Aṅgakūṭaṃ nāma gaṇhanto pacchābhāge hatthena tulaṃ akkamati, dadanto pubbabhāge. Gahaṇakūṭaṃ nāma gaṇhanto mūle rajjuṃ gaṇhāti, dadanto agge. Paṭicchannakūṭaṃ nāma tulaṃ susiraṃ katvā anto ayacuṇṇaṃ pakkhipitvā gaṇhanto taṃ pacchābhāge karoti, dadanto aggabhāge.

Messenger duty is called the task of a messenger: taking a letter or message sent by householders and going here and there. Going after being sent is called the minor going of one dispatched to another's house. Practice means performing both of these tasks. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as the practice of messenger duty and going after being sent. Buying and selling—both buying and selling. In the case of false scales and such—'false' means deception. There, false scales are of four kinds: false in appearance, false in parts, false in handling, and false in concealment. False in appearance means making two scales look alike, then taking with the large one and giving with the small one. False in parts means when taking, pressing down on the scale with the hand at the back part, but when giving, doing so at the front part. False in handling means when taking, holding the rope at the base, but when giving, holding it at the tip. False in concealment means making the scale hollow, filling it inside with iron powder, and when taking, tilting it toward the back part, but when giving, tilting it toward the front part.

Kaṃso vuccati suvaṇṇapāti. Tāya vañcanaṃ kaṃsakūṭaṃ. Kathaṃ? Ekaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ katvā aññā dve tisso lohapātiyo suvaṇṇavaṇṇā karonti, tato janapadaṃ gantvā kiñcideva aḍḍhakulaṃ pavisitvā suvaṇṇabhājanāni kiṇathā’ti vatvā agghe pucchite samagghataraṃ dātukāmā honti. Tato tehi ‘kathaṃ imesaṃ suvaṇṇabhāvo jānitabbo’ti vutte ‘vīmaṃsitvā gaṇhathā’ti suvaṇṇapātiṃ pāsāṇe ghaṃsitvā sabbapātiyo datvā gacchanti.

A kaṃsa is called a golden bowl. Deception using it is called kaṃsakūṭa. How? They make one golden bowl and two or three iron bowls colored like gold. Then they go to a district, enter a somewhat wealthy household, and say, "Buy these golden vessels." When asked the price, they wish to give them for a higher price. Then, when asked, "How can we know these are truly golden?" they reply, "Test them and take them." They rub the golden bowl on a stone, give all the bowls, and leave.

Mānakūṭaṃ nāma hadayabhedasikhābhedarajjubhedavasena tividhaṃ hoti. Tattha hadayabhedo sappitelādiminanakāle labbhati. Tāni hi gaṇhanto heṭṭhā chiddena mānena ‘saṇikaṃ āsiñcā’ti vatvā antobhājane bahuṃ paggharāpetvā gaṇhāti. Dadanto chiddaṃ pidhāya sīghaṃ pūretvā deti. Sikhābhedo tilataṇḍulādiminanakāle labbhati. Tāni hi gaṇhanto saṇikaṃ sikhaṃ ussāpetvā gaṇhāti. Dadanto vegena pūretvā sikhaṃ chindanto deti. Rajjubhedo khettavatthuminanakāle labbhati. Lañjaṃ alabhantā hi khettaṃ amahantampi mahantaṃ katvā minanti.

Measuring fraud is of three kinds: by breaking the bottom, by breaking the heap, and by breaking the rope. Here, 'breaking the bottom' occurs when measuring ghee, oil, and the like. For when taking these, one uses a measure with a hole at the bottom, says, 'Pour slowly,' and causes much to flow into an inner vessel before taking it. When giving, however, one covers the hole, fills it quickly, and gives it. 'Breaking the heap' occurs when measuring sesame, rice, and the like. For when taking these, one slowly raises the heap and takes it. When giving, however, one fills it quickly, cutting off the heap, and gives it. 'Breaking the rope' occurs when measuring fields and plots of land. For, not receiving a bribe, they measure even a small field as if it were large.

Ukkoṭanādīsu [M 0.0091] – ukkoṭananti assāmike sāmike kātuṃ lañjaggahaṇaṃ. Vañcananti tehi tehi upāyehi paresaṃ vañcanaṃ. Tatridamekaṃ vatthu – eko kira luddako migañca migapotakañca gahetvā āgacchati. Tameko dhutto – “kiṃ bho migo agghati, kiṃ migapotako”ti āha. “Migo dve kahāpaṇe, migapotako eka”nti ca vutte kahāpaṇaṃ datvā migapotakaṃ gahetvā thokaṃ gantvā nivatto[P 0.0241], “na me bho migapotakena attho, migaṃ me dehī”ti āha. Tena hi “dve kahāpaṇe dehī”ti. So āha – “nanu te, bho, mayā paṭhamaṃ [V 0.0087] eko kahāpaṇo dinno”ti? “Āma dinno”ti. Idampi migapotakaṃ gaṇha, evaṃ so ca kahāpaṇo ayañca kahāpaṇagghaṇako migapotakoti dve kahāpaṇā bhavissantīti. So “kāraṇaṃ vadatī”ti sallakkhetvā migapotakaṃ gahetvā migaṃ adāsīti.

Regarding extortion and so forth: Extortion means taking a bribe to make what belongs to a non-owner belong to an owner. Deception means deceiving others by various means. Here is one case: Once, a certain hunter caught a deer and a fawn and was bringing them back. A certain rogue asked him, 'Sir, what is the deer worth, and what is the fawn?' When told, 'The deer is two kahāpaṇas, the fawn one,' he gave one kahāpaṇa, took the fawn, went a short distance, then turned back and said, 'Sir, I have no need for the fawn; give me the deer instead.' Then the hunter said, 'Then give me two kahāpaṇas.' He replied, 'Sir, did I not already give you one kahāpaṇa earlier?' 'Yes, you did,' the hunter said. He then said, 'Take this fawn as well; in this way, that kahāpaṇa and this fawn, which is worth a kahāpaṇa, will become two kahāpaṇas.' Realizing that he was making a valid point, the hunter took the fawn and gave him the deer.

Nikatīti yogavasena vā māyāvasena vā apāmaṅgaṃ pāmaṅganti, amaṇiṃ maṇīti, asuvaṇṇaṃ suvaṇṇanti katvā patirūpakena vañcanaṃ. Sāciyogoti kuṭilayogo. Etesaṃyeva ukkoṭanādīnametaṃ nāmaṃ. Tasmā ukkoṭanasāciyogo vañcanasāciyogo nikatisāciyogoti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Keci aññaṃ dassetvā aññassa parivattanaṃ ‘sāciyogo’ti vadanti. Taṃ pana vañcaneneva saṅgahitaṃ.

Nikatī (deceit) means deceiving by means of a counterfeit, making something inferior appear superior, a false gem a genuine one, or base metal gold, whether by artifice or by trickery. Sāciyoga (fraudulent practice) means crooked dealing. This is merely another name for these very practices of extortion and so forth. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as 'fraudulent practice of extortion,' 'fraudulent practice of deception,' and 'fraudulent practice of deceit.' Some, however, say that 'sāciyoga' is showing one thing and substituting another. But that is included within deception itself.

Chedanādīsu – chedananti hatthacchedanādi. Vadhoti māraṇaṃ. Bandhoti rajjubandhanādīhi bandhanaṃ. Viparāmosoti himaviparāmoso, gumbaviparāmosoti duvidho. Yañhi himapātasamaye himena paṭicchannā hutvā maggappaṭipannaṃ janaṃ musanti, ayaṃ himaviparāmoso. Yaṃ gumbādīhi paṭicchannā musanti, ayaṃ gumbaviparāmoso. Ālopo vuccati gāmanigamādīnaṃ vilopakaraṇaṃ. Sahasākāroti sāhasikakiriyā. Gehaṃ pavisitvā manussānaṃ ure satthaṃ ṭhapetvā icchitabhaṇḍaggahaṇaṃ. Evametasmā chedana…pe… sahasākārā paṭivirato hoti.

Regarding cutting off and so forth: 'Cutting off' means cutting off hands and so on. 'Killing' means murder. 'Binding' means binding with ropes and the like. Viparāmoso (robbery with violence) is of two kinds: snow robbery with violence and thicket robbery with violence. When, during snowfall, people concealed by snow rob those traveling on the road, this is snow robbery with violence. When people concealed in thickets and the like rob others, this is thicket robbery with violence. Ālopo (plundering) means the plundering of villages, towns, and so forth. Sahasākāro (violence) means a violent act. It is entering a house, placing a knife at people's chests, and seizing desired goods. Thus, one abstains from cutting off... up to... violence.

180. So santuṭṭho hotīti so catūsu paccayesu dvādasavidhena itarītarapaccayasantosena samannāgato hoti. Kāyaparihārikenāti kāyaṃ pariharaṇamattakena. Kucchiparihārikenāti kucchipariharaṇamattakena. Samādāyeva pakkamatīti aṭṭhavidhaṃ bhikkhu parikkhāramattakaṃ sabbaṃ gahetvāva kāyapaṭibaddhaṃ katvāva gacchati. “Mama [M 0.0092] vihāro pariveṇaṃ upaṭṭhāko”ti saṅgo vā baddho vā na hoti. So jiyā muttasaro viya yūthā pakkanto, mattahatthī viya icchiticchitaṃ senāsanaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ vanapatthaṃ pabbhāraṃ paribhuñjanto ekova tiṭṭhati, ekova nisīdati. Sabbiriyāpathesu ekova adutiyo.

180. 'He is content' means he is endowed with contentment regarding the four requisites in twelve ways, with contentment with whatever comes to hand. 'With only what is necessary to maintain the body' means with only so much as is needed to maintain the body. 'With only what is necessary to maintain the belly' means with only so much as is needed to maintain the belly. 'He departs, taking only what he has adopted' means the bhikkhu goes, taking all the eight kinds of requisites, having made them bound to his body. He has no attachment or bond, thinking, 'This is my dwelling, my enclosure, my attendant.' Like an arrow released from the bow, he departs from the herd; like a solitary elephant, he enjoys whatever dwelling place he wishes—a forest thicket, the foot of a tree, a forest wilderness, a mountain slope—he stands alone, he sits alone. In all his postures, he is alone, without a second.

“Cātuddiso [P 0.0242] appaṭigho ca hoti,

Santussamāno itarītarena;

Parissayānaṃ [V 0.0088] sahitā achambhī,

Eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti. (su. ni. 42);

He is friendly in all directions and unresisting, content with whatever comes to hand; enduring dangers, fearless, he wanders alone like a rhinoceros.

Evaṃ vaṇṇitaṃ khaggavisāṇakappataṃ āpajjati.

Thus he attains the state of one like a rhinoceros horn, as described.

Idāni tamatthaṃ upamāya sādhento, “seyyathāpī”tiādimāha. Tattha pakkhī sakuṇoti pakkhayutto sakuṇo. Ḍetīti uppatati. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – sakuṇo nāma “asukasmiṃ padese rukkho paripakkaphalo”ti ñatvā nānādisāhi āgantvā nakhapakkhatuṇḍādīhi tassa phalāni vijjhantā vidhunantā khādanti. “Idaṃ ajjatanāya, idaṃ svātanāya bhavissatī”ti tesaṃ na hoti. Phale pana khīṇe neva rukkhassa ārakkhaṃ ṭhapenti, na tattha pattaṃ vā nakhaṃ vā tuṇḍaṃ vā ṭhapenti. Atha kho tasmiṃ rukkhe anapekkho hutvā yo yaṃ disābhāgaṃ icchati, so tena sapattabhārova uppatitvā gacchati. Evameva ayaṃ bhikkhu nissaṅgo nirapekkhoyeva pakkamati, tena vuttaṃ samādāyeva pakkamatīti. Ariyenāti niddosena. Ajjhattanti sake attabhāve. Anavajjasukhanti niddosasukhaṃ.

Now, illustrating that meaning by means of a simile, he says, 'Just as,' and so forth. Here, 'pakkhī sakuṇo' means a winged bird. 'Ḍeti' means it flies up. The concise meaning here is this: A bird, knowing that 'in such-and-such a place there is a tree with ripe fruit,' comes from various directions and, with its claws, wings, beak, and so forth, pierces, shakes, and eats its fruits. They do not think, 'This is for today; this will be for tomorrow.' When the fruits are exhausted, they neither place a guard on the tree nor leave behind a leaf, claw, or beak there. Then, indifferent to that tree, each one flies away with its own wings to whatever direction it desires. In the same way, this bhikkhu departs unattached and indifferent. Therefore, it is said, 'He departs taking only his requisites.' 'By the noble one' means by the faultless one. 'Internally' means within one's own person. 'Blameless happiness' means happiness free from fault.

181. So cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvāti so iminā ariyena sīlakkhandhena samannāgato bhikkhu cakkhuviññāṇena rūpaṃ passitvāti attho. Sesapadesupi yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.
