Abyāsekasukhanti kilesehi anavasittasukhaṃ. Avikiṇṇasukhantipi vuttaṃ. Indriyasaṃvarasukhañhi diṭṭhādīsu diṭṭhamattādivasena pavattatāya avikiṇṇaṃ hoti.

181. 'Having seen a form with the eye' means this bhikkhu, endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, having seen a form with eye-consciousness. Whatever needs to be said regarding the remaining phrases has already been stated below. 'Abyāsekasukha' means happiness not saturated by defilements. It is also called 'avikiṇṇasukha' (unscattered happiness). For the happiness of sense restraint is unscattered because it proceeds in the case of sights and so on, merely with seeing, and so forth.

182. So [M 0.0093] abhikkante paṭikkanteti so manacchaṭṭhānaṃ indriyānaṃ saṃvarena samannāgato bhikkhu imesu abhikkantapaṭikkantādīsu sattasu ṭhānesu satisampajaññavasena sampajānakārī hoti. Tattha yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ jhānavibhaṅge vuttameva.

182. 'When going forward and backward' means this bhikkhu, endowed with sense-restraint over the six sense faculties, acts with full awareness in these seven instances beginning with going forward and backward, through mindfulness and full comprehension. Whatever needs to be said about this has already been said in the exposition of jhāna.

So iminā cātiādinā kiṃ dasseti? Araññavāsassa paccayasampattiṃ dasseti. Yassa hi ime cattāro paccayā natthi[P 0.0243], tassa araññavāso na ijjhati, tiracchānagatehi vā vanacarakehi vā saddhiṃ vattabbataṃ āpajjati. Araññe adhivatthā devatā “kiṃ evarūpassa pāpabhikkhuno araññavāsenā”ti bheravaṃ saddaṃ sāventi. Hatthehi sīsaṃ paharitvā palāyanākāraṃ karonti[V 0.0089]. “Asuko bhikkhu araññaṃ pavisitvā idañcidañca pāpakammaṃ akāsī”ti ayaso pattharati. Yassa panete cattāro paccayā atthi, tassa araññavāso ijjhati. So hi attano sīlaṃ paccavekkhanto kiñci kāḷakaṃ vā tilakaṃ vā apassanto pītiṃ uppādetvā taṃ khayato vayato sammasanto ariyabhūmiṃ okkamati. Araññe adhivatthā devatā attamanā vaṇṇaṃ bhāsanti. Itissa udake pakkhittatelabindu viya yaso vitthāriko hoti. Vivittantiādīni heṭṭhā vuttatthāneva. So evaṃ samāhite citte…pe… yathākammūpage satte pajānātīti ettake ṭhāne yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge vuttameva.

What does 'And with this...' and so forth indicate? It indicates the accomplishment of the conditions for forest dwelling. For one who lacks these four conditions, forest dwelling does not succeed; he is reduced to consorting with animals or forest dwellers. The deities dwelling in the forest utter terrifying sounds, saying, 'What use is forest dwelling for such a wicked bhikkhu?' They strike their heads with their hands and make gestures as if fleeing. The ill-fame spreads, 'That bhikkhu entered the forest and committed such and such evil deeds.' But for one who possesses these four conditions, forest dwelling succeeds. Reflecting on his own virtue and seeing no fault or blemish, he generates joy, and contemplating its decay and vanishing, he enters the noble ground. The deities dwelling in the forest, delighted, speak his praises. Thus his fame spreads widely like a drop of oil cast upon water. The terms beginning with 'vivitta' (secluded) have the meanings as stated earlier. Whatever should be said regarding the passage 'With his mind thus concentrated... he understands beings according to their deeds' is already stated in the Visuddhimagga.

185. Tatiyavijjāya so evaṃ samāhite citteti vipassanāpādakaṃ catutthajjhānacittaṃ veditabbaṃ. Āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāyāti arahattamaggañāṇatthāya. Arahattamaggo hi āsavānaṃ vināsanato āsavānaṃ khayoti vuccati. Tatra cetaṃ ñāṇaṃ tappariyāpannattāti. Cittaṃ abhininnāmetīti vipassanācittaṃ abhinīharati. So idaṃ dukkhanti evamādīsu – “ettakaṃ dukkhaṃ, na ito bhiyyo”ti sabbampi dukkhasaccaṃ sarasalakkhaṇappaṭivedhena yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, paṭivijjhati. Tassa ca dukkhassa nibbattikaṃ taṇhaṃ – ayaṃ dukkhasamudayoti; tadubhayampi yaṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā nirujjhati, taṃ tesaṃ appavattiṃ nibbānaṃ – ayaṃ dukkhanirodhoti; tassa ca sampāpakaṃ ariyamaggaṃ – ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti sarasalakkhaṇapaṭivedhena yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, paṭivijjhatīti – evamattho veditabbo.

185. Regarding the third knowledge, 'with his mind thus concentrated,' this should be understood as the fourth jhāna consciousness, which is the basis for insight. 'For the knowledge of the destruction of the taints' means for the purpose of the knowledge of the path of arahantship. The path of arahantship is called the destruction of the taints because it destroys them, and this knowledge is included within it. 'He directs his mind' means he brings forth the mind towards insight. Thus, regarding 'This is suffering,' etc., he understands and penetrates the entire truth of suffering as it really is, through penetration of its characteristic and function, thinking: 'This much is suffering, no more than this.' He understands and penetrates the craving that produces that suffering—'This is the origin of suffering'—as it really is, through penetration of its characteristic and function; and that state where both of these cease, their non-occurrence, Nibbāna—'This is the cessation of suffering'—as it really is, through penetration of its characteristic and function; and the noble path that leads to that—'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering'—as it really is, through penetration of its characteristic and function. This is how the meaning should be understood.

Evaṃ [M 0.0094] sarūpato saccāni dassetvā idāni kilesavasena pariyāyato dassento ime āsavātiādimāha. Tassa evaṃ jānato evaṃ [P 0.0244] passatoti tassa evaṃ jānantassa evaṃ passantassa saha vipassanāya koṭippattaṃ maggaṃ katheti. Kāmāsavāti kāmāsavato. Vimuccatīti iminā maggakkhaṇaṃ dasseti. Vimuttasminti iminā phalakkhaṇaṃ dasseti. Maggakkhaṇe hi cittaṃ vimuccati, phalakkhaṇe vimuttaṃ hoti. Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇanti iminā paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ dasseti. Khīṇā jātītiādīhi tassa bhūmiṃ. Tena hi ñāṇena so paccavekkhanto ‘khīṇā jātī’tiādīni pajānāti. Vusitanti vuṭṭhaṃ parivuṭṭhaṃ kataṃ caritaṃ niṭṭhitanti attho. Brahmacariyanti maggabrahmacariyaṃ. Puthujjanakalyāṇakena hi saddhiṃ satta sekkhā brahmacariyavāsaṃ vasanti nāma. Khīṇāsavo vuṭṭhavāso. Tasmā so attano brahmacariyavāsaṃ paccavekkhanto vusitaṃ brahmacariyanti pajānāti. Kataṃ karaṇīyanti catūsu saccesu catūhi maggehi [V 0.0090] pariññāpahānasacchikiriyābhāvanāvasena soḷasavidhampi kiccaṃ niṭṭhāpitanti attho. Puthujjanakalyāṇakādayo hi taṃ kiccaṃ karonti; khīṇāsavo katakaraṇīyo. Tasmā so attano karaṇīyaṃ paccavekkhanto. “Kataṃ karaṇīya”nti pajānāti. Nāparaṃ itthattāyāti “idāni puna etthabhāvāya evaṃ soḷasakiccabhāvāya kilesakkhayāya vā maggabhāvanākiccaṃ natthī”ti pajānāti.

Having thus shown the truths in their own nature, he now shows them in a different way by means of defilements, beginning with 'these taints.' 'For one who knows thus, who sees thus'—for one knowing and seeing thus, he speaks of the path that has reached its culmination together with insight. 'From the taint of sensual desire' means from the taint of sensual desire. 'He is liberated'—this indicates the moment of the path. 'In one who is liberated'—this indicates the moment of fruition. For at the moment of the path, the mind is being liberated; at the moment of fruition, it is liberated. 'In one who is liberated, the knowledge arises: "I am liberated"'—this indicates the reviewing knowledge. 'Destroyed is birth,' etc.—this indicates his stage. For with that knowledge, while reviewing, he understands: 'Destroyed is birth,' etc. 'The holy life has been lived'—means it has been dwelt, fully dwelt, done, practiced, and completed. 'The holy life'—refers to the holy life of the path. For together with the virtuous worldling, the seven trainees are said to live the holy life. The one whose taints are destroyed has completed the living. Therefore, reviewing his own living of the holy life, he understands: 'The holy life has been lived.' 'What was to be done has been done'—means the sixteenfold task has been completed by way of full understanding, abandoning, realization, and development with regard to the four truths by the four paths. The virtuous worldling and others perform that task; the one whose taints are destroyed has done what was to be done. Therefore, reviewing his own task, he understands: 'What was to be done has been done.' 'There is nothing further for this state'—he understands: 'Now there is no further task of developing the path for this state, that is, for the state of the sixteen tasks, or for the destruction of defilements.'

186. Sarāgādīsu – appahīnoti vikkhambhanappahānena vā tadaṅgappahānena vā samucchedappahānena vā appahīno.

186. Regarding 'with lust,' etc.—'not abandoned' means not abandoned by suppression, by substitution of opposites, or by eradication.

187. Lābhī hotītiādīsu – lābhīti lābhavā paṭilabhitvā ṭhito. Ajjhattaṃ cetosamathassāti niyakajjhattasaṅkhāte attano citte uppannassa cetosamathassa. Adhipaññādhammavipassanāyāti adhipaññāsaṅkhātāya khandhadhammesu aniccādivasena pavattāya vipassanāya. Rūpasahagatānanti rūpanimittārammaṇānaṃ rūpāvacarasamāpattīnaṃ. Arūpasahagatānanti na rūpanimittārammaṇānaṃ arūpasamāpattīnaṃ. Ettha ca paṭhamo aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī puthujjano. Dutiyo sukkhavipassakaariyasāvako. Tatiyo aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī [P 0.0245] ariyasāvako. Catuttho lokiyamahājano veditabbo.

187. In 'is an obtainer,' etc.—'an obtainer' means one who possesses, having obtained and being established. 'Of internal serenity of mind'—refers to the serenity of mind arisen in one's own mind, which is designated as internal. 'Of insight into phenomena as higher wisdom'—refers to the insight, designated as higher wisdom, which proceeds by way of impermanence, etc., with regard to the phenomena of the aggregates. 'Accompanied by form'—refers to the form-sphere attainments that have a form-sign as their object. 'Accompanied by the formless'—refers to the formless attainments that do not have a form-sign as their object. Here, the first is a worldling who is an obtainer of the eight attainments. The second is a noble disciple who is a dry-insight meditator. The third is a noble disciple who is an obtainer of the eight attainments. The fourth should be understood as the great mass of worldly people.

188. Anusotagāmīādīsu – anusotagāmīti vaṭṭasotaṃ anugato, vaṭṭasote nimuggo puthujjano veditabbo. Paṭisotagāmīti paṭisotagamano[M 0.0095]. Anusotaṃ agantvā paṭisotaṃ gacchantassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Pāpañca kammaṃ na karotīti paññattaṃ vītikkamanto na karoti. Sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassenāti kilesapariyuṭṭhāne sati uppannena dukkhadomanassena saddhimpi. Paripuṇṇanti tissannaṃ sikkhānaṃ ekāyapi anūnaṃ. Parisuddhanti nirupakkilesaṃ. Brahmacariyanti seṭṭhacariyaṃ. Iminā vārena sotāpannasakadāgāmino kathitā. Kiṃ pana te rudantā brahmacariyaṃ carantīti? Āma. Kilesarodanena rudantā caranti nāma. Sīlasampanno puthujjanabhikkhupi ettheva saṅgahito.

188. Regarding 'one who goes with the stream' and so on—'one who goes with the stream' means one who follows the stream of the round of rebirths; a worldling submerged in the stream of the round should be understood. 'One who goes against the stream' means one who goes against the stream. This is a designation for one who does not go with the stream but goes against the stream. 'He does not do evil deeds' means he does not transgress what has been laid down. 'Even with suffering, even with sorrow' means even with the suffering and sorrow that arise when defilements beset him. 'Perfect' means not deficient in even one of the three trainings. 'Pure' means without defilements. 'The holy life' means the excellent conduct. By this section, the stream-enterer and the once-returner are spoken of. 'But do they practice the holy life while weeping?' Yes, they are said to practice it while weeping with the weeping of defilements. Even a virtuous worldling monk is included here.

Ṭhitattoti ṭhitasabhāvo. Anāgāmīti kāmarāgabyāpādehi akampanīyacittatāya ca tamhā lokā anāvattidhammatāya ca ṭhitasabhāvo nāma. Tiṇṇoti taṇhāsotaṃ uttiṇṇo. Pāraṅgatoti nibbānapāraṃ [V 0.0091] gato. Thale tiṭṭhatīti arahattaphalasamāpattithale tiṭṭhati. Cetovimuttinti phalasamādhiṃ. Paññāvimuttinti phalañāṇaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ khīṇāsavo “tiṇṇo pāraṅgato thale tiṭṭhati brāhmaṇo”ti vuccati. Bāhitapāpatāya hi esa brāhmaṇo nāma.

'One of steadfast self' means one of steadfast nature. The non-returner is called one of steadfast nature because his mind is unshakeable by sensual desire and ill will, and because of his nature of not returning from that world. 'Crossed over' means he has crossed the stream of craving. 'Gone to the far shore' means he has gone to the far shore of Nibbāna. 'He stands on dry ground' means he stands on the dry ground of the fruition attainment of arahantship. 'Liberation of mind' refers to the fruition-concentration. 'Liberation by wisdom' refers to the fruition-knowledge. 'This one is called' means this one whose taints are destroyed is called 'one who has crossed over, gone to the far shore, stands on dry ground, a brahmin.' For he is indeed a brahmin by having banished evil.

189. Appassutādīsu – appakaṃ sutaṃ hotīti navaṅge satthusāsane kiñcideva thokaṃ sutaṃ hoti. Na atthamaññāya, na dhammamaññāya dhammānudhammapaṭipanno hotīti aṭṭhakathañca pāḷiñca jānitvā lokuttaradhammassa anurūpadhammaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno na hoti. Iminā nayena sabbattha attho veditabbo.

189. Regarding 'one of little learning' and so on—'he has little learning' means that in the ninefold teaching of the Teacher, he has heard only a little, just a trifle. 'Not having understood the meaning, not having understood the Dhamma, he is not one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma' means that, not knowing the commentary and the Pāli text, he has not entered upon the preliminary practice that is in conformity with the supramundane Dhamma. The meaning should be understood in this way in all cases.

190. Samaṇamacalādīsu – samaṇamacaloti samaṇaacalo, makāro padasandhikaro. Niccalasamaṇo, thirasamaṇoti attho[P 0.0246]. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ sotāpanno sāsane mūlajātāya saddhāya patiṭṭhitattā ‘samaṇamacalo’ti vuccati. Sakadāgāmī pana rajjanakilesassa atthitāya samaṇapadumoti vutto. Rattaṭṭho hi idha padumaṭṭho nāmāti vuttaṃ. Anāgāmī kāmarāgasaṅkhātassa rajjanakilesassa natthitāya samaṇapuṇḍarīkoti vutto. Paṇḍaraṭṭho hi idha puṇḍarīkaṭṭho nāmāti vuttaṃ[M 0.0096]. Khīṇāsavo ca thaddhabhāvakarānaṃ kilesānaṃ abhāvena samaṇesu samaṇasukhumālo nāmāti vutto. Appadukkhaṭṭhenapi cesa samaṇasukhumāloyevāti.

190. Regarding 'the steadfast ascetic' and so on—'the steadfast ascetic' means an unshaken ascetic, the letter 'm' being a euphonic link. The meaning is a steady ascetic, a firm ascetic. 'This is called' means this stream-enterer is called 'the steadfast ascetic' because he is established in faith that has taken root in the Dispensation. The once-returner, however, is called 'the ascetic lotus' because of the existence of the defilement of lust. For here the meaning of 'lotus' is said to be 'tinged with red.' The non-returner is called 'the ascetic white lotus' because there is no defilement of lust in the form of sensual desire. For here the meaning of 'white lotus' is said to be 'white.' And the one whose taints are destroyed is called 'the delicate ascetic among ascetics' because of the absence of defilements that cause rigidity. And also in the sense of having little suffering, he is indeed the delicate ascetic.

Catukkaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Fours.

5. Pañcakaniddesavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Exposition of the Fives.

191. Pañcake – tatrāti tesu “ārabhati ca vippaṭisārī ca hotī”tiādinā nayena heṭṭhā uddiṭṭhapuggalesu. Yvāyanti yo ayaṃ. Ārabhatīti ettha ārambhasaddo kammakiriyāhiṃsanavīriyavikopanāpattivītikkamesu vattati. Tathā hesa “yaṃkiñci dukkhaṃ sambhoti, sabbaṃ ārambhapaccayā”ti (su. ni. 748) kamme āgato. “Mahāyaññā mahārambhā, na te honti mahapphalā”ti (a. ni. 4.39) kiriyāyaṃ. “Samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ uddissa [V 0.0092] pāṇaṃ ārabhantī”ti (ma. ni. 2.51-52) hiṃsane. “Ārabhatha, nikkhamatha, yuñjatha buddhasāsane”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.185) vīriye. “Bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā paṭivirato hotī”ti (dī. ni. 1.10, 194; ma. ni. 1.293) vikopane. “Ārabhati ca vippaṭisārī ca hotī”ti (a. ni. 5.142) ayaṃ pana āpattivītikkame āgato. Tasmā āpattivītikkamavasena ārabhati ceva tappaccayā vippaṭisārī ca hotīti ayamettha attho.

191. In the Pentad – among them: Here, among those individuals previously mentioned in the passage 'he commits and feels remorse,' and so on. Yvāyanti: that is, 'whoever he is.' As for 'commits' (ārabhati): in this context, the word 'ārambha' applies to actions, deeds, harm, exertion, disruption, and transgression. Thus, it is said: 'Whatever suffering arises, all of it has committing as its cause' (Sutta Nipāta 748)—here it refers to action (kamma). 'Great sacrifices, great commitments, they do not bear great fruit' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.39)—here it refers to deeds (kiriya). 'They commit violence against living beings for the sake of the ascetic Gotama' (Majjhima Nikāya 2.51-52)—here it refers to harm (hiṃsana). 'Begin, strive, exert yourselves in the Buddha’s dispensation' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.185)—here it refers to exertion (vīriya). 'He abstains from damaging seed and plant life' (Dīgha Nikāya 1.10, 194; Majjhima Nikāya 1.293)—here it refers to disruption (vikopana). But in the phrase, 'He commits and feels remorse' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.142), this refers to transgression (āpattivītikkama). Therefore, the meaning here is: he commits by way of transgression, and because of that, he feels remorse.

Yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātīti anadhigatattā yathāsabhāvato na jānāti. Yatthassāti yasmiṃ assa, yaṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā etassa puggalassa uppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhantīti attho. Kiṃ pana patvā te nirujjhantīti? Arahattamaggaṃ. Phalappattassa pana niruddhā nāma honti. Evaṃ [P 0.0247] santepi idha maggakiccavasena phalameva vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Ārambhajāti āpattivītikkamasambhavā. Vippaṭisārajāti vippaṭisārato jātā. Pavaḍḍhantīti punappunaṃ uppajjanena vaḍḍhanti. Sādhūti āyācanasādhu. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yāva aparaddhañca vata āyasmatā, evaṃ santepi mayaṃ āyasmantaṃ yācāma – “desetabbayuttakassa desanāya, vuṭṭhātabbayuttakassa vuṭṭhānena, āvikātabbayuttakassa āvikiriyāya, ārambhaje āsave [M 0.0097] pahāya, suddhante ṭhitabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena vippaṭisāraje āsave paṭivinodetvā nīharitvā vipassanācittañceva vipassanāpaññañca bhāvetū”ti. Amunā pañcamena puggalenāti etena pañcamena khīṇāsavapuggalena. Samasamo bhavissatīti lokuttaraguṇehi samabhāveneva samo bhavissatīti evaṃ khīṇāsavena ovaditabboti attho.

He does not understand as it really is—because he has not comprehended it, he does not know according to its true nature. Where for him—in whatever place, having reached which, all the arisen unwholesome states of this person cease without remainder—this is the meaning. But having reached what do they cease? The path of arahantship. But for one who has attained the fruit, they are said to be ceased. Even so, here it should be understood that the fruit is spoken of in terms of the function of the path. Ārambhajā: born from the transgression of an offense. Vippaṭisārajā: born from remorse. They increase—they grow by arising again and again. 'Good'—this is an expression of request. This is what is meant: 'Even though the venerable one has indeed transgressed, still we entreat him: "Having abandoned the taints born of transgression by confessing what ought to be confessed, rising from what ought to be risen from, and disclosing what ought to be disclosed; and having dispelled and removed the taints born of remorse by reviewing his state of being established in purity, may he develop both the mind of insight and the wisdom of insight."' By this fifth person—that is, by this fifth person, the taint-destroyed one. He will become equal—he will become equal in supramundane qualities, thus he should be advised by a taint-destroyed one—this is the meaning.

Ārabhati na vippaṭisārī hotīti āpattiṃ āpajjati. Taṃ pana desetuṃ sabhāgapuggalaṃ pariyesati. Tasmā na vippaṭisārī hoti. Aṅguttaraṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “vuṭṭhitattā na vippaṭisārī hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Na ārabhati vippaṭisārī hotīti āpattiṃ nāpajjati, vinayapaññattiyaṃ pana akovidattā anāpattiyaṃ āpattisaññī hutvā vippaṭisārī hoti. Aṅguttaraṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “sakiṃ āpattiṃ āpajjitvā tato vuṭṭhāya pacchā kiñcāpi nāpajjati, vippaṭisāraṃ pana vinodetuṃ na sakkotī”ti vuttaṃ. Na ārabhati na vippaṭisārī hotīti neva āpattiṃ āpajjati, na vippaṭisārī hoti. Katamo panesa puggaloti? Ossaṭṭhavīriyapuggalo. So hi “kiṃ me imasmiṃ buddhakāle parinibbānena, anāgate metteyyasammāsambuddhakāle parinibbāyissāmī”ti [V 0.0093] visuddhasīlopi paṭipattiṃ na pūreti. Sopi “kimatthaṃ āyasmā pamatto viharati puthujjanassa nāma gati anibaddhā. Āyasmā hi metteyyasammāsambuddhassa sammukhabhāvaṃ labheyyapi na labheyyāpīti arahattatthāya vipassanaṃ bhāvehī”ti ovaditabbova. Sesaṃ sabbattha vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

He commits an offense and does not feel remorse—thus he incurs an offense. He seeks a suitable person to whom to declare it. Therefore, he does not feel remorse. In the Aṅguttara commentary, however, it is said, 'Because he has arisen from the offense, he does not feel remorse.' He does not commit an offense but feels remorse—thus he does not incur an offense. Yet, due to not being skilled in the Vinaya regulations, considering a non-offense as an offense, he feels remorse. In the Aṅguttara commentary, however, it is said, 'Having incurred an offense once and then arisen from it, even if he does not incur it again later, he is still unable to dispel his remorse.' He neither commits an offense nor feels remorse—thus he neither incurs an offense nor feels remorse. But who is this person? It is the person of slackened effort. For even though his virtue is pure, he does not fulfill the practice, thinking, 'What is the use of my attaining final Nibbāna in this Buddha-era? I will attain final Nibbāna in the future era of Metteyya, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.' He too should be advised: 'Why, venerable one, do you dwell heedlessly? The destiny of an ordinary person is unfixed. The venerable one might or might not obtain the presence of Metteyya, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One; therefore, you should develop insight for the sake of arahantship.' The rest should be understood in the same way as explained everywhere else.

192. Datvā [P 0.0248] avajānātītiādīsu – eko bhikkhu mahāpuñño catupaccayalābhī hoti. So cīvarādīni labhitvā aññaṃ appapuññaṃ āpucchati. Sopi tasmiṃ punappunaṃ āpucchantepi gaṇhātiyeva. Athassa itaro thokaṃ kupito hutvā maṅkubhāvaṃ uppādetukāmo vadati – “ayaṃ attano dhammatāya cīvarādīni na labhati, amhe nissāya labhatī”ti. Evaṃ puggalo datvā avajānāti nāma. Eko pana ekena saddhiṃ dve tīṇi vassāni vasanto pubbe taṃ puggalaṃ garuṃ katvā pacchā gacchante gacchante kāle cittīkāraṃ na karoti, āsanāpi na vuṭṭhāti, upaṭṭhānampi na gacchati. Evaṃ puggalo saṃvāsena avajānāti nāma.

192. In the cases of 'giving and then despising' and so on: One monk is of great merit and obtains the four requisites. Having obtained robes and other items, he offers them to another monk of little merit. And that monk, even when the other repeatedly offers, just accepts. Then, the first monk becomes slightly annoyed and, wishing to create discomfiture, says, 'This one does not obtain robes and other items through his own nature; he obtains them by relying on us.' Such a person is called one who gives and then despises. Another case: A monk who has lived together with another for two or three years, having previously respected that person, later, as time passes, no longer shows him respect, does not rise from his seat, and does not go to serve him. Such a person is called one who despises through association.

Ādheyyamukhoti [M 0.0098] ādito dheyyamukho. Paṭhamavacanasmiṃyeva ṭhapitamukhoti attho. Adhimuccitā hotīti saddhātā hoti. Tatrāyaṃ nayo – eko puggalo sāruppaṃyeva bhikkhuṃ ‘asāruppo eso’ti katheti, taṃ sutvā esa niṭṭhaṃ gacchati. Puna aññena sabhāgena bhikkhunā ‘sāruppo aya’nti vuttepi tassa vacanaṃ na gaṇhāti “asukena nāma ‘asāruppo aya’nti amhākaṃ kathita”nti purimabhikkhunova kathaṃ gaṇhāti. Aparopissa dussīlaṃ ‘sīlavā’ti katheti. Tassa vacanaṃ saddahitvā puna aññena “asāruppo esa bhikkhu, nāyaṃ tumhākaṃ santikaṃ upasaṅkamituṃ yutto”ti vuttopi tassa vacanaṃ aggahetvā purimasseva kathaṃ gaṇhāti. Aparo vaṇṇampi kathitaṃ gaṇhāti, avaṇṇampi kathitaṃ gaṇhātiyeva. Ayampi ādheyyamukhoyeva nāma. Ādhātabbamukho yaṃ yaṃ suṇāti, tattha tattha ṭhapitamukhoti attho.

He is called 'credulous' because he is receptive from the start. The meaning is that his attention is fixed on the very first statement. 'He becomes convinced' (adhimuccitā hoti) means he becomes one who believes. Here is the method: One person speaks about a suitable monk, saying, 'He is unsuitable.' Hearing this, the other becomes settled in that view. Then, when another monk of the same disposition says, 'This monk is suitable,' he does not accept his words, thinking, 'A certain monk has already told us that this monk is unsuitable,' and he accepts only the first monk’s statement. Another declares an immoral person to be virtuous. Trusting that statement, even when someone else later says, 'This monk is unsuitable; he is not fit to approach you,' he does not accept those words and accepts the earlier statement. Another accepts both praise that is spoken and blame that is spoken. He too is called 'credulous.' 'Having a receptive mouth' means that whatever he hears, his attention is fixed on that; this is the meaning.

Loloti saddhādīnaṃ ittarakālaṭṭhitikattā assaddhiyādīhi lulitabhāvena lolo. Ittarasaddhoti parittasaddho, aparipuṇṇasaddho. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Ettha pana punappunaṃ bhajanavasena saddhāva bhatti. Pemaṃ saddhāpemaṃ gehasitapemampi vaṭṭati. Pasādo saddhāpasādova. Evaṃ puggalo lolo hotīti evaṃ ittarasaddhāditāya puggalo lolo nāma hoti. Haliddirāgo viya[V 0.0094], thusarāsimhi koṭṭitakhāṇuko viya, assapiṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhapitakumbhaṇḍaṃ [P 0.0249] viya ca anibaddhaṭṭhāno muhuttena pasīdati, muhuttena kuppati.

One is called 'wavering' (lolo) because of the short duration of faith and other qualities, and because one is agitated by lack of faith and similar tendencies. 'Of little faith' (ittarasaddho) means one with limited faith, incomplete faith. The same principle applies to the rest. Here, however, devotion is faith in the sense of repeated engagement. Affection is faith-based affection; even household affection is applicable. Serene confidence is simply faith-based serene confidence. Thus, a person is called 'wavering' because of such limited faith and other qualities. Like the color of turmeric, like a stake pounded in a heap of chaff, and like a gourd placed on a donkey's back—such a person is unsteady, pleased in a moment, angered in a moment.

Mando momūhoti aññāṇabhāvena mando avisadatāya momūho. Mahāmūḷhoti attho.

'Dull and confused' (mando momūho): one is dull (mando) because of ignorance, and confused (momūho) because of a lack of clarity. The meaning is 'greatly deluded' (mahāmūḷho).

193. Yodhājīvūpamesu – yodhājīvāti yuddhūpajīvino. Rajagganti hatthiassādīnaṃ pādappahārabhinnāya bhūmiyā uggataṃ rajakkhandhaṃ. Na santhambhatīti santhambhitvā ṭhātuṃ na sakkoti. Sahati rajagganti rajakkhandhaṃ disvāpi adhivāseti. Dhajagganti hatthiassādipiṭṭhesu vā rathesu vā ussāpitānaṃ dhajānaṃ aggaṃ. Ussāraṇanti hatthiassarathādīnañceva balakāyassa ca uccāsaddamahāsaddaṃ. Sampahāreti samāgate appamattakepi pahāre. Haññatīti vihaññati, vighātaṃ āpajjati. Byāpajjatīti vipattiṃ āpajjati, pakatibhāvaṃ jahati. Sahati sampahāranti dve tayo pahāre patvāpi sahati, adhivāseti[M 0.0099]. Tameva saṅgāmasīsanti tameva jayakhandhāvāraṭṭhānaṃ. Ajjhāvasatīti sattāhamattaṃ abhibhavitvā āvasati. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Laddhappahārānaṃ pahārajagganatthañceva katakammānaṃ visesaṃ ñatvā ṭhānantaradānatthañca issariyasukhānubhavanatthañca.

193. In the similes of the warrior: 'warriors' (yodhājīvā) means those who live by warfare. 'The cloud of dust' (rajaggaṃ) means the mass of dust arisen from the ground broken by the trampling of elephants, horses, and so forth. 'He does not stand firm' (na santhambhati) means he is unable to stand firm. 'He endures the cloud of dust' (sahati rajaggaṃ) means he tolerates it, even upon seeing the mass of dust. 'The banner-tip' (dhajaggaṃ) means the top of the banners raised on the backs of elephants and horses, or on chariots. 'The battle-cry' (ussāraṇaṃ) means the loud clamor and great noise of the elephants, horses, chariots, and the army. 'Blows' (sampahāraṃ) means even a small number of blows encountered. 'He is struck' (haññati) means he is afflicted, he comes to distress. 'He perishes' (byāpajjati) means he comes to ruin, he abandons his natural state. 'He endures the blows' (sahati sampahāraṃ) means he endures, he tolerates, even after receiving two or three blows. 'That very head of the battle' (tameva saṅgāmasīsaṃ) means that very place of the victory camp. 'He dwells there' (ajjhāvasati) means he dwells there for about a week, having conquered. For what reason? For the purpose of tending to the wounds of those who have been struck, for granting a higher position after recognizing the distinction of their deeds, and for experiencing the pleasure of sovereignty.

194. Idāni yasmā satthu yodhājīvehi kiccaṃ natthi, imasmiṃ pana sāsane tathārūpe pañca puggale dassetuṃ idaṃ opammaṃ ābhataṃ, tasmā te puggale dassento evamevantiādimāha.

194. Now, since the Teacher has no need for warriors, but this simile has been brought forth in this Dispensation to demonstrate five such individuals, therefore, pointing out those individuals, he spoke beginning with 'Just so...'

Tattha saṃsīdatīti micchāvitakkasmiṃ visīdati, anupavisati. Na sakkoti brahmacariyaṃ sandhāretunti brahmacariyavāsaṃ anupacchijjamānaṃ gopetuṃ na sakkoti. Sikkhādubbalyaṃ āvikatvāti sikkhāya dubbalabhāvaṃ pakāsetvā. Kimassa rajaggasminti kiṃ tassa puggalassa rajaggaṃ nāmāti vadati. Abhirūpāti abhirūpavatī. Dassanīyāti dassanayoggā. Pāsādikāti dassaneneva cittappasādāvahā. Paramāyāti uttamāya. Vaṇṇapokkharatāyāti sarīravaṇṇena ceva aṅgasaṇṭhānena ca.

Herein, 'he sinks down' (saṃsīdati) means he sinks into wrong thoughts, he enters into them. 'He is unable to maintain the holy life' (na sakkoti brahmacariyaṃ sandhāretuṃ) means he is unable to protect the practice of the holy life without interruption. 'Having declared his weakness in the training' (sikkhādubbalyaṃ āvikatvā) means having revealed the weakness of his training. As to 'What is his cloud of dust?': this means one asks, 'What is this person's cloud of dust called?' 'Well-formed' (abhirūpā) means possessing a beautiful form. 'Lovely' (dassanīyā) means worthy of being seen. 'Inspiring' (pāsādikā) means bringing serenity of mind just by being seen. 'Supreme' (paramāya) means highest. 'Beauty of complexion' (vaṇṇapokkharatāya) means by the complexion of the body and the proportion of the limbs.

196. Ūhasatīti avahasati. Ullapatīti katheti. Ujjagghatīti pāṇiṃ paharitvā mahāhasitaṃ [P 0.0250] hasati. Uppaṇḍetīti uppaṇḍanakathaṃ katheti.

196. 'Ūhasati' means one scoffs. 'Ullapati' means one speaks. 'Ujjagghati' means one laughs a great laugh, striking the hands. 'Uppaṇḍeti' means one speaks jesting talk.

197. Abhinisīdatīti [V 0.0095] abhibhavitvā santike vā ekāsane vā nisīdati. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Ajjhottharatīti avattharati.

197. 'Abhinisīdati' means one sits down, having overcome, either close by or on the same seat. The same method applies to the second word. 'Ajjhottharati' means one covers over.

198. Viniveṭhetvā vinimocetvāti gahitaṭṭhānato tassa hatthaṃ viniveṭhetvā ceva, mocetvā ca. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

198. 'Viniveṭhetvā vinimocetvā' means having unwrapped and released his hand from the place where it was grasped. The rest here is of straightforward meaning.

199. Piṇḍapātikesu – mandattā momūhattāti neva samādānaṃ jānāti, na ānisaṃsaṃ; attano pana mandattā momūhattā aññāṇeneva piṇḍapātiko hoti. Pāpiccho icchāpakatoti piṇḍapātikassa me sato “ayaṃ piṇḍapātiko”ti catupaccayasakkāraṃ karissanti. Lajjī, appicchotiādīhi ca guṇehi sambhāvessantīti. Evaṃ pāpikāya icchāya ṭhatvā tāya pāpicchāya abhibhūto hutvā piṇḍapātiko hoti. Ummādavasena piṇḍāya caranto pana ummādā cittavikkhepā piṇḍapātiko [M 0.0100] nāma hoti. Vaṇṇitanti idaṃ piṇḍapātikaṅgaṃ nāma buddhehi ca buddhasāvakehi ca vaṇṇitaṃ pasatthanti piṇḍapātiko hoti. Appicchataṃyeva nissāyātiādīsu – “iti appiccho bhavissāmi, idaṃ me piṇḍapātikaṅgaṃ appicchatāya saṃvattissati; ‘iti santuṭṭho bhavissāmi idaṃ me piṇḍapātikaṅgaṃ santuṭṭhiyā saṃvattissati’; ‘iti kilese saṃlikhissāmi’, idaṃ me piṇḍapātikaṅgaṃ kilesasallekhanatthāya saṃvattissatī”ti piṇḍapātiko hoti. Idamatthitanti imāya kalyāṇāya paṭipattiyā atthikabhāvaṃ, iminā vā piṇḍapātamattena atthikabhāvaṃ. Yaṃ yaṃ laddhaṃ tena teneva yāpanabhāvaṃ nissāyāti attho. Aggoti jeṭṭhako. Sesāni tasseva vevacanāni.

199. Among alms-gatherers: 'due to dullness and delusion' means one neither understands the undertaking nor its benefits; but due to one's own dullness and delusion, one becomes an alms-gatherer simply out of ignorance. 'One with evil desires, hoping for gain' means thinking, 'When I am an alms-gatherer, people will offer me honor with the four requisites, and they will esteem me for qualities such as modesty and fewness of wishes.' Thus, abiding in such evil desire, and being overcome by that evil desire, one becomes an alms-gatherer. However, one who wanders for alms due to madness, due to mental derangement, is called an alms-gatherer. 'Praised' means this practice of gathering alms-food is praised and commended by the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha, so one becomes an alms-gatherer. In phrases such as 'relying on fewness of wishes': one becomes an alms-gatherer thinking, 'Thus I will be one of few wishes; this practice of gathering alms-food will lead me to fewness of wishes'; 'Thus I will be content; this practice of gathering alms-food will lead me to contentment'; 'Thus I will scour away the defilements; this practice of gathering alms-food will serve to scour away the defilements.' 'Having an interest in this' means having an interest in this wholesome practice, or having an interest merely in this alms-food. The meaning is: relying on whatever is obtained, one maintains oneself. 'Foremost' means chief. The rest are synonyms for that.

Gavā khīranti gāvito khīraṃ nāma hoti, na vinā gāviyā. Khīramhā dadhītiādīsupi eseva nayo. Evamevanti yathā etesu pañcasu gorasesu sappimaṇḍo aggo; evamevaṃ imesu pañcasu piṇḍapātikesu yvāyaṃ appicchatādīni nissāya piṇḍapātiko hoti. Ayaṃ aggo ca seṭṭho ca pāmokkho ca uttamo ca pavaro ca. Imesu pana pañcasu piṇḍapātikesu dveva janā piṇḍapātikā[P 0.0251], tayo na piṇḍapātikā. Nāmamattena pana piṇḍapātikāti veditabbā. Khalupacchābhattikādīsupi eseva nayoti.

'Milk from a cow' means milk comes from a cow, not without a cow. The same method applies to 'curd from milk' and so forth. 'Just so' means just as among these five products of a cow, cream is the foremost; so too among these five alms-gatherers, the one who becomes an alms-gatherer relying on fewness of wishes and so forth, he is the foremost, the best, the chief, the highest, and the most excellent. However, among these five alms-gatherers, only two types of people are truly alms-gatherers, while three are not. Yet, they should be known as alms-gatherers in name only. The same method applies to those who refuse food offered subsequently, and so forth.

Pañcakaniddesavaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Exposition of the Fives.

6. Chakkaniddesavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Exposition of the Six.

202. Chakke [V 0.0096] – tatrāti tesu chasu puggalesu. Sammāsambuddho tena daṭṭhabboti so puggalo tena anācariyakena attanā uppāditena sabbaññutaññāṇena sabbaññubuddho daṭṭhabbo.

202. In the group of six: 'therein' means among those six persons. 'The Perfectly Self-Enlightened One should be understood by that' means that person should be understood as the All-Knowing Buddha by means of the omniscience knowledge generated by himself, without a teacher.

Paccekasambuddho tenātiādīsupi tena paccekasambodhiñāṇena so puggalo paccekasambuddho. Tena sāvakapāramīñāṇena te puggalā sāriputtamoggallānā. Tena dukkhassa antakaraṇena te puggalā avasesā arahanto. Tena itthattaṃ anāgamanena so puggalo anāgāmī. Tena itthattaṃ āgamanena te puggalā sotāpannasakadāgāmino daṭṭhabbāti.

In 'the Solitary Buddha by that,' and so forth: that person is a Solitary Buddha by means of that knowledge of solitary enlightenment. By means of that knowledge of the perfection of disciples, those persons are Sāriputta and Moggallāna. By means of making an end to suffering, those persons are the remaining arahants. By means of not returning to this state of existence, that person is a non-returner. By means of returning to this state of existence, those persons should be understood as stream-enterers and once-returners.

Chakkaniddesavaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Exposition of the Six.

7. Sattakaniddesavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Exposition of the Sevens.

203. Sattake [M 0.0101] – sakiṃ nimuggoti ekavāraṃ nimuggo. Ekantakāḷakehīti ekanteneva kāḷakehi natthikavādaahetukavādaakiriyavādasaṅkhātehi niyatamicchādiṭṭhidhammehi. Evaṃ puggaloti iminā kāraṇena puggalo ekavāraṃ nimuggo tathā nimuggova hoti. Etassa hi puna bhavato vuṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthīti vadanti. Makkhaligosālādayo viya heṭṭhā narakaggīnaṃyeva āhāro hoti.

203. In the group of seven: 'sinks once' means he sinks one time. 'By what is entirely dark' means entirely by the dark doctrines—namely the nihilistic doctrine, the causeless doctrine, and the inaction doctrine—which are reckoned as fixed wrong views. 'Thus, the person' means that for this reason, the person sinks once and remains so sunk. For him, they say, there is no rising up again from existence. Like Makkhali Gosāla and others, he becomes fuel only for the fires of hell below.

Sāhu saddhā kusalesu dhammesūti kusaladhammesu saddhā nāma sādhuladdhikāti ummujjati. So tāvatakeneva kusalena ummujjati nāma. Sādhu hirītiādīsupi eseva nayo. Hāyatiyevāti caṅkavāre āsittaudakaṃ viya ekantena parihāyateva. Evaṃ puggaloti evaṃ sāhu saddhāti. Imesaṃ saddhādīnaṃ vasena ekavāraṃ ummujjitvā tesaṃ parihāniyā puna nimujjatiyeva, devadattādayo viya. Devadatto hi aṭṭha samāpattiyo, pañca ca abhiññāyo nibbattetvāpi puna buddhānaṃ paṭikaṇṭakatāya tehi guṇehi parihīno ruhiruppādakammaṃ [P 0.0252] saṅghabhedakammañca [V 0.0097] katvā kāyassa bhedā dutiyacittavārena niraye nibbatti. Kokāliko dve aggasāvake upavaditvā padumaniraye nibbatto.

'Excellent is faith in wholesome qualities' means that because faith in wholesome qualities is well-acquired, one emerges. By just that much which is wholesome, one is said to emerge. The same principle applies to 'excellent is moral shame,' and so on. 'It inevitably declines': just as water sprinkled on a walking path inevitably disappears entirely. 'Thus the person' means that in this way, having emerged once through these qualities like faith, one inevitably sinks again due to their decline, like Devadatta and others. For Devadatta, though he had produced the eight attainments and the five higher knowledges, later lost those qualities due to being an adversary to the Buddhas. He committed the deeds of causing the Buddha's blood to flow and causing schism in the Sangha, and upon the breakup of his body, he was reborn in hell at the second moment of consciousness. Kokālika, having slandered the two foremost disciples, was reborn in the Paduma hell.

Neva hāyati no vaḍḍhatīti appahonakakālepi na hāyati, pahonakakālepi na vaḍḍhati. Ubhayampi panetaṃ agārikenapi anagārikenapi dīpetabbaṃ. Ekacco hi agāriko appahonakakāle pakkhikabhattaṃ vā salākabhattaṃ vā vassāvāsikaṃ vā upanibandhāpeti. So pacchā pahonakakālepi pakkhikabhattādimattameva pavatteti. Anagārikopi ādimhi appahonakakāle uddesaṃ vā dhutaṅgaṃ vā gaṇhāti, medhābalavīriyasampattiyā pahonakakālepi tato uttariṃ na karoti. Evaṃ puggaloti evaṃ imāya saddhādīnaṃ ṭhitiyā puggalo ummujjitvā ṭhito nāma hoti.

'It neither declines nor does it increase' means it does not decline even in a time of scarcity, nor does it increase in a time of abundance. This should be illustrated with reference to both a householder and a monastic. A certain householder, in a time of scarcity, arranges for fortnightly meals, ticket meals, or rains-residence requisites. Later, even in a time of abundance, he continues only with the fortnightly meals and the like. A monastic, too, initially in a time of scarcity, undertakes recitation or an ascetic practice. But even when endowed with an abundance of wisdom, strength, and energy, he does not go beyond that. 'Thus the person' means that in this way, by the stability of faith and other such qualities, the person is said to have emerged and stands firm.

Ummujjitvā vipassati viloketīti sotāpanno puggalo uṭṭhahitvā gamanamaggaṃ gantabbaṃ disaṃ vā āloketi nāma.

'Having emerged, he sees clearly, he looks around' means the stream-enterer, having risen, is said to look toward the path to be traveled or the direction to be gone.

Ummujjitvā [M 0.0102] pataratīti sakadāgāmipuggalo kilesatanutāya uṭṭhahitvā gantabbadisābhimukho patarati nāma.

'Having emerged, he crosses over' means the once-returner, due to the attenuation of defilements, having risen, is said to cross over facing the direction to be gone.

Patigādhappatto hotīti anāgāmipuggalo uṭṭhāya viloketvā pataritvā gantvā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne patiṭṭhāpatto nāma hoti, tiṭṭhati, na punāgacchati.

'He has reached a firm footing' means the non-returner, having risen up, looked around, crossed over, and gone, is said to have attained a firm footing in one place; he stands there and does not come back again.

Tiṇṇo pāraṅgato thale tiṭṭhatīti sabbakilesoghaṃ taritvā paratīraṃ gantvā nibbānathale ṭhito nāma hoti. Ime pana satta puggalā udakopamena dīpitā.

‘Having crossed over, gone to the far shore, standing on dry land’ means that having crossed the flood of all defilements and gone to the far shore, one is said to stand on the ground of Nibbāna. Now, these seven individuals are illustrated by the simile of water.

Satta kira jaṅghavāṇijā addhānamaggapaṭipannā antarāmagge ekaṃ puṇṇanadiṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Tesu paṭhamaṃ otiṇṇo udakabhīruko puriso otiṇṇaṭṭhāneyeva nimujjitvā puna uṭṭhātuṃ nāsakkhi, antoyeva macchakacchapabhakkho jāto. Dutiyo otiṇṇaṭṭhāne nimujjitvā sakiṃ uṭṭhahitvā puna nimuggo uṭṭhātuṃ nāsakkhi, antoyeva macchakacchapabhakkho jāto. Tatiyo nimujjitvā uṭṭhahi. So majjhe nadiyā ṭhatvā neva orato āgantuṃ, na parato gantuṃ asakkhi[V 0.0098]. Catuttho uṭṭhāya ṭhito uttaraṇatitthaṃ olokesi. Pañcamo otaraṇatitthaṃ oloketvā patari. Chaṭṭho taritvā pārimatīraṃ gantvā kaṭippamāṇe udake ṭhito. Sattamo pārimatīraṃ gantvā gandhacuṇṇādīhi nhātvā varavatthāni [P 0.0253] nivāsetvā surabhivilepanaṃ vilimpitvā nīluppalādīni piḷandhitvā nānālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito mahānagaraṃ pavisitvā pāsādavaramāruyha uttamabhojanaṃ bhuñji.

Seven merchants traveling on foot, it is said, were journeying along a road when they came upon a full river along the way. Among them, the first man, being afraid of water, sank at the very place he entered and could not rise again—he was devoured by fish and turtles right there in the water. The second man sank at the place he entered, rose once, but then sank again and could not rise—he too was devoured by fish and turtles right there in the water. The third man sank and rose up, but he stood in the middle of the river, unable to return to this shore or to go to the far shore. The fourth man rose up and stood, looking for a ford to cross. The fifth man, having seen the ford, swam across. The sixth man, having crossed, reached the far shore and stood in water up to his waist. The seventh man, having reached the far shore, bathed with fragrant powders, dressed in fine garments, anointed himself with fragrant unguents, adorned himself with blue lotuses and other ornaments, entered the great city, ascended a splendid palace, and enjoyed an excellent meal.

Tattha satta jaṅghavāṇijā viya ime satta puggalā. Nadī viya vaṭṭaṃ. Paṭhamassa udakabhīrukassa purisassa otiṇṇaṭṭhāneyeva nimujjanaṃ viya micchādiṭṭhikassa vaṭṭe nimujjanaṃ. Ummujjitvā nimuggapuriso viya saddhādīnaṃ uppattimattakena ummujjitvā tesaṃ parihāniyā nimuggapuggalo. Majjhe nadiyā ṭhito viya saddhādīnaṃ ṭhitiyā ṭhitapuggalo. Uttaraṇatitthaṃ olokento viya gantabbamaggaṃ gantabbadisaṃ vā olokento sotāpanno. Pataritapuriso viya kilesatanutāya pataranto sakadāgāmī. Taritvā kaṭimatte udake ṭhitapuriso viya anāvattitadhammatāya ṭhito anāgāmī. Nhatvā pārimatīraṃ [M 0.0103] uttaritvā thale ṭhitapuriso viya cattāro oghe atikkamitvā nibbānathale ṭhito khīṇāsavabrāhmaṇo. Thale ṭhitapurisassa nagaraṃ pavisitvā pāsādavaraṃ āruyha uttamabhojanabhuñjanaṃ viya khīṇāsavassa nibbānārammaṇaṃ phalasamāpattiṃ appetvā vītināmanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ubhatobhāgavimuttādayo heṭṭhā pakāsitāyevāti.

Here, these seven individuals are like the seven merchants traveling on foot. The round of existence is like the river. The sinking of the first man, who is afraid of water, at the very place he entered is like the sinking of one with wrong view into the round of existence. The man who surfaces and then sinks again is like the person who surfaces by the mere arising of faith and so on, and then sinks due to their decline. The man standing in the middle of the river is like the person who is established due to the stability of faith and so on. The one looking for a ford to cross is like the stream-enterer looking for the path to be traversed or the direction to be taken. The man who swims across is like the once-returner, swimming across due to the attenuation of defilements. The one who crosses and stands in water up to his waist is like the non-returner, established due to his nature of not returning. The man who bathes, crosses to the far shore, and stands on dry land is like the taint-destroyed brahmin, the arahant, who has crossed the four floods and stands on the ground of Nibbāna. The man standing on dry land entering the city, ascending an excellent palace, and enjoying the finest food should be understood to be like the taint-destroyed one spending his time having entered into the attainment of fruition with Nibbāna as its object. The doubly liberated and others have indeed been explained previously.

Sattakaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Sevens.

207. Aṭṭhakanavakaniddesāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

207. The expositions of the Eights and Nines should also be understood in the very same way as explained previously.

10. Dasakaniddesavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Exposition of the Tens

209. Dasakaniddese – idhāti kāmāvacarabhūmiyaṃ. Kāmāvacarabhūmiyañhi sattakkhattuparamādīnaṃ kāmāvacarabhūmiyaññeva niṭṭhā hoti. Kāmāvacarattabhāveneva arahattappatti ca anupādisesanibbānappatti ca hotīti attho.

209. In the Exposition of the Tens—‘here’ (idha) means in the sense-sphere realm. For those who are seven-times-at-most and so forth, their culmination occurs only in the sense-sphere realm. The attainment of arahantship and the attainment of Nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna) occurs precisely through the state of existence in the sense-sphere—this is the meaning.

Idha [V 0.0099] vihāyāti idha kāmāvacare attabhāve vihāya suddhāvāsattabhāve ṭhitānaṃ niṭṭhā hotīti attho. Antarāparinibbāyiādayo hi idha anāgāmiphalaṃ patvā ito cutā suddhāvāsesu uppajjitvā tena attabhāvena arahattañceva anupādisesanibbānadhātuñca [P 0.0254] pāpuṇanti. Tena vuttaṃ – “imesaṃ pañcannaṃ idha vihāya niṭṭhā”ti.

‘Having abandoned [existence] here’ (idha vihāya) means that for those established in the Pure Abodes, their culmination occurs after abandoning the sense-sphere existence here. For the one who attains parinibbāna in the interim and the others, having attained the fruit of non-returning here, and passing away from here, they are reborn in the Pure Abodes, and by that existence they attain arahantship and the Nibbāna-element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). Therefore it was said: ‘For these five, culmination occurs after abandoning [existence] here.’

Dasakaniddesavaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Tens.

Nigamanakathā

Conclusion

Ettāvatā ca –

And thus far—

Yaṃ ve puggalapaññattiṃ, loke appaṭipuggalo;

Nātisaṅkhepato satthā, desesi tidasālaye.

The Teacher, without equal in the world, taught the Designation of Persons in the abode of the Thirty-three, not too concisely.

Tassā aṭṭhakathañceva, dīpabhāsāya saṅkhataṃ;

Āgamaṭṭhakathāyo ca, ogāhetvā asesato.

Its commentary, compiled in the language of the island, and having thoroughly immersed myself in all the traditional commentaries,

Suvibhatto [M 0.0104] asaṃkiṇṇo, yo yo attho yahiṃ yahiṃ;

Tato tato taṃ gahetvā, pahāya ativitthāraṃ.

Well-divided and unmixed, whatever meaning is found wherever, taking that from each place, having abandoned excessive elaboration.

Visuddhimagge yaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ anādāya saṅkhatā;

Nātisaṅkhepavitthāra-nayenaṭṭhakathā ayaṃ.

This commentary has been composed without drawing upon what was stated in the Visuddhimagga, following a method that is neither too concise nor too expanded.

Taṃ etaṃ sattamattehi, bhāṇavārehi tantiyā;

Ciraṭṭhitatthaṃ dhammassa, saṅkharontena yaṃ mayā.

This very commentary, which was compiled by me in the text by means of merely seven recitation sections, for the long endurance of the Dhamma.

Sampattaṃ kusalaṃ tena, saddhammaṃ sukhumaṃ sivaṃ;

Olokentu visuddhena, pāṇayo dhammacakkhunāti.

By the merit thus attained, may all beings behold, with the purified eye of Dhamma, the subtle, auspicious True Dhamma.

Puggalapaññatti-aṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Designation of Persons is concluded.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Abhidhammapiṭake

In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka

Kathāvatthu-aṭṭhakathā

The Commentary on the Kathāvatthu

Nisinno [P 0.0001][M 0.0105][V 0.0100] devalokasmiṃ, devasaṅghapurakkhato;

Sadevakassa lokassa, satthā appaṭipuggalo.

Seated in the world of the devas, honored by the assembly of devas, the Teacher, an unequalled person in the world with its devas.

Sabbapaññattikusalo, paññattiparidīpanaṃ;

Vatvā puggalapaññattiṃ, loke uttamapuggalo.

The supreme person in the world, skilled in all designations, the illuminator of designations, having taught the Puggalapaññatti,

Yaṃ puggalakathādīnaṃ, kathānaṃ vatthubhāvato;

Kathāvatthuppakaraṇaṃ, saṅkhepena adesayī.

He briefly taught the treatise called the Kathāvatthu, because it is the basis of discussions such as the discussion of individuals.

Mātikāṭhapaneneva[V 0.0101], ṭhapitassa surālaye;

Tassa moggaliputtena, vibhattassa mahītale.

Of that which was established in the abode of the devas by the mere laying down of the matrix, and which was analyzed by Moggalliputta on the great earth.

Idāni yasmā sampatto, atthasaṃvaṇṇanākkamo;

Tasmā naṃ vaṇṇayissāmi, taṃ suṇātha samāhitāti.

Now, because the turn for the exposition of the meaning has arrived, therefore I will explain it; listen to it attentively.

Nidānakathā

The Introductory Account

Yamakapāṭihīrāvasānasmiñhi bhagavā tidasapure pāricchattakamūle paṇḍukambalasilāyaṃ vassaṃ upagantvā mātaraṃ kāyasakkhiṃ katvā devaparisāya abhidhammakathaṃ kathento dhammasaṅgaṇīvibhaṅgadhātukathāpuggalapaññattippakaraṇāni desayitvā kathāvatthudesanāya vāre sampatte “anāgate mama sāvako mahāpañño moggaliputtatissatthero nāma uppannaṃ sāsanamalaṃ sodhetvā tatiyasaṅgītiṃ karonto bhikkhusaṅghassa majjhe nisinno sakavāde pañca suttasatāni paravāde pañcāti suttasahassaṃ [P 0.0002] samodhānetvā imaṃ pakaraṇaṃ bhājessatī”ti tassokāsaṃ karonto yā cesā puggalavāde tāva catūsu pañhesu dvinnaṃ pañcakānaṃ vasena aṭṭhamukhā vādayutti, taṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbakathāmaggesu asampuṇṇabhāṇavāramattāya tantiyā mātikaṃ ṭhapesi. Athāvasesaṃ [M 0.0106] abhidhammakathaṃ vitthāranayeneva kathetvā vutthavasso suvaṇṇarajatasopānamajjhe maṇimayena sopānena devalokato saṅkassanagare oruyha sattahitaṃ sampādento yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyi.

At the conclusion of the Twin Miracle, the Blessed One, having entered the rains retreat at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, seated on the Paṇḍukambala stone, and making his mother a bodily witness, taught the Abhidhamma discourse to the assembly of devas. He expounded the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, and Puggalapaññatti treatises. When it was time for the teaching of the Kathāvatthu, he foresaw: "In the future, my disciple named the Elder Moggalliputtatissa, a man of great wisdom, will arise, cleanse the impurities of the Dispensation, and convene the Third Council. Seated amidst the community of monks, he will combine a thousand discourses—five hundred from his own school and five hundred from others—and will analyze this treatise." Making an opportunity for him, he first laid down the matrix in the text for all the paths of discussion, only to the extent of an incomplete recitation section, beginning with that argumentative method which has eight openings by way of four questions and two pentads in the discussion of individuals. Then, having taught the remaining Abhidhamma discourse in detail, he emerged from the rains retreat. Descending from the world of devas to the city of Saṅkassa by a jeweled staircase between staircases of gold and silver, accomplishing the welfare of beings, he remained for the rest of his lifespan and then passed into final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without residue.

Athassa mahākassapappamukho vasīgaṇo ajātasatturājānaṃ sahāyaṃ gahetvā dhammavinayasarīraṃ saṅgahaṃ āropesi. Tato vassasatassa accayena vajjiputtakā bhikkhū dasa vatthūni dīpayiṃsu. Tāni sutvā kākaṇḍakassa brāhmaṇassa putto yasatthero susunāgaputtaṃ kālāsokaṃ nāma rājānaṃ sahāyaṃ gahetvā dvādasannaṃ bhikkhusatasahassānaṃ antare sattatherasatāni uccinitvā tāni dasavatthūni madditvā dhammavinayasarīraṃ saṅgahaṃ āropesi.

Thereafter, the company of masters headed by Mahākassapa, with King Ajātasattu as their supporter, brought the body of the Dhamma and Vinaya into a compilation. After the lapse of a hundred years, the Vajjiputtaka monks proclaimed ten points. Hearing this, the Elder Yasa, son of the brahmin Kākaṇḍaka, with King Kālāsoka, son of Susunāga, as his supporter, selected seven hundred elders from among twelve hundred thousand monks, crushed those ten points, and brought the body of the Dhamma and Vinaya into a compilation.

Tehi pana dhammasaṅgāhakattherehi niggahitā dasasahassā vajjiputtakā bhikkhū pakkhaṃ pariyesamānā attano anurūpaṃ dubbalapakkhaṃ labhitvā visuṃ mahāsaṅghikācariyakulaṃ nāma akaṃsu[V 0.0102]. Tato bhijjitvā aparāni dve ācariyakulāni jātāni – gokulikā ca ekabyohārikā ca. Gokulikanikāyato bhijjitvā aparāni dve ācariyakulāni jātāni – paṇṇattivādā ca bāhuliyā ca. Bahussutikātipi tesaṃyeva nāmaṃ. Tesaṃyeva antare cetiyavādā nāma apare ācariyavādā uppannā. Evaṃ mahāsaṅghikācariyakulato dutiye vassasate pañcācariyakulāni uppannāni. Tāni mahāsaṅghikehi saddhiṃ cha honti.

However, the ten thousand Vajjiputtaka monks, having been expelled by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma, seeking a party, found a weak faction suitable for themselves and formed a separate school of teachers called the Mahāsaṅghika. Having split from this, two other schools of teachers arose—the Gokulikas and the Ekabyohārikas. Having split from the Gokulika sect, two more schools of teachers arose—the Paṇṇattivādins and the Bāhuliyas. Bahussutikas is also their name. Among them, another school of teachers called the Cetiyavādins arose. Thus, in the second century, five schools of teachers arose from the Mahāsaṅghika school. Together with the Mahāsaṅghikas, they are six.

Tasmiṃyeva [P 0.0003] dutiye vassasate theravādato bhijjitvā dve ācariyavādā uppannā – mahisāsakā ca vajjiputtakā ca. Tattha vajjiputtakavādato bhijjitvā apare cattāro ācariyavādā uppannā – dhammuttariyā, bhadrayānikā, channāgārikā, samitiyāti. Puna tasmiṃyeva dutiye vassasate mahisāsakavādato bhijjitvā sabbatthivādā dhammaguttikāti dve ācariyavādā uppannā. Puna sabbatthivādakulato bhijjitvā kassapikā nāma jātā. Kassapikesu bhinnesu apare saṅkantikā nāma jātā. Saṅkantikesu bhinnesu suttavādā nāma jātāti theravādato bhijjitvā ime ekādasa [M 0.0107] ācariyavādā uppannā. Te theravādehi saddhiṃ dvādasa honti. Iti ime ca dvādasa, mahāsaṅghikānañca cha ācariyavādāti sabbeva aṭṭhārasa ācariyavādā dutiye vassasate uppannā. Aṭṭhārasa nikāyātipi, aṭṭhārasācariyakulānītipi etesaṃyeva nāmaṃ. Etesu pana sattarasa vādā bhinnakā, theravādo asambhinnakoti veditabbo. Vuttampi cetaṃ dīpavaṃse –

In that very second century, having split from the Theravāda, two schools of teachers arose—the Mahīśāsakas and the Vajjiputtakas. From the Vajjiputtaka school, four more schools of teachers arose—the Dhammuttariyas, the Bhadrayānikas, the Channāgārikas, and the Samitiyas. Again, in that same second century, having split from the Mahīśāsaka school, two more schools of teachers arose—the Sabbatthivādins and the Dhammaguttikas. Again, having split from the Sabbatthivāda lineage, those called Kassapikas arose. When the Kassapikas split, others called Saṅkantikas arose. And when the Saṅkantikas split, those called Suttavādins arose. Thus, having split from the Theravāda, these eleven schools of teachers arose. Together with the Theravāda, they are twelve. So these twelve, along with the six schools of teachers of the Mahāsaṅghikas, make a total of eighteen schools of teachers that arose in the second century. Eighteen Nikāyas and Eighteen Schools of Teachers are also their names. Among these, seventeen schools are split, and the Theravāda is to be understood as unsplit. And this is also stated in the Dīpavaṃsa—

“Nikkaḍḍhitā pāpabhikkhū, therehi vajjiputtakā;

Aññaṃ pakkhaṃ labhitvāna, adhammavādī bahū janā.

"The wicked monks, the Vajjiputtakas, were expelled by the elders. Having gained another faction, many people spoke against the Dhamma."

“Dasasahassā samāgantvā, akaṃsu dhammasaṅgahaṃ;

Tasmāyaṃ dhammasaṅgīti, mahāsaṅgīti vuccati.

"Ten thousand having come together, they made a Dhamma compilation; therefore this Dhamma compilation is called the Great Compilation."

“Mahāsaṅgītikā bhikkhū, vilomaṃ akaṃsu sāsane;

Bhinditvā mūlasaṅgahaṃ, aññaṃ akaṃsu saṅgahaṃ.

"The Mahāsaṅgīti monks acted contrary to the Dispensation; having broken up the original compilation, they made another compilation."

“Aññatra [P 0.0004][V 0.0103] saṅgahitā suttaṃ, aññatra akariṃsu te;

Atthaṃ dhammañca bhindiṃsu, vinaye nikāyesu ca pañcasu.

"They rendered the compiled Sutta otherwise, and made it different; they broke apart the meaning and the Dhamma in the Vinaya and in the five Nikāyas."

“Pariyāyadesitañcāpi, atho nippariyāyadesitaṃ;

Nītatthañceva neyyatthaṃ, ajānitvāna bhikkhavo.

"Both what was taught by implication and what was taught directly; both the explicit meaning and the implicit meaning—not knowing these, O monks,"

“Aññaṃ sandhāya bhaṇitaṃ, aññaṃ atthaṃ ṭhapayiṃsu te;

Byañjanacchāyāya te bhikkhū, bahuṃ atthaṃ vināsayuṃ.

"What was spoken with one intention, they established another meaning. Those monks, by the shadow of the letter, destroyed much meaning."

“Chaḍḍetvāna ekadesaṃ, suttaṃ vinayagambhīraṃ;

Patirūpaṃ suttaṃ vinayaṃ, tañca aññaṃ kariṃsu te.

"Having discarded a part of the profound Sutta and Vinaya, they made a counterfeit Sutta and Vinaya, and they made it otherwise."

“Parivāraṃ atthuddhāraṃ, abhidhammaṃ chappakaraṇaṃ;

Paṭisambhidañca niddesaṃ, ekadesañca jātakaṃ.

"The Parivāra, the Atthuddhāra, the six treatises of the Abhidhamma; the Paṭisambhidā and the Niddesa, and a part of the Jātaka."

“Ettakaṃ vissajjitvāna, aññāni akariṃsu te;

Nāmaṃ liṅgaṃ parikkhāraṃ, ākappakaraṇāni ca.

"Having abandoned so much, they made other things: name, sign, requisites, and modes of conduct."

“Pakatibhāvaṃ jahitvā, tañca aññaṃ akaṃsu te;

Pubbaṅgamā bhinnavādā, mahāsaṅgītikārakā.

"Having abandoned their original state, they made it something else; they were the leaders of the schismatics, the conveners of the Great Council."

“Tesañca [M 0.0108] anukārena, bhinnavādā bahū ahu;

Tato aparakālamhi, tasmiṃ bhedo ajāyatha.

"And following their example, many schismatic views arose; then, at a later time, schism arose among them."

“Gokulikā ekabyohāri, dvidhā bhijjittha bhikkhavo;

Gokulikānaṃ dve bhedā, aparakālamhi jāyatha.

"The Gokulikas, who were of one practice, split into two, O monks; two divisions of the Gokulikas arose at a later time."

“Bahussutikā [V 0.0104] ca paññatti, dvidhā bhijjittha bhikkhavo;

Cetiyā ca punavādī, mahāsaṅgītibhedakā.

The Bahussutikas and the Paññattis, O monks, split into two; and the Cetiyas and the Punavādins, schismatics from the Mahāsaṅgīti.

“Pañcavādā ime sabbe, mahāsaṅgītimūlakā;

Atthaṃ dhammañca bhindiṃsu, ekadesañca saṅgahaṃ.

All these five schools originated from the Great Council; they split the meaning and the Dhamma, and a part of the Collection.

“Ganthañca ekadesañhi, chaḍḍetvā aññaṃ akaṃsu te;

Nāmaṃ [P 0.0005] liṅgaṃ parikkhāraṃ, ākappakaraṇāni ca.

Indeed, having discarded a part of the texts, they made others: name, sign, requisites, and modes of conduct.

“Pakatibhāvaṃ jahitvā, tañca aññaṃ akaṃsu te;

Visuddhattheravādamhi, puna bhedo ajāyatha.

Having abandoned their original state, they made it something else; in the pure Theravāda doctrine, a further schism arose.

“Mahisāsakā vajjiputtakā, dvidhā bhijjittha bhikkhavo;

Vajjiputtakavādamhi, catudhā bhedo ajāyatha.

The Mahisāsakas and the Vajjiputtakas, O monks, split into two; within the Vajjiputtaka school, a fourfold schism arose.

“Dhammuttarikā bhaddayānikā, channāgārikā ca samiti;

Mahisāsakānaṃ dve bhedā, aparakālamhi ajāyatha.

The Dhammuttarikas, the Bhaddayānikas, and the Channāgārikas, along with the Sammitīyas; two divisions of the Mahisāsakas arose at a later time.

“Sabbatthivādā dhammaguttā, dvidhā bhijjittha bhikkhavo;

Sabbatthivādānaṃ kassapikā, saṅkantikassapikena ca.

The Sabbatthivādins and the Dhammaguttas, O monks, split into two; from the Sabbatthivādins arose the Kassapikas, and also the Saṅkantikas.

“Saṅkantikānaṃ suttavādī, anupubbena bhijjatha;

Ime ekādasa vādā, sambhinnā theravādato.

From the Saṅkantikas, the Suttavādins gradually split off; these eleven schools split off from the Theravāda.

“Atthaṃ dhammañca bhindiṃsu, ekadesañca saṅgahaṃ;

Ganthañca ekadesañhi, chaḍḍetvā aññaṃ akaṃsu te.

They split the meaning and the Dhamma, and a part of the Collection; and having discarded a part of the texts, they made others.

“Nāmaṃ [V 0.0105] liṅgaṃ parikkhāraṃ, ākappakaraṇāni ca;

Pakatibhāvaṃ jahitvā, tañca aññaṃ akaṃsu te.

Name, sign, requisites, and modes of conduct; having abandoned their original state, they made them something else.

“Sattarasa bhinnavādā, ekavādo abhinnako;

Sabbevaṭṭhārasa honti, bhinnavādena te saha.

Seventeen are the schismatic schools, one is the undivided school; all together they are eighteen, together with the schismatic schools.

“Nigrodhova [M 0.0109] mahārukkho, thera vādānamuttamo;

Anūnaṃ anadhikañca, kevalaṃ jinasāsanaṃ.

Like a great banyan tree, the Theravāda is supreme among schools; neither deficient nor excessive, the Victor's teaching is complete.

“Santakā viya rukkhamhi, nibbattā vādasesakā;

Paṭhame vassasate natthi, dutiye vassasatantare;

Bhinnā sattarasa vādā, uppannā jinasāsane”ti.

Like offshoots on a tree, the remaining schools arose; in the first hundred years there were none, but in the second hundred years, seventeen schismatic schools arose in the Dispensation of the Conqueror.

Aparāparaṃ pana hemavatikā, rājagirikā, siddhatthikā, pubbaseliyā, aparaseliyā, vājiriyāti aññepi cha ācariyavādā uppannā. Te idha anadhippetā. Purimakānaṃ [P 0.0006] pana aṭṭhārasannaṃ ācariyavādānaṃ vasena pavattamāne sāsane paṭiladdhasaddho asoko dhammarājā divase divase buddhapūjāya satasahassaṃ, dhammapūjāya satasahassaṃ, saṅghapūjāya satasahassaṃ, attano ācariyassa nigrodhattherassa satasahassaṃ, catūsu dvāresu bhesajjatthāya satasahassanti pañcasatasahassāni pariccajanto sāsane uḷāraṃ lābhasakkāraṃ pavattesi.

Furthermore, later on, six other schools of teachers arose: the Hemavatikas, Rājagirikas, Siddhatthikas, Pubbaseliyas, Aparaseliyas, and Vājiriyas. These are not dealt with here. However, while the Dispensation was proceeding according to the eighteen earlier schools of teachers, King Asoka, the righteous king, having gained faith, donated five hundred thousand daily: one hundred thousand for offerings to the Buddha, one hundred thousand for offerings to the Dhamma, one hundred thousand for offerings to the Sangha, one hundred thousand for his teacher, the Elder Nigrodha, and one hundred thousand for medicine at the four gates. Thus, he caused splendid gain and honor to arise in the Dispensation.

Titthiyā hatalābhasakkārā antamaso ghāsacchādanamattampi alabhantā lābhasakkāraṃ patthayamānā bhikkhūsu pabbajitvā sakāni sakāni diṭṭhigatāni – “ayaṃ dhammo, ayaṃ vinayo, idaṃ satthusāsana”nti dīpenti. Pabbajjaṃ alabhamānāpi sayameva kese chinditvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā vihāresu vicarantā uposathakammādikaraṇakāle saṅghamajjhaṃ pavisanti. Te bhikkhusaṅghena dhammena vinayena satthusāsanena niggayhamānāpi dhammavinayānulomāya paṭipattiyā asaṇṭhahantā anekarūpaṃ sāsanassa abbudañca malañca kaṇṭakañca samuṭṭhāpenti. Keci aggiṃ paricaranti, keci pañcātape tapanti, keci ādiccaṃ anuparivattanti, keci “dhammañca vinayañca vobhindissāmā”ti tathā tathā paggaṇhiṃsu. Tadā bhikkhusaṅgho na tehi saddhiṃ [V 0.0106] uposathaṃ vā pavāraṇaṃ vā akāsi. Asokārāme satta vassāni uposatho upacchijji.

The sectarians, deprived of gain and honor, not even obtaining the bare necessities of food and clothing, desiring gain and honor, went forth among the monks and proclaimed their own views: 'This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher's instruction.' Even without obtaining ordination, they cut off their own hair, put on ochre robes, and wandered about the monasteries. At the time of performing the Uposatha and other formal acts, they entered the midst of the Sangha. Though the community of monks rebuked them according to the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher's instruction, they did not conform to the practice in line with the Dhamma and Vinaya. They created various kinds of growths, blemishes, and thorns for the Dispensation. Some tended the fire, some practiced the five austerities, some followed the sun's course, and some took up the view, 'We will corrupt the Dhamma and Vinaya,' and thus they persisted. At that time, the community of monks did not perform the Uposatha or Pavāraṇa with them. For seven years, the Uposatha was interrupted in the Asokārāma.

Rājā “āṇāya kāressāmī”ti vāyamantopi kāretuṃ nāsakkhi, aññadatthu duggahitagāhinā bālena amaccena anekesu bhikkhūsu jīvitā voropitesu vippaṭisārī ahosi. So tañca vippaṭisāraṃ tañca sāsane uppannaṃ abbudaṃ vūpasametukāmo “ko nu kho imasmiṃ atthe paṭibalo”ti [M 0.0110] saṅghaṃ pucchitvā “moggaliputtatissatthero, mahārājā”ti sutvā saṅghassa vacanena ahogaṅgāpabbatato theraṃ pakkosāpetvā iddhipāṭihāriyadassanena therassa ānubhāve nibbicikiccho attano kukkuccaṃ pucchitvā vippaṭisāraṃ vūpasamesi. Theropi taṃ rājuyyāneyeva vasanto satta divasāni samayaṃ uggaṇhāpesi. So uggahitasamayo sattame divase asokārāme bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātāpetvā sāṇipākāraṃ parikkhipāpetvā sāṇipākārantare nisinno ekaladdhike ekaladdhike bhikkhū [P 0.0007] ekato ekato kāretvā ekamekaṃ bhikkhusamūhaṃ pakkosāpetvā pucchi – “bhante, kiṃvādī sammāsambuddho”ti? Tato sassatavādino – “sassatavādī”ti āhaṃsu. Ekaccasassatikā, antānantikā, amarāvikkhepikā, adhiccasamuppannikā, saññīvādā, asaññīvādā, nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā, ucchedavādā, diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā – “diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādī”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā paṭhamameva samayassa uggahitattā nayime bhikkhū aññatitthiyā imeti ñatvā tesaṃ setakāni vatthāni datvā uppabbājesi. Te sabbepi saṭṭhisahassā ahesuṃ.

The king, though striving with the thought, 'I will have it done by my command,' was unable to do so. Indeed, due to a foolish minister who had wrongly grasped the matter, many monks were deprived of their lives, and the king became remorseful. Desiring to pacify both that remorse and the growth that had arisen in the Dispensation, he asked the Sangha, 'Who is capable in this matter?' Hearing the reply, 'The Elder Moggaliputtatissa, O great king,' at the Sangha's word, he had the elder summoned from the Ahogaṅga mountain. Through witnessing the elder's supernormal powers, his doubts about the elder's power were dispelled, and he inquired about his own scruples, thus pacifying his remorse. The elder, residing in that royal park, had the king learn the doctrine for seven days. The king, having learned the doctrine, on the seventh day had the community of monks assembled in the Asokārāma, had a cloth curtain put up as an enclosure, and, seated within that enclosure, he had the monks of each single doctrine gathered together, group by group. Summoning each group of monks, he asked, 'Venerable sirs, what does the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One teach?' Then those who advocated eternalism said, 'He teaches eternalism.' The partial-eternalists, the finity-and-infinity theorists, the eel-wrigglers, the fortuitous-originists, the perceptionists, the non-perceptionists, the neither-perception-nor-non-perceptionists, the annihilationists, and the believers in Nibbāna in this very life said, 'He teaches Nibbāna in this very life.' The king, having already learned the doctrine from the start, knew, 'These are not monks, they are adherents of other sects.' He gave them white robes and had them disrobed. All of them numbered sixty thousand.

Athaññe bhikkhū pakkosāpetvā pucchi – “kiṃvādī, bhante, sammāsambuddho”ti? “Vibhajjavādī, mahārājā”ti. Evaṃ vutte rājā theraṃ pucchi – “vibhajjavādī, bhante, sammāsambuddho”ti? “Āma, mahārājā”ti. Tato rājā ‘suddhaṃ dāni, bhante, sāsanaṃ, karotu bhikkhusaṅgho uposatha’nti ārakkhaṃ datvā nagaraṃ pāvisi. Samaggo saṅgho sannipatitvā uposathaṃ akāsi. Tasmiṃ sannipāte saṭṭhibhikkhusatasahassāni ahesuṃ. Tasmiṃ samāgame moggaliputtatissatthero yāni ca tadā uppannāni vatthūni, yāni ca āyatiṃ uppajjissanti, sabbesampi tesaṃ paṭibāhanatthaṃ satthārā dinnanayavaseneva tathāgatena ṭhapitamātikaṃ vibhajanto sakavāde pañca suttasatāni paravāde pañcāti suttasahassaṃ āharitvā imaṃ parappavādamathanaṃ āyatilakkhaṇaṃ kathāvatthuppakaraṇaṃ abhāsi.

Then, having summoned the other monks, he asked, 'Venerable sirs, what does the Perfectly Enlightened One teach?' 'He is an analyst, O great king,' they replied. When this was said, the king asked the elder, 'Is the Perfectly Enlightened One an analyst, venerable sir?' 'Yes, O great king.' Then the king said, 'Now, venerable sir, the Dispensation is pure. Let the Sangha of monks perform the Uposatha.' Having provided protection, he entered the city. The united Sangha gathered and performed the Uposatha. In that gathering, there were sixty hundred thousand monks. In that assembly, the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, analyzing the matrix established by the Tathagata according to the method given by the Teacher for refuting all those points of controversy that had arisen then and that would arise in the future, and having brought forth five hundred suttas on his own doctrine and five hundred on the doctrines of others—a thousand suttas in all—recited this Kathāvatthuppakaraṇa, the crusher of others' views, marked for the future.

Tato [V 0.0107] saṭṭhisatasahassasaṅkhyesu bhikkhū uccinitvā tipiṭakapariyattidharānaṃ pabhinnapaṭisambhidānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sahassamekaṃ gahetvā yathā mahākassapatthero ca yasatthero ca dhammañca vinayañca saṅgāyiṃsu; evameva saṅgāyanto [M 0.0111] sāsanamalaṃ visodhetvā tatiyasaṅgītiṃ akāsi. Tattha abhidhammaṃ saṅgāyanto imaṃ yathābhāsitaṃ pakaraṇaṃ saṅgahaṃ āropesi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then, having selected from the sixty hundred thousand monks, and having taken one thousand monks who were bearers of the scriptural learning of the Tipiṭaka and had attained the analytical knowledges, just as the Elder Mahākassapa and the Elder Yasa had recited the Dhamma and the Vinaya, so too, while reciting, he purified the defilements of the Dispensation and held the Third Council. There, while reciting the Abhidhamma, he included this treatise in the collection as it had been spoken. Therefore, it is said:

“Yaṃ [P 0.0008] puggalakathādīnaṃ, kathānaṃ vatthubhāvato;

Kathāvatthuppakaraṇaṃ, saṅkhepena adesayī.

Because it is the basis of discussions such as the discussion of the person, he taught the Kathāvatthu treatise in brief.

“Mātikāṭhapaneneva, ṭhapitassa surālaye;

Tassa moggaliputtena, vibhattassa mahītale.

Of that which was established in the abode of the gods by the laying down of the matrix, and analyzed on the great earth by Moggaliputta,

“Idāni yasmā sampatto, atthasaṃvaṇṇanākkamo;

Tasmā naṃ vaṇṇayissāmi, taṃ suṇātha samāhitā”ti.

Now, since the occasion for expounding the meaning has arrived, therefore I shall explain it. Listen to it with concentrated minds.

Nidānakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Introduction is concluded.

Mahāvaggo

The Great Division

1. Puggalakathā

1. Discussion of the Person

1. Suddhasaccikaṭṭho

1. The Purely True State

1. Anulomapaccanīkavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Forward and Reverse Order

1. Tattha [M 0.0112][P 0.0009][V 0.0108] puggalo upalabbhati saccikaṭṭhaparamatthenāti ayaṃ pucchā. Āmantāti ayaṃ paṭijānanā. Kassa panāyaṃ pucchā, kassa paṭijānanāti? Asukassāti na vattabbā. Bhagavatā hi imasmiṃ pakaraṇe nānappakārānaṃ laddhīnaṃ visodhanatthaṃ tantivasena mātikā ṭhapitā. Sā therena satthārā dinnanaye ṭhatvā tantivasena vibhattā. Na hi thero yattakā ettha vādamaggā dassitā, tattakehi vādīhi saddhiṃ vādena viggāhikakathaṃ kathesi. Evaṃ santepi pana tāsaṃ tāsaṃ kathānaṃ atthassa sukhāvadhāraṇatthaṃ sakavādīpucchā, paravādīpucchā, sakavādīpaṭiññā, paravādīpaṭiññāti evaṃ vibhāgaṃ dassetvāva atthavaṇṇanaṃ karissāma.

1. Therein, 'Is a person apprehended in the real and ultimate sense?'—this is the question. 'Yes'—this is the affirmation. But whose question is this, and whose affirmation? It should not be said, 'It is so-and-so's.' For in this treatise, the Blessed One established the matrix by way of a system for the purpose of purifying various views. That matrix was analyzed by the Elder, abiding by the method given by the Teacher, by way of a system. Indeed, the Elder did not engage in contentious debate with as many debaters as there are paths of debate shown here. Even so, for the easy comprehension of the meaning of those various discussions, we shall provide the explanation of the meaning only after showing the division thus: the question of the proponent, the question of the opponent, the affirmation of the proponent, and the affirmation of the opponent.

Puggalo upalabbhati saccikaṭṭhaparamatthenāti hi ayaṃ sakavādīpucchā. Tāya “ye atthi puggaloti evaṃladdhikā puggalavādino, te evaṃ pucchitabbā”ti dīpeti. Ke pana puggalavādinoti? Sāsane vajjiputtakā ceva samitiyā ca bahiddhā ca bahū aññatitthiyā. Tattha puggaloti attā, satto jīvo. Upalabbhatīti paññāya upagantvā labbhati, ñāyatīti attho. Saccikaṭṭhaparamatthenāti ettha saccikaṭṭhoti māyāmarīciādayo viya abhūtākārena aggahetabbo bhūtaṭṭho. Paramatthoti anussavādivasena aggahetabbo uttamattho. Ubhayenāpi yo parato [V 0.0109] “puggalo upalabbhati saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena, rūpañca upalabbhatī”tiādinā khandhāyatanadhātuindriyavasena sattapaññāsavidho dhammappabhedo dassito[P 0.0010]. Yathā so bhūtena sabhāvaṭṭhena upalabbhati, evaṃ tava puggalo upalabbhatīti pucchati. Paravādī āmantāti paṭijānāti. Paṭijānanañhi katthaci “āma, bhante”ti āgacchati, katthaci “āmo”ti paṭijānanaṃ āgacchati. Idha pana “āmantā”ti āgataṃ. Tatrāyaṃ adhippāyo – so hi yaṃ taṃ parato vuttaṃ bhagavatā – “atthi puggalo attahitāya paṭipanno”ti suttaṃ [M 0.0113] āgataṃ, taṃ gahetvā yasmā pana bhagavā saccavādī na visaṃvādanapurekkhāro vācaṃ bhāsati, nāpi anussavādivasena dhammaṃ deseti, sadevakaṃ pana lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedeti, tasmā yo tena vutto “atthi puggalo attahitāya paṭipanno”ti, so saccikaṭṭhaparamattheneva atthīti laddhiṃ gahetvā “āmantā”ti paṭijānāti.

Indeed, 'Is a person apprehended in the real and ultimate sense?'—this is the proponent's question. By this, it is indicated that 'those personalists who hold the view, "A person exists," should be questioned thus.' Who, then, are the personalists? Within the Dispensation, they are the Vajjiputtakas and the Sammitiyas, and outside, many other sectarians. Here, 'person' means self, being, life principle. 'Is apprehended' means it is obtained by approaching with wisdom; it is known—this is the meaning. Here, in 'in the real and ultimate sense': 'real sense' means the actual state, not to be grasped in an unreal form like a mirage or illusion. 'Ultimate sense' means the supreme meaning, not to be grasped by way of tradition or the like. By both is meant the fifty-sevenfold classification of phenomena in terms of aggregates, sense bases, elements, and faculties, which is shown further on with phrases like 'a person is apprehended in the real and ultimate sense, and form is apprehended.' Just as that is apprehended as actually existing by its intrinsic nature, so too is your person apprehended?—thus he asks. The opponent affirms, 'Yes.' For affirmation sometimes comes as 'Yes, venerable sir,' and sometimes as 'Yes.' Here, however, it comes as 'Yes.' The intention here is this: he takes the Sutta passage stated elsewhere by the Blessed One—'There is a person striving for his own welfare'—and since the Blessed One speaks truthfully, not uttering words with the intent to deceive, nor teaching the Dhamma based on tradition or the like, but having directly known and realized the world with its gods, he declares it, therefore, having adopted the view that what was said by him—'There is a person striving for his own welfare'—exists in the real and ultimate sense, he affirms, 'Yes.'

Athassa tādisassa lesavacanassa chalavādassa okāsaṃ adadamāno sakavādī yo saccikaṭṭhotiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ adhippāyo – yvāyaṃ parato “sappaccayo appaccayo, saṅkhato asaṅkhato, sassato, asassato sanimitto animitto”ti evaṃ paridīpito rūpādisattapaññāsavidho dhammappabhedo āgato; na sammutisaccavasena, nāpi anussavādivasena gahetabbo. Attano pana bhūtatāya eva saccikaṭṭho, attapaccakkhatāya ca paramattho. Taṃ sandhāyāha – “yo saccikaṭṭho paramattho, tato so puggalo upalabbhati saccikaṭṭhaparamatthenā”ti.

Then, not giving an opportunity for such quibbling and fraudulent talk, the proponent says, 'That which is the real sense...' and so on. The intention here is this: whatever fifty-sevenfold classification of phenomena beginning with form, which is set forth further on thus: 'with a cause, without a cause; conditioned, unconditioned; eternal, non-eternal; with a sign, without a sign,' should not be grasped by way of conventional truth, nor by way of tradition and so on. But by its own actual nature it is the real sense, and by one's own direct experience it is the ultimate sense. Referring to that, he says: 'That which is the real sense, the ultimate sense—is that person apprehended thereby in the real and ultimate sense?'

Tatoti karaṇavacanametaṃ, tasmā tena saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena so puggalo upalabbhatīti ayamettha attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ruppanādibhedena vā sappaccayādibhedena vā ākārena yo saccikaṭṭhaparamattho upalabbhati, kiṃ te puggalopi tenākārena upalabbhatīti? Na hevaṃ vattabbeti avajānanā paravādissa. So hi tathārūpaṃ puggalaṃ anicchanto avajānāti. Tatrāyaṃ padacchedo – ‘na hi evaṃ vattabbe’ti, na hi evantipi vaṭṭati. Dvinnampi evaṃ na vattabboti attho.
