‘Tato’ is an instrumental term. Therefore, ‘is that person apprehended by means of that ultimate reality?’—this is the meaning here. This is what is said: ‘That ultimate reality which is apprehended by way of distinctions such as disintegration or by way of distinctions such as being with conditions—is the person also apprehended by you in that same manner?’ ‘It should certainly not be said so’—this is the opponent's rejection. For, not desiring such a person, he rejects it. Here is the word division: ‘na hi evaṃ vattabbe’ (it should certainly not be said thus), or ‘na hi evaṃ’ (it is certainly not thus) will also do. The meaning in both cases is that it should not be said thus.

Ājānāhi niggahanti sakavādivacanaṃ. Yasmā te purimāya vattabbapaṭiññāya pacchimā navattabbapaṭiññā, pacchimāya ca purimā na sandhiyati, tasmāpi niggahaṃ patto. Taṃ niggahaṃ dosaṃ [V 0.0110] aparādhaṃ sampaṭicchāhīti attho. Evaṃ [P 0.0011] niggahaṃ ājānāpetvā idāni taṃ ṭhapanāya ceva anulomapaṭilomato pāpanāropanānañca vasena pākaṭaṃ karonto hañci puggalotiādimāha. Tattha hañci puggalo upalabbhatīti yadi puggalo upalabbhati, sace puggalo upalabbhati saccikaṭṭhaparamatthenāti attho. Ayaṃ tāva paravādīpakkhassa ṭhapanato niggahapāpanāropanānaṃ lakkhaṇabhūtā [M 0.0114] anulomaṭhapanā nāma. Tena vata retiādi anulomapakkhe niggahassa pāpitattā anulomapāpanā nāma. Tattha tenāti kāraṇavacanaṃ. Vatāti okappanavacanaṃ. Reti āmantanavacanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tena, re vattabbe vata, re hambho, bhadramukha, tena kāraṇena vattabboyevāti. Yaṃ tattha vadesītiādi anulomapakkhe niggahassa āropitattā anulomaropanā nāma. Yaṃ tassa pariyosāne micchātipadaṃ tassa purato idaṃ te’ti āharitabbaṃ. Idaṃ te micchāti ayañhettha attho. Parato ca pāḷiyaṃ etaṃ āgatameva.

‘Acknowledge the refutation’—this is the statement of the proponent. Since your earlier affirmation of what should be said does not align with your later affirmation of what should not be said, and the later does not align with the former, you have therefore incurred refutation. The meaning is: ‘Accept that refutation, that fault, that offense.’ Having thus made the refutation known, now, making it evident by way of establishing, and by leading to and attributing it forward and backward, he says, ‘If indeed a person…’ and so on. Herein, ‘If indeed a person is apprehended’ means ‘if a person is apprehended, if a person is apprehended as an ultimate reality in the true sense.’ This, first of all, is called the ‘forward establishing,’ which is characteristic of establishing the opponent's position and of leading to and attributing the refutation. Then, ‘Therefore, indeed, O friend…’ and so on, is called the ‘forward leading-to,’ because the refutation is brought forward in the forward argument. Herein, ‘tena’ is a word of reason. ‘Vata’ is a word of affirmation. ‘Re’ is a word of address. This is what is said: ‘Therefore, O friend, it should indeed be said. O good sir, O gentle sir, for that reason it must indeed be said.’ ‘What you say there…’ and so on, is called the ‘forward attributing,’ because the refutation is attributed in the forward argument. At its conclusion, the word ‘wrong’ should be brought forward with ‘this is yours’ before it. The meaning here is: ‘This of yours is wrong.’ Moreover, this appears in the Pāli text later on.

No ce pana vattabbetiādi “na hevaṃ vattabbe”ti paṭikkhittapakkhassa ṭhapitattā paṭilomato niggahapāpanāropanānaṃ lakkhaṇabhūtā paṭilomaṭhapanā nāma. No ca vata retiādi paṭilomapakkhe niggahassa pāpitattā paṭilomapāpanā nāma. Puna yaṃ tattha vadesītiādi paṭilomapakkhe niggahassa āropitattā paṭilomaropanā nāma. Idhāpi pariyosāne micchātipadassa purato idaṃ teti āharitabbameva. Paratopi evarūpesu ṭhānesu eseva nayo.

‘But if it should not be said…’ and so on, is called the ‘reverse establishing,’ as it is characteristic of establishing the rejected position, ‘it should not be said thus,’ and of leading to and attributing the refutation in reverse. ‘But not indeed, O friend…’ and so on, is called the ‘reverse leading-to,’ because the refutation is brought forward in the reverse argument. Again, ‘What you say there…’ and so on, is called the ‘reverse attributing,’ because the refutation is attributed in the reverse argument. Here too, at the conclusion, the word ‘wrong’ must indeed be brought forward with ‘this is yours’ before it. In other such instances hereafter, this same method applies.

Tatrāyaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya saṅkhepattho – yadi puggalo upalabbhati saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena, tena vata bho so upalabbhatīti vattabbo. Yaṃ pana tattha vadesi “vattabbo kho purimapañhe ‘saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena upalabbhatī’ti, no ca vattabbo dutiyapañhe ‘tato so puggalo upalabbhatī’”ti, idaṃ te micchāti evaṃ tāva anulomato ṭhapanāpāpanāropanā honti. Atha na vattabbo dutiyapañhe “tato so upalabbhatī”ti, purimapañhepi na vattabbova. Yaṃ panettha vadesi “vattabbo kho purimapañhe ‘saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena upalabbhatī’ti, no [P 0.0012] ca vattabbo dutiyapañhe ‘tato so puggalo upalabbhatī’”ti, idaṃ te micchāti evaṃ paṭilomato ṭhapanāpāpanāropanā honti. Evametaṃ niggahassa ca anulomapaṭilomato catunnaṃ pāpanāropanānañca vuttattā upalabbhatītiādikaṃ anulomapañcakaṃ nāma. Ettha ca kiñcāpi anulomato pāpanāropanāhi eko, paṭilomato pāpanāropanāhi ekoti dve niggahā katā. ‘Ājānāhi [V 0.0111] niggaha’nti etasseva panettha [M 0.0115] puggalo upalabbhatīti paṭhamaṃ vādaṃ nissāya paṭhamassa niggahassa dvīhākārehi āropitattā ekovāyaṃ niggahoti paṭhamo niggaho.

Here, the summary from the beginning is as follows: If a person is apprehended as an ultimate reality in the true sense, then indeed, good sir, it should be said, ‘He is apprehended by that means.’ But when you say, ‘It should be said in the first question, “He is apprehended as an ultimate reality in the true sense,” but it should not be said in the second question, “Therefore, that person is apprehended,”’ this of yours is wrong. Thus, first, the establishing, leading-to, and attributing occur in the forward order. Then, if it should not be said in the second question, ‘Therefore, he is apprehended,’ then in the first question too, it should not be said at all. But when you say here, ‘It should be said in the first question, “He is apprehended as an ultimate reality in the true sense,” but it should not be said in the second question, “Therefore, that person is apprehended,”’ this of yours is wrong. Thus, the establishing, leading-to, and attributing occur in the reverse order. In this way, because the refutation has been stated in both forward and reverse orders, and because the four instances of leading-to and attributing have been stated, the section beginning with ‘is apprehended’ is called the forward pentad. And here, although two refutations are made—one by the forward leading-to and attributing, and another by the reverse leading-to and attributing—this is considered one refutation. Because the first refutation, based on the first thesis ‘a person is apprehended’, is attributed in two ways, the statement ‘Acknowledge the refutation’ refers to this single refutation. This is the first refutation.

2. Idāni paccanīkanayo hoti. Tattha pucchā paravādissa. So hi “atthi puggalo attahitāya paṭipanno”ti gahitattā “nupalabbhatī”ti asampaṭicchanto evaṃ pucchati. Sakavādī yathā rūpādidhammā upalabbhanti, evaṃ anupalabbhanīyato āmantāti paṭijānāti. Puna itaro attanā adhippetaṃ saccikaṭṭhaṃyeva sandhāya yo saccikaṭṭhotiādimāha. Sammutisaccaparamatthasaccāni vā ekato katvāpi evamāha. Sakavādī ‘puggalo’ti upādāpaññattisabbhāvatopi dvinnaṃ saccānaṃ ekato katvā pucchitattāpi na hevanti paṭikkhipati.

2. Now comes the opposing method. Here, the question is from the opponent. For he, having accepted the view ‘There is a person practicing for his own welfare,’ and not accepting ‘is not apprehended,’ asks thus. The proponent professes, ‘Yes,’ on account of the person's not being apprehended in the same way that phenomena such as form are apprehended. Again, the other, referring only to what he himself intends as ultimate reality, says, ‘That which is ultimate reality…’ and so on. Or, having combined conventional truth and ultimate truth, he also speaks thus. The proponent rejects this, saying ‘Not so,’ because the question was asked by combining the two truths, and also because ‘person’ is merely a designation dependent on grasping.

Idāni kiñcāpi tena paṭhamaṃ paramatthasaccavasena nupalabbhanīyatā sampaṭicchitā, pacchā sammutisaccavasena vomissakavasena vā paṭikkhittā. Paravādī pana ‘nupalabbhatī’ti vacanasāmaññamattaṃ chalavādaṃ nissāya yaṃ tayā paṭhamaṃ paṭiññātaṃ, taṃ pacchā paṭikkhittanti bhaṇḍanassa paṭibhaṇḍanaṃ viya attano katassa niggahakammassa paṭikammaṃ karonto ājānāhi paṭikammanti āha. Idāni yathāssa anulomapañcake sakavādinā vādaṭṭhapanaṃ katvā anulomapaṭilomato pāpanāropanāhi niggaho pākaṭo kato, evaṃ paṭikammaṃ pākaṭaṃ karonto hañci puggalotiādimāha. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva atthato veditabbaṃ. Yasmā panettha ṭhapanā nāma paravādīpakkhassa ṭhapanato [P 0.0013] “ayaṃ tava doso”ti dassetuṃ ṭhapanamattameva hoti, na niggahassa vā paṭikammassa vā pākaṭabhāvakaraṇaṃ, pāpanāropanāhi panassa pākaṭakaraṇaṃ hoti. Tasmā idaṃ anulomapaṭilomato pāpanāropanānaṃ vasena catūhākārehi. Paṭikammassa katattā paṭikammacatukkaṃ nāmāti ekaṃ catukkaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Now, although initially the non-apprehensibility of a person was accepted in terms of ultimate reality, it was later rejected either in terms of conventional reality or in a mixed manner. The opponent, however, relying on the mere verbal similarity of the statement 'is not apprehended' as a sophistry, says: 'What you first acknowledged, you later rejected—this is like countering a dispute with a counter-dispute, or undoing the act of censure you yourself have performed. Understand this as a counter-action.' Now, just as in the direct-order pentad the proponent established his position and then, through leading forward and imputation in both direct and reverse orders, made the censure evident, so too, by making the counter-action evident, he says, 'If a person…,' and so forth. This should be understood in terms of its meaning in the same way as explained below. For here, 'establishment' (ṭhapanā) is merely the establishment of the opponent's position in order to show, 'This is your fault'; it is only an establishment and does not make the censure or the counter-action evident. Rather, it is made evident through leading forward and imputation. Therefore, because this counter-action is performed in four ways by means of leading forward and imputation in direct and reverse orders, it is called the 'counter-action tetrad.' Thus, this should be understood as one tetrad.

3. Evaṃ paṭikammaṃ katvā idāni yvāssa anulomapañcake sakavādinā niggaho kato, tassa tameva chalavādaṃ nissāya dukkaṭabhāvaṃ dassento tvañce pana maññasītiādimāha. Tattha tvaṃ ce pana maññasīti yadi tvaṃ maññasi. Vattabbe khoti idaṃ paccanīke āmantāti paṭiññaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ[M 0.0116]. No ca vattabbeti idaṃ pana na hevāti avajānanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tena tava tatthāti tena kāraṇena tvaṃyeva tasmiṃ nupalabbhatīti pakkhe – “hevaṃ paṭijānantanti āmantā”ti [V 0.0112] evaṃ paṭijānanto. Hevaṃ niggahetabbeti puna na hevāti avajānanto evaṃ niggahetabbo. Atha taṃ niggaṇhāmāti athevaṃ niggahārahaṃ taṃ niggaṇhāma. Suniggahito ca hosīti sakena matena niggahitattā suniggahito ca bhavasi.

3. Having thus performed the counter-action, now, showing the faultiness of the censure made by the proponent in the direct-order pentad, relying on that very sophistry, he says, 'But if you think…,' and so forth. Herein, 'But if you think' means 'if you think so.' 'It should be said' is stated in reference to the admission 'yes' in the counter-position. 'But it should not be said' is stated in reference to the denial 'not so.' Therefore, 'your position there' means: for that reason, you yourself, in that position of 'is not apprehended'—acknowledging thus, 'yes'—are so acknowledging. 'One should be censured thus' means: denying again with 'not so,' one should be censured thus. 'Then we censure you' means: then we censure you who are deserving of censure. 'And you are well-censured' means: you are well-censured because you are refutable by your own view.

Evamassa niggahetabbabhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni taṃ niggaṇhanto hañcītiādimāha. Tattha ṭhapanāpāpanāropanā heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Pariyosāne pana idaṃ te micchāti idaṃ tava vacanaṃ micchā hotīti attho. Idaṃ chalavādena catūhi ākārehi niggahassa katattā niggahacatukkaṃ nāma.

Having thus shown his state of being censurable, now, censuring him, he says, 'If…,' and so forth. Herein, the establishment, leading forward, and imputation should be understood in the same way as explained below. At the conclusion, however, 'this is wrong for you' means 'this statement of yours is false.' Because this censure is performed in four ways through sophistry, it is called the 'censure tetrad.'

4. Evaṃ niggahaṃ katvāpi idāni “yadi ayaṃ mayā tava matena kato [P 0.0014] niggaho dunniggaho, yo mama tayā heṭṭhā anulomapañcake kato niggaho, sopi dunniggaho”ti dassento ese ce dunniggahitetiādimāha. Tattha ese ce dunniggahiteti eso ce tava vādo mayā dunniggahito. Atha vā eso ce tava mayā kato niggaho dunniggaho. Hevamevaṃ tattha dakkhāti tatthāpi tayā mama heṭṭhā kate niggahe evamevaṃ passa. Idāni yvāssa heṭṭhā sakavādinā niggaho kato, taṃ “vattabbe kho”tiādivacanena dassetvā puna taṃ niggahaṃ aniggahabhāvaṃ upanento no ca mayaṃ tayātiādimāha. Tattha no ca mayaṃ tayā tattha hetāya paṭiññāyātiādīsu ayamattho – yasmā so tayā mama kato niggaho dunniggaho, tasmā mayaṃ tayā tattha anulomapañcake āmantāti etāya paṭiññāya evaṃ paṭijānantā puna na hevāti paṭikkhepe katepi “ājānāhi niggaha”nti evaṃ na niggahetabboyeva. Evaṃ aniggahetabbampi maṃ niggaṇhāsi, īdisena pana niggahena dunniggahitā mayaṃ homa.

4. Even after having performed this censure, now, showing that 'if this censure I made according to your view is an ill-censure, then the censure you made against me below in the direct-order pentad is also an ill-censure,' he says, 'If this is ill-censured…,' and so forth. Herein, 'If this is ill-censured' means 'if this statement of yours is ill-censured by me.' Or, 'if this censure made by me against you is an ill-censure.' 'See it likewise there' means 'see it likewise in the censure made by you against me below.' Now, having shown the censure made below by the proponent with the words 'It should be said…,' and so forth, he then brings that censure to a state of non-censure, saying, 'But we are not by you…,' and so forth. Herein, in 'But we are not by you there by that admission…,' and so on, this is the meaning: because that censure you made against me is an ill-censure, therefore we, acknowledging thus with the admission 'yes' in the direct-order pentad, should not be censured by you with 'Acknowledge the censure,' even when a rejection of 'not so' is made again. Censuring me who am thus not to be censured, you do so; but by such a censure, we are ill-censured.

Idāni yaṃ niggahaṃ sandhāya “dunniggahitā ca homā”ti avoca, taṃ dassetuṃ hañci puggalo…pe… idaṃ te micchātiāha. Evamidaṃ anulomapaṭilomato [M 0.0117] catūhi pāpanāropanāhi niggahassa upanītattā upanayanacatukkaṃ nāma hoti.

Now, to show the censure with reference to which he said, 'we are ill-censured,' he says, 'If a person… this is wrong for you.' Thus, because the censure is presented by means of four instances of leading forward and imputation in direct and reverse orders, this is called the 'application tetrad.'

5. Idāni “na hevaṃ niggahetabbe”tiādikaṃ niggamanacatukkaṃ nāma hoti. Tattha na hevaṃ niggahetabbeti yathāhaṃ tayā niggahito, na hi evaṃ niggahetabbo. Etassa hi niggahassa dunniggahabhāvo mayā sādhito. Tena hīti tena kāraṇena, yasmā esa niggaho dunniggaho, tasmā [V 0.0113] yaṃ maṃ niggaṇhāsi hañci puggalo…pe… idaṃ te micchāti, idaṃ niggaṇhanaṃ tava micchāti attho. Tena hi ye kate niggaheti yena kāraṇena idaṃ micchā, tena kāraṇena yo tayā niggaho kato, so dukkaṭo. Yaṃ mayā paṭikammaṃ kataṃ, tadeva sukataṃ. Yāpi [P 0.0015] cesā paṭikammacatukkādivasena kathāmaggasampaṭipādanā katā, sāpi sukatā. Evametaṃ puggalo upalabbhatītiādikassa anulomapañcakassa nupalabbhatītiādikānaṃ paṭikammaniggahopanayananiggamanacatukkānaṃ vasena anulomapaccanīkapañcakaṃ nāma niddiṭṭhanti veditabbaṃ. Ettāvatā sakavādino pubbapakkhe sati paravādino vacanasāmaññamattena chalavādena jayo hoti.

5. Now, what begins with 'One should not be censured thus' is called the 'conclusion tetrad.' Herein, 'one should not be censured thus' means: just as I have been censured by you, one should not be censured in this way. For the ill-censured nature of this censure has been demonstrated by me. 'Therefore' means 'for that reason'; because this censure is an ill-censure, therefore, when you censure me, saying, 'If a person… this is wrong for you,' this censuring of yours is wrong. 'Therefore, the censure made' means: for the reason that this is wrong, for that reason the censure you have made is ill-done. The counter-action I have made is well-done. And this exposition of the path of discourse that has been conducted by way of the counter-action tetrad and so on is also well-done. Thus, it should be understood that what begins with 'a person is apprehended' is designated as the 'direct and counter-position pentad,' by way of the direct-order pentad and the counter-action, censure, application, and conclusion tetrads, which begin with 'is not apprehended.' To this extent, when the proponent’s initial position is established, the opponent’s victory comes about merely through sophistry based on the general similarity of words.

2. Paccanīkānulomavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Counter-Position and the Direct-Position

6. Idāni yathā paravādino pubbapakkhe sati sakavādino dhammeneva tathena sujayo hoti, tathā vāduppattiṃ dassetuṃ puggalo nupalabbhatīti paccanīkānulomapañcakaṃ āraddhaṃ. Tattha paccanīke pucchā paravādissa, rūpādibhedaṃ saccikaṭṭhaparamatthaṃ sandhāya paṭiññā sakavādissa. Suddhasammutisaccaṃ vā paramatthamissakaṃ vā sammutisaccaṃ sandhāya yo saccikaṭṭhoti puna anuyogo paravādissa, sammutivasena nupalabbhatīti navattabbattā missakavasena vā anuyogassa saṃkiṇṇattā na hevanti paṭikkhepo sakavādissa. Paṭiññātaṃ paṭikkhipatīti vacanasāmaññamattena ājānāhi niggahantiādivacanaṃ paravādissa. Evamayaṃ puggalo nupalabbhatīti dutiyavādaṃ nissāya dutiyo niggaho hotīti veditabbo. Evaṃ tena chalena niggaho āropito.

6. Now, to show how, when the opponent’s initial position is present, the proponent achieves a good victory by means of the Dhamma and truth, the fivefold argument concerning opposition and accordance, beginning with 'a person is not found,' is introduced. Herein, in the opposition, the question is the opponent's, while the affirmation is the proponent's, with reference to the ultimate truth in the sense of reality, differentiated as form, etc. When the opponent again cross-examines with reference to pure conventional truth or conventional truth mixed with ultimate truth, asking 'is this in the sense of reality?', the proponent rejects it with 'no,' because it is not to be said that 'a person is not found' in the conventional sense, or because the cross-examination is confused due to its mixed nature. The opponent's statement, such as 'understand the refutation,' is merely based on the general wording, 'he rejects what was affirmed.' Thus, it should be understood that the second refutation occurs relying on the second statement, 'a person is not found.' In this way, a refutation is imposed through deception.

7-10. Idāni [M 0.0118] dhammena samena attano vāde jayaṃ [P 0.0016] dassetuṃ anulomanaye pucchā sakavādissa, attano laddhiṃ nissāya paṭiññā paravādissa. Laddhiyā okāsaṃ adatvā paramatthavasena puna anuyogo sakavādissa, paramatthavasena puggalassa abhāvato paṭikkhepo paravādissa. Tato paraṃ dhammena samena attano jayadassanatthaṃ ājānāhi paṭikammantiādi sabbaṃ sakavādīvacanameva hoti. Tattha sabbesaṃ paṭikammaniggahopanayananiggamanacatukkānaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Evamidaṃ puggalo nupalabbhatītiādikassa paccanīkapañcakassa upalabbhatītiādīnaṃ paṭikammaniggahopanayananiggamanacatukkānañca vasena paccanīkānulomapañcakaṃ nāma niddiṭṭhaṃ hoti. Evametāni paṭhamasaccikaṭṭhe dve pañcakāni niddiṭṭhāni. Tattha purimapañcake [V 0.0114] paravādissa sakavādinā kato niggaho suniggaho. Sakavādissa pana paravādinā chalavādaṃ nissāya paṭikammaṃ katvā attanā sādhito jayo dujjayo. Dutiyapañcake sakavādissa paravādinā kato niggaho dunniggaho. Paravādissa pana sakavādinā dhammavādaṃ nissāya paṭikammaṃ katvā attanā sādhito jayo sujayoti paṭhamasaccikaṭṭho. Tatthetaṃ vuccati –

Now, to demonstrate victory in one's own doctrine by means of the Dhamma and fairness, the question is the proponent's in the way of accordance, and the affirmation is the opponent's, relying on their own doctrine. Without granting an opportunity for that doctrine, the further questioning is the proponent's, based on ultimate truth; the rejection is the opponent's, due to the non-existence of a person in the ultimate sense. Thereafter, all statements made by the proponent—such as 'understand the counter-action' and so on—are for the purpose of showing victory by means of the Dhamma and fairness. Here, the meaning of all four aspects—counter-action, refutation, leading in, and leading out—should be understood in the manner explained before. Thus, by way of the fivefold argument of opposition beginning with 'a person is not found,' and the fourfold sequence of counter-action, refutation, leading in, and leading out beginning with 'is found,' this is designated as the fivefold argument concerning opposition and accordance. In this first sense of reality, these two fivefold sets have been presented. Herein, in the first fivefold set, the refutation of the opponent by the proponent is a good refutation. However, the counter-action performed by the opponent against the proponent, relying on a deceptive argument, and the victory thereby achieved is a wrongful victory. In the second fivefold set, the refutation of the proponent by the opponent is a poor refutation. But the counter-action performed by the proponent against the opponent, relying on the Dhamma-based argument, and the victory thereby achieved is a good victory. This is the first sense of reality. Herein, it is said:

“Niggaho paravādissa, suddho paṭhamapañcake;

Asuddho pana tasseva, paṭikammajayo tahiṃ.

"The refutation of the opponent is faultless in the first pentad; but his victory through counter-action there is flawed."

“Niggaho sakavādissa, asuddho dutiyapañcake;

Visuddho pana tasseva, paṭikammajayo tahiṃ.

"The refutation of the proponent is flawed in the second pentad; but his victory through counter-action there is faultless."

“Tasmā dvīsupi ṭhānesu, jayova sakavādino;

Dhammena hi jayo nāma, adhammena kuto jayo.

"Therefore, in both situations, victory belongs to the proponent; for victory is indeed by the Dhamma—how can there be victory through non-Dhamma?"

“Saccikaṭṭhe yathā cettha, pañcakadvayamaṇḍite;

Dhammādhammavaseneva, vutto jayaparājayo.

"Just as here in the sense of reality, adorned with the two pentads, victory and defeat are declared by way of Dhamma and non-Dhamma."

“Ito paresu sabbesu, saccikaṭṭhesu paṇḍito;

Evameva vibhāveyya, ubho jayaparājaye”ti.

"In all other senses of reality beyond this, the wise one should discern both victory and defeat in exactly the same way."

2. Okāsasaccikaṭṭho

2. The Sense of Reality concerning Location

1. Anulomapaccanīkavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of Accordance and Opposition

11. Evaṃ [P 0.0017][M 0.0119] suddhikasaccikaṭṭhaṃ vitthāretvā idāni tameva aparehi okāsādīhi nayehi vitthāretuṃ puna puggalo upalabbhatītiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā paravādissa. Puna sabbatthāti sarīraṃ sandhāya anuyogo sakavādissa, rūpasmiṃ attānaṃ samanupassanādosañca ‘aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīra’nti āpajjanadosañca disvā paṭikkhepo paravādissa. Sesamettha anulomapaccanīkapañcake heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Pāṭho pana saṅkhitto[V 0.0115]. Tattha yasmā sarīraṃ sandhāya “sabbattha na upalabbhatī”ti vutte sarīrato bahi upalabbhatīti āpajjati. Tasmā paccanīke paṭikkhepo sakavādissa, paṭhamaṃ anujānitvā pacchā avajānātīti chalavādassa vasena paṭikammaṃ paravādissa. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

11. Having thus elaborated the pure sense of reality, now, to elaborate the same by other methods such as location, etc., the argument beginning with 'is a person found?' is introduced. Herein, the question is the proponent's, the affirmation is the opponent's. Again, the proponent's questioning, 'everywhere?', is with reference to the body; the rejection is the opponent's, seeing the fault of regarding self in form and the fault of falling into the view 'the soul is one thing, the body another.' The rest here in the fivefold argument of accordance and opposition should be understood in the manner stated before. The text, however, is condensed. Herein, because when it is said 'is not found everywhere' with reference to the body, it follows that it is found outside the body. Therefore, in the opposition, the rejection is the proponent's; the opponent's counter-action is based on the deceptive argument that the proponent first agrees and then rejects. The rest is evident.

3. Kālasaccikaṭṭho

3. The Sense of Reality concerning Time

1. Anulomapaccanīkavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of Accordance and Opposition

12. Dutiyanaye sabbadāti purimapacchimajātikālañca dharamānaparinibbutakālañca sandhāya anuyogo sakavādissa, sveva khattiyo so brāhmaṇotiādīnaṃ āpattidosañca dharamānaparinibbutānaṃ visesābhāvadosañca disvā paṭikkhepo paravādissa. Sesaṃ paṭhamanaye vuttasadisameva.

12. In the second method, the proponent's questioning, 'always?', is with reference to the time of the first and last birth and the time of being alive and of final extinguishment; the rejection is the opponent's, seeing the fault of incurring views such as 'that very khattiya is this brahmin,' and the fault of there being no distinction between the living and the finally extinguished. The rest is just like what was stated in the first method.

4. Avayavasaccikaṭṭho

4. The Sense of Reality concerning Parts

1. Anulomapaccanīkavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of Accordance and Opposition

13. Tatiyanaye sabbesūti khandhāyatanādīni sandhāya anuyogo sakavādissa, rūpasmiṃ attā, cakkhusmiṃ attātiādidosabhayena paṭikkhepo paravādissa. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

13. In the third method, the proponent's questioning, 'in all?', is with reference to the aggregates, sense bases, and so on; the rejection is the opponent's, due to fear of the fault of such views as 'self in form' and 'self in the eye.' The rest is just the same.

Okāsadisaccikaṭṭhādi

The Senses of Reality concerning Location, etc.

2. Paccanīkānulomavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of Opposition and Accordance

14. Evametāni [P 0.0018][M 0.0120] tīṇi anulomapaccanīkapañcake anulomamattavaseneva tāva paṭipāṭiyā bhājetvā puna paccanīkānulomapañcake paccanīkamattavaseneva bhājetuṃ puggalo nupalabbhatītiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha anulomapañcakassa pāḷiyaṃ saṅkhipitvā āgate paccanīke vuttanayeneva paccanīkassa ca pāḷiyaṃ saṅkhipitvā āgate anulome vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Ettāvatā suddhikassa ceva imesañca tiṇṇanti catunnaṃ saccikaṭṭhānaṃ ekekasmiṃ saccikaṭṭhe [V 0.0116] anulomapaccanīkassa paccanīkānulomassa cāti dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ paccanīkānaṃ vasena ayaṃ aṭṭhamukhā nāma vādayutti niddiṭṭhā hotīti veditabbā. Yā ekekasmiṃ mukhe ekekassa niggahassa vasena aṭṭhakaniggahoti pāḷiyaṃ likhiyati. Tatthetaṃ vuccati –

14. Thus, it is begun with: 'These three pentads of forward-and-reverse are first divided in sequence by way of the forward method alone; then, to divide the pentads of reverse-and-forward by way of the reverse method alone, no person is found,' and so on. Therein, for the forward pentad, when the Pāli text is condensed, the meaning of the reverse section that follows is to be understood in the manner stated. And for the reverse pentad, when the Pāli text is condensed, the meaning of the forward section that follows is to be understood in the manner stated. Thus far, for the four grounds of reality—namely, the pure one and these three—in each ground of reality, by means of two pairs of reversals, that is, the forward-and-reverse and the reverse-and-forward, this logical argument named 'the eight-faced' has been set forth; it should be so understood. This, by means of one refutation for each face, is written in the Pāli as 'the eightfold refutation.' Therein, this is said:

“Evaṃ catubbidhe pañhe, pañcakadvayabhedato;

Esā aṭṭhamukhā nāma, vādayutti pakāsitā.

"Thus, in the fourfold question, through the division into two pentads, this logical argument named 'the eight-faced' has been elucidated.

“Aṭṭheva niggahā tattha, cattāro tesu dhammikā;

Adhammikā ca cattāro, sabbattha sakavādino;

Jayo parājayo ceva, sabbattha paravādino”ti.

"There are indeed eight refutations therein; four of them are righteous, and four are unrighteous. In every case, they apply to one's own proponent; and victory and defeat, in every case, apply to the other proponent."

Saccikaṭṭhavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Ground of Reality is concluded.

5. Suddhikasaṃsandanavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Simple Conjunction

17-27. Idāni rūpādīhi saddhiṃ saccikaṭṭhasaṃsandanaṃ hoti. Tattha rūpañcāti yathā rūpaṃ paramatthato upalabbhati, kiṃ te puggalopi tatheva upalabbhatīti sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, atthi puggaloti vacanamattaṃ gahetvā paṭiññā paravādissa. Yadi te rūpaṃ viya paramatthato puggalo atthi, rūpato vedanādīnaṃ viya [P 0.0019] puggalassāpi aññattaṃ āpajjatīti anuyogo sakavādissa, samayasuttavirodhaṃ disvā paṭikkhepo paravādissa. Sesaṃ atthato [M 0.0121] pākaṭameva. Dhammato panettha sattapaññāsabhedassa saccikaṭṭhaparamatthassa vasena sakavādīpakkhamūlake anulomapaccanīke sattapaññāsa anulomapañcakāni dassitāni. Paṭikammacatukkādīni saṅkhittāni. Paravādīpakkhamūlakepi paccanīkānulome sattapaññāsa paṭilomapañcakāni dassitāni. Paṭikammacatukkādīni saṅkhittāni. Tattha “vuttaṃ bhagavatā”ti vacanamattena puggalassa atthitaṃ rūpassa ca saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasena upalabbhanīyataṃ dassetvā ubhinnaṃ aññattaṃ paṭijānāpanatthaṃ [V 0.0117] vuttaṃ bhagavatāti anuyogo paravādissa, sammutiparamatthānaṃ ekattanānattapañhassa ṭhapanīyattā paṭikkhepo sakavādissa. Sesamidhāpi atthato pākaṭamevāti.

Now, there is a conjunction of the ground of reality with form and so forth. Therein, with reference to 'And form,' the proponent's question is: 'Just as form is apprehended in an ultimate sense, is the person also apprehended by you in the same way?' The opponent's admission is made by taking merely the statement, 'a person exists.' The proponent's challenge is: 'If, for you, a person exists in an ultimate sense like form, then just as feeling and so forth are other than form, the person also would attain a state of otherness.' Seeing a contradiction with a doctrinal text, the opponent makes a rejection. The rest is clear in meaning. Here, from a doctrinal perspective, by way of the fifty-seven-fold ultimate ground of reality, fifty-seven forward pentads are shown in the forward-and-reverse section, which is rooted in the proponent's position. The preparatory tetrads and so forth are summarized. Also, in the reverse-and-forward section, which is rooted in the opponent's position, fifty-seven reverse pentads are shown. The preparatory tetrads and so forth are summarized. Therein, the opponent's challenge, 'It was spoken by the Blessed One,' is for the purpose of making the proponent admit the otherness of the two, having shown the existence of the person by that mere statement and the apprehendability of form by way of the ultimate ground of reality. The proponent's rejection is because the question of the oneness or otherness of conventional and ultimate realities is to be set aside. The rest here is also clear in meaning.

Suddhikasaṃsandanavaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Simple Conjunction.

6. Opammasaṃsandanavaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Conjunction by Way of Simile

28-36. Idāni rūpādīheva saddhiṃ opammavasena saccikaṭṭhasaṃsandanaṃ hoti. Tattha rūpavedanānaṃ upaladdhisāmaññena aññattapucchā ca puggalarūpānaṃ upaladdhisāmaññapucchā cāti pucchādvayampi sakavādissa, ubhopi paṭiññā paravādissa. Paravādinā anuññātena upaladdhisāmaññena rūpavedanānaṃ viya rūpapuggalānaṃ aññattānuyogo sakavādissa, paṭikkhepo itarassa. Sesamidhāpi atthato pākaṭameva. Dhammato panettha rūpamūlakādīnaṃ cakkānañca vasena sakavādīpakkhe vīsādhikāni nava niggahapañcakasatāni dassitāni. Kathaṃ? Khandhesu tāva rūpamūlake cakke cattāri, tathā vedanādimūlakesūti vīsati. Āyatanesu cakkhāyatanamūlake cakke ekādasa, tathā sesesūti dvattiṃsasataṃ. Dhātūsu cakkhudhātumūlake cakke sattarasa, tathā sesesūti chādhikāni tīṇi satāni. Indriyesu cakkhundriyamūlake [P 0.0020] cakke ekavīsati, tathā sesesūti dvāsaṭṭhādhikāni cattāri satāni. Evaṃ sabbānipi vīsādhikāni nava niggahapañcakasatāni honti.

Now, there is a conjunction of the ground of reality with form and so forth by way of simile. Therein, two questions are from the proponent: one concerning the otherness of form and feeling by way of their commonality of apprehension, and another concerning the commonality of apprehension of a person and form. Both admissions are from the opponent. When the commonality of apprehension is admitted by the opponent, the proponent challenges regarding the otherness of form and person, just as with form and feeling; the rejection is from the other. The rest here is also clear in meaning. Here, from a doctrinal perspective, in the proponent's position, nine hundred and twenty refutation-pentads are shown by way of the cycles rooted in form and so forth. How so? In the aggregates, first, in the cycle rooted in form, there are four; similarly, in the cycles rooted in feeling and so forth, there are twenty. In the sense bases, in the cycle rooted in the eye-base, there are eleven; similarly, in the rest, there are one hundred and thirty-two. In the elements, in the cycle rooted in the eye-element, there are seventeen; similarly, in the rest, there are three hundred and six. In the faculties, in the cycle rooted in the eye-faculty, there are twenty-one; similarly, in the rest, there are four hundred and sixty-two. Thus, all together, there are nine hundred and twenty refutation-pentads.

37-45. Paravādīpakkhepi rūpaṃ upalabbhatīti anulomavaseneva rūpavedanādīnaṃ aññattapaṭiññaṃ kāretvā puna atthi puggaloti suttaṃ nissāya chalavasena [M 0.0122] puggalassa rūpādīhi upaladdhisāmaññaṃ āropetvā aññattānuyogo kato. Sesamidhāpi atthato uttānameva. Dhammatopi sakavādīpakkhe vuttanayena vīsādhikāni nava paṭikammapañcakasatāni dassitāni.

Also in the opponent's position, having caused an admission of the otherness of form, feeling, and so forth by way of the forward sequence, that is, 'form is apprehended,' then, relying on the text that says 'a person exists,' a challenge regarding otherness is made by deceitfully imposing a commonality of apprehension of the person with form and so forth. The rest here is also clear in meaning. From a doctrinal perspective as well, in the proponent's position, nine hundred and twenty preparatory pentads have been shown in the manner stated.

Rūpādīhi saddhiṃ opammavasena saccikaṭṭhasaṃsandanaṃ.

The Conjunction of the Ground of Reality with Form and so forth by Way of Simile.

7. Catukkanayasaṃsandanavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Conjunction by the Fourfold Method

46-52. Idāni [V 0.0118] yaṃ saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena upalabbhati, tena yasmā rūpādīsu sattapaññāsāya saccikaṭṭhaparamatthesu aññatarena bhavitabbaṃ; rūpādinissitena vā, aññatra vā rūpādīhi, rūpādīnaṃ vā nissayena, tasmā iminā catukkanayena saccikaṭṭhasaṃsandanaṃ āraddhaṃ. Tattha rūpaṃ puggaloti anuyogo sakavādissa, ucchedadiṭṭhibhayena na hevāti paṭikkhepo paravādissa, niggahāropanaṃ sakavādissa. Kiṃ panetaṃ yuttaṃ, nanu rūpaṃ vedanāti vuttampi paṭikkhipitabbamevāti? Āma paṭikkhipitabbaṃ. Taṃ pana rūpato vedanāya aññasabhāvasabbhāvato, na aññattābhāvato. Ayañca rūpādīsu ekadhammatopi puggalassa aññattaṃ na icchati, tasmā yuttaṃ. Ayañca anuyogo rūpaṃ puggalo…pe… aññātāvindriyaṃ puggaloti sakalaṃ paramatthasaccaṃ sandhāya āraddho. Sakalaṃ pana paccattalakkhaṇavasena ekato vattuṃ na sakkāti tantivasena anuyogalakkhaṇamattametaṃ ṭhapitaṃ. Tena viññū atthaṃ vibhāventi. Vādakāmena pana imaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ gahetvā yathā yathā paravādissa okāso na hoti, tathā tathā [P 0.0021] vattabbaṃ. Iti tantivasena anuyogalakkhaṇassa ṭhapitattāpi yuttameva. Iminā nayena sabbānuyogesu attho veditabbo.

Now, since whatever is apprehended as ultimate reality must be one of the fifty-seven ultimate realities—either dependent on form, etc., or independent of form, etc., or the basis for form, etc.—therefore, this fourfold method is begun to establish the concordance with ultimate reality. Here, the proposition “form is the person” is by the proponent; the denial “it is not so” is the opponent’s rebuttal, fearing the annihilationist view; and the imposition of censure is by the proponent. But is this appropriate? Should not even the statement “form is feeling” be rejected? Indeed, it should be rejected. However, that is because of the distinct individual natures of form and feeling, not because of the absence of otherness. This proponent does not accept the distinctness of the person even from a single phenomenon among form, etc.; therefore, it is appropriate. This proposition—“form is the person… the faculty of one who will know is the person”—is begun with reference to all ultimate truths. However, since all of these cannot be stated together based on their individual characteristics, this is established as merely a characteristic of inquiry by way of the treatise. Thus, the wise discern the meaning. But one who desires to debate, having grasped this characteristic, should speak in whatever way leaves no opportunity for the opponent. Therefore, since the characteristic of inquiry is established by way of the treatise, it is entirely appropriate. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all such propositions.

Ayaṃ pana viseso – rūpasmiṃ puggalotiādīsu yathā ekaṃ mahābhūtaṃ nissāya tayo mahābhūtā, vatthurūpaṃ nissāya viññāṇaṃ rūpasminti vattuṃ vaṭṭati, kiṃ te evaṃ rūpasmiṃ puggalo? Yathā ca sabhāgavinibbhogato vedanādayo sabbadhammā, arūpā vā pana cattāro khandhā, nibbānameva vā “aññatra rūpā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati, kiṃ te evaṃ puggalo? Yathā [M 0.0123] ca cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ rūpānaṃ nissayavasena “vedanāya rūpaṃ…pe… viññāṇasmiṃ rūpa”nti vattuṃ vaṭṭati, kiṃ te evaṃ puggaloti? Sabbānuyogesu pana ucchedadiṭṭhibhayena ceva samayavirodhena ca paṭikkhepo paravādissa. Sesamettha atthato pākaṭameva. Dhammato panettha sattapaññāsāya saccikaṭṭhesu ekekasmiṃ cattāri cattāri katvā niggahavasena aṭṭhavīsādhikāni dve pañcakasatāni dassitāni. Paravādīpakkhepi paṭikammavasena tattakāneva. Yā panettha atthi puggaloti vutte sakavādissa paṭiññā, sā sutte āgatena sammutivasena. Yo rūpaṃ puggalotiādīsu paṭikkhepo, so sakkāyadiṭṭhipañhassa ṭhapanīyattā. Paravādissa paṭikammaṃ chalavasenevāti.

Here, however, is the distinction: In statements like “a person in form,” just as three great elements depend on one great element, and it is proper to say that consciousness is “in form” by depending on a physical basis, how then, for you, is a person “in form”? Similarly, just as it is proper to say that all phenomena, such as feeling and the rest, are “other than form” due to their classification by commonality and division, or the four immaterial aggregates, or even Nibbāna itself, how then, for you, is a person so? And just as it is proper to say “form by feeling… form in consciousness” by way of dependence for mind-originated material forms, how then, for you, is a person so? In all these inquiries, however, the refutation by the opponent is due to both the fear of annihilationist views and contradiction with the doctrine. The rest here is clear in meaning. From the standpoint of the Dhamma, in each of the fifty-seven ultimate realities, taking four each, two hundred and twenty-eight points are shown by way of censure. In the opponent’s position also, there are just as many by way of counter-attack. As for the assertion here—“there is a person”—when it is stated, this is the proponent’s assertion, based on conventional truth as found in the suttas. The rejection of statements like “form is a person” is because the question of identity view is one to be set aside. The opponent’s counter-attack is merely by way of stratagem.

Catukkanayasaṃsandanaṃ.

The Concordance of the Fourfold Method.

Niṭṭhitā ca saṃsandanakathā.

The Discussion on Concordance is concluded.

8. Lakkhaṇayuttivaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Consistency of Characteristics

53. Idāni [V 0.0119] lakkhaṇayutti nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā ṭhapetvā nibbānaṃ seso saccikaṭṭhaparamattho paccayapaṭibaddhatāya sappaccayo, paccayehi samāgamma katattā saṅkhato, uppajjitvā nirujjhanato sadā abhāvato asassato, uppattikāraṇasaṅkhātassa nimittassa atthitāya sanimitto, nibbānaṃ vuttappakārābhāvato appaccayaṃ asaṅkhataṃ sassataṃ animittanti idaṃ saccikaṭṭhassa lakkhaṇaṃ. Tasmā yadi puggalopi saccikaṭṭhaparamatthova tassāpi iminā lakkhaṇena bhavitabbanti sandhāya puggalo sappaccayotiādayo aṭṭhapi anuyogā sakavādissa[P 0.0022], paṭikkhepo paravādissa. Ājānāhi niggahantiādi panettha saṅkhittaṃ. Evametāni sakavādīpakkhe anulomapaccanīke anulomamattavasena aṭṭha pañcakāni veditabbāni.

53. Now comes the explanation called the Consistency of Characteristics. Herein, except for Nibbāna, the rest of ultimate reality in its true sense is dependent on conditions, being tied to causes. Because it is made by coming together with conditions, it is conditioned. Since it arises and ceases, due to its constant non-existence, it is impermanent. Because there is the existence of a sign, which is called the cause of arising, it has a sign. Nibbāna, however, due to the absence of the aforementioned characteristics, is not dependent on conditions, unconditioned, permanent, and signless. This is the characteristic of ultimate reality. Therefore, if a person is also ultimate reality in the true sense, they too must possess these characteristics. Hence, the eight inquiries—such as “is a person dependent on conditions?”—are by the proponent, and the refutation is by the opponent. “Understand the censure,” etc., is abbreviated here. Thus, these eight groups of five should be understood in the proponent's side, in their consistent and contradictory aspects, specifically by way of the consistent aspect.

54. Paravādīpakkhepi paccanīkānulome paccanīkamattavasena aṭṭheva. Tattha yasmā paravādinā suttavasena sammutisaccaṃ sādhitaṃ, sammutiyā ca sappaccayādibhāvo [M 0.0124] natthi, tasmā yāthāvato ca paṭikkhepo sakavādissa. Chalavasena pana vattabbaṃ “ājānāhi paṭikamma”ntiādi sabbaṃ idhāpi saṅkhittameva.

54. From the opponent’s perspective also, in the contradictory and consistent aspects, there are eight points, specifically by way of the contradictory aspect. Herein, since the opponent has established conventional truth by way of the suttas, and conventional truth does not have the nature of being dependent on conditions, etc., therefore, the refutation by the proponent is in accordance with reality. But regarding what is to be said by way of stratagem, everything, such as “Understand the counter-action,” is also abbreviated here.

Lakkhaṇayuttikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on the Consistency of Characteristics is concluded.

9. Vacanasodhanavaṇṇanā

9. The Explanation of the Examination of Statements

55-59. Idāni vacanasodhanaṃ hoti. Tattha yadetaṃ puggalo upalabbhatīti vacanaṃ, taṃ sodhetuṃ puggalo upalabbhati, upalabbhati puggaloti. Pucchā sakavādissa. Tassattho – yadetaṃ puggalo upalabbhatīti padadvayaṃ, taṃ ekatthaṃ vā bhaveyya nānatthaṃ vā. Yadi tāva nānatthaṃ, yathā aññaṃ rūpaṃ, aññā vedanā, evaṃ añño puggalo, añño upalabbhatīti āpajjati. Athekatthaṃ, yathā yaṃ cittaṃ taṃ mano, evaṃ sveva puggalo, so upalabbhatīti āpajjati. Tena taṃ vadāmi “yadi te yo puggalo, so upalabbhati, evaṃ sante yo yo upalabbhati, so so puggaloti āpajjati, kiṃ sampaṭicchasi eta”nti? Tato puggalavādī yasmā puggalassa upalabbhataṃ [V 0.0120] icchati, na upalabbhamānānampi rūpādīnaṃ puggalabhāvaṃ, tasmā puggalo upalabbhati, upalabbhati ke hi ci puggalo ke hi ci na puggalotiādimāha. Tassattho – mama puggalo atthi puggaloti satthu vacanato upalabbhati. Yo pana upalabbhati, na so sabbo puggalo, atha kho ke hi ci puggalo ke hi ci na puggaloti. Tattha ko-kāratthe ke-kāro, hi-kāro ca nipātamatto. Koci puggalo, koci na puggaloti ayaṃ panettha attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – puggalopi hi rūpādīsupi yo koci dhammo upalabbhatiyeva, tattha puggalova puggalo. Rūpādīsu [P 0.0023] pana kocipi na puggaloti. Tato taṃ sakavādī āha – puggalo ke hi ci upalabbhati ke hi ci na upalabbhatīti. Tassattho – puggalo upalabbhatīti padadvayassa atthato ekatte yadi upalabbhatīti anuññāto dhammo puggalato anaññopi koci puggalo koci na puggalo, puggalopi [M 0.0125] te koci upalabbhati, koci na upalabbhatīti āpajjati, kiṃ sampaṭicchasi etanti? So puggalassa anupaladdhiṃ anicchanto na hevanti paṭikkhipati. Ito paraṃ “ājānāhi niggaha”ntiādi sabbaṃ saṅkhittaṃ. Vitthārato pana veditabbaṃ. Puggalo saccikaṭṭhotiādīsupi eseva nayo. Sabbāni hetāni upalabbhativevacanāneva, apica yasmā “puggalo upalabbhatisaccikaṭṭhaparamatthenā”ti ayaṃ puggalavādino paṭiññā, tasmāssa yatheva puggalo upalabbhatīti laddhi, evamevaṃ puggalo saccikaṭṭhotipi āpajjati. Yā panassa puggalo atthīti laddhi, tassā vijjamānotivevacanameva, tasmā sabbānipetāni vacanāni sodhitāni.

Now comes the examination of statements. Herein, to examine the statement, “a person is apprehended,” [the question is posed]: “Is a person apprehended? Is what is apprehended a person?” The question is for the proponent of his own doctrine. Its meaning is this: do these two terms, “a person is apprehended,” have the same meaning or different meanings? If they have different meanings, it would follow that just as form is one thing and feeling another, so too a person is one thing and ‘is apprehended’ is another. But if they have the same meaning, it would follow that just as that which is mind is mentality, so too the very person is the one who is apprehended. Therefore, I say to you: “If for you the person is the one who is apprehended, then it follows that whatever is apprehended is a person. Do you accept this?” Then, because the personalist desires that a person be apprehended, but not that things which are apprehended, such as form, have the nature of a person, he says, “A person is apprehended; what is apprehended is in some cases a person, in some cases not a person.” Its meaning is this: my ‘person’ is apprehended in accordance with the Teacher’s statement, “a person exists.” But what is apprehended is not entirely a person; rather, in some cases it is a person, in some cases it is not a person. Here, the word ‘ke’ is in the sense of ‘ko,’ and ‘hi’ is merely a particle. The meaning here is: something is a person, something is not a person. This is what is said: a person is indeed apprehended, just as any phenomenon whatsoever, such as form, is apprehended. Therein, only the person is the person. But among things such as form, nothing at all is a person. Then the proponent of his own doctrine says to him: “A person is apprehended in some respects, and not apprehended in some respects?” Its meaning is this: if the two terms “a person is apprehended” are identical in meaning, and if the phenomenon acknowledged as ‘apprehended’ is not other than the person, and [you say] “something is a person, something is not a person,” then it follows that for you, the person itself is in some respects apprehended and in some respects not apprehended. Do you accept this? Not wishing for the non-apprehension of a person, he rejects this, saying, “Not so.” From here on, everything is summarized as “know the refutation,” and so on. But it should be understood in detail. The same method applies to statements such as “a person is a reality in the true sense.” All these are simply synonyms for “is apprehended.” Moreover, since the personalist’s assertion is, “a person is apprehended in the true and ultimate sense,” it follows that just as he holds the view that “a person is apprehended,” so too he holds the view that “a person is a reality in the true sense.” And as for his view that “a person exists,” that is simply a synonym for “is existent.” Thus, all these statements have been examined.

60. Tattha yaṃ avasāne “puggalo atthi, atthi na sabbo puggalo”tiādi vuttaṃ, tatrāyamadhippāyo – yañhetaṃ paravādinā “puggalo atthi, atthi kehici puggalo, kehici na puggalo”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ yasmā atthato puggalo atthi, atthi na sabbo puggaloti ettakaṃ hoti, tasmā naṃ sakavādī sampaṭicchāpetvā idāni naṃ evaṃ anuyuñjati. Tayā hi “atthi puggalo attahitāya paṭipanno”ti vacanamattaṃ nissāya “puggalo atthī”ti laddhi gahitā, yathā ca bhagavatā etaṃ vuttaṃ, tathā “suññato lokaṃ avekkhassu, mogharājā, sadā sato”tiādinā (su. ni. 1125) nayena “natthī”tipi vuttaṃ, tasmā yatheva te “puggalo atthi, atthi na sabbo puggalo”ti laddhi, tathā puggalo natthi, natthi na sabbo puggalotipi āpajjati, kiṃ etaṃ sampaṭicchasīti? Atha naṃ asampaṭicchanto na hevāti paṭikkhipati. Sesamettha niggahādividhānaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

60. Herein, regarding what was stated at the end, “A person exists; what exists is not entirely a person,” and so on, the intention is this: What the opponent said, “A person exists; what exists is in some cases a person, in some cases not a person,” amounts in meaning to this much: “A person exists; what exists is not entirely a person.” Therefore, the proponent of his own doctrine, having made him accept this, now interrogates him thus: “You, relying merely on the statement, ‘There is a person who is practicing for his own welfare,’ have adopted the view that ‘a person exists.’ But just as the Blessed One has said this, so too, by the method of ‘Look upon the world as empty, Mogharāja, ever mindful,’ and so on (Snp 5.15), it is also said that ‘there is not.’ Therefore, just as you hold the view, ‘A person exists; what exists is not entirely a person,’ so too it would follow that ‘A person does not exist; what does not exist is not entirely a person.’ Do you accept this?” Then, not accepting it, he rejects it, saying, “Not so.” The remainder here, the method of refutation and so on, should be understood in the manner already explained.

Vacanasodhanavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the examination of statements is concluded.

10. Paññattānuyogavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Application of Designation

61-66. Idāni [V 0.0121] paññattānuyogo nāma hoti. Rūpadhātuyā hi puggalavādī [P 0.0024] rūpiṃ puggalaṃ paññapeti, tathā arūpadhātuyā arūpiṃ. Tassa taṃ laddhiṃ bhindituṃ sabbāpi pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā ca paṭikkhepo ca itarassa[M 0.0126]. So hi rūpīti vutte rūpakāyasabbhāvato ceva tathārūpāya ca paññattiyā atthitāya paṭijānāti. Kāmīti vutte vītarāgasabbhāvato ceva tathārūpāya ca paññattiyā natthitāya paṭikkhipati. Arūpīti vuttepi arūpakkhandhasabbhāvato ceva tathārūpāya ca paññattiyā atthitāya paṭijānāti. Dvīsupi nayesu sattoti puggalassa vevacanavasena vuttaṃ.

61-66. Now, there is what is called the application of designation. For, in the form realm, the personalist designates a person as having form; similarly, in the formless realm, as formless. To break down this view of his, all the questions belong to the proponent of his own doctrine, while the affirmation and the denial belong to the other. For when it is said “has form,” he affirms it due to the existence of the form aggregate and the existence of such a designation. When it is said “has sensual desire,” he denies it due to the existence of freedom from passion and the non-existence of such a designation. When it is said “is formless,” he also affirms it due to the existence of the formless aggregates and the existence of such a designation. In both methods, “a being” is said as a synonym for “a person.”

67. Idāni yasmā so “kāye kāyānupassī”ti āgataṭṭhāne añño kāyo añño puggaloti icchati, tasmā taṃ laddhiṃ bhindituṃ kāyoti vā sarīranti vātiādi sakavādīpucchā hoti. Tattha kāyaṃ appiyaṃ karitvāti kāyaṃ appetabbaṃ allīyāpetabbaṃ ekībhāvaṃ upanetabbaṃ avibhajitabbaṃ katvā pucchāmīti attho. Eseseti eso soyeva. Ese esetipi pāṭho. Eso esoyevāti attho. Ekaṭṭheti ekaṭṭho. Same samabhāge tajjāteti samo samabhāgo tajjātiko. Vacanamatteyevettha bhedo. Atthato pana kāyova esoti pucchati. Paravādī nānattaṃ apassanto āmantāti paṭijānāti. Puggaloti vā jīvoti vāti pucchāyapi eseva nayo. Añño kāyoti puṭṭho pana kāyānupassanāya evaṃladdhikattā paṭijānāti. Aññaṃ jīvanti puṭṭho pana āhacca bhāsitaṃ suttaṃ paṭikkhipituṃ asakkonto avajānāti. Tato paraṃ “ājānāhi niggaha”ntiādi uttānatthameva.

67. Now, because he holds that in the passage 'contemplating the body in the body,' the body is one thing and the person another, therefore, to break down his position, the proponent asks, 'Is it body or is it physical body?' Here, the phrase kāyaṃ appiyaṃ karitvā means that I ask the question by treating the body as something to be reached, to be clung to, to be brought into oneness, not to be divided—this is the meaning. The term 'eseti' means 'that is that very one'. There is also the reading 'Ese eseti'. The meaning is 'this is that very one'. 'Ekaṭṭheti' means 'it is of one meaning/essence'. 'Same, similar, of the same kind' means equal, similar, of the same type. Here, the distinction is merely verbal. In essence, he asks, 'Is this the very body?' The opponent, not seeing a difference, agrees. The same method applies to the questions, 'Is it a person or is it a life-principle?' When asked, 'Is the body another?' he admits it because of his view regarding the contemplation of the body. When asked, 'Is the life-principle another?' unable to refute the explicitly stated sutta, he disregards it. Thereafter, 'Acknowledge the refutation,' etc., is clear in meaning.

68. Paravādīpakkhe pana añño kāyo añño puggaloti puṭṭho sakavādī ṭhapanīyapañhattā paṭikkhipati, paravādī chalavasena paṭikammaṃ karoti. Tampi uttānatthamevāti.

68. On the opponent's side, when asked, 'Is the body one thing and the person another?' the proponent, because it is a question to be set aside, rejects it; and the opponent makes a counter-attack by means of evasion. That too is clear in meaning.

Paññattānuyogavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Investigation into Designation is concluded.

11. Gatianuyogavaṇṇanā

11. Explanation of the Investigation into Destinations

69-72. Idāni [V 0.0122] gatiparivattanamukhena cutipaṭisandhianuyogo hoti. Tattha yasmā puggalavādī “sa sattakkhattuparamaṃ sandhāvitvāna [P 0.0025] puggalo”tiādīni (saṃ. ni. 2.133; itivu. 24) suttāni nissāya puggalo sandhāvatīti laddhiṃ gahetvā voharati[M 0.0127], tasmāssa taṃ laddhiṃ bhindituṃ sandhāvatīti pucchā sakavādissa. Tattha sandhāvatīti saṃsarati gamanāgamanaṃ karoti. Attano laddhivasena paṭiññā paravādissa. So puggalotiādayo anuyogopi sakavādissa, paṭikkhepo itarassa. Tattha soti soyevāti attho. Evaṃ pana anuyutto sassatadiṭṭhibhayena paṭikkhipati. Aññoti puṭṭho ucchedadiṭṭhibhayena. So ca añño cāti puṭṭho ekaccasassatadiṭṭhibhayena. Neva so na aññoti puṭṭho amarāvikkhepadiṭṭhibhayena. Puna cattāropi pañhe ekato puṭṭho catunnampi diṭṭhīnaṃ bhayena paṭikkhipitvā puna yānissa suttāni nissāya laddhi uppannā tāni dassento tena hi puggalo sandhāvatītiādimāha.

69-72. Now, the investigation into passing away and rebirth follows by way of the turning of destinations. Here, since the Personalist, relying on such suttas as 'A person, having transmigrated, is at most a seven-times-returner,' adopts and declares the doctrine that a person transmigrates, the proponent's question is, 'Does one transmigrate?' Here, 'transmigrates' means wanders on, goes and comes. The affirmation, according to his own doctrine, belongs to the opponent. The investigation beginning with 'Is that a person?' also belongs to the proponent, and the denial to the other. Here, 'that' means 'that very one'. When questioned thus, he denies it out of fear of the eternalist view. When asked, 'Another?' he denies it out of fear of the annihilationist view. When asked, 'Both the same and another?' he denies it out of fear of the partial eternalist view. When asked, 'Neither the same nor another?' he denies it out of fear of the view of the eel-wrigglers. Again, when all four questions are asked together, he denies them out of fear of all four views. Then, to show the suttas on which his doctrine is based, he says, 'Therefore, a person transmigrates,' and so on.

76. Puna sakavādinā “yvāyaṃ tava laddhiyā sandhāvati, kiṃ so asmiñca parasmiñca loke ekoyevā”ti adhippāyena svevāti niyametvā puṭṭho sassatabhayā paṭikkhipitvā puna daḷhaṃ katvā tatheva puṭṭho yasmā so puggalova na añño bhāvo, “so tato cuto idhūpapanno”tiādisuttampi (pārā. 12; dī. ni. 1.245) atthi, tasmā paṭijānāti. Sveva manussoti puṭṭho manussasseva devattābhāvato paṭikkhipati.

76. Again, when questioned by the proponent with the intention, 'According to your doctrine, the one who transmigrates—is he exactly the same in this world and the next?', the question being specified as 'Is it the very same one?', he denies it out of fear of eternalism. But when questioned firmly again in the same way, he acknowledges it, because it is that very person and not another being, and because there is also a sutta stating, 'That one, having passed away from there, is reborn here,' etc. (Pārā. 12; Dī. Ni. 1.245). When asked, 'Is it the very same human being?', he denies it, since a human being does not have the state of being a deva.

77. Puna puṭṭho “ahaṃ tena samayena sunetto nāma satthā ahosi”ntiādisuttavasena (a. ni. 7.66 atthato samānaṃ) paṭijānāti. Athassa sakavādī devamanussupapattīnaṃ nānattato vacanaṃ micchāti pakāsento manusso hutvātiādimāha.

77. When asked again, he agrees, according to the sutta that says, 'At that time, I was the teacher named Sunetta,' and so on (A.N. 7.66, similar in meaning). Then the proponent, showing his statement to be wrong due to the diversity of rebirths among devas and humans, says, 'Having been a human...' and so forth.

78. Tattha hevaṃ maraṇaṃ na hehitīti evaṃ sante maraṇaṃ na bhavissatīti attho. Ito paraṃ yakkho petoti attabhāvanānattavasena anuyoganānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

78. Here, 'death will not occur in this way' means that in such a case, death will not occur. Beyond this, one should understand the diversity of questioning due to the diversity of individual existences, such as yakkhas and petas.

82. Khattiyotiādīni jātivasena ceva aṅgavekallādivasena ca vuttāni.

82. The terms 'Khattiya' and so on are mentioned in terms of birth as well as physical defects and so on.

87. Puna [M 0.0128][V 0.0123] na vattabbanti paravādinā puṭṭho idhaṭṭhakassa upapattivasena paralokassa gamanābhāvato paṭiññā sakavādissa puna sotāpannassa bhavantarepi sotāpannabhāvāvijahanato dutiyapaṭiññāpi tasseva. Hañcītiādivacanaṃ paravādissa.

87. Again, when asked by the opponent, 'Should it not be said...?', the affirmation belongs to the proponent, because for one in this present existence, there is no going to the next world by way of rebirth. And again, because a stream-enterer does not abandon the state of a stream-enterer even in another existence, the second affirmation also belongs to him. The statement 'If so...' belongs to the opponent.

88. Puna devaloke upapannassa manussattābhāvadassanena anuyogo sakavādissa.

88. Again, the investigation belongs to the proponent, by showing the absence of the human state for one reborn in the deva-world.

89. Tato paraṃ anañño avigatoti ettha anaññoti sabbākārena ekasadiso. Avigatoti ekenāpi ākārena avigatoti attho. Na hevanti devaloke upapannassa manussabhāvābhāvato evamāha.

89. Beyond that, concerning 'not another, not departed', here 'not another' means completely identical in every way. 'Not departed' means not departed in any way. 'Not so'—thus it is said because one reborn in the deva-world lacks the state of being human.

90. Puna [P 0.0026] daḷhaṃ katvā anuyutto “sveva puggalo sandhāvatī”ti laddhiyā anujānāti. Hatthacchinnotiādi ākāravigamanadassanena avigato sandhāvatīti laddhibhindanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha aḷacchinnoti yassa aṅguṭṭhakā chinnā. Kaṇḍaracchinnoti yassa mahānhārū chinnā.

90. Again, when firmly questioned, he assents to the view that 'the same person transmigrates'. The phrase 'one whose hands are cut off' and so on is stated to break the view that one transmigrates without departing from one's characteristics, by showing the disappearance of those characteristics. Here, 'one whose fingers are cut off' refers to someone whose fingers are severed. 'One whose tendons are cut off' refers to someone whose major tendons are severed.

91. Sarūpotiādīsu paṭhame pañhe iminā rūpakāyena saddhiṃ agamanaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Dutiye antarābhavapuggalaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. So hi tassa laddhiyā sarūpova gantvā mātukucchiṃ pavisati. Athassa taṃ rūpaṃ bhijjati. Taṃ jīvanti yena rūpasaṅkhātena sarīrena saddhiṃ gacchati, kimassa tadeva jīvaṃ taṃ sarīranti pucchati. Paravādī idha sarīranikkhepā suttavirodhā ca paṭikkhipati.

91. In the first question regarding 'having the same form,' etc., he denies it, referring to not going together with this physical body. In the second, he agrees, referring to the intermediate-existence being. For according to his view, that being goes with the same form and enters the mother's womb. Then that form breaks apart. The proponent asks: 'That body designated as form, with which it goes—is that very body its life-principle?' The opponent denies this due to the contradiction with the suttas about the laying down of the body here.

Savedanotiādīsu asaññūpapattiṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati, tadaññaṃ upapattiṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Taṃ jīvanti yena vedanādisaṅkhātena sarīrena saddhiṃ gacchati. Kimassa tadeva jīvaṃ taṃ sarīranti pucchati. Taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīraṃ, aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīranti etissā hi laddhiyā pañcapi khandhā sarīranti adhippetā. Paravādī suttavirodhā paṭikkhipati.

In the questions beginning 'with feeling,' and so on, he denies it with reference to rebirth in the non-percipient realm and affirms it with reference to another rebirth. 'That is the life' means that with which one goes along, together with the body characterized by feeling and so on. He asks, 'Is that very thing the life, that body?' For according to this view—'the life is that body, or the life is another and the body is another'—the five aggregates are intended as the body. The opponent denies this due to a contradiction with the Suttas.

92. Arūpotiādīsu paṭhame pañhe antarābhavaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Dutiye arūpā rūpaṃ upapajjamānaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Aññaṃ, jīvanti yaṃ [M 0.0129] rūpasaṅkhātaṃ sarīraṃ pahāya arūpo [V 0.0124] sandhāvati, kiṃ te taṃ sarīraṃ aññaṃ, aññaṃ jīvanti pucchati. Itaro suttavirodhā paṭikkhipati.

92. In the questions beginning 'formless,' and so on, in the first question he denies it with reference to the intermediate existence. In the second, he affirms it with reference to a formless being being reborn into a form realm. He asks, 'Is the life another? That is, when the formless one transmigrates, having abandoned the body designated as form, is that body of yours another, and is the life another?' The other denies it due to a contradiction with the Suttas.

Avedanotiādīsu saññībhavaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati, tadaññaṃ upapattiṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Aññaṃ jīvanti yaṃ vedanādisaṅkhātaṃ sarīraṃ pahāya avedano aviññāṇo sandhāvati, kiṃ te taṃ aññaṃ sarīraṃ, aññaṃ jīvanti pucchati. Itaro suttavirodhā paṭikkhipati.

In the questions beginning 'without feeling,' and so on, he denies it with reference to the percipient state of existence, and affirms it with reference to another rebirth. He asks: 'Is the life another? When one without feeling and without consciousness transmigrates, having abandoned the body designated as feeling and so on, is that body of yours another, and is the life another?' The other denies it due to a contradiction with the Suttas.

93. Rūpaṃ sandhāvatītiādīsu ye rūpādayo khandhe upādāya puggalaṃ paññapeti, kiṃ te tasmiṃ puggale sandhāvante tampi rūpaṃ sandhāvatīti pucchati. Paravādī “avijjānīvaraṇānaṃ sattānaṃ taṇhāsaṃyojanānaṃ sandhāvataṃ saṃsarata”nti sattasseva sandhāvanavacanato [P 0.0027] paṭikkhipati. Puna puṭṭho yasmā rūpādidhamme vinā puggalo natthi, tasmā tasmiṃ sandhāvante tenapi rūpena sandhāvitabbanti saññāya paṭijānāti. Vedanādīsupi eseva nayo.

93. In the questions beginning 'Does form transmigrate?' and so on, he who designates a person in dependence on the aggregates such as form asks: 'When that person transmigrates, does that form also transmigrate?' The opponent denies this, because of the statement that only beings transmigrate, 'beings hindered by ignorance, fettered by craving, transmigrating and wandering on.' When questioned again, he acknowledges, with the understanding that since there is no person without the phenomena of form and so on, therefore, when that person transmigrates, form also must transmigrate. The same method applies to feeling and so on.

94. Rūpaṃ na sandhāvatītiādīsu yasmā te rūpaṃ puggalo na hoti, sveva ca sandhāvatīti vadesi, tasmā taṃ pucchāmi, kiṃ te rūpaṃ na sandhāvatīti attho. Itaro puggale sandhāvante na sakkā tassa upādānabhūtena rūpena sandhāvitunti saññāya paṭikkhipati. Puna puṭṭho sattānaññeva sandhāvanavacanato paṭijānāti. Sesamettha uttānameva.

94. In the questions beginning 'Does form not transmigrate?' and so on, the meaning is: 'Since for you form is not the person, and you say that the person himself transmigrates, therefore I ask you: Does form not transmigrate for you?' The other denies it, with the understanding that when the person transmigrates, it is not possible for form, which is the basis of clinging for that person, to transmigrate. When questioned again, he acknowledges it because of the statement that only beings transmigrate. The rest here is quite clear.

Gāthānaṃ pana ayamattho – āyasmato matena rukkhaṃ upādāya chāyā viya, indhanaṃ upādāya aggi viya ca, khandhe upādāya puggalo; rūpādīnaṃ sandhāvane asati tesu khandhesu bhijjamānesu so tava puggalo bhijjati ce, evaṃ sante ucchedā bhavati diṭṭhi, ucchedadiṭṭhi te āpajjati. Katarā yā buddhena vivajjitā akusaladiṭṭhi. Yā pana “ucchedavādī samaṇo gotamo”ti pariyāyabhāsitā, na taṃ vadāmāti dasseti. Athāpi tesu khandhesu bhijjamānesu so puggalo na bhijjati, evaṃ sante sassato puggalo hoti. Tato so nibbānena samasamo āpajjati[M 0.0130]. Samasamoti ativiya samo, samena vā samo, samabhāveneva samo. Yatheva nibbānaṃ nuppajjati na bhijjati, evaṃ te puggalopi tena samasamoti.

Now, the meaning of the verses is this: According to the venerable one's view, a person depends on the aggregates just as a shadow depends on a tree and fire depends on fuel. If, in the absence of the transmigration of form and so on, that person of yours breaks apart when those aggregates break apart, then in that case it becomes the view of annihilation; the annihilationist view befalls you. Which one? The unwholesome view rejected by the Buddha. He shows, 'We do not say that which was spoken of indirectly: "The ascetic Gotama is an annihilationist."' Furthermore, if that person does not break apart when those aggregates break apart, in that case, the person becomes eternal. Then that person becomes exactly equal to Nibbāna. 'Exactly equal' means exceedingly equal, or equal by equality, or equal in its very nature. Just as Nibbāna neither arises nor breaks apart, so too, according to you, is that person exactly equal to it.

Gatiparivattanamukhena cutipaṭisandhānuyogo niṭṭhito.

The investigation of decease and re-linking by way of the change of destinies is concluded.

Anuyogavaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Investigation.

12. Upādāpaññattānuyogavaṇṇanā

12. Commentary on the Investigation of Designations Based on Clinging.

95. Idāni [V 0.0125] upādāpaññattānuyogo hoti. Tattha pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññāpaṭikkhepo paravādissa. So hi rukkhaṃ upādāya chāyāya viya, indhanaṃ upādāya aggissa viya ca, rūpādīni upādāya [P 0.0028] puggalassa paññattiṃ paññāpanaṃ avabodhanaṃ icchati, tasmā “rūpaṃ upādāyā”ti puṭṭho paṭijānāti. Puna yathā rukkhupādānā chāyā rukkho viya, indhanupādāno ca aggi indhanaṃ viya aniccādidhammo, evaṃ te rūpādiupādāno puggalo rūpādayo viya aniccoti imamatthaṃ puṭṭho attano laddhiyaṃ ṭhatvā paṭikkhipati.

95. Now comes the investigation of designations based on clinging. Here, the question is for the proponent, while the rejection of the admission is for the opponent. For he desires the designation, the making known, and the understanding of a person in dependence on form and so on, just as a shadow depends on a tree, and fire depends on fuel. Therefore, when asked, 'In dependence on form?' he admits it. Again, just as the shadow, depending on the tree, is like the tree, and the fire, depending on the fuel, is like the fuel—subject to impermanence and so on—so too, the person depending on form and so on is impermanent like form and so on. When asked about this meaning, he rejects it, standing firm in his own doctrine.

97. Nīlaṃ rūpaṃ upādāya nīlotiādīsu nīlarūpena saddhiṃ puggalassa ekattaṃ, ekasarīre nīlādīnaṃ bahūnaṃ vasena bahubhāvañca anicchanto paṭikkhipati.

97. In the questions beginning 'Is one blue, in dependence on blue form?' and so on, not wishing for the oneness of the person with blue form, nor for multiplicity by way of many things such as blue and so on in a single body, he denies it.

98. Kusalaṃ vedananti etthāpi vedanāya saddhiṃ ekattaṃ ekasantāne bahūnaṃ kusalavedanānaṃ vasena bahubhāvañca anicchanto paṭikkhipati. Dutiyanaye maggakusalotiādivacanasabbhāvato chekaṭṭhaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Saphalotiādīni puṭṭho tathārūpassa vohārassa abhāvato paṭikkhipati.

98. Regarding 'wholesome feeling,' here too, not wishing for oneness with feeling, nor for multiplicity by way of many wholesome feelings in a single continuum, he denies it. In the second method, because of the existence of expressions such as 'the path is wholesome,' and so on, he acknowledges it with reference to the meaning of 'skillful.' When questioned about 'fruitful' and so on, he rejects it due to the absence of such a usage.

99. Akusalapakkhe achekaṭṭhaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti.

99. In the case of the unwholesome, he acknowledges it with reference to the meaning of 'unskillful.'

100. Abyākatapakkhe sassatādivasena abyākatabhāvaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Sesamettha heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

100. In the case of the undeclared, he acknowledges its undeclared nature with reference to eternalism and so on. The rest here should be understood in the same way as stated above.

104. Cakkhuṃ [M 0.0131] upādāyātiādīsu “cakkhumā visamānīva…pe… pāpāni parivajjaye”ti(udā. 43) ādivohārasabbhāvato paṭijānāti. Cakkhumattādinirodhena puggalanirodhaṃ anicchanto paṭikkhipati.

104. In the questions beginning 'In dependence on the eye?' and so on, he acknowledges it because of the existence of conventional expressions such as, 'One with eyes, as if on uneven ground... should avoid evil deeds' (Udāna 43). Not wishing for the cessation of the person through the cessation of the mere eye and so on, he denies it.

107. Rūpaṃ upādāya vedanaṃ upādāyāti ettha aññepi rūpamūlakā dukatikacatukkā veditabbā. Yasmā pana khandhe upādāya puggalassa paññatti, tasmā dvepi tayopi cattāropi pañcapi [V 0.0126] upādāya paññattiṃ paṭijānāti. Ekasantāne pana dvinnaṃ pañcannaṃ vā abhāvā paṭikkhipati. Āyatanādīsupi eseva nayo.

107. In 'in dependence on form, in dependence on feeling,' here other dyads, triads, and tetrads rooted in form should also be understood. However, since the designation of a person is in dependence on the aggregates, he acknowledges designation based on two, three, four, or all five aggregates. But he denies it due to the absence of two or five in a single continuum. The same method applies to the sense bases and so on.

112. Idāni yaṃ upādāya yassa paññatti, yathā tassa aniccatāya tassāpi aniccatā, tato ca aññattaṃ siddhaṃ, evaṃ tassa puggalassāpi āpajjatīti dassetuṃ yathā rukkhantiādimāha. Tattha upādāyāti paṭicca āgamma, na vinā tanti attho. Paravādī pana tathā anicchanto laddhiyaṃ ṭhatvā paṭikkhipati.

112. Now, to show that just as the designation which depends on something is impermanent because that thing is impermanent, and from that, otherness is established, so too this applies to the person, he says 'like a tree' and so on. Herein, 'depending on' means 'dependent on, having come to,' meaning 'not without it.' But the opponent, not wishing for it to be so, stands firm in his doctrine and denies it.

115. Nigaḷoti saṅkhalikabandhanaṃ. Negaḷikoti tena bandhako yassa rūpaṃ so rūpavāti yasmā yassa rūpaṃ so rūpavā hoti, tasmā yathā na nigaḷo [P 0.0029]…pe… añño rūpavāti attho.

115. 'Nigaḷa' means a chain or bond. 'Negaḷika' means one who binds with it. The meaning is: 'Since he whose form exists is one with form, therefore, just as "not a chain" [...], so the one with form is different.'

116. Citte cittetiādīsu sarāgādicittavasena sarāgāditaṃ sandhāya cittānupassanāvasena paṭijānāti. Jāyatītiādinā nayena puṭṭho puggalassa khaṇikabhāvaṃ anicchanto paṭikkhipati. “So”ti vā “añño”ti vā puṭṭho sassatucchedabhayena paṭikkhipati. Puna na vattabbaṃ “kumārako”ti vā “kumārikā”ti vā puṭṭho lokavohārasamucchedabhayena vattabbanti paṭijānāti. Sesamettha pākaṭameva.

116. In 'mind, mind' and so on, he acknowledges it by way of the contemplation of mind, with reference to its being affected by lust and so on, as in the case of a mind affected by lust and so on. When asked in the manner of 'it arises' and so on, not wishing for the momentary nature of the person, he denies it. When asked 'Is it the same?' or 'Is it different?', he denies it out of fear of eternalism or annihilationism. Again, when asked 'Should it not be said "a boy" or "a girl"?', he acknowledges that it should be spoken of out of fear of destroying worldly convention. The rest here is quite clear.

118. Idāni paravādī aññenākārena laddhiṃ patiṭṭhāpetukāmo na vattabbaṃ puggalo upalabbhatītiādimāha. Tattha na vattabbanti kiṃ te iminā evaṃ bahunā upādāpaññattānuyogena, idaṃ tāva vadehi, kiṃ na vattabbaṃ “puggalo upalabbhati saccikaṭṭhaparamatthenā”ti. Tato sakavādinā āmantāti vutte nanu yo passatītiādimāha. Tattha yoti puggalo[M 0.0132]. Yanti rūpaṃ. Yenāti cakkhunā. Soti puggalo. Tanti rūpaṃ. Tenāti cakkhunā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – nanu yo yaṃ rūpaṃ yena cakkhunā passati, so taṃ rūpaṃ tena cakkhunā passanto puggaloti. Sakavādī kiñcāpi cakkhuviññāṇassa nissayabhāvaṃ gacchantaṃ cakkhumeva rūpaṃ passati, tathā sotameva saddaṃ suṇāti…pe… viññāṇameva dhammaṃ vijānāti, “atthi arahato cakkhu, passati arahā cakkhunā rūpa”ntiādisammutivasena pana āmantāti paṭijānāti.

118. Now, the opponent, wishing to establish his doctrine in another way, says 'It should not be said that a person is found' and so on. Herein, 'it should not be said' means: 'What use is this extensive investigation of designations based on clinging to you? First, tell me this: should it not be said that "a person is found in the real and ultimate sense"?' Then, when the proponent says 'Yes,' he says 'Is it not so that one sees?' and so on. Herein, 'who' refers to the person. 'What' refers to form. 'With which' refers to the eye. 'He' refers to the person. 'That' refers to form. 'With that' refers to the eye. This is what is said: 'Is not the one who sees a form with the eye, while seeing that form with that eye, a person?' Although the eye itself sees form, becoming the basis for eye-consciousness, and similarly the ear hears sound [...], and consciousness cognizes mental objects, yet the proponent acknowledges it conventionally, saying, 'The Arahant has an eye, the Arahant sees form with the eye,' and so on.

120. Tato [V 0.0127] chalavādaṃ nissāya paravādinā puggalassa vattabbatāya sādhitāya tameva vādaṃ parivattetvā puggalo upalabbhatītiādimāha. Tattha yo na passatīti andho asaññasatto arūpaṃ upapanno nirodhaṃ samāpanno, anandhopi ca aññatra dassanasamayā na passati nāma. Sesavāresupi eseva nayo. Sesaṃ pāḷivaseneva atthato veditabbaṃ.

120. Then, relying on sophistry, the opponent, having established the necessity of speaking about a person, turns the same argument around and says, 'a person is found,' and so on. Herein, 'who does not see' refers to a blind person, a non-percipient being, one reborn in the formless realm, or one who has attained cessation. And even a non-blind person does not see apart from the time of seeing. The same principle applies in the remaining instances. The rest should be understood according to the meaning of the Pāli text itself.

122. Suttasaṃsandanāyaṃ dibbassa cakkhuno rūpagocarattā rūpaṃ passatīti āha. Dutiyavāre “satte passāmī”tivacanato puggalaṃ passatīti āha. Tatiyavāre “rūpaṃ disvā puggalaṃ vibhāvetī”ti laddhito ubho passatīti āha. Yasmā pana passitabbaṃ nāma diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ viññātanti catubbidhe rūpasaṅgahe rūpāyatanameva saṅgahitaṃ, tasmā sakavādī “rūpaṃ puggalo, puggalo rūpaṃ, ubho rūpa”nti anuyogaṃ karoti. Tassattho pākaṭoyevāti.

122. In the correlation with the suttas, because the divine eye has form as its object-range, it is said that it sees form. In the second instance, from the statement 'I see beings,' it is said that it sees the person. In the third instance, from the doctrine that 'having seen form, one distinguishes the person,' it is said that it sees both. However, since the perceivable is fourfold—seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—but in the category of form, only the sense-object of form is included, therefore the proponent poses the question: 'Is form the person? Is the person form? Are both form?' The meaning of this is quite clear.

Upādāpaññattānuyogavaṇṇanā.

Exposition on the Inquiry into Designations Based on Clinging.

13. Purisakārānuyogavaṇṇanā

13. Exposition on the Inquiry into Personal Effort.

123. Idāni [P 0.0030] purisakārānuyogo hoti. Tattha kamme sati niyamato tassa kārakenapi bhavitabbanti laddhiyā pucchā paravādissa, tathārūpānaṃ kammānaṃ atthitāya paṭiññā sakavādissa. Puna kattā kāretāti pucchā paravādissa. Tattha kattāti tesaṃ kammānaṃ kārako. Kāretāti āṇattidesanādīhi upāyehi kārāpako. Idāni yasmā [M 0.0133] paravādī puggalaṃ sandhāya kattāti pucchati, na karaṇamattaṃ, tasmā paṭikkhepo sakavādissa.

123. Now comes the inquiry into personal effort. Here, the opponent's question is based on the tenet that when an action exists, it must necessarily have a doer. The proponent acknowledges the existence of such actions. Then the opponent asks, 'Is there a doer? Is there an instigator?' Here, 'doer' refers to the performer of those actions. 'Instigator' means the one who causes them to be done through commands, instructions, and other such means. Now, since the opponent asks about the 'doer' with reference to a person, not merely the means of doing, the proponent rejects this.

124. Tassa kattā kāretāti ettha yadi yaṃ yaṃ upalabbhati, tassa tassa kattā puggalo te upalabbhati, kiṃ tassāpi kārako ca kārāpako ca añño puggalo upalabbhatīti attho. Paravādī tathā anicchanto issaranimmānavādabhayena paṭikkhipati. Puna puṭṭho yasmā puggalaṃ mātāpitaro janenti nāmaṃ karonti posenti, tasmāssa te kārakā. Ye ca pana taṃ kalyāṇamittā vā ācariyā vā tāni tāni vijjāṭṭhānasippāyatanāni sikkhāpenti[V 0.0128], te kārāpakā nāmāti imamatthaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Purimakammameva tassa kattā ceva kārāpetā cāti adhippetaṃ.

124. Regarding 'its doer and instigator,' the meaning is this: if for whatever is apprehended, a person is apprehended by you as its doer, is another person also apprehended who is both the doer and the instigator of that person?
