The opponent, unwilling to accept this, rejects it out of fear of the doctrine of creation by a supreme being. When questioned again, they concede this meaning: since parents give birth to, name, and nurture a person, they are the doers. And since good friends or teachers teach various branches of knowledge, crafts, and skills, they are the instigators. The intended meaning is that past action itself is both its doer and its instigator.

125. Tassa tassevāti iminā idaṃ pucchati – yadi kammānaṃ kārakassa kattā tassāpi kattā tassāpi kattā attheva, evaṃ sante purimena purimena avassaṃ pacchā pacchā puggalo kātabboti imināpi te kammānaṃ kārakena puggalena āyatiṃ añño puggalo kātabbo, tenāpi aññoti natthi dukkhassa antakiriyā, natthi vaṭṭassa upacchedo, natthi appaccayaparinibbānaṃ. Paccayābhāvena paccayapaṭibaddhassa dukkhassa abhāvā yaṃ nibbānaṃ vuttaṃ, natthi te tanti. Atha vā tassa tassevāti yadi kammaṃ kammamattaṃ na hoti, tassa pana kārako puggalo, tassāpi kārako, tassāpi kārakoti evaṃ puggalaparamparā atthi. Evaṃ sante yā esā kammavaṭṭassa appavattikaraṇena dukkhassa antakiriyā vuttā, sā natthīti attho. Paravādī taṃ anicchanto paṭikkhipati. Ito aparāsupi upalabbhati sāmaññena kārakapucchāsu puggalaṃyeva sandhāya “kattā kāretā”ti [P 0.0031] vuttaṃ, na paccaye. Na hi mahāpathavīādīnaṃ paccayā natthi.

125. By 'for that very one,' this is asked: if an action is not merely an action, but there is a person as its agent, and a doer of that one, and a doer of that one—thus there is a succession of persons. This being so, that making an end of suffering, which is spoken of as being brought about by the non-continuation of the cycle of action, would not exist—this is the meaning. The opponent, not wishing for this, rejects it. Hereafter as well, in general questions about the agent, it is found that 'doer and instigator' is said with reference to a person, not to conditions. For it is not that conditions such as the great earth element do not exist.

135. Añño kalyāṇapāpakānaṃ kammānaṃ kattāti pañho “saṅkhāravantaṃ vā attāna”ntiādidiṭṭhibhayā paṭikkhitto.

135. The question, "Is another the doer of good and bad actions?" is rejected due to the fear of views such as "a self possessed of volitional formations," etc.

136. Vipāko upalabbhatītiādi vipākapaṭisaṃvedīvasena puggalaṃ dassentassa laddhibhindanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha vipākapaṭisaṃvedīti anuyogo paravādissa[M 0.0134], vipākapavattito aññassa vedakassa abhāvā paṭikkhepo sakavādissa. Puna pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa.

136. "The result is found," etc., is stated to refute the view of one who presents a person as experiencing the result. Here, "experiencer of the result" is the opponent's inquiry, while the proponent rejects it because, other than the arising of the result, there is no other experiencer. Then comes the proponent's question and the opponent's acknowledgement.

138. Tassa paṭisaṃvedīti tassa vipākapaṭisaṃvedakassa paṭisaṃvedī yasmā pana paṭisaṃveditabbo nāma vipāko, na ca puggalo vipāko, tasmā paṭikkhepo paravādissa. Puna puṭṭho yasmā puññavipāke ṭhitattā vipākapaṭisaṃvedī puttaṃ vā patiṃ vā mātā vā jāyā vā paricumbati parisajjati, tasmā tathārūpaṃ paṭisaṃveditaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti paravādī.

138. By 'an experiencer of that,' an experiencer of that experiencer of the result is meant. Since what is to be experienced is the result, and a person is not the result, therefore the opponent rejects it. When questioned again, because one is established in the result of merit, the experiencer of the result kisses or embraces a son, husband, mother, or wife. Therefore, with reference to such an experience, the opponent acknowledges it.

Tassa [V 0.0129] tassevāti yadi vipāko vipākamattaṃ na hoti, tassa pana paṭisaṃvedī puggalo, tassāpi paṭisaṃvedī tassāpi paṭisaṃvedīti evaṃ puggalaparamparā atthi. Evaṃ sante yā esā vipākavaṭṭassa appavattikaraṇena dukkhassa antakiriyā vuttā, sā natthīti attho. Ito paraṃ upalabbhatisāmaññena paṭisaṃvedīpucchāsu heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo.

By 'for that very one,' if the result is not merely the result, but there is a person as its experiencer, and an experiencer of that one, and an experiencer of that one—thus there is a succession of persons. This being so, that making an end of suffering, which is spoken of as being brought about by the non-continuation of the cycle of results, would not exist—this is the meaning. From here on, in questions about the experiencer, the meaning should be understood in the same way as stated above, in accordance with the general term 'is found'.

142. Añño kalyāṇapāpakānaṃ kammānaṃ vipākapaṭisaṃvedīti pañho “vedanavantaṃ vā attāna”ntiādidiṭṭhibhayā paṭikkhitto.

142. The question, "Is another the experiencer of the results of good and bad actions?" is rejected due to the fear of views such as "the self possesses feeling," etc.

143. Dibbaṃ sukhantiādi kalyāṇapāpakānaṃ kammānaṃ vipākaṃ bhājetvā dassanavasena āraddhaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Sakavādino cettha puggalavaseneva paṭisaṃvedīpaṭikkhepo veditabbo, na vedayitavasena.

143. "Divine pleasure," etc., is begun by way of showing the classification of the results of good and bad actions. All this should be understood in the same way as previously stated. Here, the proponent's rejection of an experiencer should be understood as being on the basis of a person, not on the basis of what is felt.

148. Mahāpathavīādīni hi ārammaṇaṃ katvā vedayitānaṃ uppatti appaṭisiddhā.

148. For the arising of experiences, having taken objects such as the great earth element, is not denied.

170. Kattā kāretā vipākapaṭisaṃvedītiādi vomissakanayavasena āraddhaṃ. Tattha so karotīti yaṃ tvaṃ kattāti ca paṭisaṃvedīti ca vadesi, kiṃ soyeva karoti, so paṭisaṃvedeti. Ayamanuyogo sakavādissa, suttavirodhabhayena paṭikkhepo paravādissa.

170. 'The doer, the instigator, the experiencer of the result,' etc., is begun by way of the mixed method. Here, 'Does he act?' means: that which you call 'doer' and 'experiencer,' does that very one act, does that one experience? This inquiry is the proponent's; the opponent's rejection is due to fear of contradicting the suttas.

171. Puna [M 0.0135] puṭṭho “idha nandati pecca nandatī”tiādisuttavasena (dha. pa. 18) paṭiññā tasseva. Athassa vacanokāsaṃ paṭibāhanto sakavādī sayaṃkataṃ sukhadukkhanti [P 0.0032] āha.

171. When questioned again, his admission is based on the sutta beginning, 'Here he rejoices, hereafter he rejoices' (Dhammapada 18). Then, obstructing his opportunity to speak, the proponent states that pleasure and pain are self-made.

172. Tattha añño karotīti kārakavedakānaṃ aññattapucchāvasena vuttaṃ. Tato paravādī suttavirodhabhayena paṭikkhipitvā puna puṭṭho “manussabhūto katvā devabhūto paṭisaṃvedetī”ti maññamāno paṭijānāti[V 0.0130]. Evaṃvādino pana paraṃkataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ āpajjatīti tassa vasena puṭṭho puna paṭikkhipati.

172. Here, 'Does another act?' is stated by way of a question about the otherness of the agent and the experiencer. Thereupon, the opponent, fearing contradiction with the suttas, rejects it. But when asked again, he concedes, thinking, 'Having acted as a human, one experiences as a deva.' However, for one who speaks thus, it follows that pleasure and pain are made by another. Questioned on that basis, he rejects it again.

174. So ca añño cāti kārakavedakānaṃ ekattaaññattapucchāvasena vuttaṃ. Tato paravādī suttavirodhabhayeneva paṭikkhipitvā puna puṭṭho purime dvepi naye ekato katvā paṭijānāti. Evaṃvādino pana sayaṃkatañca paraṃkatañca sukhadukkhaṃ āpajjatīti tassa vasena puṭṭho puna paṭikkhipati.

174. "Is it that one and another?" is stated by way of a question about the oneness and otherness of the agent and the experiencer. Thereupon, the opponent, fearing contradiction with the suttas, rejects it. But when questioned again, he combines the two previous methods and concedes. However, for one who speaks thus, it follows that pleasure and pain are both self-made and other-made. Questioned on that basis, he rejects it again.

176. Neva so karotīti kārakavedakānaṃ ekattaaññattapaṭikkhepavasena vuttaṃ. Tato paravādī suttavirodhavaseneva paṭikkhipitvā puna puṭṭho yasmā manusso devalokūpapattiyā kammaṃ katvā na manussabhūtova paṭisaṃvedeti, nāpi yena kammaṃ kataṃ, tato aññova paṭisaṃvedeti, tasmā kārakato vedako neva so hoti, na aññoti maññamāno paṭijānāti. Laddhimattamevetaṃ? Evaṃvādino pana asayaṃkāraṃ aparaṃkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ āpajjatīti tassa vasena puṭṭho puna paṭikkhipati. Apica imasmiṃ vomissakanaye ādito paṭṭhāya imināpi nayena attho veditabbo. Yasmā hi ayaṃ puggalavādī kammānaṃ kārakañceva vedakañca icchati, tasmāssa yo kārako, teneva vā vedakena bhavitabbaṃ, aññena vā ubhohi vā bhavitabbaṃ, ubhohi vāpi na bhavitabbanti idamāpannaṃ hoti. Evamāpannameva anuyogaṃ anuyuñjanto sakavādī “so karotī”tiādayo cattāropi vikappe āha. Sesaṃ vuttappakārameva.

176. "He does not act" is stated by way of rejecting the identity and difference of the doer and the experiencer of deeds. Then, the opponent, having refuted it precisely on the grounds of contradicting the suttas, when questioned again, asserts, thinking it to be so, that since a human, having performed deeds leading to rebirth in the heavenly world, does not experience it in the human state, nor does someone other than the one who performed the deeds experience it, therefore, from the perspective of the doer, the experiencer is neither the same nor another. Is this merely a view? However, proponents of this view, when further questioned on the basis that pleasure and pain arise without self-causation, without other-causation, or are accidentally produced, again reject it. Moreover, in this mixed method, the meaning should be understood from the beginning in this way as well. For since this personalist desires that there be both a doer and an experiencer of actions, it follows for him that the experiencer must either be the same as the doer, or another, or both, or neither—this dilemma arises. Engaging in this very dilemma, the proponent of his own doctrine states the four alternatives beginning with "he acts," etc. The rest is as previously explained.

Pariyosāne pana cattāropi pañhā ekato puṭṭhā. Tattha paṭikkhepo ca paṭijānanā ca sayaṃkatādidosappatti ca purimanayeneva veditabbā. Ito [M 0.0136] paraṃ “kalyāṇapāpakānī”ti avatvā heṭṭhā vuttanayā eva “kammaṃ atthī”tiādinā vikappena dassitā. Tesampi heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo.

At the conclusion, however, all four questions are asked together. There, the rejection, the assertion, and the arising of faults such as self-making are to be understood in the same way as before. From here onward, instead of stating "good and evil," the alternatives are shown by the method previously mentioned, with "there is kamma," etc. Their meaning should also be understood in the way previously explained.

Purisakārānuyogavaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Inquiry into Human Effort.

Kalyāṇavaggotipi etasseva nāmaṃ.

The Chapter on the Good is also its name.

14. Abhiññānuyogavaṇṇanā

14. The Explanation of the Inquiry into Direct Knowledge.

193. Ito [P 0.0033] paraṃ abhiññānuyogādivasena arahattasādhanā hoti. Tattha āmantāti sakavādinā paṭiññāte paravādī “bahiddhā anindriyabaddharūpe iddhividhādivisesādhigamo natthi, ajjhattaṃ [V 0.0131] atthi, tasmā iddhādinibbattakena puggalena bhavitabba”nti maññamāno nanu atthi koci iddhiṃ vikubbatītiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ uttānatthameva.

193. From here onward, the attainment of arahantship is accomplished by way of the inquiry into direct knowledge, and so on. Here, when the proponent of his own doctrine affirms, 'Yes,' the opponent, thinking, "There is no attainment of special powers like psychic abilities, etc., in external forms not bound by the senses, but internally there is; therefore, there must be a person who produces psychic powers, etc.," asks, "Is there not someone who performs psychic powers?" etc. All this is clear in meaning.

Abhiññānuyogavaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Inquiry into Direct Knowledge.

15-18. Ñātakānuyogādivaṇṇanā

15-18. The Explanation of the Inquiry into Relatives, and so on.

197. Idāni mātātiādiko ñātakānuyogo. Khattiyotiādiko jātianuyogo. Gahaṭṭho pabbajitoti paṭipattianuyogo. Devo manussoti upapattianuyogo. Sotāpannotiādiko paṭivedhānuyogo, ariyānuyogotipi vuccati. Te sabbe uttānatthāyeva. “Arahā hutvā na arahā”ti panettha moghapañhattā na vuttaṃ.

197. Now, the inquiry into relatives begins with "mother," and so on. The inquiry into caste begins with "khattiya," and so on. The inquiry into practice is "householder or renunciate." The inquiry into rebirth is "deva or human being." The inquiry into penetration begins with "stream-enterer," and so on; it is also called the noble inquiry. All these are clear in meaning. Here, "having been an arahant, is not an arahant" is not stated because of it being a vain pronouncement.

206. Cattāro purisayugātiādi saṃghānuyogo, sopi uttānatthoyeva.

206. "The four pairs of persons," etc., is the inquiry into the Sangha, and its meaning is also clear.

209. Saṅkhatotiādi saccikaṭṭhasabhāvānuyogo. Tattha tatiyā koṭīti pucchā sakavādissa. Tathārūpassa saccikaṭṭhassa abhāvato paṭikkhepo paravādissa. Puna puṭṭho puggalaṃ sandhāya paṭiññā tasseva.

209. "Conditioned," etc., is the inquiry into the nature of ultimate reality. Here, the third category is a question for the proponent of his own doctrine. The rejection is by the opponent due to the absence of such an ultimate reality. When questioned again, the assertion is his, referring to the person.

211. Añño [M 0.0137] puggalotipañhepi saṅkhatehi khandhehi aññattaṃ anicchanto paṭikkhepo tasseva.

211. In the question "is the person another?" as well, the rejection is his, as he does not desire difference from the conditioned aggregates.

212. Khandhā saṅkhatātiādi saṅkhatāsaṅkhatāni sarūpena dassetvā aññattapucchanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

212. "The aggregates are conditioned," etc., is stated to show the conditioned and unconditioned in their own nature, for the purpose of asking about difference.

213. Rūpaṃ saṅkhatantiādi khandhe vibhāgato dassetvā aññattapucchanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

213. "Form is conditioned," etc., is stated after showing the aggregates in detail, for the purpose of inquiring about difference.

214. Puggalassa uppādoti pucchā sakavādissa, “jātidhammā jarādhammā, atho maraṇadhammino”tiādisuttavasena [V 0.0132] paṭiññā paravādissa. Saṅkhatabhāvaṃ panassa so na icchati, tasmā paṭikkhipati.

214. The question 'Is there the arising of a person?' is for the proponent of his own doctrine, while the opponent's assertion is by way of suttas such as, "Subject to birth, subject to aging, and also subject to death." But he does not desire its conditioned nature; therefore, he rejects it.

215. Puna na uppādo paññāyatītiādinā nayena puṭṭho “dukkhameva hi sambhoti[P 0.0034], dukkhaṃ tiṭṭhati veti cā”tiādivacanato (saṃ. ni. 1.171) puggalassa uppādādayo nāma na yujjantīti paṭijānāti.

215. Again, when questioned in the manner of "No arising is discerned," and so on, he declares, based on the statement, "Only suffering arises, suffering remains and passes away" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.171), that notions like the arising of a person, etc., are not tenable.

216. Atthatthamhīti atthaṃ vuccati nibbānaṃ. Tattha atthīti pucchati. Tassa atthitāya sassataṃ, natthitāya. Ucchedo āpajjati. Tadubhayampi anicchanto pacchā paṭikkhipati.

216. In 'Is there the goal?', 'goal' is said to be Nibbāna. Therein, one asks, 'Does it exist?' By its existence, eternalism follows; by its non-existence, annihilationism. Not desiring either of these two, one later rejects it.

Ñātakānuyogādivaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Inquiry into Relatives, and So On.

19. Paṭivedhānuyogādivaṇṇanā

19. The Explanation of the Inquiry into Penetration, and so forth.

217. Bhavaṃ nissāya pañhe bhavanti upapattibhavaṃ.

217. Dependent on existence—that is, rebirth-existence—questions arise.

218. Vedanaṃ vediyamānapañhe vedanaṃ vediyamāno pariggahitavedano yogāvacarova pajānāti, bālaputhujjano nappajānāti.

218. In the question about experiencing a feeling, only a practitioner who has comprehended feeling understands while experiencing a feeling; a foolish ordinary person does not understand.

224. Kāyānupassanādipañhā uttānatthāyeva.

224. The questions on the contemplation of the body, and so forth, are indeed straightforward in meaning.

226. Pārāyanagāthāya [M 0.0138] suññato lokaṃ avekkhassūti sattasuññatavasena khandhalokaṃ olokehīti attho.

226. In the Pārāyana verses, "Look upon the world as empty" means: "Observe the world of aggregates by way of the seven kinds of emptiness."

228. Puggalo avekkhatīti sakavādipucchā. Paravādissa hi “suññato lokaṃ avekkhassū”ti gāthāya yo avekkhati, so puggaloti laddhi, tasmā naṃ evaṃ pucchati. Saha rūpenāti [V 0.0133] rūpakāyena saddhiṃ. Tato anissaṭo hutvāti attho. Idaṃ pañcavokāravasena anujānitvā puna taṃ jīvanti puṭṭho suttavirodhabhayena paṭikkhipati. Vinā rūpenāti idaṃ catuvokāravasena anujānitvā puna aññaṃ jīvanti puṭṭho suttavirodhabhayeneva paṭikkhipati. “Abbhantaragato”ti ca “bahiddhā nikkhamitvā”ti ca idaṃ “saha rūpena vinā rūpenā”ti heṭṭhā vuttassa lakkhaṇavacanaṃ. Tattha abbhantaragatoti rūpassa antogato, ito vā etto vā anikkhamitvā rūpaparicchedavaseneva ṭhito hutvāti attho. Nikkhamitvāti rūpaparicchedaṃ atikkamitvā. Rūpaṃ anissito hutvāti attho.

228. The question, 'Does a person observe?' is from the proponent of his own doctrine. For the opponent's view is that the one who observes in the verse 'Look upon the world as empty' is a person; therefore, he is asked thus. 'Together with form' means along with the body of form. The meaning is 'not having departed from it.' This is acknowledged in terms of the five-constituent existence, but when asked further, 'Is that the soul?' he rejects it out of fear of contradicting the suttas. 'Without form' is acknowledged in terms of the four-constituent existence, but when asked, 'Is the soul another?' he again rejects it for the same reason of fear of contradicting the suttas. 'Entered within' and 'gone outside' are descriptive terms for what was earlier stated as 'together with form' and 'without form.' Here, 'entered within' means having entered inside form, remaining within the confines of form without departing from here or there. 'Gone outside' means having transcended the confines of form—that is, being unsupported by form.

231. Anattāti attanā jīvena puggalena rahito. Ekadhammepi puggalo natthīti attho. Evaṃ sabbasuttānaṃ āgamaṭṭhakathāsu vuttanayeneva [P 0.0035] attho veditabbo. Idha pana sandhāyabhāsitamattameva vakkhāma.

231. "Not-self" means devoid of a self, a living soul, or a person. The meaning is that not even in a single phenomenon is there a person. Thus, the meaning should be understood in accordance with the method stated in the commentaries on all the suttas. Here, however, we will only speak of what is spoken with reference to something else.

237. Vuttaṃ bhagavatā sappikumbhotiādi “sabbāva desanā yathārutavaseneva atthato na gahetabbā”ti dassanatthaṃ ābhataṃ. Yathā hi suvaṇṇaṃ gahetvā kato suvaṇṇavikāro kumbho suvaṇṇakumbhoti vuccati, na evaṃ sappiṃ gahetvā kato sappissa vikāro sappikumbho nāma atthi. Yasmiṃ pana kumbhe sappi pakkhittaṃ, so sappikumbho nāmāti ayamettha attho. Telakumbhādīsupi eseva nayo. Yathā ca nibbānaṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ, na evaṃ bhattaṃ vā yāgu vā atthi. Kālaparicchedaṃ pana akatvā divase divase dassāmāti paññattavasena “niccabhattaṃ dhuvayāgū”ti vuccatīti ayamettha attho.

237. What was said by the Blessed One, "a pot of ghee," and so forth, is adduced to show that "the entire teaching should not be taken literally according to the words themselves." Just as a golden vessel made by taking gold, a transformation of gold, is called a golden vessel, so there is no such thing as a ghee vessel made by taking ghee, a transformation of ghee. But a vessel in which ghee is placed is called a ghee vessel—this is the meaning here. The same principle applies to oil vessels, and so forth. And just as Nibbāna is permanent and lasting, so food or gruel is not. However, without stipulating a time limit, but declaring, "We will give daily," it is conventionally called "permanent food, lasting gruel"—this is the meaning here.

“Atthi puggalo attahitāya paṭipanno”tiādīsupi yathā rūpādayo dhammā paccattalakkhaṇasāmaññalakkhaṇavasena atthi, na evaṃ puggalo[M 0.0139]. Rūpādīsu pana sati ‘evaṃnāmo’‘evaṃgotto’ti vohāro hoti. Iti iminā lokavohārena lokasammutiyā lokaniruttiyā atthi puggaloti ayamettha attho. Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā – “imā kho citta, lokasamaññā lokaniruttiyo lokavohārā lokapaññattiyo”ti (dī. ni. 1.440). Rūpādidhammā pana vināpi lokasammutiṃ paccattasāmaññalakkhaṇavasena paññāpanato atthīti ayamettha attho.

"There is a person who practices for their own welfare," and so forth—in such statements, just as phenomena like form and so forth exist by way of individual characteristic and general characteristic, the person does not exist in the same way. However, when there is form and so forth, conventional expressions like "so-and-so by name" or "of such-and-such clan" are used. Thus, in this context, the meaning is that a person exists by worldly expression, worldly convention, and worldly designation. This has also been stated by the Blessed One: "These, Citta, are worldly conventions, worldly designations, worldly expressions, worldly concepts" (DN 9). But phenomena like form and so forth are established as existing by their individual and general characteristics, even without worldly convention—this is the meaning here.

Buddhānaṃ [V 0.0134] pana dve kathā sammutikathā ca paramatthakathā ca. Tattha satto, puggalo, devo, brahmātiādikā sammutikathā nāma. Aniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ, anattā, khandhā, dhātuyo, āyatanāni, satipaṭṭhānā, sammappadhānātiādikā paramatthakathā nāma.

For the Buddhas, there are two kinds of discourse: conventional discourse and ultimate discourse. Of these, conventional discourse includes terms like "being," "person," "deva," "Brahmā," and so forth. Ultimate discourse includes terms like "impermanent," "suffering," "not-self," "aggregates," "elements," "sense bases," "foundations of mindfulness," "right exertions," and so forth.

Tattha yo sammutidesanāya sattoti vā…pe… brahmāti vāti vutte jānituṃ paṭivijjhituṃ niyyātuṃ arahattajayaggāhaṃ gahetuṃ sakkoti, tassa bhagavā āditova sattoti vā puggaloti vā posoti vā devoti vā brahmāti vā katheti. Yo paramatthadesanāya aniccanti vā dukkhanti vātiādīsu aññataraṃ sutvāva jānituṃ paṭivijjhituṃ niyyātuṃ arahattajayaggāhaṃ gahetuṃ sakkoti. Tassa aniccantiādīsu aññataraṃ katheti. Tathā sammutikathāya bujjhanakasattassa na paṭhamaṃ paramatthakathaṃ katheti. Sammutikathāya pana bodhetvā pacchā paramatthakathaṃ katheti[P 0.0036]. Paramatthakathāya bujjhanakasattassāpi na paṭhamaṃ sammutikathaṃ katheti. Paramatthakathāya pana bodhetvā pacchā sammutikathaṃ katheti. Pakatiyā pana paṭhamameva paramatthakathaṃ kathentassa desanā lūkhākārā hoti. Tasmā buddhā paṭhamaṃ sammutikathaṃ kathetvā pacchā paramatthakathaṃ kathenti. Te sammutikathaṃ kathentāpi saccameva sabhāvameva amusāva kathenti. Paramatthakathaṃ kathentāpi saccameva sabhāvameva amusāva kathenti. Ayañhi –

Here, if someone is capable of understanding, penetrating, emerging, and grasping the victory of arahantship when "being," or...or "Brahmā" is spoken in the conventional teaching, the Blessed One initially teaches them using terms like "being," "person," "individual," "deva," or "Brahmā." If someone is capable of understanding, penetrating, emerging, and grasping the victory of arahantship merely upon hearing one of the ultimate teachings, such as "impermanent" or "suffering," and so forth, the Blessed One teaches them one of these, such as "impermanent." Similarly, for a being who awakens through conventional discourse, the Buddha does not teach ultimate discourse first. Rather, after awakening them through conventional discourse, he later teaches ultimate discourse. Likewise, for a being who awakens through ultimate discourse, the Buddha does not teach conventional discourse first. Rather, after awakening them through ultimate discourse, he later teaches conventional discourse. By nature, if one teaches ultimate discourse first, the teaching becomes harsh in manner. Therefore, the Buddhas first teach conventional discourse and later ultimate discourse. Even when teaching conventional discourse, they speak only what is true, factual, and not false. Likewise, when teaching ultimate discourse, they speak only what is true, factual, and not false. For it is said:

“Duve saccāni akkhāsi, sambuddho vadataṃ varo;

Sammutiṃ paramatthañca, tatiyaṃ nupalabbhati”.

"The Fully Enlightened One, the best of speakers, proclaimed two truths: conventional truth and ultimate truth; a third is not found."

Tattha [M 0.0140] –

Therein:

“Saṅketavacanaṃ saccaṃ, lokasammutikāraṇaṃ;

Paramatthavacanaṃ saccaṃ, dhammānaṃ tathalakkhaṇa”nti.

"Conventional speech is true, being the cause of worldly convention. Ultimate speech is true, being the actual characteristic of phenomena."

Aparo nayo – dve bhagavato desanā paramatthadesanā ca khandhādivasena, sammutidesanā ca sappikumbhādivasena. Na hi bhagavā samaññaṃ atidhāvati. Tasmā “atthi puggalo”ti vacanamattato abhiniveso na kātabbo. Satthārā hi –

Another approach: The Blessed One's teaching is twofold—ultimate teaching, such as in terms of the aggregates and so forth, and conventional teaching, such as in terms of "a pot of ghee" and so forth. For the Blessed One does not transgress convention. Therefore, one should not form an attachment based on the mere statement "there is a person." For the Teacher has said:

“Paññattiṃ [V 0.0135] anatikkamma, paramattho pakāsito;

Samaññaṃ nātidhāveyya, tasmā aññopi paṇḍito;

Paramatthaṃ pakāsento, samaññaṃ nātidhāvaye”.

"Without transgressing convention, the ultimate is revealed. One should not overstep convention; therefore, another wise person, while revealing the ultimate, should not overstep convention."

Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

The rest is of clear meaning everywhere.

Puggalakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Person is concluded.

2. Parihānikathā

2. The Discourse on Decline

1. Vādayuttiparihānivaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of Decline in Argumentation

239. Idāni [M 0.0141][V 0.0136] parihānikathā hoti. Parihānidhammo aparihānidhammo, “dveme, bhikkhave, dhammā sekkhassa, bhikkhuno parihānāya saṃvattanti” (a. ni. 2.185), “pañcime, bhikkhave, dhammā [P 0.0037] samayavimuttassa bhikkhuno parihānāya saṃvattantī”ti (a. ni. 5.149) evamādīni hi suttāni nissāya sammitiyā vajjiputtakā sabbatthivādino ekacce ca mahāsaṅghikā arahatopi parihāniṃ icchanti, tasmā te vā hontu aññeyeva vā, yesaṃ ayaṃ laddhi, tesaṃ laddhibhindanatthaṃ parihāyati arahā arahattāti pucchā sakavādissa. Tatra parihāyatīti dve parihāniyo pattaparihāni ca appattaparihāni ca. Tattha “dutiyampi kho āyasmā godhiko tamhā sāmayikāya cetovimuttiyā parihāyī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.159) ayaṃ pattaparihāni nāma. “Mā vo sāmaññatthikānaṃ sataṃ sāmaññattho parihāyī”ti (ma. ni. 1.416-418) ayaṃ appattaparihāni. Tāsu idha pattaparihāni adhippetā. Tañhi sandhāya āmantāti paṭiññā paravādissa. Sakasamaye pana imaṃ pattaparihāniṃ nāma lokiyasamāpattiyāva icchanti, na arahattādīhi sāmaññaphalehi. Parasamayepi naṃ sabbasāmaññaphalesu sabbabhavesu sabbakālesu sabbesañca puggalānaṃ na icchanti. Taṃ pana tesaṃ laddhimattamevāti sabbaṃ laddhijālaṃ bhindituṃ puna sabbatthātiādinā nayena desanā vaḍḍhitā.

239. Now there is a discussion on decline. There is the quality of decline and the quality of non-decline. Based on such discourses as, “These two things, monks, lead to the decline of a bhikkhu in training” (A. 2.185), and “These five things, monks, lead to the decline of a bhikkhu liberated at times” (A. 5.149), the Sammityas, the Vajjiputtakas, the Sabbatthivādins, and some Mahāsaṅghikas hold that even an arahant can decline. Therefore, whether it be they or any others who hold this view, to shatter their view, the proponent's question is: “Does an arahant decline from arahantship?” Here, “decline” is of two kinds: decline from what has been attained and decline from what has not been attained. In this context, “For a second time, the Venerable Godhika declined from that temporary liberation of mind” (S. 1.159) is called decline from what has been attained. “May the goal of asceticism not decline for you who are seekers of the ascetic goal” (M. 1.416-418) is decline from what has not been attained. Of these, decline from what has been attained is intended here. In reference to this, the opponent's admission is 'Yes'. However, in our own doctrine, this 'decline from what has been attained' is accepted only with regard to mundane attainments, not with regard to the fruits of asceticism such as arahantship. And even in the opponent's doctrine, they do not accept it for all fruits of asceticism, in all states of existence, at all times, and for all individuals. But since this is merely their view, to dismantle this entire web of views, the discourse is further developed by the method beginning with “in all cases,” and so on.

Tattha yasmā paravādī kamena parihāyitvā sotāpattiphale ṭhitassa arahato parihāniṃ na icchati, upariphalesu ṭhitasseva icchati. Yasmā ca rūpārūpabhavesu ṭhitassa na icchati, kammārāmatādīnaṃ pana parihāniyadhammānaṃ bhāvato kāmabhave ṭhitasseva icchati, tasmā “sabbatthā”ti [V 0.0137] puṭṭho paṭikkhipati. Puna daḷhaṃ katvā puṭṭho kāmabhavaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Sabbasmimpi hi kāmabhave parihānikarā kāmaguṇā atthi, tasmā tattha parihāyatīti tassa laddhi.

There, because the opponent does not accept that an arahant, who is established in the fruit of stream-entry, can decline from it, but accepts decline only for one established in the higher fruits; and because he does not accept decline for one established in the realms of form or formlessness, but accepts it only for one established in the realm of sensual existence—due to the presence of qualities conducive to decline, such as delight in activity—therefore, when asked “in all cases,” he denies it. When questioned firmly again, however, he admits it with reference to the realm of sensual existence. For in the entire realm of sensual existence there are sensual qualities that cause decline; thus, his view is that one declines there.

Tatiyapucchāya [M 0.0142] parihānīti parihānikare dhamme pucchati. Tattha yasmā parihāni nāma kammārāmatādidhammā, visesato vā kāmarāgabyāpādā eva, te ca rūpārūpabhave natthi, tasmā “na heva”nti paṭikkhepo paravādissa.

In the third question, by ‘decline,’ he asks about the factors that cause decline. Here, since decline refers to states such as delight in activity and the like, or specifically to sensual lust and ill-will, and these do not exist in the realms of form and formlessness, therefore the opponent’s rejection is, “Certainly not.”

Sabbadāti kālapucchā. Tattha paṭhamapañhe yonisomanasikārakāle aparihāyanato paṭikkhipati. Dutiye ayonisomanasikaroto rattibhāge vā divasabhāge vā sabbadā parihāyanato paṭijānāti. Tatiye parihānikaradhammasamāyoge [P 0.0038] sati muhuttameva parihāni nāma hoti, tato pubbe aparihīnassa pacchā parihīnassa ca parihāni nāma natthīti paṭikkhipati.

“Always” is a question about time. There, in the first question, he rejects it because one does not decline at a time of wise attention. In the second, he accepts it because one who applies unwise attention declines at all times, whether during the day or during the night. In the third, he rejects it, stating that decline occurs only for a moment when there is an association with qualities that cause decline, and that there is no such thing as decline for one before having declined or for one after having declined.

Sabbeva arahantoti pañhānaṃ paṭhamasmiṃ tikkhindriye sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Dutiyasmiṃ mudindriye sandhāya paṭijānāti. Tatiyasmimpi tikkhindriyāva adhippetā. Tesañhi sabbesampi parihāni na hotīti tassa laddhi.

Regarding the questions about ‘all arahants’: in the first, he rejects it, with reference to one with sharp faculties. In the second, he accepts it, with reference to one with dull faculties. In the third also, those with sharp faculties are intended. For his view is that for all of them, there is no decline.

Seṭṭhiudāharaṇe paṭhamapucchā paravādissa, dutiyā sakavādissa. Tatrāyaṃ adhippāyo – yaṃ maṃ tumhe pucchatha – “arahā arahattā parihāyanto catūhi phalehi parihāyatī”ti, tatra vo paṭipucchāmi – “catūhi satasahassehi seṭṭhī seṭṭhittaṃ karonto satasahassehi parihīne seṭṭhī seṭṭhittā parihīno hotī”ti. Tato sakavādinā ekadesena parihāniṃ sandhāya “āmantā”ti vutte sabbasāpateyyā parihīno hotīti pucchati. Tathā aparihīnattā sakavādī na hevāti vatvā atha naṃ “evameva arahāpi parihāyati ca. Na ca catūhi phalehī”ti uppannaladdhikaṃ dutiyaṃ bhabbapañhaṃ pucchati. Paravādī seṭṭhino abhabbatāya niyamaṃ apassanto paṭijānitvā arahato catūhi phalehi parihānibhabbataṃ puṭṭho “niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo”ti (a. ni. 3.87) vacanassa ayoniso atthaṃ gahetvā laddhiyaṃ ṭhito sotāpattiphalato parihāyituṃ abhabbataṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Taṃ panassa laddhimattamevāti.

In the example of the wealthy man, the first question is the opponent's, the second is the proponent's. Here is the meaning: You ask me, “Does an arahant, in declining from arahantship, decline from the four fruits?” To that I ask you in return: “Does a wealthy man, being wealthy with four hundred thousand, become bereft of his wealth when he has lost one hundred thousand?” Then, when the proponent, referring to a partial decline, says, “Yes,” the opponent asks if he is bereft of all his property. Because he is not bereft in that way, the proponent says, “Certainly not,” and then asks him the second question, a question of possibility which arises from the established view: “In the same way, an arahant declines, but not from the four fruits?” The opponent, not seeing any fixed rule regarding the wealthy man’s impossibility of losing everything, concedes. Then, being asked about the possibility of an arahant declining from the four fruits, he, standing on his own view and having unwisely grasped the meaning of the statement, “He is certain, destined for enlightenment” (A. 3.87), rejects it, with reference to the impossibility of declining from the fruit of stream-entry. But this is merely his view.

Ettāvatā vādayutti nāma niṭṭhitā hoti.

With this, the section on the logic of the debate is concluded.

2. Ariyapuggalasaṃsandanaparihānivaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of Decline and the Comparison of Noble Individuals.

240. Idāni [M 0.0143][V 0.0138] ariyapuggalasaṃsandanā āraddhā. Tattha yasmā keci arahatova parihāniṃ icchanti, keci anāgāminopi, keci sakadāgāmissapi. Sotāpannassa pana sabbepi na icchantiyeva. Ye arahattā parihāyitvā anāgāmisakadāgāmibhāve ṭhitā, tesaṃ parihāniṃ icchanti, na itaresaṃ anāgāmisakadāgāmīnaṃ. Sotāpannassa [P 0.0039] pana tepi sabbathāpi na icchantiyeva, tasmā peyyālamukhena pucchā katā. Tattha tesaṃ laddhivasena paṭiññā ca paṭikkhepo ca veditabbā. “Parihāyati anāgāmī anāgāmiphalā”ti hi pañhasmiṃ ye anāgāmino parihāniṃ na icchanti, tesaṃ vasena paṭikkhepo. Ye pakatianāgāmino vā arahattā parihāyitvā ṭhitaanāgāmino vā parihāniṃ icchanti, tesaṃ vasena paṭiññāti idamettha nayamukhaṃ. Tassānusārena sabbapeyyālā atthato veditabbā.

240. Now the comparison of noble individuals is commenced. Herein, some posit the decline of only arahants, some of non-returners also, and some of once-returners also. However, all are agreed that a stream-enterer does not decline. They posit the decline of those who have fallen from arahantship and remain in the state of non-returners or once-returners, but not that of other non-returners or once-returners. As for a stream-enterer, even they do not posit their decline at all. Therefore, the question is posed by way of a repetitive series. Herein, their affirmation and denial should be understood according to their doctrine. In the question, “Does a non-returner decline from the fruit of non-returning?” the denial is from the perspective of those who do not posit the decline of non-returners. The affirmation is from the perspective of those who posit the decline of ordinary non-returners or those who have fallen from arahantship and remain as non-returners. This is the guiding principle here. Following this principle, all the repetitive series should be understood in terms of their meaning.

241. Yaṃ panettha “sotāpattiphalassa anantarā arahattaṃyeva sacchikarotī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ parihīnassa puna vāyamato arahattappattiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Itaro sotāpattiphalānantaraṃ arahattassa abhāvā paṭikkhipati.

241. However, the statement here, “Immediately after the fruit of stream-entry, one realizes arahantship,” was said with reference to the attainment of arahantship by one who has declined and strives again. The other rejects it because arahantship is not attained immediately after the fruit of stream-entry.

242. Tato paraṃ “parihāni nāmesā kilesappahānassa vā mandatāya bhaveyya, maggabhāvanādīnaṃ vā anadhimattatāya, saccānaṃ vā adassanenā”ti evamādīnaṃ vasena anuyuñjituṃ kassa bahutarā kilesā pahīnātiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ uttānādhippāyameva suttānaṃ panattho āgamaṭṭhakathāsu vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

242. After that, in order to inquire by such means as, “This decline could be due to weakness in abandoning defilements, or to the insufficient development of the path and so on, or to the non-seeing of the truths,” and so forth, it was said, “For whom have more defilements been abandoned?” and so on. All of this is of plain intent. However, the meaning of the suttas should be understood according to the method stated in the commentaries on the scriptures.

262. Samayavimutto arahā arahattā parihāyatīti ettha mudindriyo samayavimutto, tikkhindriyo asamayavimuttoti tesaṃ laddhi. Sakasamaye pana avasippatto jhānalābhī samayavimutto, vasippatto jhānalābhī ceva sabbe ca ariyapuggalā ariye vimokkhe asamayavimuttāti sanniṭṭhānaṃ. So pana taṃ attano laddhiṃ gahetvā samayavimutto [M 0.0144] parihāyati, itaro na parihāyatī”ti āha. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

262. In the question, “Does a temporarily liberated arahant fall away from arahantship?” their view is that an arahant with dull faculties is temporarily liberated, while one with sharp faculties is non-temporarily liberated. In our own doctrine, however, the established conclusion is that an attainer of jhāna who has not achieved mastery is temporarily liberated, while an attainer of jhāna who has achieved mastery, as well as all noble individuals, are non-temporarily liberated in the noble emancipations. But he, holding to his own view, says, “The temporarily liberated one falls away, while the other does not.” The rest here is of plain meaning.

Ariyapuggalasaṃsandanaparihānivaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Comparison of Noble Individuals with regard to Decline.

3. Suttasādhanaparihānivaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of Proving Decline by means of the Suttas

265. Idāni [V 0.0139] suttasādhanā hoti. Tattha uccāvacāti uttamahīnabhedato uccā ca avacā ca. Paṭipādāti paṭipadā. Samaṇena pakāsitāti buddhasamaṇena jotitā. Sukhāpaṭipadā hi khippābhiññā uccā. Dukkhāpaṭipadā dandhābhiññā avacā. Itarā dve ekenaṅgena [P 0.0040] uccā, ekena avacā. Paṭhamaṃ vuttā eva vā uccā, itaro tissopi avacā. Tāya cetāya uccāvacāya paṭipadāya na pāraṃ diguṇaṃ yanti, ekamaggena dvikkhattuṃ nibbānaṃ na gacchantīti attho. Kasmā? Yena maggena ye kilesā pahīnā, tena tesaṃ puna appahātabbato. Etena parihānidhammābhāvaṃ dīpeti. Nayidaṃ ekaguṇaṃ mutanti tañca idaṃ pāraṃ ekavāraṃyeva phusanārahaṃ na hoti. Kasmā? Ekena maggena sabbakilesānaṃ appahānato. Etena ekamaggeneva arahattābhāvaṃ dīpeti.

265. Now the proof by means of the suttas is presented. Herein, “various” (uccāvacā) means both high (uccā) and low (avacā) by way of the distinction between superior and inferior. “Practice” (paṭipādā) means the path. “Declared by the ascetic” (samaṇena pakāsitā) means illuminated by the Buddha, the Ascetic. The pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge is high; the painful practice with slow direct knowledge is low. The other two are high in one aspect and low in another. Or, the first mentioned is high, and the other three are low. By these various practices, they do not go to the far shore twice; that is, they do not attain Nibbāna twice by one and the same path. Why? Because the defilements abandoned by a certain path are not to be abandoned again by it. By this, he indicates the absence of a nature of decline. “Nor is this understood as a single attainment” (nayidaṃ ekaguṇaṃ mutaṃ)—and this far shore is not something that can be attained in a single instance. Why? Because not all defilements are abandoned by a single path. By this, he indicates the absence of attaining Arahantship by one path alone.

Atthi chinnassa chediyanti chinnassa kilesavaṭṭassa puna chinditabbaṃ kiñci atthīti pucchati. Itaro tikkhindriyaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipitvā puna puṭṭho mudindriyaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Sakavādī suttaṃ āharitvā natthibhāvaṃ dasseti. Tattha oghapāsoti kilesogho ceva kilesapāso ca.

“Is there anything to be cut for one who has already cut?” (Atthi chinnassa chediyaṃ?) This asks if there is anything to be cut again for one who has severed the cycle of defilements. The other, referring to one with keen faculties, denies it, but when asked again, he affirms it, referring to one with dull faculties. The proponent of his own doctrine cites a sutta to show its non-existence. There, “flood and noose” (ogha-pāso) means both the flood of defilements and the noose of defilements.

266. Katassa paṭicayoti bhāvitassa maggassa puna bhāvanā. Idhāpi paṭikkhepapaṭijānanāni purimanayeneva veditabbāni.

266. “Accumulation of what has been done” (katassa paṭicayo) means further cultivation of the path that has been developed. Here too, the denials and affirmations should be understood in the same way as before.

267. Parihānāya saṃvattantīti paravādinā ābhate sutte pañca dhammā appattaparihānāya ceva lokiyasamāpattiparihānāya ca saṃvattanti. So pana pattassa arahattaphalassa parihānāya sallakkheti. Teneva atthi arahato kammārāmatāti āha. Itaropi asamayavimuttaṃ [M 0.0145] sandhāya paṭikkhipitvā itaraṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Kāmarāgavasena vā pavattamānaṃ taṃ paṭikkhipitvā itarathā pavattamānaṃ paṭijānāti. Rāgādīnaṃ pana atthitaṃ puṭṭho paṭijānituṃ na sakkoti.

267. “Lead to decline” (parihānāya saṃvattanti)—in the sutta cited by the opponent, five things lead to the non-attainment of what has not been attained and to the decline from mundane attainments. But he considers them as leading to the decline from the fruit of Arahantship that has been attained. Therefore, he says, “There is delight in activity for an Arahant.” The other, denying this with reference to the non-temporarily liberated one, affirms it with reference to the other. Or, denying that which proceeds from sensual lust, he affirms that which proceeds otherwise. But when asked about the existence of lust and so on, he is unable to affirm it.

268. Kiṃ pariyuṭṭhitoti kena pariyuṭṭhito anubaddho ajjhotthato vā hutvāti attho. Anusayapucchāyapi tikkhindriyamudindriyavaseneva paṭikkhepapaṭijānanāni veditabbāni. Kalyāṇānusayoti [V 0.0140] vacanamattasāmaññena vā paṭijānāti. Rāgo upacayaṃ gacchatīti bhāvanāya pahīnaṃ sandhāyāha. Parato dosamohesupi eseva nayo. Sakkāyadiṭṭhiādīnaṃ pana dassanena pahīnattā upacayaṃ na icchati. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

268. “Obsessed by what?” (Kiṃ pariyuṭṭhito?) means: by what is he obsessed, pursued, or overwhelmed? In the question on latent tendencies, the denials and affirmations should be understood as based on keen and dull faculties. “With wholesome latent tendencies” (kalyāṇānusayo)—he affirms this by the mere generality of the term. “Lust increases” (rāgo upacayaṃ gacchati)—he speaks with reference to that which is abandoned by cultivation. The same method applies also to hatred and delusion. But since personality belief and so on are abandoned by seeing, he does not accept their increase. The rest is of plain meaning in all instances.

Suttasādhanā.

The Proof by Means of the Suttas.

Parihānikathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on Decline is Concluded.

3. Brahmacariyakathā

3. The Discourse on the Holy Life

1. Suddhabrahmacariyakathāvaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Pure Holy Life

269. Idāni [P 0.0041][M 0.0146][V 0.0141] brahmacariyakathā hoti. Tattha dve brahmacariyavāsā, maggabhāvanā ca pabbajjā ca. Pabbajjā sabbadevesu natthi. Maggabhāvanā ṭhapetvā asaññasatte sesesu appaṭisiddhā. Tattha ye paranimmitavasavattideve upādāya taduparidevesu maggabhāvanampi na icchanti seyyathāpi sammitiyā, te sandhāya natthi devesūti pucchā sakavādissa. “Tīhi, bhikkhave, ṭhānehi jambudīpakā manussā uttarakuruke ca manusse adhiggaṇhanti deve ca tāvatiṃse. Katamehi tīhi? Sūrā satimanto idha brahmacariyavāso”ti (a. ni. 9.21) idaṃ suttaṃ nissāya dvepi brahmacariyavāsā natthi devesūti uppannaladdhivasena paṭiññā paravādissa. Puna dvinnampi brahmacariyānaṃ antarāyikadhammavaseneva sabbe devā jaḷāti pucchā sakavādissa. Tattha hatthasaṃvācikāti mūgā viya hatthamuddhāya vattāro. Parato atthi devesūti pucchā paravādissa, maggabhāvanaṃ sandhāya paṭiññā sakavādissa. Paṭiññāya adhippāyaṃ asallakkhetvā pabbajjāvasena anuyogo paravādissa.

269. Now comes the discussion on the holy life. Herein, there are two ways of living the holy life: the cultivation of the path and the going forth. The going forth does not exist among any of the gods. The cultivation of the path, excepting among the non-percipient beings, is not prohibited among the remaining beings. Regarding this, it is with reference to those who, like the Sammitiyas, hold that beginning with the Paranimmitavasavatti devas, even the cultivation of the path is not desired among the gods above them, that the proponent of his own doctrine asks, 'Is there no holy life among the gods?' Based on this sutta, 'Monks, the people of Jambudīpa surpass the humans of Uttarakuru and the Tāvatiṃsa gods in three respects. What are the three? They are courageous, mindful, and here the holy life is lived' (AN 9.20), the opponent asserts, by way of a view that has arisen, that neither way of living the holy life exists among the gods. Again, the proponent of his own doctrine asks whether all gods are dull-witted on account of obstructive states concerning both ways of living the holy life. Here, 'those who communicate by gestures' refers to those who speak by means of hand-gestures, like the mute. From the other side, the opponent asks, 'Does it exist among the gods?', and the proponent's assertion is with reference to the cultivation of the path. Without discerning the intention behind the assertion, the opponent presses the point regarding the going forth.

270. Yattha natthi pabbajjāti pañhe gihīnañceva ekaccānañca devānaṃ maggapaṭilābhaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhepo tasseva. Puna puṭṭho paccantavāsino ceva asaññasatte ca sandhāya paṭiññā tasseva. Yo pabbajatītiādīsu pucchāsupi eseva nayo. Puna “atthi devesū”ti pañhepi maggabhāvanaṃ sandhāyeva paṭiññā sakavādissa, “sabbadevesū”ti vutte asaññasatte sandhāya paṭikkhepo tasseva.

270. In the question, 'Where is there no going forth?', the rejection by that same proponent is with reference to the attainment of the path by householders and certain devas. When asked again, the assertion by that same proponent is with reference to border-dwellers and non-percipient beings. The same method applies in questions such as, 'Who goes forth?' Again, in the question, 'Does it exist among the gods?', the proponent of his own doctrine's assertion is with reference to the cultivation of the path. When 'among all gods' is stated, the rejection by that same proponent is with reference to non-percipient beings.

271. Manussesūti [V 0.0142] pañhadvaye jambudīpake sandhāya paṭiññā. Paccantavāsino sandhāya paṭikkhepo veditabbo.

271. In the two questions concerning 'among humans', the assertion is with reference to the inhabitants of Jambudīpa. The rejection should be understood as referring to border-dwellers.

Atthi yattha atthīti atthi te devā, atthi vā so padeso, yattha atthīti evaṃ sattapadesavibhāgamukhena vissajjanaṃ sakavādissa. Iminā nayena sabbe ekantarikapañhā veditabbā.

In the question, 'Is there where there is?', the proponent of his own doctrine answers by way of a seven-term classification, explaining, 'There are those gods, or there is that place, where it exists.' In this manner, all one-sided questions should be understood.

272. Suttānuyoge [M 0.0147] kuhiṃ phaluppattīti tassa anāgāmino arahattaphaluppatti kuhinti pucchā sakavādissa. Tatthevāti suddhāvāsesūti attho.

272. Regarding the application of the Suttas, the proponent of his own doctrine asks, 'Where does the fruit arise? Where does the fruit of arahantship arise for that non-returner?' The meaning of 'right there' is 'in the Pure Abodes'.

Handa hīti kāraṇatthe nipāto. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yasmā anāgāmipuggalo idha loke bhāvitena maggena tattha suddhāvāsesu phalaṃ sacchikaroti, na tattha aññaṃ maggaṃ bhāveti, tasmā natthi devesu brahmacariyavāsoti.

'Handa hi' is a particle in the sense of a reason. This is what is meant: because the non-returner, by means of the path developed here in this world, realizes the fruit there in the Pure Abodes, and does not develop another path there, therefore there is no living of the holy life among the gods.

2. Saṃsandanabrahmacariyavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Comparison Regarding the Holy Life

273. Idāni [P 0.0042] yadi aññattha bhāvitena maggena aññattha phalasacchikiriyā hoti, sotāpannādīnampi siyāti etamatthaṃ dassetuṃ puna anāgāmītiādīnaṃ saṃsandanapucchā sakavādissa. Tattha anāgāmissa phalasacchikiriyāya paṭiññā, sesānaṃ phalasacchikiriyāya paṭikkhepo paravādissa. Idha bhāvitamaggo hi anāgāmī idhavihāyaniṭṭho nāma hoti. So idha anāgāmimaggaṃ bhāvetvā “opapātiko tatthaparinibbāyī”ti vacanato “puna maggabhāvanaṃ vinā upapattivaseneva arahattaphalaṃ sacchikarotī”ti tassa laddhi. Sotāpannasakadāgāmino pana tattha maggaṃ bhāvetvā tatrupapattikā nāma hontīti tesaṃ idhāgamanaññeva natthi. Iti so anāgāmissa phalasacchikiriyaṃ puṭṭho paṭijānāti. Itaresaṃ paṭikkhipati.

273. Now, to show this point—that if the realization of the fruit in one place occurs by a path developed in another, it could also apply to stream-enterers and others—the proponent of his own doctrine again raises a comparative question regarding the non-returner and others. There, the opponent acknowledges the realization of the fruit for the non-returner, but rejects the realization of the fruit for the others. For the non-returner whose path has been developed here is called 'one whose finality is established apart from this existence'. Having developed the non-returner's path here, his view is that, according to the statement 'one spontaneously reborn, attaining final Nibbāna there,' he realizes the fruit of arahantship by the power of that rebirth, without further path development. Stream-enterers and once-returners, however, having developed the path there, are called 'those who are reborn there,' and for them there is no coming here at all. Thus, when asked about the non-returner's realization of the fruit, he acknowledges it, but rejects it for the others.

Anāgāmī puggalo tattha bhāvitena maggenāti pañhe “anāgāmino tattha maggabhāvanāva natthī”ti laddhiyā paṭikkhipati. Maggo ca bhāvīyati, na ca kilesā pahīyantīti pucchā sakavādissa[V 0.0143], rūpāvacaramaggaṃ sandhāya paṭiññā itarassa. Rūpāvacaramaggena hi so idhavihāyaniṭṭho nāma jāto.

When asked, '[Does the non-returner attain the fruit] by a path developed there?', he rejects it with the view, 'There is no path development for the non-returner there.' The proponent of his own doctrine asks, 'Is the path developed, and yet the defilements are not abandoned?', and the other opponent acknowledges it with reference to the form-sphere path. For it is by the form-sphere path that he became one whose finality is established apart from this existence.

Anāgāmī puggalo katakaraṇīyoti pañhe “opapātiko tatthaparinibbāyī”ti vacanato upapattiyāvassa katakaraṇīyādibhāvaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Arahāti pañhe idhaparinibbāyino arahato vaseneva paṭikkhipati. Puna puṭṭho tatthaparinibbāyino vasena paṭijānāti.

When asked, 'Is the non-returner a person who has done what was to be done?', he acknowledges it with reference to his state of having done what was to be done by the very fact of his rebirth, based on the statement, 'Being spontaneously reborn, he attains final Nibbāna there.' In the question, 'Is he an arahant?', he rejects it by way of the arahant who attains final Nibbāna here. When asked again, he acknowledges it by way of one who attains final Nibbāna there.

Atthi arahato punabbhavotiādīsupi tatthaparinibbāyī idhaparinibbāyīnaṃ vaseneva attho veditabbo. Appaṭividdhākuppova tatthaparinibbāyatīti puṭṭho [M 0.0148] idheva bhāvitena maggena tassa akuppapaṭivedhaṃ icchanto paṭikkhipati.

Similarly, in questions like, 'Does the arahant have future rebirth?', the meaning should be understood by way of the one who attains final Nibbāna there and those who attain final Nibbāna here. When asked, 'Does one attain final Nibbāna there with the unshakable unpenetrated?', he rejects it, holding that the penetration of the unshakable for that person occurs only here through the path developed here.

Yathā migoti paṭhamaṃ udāharaṇaṃ paravādissa, dutiyaṃ sakavādissa. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

The first example, 'like a deer,' is the opponent's, while the second is the proponent's. The rest is straightforward in meaning everywhere.

Brahmacariyakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discussion on the Holy Life is concluded.

3. Odhisokathāvaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Discussion on the Partial

274. Idāni odhisokathā nāma hoti. Tattha ye sotāpannādīnaṃ nānābhisamayavasena dukkhadassanādīhi odhiso odhiso [P 0.0043] ekadesena ekadesena kilesappahānaṃ icchanti seyyathāpi etarahi sammitiyādayo, tesaṃ taṃ laddhiṃ bhindituṃ odhisoti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā paravādissa. Puna anuyogo sakavādissa, ekadesena sotāpannādibhāvassa abhāvato paṭikkhepo paravādissa. Iminā upāyena sabbavāresu attho veditabboti.

274. Now comes the discussion on the partial. Here, there are those who, like the Sammitiyas and others nowadays, hold that the abandoning of defilements occurs partially, bit by bit, through seeing suffering and so forth, by way of the various realizations of stream-entry and so on. To break their view, the proponent asks, 'Partially?', and the opponent admits it. Again, the cross-examination is from the proponent; the rejection by the opponent is due to the non-existence of the state of stream-entry and so forth in parts. By this method, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

Odhisokathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discussion on the Partial.

4. Jahatikathā

4. The Discussion on Abandoning

1. Nasuttāharaṇakathāvaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Discussion on Not Citing a Sutta

279. Idāni [V 0.0144] jahatikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “jhānalābhī puthujjano saha saccābhisamayā anāgāmī nāma hoti, tassa puthujjanakāleyeva kāmarāgabyāpādā pahīnā”ti laddhi seyyathāpi etarahi sammitiyānaṃ, tesaṃ taṃ laddhiṃ bhindituṃ jahati puthujjanoti pucchā sakavādissa, jhānavikkhambhitānaṃ pana tesaṃ pariyuṭṭhānaṃ apassantassa paṭiññā paravādissa. Yasmā pana tesaṃ jhānavikkhambhitānampi anāgāmimaggeneva accantaṃ [M 0.0149] pahānaṃ hoti, tasmā puna accantantiādianuyogo sakavādissa, tathārūpassa pahānassa abhāvato paṭikkhepo itarassa. Vikkhambhetīti accantavikkhambhanameva sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa. Tato paraṃ anāgāmimaggaṭṭhena saddhiṃ puthujjanasaṃsandanaṃ hoti. Taṃ uttānatthameva.

279. Now comes the discussion on abandoning. Here, to break the view of those—such as the Sammitiyas nowadays—who hold that "a worldling who attains jhāna becomes a non-returner upon the penetration of the truths, and for him, sensual desire and ill-will are abandoned even while still a worldling," the question 'Does a worldling abandon?' is posed by the proponent. But the admission is made by the opponent, who does not see the manifestation of those defilements suppressed by jhāna. However, since for them, even those defilements suppressed by jhāna are ultimately abandoned only by the path of non-returning, therefore, again, the cross-examination 'Ultimately?' and so forth is posed by the proponent; the rejection by the other is due to the non-existence of such an abandonment. The question 'Does it suppress?' is posed by the proponent, referring only to ultimate suppression. Thereafter, a comparison of the worldling is made with one established in the path of non-returning. That meaning is straightforward.

280. Tato paraṃ anāgāmiphale saṇṭhātīti puṭṭho jhānānāgāmitaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Arahatte saṇṭhātīti puṭṭho dassanamaggena uddhambhāgiyānaṃ pahānābhāvato paṭikkhipati.

280. Thereafter, when asked, 'Is one established in the fruition of non-returning?', he admits it, referring to the jhāna-non-returner. When asked, 'Is one established in arahantship?', he rejects it due to the non-abandonment of the higher fetters by the path of vision.

Apubbaṃ acarimaṃ tayo maggeti puṭṭho tathārūpāya bhāvanāya abhāvā paṭikkhipati. Puna puṭṭho tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ kiccasabbhāvaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Sāmaññaphalapucchāsupi eseva nayo. Katamena maggenāti puṭṭho anāgāmimaggenāti jhānānāgāmitaṃ sandhāya vadati. Puna saṃyojanappahānaṃ puṭṭho tiṇṇaṃ anāgāmimaggena tesaṃ kilesānaṃ appaheyyattā paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho paṭhamamaggasseva [P 0.0044] jhānānāgāmimaggabhāvaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

When asked, 'Are the three paths without prior and without subsequent?', he rejects it due to the absence of such a development. When asked again, he admits it with reference to the existence of the function of the three paths. This same method applies to questions about the fruits of recluseship. When asked, 'By which path?', he says, 'By the path of non-returning,' referring to the jhāna-non-returner. When asked again about the abandoning of fetters, he rejects it concerning the three, because those defilements are not to be abandoned by the path of non-returning. When asked a second time, he admits it, referring to the first path itself being the path of the jhāna-non-returner. The rest here is straightforward in meaning.

Jahatikathā.

The Discussion on Abandoning.

5. Sabbamatthītikathā

5. The Discussion on 'All Exists'.

1. Vādayuttivaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Method of Debate.

282. Idāni [V 0.0145] sabbamatthītivādakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ…pe… ayaṃ vuccati rūpakkhandho”tiādivacanato (vibha. 2) “sabbepi atītādibhedā dhammā khandhasabhāvaṃ na vijahanti, tasmā sabbaṃ atthiyeva nāmā”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi sabbamatthivādānaṃ, tesaṃ laddhivisodhanatthaṃ sabbamatthīti pucchā sakavādissa, vuttappakārāya laddhiyā ṭhatvā paṭiññā itarassa. Sabbathāti sabbasmiṃ sarīre sabbamatthīti pucchati. Sabbadāti sabbasmiṃ kāle sabbamatthīti pucchati. Sabbena sabbanti sabbenākārena sabbamatthīti pucchati. Sabbesūti sabbesu dhammesu sabbamatthīti pucchati. Ayoganti [M 0.0150] ayuttaṃ. Nānāsabhāvānañhi yogo hoti, na ekasabhāvassa. Iti imasmiṃ pañhe rūpaṃ vedanāya, vedanaṃ vā rūpena anānaṃ ekalakkhaṇameva katvā sabbamatthīti pucchati. Yampi natthi tampatthīti yampi chaṭṭhakhandhādikaṃ sasavisāṇādikaṃ vā kiñci natthīti siddhaṃ, tampi te atthīti pucchati. Sabbamatthīti yā diṭṭhi sā diṭṭhi micchādiṭṭhīti, yā diṭṭhi sā diṭṭhi sammādiṭṭhīti hevamatthīti iminā idaṃ pucchati – yā te esā sabbamatthīti diṭṭhi, sā diṭṭhi ayāthāvakattā micchādiṭṭhīti evaṃ yā amhākaṃ diṭṭhi, sā diṭṭhi yāthāvakattā sammādiṭṭhīti evaṃ tava samaye atthīti pucchati. Itaro sabbesupi etesu nayesu vuttappakārāya atthitāya abhāvato paṭikkhipati. Imesu pana sabbesupi nayesu “ājānāhi niggaha”nti ādiṃ katvā sabbo kathāmaggabhedo vitthārato veditabboti ayaṃ tāvettha vādayutti.

282. Now comes the discussion on the 'All Exists' view. Here, there are those who hold the view—based on statements like "Whatever form, past, future, or present… this is called the aggregate of form" (Vibh. 2)—that "all phenomena, even those classified as past, etc., do not abandon the nature of aggregates; therefore, all indeed exists." Such are the present-day advocates of the 'All Exists' view. For the purpose of clarifying their view, the question 'Does all exist?' is posed by the proponent, while the other, standing on the described view, makes an admission. By 'In every way,' he asks whether all exists in every body. By 'At all times,' he asks whether all exists at every moment. By 'All with all,' he asks whether all exists in every manner. By 'In all,' he asks whether all exists in all phenomena. By 'Incongruous,' it is meant 'unsuitable.' For a connection applies to things of diverse natures, not to a single nature. Thus, in this question, treating form and feeling, or feeling and form, as non-diverse and having a single characteristic, he asks whether all exists. By 'Even what does not exist, that exists,' he asks whether even that which is established as non-existent, such as a sixth aggregate or a hare’s horn, exists for them. By the question, 'Is the view that "all exists" a wrong view, and is the [contrary] view a right view, thus does it exist?' he asks this: 'Is this view of yours, that "all exists," a wrong view because it is untrue? And is our view a right view because it is true? Thus, does this hold in your system?' The other rejects this in all these methods due to the non-existence of the described existence. However, in all these methods, starting with 'Acknowledge the refutation,' the entire course of the discussion should be understood in detail. This, for now, is the method of debate here.

2. Kālasaṃsandanavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Conjunction of Time.

283-284. Idāni [P 0.0045] atītaṃ atthīti kālasaṃsandanaṃ hoti. Tattha atītaṃ atthītiādikaṃ suddhikasaṃsandanaṃ. Atītaṃ rūpaṃ atthītiādikaṃ khandhavasena kālasaṃsandanaṃ.

Now, there is the conjunction of time with the statement 'the past exists.' Here, 'the past exists' and so on is a pure conjunction. 'Past form exists' and so on is the conjunction of time by way of the aggregates.

285. Paccuppannaṃ rūpaṃ appiyaṃ karitvāti atītānāgataṃ pahāya paccuppannarūpameva appiyaṃ [V 0.0146] avibhajitabbaṃ karitvā. Rūpabhāvaṃ jahatītipañhe niruddhassāpi rūpassa rūpakkhandhasaṅgahitattā paṭikkhipati. Rūpabhāvaṃ na jahatīti paṭilomapañhepi rūpakkhandhena saṅgahitattāva paṭijānāti. Odātaṃ vatthaṃ appiyaṃ karitvāti ettha kiñcāpi na sabbaṃ vatthaṃ odātaṃ, iminā pana vatthanti avatvā “odātaṃ vatthaṃ appiyaṃ karitvā”ti vutte sakavādinā ekatthatā anuññātā. Odātabhāvaṃ jahatīti pañhe vaṇṇavigamaṃ sandhāya paṭiññā sakavādissa. Vatthabhāvaṃ jahatīti ettha pana paññattiyā avigatattā paṭikkhepo tasseva. Paṭilomepi eseva nayo.

285. Regarding the phrase 'having made the present form unlovely,' it means having abandoned the past and future, and having made only the indivisible present form unlovely. In the question, 'Does one abandon the state of form?', he denies it because even ceased form is included in the aggregate of form. In the reverse question, 'Does one not abandon the state of form?', he affirms it precisely because it is included in the aggregate of form. Regarding the statement, 'Having made the white cloth unlovely,' here, although not all cloth is white, by not saying 'this cloth' but stating 'having made the white cloth unlovely,' a unity of subject is conceded by the proponent. In the question, 'Does one abandon the state of whiteness?', the proponent acknowledges it with reference to the disappearance of color. But in the question, 'Does one abandon the state of cloth?', he denies it because the designation has not disappeared. The same method applies in the reverse case.

286. Atītaṃ atītabhāvaṃ na jahatīti puṭṭho “yadi jaheyya, anāgataṃ vā paccuppannaṃ vā siyā”ti maññamāno paṭijānāti. Anāgataṃ anāgatabhāvaṃ na jahatīti puṭṭho pana “yadi na jaheyya, anāgatamevassa[M 0.0151], paccuppannabhāvaṃ na pāpuṇeyyā”ti maññamāno paṭikkhipati. Paccuppannapañhepi atītabhāvaṃ anāpajjanadoso siyāti paṭikkhipati. Anulomapañhesupi imināva nayena attho veditabbo.

286. When asked, 'Does the past not abandon its past state?', he affirms it, thinking, 'If it were to abandon it, it would become either future or present.' But when asked, 'Does the future not abandon its future state?', he denies it, thinking, 'If it did not abandon it, it would remain future and not attain the present state.' In the question about the present, he also denies it, considering that there would be the fault of not arriving at the past state. The meaning should be understood in this same way for the questions in direct order.

287. Evaṃ suddhikanayaṃ vatvā puna khandhavasena dassetuṃ atītaṃ rūpantiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ pāḷianusāreneva sakkā jānituṃ.

287. Having thus explained the pure method, 'past form' and so on is further stated to show by way of aggregates. All that can be understood by following the Pāli text itself.

Vacanasodhanavaṇṇanā

The Description of the Clarification of Statements

288. Idāni “atītaṃ nvatthī”tiādi vacanasodhanā hoti. Tattha hañci atītaṃ nvatthīti yadi atītaṃ no atthīti attho. Atītaṃ [P 0.0046] atthīti micchāti atītañca taṃ atthi cāti micchā eva. Taññeva anāgataṃ taṃ paccuppannanti puṭṭho anāgatakkhaṇeyevassa paccuppannatāya abhāvaṃ sandhāya kālanānattena paṭikkhipati.

288. Now, the clarification of statements like 'the past does not exist' occurs. Here, if 'the past does not exist' means 'the past is not existent,' that is the meaning. To say 'the past exists' is wrong; and that it is past and exists is indeed wrong. When asked, 'Is that very future the present?', he rejects it with reference to the absence of presentness in the future moment itself, due to the difference in time.

Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho yaṃ uppādato pubbe anāgataṃ ahosi, tassa uppannakāle paccuppannattā paṭijānāti. Hutvā hoti hutvā hotīti yadetaṃ tayā “anāgataṃ hutvā paccuppannaṃ hotī”ti vadatā taññeva anāgataṃ taṃ paccuppannanti laddhivasena “anāgataṃ vā paccuppannaṃ vā hutvā hotī”ti [V 0.0147] vuttaṃ. Kiṃ te tampi hutvā hotīti? Itaro hutvā bhūtassa puna hutvā abhāvato na hevanti paṭikkhipati.

When asked a second time, he affirms it because that which was future before its arising becomes present at the time of its arising. When you say 'the future, having been, becomes present,' then by accepting 'that very future is the present,' it is said 'having been, it is,' whether future or present. Do you also say 'having been, it is' regarding that? The other denies it, saying, 'No, indeed,' because what has become, having been, does not exist again as having been.

Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho yasmā taṃ anāgataṃ hutvā paccuppannaṃ hontaṃ “hutvā hotī”ti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ, tasmā paṭijānāti. Atha naṃ sakavādī “yadi te taṃ anāgataṃ hutvā paccuppannaṃ hontaṃ ‘hutvā hotī’ti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ, puna hutvā hoti, yaṃ anāgataṃ na hutvā paccuppannaṃ na hontaṃ ‘na hutvā na hotī’ti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ sasavisāṇaṃ, kiṃ te tampi puna na hutvā na hotī”tiadhippāyena na hutvā na hoti na hutvā na hotīti pañhaṃ pucchati. Itaro “yaṃ natthi, taṃ natthitāya, eva anāgataṃ na hutvā paccuppannaṃ na hotīti nahutvānahoti nāma tāva hotu, puna nahutvānahotibhāvo panassa kuto”ti maññamāno paṭikkhipati. Taññeva paccuppannaṃ taṃ atītanti pañhepi paccuppannakkhaṇeyevassa atītatāya abhāvaṃ sandhāya kālanānattā paṭikkhipati.

When asked a second time, he affirms it because that which is future, having been, becomes present, has attained the designation 'having been, it is.' Then his own proponent asks him, 'If, for you, that which is future, having been, becomes present, has attained the designation 'having been, it is,' does it again become 'having been, it is'? That which is future, not having been, not becoming present, has attained the designation 'not having been, it is not'—like a hare's horn—does that too again become 'not having been, it is not'?' With this intention, he asks the question, 'Not having been, it is not; not having been, it is not?' The other, thinking, 'What does not exist, by its non-existence, thus the future not having been does not become present—so let it first have the name 'not having been, it is not'; but whence comes its state of again not having been, it is not?', rejects it. Regarding the question, 'Is that very present the past?', he also rejects it with reference to its absence as past in the present moment itself, due to the difference in time.

Dutiyapañhe [M 0.0152] puṭṭho yaṃ atītabhāvato pubbe paccuppannaṃ ahosi, tasseva atītattā paṭijānāti. Hutvā hoti hutvā hotīti yadetaṃ tayā “paccuppannaṃ hutvā atītaṃ hotī”ti vadatā “taññeva paccuppannaṃ taṃ atīta”nti laddhivasena “paccuppannaṃ vā atītaṃ vā hutvā hotī”ti vuttaṃ, kiṃ te tampi hutvā hotīti? Itaro hutvā bhūtassa puna hutvā abhāvato na hevanti paṭikkhipati.

In the second question, when asked, he affirms it because that which was present before becoming past is itself past. When you say 'the present, having been, becomes past,' then by accepting 'that very present is the past,' it is said 'having been, it is,' whether present or past. Do you also say 'having been, it is' regarding that? The other denies it, saying, 'No, indeed,' because what has become, having been, does not exist again as having been.

Dutiyapañhe yasmā taṃ paccuppannaṃ hutvā atītaṃ hontaṃ “hutvā hotī”ti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ, tasmā paṭijānāti[P 0.0047]. Atha naṃ sakavādī “yadi te taññeva paccuppannaṃ hutvā atītaṃ hontaṃ ‘hutvā hotī’ti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ, puna hutvā hoti, yaṃ paccuppannaṃ na hutvā atītaṃ na hontaṃ ‘na hutvā na hotī’ti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ sasavisāṇaṃ, kiṃ te tampi puna na hutvā na hotī”ti adhippāyena na hutvā na hoti na hutvā na hotīti pañhaṃ pucchati. Itaro “yaṃ natthi, taṃ natthitāya eva paccuppannaṃ na hutvā atītaṃ na hotīti nahutvānahoti nāma tāva hotu. Puna nahutvānahotibhāvo panassa kuto”ti maññamāno paṭikkhipati. Ubhayaṃ ekato katvā āgate tatiyapañhepi imināvupāyena yojanā kātabbā.

In the second question, he affirms it because that which is present, having been, becomes past, has attained the designation 'having been, it is.' Then his own proponent asks him, 'If, for you, that which is present, having been, becomes past, has attained the designation 'having been, it is,' does it again become 'having been, it is'? That which is present, not having been, not becoming past, has attained the designation 'not having been, it is not'—like a hare's horn—does that too again become 'not having been, it is not'?' With this intention, he asks the question, 'Not having been, it is not; not having been, it is not?' The other, thinking, 'What does not exist, by its non-existence, thus the present, not having been, does not become past—so let it first have the name 'not having been, it is not'; but whence comes its state of again not having been, it is not?', rejects it. Combining both, the third question should also be analyzed in this same way.

Aparo [V 0.0148] nayo – yadi taññeva anāgataṃ taṃ paccuppannaṃ, anāgatassa paccuppanne vutto hotibhāvo, paccuppannassa ca anāgate vutto hutvābhāvo āpajjati. Evaṃ sante anāgatampi hutvāhoti nāma. Paccuppannampi hutvāhotiyeva nāma. Tena taṃ pucchāma – “kiṃ te etesu ekekaṃ hutvā hoti hutvā hotī”ti? Itaro – “taññeva anāgataṃ taṃ paccuppanna”nti pañhe paṭikkhittanayeneva paṭikkhipitvā puna puṭṭho dutiye pañhe paṭiññātanayeneva paṭijānāti. Atha naṃ sakavādī “taññeva anāgataṃ taṃ paccuppanna”nti pañhāvasena tesu ekekaṃ hutvā hoti hutvā hotīti paṭijānantaṃ purimaṃ paṭikkhittapañhaṃ parivattitvā pucchanto na hutvā na hoti na hutvā na hotīti pucchati. Tassattho – nanu “tayā taññeva anāgataṃ taṃ paccuppanna”nti vutte paṭhamapañhaṃ paṭikkhipantena anāgatassa hotibhāvo paccuppannassa ca hutvābhāvo paṭikkhittoti. Tena anāgataṃ na hoti nāma, paccuppannaṃ na hutvā nāma.

Another approach: If that very future is the present, then the state of 'it is' for the future would be stated in the present, and the state of 'having been' for the present would be stated in the future. This being so, even the future would be called 'having been, it is.' And the present would also be called 'having been, it is.' Therefore, we ask you: 'Does each of these, individually, become 'having been, it is; having been, it is' for you?' The other, having rejected it by the very method of rejection in the question 'Is that very future the present?', when asked again in the second question, affirms it by the very method of affirmation. Then his own proponent, by way of the question 'Is that very future the present?', asks the one who acknowledges that each of these becomes 'having been, it is; having been, it is,' by reversing the previously rejected question: 'Not having been, it is not; not having been, it is not?' The meaning of that is: 'Indeed, when you said 'that very future is the present,' by rejecting the first question, the state of 'it is' for the future and the state of 'having been' for the present were rejected. Therefore, the future is called 'it is not,' and the present is called 'not having been.'

Dutiyapañhe [M 0.0153] ca taññeva anāgataṃ taṃ paccuppannanti paṭiññātaṃ. Evaṃ sante anāgatampi na hutvā na hoti nāma. Paccuppannampi na hutvā na hotiyeva nāma. Tena taṃ pucchāma – “kiṃ te etesu ekekaṃ na hutvā na hoti na hutvā na hotī”ti? Paravādī sabbato andhakārena pariyonaddho viya tesaṃ nahutvānahotibhāvaṃ apassanto na hevanti paṭikkhipati.

And in the second question, it is acknowledged that 'that very future is the present.' This being so, even the future is called 'not having been, it is not.' And the present is also called 'not having been, it is not.' Therefore, we ask you: 'Does each of these, individually, become 'not having been, it is not; not having been, it is not' for you?' The opponent, as if utterly enveloped in darkness, not seeing their state of 'not having been, it is not,' rejects it by saying, 'No, indeed.'

Dutiyavārepi yadi taññeva [P 0.0048] paccuppannaṃ taṃ atītaṃ, paccuppannassa atīte vutto hotibhāvo, atītassa ca paccuppanne vutto hutvābhāvo āpajjati, evaṃ sante paccuppannampi hutvāhoti nāma, atītampi hutvāhotiyeva nāma. Tena taṃ pucchāma – “kiṃ te etesu ekekaṃ hutvā hoti hutvā hotī”ti? Itaro taññeva paccuppannaṃ taṃ atītantipañhe paṭikkhittanayeneva paṭikkhipitvā puna puṭṭho dutiyapañhe paṭiññātanayeneva paṭijānāti. Atha naṃ sakavādī “taññeva paccuppannaṃ taṃ atīta”nti pañhāvasena tesu ekekaṃ hutvā hoti hutvā hotīti paṭijānantaṃ purimaṃ paṭikkhittapañhaṃ parivattitvā pucchanto na hutvā na hoti na hutvā na hotīti pucchati. Tassattho – nanu tayā taññeva paccuppannaṃ taṃ atītanti vutte paṭhamapañhaṃ paṭikkhipantena paccuppannassa hotibhāvo, atītassa ca hutvābhāvo paṭikkhittoti. Tena paccuppannaṃ nahoti nāma. Atītaṃ nahutvā nāma.

Also in the second turn, if that very present is that past, it would follow that the present's state of being is spoken of in the past, and the past's state of having been is spoken of in the present. Thus, in that case, even the present would be called 'has been and is', and the past would also be called 'has been and is'. Therefore, we ask you: 'Is each of these, for you, 'has been and is', 'has been and is'?' The opponent, having rejected the question 'that very present is that past' in the manner of rejection, when asked again, affirms the second question in the manner of affirmation. Then the proponent, seeing him affirm that each of these, one by one, 'has been and is', 'has been and is' in response to the question 'that very present is that past', turns the previously rejected question around and asks, 'has not been and is not', 'has not been and is not'. Its meaning is: When you said 'that very present is that past', did you not, in rejecting the first question, reject the present's state of being and the past's state of having been? Therefore, the present is called 'is not'. The past is called 'has not been'.

Dutiyapañhe ca te “taññeva paccuppannaṃ taṃ atīta”nti paṭiññātaṃ. Evaṃ sante paccuppannampi [V 0.0149] na hutvā na hoti nāma, atītampi na hutvā na hotiyeva nāma. Tena taṃ pucchāma – “kiṃ te etesu ekekaṃ na hutvā na hoti, na hutvā na hotī”ti. Paravādī sabbato andhakārena pariyonaddho viya tesaṃ nahutvānahotibhāvaṃ apassanto na hevanti paṭikkhipati.

And in the second question, you affirmed 'that very present is that past'. Thus, in that case, even the present would be called 'has not been and is not', and the past would also be called 'has not been and is not'. Therefore, we ask you: 'Is each of these, for you, 'has not been and is not', 'has not been and is not'?' The opponent, as if completely enveloped in darkness, not seeing their state of 'has not been and is not', denies it, saying, 'Not so'.

Tatiyavārepi yadi taññeva anāgataṃ taṃ paccuppannaṃ taṃ atītaṃ; anāgatapaccuppannānaṃ paccuppannātītesu vutto hotibhāvo, paccuppannātītānañca anāgatapaccuppannesu vutto hutvābhāvo āpajjati. Evaṃ sante anāgatampi hutvāhoti nāma. Paccuppannampi atītampi hutvā hotiyeva nāma. Tena taṃ pucchāma – “kiṃ te tīsupi etesu ekekaṃ hutvā hoti [M 0.0154] hutvā hotī”ti? Itaro “taññeva anāgataṃ, taṃ paccuppannaṃ, taṃ atīta”ntipañhe paṭikkhittanayeneva paṭikkhipitvā puna puṭṭho dutiyapañhe paṭiññātanayeneva paṭijānāti. Atha naṃ sakavādī “taññeva anāgataṃ, taṃ paccuppannaṃ, taṃ atīta”nti pañhāvasena tesu ekekaṃ hutvā hoti, hutvā hotīti paṭijānantaṃ purimaṃ paṭikkhittapañhaṃ parivattitvā pucchanto na hutvā na hoti na hutvā na hotīti pucchati. Tassattho [P 0.0049] – nanu tayā taññeva anāgataṃ, taṃ paccuppannaṃ, taṃ atītanti vutte paṭhamapañhaṃ paṭikkhipantena anāgatapaccuppannānaṃ hotibhāvo; paccuppannātītānañca hutvābhāvo paṭikkhittoti? Tena anāgataṃ paccuppannañca na hoti nāma. Paccuppannañca atītañca na hutvā nāma.

Also in the third turn, if that very future is that present and that past, it would follow that the state of being of the future and present is spoken of in relation to the present and past, and the state of having been of the present and past is spoken of in relation to the future and present. Thus, in that case, even the future would be called 'has been and is'. The present and past would also be called 'has been and is'. Therefore, we ask you: 'Is each of these three, for you, 'has been and is', 'has been and is'?' The opponent, having rejected the question 'that very future is that present, that past' in the manner of rejection, when asked again, affirms the second question in the manner of affirmation. Then the proponent, seeing him affirm that each of these, one by one, 'has been and is', 'has been and is' in response to the question 'that very future is that present, that past', turns the previously rejected question around and asks, 'has not been and is not', 'has not been and is not'. Its meaning is: When you said 'that very future is that present, that past', did you not, in rejecting the first question, reject the state of being of the future and present, and the state of having been of the present and past? Therefore, the future and present are called 'is not'. And the present and past are called 'has not been'.

Dutiyapañhe ca te “taññeva anāgataṃ, taṃ paccuppannaṃ, taṃ atīta”nti paṭiññātaṃ. Evaṃ sante anāgatampi na hutvā na hoti nāma, paccuppannampi atītampi na hutvā na hotiyeva nāma. Tena taṃ pucchāma – “kiṃ te etesu ekekaṃ na hutvā na hoti na hutvā na hotī”ti? Paravādī sabbato andhakārena pariyonaddho viya tesaṃ na hutvā na hotibhāvaṃ apassanto na hevanti paṭikkhipatīti. Niggahādīni panettha heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva yojetabbāni.

And in the second question, you affirmed 'that very future is that present, that past'. Thus, in that case, even the future would be called 'has not been and is not', and the present and past would also be called 'has not been and is not'. Therefore, we ask you: 'Is each of these, for you, 'has not been and is not', 'has not been and is not'?'
