The opponent, as if completely enveloped in darkness, not seeing their state of 'has not been and is not', denies it, saying, 'Not so'. Here, the refutations and so forth should be applied in the manner previously stated.

Vacanasodhanavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Clarification of Terms is concluded.

Atītacakkhurūpādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discussion on Past Eye, Form, and So On

289. Atītaṃ [V 0.0150] cakkhu atthītiādīsupi cakkhādibhāvāvijahaneneva atthitaṃ paṭijānāti. Passatītiādīni puṭṭho pana tesaṃ viññāṇānaṃ kiccābhāvavasena paṭikkhipati.

289. Even in statements such as 'the past eye exists,' one acknowledges its existence precisely by not abandoning the nature of the eye, and so on. But when asked about 'sees,' and so on, one denies them on account of the absence of function of those consciousnesses.

Atītañāṇādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discussion on Past Knowledge, and So On

290. Tena ñāṇena ñāṇakaraṇīyaṃ karotīti pañhe tassa ñāṇassa niruddhattā kiccabhāvamassa apassanto paṭikkhipati. Puna puṭṭho atītārammaṇaṃ paccuppannaṃ ñāṇaṃ atītānaṃ dhammānaṃ jānanato atītaṃ ñāṇanti [M 0.0155] lesena paccuppannameva “atītaṃ ñāṇa”nti katvā tena ñāṇena ñāṇakaraṇīyassa atthitāya paṭijānāti. Athassa sakavādī lesokāsaṃ adatvā tena ñāṇena dukkhaṃ parijānātītiādimāha. Itaro atītārammaṇeneva ñāṇena imesaṃ catunnaṃ kiccānaṃ abhāvā [P 0.0050] paṭikkhipati. Anāgatapañhepi eseva nayo. Paccuppannapañho ceva saṃsandanapañho ca uttānatthāyeva.

290. When asked, 'Does one perform with that knowledge what is to be done by knowledge?', one denies it, not seeing its function because that knowledge has ceased. When questioned again, one acknowledges the existence of what is to be done by that knowledge, by way of a pretext that present knowledge with a past object is 'past knowledge' because it knows past phenomena, thus treating the present knowledge itself as 'past knowledge.' Then the proponent, giving no opportunity for a pretext, says, 'By that knowledge one fully understands suffering,' and so on. The other denies this, because of the absence of these four functions for a knowledge with only a past object. The same method applies to questions about the future. The question about the present and the question of comparison are of plain meaning.

Arahantādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discussion on the Arahant, and So On

291. Arahato atīto rāgo atthītiādīsupi rāgādibhāvāvijahanto evaṃ paṭijānāti. Sarāgotiādīsu suttavirodhabhayena ceva yuttivirodhabhayena ca paṭikkhipati.

291. Even in statements such as 'an arahant has past lust,' one acknowledges it precisely by not abandoning the nature of lust, and so on. But in cases such as 'one with lust,' one rejects it out of fear of contradicting the suttas and out of fear of contradicting reason.

Padasodhanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discussion on the Analysis of Terms

295. Evaṃ sabbampi pāḷianusāreneva viditvā parato atthi siyā atītaṃ, siyā nvātītanti ettha evamattho veditabbo. Yaṃ atītameva atthi, taṃ atītaṃ. Yaṃ paccuppannānāgataṃ atthi, taṃ no atthi, taṃ no atītaṃ. Tenātītaṃ nvātītaṃ, nvātītaṃ atītanti tena kāraṇena atītaṃ no atītaṃ, no atītaṃ atītanti. Anāgatapaccuppannapucchāsupi eseva nayo.

295. Having understood all this precisely in accordance with the Pāli, hereafter the meaning should be understood as follows regarding 'there may be something past, or there may be something not past.' What exists as past is the past. What exists as present or future, that does not exist as past, that is not past. Therefore, the past is not past, and the not-past is past. For that reason, the past is not past, and the not-past is past. The same method applies to questions about the future and the present.

Suttasādhanavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Sutta Method

296. Na [V 0.0151] vattabbaṃ “atītaṃ atthi anāgataṃ atthī”ti suttasādhanāya pucchā paravādissa, paṭiññā sakavādissa. Puna attano laddhiṃ nissāya yaṃkiñci, bhikkhave, rūpanti anuyogo paravādisseva. Dutiyanaye pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Evaṃ sabbattha pucchā ca paṭiññā ca veditabbā. Yaṃ panetaṃ paravādinā anāgatassa atthibhāvasādhanatthaṃ “nanu vuttaṃ bhagavatā kabaḷīkāre, ce, bhikkhave”ti suttassa pariyosāne atthi tattha āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbattītiādi dassitaṃ na taṃ anāgatassa atthibhāvasādhakaṃ[M 0.0156]. Tañhi hetūnaṃ pariniṭṭhitattā avassaṃ bhāvitaṃ sandhāya tattha vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ suttādhippāyo. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

296. The question for the purpose of establishing the sutta that states, 'It should not be said, "The past exists, the future exists,"' belongs to the opponent, and the acknowledgement belongs to the proponent. Again, relying on his own view, the interrogation, 'Whatever, bhikkhus, is form?' belongs to the opponent himself. In the second method, the question belongs to the proponent, and the acknowledgement belongs to the other. Thus, in all cases, both the question and the acknowledgement should be understood. As for that which is shown by the opponent to prove the existence of the future by citing, 'Was it not said by the Blessed One, "Bhikkhus, in the case of edible food..."?' and so on, and at the conclusion of the sutta, '...therein is future rebirth and re-becoming,' and so on—this does not prove the existence of the future. For that was said there with reference to what must inevitably come to be due to the completion of its causes. This is the intended meaning of the sutta. The rest is everywhere of straightforward meaning.

Sabbamatthītikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on 'All Exists' is concluded.

6. Atītakkhandhādikathā

6. The Discussion on the Past Aggregates, and so on.

1. Nasuttasādhanakathāvaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Discussion on Non-Establishment by Sutta.

297. Idāni “atītaṃ khandhā”tiādikathā hoti. Tattha khandhādibhāvāvijahanato atītānāgatānaṃ atthitaṃ icchantassa atītaṃ khandhāti pucchā paravādissa, atītassa khandhasaṅgahitattā āmantāti paṭiññā sakavādissa. Puna atītaṃ [P 0.0051] natthīti pucchā paravādissa, tassa niruttipathasuttena atthitāya vāritattā paṭikkhepo sakavādissa. Āyatanadhātupucchāsupi anāgatapañhesupi paccuppannena saddhiṃ saṃsanditvā anulomapaṭilomato āgatapañhesupi “atītaṃ rūpa”ntiādipañhesupi imināvupāyena attho veditabbo.

297. Now there is the discussion on 'Is the past aggregates?' and so on. Here, for one who desires the existence of past and future by not abandoning the nature of aggregates, and so on, the question 'Is the past aggregates?' belongs to the opponent, and the acknowledgment 'Yes' belongs to the proponent, because the past is included within the aggregates. Again, the question 'Does the past not exist?' belongs to the opponent, and the rejection belongs to the proponent because its existence is refuted by the Niruttipatha-sutta. Similarly, in questions about sense-bases and elements, in future questions, in questions that arise through direct and reverse comparison with the present, and in questions like 'Is form past?' and so on, the meaning should be understood by this method.

2. Suttasādhanavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Proof by Sutta.

298. Suttasādhane [V 0.0152] pana na vattabbanti pucchā sakavādissa. Tattha natthi ceteti natthi ca ete dhammāti attho. Khandhādibhāve sati natthitaṃ anicchantassa āmantāti paṭiññā paravādissa, atha nesaṃ natthibhāvasādhanatthaṃ suttāharaṇaṃ sakavādissa. Dutiyapucchāpi paravādissa, paṭiññā sakavādissa, suttāharaṇaṃ paravādissa. Taṃ pana nesaṃ khandhādibhāvameva sādheti, na atthibhāvanti āhaṭampi anāhaṭasadisamevāti.

298. In the proof by sutta, however, the question, 'Should it not be said...?' belongs to the proponent. Here, the meaning of 'if these do not exist' is 'and these phenomena do not exist.' When the state of being aggregates, etc., is present, the opponent, not wishing for their non-existence, acknowledges this with 'Yes.' Then, the proponent cites a sutta to prove their non-existence. The second question also belongs to the opponent, the acknowledgment to the proponent, and the sutta citation to the opponent. However, that only proves their state as aggregates, etc., not their existence; thus, even when cited, it is as if it were not cited.

Atītaṃ khandhātiādikathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the discussion beginning with 'Is the past aggregates?'

7. Ekaccaṃatthītikathā

7. The Discussion on 'Some Exist'.

1. Atītādiekaccakathāvaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Discussion on the Past, etc., and 'Some Exist'.

299. Idāni [M 0.0157] ekaccaṃ atthīti kathā hoti. Tattha ye “ekaccaṃ atītaṃ atthī”ti maññanti, seyyathāpi kassapikā; tesaṃ laddhibhindanatthaṃ atītaṃ atthīti pucchā sakavādissa, ekaccaṃ atthīti vissajjanaṃ paravādissa. Ayañhi adhippāyo – avipakkavipākaṃ atthi, vipakkavipākaṃ natthīti. Ekaccaṃ niruddhanti anuyogo sakavādissa. Tassattho – yadi te atītaṃ ekaccaṃ atthi ekaccaṃ natthi, evaṃ sante ekaccaṃ atītaṃ niruddhaṃ, ekaccaṃ atītaṃ aniruddhaṃ, tatheva ṭhitanti āpajjati. Vigatantiādīsupi eseva nayo.

299. Now, there is a discussion on 'some exist.' Here, to refute the view of those who think 'some of the past exists,' such as the Kassapikas, the proponent asks, 'Does the past exist?' and the opponent replies, 'Some exists.' Indeed, the intention here is: 'What has not yet ripened into its result exists, but what has ripened into its result does not.' The proponent then poses the counter-question, 'Has some ceased?' Its meaning is: If for you some of the past exists and some does not, then it follows that some of the past has ceased, and some of the past has not ceased, thus remaining just as it was. The same principle applies to 'has vanished,' etc.

Avipakkavipākadhammā ekacceti idaṃ yasmā yesaṃ so avipakkavipākānaṃ atthitaṃ icchati, tepi atītāyeva. Tasmā yathā te atītaṃ ekaccaṃ atthi, kiṃ tathā avipakkavipākāpi dhammā [P 0.0052] ekacce atthī ekacce natthīti codetuṃ vuttaṃ. Vipakkavipākāti idaṃ yesaṃ so natthitaṃ icchati, tesaṃ vasena codetuṃ vuttaṃ. Avipākāti idaṃ abyākatānaṃ vasena codetuṃ vuttaṃ. Iti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ rāsīnaṃ vasena sabbesu anulomapaṭilomesu paṭiññā ca [V 0.0153] paṭikkhepo ca veditabbā. Atītā ekadesaṃ vipakkavipākā, ekadesaṃ avipakkavipākāti vippakatavipākā vuccanti. Yena hi kammena paṭisandhi nibbattitā, bhavaṅgampi cutipi tasseva vipāko. Tasmā paṭisandhito yāva cuti, tāva taṃ vippakatavipākaṃ nāma hoti. Tathārūpe dhamme sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

'Some phenomena that have not yet ripened into results': This is said because those whose existence he desires, namely, those that have not yet ripened into results, are also past. Therefore, just as some of the past exists for them, this is said to challenge them: 'Are some phenomena that have not yet ripened into results existent and some non-existent?' 'What has ripened into results': This is said to challenge them in terms of what he desires to be non-existent. 'Without result': This is said to challenge them in terms of indeterminate phenomena. Thus, in terms of these three categories, affirmation and denial should be understood in all forward and reverse arguments. The past, a portion of which has ripened into results and a portion of which has not ripened into results, is called 'results that have ripened in a divided way.' For by the kamma by which rebirth-linking is produced, the life-continuum and death are also its result. Therefore, from rebirth-linking until death, that is called 'results ripened in a divided way.' This is said in reference to such a phenomenon.

Vipaccissantīti katvā te atthīti pucchā sakavādissa. Yathā dhammadharassa puggalassa niddāyantassāpi bahupavattino dhammā atthīti vuccanti, evaṃ lokavohāravasena atthitaṃ sandhāya paṭiññā paravādissa. Vipaccissantīti katvā paccupannāti dutiyapañhe “kammānaṃ avināsasaṅkhāto kammūpacayo nāmeko atthī”ti laddhiyaṃ ṭhatvā paṭiññā paravādissa.

Having considered that 'they will ripen,' the proponent asks, 'Do they exist?' Just as it is said that a person who upholds the Dhamma, even while sleeping, has many active qualities, so too the opponent's acknowledgment is made with reference to existence in terms of worldly convention. Having considered that 'they will ripen,' in the second question, 'Are they present?', the opponent's acknowledgment stands on the doctrine that 'there is a certain accumulation of kamma, designated as the non-perishing of kamma.'

2. Anāgatādiekaccakathāvaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Discussion on the Future, etc., and 'Some Exist'.

300. Anāgataṃ [M 0.0158] atthītiādīsupi ekaccaṃ atthīti uppādino dhamme sandhāya vadati. Sesaṃ sabbattha heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthamevāti.

300. In statements such as, 'Does the future exist?' and so on, when he says 'some exist,' he speaks with reference to phenomena that are to arise. The rest, everywhere, is of straightforward meaning because of the method stated below.

Ekaccaṃatthītikathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discussion on 'Some Exists'.

8. Satipaṭṭhānakathāvaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Discussion on the Establishments of Mindfulness.

301. Idāni satipaṭṭhānakathā hoti. “Tattha – catunnaṃ, bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca desessāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.408) satipaṭṭhānasaṃyutte vuttanayeneva yesaṃ kāyādayo satiyā ārammaṇadhamme gahetvā “sabbe dhammā satipaṭṭhānā”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi andhakānaṃ. Andhakā nāma pubbaseliyā, aparaseliyā, rājagiriyā, siddhatthikāti ime pacchā uppannanikāyā. Tesaṃ laddhivivecanatthaṃ pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā paravādissa. Tattha yasmā “patiṭṭhāti etesūti paṭṭhānā[P 0.0053]. Kā patiṭṭhāti? Sati. Satiyā paṭṭhānā satipaṭṭhānā”ti iminā atthena satigocarāpi satipaṭṭhānā. “Patiṭṭhahantīti paṭṭhānā. Kā [V 0.0154] patiṭṭhahanti? Satiyo. Satiyova paṭṭhānā satipaṭṭhānā”ti iminā atthena satiyova satipaṭṭhānā. Tasmā dvepi vādā pariyāyena yujjanti. Ye pana taṃ pariyāyaṃ pahāya ekanteneva “sabbe dhammā satipaṭṭhānā”ti vadanti, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, ārammaṇavasena paṭiññā paravādissa. Sabbe dhammā satīti anuyuttassa pana sabbesaṃ satisabhāvābhāvato paṭikkhepo tasseva. Tattha khayagāmītiādīni maggavisesanāni. Ekāyanamaggo hi kilesānaṃ khayabhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ gacchatīti khayagāmī. Cattāri saccāni bujjhanto gacchatīti bodhagāmī. Vaṭṭaṃ apacinanto gacchatīti apacayagāmī. Evametehi padehi “kiṃ te sabbe dhammā evarūpo te ekāyano maggo hotī”ti pucchati. Anāsavā asaṃyojaniyātiādīnipi lokuttarabhāvaṃ pucchanatthāya vuttāni. Buddhānussatītiādīni pabhedapucchāvasena vuttāni.

301. Now there is the discussion on the foundations of mindfulness. Therein—'Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the arising and passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness' (SN 5.408). In accordance with the method stated in the Satipaṭṭhāna Saṃyutta, there is the view of those who, taking the body and so forth as the objective phenomena for mindfulness, hold that 'all phenomena are foundations of mindfulness,' such as the Andhakas nowadays. The Andhakas are the later schools, namely, the Pubbaseliyas, Aparaseliyas, Rājagiriyas, and Siddhatthikas. For the purpose of analyzing their view, the question is from the proponent, and the assertion is from the opponent. Herein, because 'one is established in these, thus they are foundations (paṭṭhānā). What is established? Mindfulness (sati). The foundations for mindfulness are the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhānā)'—by this meaning, even the objects of mindfulness are foundations of mindfulness. 'They are established, thus they are foundations. What are established? Mindfulnesses (satiyo). Mindfulnesses themselves are the foundations, thus foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhānā)'—by this meaning, mindfulnesses themselves are the foundations of mindfulness. Therefore, both views are tenable by way of interpretation. But those who abandon that interpretation and categorically state that 'all phenomena are foundations of mindfulness'—with reference to them, the question is from the proponent, and the assertion, by way of the object, is from the opponent. However, for one who is questioned, 'Are all phenomena mindfulness?', the refutation is for that very one, due to the absence of the nature of mindfulness in all things. Herein, 'leading to destruction' and so forth are qualifiers of the path. For the one-way path goes to Nibbāna, which is the destruction of the defilements; thus it is 'leading to destruction.' It goes while awakening to the four truths; thus it is 'leading to awakening.' It goes while diminishing the round; thus it is 'leading to diminution.' Thus, with these terms, he asks: 'Are all those phenomena for you such a one-way path?' Terms like 'taintless,' 'not connected with the fetters,' and so forth, are also stated for the purpose of asking about the supramundane state. 'Recollection of the Buddha,' and so forth, are stated by way of asking about the classifications.

Cakkhāyatanaṃ [M 0.0159] satipaṭṭhānantiādi sabbadhammānaṃ pabhedapucchāvasena vuttaṃ. Tatthāpi sativasena paṭikkhepo, ārammaṇavasena paṭiññāti. Evaṃ sabbapañhesu attho veditabbo. Suttasādhanā uttānatthāyevāti.

'The eye-base is a foundation of mindfulness,' and so forth, is stated by way of asking about the classifications of all phenomena. Therein too, the refutation is by way of mindfulness, and the assertion is by way of the object. Thus, the meaning should be understood in all questions. The adducing of the sutta is indeed of clear meaning.

Satipaṭṭhānakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discussion of the Foundations of Mindfulness is concluded.

9. Hevatthikathāvaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Hevatthika Discussion

304. Idāni hevatthikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “sabbepi atītādibhedā dhammā rūpādivasena atthi, atītaṃ anāgatapaccuppannavasena, anāgatapaccuppannāni vā atītādivasena natthi; tasmā sabbamevidaṃ evaṃ atthi evaṃ natthī”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi vuttappabhedānaṃ andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya atītaṃ atthīti pucchā sakavādissa. Hevatthi heva natthīti vissajjanaṃ paravādissa. Tattha hevāti evaṃ[P 0.0054]. Atha naṃ sakavādī “yadi atītova evaṃ atthi, evaṃ natthīti laddhi, evaṃ sante soyeva atthi, soyeva natthi nāmā”ti pucchanto sevatthi, seva natthīti āha. Itaro teneva sabhāvena atthitaṃ, teneva natthitaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho [V 0.0155] sakabhāveneva atthitaṃ, parabhāveneva natthitaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Tato paraṃ atthaṭṭho natthaṭṭhoti atthisabhāvo natthisabhāvo nāma hotīti pucchati. Imināvupāyena sabbavāresu attho veditabbo. Pariyosāne pana “tena hi atītaṃ hevatthi, heva natthī”ti ca “tena hi rūpaṃ hevatthi, heva natthī”ti cātiādīni vatvā kiñcāpi paravādinā laddhi patiṭṭhāpitā, ayoniso patiṭṭhāpitattā panesā appatiṭṭhāpitāyevāti.

304. Now there is the discussion called the Hevatthikathā. Herein, with reference to those who hold the view that 'all phenomena, distinguished as past and so forth, exist by way of form and so forth, but the past does not exist by way of the future and present, nor do the future and present exist by way of the past; therefore, all of this thus exists and thus does not exist'—such as the various kinds of Andhakas mentioned earlier—the question 'Does the past exist?' is from the proponent. The reply 'It thus exists, it thus does not exist' is from the opponent. Herein, `heva` means `evaṃ` (thus). Then the proponent, questioning him, said: 'If the past is thus existent and thus non-existent according to your view, then is it the very same thing that exists and the very same thing that does not exist?' The other refutes this, referring to its existence and non-existence by that same nature. When asked a second time, he agrees, referring to its existence by its own nature and its non-existence by another's nature. Thereafter, he asks whether 'the meaning of existence' and 'the meaning of non-existence' means there is a nature of existence and a nature of non-existence. By this method, the meaning should be understood in all sections of the debate. At the conclusion, however, although the opponent's view is established by stating, 'Therefore, the past thus exists and thus does not exist,' and 'Therefore, form thus exists and thus does not exist,' and so forth, because it is established unsystematically, it is in fact not established at all.

Hevatthikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Hevatthika Discussion.

Mahāvaggo niṭṭhito.

The Great Chapter is concluded.

2. Dutiyavaggo

2. The Second Chapter

1. Parūpahāravaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on Derogation

307. Idāni [P 0.0055][M 0.0160] parūpahārakathā nāma hoti. Tattha ye arahattaṃ paṭijānantānaṃ appatte pattasaññīnaṃ adhimānikānaṃ kuhakānaṃ vā arahattaṃ paṭijānantānaṃ sukkavissaṭṭhiṃ disvā “mārakāyikā devatā arahato asuciṃ upasaṃharantī”ti maññanti; seyyathāpi etarahi pubbaseliyā ca aparaseliyā ca; te sandhāya atthi arahatoti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Idāni yasmā sukkavissaṭṭhi nāma rāgasamuṭṭhānā hoti, tasmā atthi arahato rāgoti anuyogo āraddho. So sabbopi uttānatthoyeva.

307. Now there is the discussion called 'Derogation.' Herein, there are those who, seeing an emission of semen from some who claim arahantship—those with conceit who perceive attainment in what is not attained, or deceivers who claim arahantship—think, 'Deities of Māra's host are presenting impurity to the Arahant.' This is the view of the Pubbaseliyas and Aparaseliyas nowadays. With reference to them, the question 'Does an Arahant have an emission of semen?' is from the proponent, and the assertion is from the other. Now, because an emission of semen arises from lust, the cross-examination 'Does an Arahant have lust?' is begun. All of this is indeed of clear meaning.

Mārakāyikā devatā attanotiādipañhe yasmā tāsaṃ devatānaṃ sukkavissaṭṭhi nāma natthi, aññesampi sukkaṃ gahetvā na upasaṃharanti, arahato pana sukkameva natthi, tasmā na hevanti paṭikkhipati.

In the question beginning 'Do deities of Māra's host [present it] from themselves?', since those deities do not have what is called an emission of semen, nor do they take the semen of others and present it, and an Arahant, for his part, has no semen at all, therefore he refutes it, saying, 'It is not so.'

Neva attanotipañhe pana nimminitvā upasaṃharantīti laddhiyā paṭijānāti. Lomakūpehītipañhe sappitelānaṃ viya lomakūpehi upasaṃharaṇābhāvaṃ disvā paṭikkhipati.

However, in the question 'Not from themselves?', he agrees with the view that they present it after creating it. In the question 'Through the hair-pores?', seeing that there is no presentation through the hair-pores as there is for ghee and oil, he refutes it.

308. Handa [V 0.0156] hīti vacasāyatthe nipāto. “Arahā nu kho ahaṃ, no”ti evaṃ vimatiṃ gāhayissāmāti evaṃ vacasāyaṃ katvā upasaṃharantīti attho. Atthi arahato vimatīti puṭṭho aṭṭhavatthukaṃ vicikicchaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati, dutiyaṃ puṭṭho itthipurisānaṃ nāmagottādīsu sanniṭṭhānābhāvaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti.

308. `Handa hi` is a particle in the sense of verbal effort. The meaning is that they present it, making a verbal effort thus: 'We will cause him to have the doubt, "Am I an Arahant or not?"' When asked, 'Does an Arahant have doubt?', he refutes it, referring to the doubt concerning the eight objects (vicikicchā). When asked a second time, he agrees, referring to the absence of a firm conclusion regarding the names, clans, and so on, of men and women.

309. Atthi tassa āsayoti tassa sukkassa uccārapassāvānaṃ viya patiṭṭhānokāso atthīti pucchati.

309. 'Does he have a repository for it?' This asks whether there is a place of establishment for that semen, like there is for feces and urine.

312. Sadhammakusalassāti attano arahattadhammamatteyeva kusalassa. Paññāvimuttaṃ sandhāyevaṃ [P 0.0056] vadati. Paradhammakusalassāti sadhammato parasmiṃ [M 0.0161] aṭṭhasamāpattidhammepi kusalassa. Ubhatobhāgavimuttaṃ sandhāyevaṃ vadati. Sesamettha pāḷianusāreneva veditabbanti.

312. 'Skilled in one's own Dhamma' means skilled only in one's own Dhamma, that is, the state of Arahantship. This is said with reference to one liberated by wisdom. 'Skilled in another's Dhamma' means skilled in the Dhamma other than one's own Dhamma, that is, in the eight attainments. This is said with reference to one liberated both ways. The rest here should be understood according to the Pāli text itself.

Parūpahārakathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discussion on Derogation.

2-3-4. Aññāṇādikathāvaṇṇanā

2-3-4. Explanation of the Discussions Beginning with Ignorance.

314. Idāni aññāṇaṃ, kaṅkhā, paravitaraṇāti tisso kathā nāma honti. Tattha yesaṃ “arahato itthipurisādīnaṃ nāmagottādīsu ñāṇappavattiyā abhāvena atthi aññāṇaṃ, tattheva sanniṭṭhānābhāvena atthi kaṅkhā. Yasmā ca nesaṃ tāni vatthūni pare vitaranti pakāsenti ācikkhanti, tasmā nesaṃ atthi paravitaraṇā”ti imā laddhiyo, seyyathāpi etarahi pubbaseliyādīnaṃ; tesaṃ tā laddhiyo bhindituṃ tīsupi kathāsu pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā ca paṭikkhepo ca itarassa. Tattha sabbesupi pañhesu ceva vissajjanesu ca pāḷiṃ anugantvāva attho veditabboti.

314. Now, there are three discussions: ignorance, doubt, and 'dependence on others.' Here, for those who hold these views—just like the Pubbaseliyas and others at present—namely, that 'there is ignorance in an Arahant because there is no arising of knowledge regarding the names, clans, and so on, of men and women; there is doubt because there is no firm conviction in these matters; and there is dependence on others because others distribute, explain, and declare these things to them'—for them, these views are to be broken down in all three discussions through questions from one's own side, and admission and refutation from the other side. In all these questions and answers, the meaning should be understood only by following the Pāli text.

Aññāṇādikathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discussions Beginning with Ignorance.

5. Vacībhedakathāvaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Discourse on Speech Interruption.

326. Idāni [V 0.0157] vacībhedakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa dukkhanti vācā bhijjatī”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi pubbaseliyādīnaṃ; te sandhāya samāpannassa atthi vacībhedoti pucchā sakavādissa, laddhiyaṃ ṭhatvā paṭiññā paravādissa. Puna sabbatthāti tayo bhave sandhāya puṭṭho arūpaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Sabbadāti [P 0.0057] kālavasena puṭṭho paṭhamamaggakkhaṇe paṭhamajjhānikasamāpattito aññaṃ sabbaṃ samāpattikālaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Sabbesaṃ samāpannānanti puṭṭho lokiyasamāpattiyo samāpanne sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Sabbasamāpattīsūti puṭṭho dutiyajjhānādikaṃ lokuttaraṃ sabbañca lokiyasamāpattiṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati.

326. Now there is the discourse called 'Speech Interruption.' Here, regarding those who hold the view that 'at the moment of the stream-entry path, for one who has attained the first jhāna, the utterance "suffering" is broken'—such as the Pubbaseliyas and others nowadays—the question 'Is there speech interruption for one in attainment?' is asked by one of their own school, and the opponent, standing by their view, acknowledges it. Furthermore, when asked about 'everywhere,' having been asked with reference to the three realms, they deny it with reference to the immaterial realm. When asked about 'always,' having been asked in terms of time, they deny all times of attainment other than the first moment of the path with the attainment of the first jhāna. When asked about 'all those who are in attainment,' they deny it with reference to those who have attained worldly attainments. When asked about 'all attainments,' they deny it with reference to the supramundane attainments beginning with the second jhāna, and all worldly attainments.

Kāyabhedoti [M 0.0162] abhikkamādivasena pavattakāyaviññatti. Idaṃ “yāni cittāni vacīviññattiṃ samuṭṭhāpenti, tāneva kāyaviññattiṃ. Evaṃ sante kasmā kāyabhedopi na hotī”ti codanatthaṃ pucchati. Itaro laddhivasena paṭikkhipati ceva paṭijānāti ca. Idāni yadi so maggakkhaṇe “dukkha”nti vācaṃ bhāsati, “samudayo”tiādikampi bhāseyya. Yadi vā taṃ na bhāsati, itarampi na bhāseyyāti codanatthaṃ dukkhanti jānantotiādayo pañhā vuttā. Itaro pana attano laddhivaseneva paṭijānāti ceva paṭikkhipati ca. Lokuttaraṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpanno dukkhadukkhanti vipassatīti hissa laddhi.

'Bodily interruption' refers to bodily intimation occurring through movements and so forth. This is questioned for the purpose of challenging: 'If those very same cittas that produce verbal intimation also produce bodily intimation, then why is there not also a bodily interruption?' The other side rejects and acknowledges based on their view. Now, if at the path moment one utters the word 'suffering,' one would also utter 'origin' and so forth. Or if one does not utter that, one would not utter the others either—thus, for the purpose of challenging, questions such as 'knowing suffering' are stated. The other side, however, acknowledges and rejects based on their own view. For their view is that one who has attained the supramundane first jhāna contemplates 'suffering as suffering'.

328. Ñāṇanti lokuttaraṃ catusaccañāṇaṃ. Sotanti sotaviññāṇaṃ adhippetaṃ, yena taṃ saddaṃ suṇāti. Dvinnaṃ phassānanti sotasamphassamanosamphassānaṃ.

328. 'Knowledge' refers to the supramundane knowledge of the four noble truths. 'Ear' here means ear-consciousness, by which one hears that sound. 'Two contacts' refers to ear-contact and mind-contact.

329. No vata re vattabbeti yadi avisesena yaṃkiñci samāpannassa natthi vacībhedo, na avisesena vattabbaṃ “samāpannassa atthi vacībhedo”ti. Sesamettha uttānatthameva saddhiṃ suttasādhanāya. Yaṃ panetena “sikhissa ānanda, bhagavato”ti pariyosāne suttaṃ ābhataṃ, tattha yena samāpatticittena so vacībhedo samuṭṭhito, kāyabhedopi tena samuṭṭhātiyeva, na ca taṃ lokuttaraṃ paṭhamajjhānacittaṃ, tasmā asādhakanti.

329. 'No, indeed, it should not be said'—if there is no speech interruption for one who has attained any state without distinction, then it should not be said without distinction that 'there is speech interruption for one who has attained.' The rest here is clear in meaning, along with the sutta's substantiation. But regarding the sutta brought up at the conclusion, 'Sikhi, O Ānanda, the Blessed One,' there, the speech interruption arises from that attainment-consciousness, and bodily interruption also arises from that very same consciousness. Yet that is not the supramundane first jhāna consciousness; therefore, it is not valid.

Vacībhedakathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discourse on Speech Interruption.

6. Dukkhāhārakathāvaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Discourse on Suffering as Nutriment.

334. Idāni [V 0.0158] dukkhāhārakathā nāma hoti. Tattha “dukkhaṃ dukkhanti vācaṃ bhāsanto dukkhe ñāṇaṃ āharati, taṃ dukkhāhāro nāma vuccati[P 0.0058]. Tañca panetaṃ maggaṅgaṃ maggapariyāpanna”nti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi pubbaseliyānaṃ; te sandhāya dukkhāhāroti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā paravādissa. Ye kecīti paṭhamapañhe avipassake sandhāya paṭikkhipati, dutiyapañhe [M 0.0163] vipassake sandhāya paṭijānāti, taṃ panassa laddhimattameva. Tasmā “sabbe te”ti vādassa bhindanatthaṃ bālaputhujjanātiādimāha. Taṃ uttānatthamevāti.

334. Now there is the discourse called 'Suffering as Nutriment.' Here, regarding those who hold the view that 'by uttering the word "suffering" as "suffering," one brings forth knowledge of suffering, and that is called "suffering as nutriment," and moreover, that this is a path factor included within the path'—such as the Pubbaseliyas nowadays—the question 'Is suffering nutriment?' is asked by one of their own school, and the opponent acknowledges it. 'Whatever others'—in the first question, he rejects it with reference to non-insightful practitioners; in the second question, he affirms it with reference to insightful practitioners. But that is merely their own view. Therefore, for the purpose of breaking down the statement 'all of them,' he speaks of 'foolish ordinary people' and so forth. That is clear in meaning.

Dukkhāhārakathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discourse on Suffering as Nutriment.

7. Cittaṭṭhitikathāvaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Discourse on the Persistence of Mind.

335. Idāni cittaṭṭhitikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ samāpatticittañceva bhavaṅgacittañca anuppabandhena pavattamānaṃ disvā “ekameva cittaṃ ciraṃ tiṭṭhatī”ti laddhi seyyathāpi etarahi heṭṭhā vuttappabhedānaṃ andhakānaṃ, taṃladdhivisodhanatthaṃ ekaṃ, cittaṃ divasaṃ tiṭṭhatīti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā paravādissa. Upaḍḍhadivaso uppādakkhaṇoti ettha ṭhitikkhaṇaṃ anāmasitvā “aniccā vata saṅkhārā, uppādavayadhammino”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.186; 2.143) desanānayena uppādavayavaseneva pucchā katā.

335. Now comes the discourse called 'The Persistence of Mind.' Here, to clarify the view of those who, seeing the absorption mind and the life-continuum mind proceeding without interruption, hold the view that 'only one mind persists for a long time'—such as the Andhakas of the types mentioned previously—the question 'Does one mind persist for a day?' is posed by the proponent of one's own doctrine, and the affirmation is from the opponent. Regarding 'Half a day is the moment of arising,' here, without touching upon the moment of persistence, the question is posed only by way of arising and passing away, in accordance with the teaching method: 'Impermanent, indeed, are conditioned things, subject to arising and passing away' (Saṃ. Ni. 1.186; 2.143).

Te dhammā cittena lahuparivattāti puṭṭho cittato lahutaraparivattino dhamme apassanto paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho yassa cittassa dīghaṭṭhitiṃ icchati, taṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Yāvatāyukaṃ tiṭṭhatīti pañhe “cullāsītisahassāni, kappā tiṭṭhanti ye marū”tiādivacanavasena (mahāni. 10) āruppato aññatra paṭikkhipati, āruppe paṭijānāti. Muhuttaṃ muhuttaṃ uppajjatīti pañhe paravādissa “uppādavayadhammino”tiādisuttavirodhabhayena paṭijānāti. Ṭhitiṃ panassa laddhivasena icchati. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

When asked, 'Are those phenomena quick to change with the mind?' he denies it, not seeing phenomena that change quicker than the mind. When asked a second time, with reference to that mind whose long persistence he desires, he affirms it. To the question, 'Does it persist for a lifetime?' he denies it for those other than the formless attainments, by way of statements such as, 'Eighty-four thousand eons, the Maras persist,' but affirms it for the formless attainments. To the question, 'Does it arise moment by moment?' the opponent affirms it out of fear of contradicting sutta passages such as 'subject to arising and passing away.' But he desires its persistence in accordance with how it has been attained. The rest here is of obvious meaning.

Cittaṭṭhitikathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discourse on the Persistence of Mind.

8. Kukkuḷakathāvaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Discourse on Hot Ash.

338. Idāni [P 0.0059][V 0.0159] kukkuḷakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, ādittaṃ (saṃ. ni. 4.28; mahāva. 54) sabbe saṅkhārā dukkhā”tiādīni (dha. pa. 278) suttāni ayoniso gahetvā [M 0.0164] “nippariyāyeneva sabbe saṅkhārā kukkuḷā vītaccitaṅgārasammissā chārikanirayasadisā”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi gokulikānaṃ; tesaṃ nānappakārasukhasandassanena taṃ laddhiṃ vivecetuṃ pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā paravādissa. Tattha anodhiṃ katvāti odhiṃ mariyādaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ akaritvā, avisesena sabbeyevāti attho. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ pāḷinayeneva veditabbaṃ saddhiṃ suttasādhanāyāti.

338. Now comes the discourse called 'Hot Ash.' Here, for those who, having improperly grasped suttas such as 'All is burning, monks' and 'All conditioned things are suffering,' hold the view that 'All conditioned things are, without exception, hot ash, like embers mixed with glowing coals, resembling the hell of cinders'—as is the case nowadays with the Gokulikas—to dispel that view by showing various kinds of happiness, the question is from the proponent, and the affirmation is from the opponent. Here, 'without setting a limit' means not making a boundary, a limit, or a division; the meaning is 'all without exception.' The rest should be understood entirely in accordance with the method of the canonical text, along with the sutta substantiation.

Kukkuḷakathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discourse on Hot Ash.

9. Anupubbābhisamayakathāvaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Discourse on Gradual Realization.

339. Idāni anupubbābhisamayakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ –

339. Now comes the discourse called 'Gradual Realization.' Here, for those who—

“Anupubbena medhāvī, thokaṃ thokaṃ khaṇe khaṇe;

Kammāro rajatasseva, niddhame malamattano”ti. (dha. pa. 239) –

‘Gradually, little by little, from moment to moment, a wise person should remove their own impurities, as a smith removes the dross from silver.’ (Dhp 239)

Ādīni suttāni ayoniso gahetvā “sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanno ekacce kilese dukkhadassanena pajahati, ekacce samudayanirodhamaggadassanena, tathā sesāpīti evaṃ soḷasahi koṭṭhāsehi anupubbena kilesappahānaṃ katvā arahattapaṭilābho hotī”ti evarūpā nānābhisamayaladdhi uppannā, seyyathāpi etarahi andhakasabbatthikasammitiyabhadrayānikānaṃ; tesaṃ laddhivivecanatthaṃ anupubbābhisamayoti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Anupubbena sotāpattimagganti puṭṭho pana ekassa maggassa bahubhāvāpattibhayena paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho dukkhadassanādivasena paṭijānāti. Tāni vā cattāripi ñāṇāni eko sotāpattimaggoyevāti [V 0.0160] paṭijānāti, phalaṃ pana ekameva icchati, tasmā paṭikkhipati. Sakadāgāmimaggādīsupi [P 0.0060] eseva nayo.

Having improperly grasped these and other suttas, a view of manifold realization has arisen, namely: 'One who has entered upon the path for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry abandons some defilements through the seeing of suffering, some through the seeing of the origin, cessation, and path, and so with the remaining defilements—in this way, having gradually abandoned the defilements through sixteen sections, the attainment of arahantship occurs'—just as it exists now among the Andhakas, Sarvāstivādins, Sammitīyas, and Bhadrayānikas. To refute their view, the question, 'Is there gradual realization?' is from the proponent, and the affirmation is from the other. However, when asked, 'Is the stream-entry path gradual?' he rejects it out of fear that the one path would become many. When asked a second time, he affirms it on the basis of the seeing of suffering and so on. Or, he affirms that those four knowledges are indeed the one stream-entry path, but he desires only a single fruit; therefore, he rejects it. The same method applies to the path of the once-returner and so on.

344. Magge diṭṭhe phale ṭhitoti pañhe yasmā dukkhadassanādīhi dassanaṃ apariniṭṭhitaṃ, maggadassanena pariniṭṭhitaṃ nāma hoti, tadā so phale ṭhitoti saṅkhaṃ gacchati, tasmā paṭijānāti.

344. To the question, 'When the path is seen, is one established in the fruit?' he affirms it, because the seeing by means of suffering and so on is incomplete, whereas it is called complete only through the seeing of the path. At that time, he is reckoned as one who is established in the fruit.

345. Dukkhe [M 0.0165] diṭṭhe cattāri saccānīti pucchā paravādissa, ekābhisamayavasena paṭiññā sakavādissa. Puna dukkhasaccaṃ cattāri saccānīti anuyoge catunnampi nānāsabhāvattā paṭikkhepo tasseva.

345. The question, 'When suffering is seen, are the four truths seen?' is from the opponent, and the affirmation from the proponent is by way of a single realization. Again, upon the follow-up question, 'Is the truth of suffering the four truths?' the rejection is from that same proponent because of the distinct natures of the four.

Rūpakkhandhe aniccato diṭṭheti pucchā sakavādissa, samuddato ekabindussa rase paṭividdhe sesaudakassa paṭivedho viya ekadhamme aniccādito paṭividdhe sabbepi paṭividdhā hontīti laddhiyā paṭiññā paravādissa.

The question, 'When the form aggregate is seen as impermanent...?' is from the proponent. The affirmation from the opponent is based on the view that, just as when the taste of one drop from the ocean is penetrated, the taste of the remaining water is penetrated, so too when impermanence and so on are penetrated in one phenomenon, they are all penetrated.

Catūhi ñāṇehīti dukkhe ñāṇādīhi. Aṭṭhahi ñāṇehīti sāvakānaṃ sādhāraṇehi saccañāṇehi ceva paṭisambhidāñāṇehi ca. Dvādasahi ñāṇehīti dvādasaṅgapaṭiccasamuppādañāṇehi. Catucattārīsāya ñāṇehīti “jarāmaraṇe ñāṇaṃ, jarāmaraṇasamudaye ñāṇa”nti evaṃ nidānavagge vuttañāṇehi. Sattasattatiyā ñāṇehīti “jarāmaraṇaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppannaṃ khayadhammaṃ vayadhammaṃ virāgadhammaṃ nirodhadhamma”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.20) evaṃ tattheva vuttañāṇehi. Sesamettha pāḷinayeneva veditabbaṃ saddhiṃ suttasādhanenāti.

'With four knowledges' means with the knowledge of suffering and so on. 'With eight knowledges' means with the truth-knowledges and the analytical knowledges, which are common to the disciples. 'With twelve knowledges' means with the knowledges of the twelve-factored dependent origination. 'With forty-four knowledges' means with the knowledges stated in the Nidāna Vagga, such as 'knowledge in aging-and-death, knowledge in the origin of aging-and-death,' and so on. 'With seventy-seven knowledges' means with the knowledges stated in that same place, such as: 'Aging-and-death, monks, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to decay, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.20). The rest here should be understood in accordance with the method of the canonical text, along with the sutta substantiation.

Anupubbābhisamayakathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discourse on Gradual Realization.

10. Vohārakathāvaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Discourse on Conventional Usage.

347. Idāni [V 0.0161] vohārakathā nāma hoti. Tattha buddho bhagavā lokuttarena vohārena voharatīti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, laddhivasena paṭiññā paravādissa. Lokuttare sotetiādīni tassa ayuttavādībhāvadīpanatthaṃ vuttāni. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – “saddāyatanameva te lokuttaraṃ, udāhu sotādīnipī”ti.

347. Now comes the discourse called 'Conventional Usage.' Here, for those whose view is that the Buddha, the Blessed One, speaks with supramundane conventional usage—as is the case with the Andhakas at present—with reference to them, the question is from the proponent, and the affirmation from the opponent is in accordance with their view. The words 'with the supramundane ear' and so on are stated to demonstrate that he is an exponent of an untenable doctrine. This is the intention here: 'Is only the sound-base supramundane for you, or are the ear and so on as well?'

Hañci buddhassa bhagavato vohāro lokiye sote paṭihaññatīti ettha yadi so lokuttare paṭihaññeyya. Lokuttaro siyāti evamattho na gahetabbo. Lokiye [P 0.0061] paṭihaññamānassa pana lokuttaratā nāma natthīti ayametthādhippāyo. Lokiyena viññāṇenāti etthāpi lokiyenevāti [M 0.0166] attho. Itarathā anekantatā siyā. Lokuttarañhi lokiyenapi ñāṇena ñāyatī. Evaṃ sabbaṃ yathānurūpato veditabbaṃ. Sabbe te maggaṃ bhāventīti pañhesu ye maggaṃ nappaṭilabhanti, te sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Ye paṭilabhanti, te sandhāya paṭijānāti.

Here, regarding the statement, 'The conventional usage of the Buddha, the Blessed One, strikes the worldly ear': if it were to strike the supramundane ear, the meaning 'it would be supramundane' should not be taken. But for that which strikes the worldly ear, there is no such thing as a supramundane nature—this is the intention here. 'By worldly consciousness'—here too, the meaning is 'only by the worldly.' Otherwise, it would not be conclusive. For the supramundane is indeed known even by worldly knowledge. Thus, everything should be understood as is appropriate. In the questions, 'Do all those develop the path?' he rejects it with reference to those who do not attain the path, and he affirms it with reference to those who do attain it.

351. Sovaṇṇamayāyāti suvaṇṇamayāya. Idaṃ paravādissa udāharaṇaṃ.

351. 'Sovaṇṇamayāya' means 'suvaṇṇamayāya' (made of gold). This is an example for the opponent.

Eḷaṇḍiyāyāti eḷaṇḍamayāya. Idaṃ sakavādissa udāharaṇaṃ. Lokiyaṃ voharantassa lokiyoti ayampi ekā laddhi. Sā etarahi ekaccānaṃ andhakānaṃ laddhi. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

'Eḷaṇḍiyāyā' means 'eḷaṇḍamayāya' (made of castor-oil plant). This is an example for the proponent. That one who speaks in a worldly way is worldly—this too is one view. That is the view of some Andhakas at present. The rest here is of clear meaning.

Vohārakathāvaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Discourse on Conventional Usage.

11. Nirodhakathāvaṇṇanā

11. Exposition of the Discourse on Cessation

353. Idāni nirodhakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ appaṭisaṅkhānirodhañca paṭisaṅkhānirodhañca dvepi ekato katvā nirodhasaccanti laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi mahisāsakānañceva andhakānañca; te sandhāya dve nirodhāti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā paravādissa[V 0.0162]. Dve dukkhanirodhāti pañhesu yasmā dve dukkhasaccāni na icchati, tasmā paṭikkhipati. Yasmā dvīhākārehi dukkhaṃ nirujjhatīti icchati, tasmā paṭijānāti. Dve nirodhasaccānītipañhesu dvinnaṃ dukkhasaccānaṃ nirodhavasenaanicchanto paṭikkhipati. Dvīhākārehi dukkhassa nirujjhanato paṭijānāti. Dve tāṇānītiādīsupi eseva nayo.

353. Now there is the discourse on cessation. Herein, for those whose view is that, having combined both cessation without discernment and cessation with discernment into one, it is the truth of cessation—just as is the view of the Mahisāsakas and Andhakas at present—with reference to them, the question, ‘Are there two cessations?’ is by the proponent, and the assertion is by the opponent. In the questions, ‘Are there two cessations of suffering?’, because he does not accept two truths of suffering, he rejects it; because he accepts that suffering ceases in two ways, he affirms it. In the questions, ‘Are there two truths of cessation?’, not accepting it on the basis of the cessation of two truths of suffering, he rejects it; he affirms it because suffering ceases in two ways. The same method applies in ‘Are there two refuges?’ and so forth.

Atthi dvinnaṃ nibbānānantiādīsu pucchāsu uccanīcatādīni apassanto paṭikkhipati.

In questions such as 'Are there two Nibbānas?' and so forth, he rejects it by not seeing high and low and so forth.

Appaṭisaṅkhāniruddheti ye paṭisaṅkhāya lokuttarena ñāṇena aniruddhā suddhapakatikattā vā uddesaparipucchādīnaṃ vā vasena na samudācaraṇato niruddhāti vuccanti, te saṅkhāre. Paṭisaṅkhā nirodhentīti. Lokuttarañāṇena nirodhenti anuppattibhāvaṃ gamenti. Nanu appaṭisaṅkhāniruddhā saṅkhārāti [P 0.0062] pucchā paravādissa[M 0.0167]. Tattha bhaggānaṃ puna abhañjanato appaṭisaṅkhāniruddhānaṃ vā ariyamagge uppanne tathā nirujjhanatova sakavādī accantabhaggataṃ paṭijānāti. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

Regarding 'ceased without discernment': this refers to those formations which, not having been ceased by supramundane knowledge with discernment, are called 'ceased' either because of their pure nature or because they do not arise by way of exposition, questioning, and so forth. 'To cause cessation with discernment' means to cause cessation with supramundane knowledge, to bring them to a state of non-arising. 'But are not formations ceased without discernment?' is the question of the opponent. Therein, the proponent affirms utter destruction, because what has been broken is not broken again, or because those things that have ceased without discernment cease in such a way when the noble path has arisen. The rest here is of clear meaning.

Nirodhakathāvaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Discourse on Cessation.

Dutiyo vaggo.

The Second Section.

3. Tatiyavaggo

3. The Third Section

1. Balakathāvaṇṇanā

1. Exposition of the Discourse on Powers

354. Idāni [P 0.0063] balakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ anuruddhasaṃyutte “imesañca panāhaṃ, āvuso, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā ṭhānañca ṭhānato aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānato yathābhūtaṃ pajānāmī”tiādīni (saṃ. ni. 5.913) dasasuttāni ayoniso gahetvā “tathāgatabalaṃ sāvakasādhāraṇa”nti laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, laddhiyaṃ ṭhatvā paṭiññā paravādissa. Tathāgatabalañca nāmetaṃ sāvakehi sādhāraṇampi atthi asādhāraṇampi sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇampi. Tattha āsavānaṃ khaye ñāṇaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ. Indriyaparopariyattiñāṇaṃ [V 0.0163] asādhāraṇaṃ. Sesaṃ sādhāraṇañca asādhāraṇañca. Ṭhānāṭṭhānādīni hi sāvakā padesena jānanti, tathāgatā nippadesena. Iti tāni uddesato sādhāraṇāni, na niddesato. Ayaṃ pana avisesena sabbampi sādhāraṇanti āha. Tamenaṃ tato vivecetuṃ tathāgatabalaṃ sāvakabalanti puna anuyogo āraddho. Tattha paṭhamapañhe niddesato sabbākāravisayataṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Dutiyapañhe uddesato ṭhānāṭṭhānamattādijānanavasena paṭijānāti. Taññevātiādipañhesu sabbākārena ninnānākaraṇatāya abhāvena paṭikkhipati. Pubbayogo ca pubbacariyā ca atthato ekaṃ, tathā dhammakkhānañca dhammadesanā ca.

354. Now there is the discourse on powers. Herein, some—like the Andhakas nowadays—wrongly grasp the ten suttas in the Anuruddha Saṃyutta, such as: “Friends, through the development and cultivation of these four foundations of mindfulness, I understand the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible as it really is,” and hold the view that “the Tathāgata’s powers are common to his disciples.” With reference to them, the question is by the proponent, and the assertion, standing firm in their view, is by the opponent. The Tathāgata’s powers are indeed both common and uncommon to his disciples, and also partly common and partly uncommon. Among them, the knowledge of the destruction of the taints is common. The knowledge of the varying maturity of others’ faculties is uncommon. The rest are both common and uncommon. For disciples know the possible and impossible, etc., partially, while the Tathāgatas know them completely. Thus, in terms of a general description, they are common, but not in terms of a detailed explanation. Yet this one asserts that all are common without distinction. To distinguish him from that, the question, 'Is the Tathāgata's power a disciple's power?' is again raised. In the first question, it is rejected by considering the all-encompassing scope in the detailed explanation. In the second question, it is acknowledged in terms of a general description, such as knowing just the possible and impossible, etc. In the questions beginning with 'Is it just this?', it is rejected due to the lack of differentiation in all aspects. Past striving and past conduct are the same in meaning, as are the proclamation of the Dhamma and the teaching of the Dhamma.

Indriyaparopariyattipañhe ekadesena sādhāraṇataṃ sandhāya sāvakavisaye paṭijānāti.

In the question on the varying maturity of others’ faculties, he affirms it with respect to the domain of disciples, considering the partial commonality.

355. Idāni [M 0.0168] yasmā uddesato ṭhānāṭṭhānādīni sāvako jānāti, tasmā sāvakassa tathā jānanaṃ pakāsetvā tena jānanamattasāmaññena tesaṃ sāvakasādhāraṇattaṃ patiṭṭhāpetuṃ sāvako ṭhānāṭṭhānaṃ [P 0.0064] jānātītiādayo paravādipañhā honti. Tattha indriyaparopariyattiñāṇaṃ channaṃ asādhāraṇañāṇānaṃ aññataranti na gahitaṃ. Āsavakkhayena vā āsavakkhayanti yaṃ tathāgatassa āsavakkhayena saddhiṃ sāvakassa āsavakkhayaṃ paṭicca vattabbaṃ siyā nānākaraṇaṃ, taṃ natthi. Vimuttiyā vā vimuttinti padepi eseva nayo. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

355. Now, because the disciple knows the possible and impossible, etc., in terms of a general description, therefore, having shown the disciple's knowledge in that way, to establish that these are common to disciples by that mere commonality of knowledge, the opponent's questions such as, "Does the disciple know the possible and impossible?" etc., are raised. Herein, the knowledge of the varying maturity of others’ faculties is not taken as one of the six uncommon knowledges. As for "by the destruction of the taints, or the destruction of the taints," whatever distinction should be stated regarding the disciple's destruction of the taints in relation to the Tathāgata's destruction of the taints, there is none. The same method applies to the phrase "by liberation, or liberation." The rest here is of clear meaning.

356. Idāni yaṃ sakavādinā “āsavānaṃ khaye ñāṇaṃ sādhāraṇa”nti anuññātaṃ, tena saddhiṃ saṃsanditvā sesānampi sādhāraṇabhāvaṃ pucchituṃ puna āsavānaṃ khayetiādayo paravādipañhāva honti. Tesaṃ vissajjane sakavādinā āsavakkhaye visesābhāvena taṃ ñāṇaṃ sādhāraṇanti anuññātaṃ. Itaresupi visesābhāvena sādhāraṇatā paṭikkhittā. Puna ṭhānāṭṭhānādīnaṃ āsavakkhayeneva saddhiṃ saṃsanditvā asādhāraṇapucchā paravādisseva. Tattha āsavakkhayañāṇe paṭikkhepo, sesesu ca paṭiññā sakavādissa. Tato indriyaparopariyattena saddhiṃ saṃsanditvā asādhāraṇapucchā paravādissa. Sā saṅkhipitvā dassitā. Tathāpi indriyaparopariyatte paṭiññā, sesesu ca paṭikkhepo sakavādissa. Tato ṭhānāṭṭhānādīhi saddhiṃ saṃsanditvā indriyaparopariyattassa sādhāraṇapucchā paravādissa. Sāpi saṅkhipitvāva dassitā. Tattha indriyaparopariyatte paṭikkhepo. Sesesu ca paṭiññā sakavādissāti.

356. Now, in order to ask about the commonality of the remaining powers by comparing them with what the proponent has acknowledged as, “the knowledge of the destruction of the taints is common,” the opponent's questions, beginning with “the destruction of the taints,” etc., are again raised. In answering them, the proponent acknowledges that knowledge as common due to the absence of distinction in the destruction of the taints. For the others, commonality is rejected due to the presence of a distinction. Again, by comparing the possible and impossible, etc., with the destruction of the taints, the questions about what is not common belong solely to the opponent. There, the proponent rejects it in the case of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, but affirms it in the case of the rest. Then, by comparing with the varying maturity of others’ faculties, the questions about what is not common belong to the opponent. This has been briefly shown. Even so, the proponent affirms it in the case of the varying maturity of others’ faculties, but rejects it in the case of the rest. Next, by comparing the possible and impossible, etc., with the varying maturity of others’ faculties, the questions about the commonality of the varying maturity of others’ faculties belong to the opponent. That too has been briefly shown. There, the proponent rejects it in the case of the varying maturity of others’ faculties, but affirms it in the case of the rest.

Balakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion of Powers.

2. Ariyantikathāvaṇṇanā

2. Exposition of the Ariyanti Discussion.

357. Idāni [V 0.0164] ariyantikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “na kevalaṃ āsavakkhayañāṇameva ariyaṃ, atha kho purimānipi nava balāni ariyāni”cceva laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya ariyanti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Puna yadi taṃ ariyaṃ, maggādīsu tena aññatarena [M 0.0169] bhavitabbanti maggādivasena pucchā sakavādissa, paṭikkhepo itarassa.

357. Now, there is what is called the Ariyanti discussion. In this regard, some hold the view that "not only the knowledge of the destruction of the taints is noble, but also the preceding nine powers are noble," just as the Andhakas do nowadays. With reference to them, the question "Is it noble?" is the proponent's question, and the other's acknowledgment. Again, if that is noble, it must be one of the path, etc.—thus the proponent's question in terms of the path, etc., and the other's rejection.

Puna suññatārammaṇādivasena pucchā sakavādissa. Tattha dve suññatā – sattasuññatā ca saṅkhārasuññatā ca. Sattasuññatā nāma diṭṭhiyā [P 0.0065] parikappitena sattena suññā pañcakkhandhā. Saṅkhārasuññatā nāma sabbasaṅkhārehi suññaṃ vivittaṃ nissaṭaṃ nibbānaṃ. Tattha paravādī nibbānārammaṇataṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati, saṅkhārārammaṇataṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Manasi karotīti puṭṭhopi nibbānameva sandhāya paṭikkhipati, saṅkhāre sandhāya paṭijānāti. Tato sakavādinā “ṭhānāṭṭhānādimanasikāro saṅkhārārammaṇo, suññatamanasikāro nibbānārammaṇo”ti imaṃ nayaṃ gahetvā “dvinnaṃ phassānaṃ dvinnaṃ cittānaṃ samodhānaṃ hotī”ti puṭṭho lesokāsaṃ alabhanto paṭikkhipati. Animittāpaṇihitesupi eseva nayo. Sattanimittābhāvato hi khandhā animittā. Saṅkhāranimittābhāvato nibbānaṃ. Ekadhammasmimpi āropetvā ṭhapetabbasaṅkhātena ca paṇidahitabbaṭṭhena paṇihitasaṅkhaṃ gatena sattapaṇidhinā appaṇihitā khandhā. Taṇhāpaṇidhinā taṇhāya vā ārammaṇabhūtena sabbasaṅkhārapaṇidhinā appaṇihitaṃ nibbānaṃ. Tasmā idhāpi paṭikkhepo ca paṭiññā ca purimanayeneva veditabbā.

Again, the proponent's question is based on the object of emptiness, and so on. Herein, there are two kinds of emptiness: emptiness of a being and emptiness of formations. Emptiness of a being means the five aggregates are empty of a being conceived by view. Emptiness of formations means Nibbāna is empty, secluded, and detached from all formations. Here, the opponent rejects by referring to Nibbāna as the object, but accepts by referring to formations as the object. Even when asked, 'Does one attend to it?', he rejects by referring to Nibbāna and accepts by referring to formations. Then, the proponent, taking up this method—'Attention to the possible and impossible has formations as its object, while attention to emptiness has Nibbāna as its object'—when asked, 'Is there a concurrence of two contacts and two consciousnesses?', and finding no opportunity for evasion, rejects it. The same method applies even in the case of the signless and the desireless. For the aggregates are signless due to the absence of a sign of a being. Nibbāna is signless due to the absence of the sign of formations. The aggregates are desireless, being free from the seven kinds of aspiration, which are designated as 'aspired to' because they are an object of aspiration and are reckoned as something to be established in relation to a single thing. Nibbāna is desireless because it is not an object of aspiration by craving, or by the aspiration for all formations that are objects of craving. Therefore, here too, rejection and acceptance should be understood in the same way as before.

358. Tato “yathā satipaṭṭhānādayo lokuttaradhammā ariyā ceva suññatādiārammaṇā ca, kiṃ te evaṃ ṭhānāṭṭhānañāṇa”nti anulomapaṭilomapucchā honti. Tattha sabbāpi paṭiññā sabbe ca paṭikkhepā paravādisseva. Imināvupāyena sesañāṇesupi pucchāvissajjanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ pana sesāni saṅkhipitvā avasāne cutūpapātañāṇameva vibhattaṃ. Tato paraṃ sakasamayepi “ariya”nti siddhena āsavānaṃ khayañāṇena saddhiṃ saṃsanditvā sesañāṇānaṃ anulomato ca paṭilomato ca ariyabhāvapucchā honti. Tā sabbā paravādissa, paṭiññā paṭikkhepo ca sakavādissa[V 0.0165]. Te uttānatthāyeva. Pāḷiyaṃ panettha paṭhamanavamāneva dassetvā satta ñāṇāni saṅkhittānīti.

358. Then, questions are asked in forward and reverse order: 'Just as the supramundane states, such as the foundations of mindfulness, are noble and have emptiness, etc., as their object, are they thus the knowledge of what is possible and impossible?' Here, all affirmations and all rejections belong solely to the opponent. By this method, the questioning and answering regarding the remaining knowledges should be understood. However, in the Pāli text, the remaining ones are summarized, and only the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings is explained in detail at the end. Thereafter, even within one's own school, questions about the nobility of the remaining knowledges are asked, both in forward and reverse order, by comparing them with the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, which is established as 'noble.' All these belong to the opponent, while affirmation and rejection belong to the proponent. These are obvious in meaning. In the Pāli text here, however, only the first and the ninth are shown, and the seven knowledges are summarized.

Ariyantikathāvaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Ariyanti Discussion.

3. Vimuttikathāvaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discussion of Liberation.

363. Idāni [P 0.0066][M 0.0170] vimuttikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “vītarāgacittānaṃ vimuttipayojanaṃ nāma natthi. Yathā pana malīnaṃ vatthaṃ dhoviyamānaṃ malā vimuccati, evaṃ sarāgaṃ cittaṃ rāgato vimuccatī”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya sarāganti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Tato rāgasahagatantiādinā nayena puṭṭho maggakkhaṇe cittaṃ vimuccati nāma. Tadā ca evarūpaṃ cittaṃ natthīti paṭikkhipati.

363. Now comes the discussion called 'Liberation'. Here, for those who hold the view that 'For those whose minds are free from lust, there is no such thing as the purpose of liberation. Just as a soiled cloth, being washed, is liberated from stains, so a lustful mind is liberated from lust'—as is the view of the Andhakas nowadays—the question 'Is it lustful?' is from the proponent, while the admission is from the other. Then, when asked in terms of 'accompanied by lust,' etc., it is said that the mind is liberated at the moment of the path. And at that time, he rejects that such a mind exists.

Saphassantiādinā nayena puṭṭhopi yathā phasso ca cittañca ubho rāgato vimuccanti, evaṃ rāgassa vimuttiṃ apassamāno paṭikkhipati. Sadosādīsupi imināvupāyena attho veditabbo.

Even when asked in terms of 'with contact,' etc., since he does not see how both contact and mind are liberated from lust, he rejects the proposition. The same method should be understood in the case of aversion, etc.

Vimuttikathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discussion of Liberation.

4. Vimuccamānakathāvaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discussion of Being Liberated.

366. Idāni vimuccamānakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “jhānena vikkhambhanavimuttiyā vimuttaṃ, maggakkhaṇe samucchedavimuttiyā vimuccamānaṃ nāma hotī”ti laddhi, te sandhāya vimuttaṃ vimuccamānanti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarasa.

366. Now comes the discussion called 'Being Liberated'. Here, for those who hold the view that 'What is liberated by jhāna is liberated by liberation through suppression, while at the moment of the path it is called being liberated by liberation through eradication'—referring to them, the proponent's question is, 'Is that which is liberated being liberated?', while the acknowledgement is from the other.

Puna ekadesanti pucchā sakavādissa. Tattha ekadesanti bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ. Yathā vimuttaṃ, ekadesena [V 0.0166] vā ekadese vā avimuttaṃ hoti kiṃ evaṃ ekadesaṃ vimuttaṃ, ekadesaṃ avimuttanti pucchati. Kiṃ kāraṇā evaṃ pucchatīti? “Vimuttaṃ vimuccamāna”nti vippakatabhāvena vuttattā. Yathā hi kariyamānā kaṭādayo vippakatattā ekadesena katā ekadesena akatā honti, tathā idampi ekadesaṃ vimuttaṃ ekadesaṃ avimuttanti āpajjati. Tato paravādī kaṭādīnaṃ viya cittassa ekadesābhāvā paṭhamapañhe paṭikkhipitvā dutiye vimuccamānassa apariniṭṭhitavimuttitāya paṭijānāti. Lokiyajjhānakkhaṇaṃ vā sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Na hi taṃ tadā samucchedavimuttiyā vimuccamānaṃ. Lokuttarajjhānakkhaṇaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Tañhi tadā samucchedavimuttiyā vimuttekadesena [P 0.0067] vimuccamānantissa laddhi. Tato sakavādī “yadi te ekameva [M 0.0171] cittaṃ ekadesaṃ vimuttaṃ ekadesaṃ avimuttaṃ, evaṃ sante yo ekeneva cittena sotāpanno hoti, sopi te ekadesaṃ sotāpanno, ekadesaṃ na sotāpanno āpajjatī”ti codanatthaṃ ekadesaṃ sotāpannotiādimāha. Itaro taṃ vidhānaṃ apassanto paṭikkhipati. Sesavāresupi eseva nayo.

Again, the proponent's question is 'partly'. Here, 'partly' is a neuter noun of state. For example, if something is liberated, is it partly or in some part unliberated? Thus, he asks, 'Is one part liberated and one part unliberated?' Why does he ask in this way? Because it is stated in terms of 'liberated' and 'being liberated,' in an incomplete state. Just as mats, etc., being made, are partly made and partly unmade due to their incomplete state, so too here, it would follow that one part is liberated and one part is unliberated. Thereupon, the opponent, due to the absence of parts in the mind, unlike in mats etc., having rejected the first question, acknowledges it in the second due to the incomplete liberation of that which is being liberated. Or he rejects it with reference to the moment of mundane jhāna, for at that time it is not being liberated by way of liberation through eradication. He acknowledges it with reference to the moment of supramundane jhāna, for then it is being liberated by way of liberation through eradication—hence his view that 'it is partly liberated while being liberated'. Then, the proponent, intending to censure, says, 'If for you, a single mind is partly liberated and partly unliberated, then in that case, one who is a stream-enterer with a single mind would, for you, also be partly a stream-enterer and partly not a stream-enterer.' To illustrate this, he says, 'partly a stream-enterer,' and so on. The other, not seeing that implication, rejects it. The same method applies in the remaining sections.

Uppādakkhaṇapañhe yadi ekameva cittaṃ vimuttañca vimuccamānañca, ekasmiṃ khaṇe vimuttaṃ ekasmiṃ vimuccamānaṃ āpajjati. Kiṃ te evarūpaṃ cittanti attho.

In the question concerning the moment of arising: if a single mind is both liberated and being liberated, it would follow that in one moment it is liberated and in another it is being liberated. The meaning is: 'What is such a mind to you?'

367. Suttasādhane paṭhamasuttaṃ paravādissa. Tatrāssāyamadhippāyo – vimuccatīti vippakataniddeso. Tasmā yaṃ tassa yogino evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato etehi āsavehi cittaṃ vimuccati, taṃ vimuccamānaṃ nāma hotīti. Dutiyasuttaṃ sakavādissa. Tatrāssāyamadhippāyo – yadi te vimuccatīti vacanato vimuttaṃ vimuccamānaṃ, idha vimuccatīti vacanābhāvato vimuttameva siyā, na vimuccamānanti.

367. In adducing the sutta proof, the first sutta is for the opponent. Herein, this is the intended meaning: 'is liberated' (vimuccati) is an incomplete designation. Therefore, when the mind of that yogi, knowing thus and seeing thus, is liberated from these taints, that is called 'being liberated'. The second sutta is for the proponent. Herein, this is the intended meaning: if, for you, on account of the statement 'is liberated' (vimuccati), what is liberated is 'being liberated', then here, due to the absence of the statement 'is liberated', it should be only 'liberated', not 'being liberated'.

Idāni “yathā te vippakatavimuttitāya vimuccamānaṃ, kiṃ evaṃ vippakatarāgāditāya rajjamānādīnipi atthī”ti codanatthaṃ puna atthi cittantiādi āraddhaṃ. Paravādināpi tathārūpaṃ cittaṃ apassantena sabbaṃ paṭikkhittaṃ. Atha naṃ sakavādī “dveyeva koṭiyo, tatiyā natthī”ti anubodhento nanu rattañceva arattañcātiādimāha. Tassattho – nanu bhadramukha, rāgasampayuttaṃ cittaṃ rattaṃ vippayuttaṃ arattanti dveva koṭiyo, rajjamānaṃ nāma tatiyā koṭi natthīti? Duṭṭhādīsupi eseva nayo. Atha naṃ āmantāti paṭijānitvā ṭhitaṃ. Vimuttipakkhepi dveyeva [V 0.0167] koṭiyo dassetuṃ hañci rattañcevātiādimāha. Tassattho – yadi etā dve koṭiyo sampaṭicchasi, avimuttañceva vimuttañcā ti imāpi sampaṭiccha. Kilesasampayuttañhi cittaṃ avimuttaṃ, vippayuttaṃ vimuttaṃ. Vimuccamānaṃ nāmāti paramatthato tatiyā koṭi natthīti.

Now, for the purpose of censure with the question, 'Just as for you there is 'being liberated' by way of incomplete liberation, are there also states of 'being lustful', etc., by way of incomplete lust, etc.?', the passage beginning 'Is there a mind?' is introduced. The opponent, not seeing such a mind, rejected it all. Then the proponent, instructing him that 'There are only two alternatives, a third does not exist,' said, 'Is it not so that there is the lustful and the lust-free?' and so on. Its meaning is: 'Good sir, is it not so that there are only two alternatives—a mind associated with lust is lustful, and one dissociated is lust-free? A third alternative, called 'being lustful,' does not exist.' The same method applies to the hateful, etc. Then, having acknowledged 'Yes,' he stands his ground. To show that in the case of liberation also there are only two alternatives, he said, 'If there is the lustful...' and so on. Its meaning is: 'If you accept these two alternatives, then accept these also: the unliberated and the liberated. For a mind associated with defilements is unliberated, while one dissociated is liberated. In an ultimate sense, a third alternative called 'being liberated' does not exist.'

Vimuccamānakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion of 'Being Liberated'.

5. Aṭṭhamakakathāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Discussion Concerning the Eighth Person.

368. Idāni [P 0.0068][M 0.0172] aṭṭhamakakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ anulomagotrabhumaggakkhaṇe kilesānaṃ samudācārābhāvato aṭṭhamakassa sotāpattimaggaṭṭhapuggalassa dve pariyuṭṭhānā pahīnāti laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi andhakānañceva sammitiyānañca; tesaṃ aññataraṃ sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, maggakkhaṇato paṭṭhāya diṭṭhiyā anuppattiṃ sandhāya paṭiññā itarassa. Tato yasmā diṭṭhi nāmesā sotāpannasseva pahīnā, na maggaṭṭhassa, tasmā aṭṭhamako puggalo sotāpannoti anuyogo sakavādissa. Vicikicchāpañhepi eseva nayo. Anusayapañhe pariyuṭṭhānato añño anusayoti tesaṃ laddhi, tasmā “na heva”nti paṭikkhittaṃ.

368. Now there is the discussion concerning the eighth person. Herein, there is the view of those who hold that for the eighth person, the individual established on the path to stream-entry, two obsessions are abandoned at the path-moment, due to the non-occurrence of defilements; such is the view of the Andhakas and the Sammitiyas nowadays. With reference to one of them, the question is the proponent's; with reference to the non-arising of wrong view from the path-moment onwards, the admission is the opponent's. Then, because this thing called wrong view is abandoned only by the stream-enterer, not by one on the path, the proponent's rejoinder is, therefore, that the eighth person is a stream-enterer. The same method applies to the question on doubt. In the question on the underlying tendencies, their view is that an obsession is different from an underlying tendency; therefore, it was rejected with 'Not so'.

Sīlabbataparāmāsapañhepi sīlabbataparāmāsapariyuṭṭhānanti vohāraṃ na passati, tasmā paṭikkhipati. Pariyuṭṭhānamevassa pahīnanti laddhi.

Also in the question concerning the clinging to precepts and observances, he does not see the usage 'obsession of clinging to precepts and observances,' and therefore he rejects it. His view is that the obsession itself is abandoned.

369. Maggo bhāvitoti pañhe tasmiṃ khaṇe bhāveti, na bhāvito. Tasmā paṭikkhipati. Amaggenātiādianuyoge paṭhamamaggeneva pahīnabhāvaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Yadi hi amaggena pahīyetha, gotrabhupuggalādīnampi pahīyethāti āpajjanato. Uppajjissatīti pucchā paravādissa, vissajjanaṃ sakavādissa. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

369. In the question, 'Is the path developed?', at that moment one is developing it, but it is not yet developed. Therefore, he rejects it. In the rejoinder, 'By the non-path?' and so on, he rejects it with reference to the fact that abandonment is by the first path itself. For if it were abandoned by a non-path, it would follow that it would be abandoned even for individuals such as the one at change-of-lineage. 'Will it arise?' is the opponent's question; the answer is the proponent's. The rest everywhere is of plain meaning.

Aṭṭhamakakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion Concerning the Eighth Person.

6. Aṭṭhamakassa indriyakathāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Discussion of the Faculties of the Eighth Person.

371. Idāni [V 0.0168] aṭṭhamakassa indriyakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “aṭṭhamako maggakkhaṇe indriyāni paṭilabhati nāma, no cassa paṭiladdhāni hontī”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya natthi saddhindriyanti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Natthi saddhāti puṭṭho pana saddhindriyato saddhāya nānattaṃ sallakkhetvā paṭikkhipati. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Yathā pana yassa atthi mano, tassa manindriyampi atthi; evaṃ yassa [M 0.0173] saddhādayo atthi, tassa atthi saddhindriyādīnipīti dīpanatthaṃ [P 0.0069] atthi mano atthi manindriyantiādi āraddhaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ uttānatthameva saddhiṃ suttasādhanenāti.

371. Now there is the discussion concerning the faculties of the eighth person. Herein, with reference to those who hold the view that 'the eighth person acquires the faculties at the path-moment, but they are not yet acquired by him'—as do the Andhakas nowadays—the question, 'Is there no faculty of faith?' is the proponent's, and the admission is the opponent's. But when asked, 'Is there no faith?', he rejects it, having noted the difference between faith and the faculty of faith. The same method applies to the remaining cases. However, to illustrate that just as one who has a mind also has the faculty of mind, so too one who has faith and so on also has the faculties of faith and so on, the passage beginning 'There is mind, there is the faculty of mind' is introduced. All of that, together with the adducing of the sutta, is of plain meaning.

Aṭṭhamakassa indriyakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion of the Faculties of the Eighth Person.

7. Dibbacakkhukathāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Discussion of the Divine Eye.

373. Idāni dibbacakkhukathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ catutthajjhānadhammūpatthaddhaṃ maṃsacakkhumeva dibbacakkhu nāma hotīti laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi andhakānañceva sammitiyānañca; te sandhāya maṃsacakkhunti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa.

373. Now there is the discussion of the divine eye. Herein, there is the view of those for whom the physical eye itself, when supported by the states of the fourth jhāna, is called the divine eye—as is the view of the Andhakas and the Sammitiyas nowadays. With reference to them, the question, 'Is it the physical eye?' is the proponent's, and the admission is the opponent's.

Puna “maṃsacakkhu dibbacakkhu, dibbacakkhu maṃsacakkhū”ti puṭṭho taṃ mattameva taṃ na hotīti paṭikkhipati. Yādisantiādipucchāsupi ubhinnaṃ ekasabhāvābhāveneva paṭikkhipati.

Again, when asked, 'Is the physical eye the divine eye, and is the divine eye the physical eye?', he rejects it, stating that it is not merely so. Also in questions such as, 'Of what kind?', he rejects it precisely because the two do not have a single, identical nature.

Visayotiādīsu ubhinnampi rūpāyatanameva visayo. Maṃsacakkhu pana āpāthagatameva passati. Itaraṃ anāpāthagataṃ tiropabbatādigatampi. Dibbacakkhussa ca atisukhumampi rūpaṃ gocaro, na tādisaṃ itarassāti evametesaṃ ānubhāvagocarā asadisā.

In questions concerning the object and so forth, the object for both is indeed the sphere of form. However, the physical eye sees only what has come into its range, while the other sees even what is beyond its range, such as what is behind a mountain and so on. And for the divine eye, even extremely subtle form is its domain, which is not so for the other. Thus, their power and range are dissimilar.

Upādiṇṇaṃ hutvā anupādiṇṇaṃ hotīti puṭṭho yasmā maṃsacakkhu upādiṇṇaṃ, dibbacakkhu anupādiṇṇaṃ, na ca maṃsacakkhumeva dibbacakkhūti icchati, tasmā paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho yasmā [V 0.0169] “maṃsacakkhussa uppādo, maggo dibbassa cakkhuno”ti vacanaṃ nissāya maṃsacakkhupaccayā dibbacakkhu uppajjati, tañca rūpāvacarikānaṃ catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ pasādoti icchati, tasmā paṭijānāti. Kāmāvacaraṃ hutvāti puṭṭhopi yasmā na maṃsacakkhumeva dibbacakkhūti icchati, tasmā paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho rūpāvacarajjhānapaccayena uppannattā rūpāvacaraṃ nāma jātanti paṭijānāti.

When asked, 'Having been clung to, does it become unclung to?' he denies it because the physical eye is clung to, the divine eye is unclung to, and he does not hold the view that the physical eye itself is the divine eye. When asked a second time, he affirms it because, relying on the statement, 'The arising of the physical eye is the path to the divine eye,' the divine eye arises dependent on the physical eye, and he holds the view that it is the sensitivity of the four great elements pertaining to the form realm. Even when asked, 'Having been of the sensual realm, does it become of the form realm?' he denies it because he does not hold the view that the physical eye itself is the divine eye. When asked a second time, he affirms that it is called 'of the form realm' because it arises dependent on the form-realm jhāna.

Rūpāvacaraṃ hutvā arūpāvacaranti puṭṭhopi tato paraṃ bhāvanāya arūpāvacarakkhaṇe rūpāvacaracittassa abhāvā paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho arūpāvacarikānaṃ [M 0.0174] catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ pasādo hutvā uppajjatīti laddhiyā [P 0.0070] paṭijānāti. Apariyāpannabhāvaṃ panassa na icchati, tasmā paṭikkhipatiyeva.

Even when asked, 'Having been of the form realm, does it become of the formless realm?' he denies it because beyond that, in the moment of the formless realm through development, the consciousness of the form realm is absent. When asked a second time, he affirms it according to the view that it arises as the sensitivity of the four great elements pertaining to the formless realm. However, he does not hold the view that it is unincluded, and thus he denies it.

374. Dibbacakkhuṃ dhammupatthaddhanti kāmāvacaradhammena upatthambhitaṃ hutvā. Puna dhammupatthaddhanti lokuttaradhammena upatthaddhaṃ. Dveva cakkhūnīti puṭṭho kiñcāpi dibbacakkhuno dhammupatthaddhassa paññācakkhubhāvaṃ na icchati, paññācakkhussa pana atthitāya paṭikkhipati. Puna puṭṭho maṃsacakkhu dhammupatthaddhaṃ dibbacakkhu hotīti laddhivasena paṭijānāti. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

374. The divine eye is 'supported by the Dhamma'—meaning, being supported by sense-sphere phenomena. Again, 'supported by the Dhamma' means supported by supramundane phenomena. When asked, 'Are there only two eyes?' although he does not hold the view that the divine eye supported by the Dhamma is the wisdom eye, he denies it because of the existence of the wisdom eye. Again, when asked, he affirms it according to the view that the physical eye, supported by the Dhamma, becomes the divine eye. The rest here is of clear meaning.

Dibbacakkhukathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discussion on the Divine Eye.

8. Dibbasotakathāvaṇṇanā

8. The Exposition of the Discussion on the Divine Ear.

375. Idāni dibbasotakathā nāma hoti. Tattha ekaṃyeva sotanti puṭṭho dvinnaṃ atthitāya paṭikkhipati. Puna puṭṭho yasmā tadeva dhammupatthaddhaṃ dibbasotaṃ nāma hoti, tasmā paṭijānāti. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayamevāti.

375. Now comes the discussion on the divine ear. Here, when asked, 'Is there only one ear?' he denies it because of the existence of two. When asked again, he affirms it because that very ear, being supported by the Dhamma, is called the divine ear. The rest is precisely as stated above.

Dibbasotakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discussion on the Divine Ear.

9. Yathākammūpagatañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

9. The Exposition of the Discussion on the Knowledge of Beings Faring According to Their Deeds.

377. Idāni [V 0.0170] yathākammūpagatañāṇakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “iti dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena…pe… yathākammūpage satte pajānātī”ti (dī. ni. 1.246; paṭi. ma. 1.106) suttaṃ ayoniso gahetvā yathākammūpagatañāṇameva dibbacakkhunti laddhi, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Puna yathākammūpagatañca manasi karotīti puṭṭho ekacittassa ārammaṇadvayābhāvā paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho nānācittavasena paṭijānāti. Puna lesokāsaṃ adatvā dvinnaṃ phassānanti puṭṭho paṭikkhipati. Iti yathā iminā yathākammūpagatapadena, evameva ime vata bhonto[P 0.0071], sattātiādipadehipi saddhiṃ yojanāsu attho veditabbo.

377. Now comes the discussion on the knowledge of beings faring according to their deeds. Here, concerning those who, taking the sutta passage “With the divine eye, purified…he understands beings faring according to their deeds” (Dī. Ni. 1.246; Paṭi. Ma. 1.106) unwisely, hold the view that the knowledge of beings faring according to their deeds is itself the divine eye—the question is posed to the proponent, and the admission is given by the other. Again, when asked whether he also attends to that which fares according to deeds, he denies it because a single consciousness cannot have two objects. When asked a second time, he concedes it by way of different consciousnesses. Further, when asked whether there are two contacts without giving any loophole, he denies it.
