Thus, just as the meaning should be understood in connection with this phrase “faring according to their deeds,” so too should it be understood in connection with phrases such as “these good sirs, beings,” and so forth, in the applications.

378. Āyasmā [M 0.0175] sāriputto yathākammūpagataṃ ñāṇaṃ jānātīti idaṃ sakavādī yasmā thero appicchatāya abhiññāñāṇāni na vaḷañjetīti ekacce na jānanti, tāni panassa neva atthīti maññanti, tasmā taṃ “dibbacakkhuno alābhī thero”ti maññamānaṃ pucchati. Teneva kāraṇena “atthāyasmato sāriputtassa dibbacakkhū”ti parato puṭṭho paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho yaṃkiñci sāvakena pattabbaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ therena anuppattanti paṭijānāti. Idānissa vikkhepaṃ karonto sakavādī nanu āyasmā sāriputtotiādimāha. Imañhi gāthaṃ thero vaḷañjanapaṇidhiyā eva abhāvena āha, na abhiññāñāṇassa abhāvena. Paravādī pana abhāvenevāti atthaṃ sallakkheti. Tasmā tassa laddhiyā therassa yathākammūpagatañāṇameva atthi, no dibbacakkhu. Tena vuttaṃ “tena hi na vattabbaṃ yathākammūpagatañāṇaṃ dibbacakkhū”ti.

378. Regarding the statement, “The Venerable Sāriputta knows the knowledge of beings faring according to their deeds,” the proponent asks this because some do not know that the elder does not exercise his higher knowledges due to his being of few wishes, and they even think that he does not possess them; therefore, he asks the opponent, who thinks, “The elder is one who has not obtained the divine eye.” For the same reason, when asked by the other, “Does the Venerable Sāriputta possess the divine eye?” the proponent denies it. When asked a second time, he admits that whatever can be attained by a disciple, all that has been attained by the elder. Now, creating a diversion, the proponent says, “Does not the Venerable Sāriputta…” and so forth. Indeed, the elder spoke this verse due to the absence of any intention to exercise them, not due to the absence of higher knowledge. The opponent, however, takes the meaning to be that it is due to the absence itself. Therefore, according to his view, the elder possesses only the knowledge of beings faring according to their deeds, not the divine eye. Hence it is said, “Therefore, it should not be said that the knowledge of beings faring according to their deeds is the divine eye.”

Yathākammūpagatañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discussion on the Knowledge of Beings Faring According to Their Deeds.

10. Saṃvarakathāvaṇṇanā

10. The Exposition of the Discussion on Restraint.

379. Idāni saṃvarakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ tāvatiṃse deve upādāya tatuttari devesu yasmā te pañca verāni na samācaranti, tasmā saṃvaro atthīti laddhi, te sandhāya pucchā [V 0.0171] sakavādissa, verasamudācāraṃ apassato paṭiññā itarassa. Tato yasmā saṃvaro nāma saṃvaritabbe asaṃvare sati hoti, tasmā asaṃvarapucchā sakavādissa, devesu pāṇātipātādīnaṃ abhāvena paṭikkhepo itarassa.

379. Now comes the discussion on restraint. Here, concerning those who hold the view that since the devas, starting from the Tāvatiṃsa devas and in the devas above them, do not engage in the five kinds of harmful conduct, they therefore possess restraint—the question is posed to the proponent, and the admission is given by the other, who does not see the practice of harmful conduct. Then, since restraint exists when there is non-restraint regarding what should be restrained, the question about non-restraint is posed to the proponent, and the other’s denial is due to the absence of killing and so forth among the devas.

Atthi manussesūtiādi saṃvare sati asaṃvarassa asaṃvare ca sati saṃvarassa pavattidassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

The statement “There is among humans,” and so forth, is said to show the occurrence of non-restraint when there is restraint, and of restraint when there is non-restraint.

380. Pāṇātipātā veramaṇīti ādipañhesu pāṇātipātādīnaṃ asamācaraṇavasena paṭiññā, pāṇātipātādīnaṃ natthitāya paṭikkhepo veditabbo. Paṭilomapañhā uttānatthāyeva.

380. In the questions beginning with “Abstaining from the taking of life,” the admission is made by way of not engaging in the taking of life and so forth, and the denial should be understood as due to the non-existence of the taking of life and so forth. The reverse questions are of obvious meaning.

Avasāne natthi devesu saṃvarotipañhe [P 0.0072] pāṇātipātādīni katvā puna tato saṃvarābhāvaṃ sandhāya paṭiññā sakavādissa. Tato chalavasena [M 0.0176] yadi saṃvaro natthi, sabbe devā pāṇātipātinotiādipucchā paravādissa. Devānaṃ verasamudācārassa abhāvena paṭikkhepo sakavādissa. Nahevanti vacanamattaṃ gahetvā laddhipatiṭṭhāpanaṃ paravādissa. Evaṃ patiṭṭhitā pana laddhi appatiṭṭhitāva hotīti.

At the end, in the question “Is there no restraint among the devas?” the proponent’s admission is made with reference to the absence of restraint from killing and so forth, after such acts have been done. Then, by way of a trick, the opponent asks, “If there is no restraint, are all devas killers of living beings?” and so forth. The proponent denies it due to the absence of the practice of harmful conduct among the devas. Seizing merely the words “It is not so,” the opponent establishes his view. Thus, the view so established is, however, unestablished.

Saṃvarakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discussion on Restraint.

11. Asaññakathāvaṇṇanā

11. The Exposition of the Discussion on Non-Perception.

381. Idāni asaññakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇa”nti vacanato vinā viññāṇena paṭisandhi nāma natthi. “Saññuppādā ca pana te devā tamhā kāyā cavantī”ti vacanato asaññasattānampi cutipaṭisandhikkhaṇe saññā atthīti laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Tato naṃ sakavādī “kiṃ te taṃ ṭhānaṃ saññābhavo”tiādīhi codetuṃ saññābhavo saññāgatītiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ tato parañca pāḷinayeneva veditabbanti.

381. Now there is the discussion called 'Non-Perception'. Herein, for those who hold the view that, because of the statement 'Conditioned by formations is consciousness,' there is no rebirth-linking without consciousness, and because of the statement 'And those devas, with the arising of perception, pass away from that body,' even non-percipient beings have perception at the moment of death and rebirth-linking—just like the Andhakas at present—the question is for the proponent, and the admission is for the other. Then, the proponent, in order to challenge him with questions such as 'Is that state of yours a perception-existence?' and so forth, states 'A perception-existence is a perception-destination,' and so forth. All that and what follows should be understood according to the method of the Pāli text.

Asaññakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Non-Perception.

12. Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanakathāvaṇṇanā

12. The Explanation of the Discourse on the Sphere of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception

384. Idāni [V 0.0172] nevasaññānāsaññāyatanakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “nevasaññānāsaññāyatana”nti vacanato na vattabbaṃ “tasmiṃ bhave saññā atthī”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha sabbaṃ pāḷinayeneva veditabbanti.

384. Now there is the discussion called 'The Sphere of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception'. Herein, for those who hold the view that, because of the expression 'the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception,' it should not be said that 'perception exists in that state of being'—just like the Andhakas at present—the question is for the proponent, and the admission is for the other. The rest here should all be understood according to the method of the Pāli text.

Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Sphere of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception.

Tatiyo vaggo.

The Third Chapter.

4. Catutthavaggo

4. The Fourth Chapter.

1. Gihissa arahātikathāvaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Discourse on a Layperson Being an Arahant.

387. Idāni [M 0.0177][P 0.0073] gihissa arahāti kathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ yasakulaputtādīnaṃ gihibyañjane ṭhitānaṃ arahattappattiṃ disvā “gihi assa arahā”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi uttarāpathakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa. Tattha gihissāti yo gihisaṃyojanasampayuttatāya gihi, so arahaṃ assāti attho. Paravādī pana adhippāyaṃ asallakkhetvā gihibyañjanamattameva passanto paṭijānāti. Idānissa “gihi nāma gihisaṃyojanena hoti, na byañjanamattena. Yathāha bhagavā –

387. Now there is the discussion called 'A Layperson is an Arahant'. Herein, for those who hold the view that 'a layperson can be an arahant,' having seen the attainment of arahantship by the clansman Yasa and others, who remained in the outward appearance of a householder—just like the Uttarāpathakas at present—the question is for the proponent. Herein, 'a layperson' means one who is a layperson on account of being connected with the fetters of a householder; the meaning is 'could such a one be an arahant?' But the opponent, not discerning the intended meaning and seeing only the outward appearance of a householder, admits it. Now, to him: 'A layperson is so called by the fetters of a householder, not merely by outward appearance. As the Blessed One has said—'

‘Alaṅkato cepi samaṃ careyya,

Santo danto niyato brahmacārī;

Sabbesu bhūtesu nidhāya daṇḍaṃ,

So brāhmaṇo so samaṇo sa bhikkhū’”ti. (dha. pa. 142);

“Though adorned, if he should live in peace,

calm, tamed, restrained, leading the holy life,

having laid aside the rod toward all beings—

he is a brahmin, he is an ascetic, he is a monk.”

Imaṃ [V 0.0173] nayaṃ dassetuṃ atthi arahatotiādi āraddhaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

To show this method, the passage beginning 'An arahant exists...' and so forth, is introduced. All of that has a clear meaning.

Gihissa arahātikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on a Layperson Being an Arahant.

2. Upapattikathāvaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Discourse on Rebirth.

388. Idāni upapattikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “opapātiko hoti tatthaparinibbāyī”tivacanāni (pu. pa. 35-40) ayoniso gahetvā suddhāvāsesu upapattiyā arahāti laddhi, “yesaṃ vā upahaccaparinibbāyī”ti [P 0.0074] padaṃ parivattitvā “upapajjaparinibbāyī”ti pariyāpuṇantānaṃ saha upapattiyā arahā hotīti laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi uttarāpathakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Tattha yasmā upapatticittaṃ nāma lokiyaṃ, tena sotāpannādayopi na honti, pageva arahā. Tasmāssa [M 0.0178] imaṃ nayaṃ dassetuṃ saha upapattiyā sotāpannotiādi āraddhaṃ.

388. Now there is the discussion called 'Rebirth'. Herein, for those who, having taken the statements 'he is spontaneously reborn, attaining final Nibbāna there' unwisely, hold the view that one becomes an arahant by way of rebirth in the Pure Abodes; or for those who, altering the phrase 'one who attains final Nibbāna after an interval' to 'one who attains final Nibbāna upon being reborn,' learn it as the view that one becomes an arahant together with rebirth—just like the Uttarāpathakas at present—the question is for the proponent, and the admission is for the other. Herein, since the rebirth-consciousness is mundane, by it one cannot even be a stream-enterer or the like, much less an arahant. Therefore, to show them this method, the passage beginning '[Is one] a stream-enterer together with rebirth?' and so forth, is introduced.

389. Sāriputtotiādi imesu mahātheresu ko ekopi saha upapattiyā arahā nāmāti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

389. Regarding Sāriputta and others, it is stated for the purpose of challenging the view: 'Is even one among these great elders an arahant together with rebirth?'

390. Upapattesiyenāti paṭisandhicittena. Tañhi upapattiṃ esati gavesati, tasmā upapattesiyanti vuccati. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

390. 'By that which seeks rebirth' means by the rebirth-linking consciousness. For that seeks or searches for rebirth, therefore it is called 'that which seeks rebirth'. The rest here has a clear meaning.

Upapattikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Rebirth.

3. Anāsavakathāvaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Discourse on the Taintless.

391. Idāni anāsavakathā nāma hoti. Tattha ye dhammā anāsavassa arahato, sabbe te [V 0.0174] anāsavāti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi uttarāpathakānaṃ; te sandhāya arahatoti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ anāsavā nāma maggādayo, kiṃ tassa teyeva uppajjantīti codanatthaṃ maggo phalantiādi āraddhaṃ. Cakkhu anāsavanti puṭṭho tassa sāsavattā paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho anāsavassetanti paṭijānāti.

391. Now there is the discussion on the taintless. Herein, for those who hold the view that all phenomena of the taintless arahant are themselves taintless—just as is the case with the Uttarāpathakas nowadays—with reference to them, the question concerning the arahant is for the proponent, and the admission is for the other. Then, to challenge him with 'Do only these, namely the path and so forth, which are called taintless, arise for him?', the discussion concerning the path, the fruit, and so on, is introduced. When asked 'Is the eye taintless?', he rejects it because it is tainted. When asked a second time, 'Does it belong to the taintless one?', he admits it.

392. Cīvarapañhe ekova dhammo anāsavo sāsavo ca hotīti lakkhaṇavirodhabhayā paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho anāsavassa hutvā sāsavassa hotīti paṭijānāti. Taññeva anāsavanti pañhādvayepi eseva nayo. Sakavādī pana taññevāti anuññātattā “maggo anāsavo hutvā”tiādīhi codeti. Iminā upāyena sabbattha attho veditabboti.

392. In the question concerning robes, he rejects the notion that a single phenomenon can be both taintless and tainted, fearing a contradiction in characteristics. When asked a second time, he admits that having belonged to a taintless one, it can belong to a tainted one. The same method applies to both questions concerning 'that very thing is taintless'. But the proponent, because 'that very thing' has been conceded, challenges with statements beginning 'the path, having been taintless...' and so on. By this method, the meaning should be understood everywhere.

Anāsavakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Taintless.

4. Samannāgatakathāvaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Discourse on Accomplishment.

393. Idāni [M 0.0179][P 0.0075] samannāgatakathā nāma hoti. Tattha dve samannāgamā paccuppannakkhaṇe samaṅgībhāvasamannāgamo ca rūpāvacarādīsu aññatarabhūmippattito paṭilābhasamannāgamo ca. So yāva adhigatavisesā na parihāyati, tāvadeva labbhati. Yesaṃ pana ṭhapetvā ime dve samannāgame añño upapattidhammavasena eko samannāgamo nāma hotīti laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi uttarāpathakānaṃ, tesaṃ pattidhammo nāma koci natthīti anubodhanatthaṃ arahā catūhi phalehi samannāgatoti pucchā sakavādissa, pattiṃ sandhāya paṭiññā itarassa. Athassa “yadi te arahā catūhi khandhehi viya catūhi phalehi samannāgato, evaṃ sante ye catūsu phalesu cattāro phassādayo, tehi te arahato samannāgatatā pāpuṇātī”ti codanatthaṃ arahā catūhi phassehītiādi āraddhaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ paravādinā ekakkhaṇe catunnaṃ phassādīnaṃ abhāvā paṭikkhittaṃ. Anāgāmipañhādīsupi eseva nayo.

393. Now there is the discussion on accomplishment. Herein, there are two kinds of accomplishment: the accomplishment of being endowed at the present moment, and the accomplishment of attainment upon reaching any one of the form realms and so forth. This is obtained only as long as the attained distinction does not decline. But for those who, setting aside these two kinds of accomplishment, hold the view that there is another kind of accomplishment based on the nature of rebirth—just as is the case with the Uttarāpathakas nowadays—to make them understand that there is no such thing as an attainment-nature for them, the question 'Is the arahant accomplished in the four fruits?' is posed by the proponent, and the admission comes from the other with reference to attainment. Then, to challenge him with 'If the arahant is accomplished in the four fruits like the four aggregates, then it would follow that the arahant is accomplished in the four contacts and so forth that are in the four fruits,' the passage beginning 'Is the arahant accomplished in the four contacts?' and so on is introduced. All this is rejected by the opponent due to the absence of the four contacts and so forth at a single moment. The same method applies to the questions concerning the non-returner and so forth.

395. Sotāpattiphalaṃ vītivattoti na paṭhamajjhānaṃ viya dutiyajjhānalābhī; puna anuppattiyā [V 0.0175] pana vītivattoti pucchati. Sotāpattimaggantiādi yaṃ vītivatto, tenassa puna asamannāgamaṃ dassetuṃ āraddhaṃ.

395. The question 'Has the fruit of stream-entry been transcended?' does not mean transcended in the way that one who attains the second jhāna transcends the first jhāna; rather, it asks whether it has been transcended in the sense of not being attained again. The passage beginning 'the path of stream-entry' and so on is introduced to show his non-possession again of that which has been transcended.

396. Tehi ca aparihīnoti pañhe yasmā yathā paccanīkasamudācārena lokiyajjhānadhammā parihāyanti, na evaṃ lokuttarā. Maggena hi ye kilesā pahīyanti, phalena ca paṭippassambhanti, te tathā pahīnāva tathā paṭippassaddhāyeva ca honti, tasmā sakavādinā āmantāti paṭiññātaṃ. Svāyamattho parato “arahatā cattāro maggā paṭiladdhā”tiādīsu pakāsitoyeva. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

396. In the question 'And not fallen away from them?', because worldly jhāna phenomena fall away due to the arising of opposing factors, supramundane phenomena do not. For the defilements abandoned by the path and tranquillized by the fruit remain abandoned and tranquillized in that way. Therefore, the proponent of one's own doctrine acknowledges with 'Yes'. This meaning is clearly shown later in statements like 'the arahant has attained the four paths' and so on. The rest is of clear meaning.

Samannāgatakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Being Endowed.

5. Upekkhāsamannāgatakathāvaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Discussion on Being Endowed with Equanimity.

397. Arahā [M 0.0180] chahi upekkhāhīti kathāyapi imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Arahā hi chasu dvāresu upekkhānaṃ uppattibhabbatāya [P 0.0076] tāhi samannāgatoti vuccati, na ekakkhaṇe sabbāsaṃ uppattibhāvenāti.

397. In the discussion 'An Arahant with six kinds of equanimity,' the meaning should be understood in this very way. For the Arahant is said to be endowed with them because of the potential for their arising at the six sense-doors, not because of the arising of all of them at a single moment.

Upekkhāsamannāgatakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on Being Endowed with Equanimity.

6. Bodhiyābuddhotikathāvaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Discussion on Being a Buddha by Means of Enlightenment.

398. Idāni bodhiyā buddhotikathā nāma hoti. Tattha bodhīti catumaggañāṇassāpi sabbaññutaññāṇassāpi adhivacanaṃ. Tasmā yesaṃ yathā odātena vaṇṇena odāto, sāmena vaṇṇena sāmo, evaṃ bodhiyā buddhoti laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi uttarāpathakānaṃyeva; te sandhāya pucchā ca anuyogo ca sakavādissa, paṭiññā ca paṭikkhepo ca itarassa.

398. Now there is the discussion called 'A Buddha by Means of Enlightenment.' Here, 'enlightenment' is a designation for both the knowledge of the four paths and the knowledge of omniscience. Therefore, for those whose view is 'a Buddha by means of enlightenment'—just as 'white' is by means of white color, and 'dark' by means of dark color—as is the case, for example, among the Uttarāpathakas nowadays; with reference to them, the question and investigation belong to the proponent of our own view, and the admission and refutation belong to the other.

Atītāyāti [V 0.0176] pañhe tasmiṃ khaṇe abhāvato paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho paṭilābhaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Puna kiccavasena puṭṭho kiccābhāvato paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho yaṃ tena tāya karaṇīyaṃ kataṃ, tattha sammohābhāvaṃ paṭijānāti. Lesokāsaṃ pana adatvā dukkhaṃ parijānātītiādinā nayena puṭṭho tassa kiccassa abhāvā paṭikkhipati.

In the question regarding the past, he rejects it because of its non-existence at that moment. When asked a second time, he acknowledges it with reference to its acquisition. Again, when asked in terms of function, he rejects it due to the absence of the function. When asked a second time, he acknowledges the absence of delusion regarding what was to be done by him through that, which has been done. However, when asked in a manner that does not allow a loophole, such as 'Is suffering fully understood?', he rejects it due to the absence of that function.

Anāgatapañhe tasmiṃ khaṇe maggañāṇassa abhāvā paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho “agamā rājagahaṃ buddho”ti (su. ni. 410) anāgatāya bodhiyā buddhabhāvaṃ maññamāno paṭijānāti. Bodhikaraṇīyaṃ karotīti puṭṭho tasmiṃ khaṇe kiccābhāvena paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho yadi na kareyya, buddhoti na vucceyya. Yasmā avassaṃ karissati, tasmā karotiyeva nāmāti paṭijānāti. Puna lesokāsaṃ adatvā puṭṭho paṭikkhipati. Paccuppannapañho saddhiṃ saṃsandanāya uttānatthova.

In the question about the future, he rejects it because of the absence of the knowledge of the path at that moment. When asked a second time, he acknowledges it, considering the future enlightenment as Buddhahood, as in the phrase, 'The Buddha went to Rājagaha' (Snp 410). When asked, 'Does he perform what is to be done by enlightenment?', he rejects it at that moment due to the absence of the task. When asked a second time, he acknowledges that if he were not to perform it, he would not be called a Buddha. Since he will inevitably do so, he affirms that he indeed performs it. Again, when asked without giving room for equivocation, he rejects it. The question about the present, in comparison, is of clear meaning.

399. Tisso bodhiyo ekato katvā puṭṭho sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ sandhāya tīhipi buddhoti vattabbabhāvato paṭijānāti. Puna tīhiti puṭṭho sabbāsaṃ [M 0.0181] ekakkhaṇe abhāvā paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho atītānāgatapaccuppannassa sabbaññutaññāṇassa vasena paṭijānāti. Puna lesokāsaṃ adatvā satataṃ samitanti puṭṭho paṭikkhipati.

399. When asked combining the three enlightenments, he acknowledges it with reference to the knowledge of omniscience, because it can be said that he is a Buddha by means of all three. Again, when asked about the three, he rejects it because of the non-existence of all of them at a single moment. When asked a second time, he acknowledges it by way of the omniscient knowledge of the past, future, and present. Again, when asked without giving room for equivocation, 'Is it continuous and constant?', he rejects it.

Na battabbaṃ bodhiyāti pucchā paravādissa, bodhiyā abhāvakkhaṇe abuddhabhāvāpattito paṭiññā sakavādissa. Nanu bodhipaṭilābhāti pañhe pana yasmiṃ santāne bodhisaṅkhātaṃ [P 0.0077] maggañāṇaṃ uppannaṃ, tattha buddhoti sammutisabbhāvato paṭiññā tasseva. Tassa adhippāyaṃ ajānitvā hañcīti laddhiṭṭhapanā paravādissa. Idānissa asallakkhaṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ bodhipaṭilābhā buddhoti bodhiyā buddhoti pucchā sakavādissa. Tassattho – “kiṃ te yasmā bodhipaṭilābhā buddho, tasmā bodhiyā buddho”ti. Itaro “bodhipaṭilābho nāma bodhiyā uppajjitvā niruddhāyapi santāne uppannabhāvoyeva. Bodhi nāma maggakkhaṇe ñāṇa”nti imaṃ vibhāgaṃ asallakkhentova puna paṭijānāti. Tato sakavādinā bodhipaṭilābhā bodhīti puṭṭho vacanokāsaṃ alabhanto paṭikkhipatīti.

The question, 'Should it not be said, "A Buddha by means of enlightenment"?' is the opponent's; the admission is the proponent's, due to the consequence of this view leading to the state of being a non-Buddha at a moment when enlightenment is absent. However, in the question, 'Is it not by the attainment of enlightenment that one is a Buddha?', his admission is due to the existence of the convention 'Buddha' for a continuum in which the knowledge of the path, called enlightenment, has arisen. Not understanding his intention, the opponent establishes his own view with 'If so...'. Now, to make his lack of discernment clear, the proponent asks, 'If one is a Buddha by the attainment of enlightenment, is one a Buddha by enlightenment?' The meaning is: 'Is it your view that because one is a Buddha by means of the attainment of enlightenment, therefore one is a Buddha by means of enlightenment?' The other, not discerning this distinction—that 'attainment of enlightenment' is the state of its having arisen in the continuum even after that enlightenment has arisen and ceased, while 'enlightenment' is the knowledge at the moment of the path—again admits it. Then, when asked by the proponent, 'Is the attainment of enlightenment enlightenment?', not finding a way to answer, he rejects it.

Bodhiyābuddhotikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on Being a Buddha by Means of Enlightenment.

Iti imā tissopi kathā uttarāpathakānaṃyeva.

Thus, these three discussions also belong solely to the Uttarāpathakas.

7. Lakkhaṇakathāvaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Discourse on Characteristics.

400. Idāni [V 0.0177] lakkhaṇakathā nāma hoti. Tattha “yehi samannāgatassa mahāpurisassa dveva gatiyo bhavantī”ti (dī. ni. 1.258) imaṃ suttaṃ ayoniso gahetvā lakkhaṇasamannāgato bodhisattova hotīti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi uttarāpathakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa.

400. Now there is the discussion called 'Characteristics.' Here, taking the sutta 'For one endowed with which, a great man has only two destinies' (DN 14) improperly, some hold the view that only a Bodhisatta is endowed with the characteristics—such as the Uttarāpathakas nowadays. With reference to them, the question is the proponent's, and the admission is the other's.

Cakkavattisattoti pañhesu yasmā cakkavattī sattopi ca bodhisattopi, tasmā abodhisattaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Bodhisattaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti.

In the questions concerning 'a wheel-turning monarch as a being,' since a wheel-turning monarch is a being and may also be a bodhisatta, he rejects it with reference to a non-bodhisatta and acknowledges it with reference to a bodhisatta.

402. Dvattiṃsimānītisuttaṃ [M 0.0182] bodhisattameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. So hi pacchime bhave buddho hoti, itaresu cakkavattī, tasmā ābhatampi anābhatasadisamevāti.

402. The sutta on the thirty-two marks was spoken with reference to the Bodhisatta alone, for in his last existence he becomes a Buddha, while in others he becomes a wheel-turning monarch. Therefore, even what is adduced is as if it were not adduced.

Lakkhaṇakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Characteristics.

8. Niyāmokkantikathāvaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Discourse on Entry into the Fixed Course.

403. Idāni [P 0.0078] niyāmokkantikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ ghaṭikārasutte jotipālassa pabbajjaṃ sandhāya “bodhisatto kassapabhagavato pāvacane okkantaniyāmo caritabrahmacariyo”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya bodhisattoti pucchā sakavādissa, laddhiyaṃ ṭhatvā paṭiññā itarassa. Tato yasmā niyāmoti vā brahmacariyanti vā ariyamaggassa nāmaṃ, bodhisattānañca ṭhapetvā pāramīpūraṇaṃ aññā niyāmokkanti nāma natthi. Yadi bhaveyya, bodhisatto sotāpanno sāvako bhaveyya. Na cetamevaṃ. Kevalañhi naṃ buddhā attano ñāṇabale ṭhatvā – “ayaṃ buddho bhavissatī”ti byākaronti, tasmā puna bodhisattoti anuyogo sakavādissa. Pacchimabhavaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhepo itarassa. Dutiyapañhe jotipālakālaṃ sandhāya paṭiññā tasseva. Sāvako hutvātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Anussaviyoti [V 0.0178] anussavena paṭividdhadhammo. Pacchimabhavaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipitvā jotipālakāle anussavaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti.

403. Now comes the discussion called 'Entry into the Fixed Course.' Herein, with reference to Jotipāla's going forth in the Ghaṭikāra Sutta, the question concerning the Bodhisatta is posed by the proponent to those who hold the view that 'the Bodhisatta entered the fixed course in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa and lived the holy life'—such as the Andhakas nowadays; the opponent makes an admission, standing on their view. Because 'fixed course' or 'holy life' are names for the Noble Path, and for Bodhisattas, apart from the fulfillment of the perfections, there is no other entry into the fixed course. If there were, the Bodhisatta would be a stream-enterer disciple. But this is not so. For the Buddhas, standing on the power of their own knowledge, declare, 'This one will become a Buddha.' Therefore, a further question concerning the Bodhisatta is posed by the proponent. The rejection is given by the opponent with reference to the final existence. In the second question, the admission is given by that same one with reference to the time of Jotipāla. The same method applies in the cases of 'having been a disciple,' and so on. 'Anussaviyo' means one who has penetrated the Dhamma through oral tradition. Having rejected with reference to the final existence, he makes an admission with reference to the time of Jotipāla, based on oral tradition.

404. Aññaṃ satthārantiāḷārañca rāmaputtañca sandhāya vuttaṃ. Āyasmā ānandotiādi “okkantaniyāmāva sāvakā honti, na itare okkantaniyāmā evarūpā hontī”ti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ.

404. 'Another teacher' is said with reference to Āḷāra and Rāmaputta. The phrase 'the Venerable Ānanda, and so on,' is stated to show that 'only disciples are those who have entered the fixed course; others are not of such a kind.'

Sāvako jātiṃ vītivattoti yāya jātiyā sāvako, taṃ vītivatto aññasmiṃ bhave asāvako hotīti pucchati. Itaro sotāpannādīnaṃ sotāpannādisāvakabhāvato paṭikkhipati. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

'A disciple has overcome birth' asks whether a disciple, having overcome a particular birth, becomes a non-disciple in another existence. The other rejects this with reference to stream-enterers and so on, on account of their being disciples as stream-enterers and so on. The rest here is self-explanatory.

Niyāmokkantikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on Entry into the Fixed Course.

9. Aparāpi samannāgatakathāvaṇṇanā

9. A Further Explanation of the Discussion on Being Endowed.

406. Idāni [M 0.0183] aparāpi samannāgatakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “catutthamaggaṭṭho puggalo pattidhammavasena tīhi phalehi samannāgato”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi andhakānaṃ[P 0.0079]; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha heṭṭhā catūhi phalehi samannāgatakathāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

406. Now there is a further discussion called 'Being Endowed.' Herein, with regard to those who hold the view that 'a person established in the fourth path is endowed with the three fruits by way of attainment'—just as the Andhakas do nowadays—the question is for the proponent, and the admission is for the opponent. The rest here should be understood in the same manner as was stated previously in the discussion on being endowed with the four fruits.

Aparāpi samannāgatakathāvaṇṇanā.

A Further Explanation of the Discussion on Being Endowed.

10. Sabbasaṃyojanappahānakathāvaṇṇanā

10. The Explanation of the Discussion on the Abandoning of All Fetters.

413. Idāni saṃyojanappahānakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “nippariyāyeneva sabbasaṃyojanappahānaṃ [V 0.0179] arahatta”nti laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Puna sabbe saṃyojanāti puṭṭho heṭṭhā vuttamaggattayena pahīne sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho tena maggena appahīnassa abhāvā paṭijānāti. Sakkāyadiṭṭhiādīsupi paṭhamamaggena pahīnabhāvaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati, catutthamaggena anavasesappahānaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Eseva nayo sabbatthāti.

413. Now there is a discussion called 'The Abandoning of the Fetters.' Herein, with regard to those who hold the view that 'the abandoning of all fetters without remainder is Arahantship'—just as the Andhakas do nowadays—the question is for the proponent, and the admission is for the opponent. When asked again about 'all the fetters,' he denies, with reference to those abandoned by the three previously mentioned paths. When asked a second time, he affirms, because there is nothing unabandoned by that path. Regarding personality view, etc., he denies, with reference to their abandonment by the first path; then he affirms, with reference to their complete abandonment without remainder by the fourth path. The same method applies throughout.

Sabbasaṃyojanappahānakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on the Abandoning of All Fetters.

Catuttho vaggo.

The Fourth Chapter.

5. Pañcamavaggo

5. The Fifth Chapter.

1. Vimuttikathāvaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Discussion on Liberation.

418. Idāni [P 0.0080] vimuttikathā nāma hoti. Tattha vipassanā, maggo, phalaṃ, paccavekkhaṇanti catunnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ vimuttiñāṇanti nāmaṃ. Tesu vipassanāñāṇaṃ niccanimittādīhi vimuttattā, tadaṅgavimuttibhāvena vā vimuttattā vimuttiñāṇaṃ. Maggo [M 0.0184] samucchedavimutti, phalaṃ paṭippassaddhivimutti, paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ pana vimuttiṃ jānātīti vimuttiñāṇaṃ. Evaṃ catubbidhe vimuttiñāṇe nippariyāyena phalañāṇameva vimutti. Sesāni “vimuttānī”ti vā “avimuttānī”ti vā na vattabbāni. Tasmā “idaṃ nāma vimuttiñāṇaṃ vimutta”nti avatvā aviseseneva “vimuttiñāṇaṃ vimutta”nti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā paravādissa. Puna yaṃkiñcīti puṭṭho paccavekkhaṇādīni sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Paṭipannassāti puṭṭho maggañāṇassa anāsavataṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Yasmā pana taṃ sotāpannassa phale ṭhitassa ñāṇaṃ na hoti, tasmā vimuttaṃ nāma na hotīti codanatthaṃ puna sakavādī sotāpannassātiādimāha. Iminā upāyena sabbattha attho veditabbo.

418. Now there is a discussion called 'Liberation.' Herein, insight, path, fruit, and reviewing—the knowledge of these four is called the knowledge of liberation. Among them, the knowledge of insight is called the knowledge of liberation because it is liberated from the signs of permanence, etc., or because it is liberated by way of provisional liberation. The path is liberation by cutting off; the fruit is liberation by tranquilization; but the reviewing knowledge is called the knowledge of liberation because it knows liberation. Thus, among the fourfold knowledge of liberation, it is the knowledge of the fruit alone that is liberation in an absolute sense. The others cannot be said to be either 'liberated' or 'not liberated.' Therefore, the proponent's question is directed at those whose doctrine is that, without specifying 'this particular knowledge of liberation is liberated,' but stating without distinction 'the knowledge of liberation is liberated'—just as the Andhakas do; the admission is made by the opponent. Further, when asked 'whatever,' he rejects it with reference to reviewing, and so on. When asked about 'one who has entered the path,' he admits it with reference to the untainted nature of the path knowledge. But since that knowledge does not exist for a stream-enterer established in the fruit, it is therefore not called 'liberated.' To make this a point of censure, the proponent then says 'for a stream-enterer,' and so on. By this method, the meaning should be understood everywhere.

Vimuttikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on Liberation.

2. Asekhañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Discussion on the Adept's Knowledge.

421. Idāni [V 0.0180] asekhakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā ānandattherādayo sekhā “uḷāro bhagavā”tiādinā nayena asekhe jānanti, tasmā [P 0.0081] “sekhassa asekhañāṇaṃ atthī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi uttarāpathakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Jānāti passatīti idaṃ attanā adhigatassa jānanavasena vuttaṃ. Gotrabhunotiādi heṭṭhimāya bhūmiyaṃ ṭhitassa uparūpariñāṇassa abhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Nanu āyasmā ānando sekho “uḷāro bhagavā”ti jānātīti paravādī asekhe bhagavati pavattattā taṃ asekhañāṇanti icchati, na panetaṃ asekhaṃ. Tasmā evaṃ patiṭṭhāpitāpi laddhi appatiṭṭhāpitāva hotīti.

421. Now there is the discussion on the adept. Herein, because trainees like the Venerable Ānanda know adepts in such ways as, 'The Blessed One is sublime,' the proponent's question is directed at those, such as the Northerners, who hold the view that 'a trainee possesses an adept's knowledge,' and the opponent makes an admission. The phrase 'he knows, he sees' is stated with reference to knowing what has been personally attained. The phrase 'the change-of-lineage being,' and so on, is stated to show the absence of higher knowledge for one established on a lower stage. The opponent—because the Venerable Ānanda, a trainee, knows 'The Blessed One is sublime,' and this knowledge pertains to the Blessed One, who is an adept—desires to consider that an adept's knowledge; but it is not an adept's knowledge. Therefore, even though this view is thus established, it remains unestablished.

Asekhañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on the Adept's Knowledge.

3. Viparītakathāvaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Discussion on Inversion.

424. Idāni viparītakathā nāma hoti. Tattha “yvāyaṃ pathavīkasiṇe pathavīsaññī samāpajjati, tassa taṃ ñāṇaṃ viparītañāṇa”nti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi [M 0.0185] andhakānaṃ, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Pathaviṃ nissāya uppannanimittañhi na pathavīyeva, tatra cāyaṃ pathavīsaññī. Tasmā viparītañāṇanti ayametassa adhippāyo. Tato sakavādī “lakkhaṇapathavīpi sasambhārapathavīpi nimittapathavīpi pathavīdevatāpi sabbā pathavīyeva, tāsu pathavīti ñāṇaṃ viparītaṃ na hoti. Anicce niccantiādivipariyeso pana viparītañāṇaṃ nāma. Kiṃ te idaṃ etesu aññatara”nti codetuṃ anicce niccantiādimāha. Itaro vipallāsalakkhaṇābhāvaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati, pathavīnimittaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti.

424. Now there is the discourse called 'Inversion'. Herein, the proponent's question is directed at those who hold the view that 'for one who attains the earth kasiṇa, perceiving earth, that knowledge is inverted knowledge'—such as the Andhakas—and the admission is from the other. For the sign that arises dependent on earth is not the earth itself, yet this person perceives it as earth. Therefore, his intention is that this is inverted knowledge. Then the proponent, to challenge him, says: 'Characteristic earth, composite earth, sign-earth, and the earth deity—all these are earth. Knowledge of earth regarding these is not inverted. However, the perversion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent, and so forth, is what is called inverted knowledge. Is this knowledge of yours any of these?' The other, referring to the absence of the characteristic of perversion, rejects this; referring to the earth-sign, he admits it.

Kusalanti sekkhaputhujjanānaṃ ñāṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Atthi arahatoti pañhesupi vipallāsalakkhaṇābhāvena paṭikkhipati. Pathavīnimittaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Sabbeva pathavīti sabbaṃ taṃ pathavīkasiṇaṃ lakkhaṇapathavīyeva [P 0.0082] hotīti pucchati. Sakavādī tathā abhāvato paṭikkhipati. Nanu pathavī atthi, atthi ca koci pathaviṃ pathavito samāpajjatīti pucchā sakavādissa[V 0.0181]. Tassattho – nanu nimittapathavī atthi, atthi ca koci taṃ pathaviṃ pathavitoyeva samāpajjati, na āpato vā tejato vāti. Pathavī atthītiādi “yadi yaṃ yathā atthi, taṃ tathā samāpajjantassa ñāṇaṃ viparītaṃ hoti, nibbānaṃ atthi, tampi samāpajjantassa sabbavipariyesasamugghātanaṃ maggañāṇampi te viparītaṃ hotū”ti dassanatthaṃ vuttanti.

The term 'wholesome' is stated with reference to the knowledge of trainees and ordinary people. In the questions such as, 'Does it exist for an Arahant?', he rejects it due to the absence of the characteristic of perversion. He admits it with reference to the earth-sign. The question 'Is all of it earth?' means 'Is all of that earth kasiṇa merely characteristic earth?' The proponent rejects this, as it is not so. The proponent's question is: 'Surely, earth exists, and does someone attain earth as earth?' Its meaning is: 'Surely, the sign-earth exists, and does someone attain that earth as earth, and not as water or fire?' The phrase 'earth exists,' etc., is stated to show: 'If the knowledge of one who attains something as it exists is inverted, then for you, even the path knowledge that eradicates all perversions regarding the existing Nibbāna would be inverted.'

Viparītakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Inversion.

4. Niyāmakathāvaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Discourse on Certainty.

428-431. Idāni niyāmakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yo puggalo sammattaniyāmaṃ okkamissati, taṃ “bhabbo esa dhammaṃ abhisametu”nti yasmā bhagavā jānāti, tasmā “aniyatassa puthujjanasseva sato puggalassa niyāmagamanāya ñāṇaṃ atthī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi uttarāpathakānaṃ; te sandhāya aniyatassāti pucchā sakavādissa. Tattha niyāmagamanāyāti niyāmo vuccati maggo, maggagamanāya maggokkamanāyāti attho. Yaṃ panassa ñāṇaṃ disvā bhagavā “bhabbo aya”nti jānāti, taṃ sandhāya paṭiññā paravādissa.

Now there is the discourse called 'Certainty'. Herein, since the Blessed One knows of the person who will enter the right course of certainty, 'This one is capable of realizing the Dhamma,' therefore the proponent's question, 'Is it for one who is undetermined?', is directed at those who hold the view that 'there is knowledge for an undetermined ordinary person, while still an ordinary person, to attain certainty,' such as the Northerners nowadays. Here, 'to attain certainty' means: certainty is called the path; the meaning is to go to the path, to enter the path. The opponent's admission is made with reference to that knowledge, seeing which the Blessed One knows, 'This one is capable.'

Athassa [M 0.0186] sakavādī ayuttavāditaṃ dīpetuṃ niyatassāti viparītānuyogamāha. Tattha paṭhamapañhe maggena niyatassa aniyāmagamanāya ñāṇaṃ nāma natthīti paṭikkhipati. Dutiye natthibhāvena paṭijānāti. Tatiye aniyatassa natthīti puṭṭhattā laddhivirodhena paṭikkhipati. Puna paṭhamapañhameva catutthaṃ katvā niyatassa niyāmagamanādivasena tayo pañhā katā. Tesu paṭhame yasmā ādimaggena niyatassa puna tadatthāya ñāṇaṃ natthi, tasmā paṭikkhipati. Dutiye [P 0.0083] natthibhāveneva paṭijānāti. Tatiye laddhivirodheneva paṭikkhipati. Puna paṭhamapañhaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ katvā aniyatassa aniyāmagamanādivasena tayo pañhā katā. Tesaṃ attho vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Puna paṭhamapañhameva dvādasamaṃ katvā taṃmūlakā atthi niyāmotiādayo pañhā katā. Tattha yasmā niyāmagamanāya ñāṇaṃ nāma maggañāṇameva hoti, tasmā taṃ sandhāya atthi niyāmoti vuttaṃ. Itaro pana niyāmoti vutte paṭikkhipati, ñāṇanti vutte paṭijānāti. Satipaṭṭhānādīsupi [V 0.0182] eseva nayo. Paccanīkaṃ uttānatthameva. Gotrabhunotiādi yena yaṃ appattaṃ, tassa taṃ natthīti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Bhagavā jānātīti attano ñāṇabalena jānāti, na tassa niyāmagamanañāṇasabbhāvato. Tasmā iminā kāraṇena patiṭṭhitāpissa laddhi appatiṭṭhitāyevāti.

Then, to show the opponent's incorrect assertion, the proponent poses a counter-question, 'Is it for one who is certain?' Here, in the first question, he rejects it because there is no knowledge for one made certain by the path to attain non-certainty. In the second, he admits it as non-existent. In the third, he rejects it due to contradiction with his doctrine, because it was asked whether it does not exist for the undetermined. Again, making the first question the fourth, three questions are formed regarding the certain one's attainment of certainty, and so on. Among these, in the first, he rejects it because for one made certain by the initial path, there is no knowledge to attain that again. In the second, he admits it as non-existent. In the third, he rejects it due to contradiction with his doctrine. Again, making the first question the eighth, three questions are formed regarding the uncertain one's attainment of non-certainty, and so on. Their meaning should be understood in the way already stated. Again, making the first question the twelfth, questions based on it, such as 'Is there certainty?', are formed. Here, because the knowledge for attaining certainty is indeed path knowledge, it is said, 'Is there certainty?' with reference to that. But when 'certainty' is mentioned, the other rejects it; when 'knowledge' is mentioned, he admits it. The same method applies to the foundations of mindfulness, etc. The opposing argument is indeed clear in meaning. The phrase 'change-of-lineage,' etc., is stated to show that for one who has not attained something, that thing does not exist. 'The Blessed One knows' means He knows by the power of His own knowledge, not because of the existence of that person's knowledge for attaining certainty. Therefore, by this reasoning, even if their view seems established, it remains unestablished.

Niyāmakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Certainty.

5. Paṭisambhidākathāvaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Discourse on Analytical Knowledges.

432-433. Idāni paṭisambhidākathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “yaṃkiñci ariyānaṃ ñāṇaṃ, sabbaṃ lokuttaramevā”ti gahetvā “sabbaṃ ñāṇaṃ paṭisambhidā”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sammutiñāṇapañhesu pathavīkasiṇasammutiyaṃ samāpattiñāṇaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati, niruttiñāṇaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Ye keci sammutinti pañhe puthujjane sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Cetopariyāyapañhesu puthujjanassa ñāṇaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati, ariyassa ñāṇaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Sabbā paññātipañhesu kasiṇasamāpattipañhaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati, lokuttaraṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Pathavīkasiṇasamāpattintiādi “yā etesu ettakesu ṭhānesu paññā, kiṃ sabbā sā paṭisambhidā”ti pucchanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tena [M 0.0187] hi sabbaṃ ñāṇanti yasmā sabbā lokuttarapaññā paṭisambhidā[P 0.0084], tasmā sabbanti vacanaṃ sāmaññaphalena saddhiṃ patiṭṭhāpetīti.

Now there is the discourse on analytical knowledges. Herein, the proponent's question is directed at those who, grasping that 'whatever knowledge of the noble ones is entirely supramundane,' hold the doctrine that 'all knowledge is analytical knowledge,' like the Andhakas; the admission is from the other. In questions concerning conventional knowledge, regarding the convention of the earth kasiṇa, one rejects it with reference to the knowledge of attainment, and affirms it with reference to the knowledge of expression. In the question concerning 'any conventional knowledge,' one rejects it with reference to ordinary people. In questions concerning knowledge of others’ minds, one rejects it with reference to the knowledge of an ordinary person, and affirms it with reference to the knowledge of a noble one. In the question, 'Is all wisdom analytical knowledge?', one rejects it with reference to kasiṇa attainment, and affirms it with reference to the supramundane. The phrase 'earth kasiṇa attainment,' and so on, is stated for the purpose of asking: 'The wisdom in these many instances—is all of it analytical knowledge?' Therefore, the statement 'In that case, all knowledge...' establishes this together with the fruit of recluseship, because all supramundane wisdom is analytical knowledge.

Paṭisambhidākathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Analytical Knowledges.

6. Sammutiñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Discourse on Conventional Knowledge

434-435. Idāni sammutiñāṇakathā nāma hoti. Tattha sammutisaccaṃ paramatthasaccanti dve [V 0.0183] saccāni. Ye pana evaṃ vibhāgaṃ akatvā saccanti vacanasāmaññena sammutiñāṇampi “saccārammaṇamevā”ti vadanti, seyyathāpi andhakā; te ayuttavādinoti tesaṃ vādavisodhanatthaṃ ayaṃ kathā āraddhā. Tattha na vattabbanti pucchā paravādissa, paramatthasaccaṃ sandhāya paṭiññā sakavādissa. Sammutisaccamhīti sammutiṃ anupaviṭṭhe saccamhi. Paccatte vā bhummavacanaṃ, sammutisaccanti attho. Sammutiñāṇaṃ saccārammaṇaññevāti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Tato naṃ “yadi taṃ avisesena saccārammaṇaññeva, tena ñāṇena dukkhapariññādīni kareyyā”ti codetuṃ tena ñāṇenātiādimāha.

434-435. Now begins the discourse on conventional knowledge. Herein, there are two truths: conventional truth and ultimate truth. But those who, without making such a distinction, say that even conventional knowledge has 'truth as its object' merely by the common usage of the word 'truth,' like the Andhakas, are speakers of what is inappropriate. This discourse is begun in order to refute their view. Here, the question 'Should it not be said?' is from the opponent; the assertion, made with reference to ultimate truth, is from one's own school. 'In conventional truth' means in a truth that has entered into convention. Or, it is a locative case in the sense of 'itself'; the meaning is 'conventional truth.' The question 'Is conventional knowledge with only truth as its object?' is from one's own school, the admission is from the other. Then, to challenge him, 'If it is indiscriminately with only truth as its object, then with that knowledge one should accomplish the full comprehension of suffering, etc.,' he said 'with that knowledge,' and so forth.

Sammutiñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discourse on Conventional Knowledge.

7. Cittārammaṇakathāvaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Discourse on Mind as Object

436-438. Idāni cittārammaṇakathā nāma hoti. Tattha cetopariyāye ñāṇanti vacanamattameva gahetvā “taṃ ñāṇaṃ cittārammaṇamevā”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Athassa “yo sarāgādivasena cittaṃ jānāti, tassa rāgādayopi ārammaṇā honti, tasmā na vattabbaṃ taṃ cittārammaṇaññevā”ti codanatthaṃ nanu atthi kocītiādi āraddhaṃ. Phassārammaṇeti [P 0.0085] phassasaṅkhāte ārammaṇe. Vedanārammaṇetiādīsupi eseva nayo. Puna phassārammaṇe ñāṇaṃ na vattabbanti puṭṭho phassassa phusanalakkhaṇaṃ [M 0.0188] manasikaroto phassovārammaṇaṃ hotīti paṭijānāti. Kiṃ panetaṃ phassapariyāye ñāṇanti puṭṭho pana tādisassa suttapadassa abhāvā paṭikkhipati. Vedanādīsupi eseva nayo. Idāni yaṃ nissāya laddhi, tadeva dassetvā laddhiṃ patiṭṭhāpetuṃ nanu cetopariyāye ñāṇantiādimāha. Sā panesā vacanamattābhinivesena patiṭṭhāpitāpi appatiṭṭhāpitāva hotīti.

436-438. Now begins the discourse on mind as object. Herein, with reference to those who, taking the mere phrase 'knowledge of penetration of mind,' hold the doctrine that 'that knowledge has only the mind as its object'—like the present-day Andhakas—the question is from one's own school, the admission from the other. Then, to challenge him by saying, 'One who knows the mind by way of lust, etc., also has lust, etc., as objects; therefore, it should not be said that it has only the mind as its object,' the phrase 'Is there not someone...' and so on is introduced. 'With contact as object' means with an object reckoned as contact. The same method applies to 'with feeling as object,' and so on. When asked again, 'Should it not be said that there is knowledge with contact as its object?', one admits that for one who attends to the characteristic of contact as touching, contact itself is the object. But when further asked, 'What then is this knowledge in terms of contact?', one denies it due to the absence of such a sutta passage. The same method applies to feeling, etc. Now, to establish the doctrine by showing that upon which it relies, he said, 'Is there not knowledge of penetration of mind?' and so on. However, this doctrine, even though established merely by attachment to the words, is as if not established at all.

Cittārammaṇakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discourse on Mind as Object.

8. Anāgatañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Discourse on Knowledge of the Future

439-440. Idāni [V 0.0184] anāgatañāṇakathā nāma hoti. Tattha anāgataṃ nāma antarampi atthi, anantarampi. Tesu anantare ekanteneva ñāṇaṃ natthi. Yathā ca anantare, tathā ekavīthiekajavanapariyāpannepi. Tattha ye sabbasmimpi anāgate ñāṇaṃ icchanti, seyyathāpi andhakā; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yaṃ te anāgate ñāṇaṃ, kiṃ tena anantaraṃ anāgataṃ mūlādivasena jānātī”ti codetuṃ anāgataṃ mūlatotiādimāha. Tattha mūlatotiādīni sabbāni kāraṇavevacanāneva. Kāraṇañhi yaṃ attano phalaṃ karoti, taṃ tattha mūlayati patiṭṭhātīti mūlaṃ. Tato ca taṃ hinoti pavattayatīti hetu. Tadeva taṃ nideti “handa naṃ gaṇhathā”ti. Niyyāteti viyāti nidānaṃ. Tato taṃ sambhavatīti sambhavo. Pabhavatīti pabhavo. Tattha ca taṃ samuṭṭhāti, taṃ vā naṃ samuṭṭhāpetīti samuṭṭhānaṃ. Tadeva naṃ āharatīti āhāro. Tañcassa apariccajitabbaṭṭhena ārammaṇaṃ. Tadeva cetaṃ paṭicca etīti paccayo. Tato naṃ samudetīti samudayoti vuccati. Yasmā [P 0.0086] pana anantaraṃ cittaṃ etehākārehi na sakkā jānituṃ, tasmā na hevanti paṭikkhipati. Anāgataṃ hetupaccayatanti yā anantarānāgate citte hetupaccayatā, taṃ jānāti. Ye tattha dhammā hetupaccayā honti, te jānātīti attho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Gotrabhunotiādi yasmiṃ anāgate ñāṇaṃ na uppajjati, taṃ sarūpato dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Pāṭaliputtassāti [M 0.0189] suttaṃ yasmiṃ anāgate ñāṇaṃ uppajjati, taṃ dassetuṃ āhaṭaṃ. Yasmā panetaṃ na sabbasmiṃ anāgate ñāṇassa sādhakaṃ; tasmā anāhaṭamevāti.

439-440. Now begins the discourse on knowledge of the future. Herein, 'the future' is both that which is non-immediate and that which is immediate. Among these, there is certainly no knowledge of the immediate. And just as with the immediate, so too with what is included in a single cognitive series and a single impulsion. Here, with reference to those who desire knowledge of the entire future, like the Andhakas, the question is from one's own school, the admission from the other. Then, to challenge him, 'That knowledge of the future which you possess—does it know the immediate future by way of its root, etc.?' he said 'the future by way of its root,' and so on. Here, 'by way of its root,' and so on, are all synonyms for cause. For a cause is that which produces its own result; it is called a root (mūla) because it grounds (mūlayati) and establishes (patiṭṭhāti) it there. And from that, it sends it forth (hinoti) and makes it proceed (pavattayati); hence it is called a cause (hetu). That very thing directs it, saying, 'Come now, take it,' and delivers it, as it were; thus it is called a source (nidāna). From that, it comes into being (sambhavati); hence it is called an origin (sambhava). It arises (pabhavati) from that; hence it is called a source (pabhava). And there, it arises (samuṭṭhāti) from that, or it causes that to arise (samuṭṭhāpeti); thus it is called an arising (samuṭṭhāna). That very thing brings it (āharati); hence it is called a nutriment (āhāra). And because it should not be abandoned, it is called an object (ārammaṇa). And that very thing comes depending on this; hence it is called a condition (paccaya). From that, it arises together (samudeti); hence it is called an origin (samudaya). But because the immediate consciousness cannot be known in these ways, he therefore rejects it, saying, 'It is not so.' As for 'knows the causal conditionality of the future,' this means one knows that causal conditionality which is in the immediate future consciousness. The meaning is: one knows those phenomena that are causal conditions there. The same method applies to the remaining terms. 'Change-of-lineage,' etc., is said to show, by its own nature, that future in which knowledge does not arise. The sutta concerning Pāṭaliputta is cited to show that future in which knowledge does arise. But because this is not proof of knowledge of the entire future, it is therefore as if not cited.

Anāgatañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discourse on Knowledge of the Future.

9. Paṭuppannañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Discourse on Knowledge of the Present

441-442. Idāni paṭuppannañāṇakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “sabbasaṅkhāresu aniccato diṭṭhesu tampi ñāṇaṃ aniccato diṭṭhaṃ hotī”ti vacanaṃ nissāya “avisesena sabbasmiṃ paccuppanne ñāṇaṃ atthī”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya paṭuppanneti pucchā [V 0.0185] sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi avisesena paṭuppanne ñāṇaṃ atthi, khaṇapaccuppannepi tena bhavitabbaṃ. Evaṃ sante dvinnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ ekato abhāvā teneva ñāṇena taṃ jānitabbaṃ hotī”ti codanatthaṃ tenāti anuyogo sakavādissa. Tattha paṭhamapañhe teneva taṃ jānituṃ na sakkāti paṭikkhepo itarassa. Dutiyapañhe santatiṃ sandhāya paṭiññā tasseva. Paṭipāṭito bhaṅgaṃ passanto bhaṅgānupassaneneva bhaṅgānupassanāñāṇaṃ passatīti adhippāyo. Tena ñāṇena taṃ ñāṇaṃ jānātītiādīsupi eseva nayo. Tena phassena taṃ phassantiādīnissa lesokāsanivāraṇatthaṃ vuttāni[P 0.0087]. Yaṃ panetena laddhipatiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ nanu sabbasaṅkhāretiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha nayato taṃ ñāṇaṃ diṭṭhaṃ hoti, na ārammaṇatoti adhippāyena paṭiññā sakavādissa. Tasmā evaṃ patiṭṭhitāpissa laddhi appatiṭṭhitāva hoti.

Now, there is a discussion called 'Knowledge of the Present.' Here, some, relying on the statement, 'When all conditioned things are seen as impermanent, that knowledge too is seen as impermanent,' hold the view that 'there is knowledge in every present without distinction,' like the Andhakas. With reference to them, the question 'Is there knowledge in the present?' is for the proponent of one's own doctrine, the admission for the other. Then, to challenge him, the proponent of one's own doctrine follows up: 'If there is knowledge in every present without distinction, then it must exist even in a momentary present. If so, since two knowledges do not arise simultaneously, it would have to be known by that very knowledge.' In the first question, the other's rejection is that it is impossible to know it by that knowledge itself. In the second question, his admission is with reference to continuity. The meaning is that one who sees dissolution sequentially sees the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution through the contemplation of dissolution itself. The same method applies to statements like 'that knowledge knows that knowledge,' and so on. Phrases like 'that contact contacts that contact,' and so on, are stated to prevent any pretext. Moreover, the statement 'Indeed, all conditioned things...' and so on, was made by him to establish his doctrine. There, the admission of the proponent of one's own doctrine is with the intention that that knowledge is seen by way of method, not as an object. Therefore, even though his doctrine is established in this way, it remains unestablished.

Paṭuppannañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge of the Present.

10. Phalañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Discussion on the Knowledge of Fruits.

443-444. Idāni phale ñāṇakathā nāma hoti. Tattha “buddhāpi sattānaṃ ariyaphalappattiyā dhammaṃ desenti sāvakāpi, iti iminā sāmaññena [M 0.0190] buddhānaṃ viya sāvakānampi tena tena sattena pattabbe phale ñāṇaṃ atthī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya sāvakassāti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi sāvakassa phale ñāṇaṃ atthi, yathā buddhā samānepi sotāpattiphale attano ñāṇabalena ‘ayaṃ ekabījī, ayaṃ kolaṃkolo, ayaṃ sattakkhattuparamo’ti phalassakataṃ paññapenti, kiṃ te evaṃ sāvakopī”ti codetuṃ sāvako phalassa kataṃ paññapetīti āha. Itaro paṭikkhipati.

Now there is the discussion on knowledge of the fruits. Here, the view of those who hold that 'just as the Buddhas teach the Dhamma for beings to attain the noble fruits, so do the disciples; thus, in this general sense, like the Buddhas, the disciples too have knowledge of the fruit attainable by each particular being,' is like that of the Andhakas. With reference to them, the question concerning the disciple is for the proponent of one's own doctrine, and the other's is the admission. Then, to challenge him, he says: 'If the disciple has knowledge of the fruits, just as the Buddhas, even regarding the same stream-entry fruit, declare the distinctness of the fruit by the power of their own knowledge, saying: "This one is a one-seeder, this one is a family-to-family goer, this one is one with at most seven more existences," does the disciple also declare the distinctness of the fruit in this way?' The other rejects it.

Atthi sāvakassa phalaparopariyattītiādi phale ñāṇassa atthitāya paccayapucchanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – buddhānaṃ “idaṃ phalaṃ paraṃ, idaṃ opara”nti evaṃ phalānaṃ uccāvacabhāvajānanasaṅkhātā phale paropariyatti nāma atthi. Tathā indriyapuggalaparopariyattiyo, tāsaṃ [V 0.0186] atthitāya tassa tassa puggalassa tesaṃ tesaṃ indriyānaṃ vasena taṃ taṃ phalaṃ jānanti, kiṃ te sāvakassāpi etā paropariyattiyo atthīti.

The question 'Does the disciple have knowledge of the higher and lower states of fruits?' and so on, is made for the purpose of inquiring into the conditions for the existence of knowledge regarding the fruits. Here, the intention is this: The Buddhas possess what is called the knowledge of the higher and lower states of fruits, which consists in knowing 'This fruit is higher, this is lower.' Similarly, there are the knowledges of the higher and lower states of faculties and individuals. Due to the existence of these, they know each particular fruit according to the faculties of each particular individual. Is it that the disciples also possess these knowledges of higher and lower states?

Atthi sāvakassa khandhapaññattītiādīnipi “yadi te sāvakassa buddhānaṃ viya phale ñāṇaṃ atthi, imā hi pissa paññattīhi [P 0.0088] bhavitabbaṃ. Kimassa tā atthi, sakkoti so etā paññattiyo attano balena jānituṃ vā paññapetuṃ vā”ti codanatthaṃ vuttāni. Sāvako jinotiādi “yadi sāvakassa buddhānaṃ viya phale ñāṇaṃ atthi, evaṃ sante sveva jino”ti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Sāvako anuppannassāti pañhepi ayameva nayo. Aññāṇīti pañhe avijjāsaṅkhātassa aññāṇassa vihatattā paṭikkhitto, na panassa buddhānaṃ viya phale ñāṇaṃ atthi. Tasmā appatiṭṭhitova paravādīvādoti.

The questions 'Does the disciple have the designation of aggregates?' and so forth, are made for the purpose of censure, meaning: 'If the disciple has knowledge of the fruits like the Buddhas, then these designations must also belong to him. Does he possess them? Can he know or establish these designations by his own power?' The statement 'The disciple is a conqueror,' and so on, is made for the purpose of censure, meaning: 'If the disciple has knowledge of the fruits like the Buddhas, then in that case, he himself would be a Conqueror.' In the question concerning the disciple and the unarisen, the same method applies. In the question 'Is he ignorant?', it is rejected because ignorance, which is reckoned as non-knowledge, has been destroyed; however, he does not possess knowledge of the fruits like the Buddhas. Therefore, the opponent's argument is indeed unestablished.

Phalañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discussion on the Knowledge of Fruits.

Pañcamo vaggo.

The Fifth Chapter.

Mahāpaṇṇāsako samatto.

The Great Fifty is concluded.

6. Chaṭṭhavaggo

6. The Sixth Chapter.

1. Niyāmakathāvaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discussion on Certainty.

445-447. Idāni [M 0.0191][P 0.0089] niyāmakathā nāma hoti. Tattha niyāmoti “bhabbo niyāmaṃ okkamituṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammatta”nti (pu. pa. 13) vacanato ariyamaggo vuccati. Yasmā pana tasmiṃ uppajjitvā niruddhepi puggalo aniyato nāma na hoti, tasmā “so niyāmo niccaṭṭhena asaṅkhato”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Tato “yadi so asaṅkhato, evarūpena tena bhavitabba”nti dīpento nibbānantiādimāha. Saṃsandanapucchā uttānatthāyeva.

Now there is the discussion on certainty. Herein, 'certainty' refers to the Noble Path, according to the statement, 'capable of entering into certainty, the rightness in wholesome states' (Pug. 13). However, because a person is not called 'uncertain' even after that path, having arisen, has ceased, some, like the Andhakas, hold the view that 'this certainty is unconditioned in the sense of being permanent.' With reference to them, the question is for the proponent of one's own doctrine, and the admission is for the other. Then, clarifying, 'If it is unconditioned, it must be of such a nature,' he states what begins with 'Nibbāna.' The question for comparison is of straightforward meaning.

Atthi [V 0.0187] kecītiādi niyāmassa saṅkhatabhāvadīpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Maggo asaṅkhatotipañhe tassa uppādanirodhabhāvato paṭikkhipatīti. Niyāmo saṅkhatotipañhe niruddhepi magge niyāmassa atthitaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Sotāpattiniyāmotiādipañhesupi anulomato ca paṭilomato ca imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Pañca asaṅkhatānīti puṭṭho pañcannaṃ asaṅkhatānaṃ āgataṭṭhānaṃ apassanto paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho catunnaṃ sammattaniyāmānaṃ niyāmavacanato nibbānassa ca asaṅkhatabhāvato paṭijānāti. Micchattaniyāmapañho niyāmavacanamattena asaṅkhatatāya ayuttabhāvadīpanatthaṃ vuttoti.

The passage beginning 'There are some,' and so on, is stated for the purpose of explaining the conditioned nature of certainty. In the question 'Is the path unconditioned?', it is rejected because of its nature of arising and ceasing. In the question 'Is certainty conditioned?', he rejects it with reference to the existence of certainty even when the path has ceased. And in questions such as 'Is the certainty of stream-entry...?', the meaning should be understood in the same way, both in direct and reverse order. Being asked 'Are there five unconditioned things?', not seeing a textual source for five unconditioned things, he rejects it. Being asked a second time, he affirms it because of the term 'certainty' for the four right certainties, and because of the unconditioned nature of Nibbāna. The question concerning the wrong certainty is stated for the purpose of explaining its inappropriateness, merely by the term 'certainty' implying an unconditioned state.

Niyāmakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discussion on Certainty.

2. Paṭiccasamuppādakathāvaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Discussion on Dependent Origination.

448. Idāni paṭiccasamuppādakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ nidānavagge “uppādā vā tathāgatānaṃ anuppādā vā tathāgatānaṃ [P 0.0090] ṭhitāva sā dhātu dhammaṭṭhitatā”tiādivacanato (saṃ. ni. 2.20) “paṭiccasamuppādo asaṅkhato”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyānañca mahisāsakānañca; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa.

448. Now there is the exposition on dependent origination. Here, concerning those who, based on statements in the Nidānavagga such as, “Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, that element stands firm, the fixedness of the Dhamma,” hold the view that “dependent origination is unconditioned,” as do the Pubbaseliyas and the Mahisāsakas—with reference to them, the question is by the proponent of their own view, the affirmation by the other.

449. Avijjā [M 0.0192] asaṅkhatāti ādayo pañhā avijjādīnaṃyeva paṭiccasamuppādabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttā. Yena panatthena tattha ekekaṃ aṅgaṃ “paṭiccasamuppādo”ti vuccati, so paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅge vuttoyeva.

449. The questions beginning with “Is ignorance unconditioned?” were stated for the purpose of showing that ignorance and so forth are themselves dependently arisen. However, the sense in which each individual factor there is called “dependent origination” has indeed been explained in the Exposition of Dependent Origination.

451. Avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti yā tattha dhammaṭṭhitatātiādi yena suttena laddhi patiṭṭhāpitā, tasseva atthadassanena laddhibhindanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Ayañhettha attho – yā ayaṃ heṭṭhā “ṭhitāva sā dhātu dhammaṭṭhitatā dhammaniyāmatā”ti vuttā na sā aññatra avijjādīhi visuṃ ekā atthi. Avijjādīnaṃ pana paccayānaṃyevetaṃ nāmaṃ. Uppannepi hi tathāgate anuppannepi avijjāto saṅkhārā sambhavanti, saṅkhārādīhi ca viññāṇādīni, tasmā “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti [V 0.0188] yā etasmiṃ pade saṅkhāradhammānaṃ kāraṇaṭṭhena ṭhitatāti dhammaṭṭhitatā. Tesaṃyeva ca dhammānaṃ kāraṇaṭṭheneva niyāmatāti dhammaniyāmatāti avijjā vuccati. Sā ca asaṅkhatā, nibbānañca asaṅkhatanti pucchati. Paravādī laddhivasena paṭijānitvā puna dve asaṅkhatānīti puṭṭho suttābhāvena paṭikkhipitvā laddhivaseneva paṭijānāti. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Heṭṭhā vuttasadisaṃ pana tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

451. The statement, 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise,' is made for the purpose of breaking down, by showing its meaning, that view which was established by the sutta concerning the fixedness of the Dhamma (dhammaṭṭhitatā) and so forth. The meaning here is this: that which was stated earlier as 'that element stands firm, the fixedness of the Dhamma, the lawfulness of the Dhamma,' does not exist as a single separate thing apart from ignorance and so forth. Rather, this is merely a name for those very conditions such as ignorance. For whether Tathāgatas have arisen or not, volitional formations arise from ignorance, and from volitional formations, consciousness and so forth. Therefore, in the phrase 'with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise,' the fixedness of the Dhamma (dhammaṭṭhitatā) is the fact of standing firm as a cause for the phenomena of volitional formations. And the lawfulness of the Dhamma (dhammaniyāmatā) is the lawfulness in the sense of being a cause for those very phenomena; it is ignorance that is so called. He asks: 'Is that unconditioned, and Nibbāna unconditioned?' The opponent, having first affirmed based on his view, when asked again whether there are two unconditioned states, rejects it due to the absence of a sutta to support it, but still affirms based on his view. The same method applies to the remaining points. However, what is similar to what was stated earlier should be understood in the same way as explained there.

Paṭiccasamuppādakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discourse on Dependent Origination.

3. Saccakathāvaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on the Truths

452-454. Idāni saccakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, tathāni avitathānī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1090) suttaṃ nissāya “cattāri saccāni niccāni asaṅkhatānī”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Ayañhissa adhippāyo – dukkhasamudayamaggesu vatthusaccaṃ saṅkhataṃ, lakkhaṇasaccaṃ [P 0.0091] asaṅkhataṃ. Nirodhe vatthusaccaṃ nāma natthi asaṅkhatameva tanti. Tasmā āmantāti āha. Taṃ panassa laddhimattameva. So hi dukkhaṃ vatthusaccaṃ icchati, tathā samudayaṃ maggañca. Yāni pana nesaṃ bādhanapabhavaniyyānikalakkhaṇāni, tāni lakkhaṇasaccaṃ nāmāti, na ca bādhanalakkhaṇādīhi aññāni dukkhādīni nāma atthīti. Tāṇānītiādīsu adhippāyo vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Now there is the exposition on the truths. Here, concerning those who, relying on the sutta, “Monks, these four are real, not unreal,” hold the view that “the four truths are permanent and unconditioned,” like the Pubbaseliyas—with reference to them, the question is by the proponent of their own view, the affirmation by the other. For this is his intention: in the truths of suffering, origin, and path, the objective truth is conditioned, while the characteristic truth is unconditioned. In cessation, there is no objective truth; it is only unconditioned. Therefore, he says, “Yes.” But that is merely his view. For he considers suffering as an objective truth, and likewise origin and path. But those characteristics of theirs that are afflictive, productive of origination, and leading to liberation, are called the characteristic truth; and there are no other sufferings, etc., apart from those afflictive characteristics and so on. In phrases beginning with “those as protection,” the intended meaning should be understood in the same way as explained above.

Dukkhasaccanti [M 0.0193] pañhe laddhivasena lakkhaṇaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Dukkhanti pañhe vatthuṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Ito paraṃ suddhikapañhā ca saṃsandanapañhā ca sabbe pāḷianusāreneva veditabbā. Avasāne laddhipatiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ āhaṭasuttaṃ atthassa micchā gahitattā anāhaṭasadisamevāti.

In the question 'Is it the truth of suffering?', he affirms based on his view, referring to the characteristic. In the question 'Is it suffering?', he rejects, referring to the objective reality. From here onward, all the simple questions and the questions of comparison should be understood in accordance with the Pāli text itself. At the end, the sutta brought forward for the purpose of establishing a view, since its meaning was wrongly grasped, is as if it were not brought forward.

Saccakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Truths.

4. Āruppakathāvaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse on the Immaterial States

455-456. Idāni [V 0.0189] āruppakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “cattāro āruppā āneñjā”ti vacanaṃ nissāya “sabbepi te dhammā asaṅkhatā”ti laddhi, te sandhāya ākāsānañcāyatananti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti. Sādhakasuttampi atthaṃ ajānitvā āhaṭattā anāhaṭasadisamevāti.

Now comes the discourse on the immaterial states. Herein, with reference to those who, relying on the statement “the four immaterial states are imperturbable,” hold the view that “all those phenomena are unconditioned,” the question “Is the sphere of infinite space...?” is for the proponent of one’s own doctrine, the affirmation for the other. The rest here is quite straightforward. And the sutta cited as proof, because it is brought forward without understanding its meaning, is as if it were not brought forward at all.

Āruppakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Immaterial States.

5. Nirodhasamāpattikathāvaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Attainment of Cessation

457-459. Idāni nirodhasamāpattikathā nāma hoti. Tattha nirodhasamāpattīti catunnaṃ khandhānaṃ appavatti. Yasmā pana sā kariyamānā kariyati, samāpajjiyamānā samāpajjiyati, tasmā nipphannāti vuccati. Saṅkhatāsaṅkhatalakkhaṇānaṃ pana [P 0.0092] abhāvena na vattabbā “saṅkhatāti vā asaṅkhatā”ti vā. Tattha yesaṃ “yasmā saṅkhatā na hoti, tasmā asaṅkhatā”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānañceva uttarāpathakānañca; te sandhāya nirodhasamāpattīti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Uppādentītiādi samāpajjanapaṭilābhavaseneva vuttaṃ. Yathā pana rūpādayo asaṅkhatadhamme uppādenti; na tathā taṃ keci uppādenti nāma. Nirodhā vodānaṃ vuṭṭhānanti phalasamāpatti veditabbā. Asaṅkhatā pana taṃ [M 0.0194] natthiyeva, tasmā paṭikkhipati. Tena hīti yasmā saṅkhatā na hoti, tasmā asaṅkhatāti laddhi. Idaṃ pana asaṅkhatabhāve kāraṇaṃ na hotīti vuttampi avuttasadisamevāti.

Now comes the discourse on the attainment of cessation. Herein, the attainment of cessation is the non-occurrence of the four aggregates. However, because it is made when being made, and entered when being entered, it is therefore called “produced.” Since it lacks the characteristics of the conditioned or the unconditioned, it cannot be said to be either “conditioned” or “unconditioned.” Here, with reference to those who hold the view that “because it is not conditioned, therefore it is unconditioned”—such as the Andhakas and the Uttarāpathakas—the question “Is the attainment of cessation...?” is for the proponent of one’s own doctrine, the affirmation for the other. The terms “producing” and so on are stated only in relation to entering and obtaining it. Just as material form and others do not produce an unconditioned phenomenon, so too does no one truly produce it. “Emergence from cessation, a purification,” should be understood as the attainment of fruition. However, that attainment is not unconditioned, therefore he rejects it. The phrase 'If that is so...' introduces the view: 'Because it is not conditioned, therefore it is unconditioned.' But since this is not a reason for its being unconditioned, what is said is as good as unsaid.

Nirodhasamāpattikathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Attainment of Cessation.

6. Ākāsakathāvaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Discourse on Space

460-462. Idāni ākāsakathā nāma hoti. Tattha tividho ākāso – paricchedākāso[V 0.0190], kasiṇugghāṭimākāso, ajaṭākāso. “Tucchākāso”tipi tasseva nāmaṃ. Tesu paricchedākāso saṅkhato, itare dve paññattimattā. Yesaṃ pana “duvidhopi yasmā saṅkhato na hoti, tasmā asaṅkhato”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi uttarāpathakānaṃ mahisāsakānañca; te sandhāya ākāsoti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

Now comes the discourse on space. Therein, space is threefold: delimited space, space from removing the kasiṇa, and unobstructed space. “Empty space” is also a name for that same thing. Among these, delimited space is conditioned, while the other two are mere designations. However, for those who hold the view that “since neither of the two is conditioned, therefore it is unconditioned”—such as the Uttarāpathakas and the Mahīsāsakas—the question “Is space...?” is for the proponent of one’s own doctrine, and the affirmation is for the other. The rest here is of plain meaning.

Ākāsakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discourse on Space.

7. Ākāso sanidassanotikathāvaṇṇanā

7. The Exposition of the Discourse on Whether Space is Visible.

463-464. Idāni ākāso sanidassanotikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ tāḷacchiddādīsu ñāṇappavattiṃ nissāya “sabbopi ajaṭākāso [P 0.0093] sanidassano”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ[V 0.0191]; te sandhāya ākāso sanidassanoti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi sanidassano, evaṃvidho bhaveyyā”ti codanatthaṃ rūpantiādi vuttaṃ. Cakkhuñca paṭiccātipañhesu evarūpassa suttassa abhāvena paṭikkhipitvā tulantarikādīnaṃ upaladdhiṃ nissāya paṭijānāti. Dvinnaṃ rukkhānaṃ antaranti ettha rukkharūpaṃ cakkhunā disvā antare rūpābhāvato ākāsanti manodvāraviññāṇaṃ uppajjati, na cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Tasmā asādhakametanti.

Now comes the discourse called “Is space visible?” Here, those who, relying on the occurrence of knowledge regarding keyholes and so on, hold the view that “all unobstructed space is visible”—such as the Andhakas—are referred to. The question “Is space visible?” is for the proponent of one’s own doctrine, and the affirmation is for the other. Then, to challenge them with, “If it were visible, it would be of such a nature,” the words “form, etc.” are stated for the purpose of censure. In the questions regarding “depending on the eye,” having rejected this due to the absence of such a sutta, they affirm it relying on the perception of gaps, such as that between pillars. Regarding “the space between two trees,” here, having seen the form of the trees with the eye, a mind-door consciousness arises thinking “space” due to the absence of form in between, not an eye-consciousness. The same method applies to the remaining cases. Therefore, this is not a valid proof.

Ākāso sanidassanotikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discourse on Whether Space is Visible.

10. Pathavīdhātusanidassanātiādikathāvaṇṇanā

10. The Exposition of the Discourse Beginning with 'Is the Earth Element Visible?'

465-470. Idāni [M 0.0195] pathavīdhātu sanidassanātiādikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ pāsāṇaudakajālarukkhacalanānañceva pañcindriyapatiṭṭhokāsānañca vaṇṇāyatanaṃ kāyaviññattikāle hatthapādādirūpañca disvā “pathavīdhātuādayo sanidassanā”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya sabbakathāsu ādipucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesaṃ sabbattha pāḷianusārena ceva heṭṭhā vuttanayena ca veditabbanti. Pathavīdhātu sanidassanāti ādiṃ katvā kāyakammaṃ sanidassananti pariyosānakathā niṭṭhitā.

Now comes the discourse beginning with 'Is the earth element visible?' Herein, for those who, upon seeing rocks, water, nets, the movement of trees, the visible object which is the basis for the establishment of the five sense faculties, and forms such as hands and feet at the time of bodily intimation, hold the view that 'the earth element and others are visible,' such as the Andhakas; referring to them, the initial question in all discourses is for the proponent of one's own doctrine, and the admission is for the other. The rest should be understood everywhere according to the Pāli text and the method stated previously. The discourse beginning with 'Is the Earth Element Visible?' and ending with 'Is Bodily Action Visible?' is concluded.

Chaṭṭho vaggo.

The Sixth Chapter.

7. Sattamavaggo

7. The Seventh Chapter.

1. Saṅgahitakathāvaṇṇanā

1. The Exposition of the Discourse on Inclusion.

471-472. Idāni [P 0.0094] saṅgahitakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā dāmādīhi balibaddādayo viya keci dhammā kehici dhammehi saṅgahitā nāma natthi, tasmā “natthi keci dhammā kehici dhammehi saṅgahitā, evaṃ sante ekavidhena rūpasaṅgahotiādi niratthaka”nti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi rājagirikānañceva siddhatthikānañca; te sandhāya aññenatthena saṅgahabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ pucchā sakavādissa, attano laddhivasena paṭiññā itarassa. Idāni yenatthena saṅgaho labbhati, taṃ dassetuṃ nanu atthi keci dhammātiādi āraddhaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthameva.
