Yā panesā paravādinā laddhipatiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ yathā dāmena vātiādikā upamā āhaṭā, sakavādinā taṃ anabhinanditvā appaṭikkositvā “hañci dāmena vā”ti tassa laddhi bhinnāti veditabbā. Ayañhettha attho – yadi te dāmādīhi balibaddādayo saṅgahitā nāma, atthi keci dhammā kehici dhammehi saṅgahitāti.

Now comes the discourse on inclusion. Herein, since some phenomena are not in fact included by other phenomena in the way that oxen and so forth are by ropes and so forth, some hold the view that 'there are no phenomena included by other phenomena, and thus statements like "inclusion of form in one way" and so forth are meaningless,' such as the Rājagirikā and the Siddhatthikā; referring to them, to show the state of inclusion in another sense, the question is for the proponent of one's own doctrine, and the admission is for the other according to his own view. Now, to show by what meaning inclusion is obtained, the discussion beginning with 'Are there not some phenomena?' is commenced. All that is of plain meaning because the method has been stated previously. But as for the simile beginning with 'just as by a rope' brought by the opponent to establish his view, it should be understood that the proponent, without approving or refuting it, broke his view by saying, 'If indeed by a rope.' The meaning here is: if oxen and so forth are indeed included by ropes and so forth, then there are some phenomena included by some other phenomena.

Saṅgahitakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discourse on Inclusion.

2. Sampayuttakathāvaṇṇanā

2. The Exposition of the Discourse on Association.

473-474. Idāni [M 0.0196] sampayuttakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā tilamhi telaṃ viya na vedanādayo saññādīsu anupaviṭṭhā, tasmā “natthi keci dhammā kehici dhammehi sampayuttā, evaṃ sante [V 0.0192] ñāṇasampayuttantiādi niratthakaṃ hotī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi [P 0.0095] rājagirikasiddhatthikānaññeva; te sandhāya aññenevatthena sampayuttataṃ dassetuṃ pucchā sakavādissa, attano laddhivasena paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamidhāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthameva. Yo panesa paravādinā “yathā tilamhi tela”ntiādiko upamāpañho āhaṭo, so yasmā vedanāsaññānaṃ viya tilatelānaṃ lakkhaṇato nānattavavatthānaṃ natthi. Sabbesupi hi tilaaṭṭhitacesu tiloti vohāramattaṃ, teneva tilaṃ nibbattetvā gahite purimasaṇṭhānena tilo nāma na paññāyati, tasmā anāhaṭasadisova hotīti.

Now comes the discourse on association. Herein, since feelings and so forth have not entered into perceptions and so forth in the way that oil has into sesame, those who hold the view that 'there are no phenomena associated with any phenomena, and thus statements such as "associated with knowledge" and so forth are meaningless,' such as the Rājagirikā and the Siddhatthikā themselves; referring to them, to show association in another sense, the question is for the proponent of one's own doctrine, and the admission is for the other according to his own view. The rest here too is of plain meaning because the method has been stated previously. But as for the question with the simile beginning with 'as oil in sesame' brought by the opponent, it is because there is no distinct determination of characteristics between sesame and oil as there is between feelings and perceptions. For in all sesame seeds and cakes, it is merely the convention 'sesame'; and because when oil is extracted from sesame, the sesame is no longer apparent in its original form, therefore it is like an inapplicable simile.

Sampayuttakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discourse on Association.

3. Cetasikakathāvaṇṇanā

3. The Exposition of the Discourse on Mental Concomitants.

475-477. Idāni cetasikakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā phassikādayo nāma natthi, tasmā “cetasikenāpi na bhavitabbaṃ, iti natthi cetasiko dhammo”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi rājagirikasiddhatthikānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sahajātoti sampayuttasahajātaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Phassikāti tādisaṃ vohāraṃ apassantassa pucchā paravādissa. Kiṃ vohārena, yathā cittanissitakoti cetasiko, evaṃ sopi phassanissitattā phassikoti vutte doso natthīti paṭiññā sakavādissa. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

Now comes the discourse on mental concomitants. Herein, since there are no such things as 'contact-factors' and so forth, some hold the view that 'there can be no mental concomitant either; thus there is no mental concomitant phenomenon,' such as the Rājagirikas and Siddhatthikas; referring to them, the question is by the proponent of one's own doctrine, and the admission is by the other. 'Co-arisen' is said in reference to that which is associated and co-arisen. 'Contact-factor' is a question from the opponent who does not see such a usage. 'What is wrong with the usage? Just as what is dependent on the mind is a mental concomitant, so too, since this is dependent on contact, there is no fault in calling it a contact-factor'—this is the assertion of the proponent of one's own doctrine. The rest is of plain meaning.

Cetasikakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discourse on Mental Concomitants.

4. Dānakathāvaṇṇanā

4. The Exposition of the Discourse on Giving.

478. Idāni [M 0.0197] dānakathā nāma hoti. Tattha dānaṃ nāma tividhaṃ – cāgacetanāpi, viratipi, deyyadhammopi. “Saddhā hiriyaṃ kusalañca [P 0.0096] dāna”nti (a. ni. 8.30) āgataṭṭhāne cāgacetanā dānaṃ. “Abhayaṃ detī”ti (a. ni. 8.39) āgataṭṭhāne virati. “Dānaṃ deti annaṃ pāna”nti āgataṭṭhāne deyyadhammo. Tattha cāgacetanā “deti vā deyyadhammaṃ, denti [V 0.0193] vā etāya deyyadhamma”nti dānaṃ. Virati avakhaṇḍanaṭṭhena lavanaṭṭhena vā dānaṃ. Sā hi uppajjamānā bhayabheravādisaṅkhātaṃ dussīlyacetanaṃ dāti khaṇḍeti lunāti vāti dānaṃ. Deyyadhammo diyyatīti dānaṃ. Evametaṃ tividhampi atthato cetasiko ceva dhammo deyyadhammo cāti duvidhaṃ hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “cetasikova dhammo dānaṃ, na deyyadhammo”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi rājagirikasiddhatthikānaṃ; te sandhāya cetasikoti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ deyyadhammavasena codetuṃ labbhāti pucchā sakavādissa, annādīni viya so na sakkā dātunti paṭikkhepo itarassa. Puna daḷhaṃ katvā puṭṭhe “abhayaṃ detī”ti suttavasena paṭiññā tasseva. Phassapañhādīsu pana phassaṃ detītiādivohāraṃ apassanto paṭikkhipateva.

478. Now comes the discussion on giving. Herein, giving is of three kinds: the intention to give, abstention, and the gift itself. In the passage, 'Faith, moral shame, and skillful giving,' the intention to give is called giving. In the passage, 'One gives safety,' abstention is called giving. In the passage, 'One gives food and drink,' the gift itself is called giving. Herein, the intention to give is called giving because one gives a gift, or because by it a gift is given. Abstention is called giving in the sense of severing or cutting. For when it arises, it severs or cuts the volition of immorality, which is designated as fear and terror—thus it is called giving. The gift is called giving because it is given. Thus, these three kinds are, in essence, of two kinds: a mental concomitant and the gift itself. Herein, for those who hold the view that 'giving is only a mental concomitant, not the gift itself,' such as the Rājagirikas and Siddhatthikas, the question about the mental concomitant is posed by the proponent of one's own doctrine, while the admission is by the other. Then, to challenge him regarding the gift itself, the proponent of one's own doctrine poses the question, while the other rejects it, saying that it cannot be given like food and so on. Again, when pressed firmly, the admission is made by that same party, citing the sutta passage, 'One gives safety.' But in questions like those about contact, not finding the conventional expression 'one gives contact' and so on, the other simply rejects it.

479. Aniṭṭhaphalantiādi acetasikassa dhammassa dānabhāvadīpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Na hi acetasiko annādidhammo āyatiṃ vipākaṃ deti, iṭṭhaphalabhāvaniyamanatthaṃ panetaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Ayampi hettha adhippāyo – yadi acetasiko annādidhammo dānaṃ bhaveyya, hitacittena aniṭṭhaṃ akantaṃ bhesajjaṃ dentassa nimbabījādīhi viya nimbādayo aniṭṭhameva phalaṃ nibbatteyya. Yasmā panettha hitapharaṇacāgacetanā dānaṃ, tasmā aniṭṭhepi deyyadhamme dānaṃ iṭṭhaphalameva hotīti.

479. The passage beginning 'undesirable result' is stated to clarify the nature of a non-mental phenomenon as giving. For a non-mental phenomenon like food and so on does not yield a future result. But it should be understood that this is said to establish the certainty of a desirable result. The intention here is also this: if a non-mental phenomenon like food and so on were giving, then when one gives unpleasant or unwanted medicine with a beneficial intention, it would produce only an undesirable result, just as from neem seeds, neem trees are produced. But since here the volition of giving, pervaded by benefit, is what constitutes giving, therefore, even if the object given is undesirable, the giving still yields a desirable result.

Evaṃ paravādinā cetasikadhammassa dānabhāve patiṭṭhāpite sakavādī itarena pariyāyena deyyadhammassa dānabhāvaṃ sādhetuṃ dānaṃ iṭṭhaphalaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatātiādimāha. Paravādī pana cīvarādīnaṃ iṭṭhavipākataṃ apassanto paṭikkhipati. Suttasādhanaṃ paravādīvādepi yujjati sakavādīvādepi, na pana ekenatthena. Deyyadhammo iṭṭhaphaloti iṭṭhaphalabhāvamattameva paṭikkhittaṃ. Tasmā tena hi na vattabbanti iṭṭhaphalabhāveneva na vattabbatā yujjati[M 0.0198]. Dātabbaṭṭhena [P 0.0097] pana deyyadhammo dānameva. Dinnañhi dānānaṃ saṅkarabhāvamocanatthameva ayaṃ kathāti.

Thus, when the opponent establishes the mental concomitant as the act of giving, the proponent of one's own doctrine, in another way, seeks to establish the gift-worthy object as the act of giving by stating that the Blessed One has declared giving to yield desirable results. The other, however, rejects this, not seeing the desirable results of robes and other gifts. The argument based on the sutta is valid whether it is the other's view or the proponent of one's own doctrine's view, but not in the sense of a single meaning. That the gift-worthy object yields desirable results—only the mere state of being a desirable result is rejected. Therefore, the statement 'it should not be said by him' is valid only regarding the state of being a desirable result. However, in the sense of being fit to be given, the gift-worthy object is precisely giving itself. Indeed, this discussion is solely for the purpose of resolving the confusion about gifts that have been given.

Dānakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on Giving.

5. Paribhogamayapuññakathāvaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Discussion on Merit Consisting of Use.

483. Idāni paribhogamayapuññakathā nāma hoti. Tattha “tesaṃ divā ca ratto ca, sadā puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.47) ca “yassa bhikkhave, bhikkhu cīvaraṃ paribhuñjamāno”ti (a. ni. 4.51) ca evamādīni suttāni ayoniso gahetvā yesaṃ paribhogamayaṃ [V 0.0194] nāma puññaṃ atthī”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi rājagirikasiddhatthikasammitiyānaṃ; te sandhāya paribhogamayanti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “puññaṃ nāma phassādayo kusalā dhammā, na tato paraṃ, tasmā phassādīhi te vaḍḍhitabba”nti codetuṃ paribhogamayo phassotiādi āraddhaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ itarena tesaṃ avaḍḍhanato paṭikkhittaṃ. Latāviyātiādīni “kiriyāya vā bhāvanāya vā vināpi yathā latādīni sayameva vaḍḍhanti, kiṃ te evaṃ vaḍḍhantī”ti codanatthaṃ vuttāni. Tathā panassa avaḍḍhanato na hevāti paṭikkhittaṃ.

483. Now there is the discussion called 'Merit Consisting of Use.' Herein, taking suttas such as “For them, day and night, merit always increases” and “Monks, when a monk uses a robe” and so on inappropriately, there is a view, 'there is merit called "consisting of use,"' as held by the Rājagirikas, Siddhatthikas, and Sammitiyas. Concerning them, the proponent asks, 'Is there merit consisting of use?' and the other acknowledges it. Then, to challenge them by saying, 'Merit is wholesome states beginning with contact, not beyond that; therefore, they should be increased by contact and so on,' the proponent begins with 'merit consisting of use is contact,' etc. All of that is rejected by the other because it does not lead to their increase. The examples of creeping plants and so on are stated for the purpose of challenging them, saying: 'Even without action or development, just as creepers and so on grow by themselves, do they grow in this way?' However, because it does not increase in that way, it is rejected with 'not so.'

484. Na samannāharatīti pañhe paṭiggāhakānaṃ paribhogena purimacetanā vaḍḍhati, evaṃ taṃ hoti puññanti laddhivasena paṭijānāti. Tato anāvaṭṭentassātiādīhi puṭṭho dāyakassa cāgacetanaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Tattha anāvaṭṭentassāti dānacetanāya purecārikena āvajjanena bhavaṅgaṃ anāvaṭṭentassa aparivaṭṭentassa. Anābhogassāti nirābhogassa. Asamannāharantassāti na samannāharantassa. Āvajjanañhi bhavaṅgaṃ vicchinditvā attano gatamagge uppajjamānaṃ dānacetanaṃ samannāharati nāma. Evaṃkiccena iminā cittena asamannāharantassa puññaṃ hotīti pucchati. Amanasikarontassāti [P 0.0098] manaṃ akarontassa. Āvajjanena hi tadanantaraṃ uppajjamānaṃ manaṃ karoti nāma. Evaṃ akarontassāti attho. Upayogavacanasmiñhi etaṃ bhummaṃ. Acetayantassāti cetanaṃ anuppādentassa. Apatthentassāti [M 0.0199] patthanāsaṅkhātaṃ kusalacchandaṃ akarontassa. Appaṇidahantassāti dānacetanāvasena cittaṃ aṭṭhapentassāti attho. Nanu āvaṭṭentassāti vāre ābhogassāti ābhogavato. Atha vā ābhogā assa, ābhogassa vā anantaraṃ taṃ puññaṃ hotīti attho.

484. In the question 'Does one not bring it to mind?', it is acknowledged in terms of the view that the donor's initial volition increases through the recipient's use, and thus it becomes merit. Then, when asked with 'for one not adverting,' and so on, the opponent rejects it, referring to the donor’s volition of generosity. Herein, 'for one not adverting' means for one not turning, not revolving, the life-continuum by the advertence that precedes the volition of giving. 'For one without effort' means for one without exertion. 'For one not bringing to mind' means for one not bringing to mind. For advertence, indeed, interrupting the life-continuum, brings to mind the volition of giving arising in its own course. Thus, the proponent asks whether merit arises for one who does not bring to mind with this mind, which performs such a function. 'For one not attending' means for one not applying the mind. For what arises immediately after advertence is called 'making mind' or attending. 'Not doing so' is the meaning. Indeed, this is a locative usage in the sense of application. 'For one not intending' means for one not arousing volition. 'For one not aspiring' means for one not generating the wholesome desire known as aspiration. 'For one not directing' means for one not fixing the mind by way of the volition of giving. Now, in the section on 'for one adverting,' 'for one with effort' means for one who possesses effort. Or alternatively, the meaning is that effort is his, or that the merit arises immediately after the effort.

485. Dvinnaṃ phassānantiādīsupi ekakkhaṇe dāyakassa dvinnaṃ phassādīnaṃ abhāvā paṭikkhipati, dāyakassa ca paribhuñjantassa cāti ubhinnaṃ phassādayo sandhāya paṭijānāti. Apicassa pañcannaṃ viññāṇānaṃ samodhānaṃ hotīti laddhi, tassāpi vasena paṭijānāti. Atha naṃ sakavādī pariyāyassa dvāraṃpidahitvā ujuvipaccanīkavasena codetuṃ kusalādipañhaṃ pucchati. Tatrāpi kusalākusalānaṃ ekassekakkhaṇe sampayogābhāvaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Paribhogamayaṃ pana cittavippayuttaṃ uppajjatīti laddhiyā paṭijānāti. Atha naṃ sakavādī suttena niggaṇhāti.

485. Even in the question 'of two contacts,' etc., the opponent rejects it because at a single moment, the donor does not have two instances of contact, etc. However, it is acknowledged with reference to the contact, etc., of both the donor and the one using the offering. Moreover, there is the view that a convergence of the five sense-consciousnesses occurs, and it is acknowledged on that basis as well. Then, the proponent, closing the door to indirect reasoning, challenges him by way of direct opposition with a question about what is skillful, etc. There too, it is rejected with reference to the absence of the simultaneous association of skillful and unskillful states at a single moment. However, it is acknowledged based on the view that merit consisting of use arises disconnected from the mind. Then, the proponent refutes him with a sutta.

486. Suttasādhane ārāmaropakādīnaṃ anussaraṇapaṭisaṅkharaṇādivasena antarantarā uppajjamānaṃ [V 0.0195] puññaṃ sandhāya sadā puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatīti vuttaṃ. Appamāṇo tassa puññābhisandoti idaṃ appamāṇavihārino dinnapaccayattā ca “evarūpo me cīvaraṃ paribhuñjatī”ti anumodanavasena ca vuttaṃ. Taṃ so paribhogamayanti sallakkheti. Yasmā pana paṭiggāhakena paṭiggahetvā aparibhuttepi deyyadhamme puññaṃ hotiyeva, tasmā sakavādīvādova balavā, tattha paṭiggāhakena paṭiggahiteti attho daṭṭhabbo. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

486. In the proof from the sutta, it is said that 'merit always increases' with reference to the merit arising intermittently through recollecting, reflecting, etc., regarding the planting of parks, etc. 'Immeasurable is his flood of merit'—this is said because of the requisites given to one dwelling in the immeasurable meditations, and also by way of rejoicing with the thought, 'Such a one is using my robe.' He (the opponent) recognizes that as 'merit consisting of use.' However, since merit indeed arises even when the offered item is accepted by the recipient but not yet used, therefore, the argument of the proponent is stronger; there, the meaning should be understood as 'accepted by the recipient.' The rest is clear in meaning.

Paribhogamayapuññakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on Merit Consisting of Use.

6. Itodinnakathāvaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Discussion on What is Given from Here.

488-491. Idāni [P 0.0099] ito dinnakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “ito dinnena yāpenti, petā kālaṅkatā tahi”nti (pe. va. 19) vacanaṃ nissāya “yaṃ ito cīvarādi dinnaṃ teneva yāpentī”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi rājagirikasiddhatthikānaṃ; te sandhāya ito dinnenāti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa[M 0.0200]. Puna cīvarādivasena anuyutto paṭikkhipati. Añño aññassa kārakoti aññassa vipākadāyakānaṃ kammānaṃ añño kārako, na attanāva attano kammaṃ karotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ puṭṭho pana itaro suttavirodhabhayena paṭikkhipati. Dānaṃ dentanti dānaṃ dadamānaṃ disvāti attho. Tattha yasmā attano anumoditattā ca tesaṃ tattha bhogā uppajjanti, tasmāssa iminā kāraṇena laddhiṃ patiṭṭhapentassāpi appatiṭṭhitāva hoti. Na hi te ito dinneneva vatthunā yāpenti. Sesesupi suttasādhanesu eseva nayoti.

488-491. Now comes the discussion called 'Given from Here.' Here, regarding those who, relying on the statement, 'They subsist on what is given from here, the departed who have passed away there' (Pe. Va. 19), hold the view that 'they subsist on that very thing which is given from here, such as robes, etc.,' like the Rājagirikas and Siddhatthikas; with reference to them, the question 'by what is given from here?' is posed by the proponent, and the other party acknowledges it. Then, being pressed concerning robes, etc., he refutes it. 'Another is the doer for another': It is said that the doer of actions that yield results for another is different; one does not perform one's own action by oneself. However, when asked thus, the other refutes it for fear of contradicting the Sutta. 'Dānaṃ dentanti': This means 'seeing someone giving a gift.' There, because their enjoyments arise there due to their own rejoicing, even when one establishes a view based on this reason, it remains unestablished. For they do not subsist solely on things given from here. In the remaining proofs from the suttas, the method is the same.

Ito dinnakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on What is Given from Here.

7. Pathavīkammavipākotikathāvaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Discussion of 'Earth as the Result of Kamma'.

492. Idāni pathavī kammavipākotikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā “atthi issariyasaṃvattaniyaṃ kammaṃ, ādhipaccasaṃvattaniyaṃ kamma”nti ettha issarānaṃ bhāvo issariyaṃ nāma[V 0.0196], adhipatīnañca bhāvo ādhipaccaṃ nāma, pathavissariyaādhipaccasaṃvattanikañca kammaṃ atthīti vuttaṃ. Tasmā yesaṃ “pathavī kammavipāko”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pathavīti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sukhavedanīyātiādi kammavipākasabhāvadassanavasena vuttaṃ. “Phasso hotī”tiādinā nayena niddiṭṭhesu vipākesu phasso sukhavedanīyādibhedo [P 0.0100] hoti. So ca saññādayo ca sukhavedanādīhi sampayuttā, vedanādayo saññādīhi, sabbepi sārammaṇā, atthi ca nesaṃ purecārikaāvaṭṭanādisaṅkhātaṃ āvajjanaṃ, kammapaccayabhūtā cetanā, yo tattha iṭṭhavipāko, tassa patthanā, paṇidhānavasena pavattā mūlataṇhā, kiṃ te evarūpā pathavīti pucchati. Itaro paṭikkhipati. Paṭilomapucchādīni uttānatthāneva.

492. Now comes the discussion called 'Earth as the Result of Kamma.' Here, because it is said, 'There is kamma conducive to sovereignty, kamma conducive to dominion,' the state of lords is called sovereignty, and the state of rulers is called dominion; and it is stated that there is kamma conducive to sovereignty and dominion over the earth. Therefore, for those who hold the view that 'earth is the result of kamma,' like the Andhakas, the question 'Is it earth?' is posed by the proponent, and the other party acknowledges it. 'Accompanied by pleasant feeling,' etc., is stated to show the nature of the result of kamma. Among the results described in the manner of 'contact arises,' etc., contact is of the kind associated with pleasant feeling, etc. That contact, along with perception, etc., is associated with pleasant feeling, etc.; and feeling, etc., is associated with perception, etc. All have objects, and there is also advertence, which is designated as the forerunner, turning towards, etc.; the volition that is the kamma-condition; and the root craving that proceeds by way of aspiration and resolve for a desired result there. He asks, 'Is the earth of such a nature for you?' The other refutes it. The counter-questions, etc., are clear in meaning.

493. Kammavipāko paresaṃ sādhāraṇoti pañhe phassādayo sandhāya paṭikkhipati, kammasamuṭṭhānaṃ rūpañca pathavīādīnaṃyeva ca sādhāraṇabhāvaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Asādhāraṇamaññesanti suttaṃ parasamayato āharitvā [M 0.0201] dassitaṃ. Sabbe sattā pathaviṃ paribhuñjantīti pañhe pathaviṃ anissite sandhāya paṭikkhipati, nissite sandhāya paṭijānāti. Pathaviṃ aparibhuñjitvā parinibbāyantīti pañhe āruppe parinibbāyantānaṃ vasena paṭijānāti. Kammavipākaṃ akhepetvāti idaṃ parasamayavasena vuttaṃ. Kammavipākañhi khepetvāva parinibbāyantīti tesaṃ laddhi. Sakasamaye pana katokāsassa kammassa uppannaṃ vipākaṃ akhepetvā parinibbānaṃ natthi. Tesañca laddhiyā pathavī sādhāraṇavipākattā uppannavipākoyeva hoti. Taṃ vipākabhāvena ṭhitaṃ akhepetvā parinibbānaṃ na yujjatīti codetuṃ vaṭṭati. Itaro laddhivasena paṭikkhipati. Cakkavattisattassa kammavipākanti pañhe asādhāraṇaṃ phassādiṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati, sādhāraṇaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Pathavīsamuddasūriyacandimādayo hi sabbesaṃ sādhāraṇakammavipākoti tesaṃ laddhi.

493. Regarding the question, 'Is the result of kamma common to others?', he refutes it with reference to contact, etc., but affirms it with reference to kamma-produced form and the common nature of earth, etc. 'Asādhāraṇamaññesaṃ' ('Not common to others'): This sutta passage is cited from another school. In the question, 'Do all beings make use of the earth?', he refutes it with reference to those not relying on earth but affirms it with reference to those relying on it. In the question, 'Do they attain final Nibbāna without making use of the earth?', he affirms it with reference to those attaining Nibbāna in the formless realms. 'Kammavipākaṃ akhepetvā' ('Without having exhausted the result of kamma'): This is stated from the perspective of another school. For they hold that one attains final Nibbāna only after exhausting the results of kamma. But in our own tradition, there is no final Nibbāna without exhausting the arisen result of kamma for which opportunity has been made. According to their view, since earth is a common result, it is only an arisen result. It is proper to object that it is not possible to attain Nibbāna without exhausting that which persists as a result. The other refutes it according to his view. In the question, 'Is it the result of kamma for a wheel-turning being?', he refutes it with reference to the uncommon contact, etc., but affirms it with reference to what is common. For they hold that the earth, ocean, sun, moon, etc., are the common results of kamma for all beings.

494. Issariyasaṃvattaniyanti ettha issariyaṃ nāma bahudhanatā. Ādhipaccaṃ nāma sesajane attano vase vattetvā tehi garukātabbaṭṭhena adhipatibhāvo. Tattha kammaṃ paṭilābhavasena taṃsaṃvattanikaṃ nāma hoti, na janakavasena. Tasmā vipākabhāve asādhakametanti.

494. Regarding 'conducive to sovereignty': here, sovereignty means abundant wealth. Dominion means the state of being a master, in the sense of making other people act according to one's will and being worthy of their respect. There, kamma is called 'conducive to that' in the sense of acquisition, not in the sense of generation. Therefore, this is not a proof for its being a state of result.

Pathavī kammavipākotikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on 'The Earth is a Result of Kamma'.

8. Jarāmaraṇaṃ vipākotikathāvaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Discussion on 'Aging and Death are a Result'.

495. Idāni [P 0.0101][V 0.0197] jarāmaraṇaṃ vipākotikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “atthi dubbaṇṇasaṃvattaniyaṃ kammaṃ appāyukasaṃvattaniyaṃ kamma”nti ettha dubbaṇṇatā nāma jarā. Appāyukatā nāma maraṇaṃ. Taṃsaṃvattaniyañca kammaṃ atthi. Tasmā jarāmaraṇaṃ vipākoti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Paṭilomapañhe anārammaṇanti rūpadhammānaṃ tāva anārammaṇameva, arūpānaṃ pana jarāmaraṇaṃ sampayogalakkhaṇābhāvā anārammaṇameva.

495. Now, the discussion called 'Aging and Death are a Result' takes place. Herein, for those who hold the view, 'There is kamma conducive to unattractiveness and kamma conducive to a short life,' unattractiveness is aging, and a short life is death. And there is kamma conducive to that. Therefore, their view is that aging and death are a result, as is the case with the Andhakas. With reference to them, the question is for the proponent, and the assertion is for the opponent. In the counter-question, regarding 'without an object': for material phenomena, it is indeed without an object; for immaterial phenomena, however, aging and death are without an object due to the absence of the characteristic of association.

496. Akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ jarāmaraṇaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ vipākoti pañhe jarāmaraṇena nāma aniṭṭhavipākena bhavitabbanti laddhiyā paṭijānāti[M 0.0202]. Teneva kāraṇena kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ jarāmaraṇassa kusalavipākataṃ paṭikkhipati. Parato cassa akusalavipākataññeva paṭijānāti.

496. In the question, 'Are aging and death the result of unwholesome phenomena?', he asserts this based on the view that aging and death must be an undesirable result. For that same reason, he rejects that the aging and death of wholesome phenomena is a wholesome result. And further, he asserts that it is only an unwholesome result.

Kusalānañca akusalānañcāti pucchāvasena ekato kataṃ, ekakkhaṇe pana taṃ natthi. Abyākatānaṃ avipākānaṃ jarāmaraṇaṃ vipākoti vattabbatāya pariyāyo natthi, tasmā abyākatavasena pucchā na katā.

The question 'Are they wholesome and unwholesome?' is made collectively, but they do not occur in a single moment. There is no way to assert that aging and death are results of indeterminate, non-resultant phenomena; therefore, the question is not framed in terms of the indeterminate.

497. Dubbaṇṇasaṃvattaniyanti ettha dubbaṇṇiyaṃ nāma aparisuddhavaṇṇatā. Appāyukatā nāma āyuno ciraṃ pavattituṃ asamatthatā. Tattha akusalakammaṃ kammasamuṭṭhānassa dubbaṇṇarūpassa kammapaccayo hoti, asadisattā panassa taṃvipāko na hoti. Utusamuṭṭhānādino pana taṃpaṭilābhavasena āyuno ca upacchedakavasena paccayo hoti. Evametaṃ pariyāyena taṃsaṃvattanikaṃ nāma hoti, na vipākaphassādīnaṃ viya janakavasena, tasmā vipākabhāve asādhakaṃ. Sesamettha heṭṭhā vuttasadisamevāti.

497. Regarding 'conducive to unattractiveness': here, unattractiveness means impure complexion. A short life means the inability of the life-faculty to continue for long. Herein, unwholesome kamma is a kamma-condition for unattractive materiality arisen from kamma, but due to its dissimilarity, it is not its result. For that which arises from temperature and so on, however, it becomes a condition by way of acquiring that and by way of cutting off the life-faculty. Thus, it is called 'conducive to that' indirectly, not in the generative sense like resultant contact and so on; therefore, it is not a proof for its being a state of result. The rest here is similar to what was stated above.

Jarāmaraṇaṃ vipākotikathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discussion on 'Aging and Death are a Result'.

9. Ariyadhammavipākakathāvaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Discussion on the Result of Noble Dhammas.

498. Idāni [P 0.0102][V 0.0198] ariyadhammavipākakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ kilesappahānamattameva sāmaññaphalaṃ, na cittacetasikā dhammāti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya natthi ariyadhammavipākoti pucchā sakavādissa. Tattha ariyadhammavipākoti maggasaṅkhātassa ariyadhammassa vipāko. Kilesakkhayamattaṃ ariyaphalanti laddhiyā paṭiññā itarassa. Sāmaññanti samaṇabhāvo, maggassetaṃ nāmaṃ. “Sāmaññañca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi sāmaññaphalañcā”ti hi vuttaṃ. Brahmaññepi eseva nayo.

498. Now, the discussion on the result of noble dhammas is thus named. Here, for those who hold the view that the fruit of recluseship is merely the abandoning of defilements, and not mind and mental factors—as is the case with the Andhakas; with reference to them, the proponent's question is: 'Is there no result of noble dhammas?' Herein, 'result of noble dhammas' means the result of the noble dhammas designated as the path. Based on their view that the noble fruit is merely the destruction of defilements, the assertion is for the opponent. 'Recluseship' means the state of a recluse; this is a name for the path. For it is said: 'Bhikkhus, I will teach you recluseship and the fruit of recluseship.' The same principle applies to the holy life.

Sotāpattiphalaṃ na vipākotiādīsu sotāpattimaggādīnaṃ apacayagāmitaṃ sandhāya ariyaphalānaṃ navipākabhāvaṃ paṭijānāti, dānaphalādīnaṃ paṭikkhipati[M 0.0203]. So hi ācayagāmittikassa evaṃ atthaṃ dhāreti – vipākasaṅkhātaṃ ācayaṃ gacchanti, taṃ vā ācinantā gacchantīti ācayagāmino, vipākaṃ apacinantā gacchantīti apacayagāminoti. Tasmā evaṃ paṭijānāti ca paṭikkhipati ca.

In statements such as, 'The fruit of stream-entry is not a result,' he asserts that noble fruits are not results, with reference to the stream-entry path and so on leading to diminution, but he rejects this for the results of giving and so on. For he understands the meaning of 'leading to accumulation' thus: 'They go to accumulation, designated as result, or they go while accumulating it'—such are 'leading to accumulation'; 'they go while diminishing result'—such are 'leading to diminution.' Therefore, he asserts in one case and rejects in another.

500. Kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ savipākaṃ ācayagāmītiādikā pucchā paravādissa, paṭiññā ca paṭikkhepo ca sakavādissa. Lokiyañhi kusalaṃ vipākacutipaṭisandhiyo ceva vaṭṭañca ācinantaṃ gacchatīti ācayagāmi. Lokuttarakusalaṃ cutipaṭisandhiyo ceva vaṭṭañca apacinantaṃ gacchatīti apacayagāmi. Evametaṃ savipākameva hoti, na apacayagāmivacanamattena avipākaṃ. Imamatthaṃ sandhāyettha sakavādino paṭiññā ca paṭikkhepo ca veditabbāti.

500. The question, 'Is sense-sphere wholesome kamma with result and leading to accumulation?' and so on, is for the opponent, while the assertion and rejection are for the proponent. For mundane wholesome kamma proceeds while accumulating results, death and rebirth-linking, and the round of existence, hence it is 'leading to accumulation.' Supramundane wholesome kamma proceeds while diminishing death and rebirth-linking and the round of existence, hence it is 'leading to diminution.' Thus, it is indeed with a result, not without a result merely because of the expression 'leading to diminution.' With reference to this meaning, the proponent's assertion and rejection here should be understood.

Ariyadhammavipākakathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discussion on the Result of Noble Dhammas.

10. Vipāko vipākadhammadhammotikathāvaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Discussion on 'A Result is a Phenomenon that is a Condition for a Result'.

501. Idāni vipāko vipākadhammadhammotikathā nāma [P 0.0103] hoti. Tattha yasmā vipāko vipākassa aññamaññādipaccayavasena paccayo hoti, tasmā vipākopi vipākadhammadhammoti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Tassa vipākoti tassa vipākadhammadhammassa vipākassa yo vipāko, sopi te vipākadhammadhammo hotīti [V 0.0199] pucchati. Itaro āyatiṃ vipākadānābhāvaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho tappaccayāpi aññassa vipākassa uppattiṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Evaṃ sante panassa kusalākusalassa viya tassāpi vipākassa vipāko, tassāpi vipākoti vaṭṭānupacchedo āpajjatīti puṭṭho samayavirodhabhayena paṭikkhipati.

501. Now, the discussion called 'A Result is a Phenomenon that is a Condition for a Result' takes place. Herein, since a result is a condition for another result by way of mutual condition and so on, some hold the view that a result is also a phenomenon that is a condition for a result, as is the case with the Andhakas. With reference to them, the question is for the proponent, and the assertion is for the opponent. He asks: 'Regarding the result of that phenomenon which is a condition for a result—is its result also a phenomenon that is a condition for a result for you?' The opponent denies it, with reference to the absence of future result-giving. When asked a second time, he affirms it, considering the arising of another result due to that condition. But when asked, 'If this is so, then just as wholesome and unwholesome kamma has its result, so too would that result have its result, and that result its result, leading to a non-cessation of the round of existence?', he denies it for fear of contradicting his own doctrine.

Vipākoti vātiādimhi vacanasādhane pana yadi vipākassa vipākadhammadhammena ekatthatā bhaveyya, kusalākusalabyākatānaṃ ekatthataṃ āpajjeyyāti paṭikkhipati. Vipāko ca vipākadhammadhammo cāti ettha [M 0.0204] ayaṃ adhippāyo – so hi catūsu vipākakkhandhesu ekekaṃ aññamaññapaccayādīsu paccayaṭṭhena vipākadhammadhammataṃ paccayuppannaṭṭhena ca vipākaṃ maññamāno “vipāko vipākadhammadhammo”ti puṭṭho āmantāti paṭijānāti. Atha naṃ sakavādī “yasmā tayā ekakkhaṇe catūsu khandhesu vipāko vipākadhammadhammopi anuññāto, tasmā tesaṃ sahagatādibhāvo āpajjatī”ti codetuṃ evamāha. Itaro kusalākusalasaṅkhātaṃ vipākadhammadhammaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Taññeva akusalanti yadi te vipāko vipākadhammadhammo, yo akusalavipāko, so akusalaṃ āpajjati. Kasmā? Vipākadhammadhammena ekattā. Taññeva kusalantiādīsupi eseva nayo.

However, in the analysis of the word 'result,' if a result were identical in substance with a resultant phenomenon, then wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states would also become identical in substance—hence the denial. The meaning here regarding 'a result and a resultant phenomenon' is this: He, considering each of the four resultant aggregates to be a resultant phenomenon in the sense of being a condition in mutual conditionality, etc., and to be a result in the sense of being produced by a condition, when asked, 'Is a result a resultant phenomenon?' affirms it. Then the proponent of his own doctrine, intending to challenge him, says, 'Since you acknowledge that in a single moment, with respect to the four aggregates, there is both a result and a resultant phenomenon, it follows that they are co-arisen,' etc. The other denies this, with reference to the resultant phenomenon that is classified as wholesome and unwholesome. 'If that very thing is unwholesome,' if for you the result is a resultant phenomenon, then the unwholesome result would become unwholesome. Why? Because of its identity with a resultant phenomenon. The same reasoning applies in the cases of 'If that very thing is wholesome,' etc.

502. Aññamaññapaccayāti idaṃ sahajātānaṃ paccayamattavasena vuttaṃ, tasmā asādhakaṃ. Mahābhūtānampi ca aññamaññapaccayatā vuttā, na ca tāni vipākāni, na ca vipākadhammadhammānīti.

502. 'Mutual conditionality' is stated here merely in terms of a condition for co-arisen states; therefore, it is inconclusive. Moreover, mutual conditionality is also stated for the great primary elements, yet they are neither results nor resultant phenomena.

Vipāko vipākadhammadhammotikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on 'A Result is a Resultant Phenomenon'.

Sattamo vaggo.

The Seventh Chapter.

8. Aṭṭhamavaggo

8. The Eighth Chapter.

1. Chagatikathāvaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Discourse on the Six Destinies.

503-504. Idāni [P 0.0104][V 0.0200] chagatikathā nāma hoti. Tattha asurakāyena saddhiṃ chagatiyoti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānañceva uttarāpathakānañca; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ sakavādī “pañca kho panimā, sāriputta, gatiyo”ti (ma. ni. 1.153) lomahaṃsanapariyāye paricchinnānaṃ gatīnaṃ vasena codetuṃ nanu pañca gatiyotiādimāha. Itaro suttavirodhabhayena paṭijānāti. Kasmā pana sakavādī cha gatiyo na sampaṭicchati, nanu “catūhāpāyehi ca vippamutto”ti ettha asurakāyopi gahitoti. Saccaṃ gahito, na panesā gati. Kasmā? Visuṃ abhāvato. Asurakāyasmiñhi kālakañcikā asurā petagatiyā saṅgahitā[M 0.0205], vepacittiparisā devagatiyā, asurakāyoti visuṃ ekā gati nāma natthi.

Now there is the discussion called 'The Six Destinies.' Herein, with reference to the view held by some—such as the Andhakas and the Uttarāpathakas—that there are six destinies including the asura realm, the question is from the proponent of his own doctrine, and the affirmation is from the other. Then the proponent of his own doctrine, intending to challenge them based on the destinies defined in the Lomahaṃsana Pariyāya, 'Sāriputta, there are these five destinies' (MN 1.73), says, 'Are there not five destinies?' and so on. The other, fearing contradiction with the sutta, concedes. But why does the proponent of his own doctrine not accept six destinies? Is it not that in the phrase 'freed from the four states of woe,' the asura realm is also included? True, it is included, but it is not a destiny. Why? Because it does not exist separately. For the Kālakañjika asuras are included in the destiny of ghosts, while the assembly of Vepacitti are included in the destiny of devas. Thus, there is no separate destiny called the asura realm.

Idāni etameva atthaṃ dassetuṃ nanu kālakañcikātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha samānavaṇṇāti sadisarūpasaṇṭhānā bībhacchā virūpā duddassikā. Samānabhogāti sadisamethunasamācārā. Samānāhārāti sadisakheḷasiṅghāṇikapubbalohitādiāhārā. Samānāyukāti sadisaāyuparicchedā. Āvāhavivāhanti kaññāgahaṇañceva kaññādānañca. Sukkapakkhe samānavaṇṇāti sadisarūpasaṇṭhānā abhirūpā pāsādikā dassanīyā pabhāsampannā. Samānabhogāti sadisapañcakaāmaguṇabhogā. Samānāhārāti sadisasudhābhojanādiāhārā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Nanu atthi asurakāyoti idaṃ asurakāyasseva sādhakaṃ. Tassa pana visuṃ gatiparicchedābhāvena na gatisādhakanti.

Now, to illustrate this very point, the passage beginning with 'Are not the Kālakañjikas...?' is introduced. Therein, 'of similar appearance' means having a similar physical form and shape—repulsive, deformed, and unpleasant to see. 'Of similar enjoyment' means sharing similar sexual conduct. 'Of similar food' means consuming similar food, such as saliva, mucus, pus, and blood. 'Of similar lifespan' means having a similar life-limit. 'Marriage' refers to both taking a maiden and giving a maiden in marriage. In the bright fortnight, 'of similar appearance' means having a similar physical form and shape—beautiful, lovely, pleasing to behold, and possessing radiance. 'Of similar enjoyment' means enjoying similar pleasures of the five sense qualities. 'Of similar food' means consuming similar food, such as ambrosial food. The rest follows the same method. 'But is there not an asura realm?' This supports the existence of the asura realm. However, since there is no distinct delineation of it as a destiny, it does not serve as proof for a separate destiny.

Chagatikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Six Destinies.

2. Antarābhavakathāvaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Discourse on the Intermediate State.

505. Idāni [P 0.0105][V 0.0201] antarābhavakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “antarā parinibbāyī”ti suttapadaṃ ayoniso gahetvā “antarābhavo nāma atthi, yattha satto dibbacakkhuko viya adibbacakkhuko, iddhimā viya aniddhimā mātāpitisamāgamañceva utusamayañca olokayamāno sattāhaṃ vā atirekasattāhaṃ vā tiṭṭhatī”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyānañceva sammitiyānañca; te sandhāya atthīti pucchā sakavādissa, laddhiyaṃ ṭhatvā paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ ye ca bhagavatā tayo bhavā vuttā, tesaṃ vasena codetuṃ kāmabhavotiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ adhippāyo – yadi te antarābhavo nāma koci bhavo atthi, tena kāmabhavādīnaṃyeva aññatarena bhavitabbaṃ pañcavokārabhavādinā viya, tena taṃ pucchāmi – “kiṃ te ayaṃ antarābhavo nāma kāmabhavo, udāhu rūpabhavo arūpabhavo vā”ti? Itaro tathā anicchanto sabbaṃ paṭikkhipati. Kāmabhavassa cātiādi yadi antarābhavo nāma atthi, imesaṃ bhavānaṃ antarā dvinnaṃ sīmānaṃ sīmantarikā [M 0.0206] viya bhaveyyāti codetuṃ āraddhaṃ. Paravādī pana tathā anicchanto sabbapañhe paṭikkhipati kevalaṃ laddhiyā, na sahadhammena. Teneva naṃ sakavādī ‘no vata re’ti paṭisedheti.

505. Now there is the discussion on the intermediate state. Herein, with reference to those who, improperly grasping the sutta phrase 'one who attains final Nibbāna in the interval,' hold the view that there is an intermediate state in which a being—like one with the divine eye, yet without the divine eye; like one with psychic power, yet without psychic power—observing the union of his parents and the proper season, remains for seven days or more than seven days (such as the Pubbaseliyas and the Sammitīyas), the question 'Does it exist?' is from the proponent of his own doctrine, and the affirmation, standing firm in their view, is from the other. Then, to challenge them based on the three existences taught by the Blessed One, he begins with 'the sensual existence,' and so on. Here, the intention is this: if for you there is indeed some existence called the intermediate state, it must be one of the sensual existence, the form existence, or the formless existence, just as with the five-constituent existence. Therefore, I ask: 'Is this so-called intermediate state the sensual existence, or the form existence, or the formless existence?' The other, not wishing it to be so, rejects everything. The passage beginning 'Of the sensual existence...' is introduced to challenge that if there is indeed an intermediate state, it would be between these existences like the space between two boundaries. But the opponent, unwilling to agree, rejects every question purely out of adherence to his view, not in accordance with the Dhamma. For that very reason, the proponent of his own doctrine refutes them, saying, 'Surely not!'

506. Pañcamī sā yonītiādīnipi yathāparicchinnayoniādīsu so samodhānaṃ na gacchati, atha tena tato tato atirekena bhavitabbanti codetuṃ vuttāni. Antarābhavūpagaṃ kammanti yadi sopi eko bhavo, yathā kāmabhavūpagādīni kammāni atthīti satthārā vibhajitvā dassitāni, evaṃ tadupagenāpi kammena bhavitabbanti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana parasamaye antarābhavūpagaṃ nāma pāṭiyekkaṃ kammaṃ natthi, yaṃ yaṃ bhavaṃ upapajjissati, tadupageneva kammena antarābhave nibbattatīti tesaṃ laddhi, tasmā ‘naheva’nti paṭikkhittaṃ. Atthi antarābhavūpagā sattāti puṭṭhopi kāmabhavūpagāyeva nāma teti laddhiyā paṭikkhipati. Jāyantītiādīni puṭṭhopi tattha jātijarāmaraṇāni ceva cutipaṭisandhiparamparañca [P 0.0106] anicchanto paṭikkhipati. Rūpādivasena puṭṭhopi yasmā antarābhavasattassa anidassanaṃ rūpaṃ, vedanādayopi aññesaṃ viya na oḷārikāti tassa laddhi, tasmā paṭikkhipati. Imināva kāraṇena pañcavokārabhavabhāvepi paṭikkhepo veditabbo.

506. The statement 'the fifth womb,' and so on, is made to challenge the opponent that the intermediate state does not fall into the categories of wombs already defined, and thus it must be something additional to them. The kamma leading to the intermediate state—if that too is an existence, just as the Teacher has distinctly shown that there are kammas leading to the sensual existence and so forth, then there must also be kamma leading to that intermediate state—this is stated for the purpose of challenging. However, because, according to the opponent's system, there is no specific kamma called 'leading to the intermediate state,' but rather, their view is that whichever existence one is about to enter, the intermediate state arises through the kamma leading to that existence; therefore, it is rejected with 'certainly not.' When asked whether there are beings bound for the intermediate state, he rejects it based on their view that they are simply called beings bound for the sensual existence. When asked about birth, and so on, he rejects it because he does not accept birth, aging, and death, or the succession of passing away and rebirth there. When asked in terms of form, and so on, he rejects it because, in their view, the being in the intermediate state has unmanifest form, and feelings and other mental states are not as gross as in others. For this very reason, the rejection should be understood even in the case of the five-constituent existence.

507. Idāni [V 0.0202] kāmabhavo bhavo gatītiādi bhavasaṃsandanaṃ nāma hoti. Tatrāyaṃ adhippāyo – yadi te antarābhavo nāma koci bhavo bhaveyya, yathā kāmabhavādīsu bhavagatiādibhedo labbhati, tathā tatrāpi labbhetha. Yathā vā tattha na labbhati, tathā imesupi na labbhetha. Samānasmiñhi bhavabhāve etesvevesa vibhāgo atthi, na itarasminti ko ettha visesahetūti. Itaro puna laddhimattavasena taṃ taṃ paṭijānāti ceva paṭikkhipati ca.

507. Now, the statement 'the sensual existence is an existence, a destination,' and so forth—this is called the linking of existences. Here, the intention is this: If that intermediate state were indeed some kind of existence, then just as distinctions like 'existence' and 'destination' are found in the sensual existence and so forth, they should also be found there. Or, just as they are not found there, so too they should not be found in these. For if the state of existence is the same, and this distinction exists in these but not in the other, what is the reason for the difference here? The other, however, merely based on adherence to views, both affirms and rejects this and that.

508. Sabbesaññeva sattānaṃ atthi antarābhavoti puṭṭho yasmā nirayūpagaasaññasattūpagaarūpūpagānaṃ antarābhavaṃ na icchati, tasmā paṭikkhipati. Teneva kāraṇena paṭilome paṭijānāti. Ānantariyassātiādi yesaṃ so antarābhavaṃ na icchati, te tāva vibhajitvā [M 0.0207] dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ pāḷianusāreneva veditabbaṃ saddhiṃ suttasādhanenāti.

508. When asked whether all beings have an intermediate state, he rejects it because he does not accept an intermediate state for those bound for hell, for non-percipient beings, or for those bound for the formless realms. For the same reason, he acknowledges it in the converse. The statement 'Of the one who commits a crime with immediate retribution,' and so on, is made to show, by distinguishing them, those for whom he does not accept an intermediate state. All this should be understood in accordance with the Pāḷi text, together with scriptural evidence.

Antarābhavakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Intermediate State.

3. Kāmaguṇakathāvaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on the Strands of Sensual Pleasure

510. Idāni kāmaguṇakathā nāma hoti. Tattha sakasamaye tāva kāmadhātūti vatthukāmāpi vuccanti – kilesakāmāpi kāmabhavopi. Etesu hi vatthukāmā kamanīyaṭṭhena kāmā, sabhāvanissattasuññataṭṭhena dhātūti kāmadhātu. Kilesakāmā kamanīyaṭṭhena ceva kamanaṭṭhena ca kāmā, yathāvuttenevatthena dhātūti kāmadhātu. Kāmabhavo kamanīyaṭṭhena [P 0.0107] kamanaṭṭhena vatthukāmapavattidesaṭṭhenāti tīhi kāraṇehi kāmo, yathāvuttenevatthena dhātūti kāmadhātu. Parasamaye pana – “pañcime, bhikkhave, kāmaguṇā”ti vacanamattaṃ nissāya pañceva kāmaguṇā kāmadhātūti gahitaṃ. Tasmā yesaṃ ayaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi pubbaseliyānaṃ; te sandhāya kāmadhātunānattaṃ bodhetuṃ pañcevāti pucchā sakavādissa, laddhivasena paṭiññā itarassa. Nanu atthītiādi kilesakāmadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha tappaṭisaṃyuttoti kāmaguṇapaṭisaṃyutto, kāmaguṇārammaṇoti attho. No ca vata re vattabbe pañcevāti imesu tappaṭisaṃyuttachandādīsu sati [V 0.0203] pañceva kāmaguṇā kāmadhātūti na vattabbaṃ. Etepi hi chandādayo kamanīyaṭṭhena kāmā ca dhātu cātipi kāmadhātu. Kamanaṭṭhena kāmasaṅkhātā dhātūtipi kāmadhātūti attho.

510. Now, this is called the discourse on the strands of sensual pleasure. Herein, in our own school, the term 'sensual element' refers to the objects of sensual pleasure, the defilements of sensual pleasure, and sensual existence. Among these, the objects of sensual pleasure are called 'sensual' in the sense of being desirable, and 'element' in the sense of being empty, devoid of a living being and an intrinsic nature—thus, 'sensual element'. The defilements of sensual pleasure are called 'sensual' in the sense of being desirable and in the sense of desiring, and 'element' in the sense previously stated—thus, 'sensual element'. Sensual existence is called 'sensual' for three reasons: in the sense of being desirable, in the sense of desiring, and in the sense of being the sphere where objects of sensual pleasure prevail; and 'element' in the sense previously stated—thus, 'sensual element'. In another school, however, based solely on the statement, 'Monks, these five are strands of sensual pleasure,' only the five strands of sensual pleasure are taken as the 'sensual element'. Therefore, for those who hold this view, such as the Pubbaseliyas of the present day, the question 'Only five?' is posed by the proponent of our own school to clarify the diversity of the sensual element, while the affirmation of the other is based on their doctrine. The statement 'Surely, do they exist?' and so forth, is spoken to show the defilements of sensual pleasure. Herein, 'associated with them' means 'associated with the strands of sensual pleasure,' which is to say, 'having the strands of sensual pleasure as their object'. But it should not be said, 'Only these five,' for when these associated desires and so forth exist, it should not be said that only the five strands of sensual pleasure constitute the sensual element. For these desires and so forth are also the sensual element, being 'sensual' in the sense of being desirable and also being an 'element'. Alternatively, they are the sensual element because they are an 'element' designated as 'sensual' in the sense of desiring. This is the meaning.

Manussānaṃ cakkhuntiādi vatthukāmadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha paravādī channampi āyatanānaṃ vatthukāmabhāvena nakāmadhātubhāvaṃ paṭikkhipitvā puna manoti puṭṭho mahaggatalokuttaraṃ sandhāya nakāmadhātubhāvaṃ paṭijānāti. Yasmā pana sabbopi tebhūmakamano kāmadhātuyeva, tasmā naṃ sakavādī suttena niggaṇhāti.

The statement 'the eye of humans' and so forth is made to show the objects of sensual pleasure. Herein, the opponent, having rejected that the six sense bases are the sensual element, when questioned again about the mind, acknowledges that it is not the sensual element, referring to the exalted and supramundane. However, since all mind belonging to the three planes of existence is indeed the sensual element, the proponent of our own school refutes him with a sutta.

511. Kāmaguṇā [M 0.0208] bhavotiādi bhavassa kāmadhātubhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana kāmaguṇamatte bhavoti vohāro natthi, tasmā paravādī nahevāti paṭikkhipati. Kāmaguṇūpagaṃ kammantiādi sabbaṃ kāmaguṇamattassa nakāmadhātubhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Kāmadhātusaṅkhātakāmabhavūpagameva hi kammaṃ atthi, kāmabhavūpagā eva ca sattā honti. Tattha jāyanti jiyanti miyanti cavanti upapajjanti, na kāmaguṇesūti iminā upāyena sabbattha attho veditabboti.

511. The statement 'strands of sensual pleasure are existence' and so forth is made to show that existence is the sensual element. However, since there is no conventional expression 'existence is merely strands of sensual pleasure,' the opponent refutes it with 'no indeed'. The statement 'kamma leading to the strands of sensual pleasure' and so forth—all this is made to show that mere strands of sensual pleasure are not the sensual element. For only kamma that leads to sensual existence, which is designated as the sensual element, exists; and beings exist only as those who have gone to sensual existence. There they are born, age, die, pass away, and are reborn—not in the mere strands of sensual pleasure. By this method, the meaning should be understood everywhere.

Kāmaguṇakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Strands of Sensual Pleasure.

4. Kāmakathāvaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse on Sensual Pleasures

513-514. Idāni [P 0.0108] kāmakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “pañcime, bhikkhave, kāmaguṇā”ti vacanamattaṃ nissāya rūpāyatanādīni pañcevāyatanāni kāmāti laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyānaṃ; tesaṃ kilesakāmasseva nippariyāyena kāmabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ pañcevāti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

513-514. Now comes the discourse on sensual pleasures. Here, for those who hold the view, like the Pubbaseliyas, that the five sense objects, such as visible forms, are themselves sensual pleasures—based merely on the statement, 'Monks, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure'—the question 'Are there only five?' is posed by the proponent of our own school, and the other affirms it. This is in order to show them that it is sensual defilement itself that is sensuality in the primary sense. The rest here is clear in meaning.

Kāmakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discourse on Sensual Pleasures.

5. Rūpadhātukathāvaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Form Realm

515-516. Idāni [V 0.0204] rūpadhātukathā nāma hoti. Tattha “rūpino dhammā rūpadhātu nāmā”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya rūpinoti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ sakavādī yasmā rūpadhātu nāma rūpabhavo, na rūpamattameva, tasmā tenatthena codetuṃ rūpadhātūtiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ kāmaguṇakathāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Sāva kāmadhātūti puṭṭho bhūmiparicchedena virodhaṃ passamāno paṭikkhipati. Puna daḷhaṃ katvā puṭṭho attano laddhivasena paṭijānāti. Evaṃ sante pana dvīhi bhavehi samannāgatatā āpajjati, tena taṃ sakavādī kāmabhavena cāti ādimāha. Itaro ekassa dvīhi samannāgatābhāvato paṭikkhipatīti.

Now comes the discussion on the form realm. Here, with reference to those who hold the view that 'material phenomena are called the form realm,' such as the Andhakas, the question 'Are they material?' is from the proponent, and the acknowledgement is from the other. Then, because the form realm is the existence of form, not merely form itself, the proponent, in order to challenge him on that point, says, 'the form realm,' and so on. All of this should be understood in the same way as explained in the discussion on sensual pleasures. When asked, 'Is that the sense-sphere realm?' he rejects it, seeing the contradiction in the distinction of planes. When asked again firmly, he acknowledges it in accordance with his own view. This being so, it would follow that one is endowed with two existences; therefore, the proponent says to him, 'with sensual existence,' and so on. The other rejects this, because one cannot be endowed with two.

Rūpadhātukathāvaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Discussion on the Form Realm.

6. Arūpadhātukathāvaṇṇanā

6. Exposition of the Discussion on the Formless Realm.

517-518. Arūpadhātukathāyapi [M 0.0209] imināvupāyena attho veditabbo. Arūpadhammesu pana vedanākkhandhameva gahetvā vedanā [P 0.0109] bhavotiādinā nayenettha desanā katā. Tattha kiṃ te arūpino dhammāti saṅkhaṃ gatā vedanādīsu aññatarā hotīti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

In the discussion on the formless realm, too, the meaning should be understood by this same method. However, concerning formless phenomena, the teaching here is given by taking only the feeling aggregate, according to the method 'feeling is existence,' and so on. Here, the meaning should be understood thus: the question 'What are those formless phenomena?' refers to any one of the phenomena reckoned as such, beginning with feeling. The rest should be understood in the same way as explained above.

Arūpadhātukathāvaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Discussion on the Formless Realm.

7. Rūpadhātuyā āyatanakathāvaṇṇanā

7. Exposition of the Discussion on the Sense Bases in the Form Realm.

519. Idāni rūpadhātuyā āyatanakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “rūpī manomayo sabbaṅgapaccaṅgī ahīnindriyo”ti (dī. ni. 1.87) suttaṃ nissāya brahmakāyikānaṃ ghānādinimittānipi āyatanānevāti kappetvā saḷāyataniko tesaṃ attabhāvoti laddhi, seyyathāpi [V 0.0205] andhakānañceva sammitiyānañca; te sandhāya saḷāyatanikoti pucchā sakavādissa, laddhivasena paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ yaṃ tattha āyatanaṃ natthi, tassa vasena codetuṃ atthi tattha ghānāyatanantiādi āraddhaṃ. Tato paravādī yaṃ tattha ajjhattikānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ āyatanānaṃ ghānādikaṃ saṇṭhānanimittaṃ tadeva āyatananti laddhiyā paṭijānāti. Bāhirānaṃ gandhāyatanādīnaṃ vasena puṭṭho ghānappasādādayo tattha na icchati, tasmā tesaṃ gocaraṃ paṭisedhento paṭikkhipati. Paṭilomapañhasaṃsandanapañhesupi imināvupāyena attho veditabbo.

519. Now comes the discussion on the sense bases in the form realm. Here, with reference to those who, relying on the sutta, 'Possessed of form, mind-made, complete with all major and minor limbs, not deficient in any faculty' (Dī. Ni. 1.87), conceive that even the features of the nose and other organs of the Brahmā-beings are sense bases, and thus hold the view that their existence has six sense bases—such as the Andhakas and the Sammitiyas—the question 'Does it have six sense bases?' is from the proponent, and the acknowledgement from the other is in accordance with their view. Then, in order to challenge him on the basis of the sense base that is not present there, the argument 'Is the nose-base there?' and so on, is initiated. Thereupon, the opponent acknowledges, according to his view, that the very configuration-sign of the three internal sense bases—the nose and so on—is the sense base there. When questioned about the external sense bases, such as the odor-base and so on, he does not accept the sensitive matter of the nose, etc., there; therefore, denying their object-domain, he rejects it. In the reverse questions and in the questions that connect the threads as well, the meaning should be understood by this method.

521. Atthi tattha ghānāyatanaṃ atthi gandhāyatanaṃ tena ghānena taṃ gandhaṃ ghāyatīti tasmiṃyeva parasamaye ekacce ācariye sandhāya vuttaṃ. Te kira tattha cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni paripuṇṇāni icchanti, āyatanena ca nāma sakiccakena bhavitabbanti tehi ghānādīhi te gandhādayo ghāyanti sāyanti phusantītipi icchanti. Taṃ laddhiṃ sandhāya paravādī āmantāti paṭijānāti.

521. 'There is the nose-base there, there is the odor-base; with that nose one smells that odor.' This was said with reference to certain teachers of that very same school. They, it seems, hold that the six internal sense bases are complete there, and that a sense base must have its own function. They also hold that with those sense organs—the nose and so on—they smell odors, taste flavors, and touch tangibles. With reference to that view, the opponent acknowledges by saying, 'Yes.'

522. Atthi [M 0.0210] tattha mūlagandhotiādīni pana puṭṭho atthibhāvaṃ sādhetuṃ asakkonto paṭikkhipati. Nanu atthi tattha [P 0.0110] ghānanimittantiādi saṇṭhānamattasseva sādhakaṃ, na āyatanassa, tasmā udāhaṭampi anudāhaṭasadisamevāti.

522. But when asked, 'Is there a root-odor there?' and so on, being unable to establish its existence, he rejects it. Surely, the question 'Is there a sign of a nose there?' and so on, proves only the mere configuration, not the sense base. Therefore, what is cited is just like what is not cited.

Rūpadhātuyā āyatanakathāvaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Discussion on the Sense Bases in the Form Realm.

8. Arūpe rūpakathāvaṇṇanā

8. Exposition of the Discussion on Form in the Formless Realm.

524-526. Idāni arūpe rūpakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti vacanato āruppabhavepi oḷārikarūpā nissaṭaṃ sukhumarūpaṃ atthīti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya atthi rūpanti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

Now comes the discussion on form in the formless realm. Here, with reference to those who, based on the statement 'Conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form arises,' hold the view that even in the formless existence there is a subtle form devoid of gross form—such as the Andhakas—the question 'Is there form?' is from the proponent, and the acknowledgement is from the other. The rest here has a plain meaning.

Arūpe rūpakathāvaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Discussion on Form in the Formless Realm.

9. Rūpaṃ kammantikathāvaṇṇanā

9. Exposition of the Discussion on 'Form is Kamma'.

527-537. Idāni [V 0.0206] rūpaṃ kammantikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ kāyavacīviññattisaṅkhātaṃ rūpameva kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma, tañca kusalasamuṭṭhānaṃ kusalaṃ, akusalasamuṭṭhānaṃ akusalanti laddhi, seyyathāpi mahisāsakānañceva sammitiyānañca; te sandhāya kusalena cittena samuṭṭhitanti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ sace taṃ kusalaṃ, yvāyaṃ sārammaṇādibhedo kusalassa labbhati, atthi te so tassāti codetuṃ sārammaṇantiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha patthanā paṇidhīti cetanāyevetaṃ vevacanaṃ. Kusalacetanāyeva hi pakappayamānā patthanāti. Pakappanavasena ṭhitattā paṇidhīti ca vuccati. Parato pana kusalena cittena samuṭṭhitā vedanā saññā cetanā saddhātiādīsu vedanādīnaññeva cettha patthanā paṇidhīti labbhati, na cetanāya. Kasmā? Dvinnaṃ cetanānaṃ ekato abhāvā, sotapatitattā pana evaṃ tanti gatāti veditabbā. Rūpāyatanantiādi [P 0.0111] purimavāre “sabbantaṃ kusala”nti saṃkhittassa pabhedadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ[M 0.0211]. Sesā saṃsandananayā, vacīkammakathā “akusalena cittena samuṭṭhita”ntiādividhānañca sabbaṃ pāḷianusāreneva veditabbaṃ. Asucīti panettha sukkaṃ adhippetaṃ. Suttasādhanaṃ uttānatthameva.

Now comes the discussion on 'Form is kamma.' Here, with reference to those who hold the view that form itself, designated as bodily and verbal intimation, is called bodily kamma and verbal kamma, and that what is originated by the wholesome is wholesome, and what is originated by the unwholesome is unwholesome—such as the Mahisāsakas and the Sammitiyas—the question 'Has it arisen from a wholesome mind?' is from the proponent, and the acknowledgement is from the other. Then, in order to challenge him, 'If that is wholesome, does it have those distinctions found in the wholesome, such as having an object?', the argument beginning 'having an object' is initiated. Here, 'aspiration' and 'resolve' are synonyms for volition. For it is wholesome volition itself that, when aspiring, is called 'aspiration.' And because it stands by way of aspiration, it is called 'resolve.' But further on, among feeling, perception, volition, faith, and so on, which have arisen from a wholesome mind, it is only feeling and the others that are obtained here as 'aspiration' and 'resolve,' not volition. Why? Because two volitions do not arise together; but it should be understood that the textual tradition proceeds in this way because it has entered the stream of the argument. 'The form-base,' etc., was said in the previous section to show the classification of the abbreviated phrase 'all that is wholesome.' The remaining methods of connection, the discussion on verbal kamma, and the procedure for 'arisen from an unwholesome mind,' etc., should all be understood by following the Pāli text. Here, by 'impure' is meant semen. The scriptural proof has a plain meaning.

Rūpaṃ kammantikathāvaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Discussion on 'Form is Kamma'.

10. Jīvitindriyakathāvaṇṇanā

10. Exposition of the Discussion on the Life Faculty.

540. Idāni jīvitindriyakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ nāma cittavippayutto arūpadhammo, tasmā rūpajīvitindriyaṃ natthīti laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyānañceva sammitiyānañca; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Natthi rūpīnaṃ dhammānaṃ āyūti pañhe upādinnarūpānampi tiṇakaṭṭhādīnampi santānavasena pavattimeva āyu ṭhiti yapanā yāpanā iriyanā vattanā pālanāti icchati, tasmā paṭikkhipati. Atthīti pañhepi iminā kāraṇena paṭijānāti. Atthi arūpajīvitindriyanti pañhe [V 0.0207] arūpadhammānaṃ cittavippayuttaṃ jīvitindriyasantānaṃ nāma atthīti icchati, tasmā paṭijānāti.

540. Now there is the discussion on the life faculty. Herein, for those who hold the view that the life faculty is a mind-disassociated immaterial phenomenon, and therefore there is no material life faculty—such as the Pubbaseliyas and the Sammitiyas—regarding them, the question is from the proponent of his own doctrine, and the affirmation is from the other. To the question, ‘Is there no life for material phenomena?’, he rejects it, because he holds that even for clung-to matter and for things such as grass and wood, their very process by way of continuity is life, persistence, duration, maintenance, subsistence, functioning, activity, and preservation. To the question, ‘Is there?’, he also affirms for this reason. To the question, ‘Is there an immaterial life faculty?’, he affirms it because he holds that for immaterial phenomena there is indeed what is called the continuity of the life faculty, which is mind-disassociated.

541. Rūpīnaṃ dhammānaṃ āyu arūpajīvitindriyanti pañhe sattasantāne rūpino vā hontu arūpino vā, sabbesaṃ cittavippayuttaṃ arūpajīvitindriyameva icchati, tasmā paṭijānāti.

541. To the question, ‘Is the life of material phenomena the immaterial life faculty?’, he holds that in the continuum of a being, whether phenomena are material or immaterial, for all of them it is precisely the mind-disassociated, immaterial life faculty; therefore, he affirms it.

542. Nirodhasamāpannapañhesupi cittavippayuttaṃ arūpajīvitameva sandhāya paṭikkhipati ca paṭijānāti ca. Sakavādī pana taṃ asampaṭicchanto yaṃ arūpapavatte asati atthi, rūpena tena bhavitabbanti codetuṃ hañcītiādimāha. Saṅkhārakkhandhapañhe phassādisaṅkhārakkhandhaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati, kāyakammādisaṅkhārakkhandhaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Kāyaviññatti [P 0.0112] vacīviññatti sammāvācā sammākammanto jīvitindriyanti evamādayopi dhammā saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpannātissa laddhi. Sakavādī pana taṃ asampaṭicchanto yadi niruddhepi arūpapavatte saṅkhārakkhandho atthi, catunnampi khandhānaṃ atthitā hotūti codetuṃ atthi vedanākkhandhoti ādimāha. Itaro antosamāpattiṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati, samāpajjantassa ca vuṭṭhahantassa ca pubbāparabhāgaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti.

542. Regarding the questions on the attainment of cessation, he denies and affirms with reference only to the mind-disassociated, immaterial life faculty. However, the proponent of his own doctrine, not accepting that, says, ‘If...’ and so on, to argue: ‘If something exists in the absence of the immaterial process, then it must be by means of form.’ To the question on the formations aggregate, he denies with reference to the formations aggregate of contact and so on, and affirms with reference to the formations aggregate of bodily action and so on. According to his view, phenomena such as bodily intimation, verbal intimation, right speech, right action, and the life faculty are also included in the formations aggregate. The proponent of his own doctrine, not accepting that, says, ‘The feeling aggregate exists,’ and so on, to argue: ‘If the formations aggregate exists even when the immaterial process has ceased, then all four aggregates must exist.’ The other denies with reference to being within the attainment and affirms with reference to the preceding and subsequent stages of one entering and emerging from it.

543. Asaññasattavārepi [M 0.0212] eseva nayo. Tassa hi laddhiyā asaññasattānaṃ paṭisandhikāle cittaṃ uppajjitvā nirujjhati, tena saha cittavippayuttaarūpajīvitindriyaṃ uppajjitvā yāvatāyukaṃ pavattati. Tasmā tesaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ natthīti puṭṭho paṭikkhipati, atthīti puṭṭho paṭijānāti. Vedanākkhandhādayopi tesaṃ pavattivasena paṭikkhipati, cutipaṭisandhivasena paṭijānāti. Sakavādī pana taṃ anicchanto “sace tattha ekakkhaṇepi vedanādayo atthi, pañcavokārabhavattaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti codetuṃ pañcavokārabhavoti āha. Itaro suttavirodhabhayā paṭikkhipati.

543. The same method applies in the section on non-percipient beings. For according to his view, at the moment of rebirth-linking for non-percipient beings, consciousness arises and ceases, and along with it, the mind-disassociated, immaterial life faculty arises and continues for the duration of the lifespan. Therefore, when asked, ‘Do they have no life faculty?’, he rejects it; when asked, ‘Is there?’, he affirms it. The feeling aggregate and so on, he also denies with regard to their ongoing process, but affirms with regard to death and rebirth-linking. However, the proponent of his own doctrine, not accepting that, says, ‘a being of the five-aggregate existence,’ in order to argue: ‘If feeling and so on exist there even for a single moment, it would attain the state of a five-aggregate existence.’ The other denies this out of fear of contradicting the suttas.

544-545. Ekadesaṃ bhijjatīti pañhe sampayuttaṃ bhijjati, vippayuttaṃ tiṭṭhatīti tassa laddhi, tasmā paṭijānāti. Dve jīvitindriyānīti pucchā paravādissa, paṭiññā sakavādissa. Rūpārūpavasena hi dve jīvitindriyāni, tehiyeva satto jīvati, tesaṃ bhaṅgena maratīti vuccati. Cutikkhaṇasmiñhi dvepi jīvitāni saheva bhijjanti.

544-545. To the question, ‘Does it break in part?’, he affirms it, because it is his view that the associated part breaks, while the disassociated part remains; therefore he affirms it. ‘Two life faculties’ is a question from the opponent; the affirmation is from the proponent of his own doctrine. For there are two life faculties, classified as material and immaterial; a being lives by means of these, and at their breaking is said to die. For at the moment of death, both life faculties break together.

Jīvitindriyakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion of the Life Faculty.

11. Kammahetukathāvaṇṇanā

11. The Commentary on the Discussion of Kamma as Cause.

546. Idāni [V 0.0208] kammahetukathā nāma hoti. Tattha yena arahatā purimabhave arahā abbhācikkhitapubbo, so tassa kammassa hetu arahattā parihāyatīti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyānañceva sammitiyānañca; te sandhāya kammahetūti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesaṃ parihānikathāyaṃ vuttanayameva[P 0.0113].

546. Now there is the discussion called 'Kamma as Cause.' Herein, concerning the view held by some—such as the Pubbaseliyas and the Sammitiyas—that an arahant, who in a former existence had previously falsely accused an arahant, falls away from arahantship because of that kamma as cause; regarding them, the question concerning kamma as cause is from the proponent of his own doctrine, while the affirmation is from the other. The rest is in accordance with the method stated in the discussion on falling away.

Handa hi arahantānaṃ abbhācikkhatīti idaṃ yassa kammassa hetu parihāyati, taṃ sampaṭicchāpetuṃ vadati. Atha naṃ sakavādī taṃ pakkhaṃ paṭijānāpetvā “yadi evaṃ yehi arahanto na abbhācikkhitapubbā, te sabbe arahattaṃ pāpuṇeyyu”nti codetuṃ ye kecītiādimāha. Itaro tassa kammassa arahattaṃ sampāpuṇane niyāmaṃ apassanto paṭikkhipati.

Indeed, to make the opponent admit that falsely accusing arahants is the kamma due to which one falls away, he speaks. Then, the proponent, having had that position acknowledged, argues: 'If so, then all those who have never falsely accused an arahant should attain arahantship,' and states, 'Whoever,' etc. The other, not seeing any certainty that such kamma leads to the attainment of arahantship, rejects it.

Kammahetukathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion of Kamma as Cause.

Aṭṭhamo vaggo.

The Eighth Chapter.

9. Navamavaggo

9. The Ninth Chapter.

1. Ānisaṃsadassāvīkathāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Discussion of Seeing the Benefits.

547. Idāni [P 0.0114][M 0.0213] ānisaṃsadassāvīkathā nāma hoti. Tattha sakasamaye saṅkhāre ādīnavato nibbānañca ānisaṃsato passantassa saṃyojanappahānaṃ hotīti nicchayo. Yesaṃ pana tesu dvīsupi ekaṃsikavādaṃ gahetvā “ānisaṃsadassāvinova saṃyojanappahānaṃ hotī”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Athassa “ekaṃsikavādo tayā gahito, ādīnavopi daṭṭhabboyevā”ti vibhāgadassanatthaṃ sakavādī saṅkhāretiādimāha.

547. Now there is the discussion called 'Seeing the Benefits.' Herein, in one's own doctrine, it is certain that for one who sees the danger in formations and the benefit of Nibbāna, the abandoning of fetters occurs. But as for those who, holding to a one-sided view in these two matters, have the doctrine that 'the abandoning of fetters occurs only for one who sees the benefits'—such as the Andhakas; regarding them, the question is from the proponent of his own doctrine, while the affirmation is from the other. Then, to show him the distinction, the proponent of his own doctrine says, ‘formations…’ and so on, arguing, 'A one-sided view has been adopted by you, but the danger, too, should indeed be seen.'

Saṅkhāre [V 0.0209] ca aniccato manasikaroti, nibbāne ca ānisaṃsadassāvī hotīti pañhasmiṃ ayamadhippāyo – ānisaṃsadassāvissa saṃyojanānaṃ pahānaṃ hotīti tesaṃ laddhi. Nanu saṅkhāre aniccato manasikaroto saṃyojanā pahīyantīti ca puṭṭho āmantāti paṭijānāti. Tena te saṅkhāre ca aniccato manasikaroti, nibbāne ca ānisaṃsadassāvī hotīti idaṃ āpajjati, kiṃ sampaṭicchasi etanti. Tato paravādī ekacittakkhaṇaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati, dutiyaṃ puṭṭho nānācittavasena paṭijānāti. Sakavādī panassa adhippāyaṃ madditvā aniccamanasikārassa ānisaṃsadassāvitāya ca ekato paṭiññātattā dvinnaṃ phassānaṃ dvinnaṃ cittānaṃ samodhānaṃ hotīti pucchati. Itaro dvinnaṃ samodhānaṃ apassanto paṭikkhipati. Dukkhatotiādipañhesupi eseva nayo. Kiṃ panettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ, kiṃ aniccādito manasikaroto saṃyojanā pahīyanti, udāhu nibbāne ānisaṃsadassāvissa, udāhu dvepi ekato karontassāti. Yadi tāva aniccādito manasikaroto pahānaṃ [P 0.0115] bhaveyya, vipassanācitteneva bhaveyya. Atha ānisaṃsadassāvino, anussavavasena nibbāne ānisaṃsaṃ passantassa vipassanācitteneva bhaveyya, atha dvepi ekato karontassa bhaveyya, dvinnaṃ phassādīnaṃ samodhānaṃ bhaveyya. Yasmā pana ariyamaggakkhaṇe aniccādimanasikārassa kiccaṃ nipphattiṃ gacchati puna niccatotiādigahaṇassa anuppattidhammabhāvato, nibbāne ca paccakkhatova ānisaṃsadassanaṃ ijjhati, tasmā kiccanipphattivasena aniccādito [M 0.0214] manasikaroto ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattivasena ca nibbāne ānisaṃsadassāvissa saṃyojanānaṃ pahānaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ.

He attends to formations as impermanent and sees the benefit in Nibbāna—this is the meaning in the question. 'For one who sees the benefit, the fetters are abandoned'—this is their tenet. When asked, 'Are the fetters abandoned for one who attends to formations as impermanent?' he acknowledges it, saying, 'Yes.' Therefore, this follows: 'He attends to formations as impermanent and sees the benefit in Nibbāna.' Do you accept this? Then, the opponent rejects it by referring to a single moment of mind, but when questioned a second time, he acknowledges it in terms of different moments of mind. The proponent, however, pressing his own view, asks whether there is a conjunction of two contacts and two minds, since it was acknowledged that attending to impermanence and seeing the benefit occur together. The other, not seeing their conjunction, rejects it. The same method applies to questions on suffering, etc. Now, what is the conclusion here? Are the fetters abandoned for one who attends to impermanence, etc., or for one who sees the benefit in Nibbāna, or for one who does both together? If the abandoning were to occur by attending to impermanence, etc., it would be through the insight-mind alone. If it were for one who sees the benefit, it would be through the insight-mind alone for one who sees the benefit of Nibbāna by way of report. If it were for one who does both together, there would be a conjunction of two contacts, etc. However, because at the moment of the noble path the function of attending to impermanence, etc., is fulfilled—since the state has been reached wherein the grasping of permanence, etc., does not arise again—and because the direct seeing of the benefit in Nibbāna is accomplished, it should be understood that the abandoning of the fetters occurs for one who attends to impermanence, etc., by way of the fulfillment of its function, and for one who sees the benefit in Nibbāna by way of its occurrence as an object.

548. Nibbāne sukhānupassīti suttaṃ nibbāne sukhānupassanādibhāvameva sādheti, na ānisaṃsadassāvitāmattena saṃyojanānaṃ pahānaṃ. Tasmā ābhatampi anābhatasadisamevāti.

548. The sutta 'Seeing happiness in Nibbāna' establishes only the state of seeing happiness in Nibbāna, etc., not the abandoning of fetters merely by seeing the benefit. Therefore, the evidence brought forward is as if it were not brought forward.

Ānisaṃsadassāvīkathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discourse on Seeing the Benefit.

2. Amatārammaṇakathāvaṇṇanā

2. The Exposition of the Discourse on the Deathless as Object.

549. Idāni amatārammaṇakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “nibbānaṃ maññatī”tiādīnaṃ [V 0.0210] ayoniso atthaṃ gahetvā amatārammaṇaṃ saṃyojanaṃ hotīti laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyānaṃ, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ sace amatārammaṇaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, amatassa saṃyojaniyādibhāvo āpajjatīti codetuṃ amataṃ saṃyojaniyantiādimāha. Itaro suttavirodhabhayena sabbaṃ paṭikkhipati. Iminā upāyena sabbavāresu attho veditabbo. Nibbānaṃ nibbānatoti āhaṭasuttaṃ pana diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ sandhāya bhāsitaṃ, tasmā asādhakanti.

549. Now begins the discourse on the Deathless as object. Herein, with reference to those who, having wrongly grasped the meaning of such phrases as 'he conceives Nibbāna,' hold the tenet that having the Deathless as an object is a fetter—such as the Pubbaseliyas—the question is put by the Sakavādin, and the admission is by the other. Then, in order to challenge him by showing that if having the Deathless as an object is a fetter, it would follow that the Deathless becomes something that can be fettered, etc., he says, 'The Deathless is something that can be fettered,' and so forth. The other rejects all of this for fear of contradicting the suttas. By this method, the meaning should be understood in all sections of the debate. The sutta brought forward, 'Nibbāna is Nibbāna,' however, was spoken with reference to Nibbāna in this very life; therefore, it is not a valid proof.

Amatārammaṇakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discourse on the Deathless as Object.

3. Rūpaṃ sārammaṇantikathāvaṇṇanā

3. The Exposition of the Discourse 'Form Has an Object'.

552-553. Idāni [P 0.0116] rūpaṃ sārammaṇantikathā nāma hoti. Tattha rūpaṃ sappaccayaṭṭhena sārammaṇaṃ nāma hoti, na aññaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karotīti ārammaṇapaccayavasena. Yesaṃ pana avisesena rūpaṃ sārammaṇanti laddhi, seyyathāpi uttarāpathakānaṃ; te sandhāya ārammaṇatthassa vibhāgadassanatthaṃ pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa.
