Sesamettha pāḷianusāreneva veditabbaṃ. Na vattabbanti pañhe olubbhārammaṇaṃ sandhāya paṭiññā sakavādissa. Dutiyapañhepi paccayārammaṇaṃ sandhāya paṭiññā tasseva. Iti sappaccayaṭṭhenevettha sārammaṇatā siddhāti.

Now begins the discourse called 'Form Has an Object.' Herein, form is called 'having an object' in the sense of being conditioned, not in the sense that it takes something else as its object by way of the object-condition. But with reference to those who hold the tenet that form has an object without distinction—such as the Uttarāpathakas—the question is put by the Sakavādin for the sake of showing the distinction in the meaning of 'object,' and the admission is by the other. The remainder here should be understood in accordance with the Pāli text itself. In the question, 'It should not be said,' the admission by the Sakavādin is with reference to engrossment in an object. In the second question too, the admission is by him with reference to the condition as object. Thus, its having an object is established here only in the sense of being conditioned.

Rūpaṃ sārammaṇantikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discourse 'Form Has an Object'.

4. Anusayā anārammaṇakathāvaṇṇanā

4. The Exposition of the Discourse 'Latent Tendencies Have No Object'.

554-556. Idāni [M 0.0215] anusayā anārammaṇātikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ anusayā nāma cittavippayuttā ahetukā abyākatā, teneva ca anārammaṇāti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānañceva ekaccānañca uttarāpathakānaṃ; te sandhāya anusayāti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā [V 0.0211] itarassa. Atha naṃ anārammaṇena nāma evaṃvidhena bhavitabbanti codetuṃ rūpantiādimāha. Kāmarāgotiādi kāmarāgānusayato anaññattā dassitaṃ. Saṅkhārakkhandho anārammaṇoti pañhe cittasampayuttasaṅkhārakkhandhaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Anusayaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ kāyakammādirūpañca saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpannaṃ, taṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Imināvupāyena sabbavāresu attho veditabbo. Sānusayoti pañhe pana appahīnānusayattā sānusayatā anuññātā. Na anusayānaṃ pavattisabbhāvā. Yo hi appahīno, na so atīto, nānāgato, na paccuppanno ca. Maggavajjhakileso panesa appahīnattāva atthīti [P 0.0117] vuccati. Evarūpassa ca idaṃ nāma ārammaṇanti na vattabbaṃ. Tasmā taṃ paṭikkhittaṃ. Taṃ panetaṃ na kevalaṃ anusayassa, rāgādīnampi tādisameva, tasmā anusayānaṃ anārammaṇatāsādhakaṃ na hotīti.

Now begins the discourse called 'Latent Tendencies Have No Object.' Herein, with reference to those who hold the tenet that latent tendencies are dissociated from mind, rootless, and indeterminate, and for that very reason have no object—such as the Andhakas and some Uttarāpathakas—the question regarding latent tendencies is put by the Sakavādin, and the admission is by the other. Then, to challenge him by showing that something without an object must be of such a nature, he says, 'Form,' and so forth. 'Sensual desire,' and so forth, is shown because of its non-difference from the latent tendency of sensual desire. In the question, 'The volitional formations aggregate has no object,' he rejects it with reference to the volitional formations aggregate associated with mind. He admits it with reference to the latent tendency, the life faculty, and bodily action, etc., which are included in the volitional formations aggregate. By this method, the meaning should be understood in all sections of the debate. In the question, 'With latent tendencies,' the state of having latent tendencies is conceded because they are unabandoned, not because of the actual occurrence of latent tendencies. For what is unabandoned is not past, nor future, nor present. But this defilement, which is to be abandoned by the path, is said to exist precisely because it is unabandoned. And for such a thing, it cannot be said, 'This is its object.' Therefore, that is rejected. This, however, applies not only to a latent tendency but also to lust, etc., which are of the same nature; therefore, it does not prove that latent tendencies are without an object.

Anusayā anārammaṇātikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discourse 'Latent Tendencies Have No Object'.

5. Ñāṇaṃ anārammaṇantikathāvaṇṇanā

5. The Exposition of the Discourse 'Knowledge Has No Object'.

557-558. Idāni ñāṇaṃ anārammaṇantikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā arahā cakkhuviññāṇasamaṅgī ñāṇīti vuccati, tassa ñāṇassa tasmiṃ khaṇe ārammaṇaṃ natthi, tasmā ñāṇaṃ anārammaṇanti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha anusayakathāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

Now comes the discourse called 'Knowledge Being Objectless'. Here, since an arahant endowed with eye-consciousness is called 'one who knows', and at that moment there is no object for that knowledge, therefore, 'knowledge is objectless'—this is the belief of some, like the Andhakas. With reference to them, the question is posed by one's own party, and the admission is made by the other. The rest here should be understood in the same way as stated in the discourse on latent tendencies.

Ñāṇaṃ anārammaṇantikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Knowledge Being Objectless.

6. Atītānāgatārammaṇakathāvaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Discourse on Past and Future Objects.

559-561. Idāni atītānāgatārammaṇakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā atītānāgatārammaṇaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā tadārammaṇena cittena ārammaṇassa [M 0.0216] natthitāya anārammaṇena [V 0.0212] bhavitabbanti atītaṃ anārammaṇanti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi uttarāpathakānaṃ, te sandhāya atītārammaṇanti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha yathāpāḷimeva niyyātīti.

Now comes the discourse on past and future objects. Here, since there is no such thing as an object of the past or future, therefore, a mind that takes such an object, due to the non-existence of the object, must be objectless—'the past is objectless' is the belief of some, such as the Uttarāpathakas. With reference to them, the question 'Is the past an object?' is posed by one's own party, and the admission is made by the other. The rest here proceeds just as in the Pāli text.

Atītānāgatārammaṇakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Past and Future Objects.

7. Vitakkānupatitakathāvaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Discourse on Being Accompanied by Applied Thought.

562. Idāni [P 0.0118] vitakkānupatitakathā nāma hoti. Tattha vitakkānupatitā nāma duvidhā – ārammaṇato ca sampayogato ca. Tattha asukacittaṃ nāma vitakkassārammaṇaṃ na hotīti niyamābhāvato siyā sabbaṃ cittaṃ vitakkānupatitaṃ, vitakkavippayuttacittasabbhāvato pana na sabbaṃ cittaṃ vitakkānupatitaṃ. Iti imaṃ vibhāgaṃ akatvā aviseseneva sabbaṃ cittaṃ vitakkānupatitanti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi uttarāpathakānaṃ, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha pāḷivaseneva niyyātīti.

562. Now comes the discourse on being accompanied by applied thought. Here, being accompanied by applied thought is of two kinds: with regard to object and with regard to association. In this regard, since there is no fixed rule that a certain mind is not the object of applied thought, all mind could be accompanied by applied thought. However, because of the existence of mind dissociated from applied thought, not all mind is accompanied by applied thought. Thus, without making this distinction, those who hold the belief that all mind is indiscriminately accompanied by applied thought—such as the Uttarāpathakas—with reference to them, the question is posed by one's own party, and the admission is made by the other. The rest here proceeds according to the Pāli text.

Vitakkānupatitakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Being Accompanied by Applied Thought.

8. Vitakkavipphārasaddakathāvaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Discourse on the Sound of Thought Diffusion.

563. Idāni vitakkavipphārasaddakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā “vitakkavicārā vacīsaṅkhārā”ti vuttā, tasmā sabbaso vitakkayato vicārayato antamaso manodhātupavattikālepi vitakkavipphāro saddoyevāti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyānaṃ; te sandhāya sabbasoti pucchā sakavādissa paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ yadi vitakkavipphāramattaṃ saddo, phassādivipphāropi saddo bhaveyyāti codetuṃ sabbaso phusayatotiādimāha. Itaro tādisaṃ suttalesaṃ apassanto paṭikkhipati. Vitakkavipphāro saddo sotaviññeyyoti vitakkassa vipphāramattameva [V 0.0213] saddoti katvā pucchati, na vitakkavipphārasamuṭṭhitaṃ suttapamattānaṃ [M 0.0217] saddaṃ, itaro paṭikkhipati. Nanu vitakkavipphārasaddo na sotaviññeyyoti idaṃ tasseva laddhiyā dasseti. So hi vitakkavipphāramattameva saddaṃ vadati, so na sotaviññeyyoti. Itaro pana “vitakkavipphārasaddaṃ sutvā ādisatī” ti (dī. ni. 3.148) vacanato sotaviññeyyovāti vadati.

563. Now comes the discourse on the sound of thought diffusion. Here, since it is said, 'Applied thought and sustained thought are verbal formations,' therefore, for those who hold the belief that when applying thought and sustaining thought in any way, even at the moment of the mind-element's arising, the diffusion of thought is indeed sound—such as the Pubbaseliyas—with reference to them, the question 'in all cases?' is posed by one's own party, and the admission is made by the other. Then, to refute him by arguing, 'If the mere diffusion of thought is sound, then the diffusion of contact, etc., would also be sound,' he says, 'in all cases, when contacting,' etc. The other, not seeing such a scriptural fragment, rejects it. 'The sound of thought diffusion is cognizable by the ear'—he asks this, taking sound to be merely the diffusion of thought, not the sound arising from the diffusion of thought of those who are heedless of the suttas. The other rejects it. 'Surely, the sound of thought diffusion is not cognizable by the ear'—this shows his own belief. For he speaks of sound as merely the diffusion of thought, and that is not cognizable by the ear. But the other, based on the statement, 'Having heard the sound of thought diffusion, he declares' (Dī. Ni. 3.148), says it is indeed cognizable by the ear.

Vitakkavipphārasaddakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Sound of Thought Diffusion.

9. Nayathācittassa vācātikathāvaṇṇanā

9. The Explanation of the Discourse on Speech Not in Accordance with Mind.

564. Idāni [P 0.0119] nayathācittassa vācātikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā koci aññaṃ bhaṇissāmīti aññaṃ bhaṇati, tasmā nayathācittassa vācā cittānurūpā cittānugatikā na hoti, vināpi cittena pavattatīti yesaṃ laddhi; seyyathāpi pubbaseliyānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi taṃsamuṭṭhāpakaṃ cittaṃ na siyā, phassādayopi tasmiṃ khaṇe na siyu”nti codetuṃ aphassakassātiādimāha. Na bhaṇitukāmotiādīsu yasmā aññaṃ bhaṇissāmīti aññaṃ bhaṇantopi bhaṇitukāmoyeva nāma hoti, tasmā na hevāti paṭikkhipati.

564. Now comes the discourse on speech not in accordance with mind. Here, because someone, thinking 'I will say one thing,' says another, therefore, speech not in accordance with mind is neither in harmony with mind nor does it follow mind, but occurs independently of mind—this is the view of some, such as the Pubbaseliyas. With reference to them, the question is posed by one's own party, and the admission is made by the other. Then, to refute them, he says, 'If the mind that produces it were not present, then contact and other factors would also not be present at that moment,' beginning with 'of one without contact.' Regarding such phrases as 'not wishing to speak,' since even one who says something other than what they intended to say is still considered one who wishes to speak, it is therefore rejected with 'it is not so.'

565. Nanu atthi koci aññaṃ bhaṇissāmītiādīsu cīvaranti bhaṇitukāmo cīranti bhaṇeyya. Tattha aññaṃ bhaṇitukāmatācittaṃ, aññaṃ bhaṇanacittaṃ, iti pubbabhāgena cittena asadisattā ayathācitto nāma hoti, tenassa kevalaṃ anāpatti nāma hoti, na pana cīranti vacanasamuṭṭhāpakacittaṃ natthi, iti acittakā sā vācāti atthaṃ sandhāya iminā udāharaṇena “nayathācittassa vācā”ti patiṭṭhāpitāpi appatiṭṭhāpitāva hotīti.

565. Is it not the case that someone, intending to say 'robe,' might say 'bark-cloth'? Here, the mind intending to say one thing and the mind uttering another are dissimilar to the preceding mind-moment, so it is called 'speech not in accordance with the mind.' For this reason, for him there is only non-offense, but it is not that the mind producing the utterance 'bark-cloth' is absent. Thus, with reference to the meaning that such speech is mindless, even though 'speech not in accordance with the mind' is established by this example, it is as if it were not established.

Nayathācittassa vācātikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Speech Not in Accordance with Mind.

10. Nayathācittassa kāyakammantikathāvaṇṇanā

10. The Explanation of the Discourse on Bodily Action Not in Accordance with Mind.

566-567. Idāni [M 0.0218][V 0.0214] nayathācittassa kāyakammantikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā koci aññatra gacchissāmīti aññatra gacchati, tasmā nayathācittassa kāyakammaṃ cittānurūpaṃ cittānugatikaṃ na hoti, vināpi cittena pavattatīti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyānaṃyeva, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

Now comes the discourse on bodily action not in accordance with mind. Here, because someone, thinking 'I will go to one place,' goes to another, therefore, bodily action not in accordance with mind is neither in harmony with mind nor does it follow mind, but occurs independently of mind—this is the view of some, such as the Pubbaseliyas themselves. With reference to them, the question is posed by one's own party, and the admission is made by the other. The rest here should be understood in the same way as stated above.

Nayathācittassa kāyakammantikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Bodily Action Not in Accordance with Mind.

11. Atītānāgatasamannāgatakathāvaṇṇanā

11. The Explanation of the Discourse on Being Endowed with the Past and Future.

568-570. Idāni [P 0.0120] atītānāgatehi samannāgatakathā nāma hoti. Tattha samannāgatapaññatti paṭilābhapaññattīti dve paññattiyo veditabbā. Tāsu paccuppannadhammasamaṅgī samannāgatoti vuccati. Aṭṭha samāpattilābhino pana samāpattiyo kiñcāpi na ekakkhaṇe pavattanti, aññā atītā honti, aññā anāgatā, aññā paccuppannā, paṭivijjhitvā aparihīnatāya pana lābhīti vuccati. Tattha yesaṃ imaṃ vibhāgaṃ aggahetvā yasmā jhānalābhīnaṃ atītānāgatāni jhānānipi atthi, tasmā “te atītenapi anāgatenapi samannāgatā”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ. Te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti. “Aṭṭhavimokkhajhāyī”tiādi pana lābhībhāvassa sādhakaṃ, na samannāgatabhāvassāti.

568-570. Now, there is what is called the discourse on being endowed with the past and future. Herein, two concepts should be understood: the concept of being endowed and the concept of obtaining. One possessing present phenomena is called 'endowed.' However, for those who have gained the eight attainments, although the attainments do not occur simultaneously—some are past, some future, and some present—they are called 'gainers' because they have penetrated and not deteriorated from them. Herein, for those who, not grasping this distinction, hold the view that because those who have gained jhāna also have past and future jhānas, therefore 'they are endowed with the past and the future'—this is a view like that of the Andhakas. With reference to them, the question is from the proponent of his own doctrine, and the affirmation is from the other. The rest here is clear in meaning. 'One who contemplates the eight deliverances,' etc., is evidence for the state of being a gainer, not for the state of being endowed.

Atītānāgatasamannāgatakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Being Endowed with the Past and Future.

Navamo vaggo.

The Ninth Chapter.

10. Dasamavaggo

10. The Tenth Chapter

1. Nirodhakathāvaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Discourse on Cessation

571-572. Idāni [P 0.0121][V 0.0215] nirodhakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “upapattesiyanti saṅkhaṃ gatassa bhavaṅgacittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇena saheva kiriyāti saṅkhaṃ gatā [M 0.0219] kusalā vā akusalā vā cattāro khandhā cittasamuṭṭhānarūpañcāti pañcakkhandhā uppajjanti. Tesu hi anuppannesu bhavaṅge niruddhe santativicchedo bhaveyyā”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya upapattesiyeti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Tattha upapattesiyeti catūsupi padesu bahuvacanabhummatthe ekavacanabhummaṃ. Upapattesiyesu pañcasu khandhesu aniruddhesūti ayañhettha attho. Dasannanti upapattesiyakhandhānañca kiriyakhandhānañca vasena vuttaṃ. Tattha paṭhamapañhe khandhalakkhaṇavasena kiriyavasena ca pañceva nāma te khandhāti paṭikkhipati. Dutiyapañhe purimapacchimavasena upapattesiyakiriyavasena ca nānattaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Dvinnaṃ pana phassānaṃ cittānañca samodhānaṃ puṭṭho suttalesābhāvena paṭikkhipati.

571-572. Now is the discourse on cessation. Herein, those who hold the view that 'at the moment of the dissolution of the life-continuum consciousness, which is reckoned as seeking rebirth, together with what is reckoned as functional, the five aggregates—namely, the four mental aggregates, wholesome or unwholesome, and mind-produced material form—arise, for if these have not arisen when the life-continuum were to cease, there would be a break in the continuity of existence'—this is a view like that of the Andhakas. With reference to them, the question 'Is one seeking rebirth?' is from the proponent of his own doctrine, while the other affirms it. Herein, regarding 'Is one seeking rebirth?', in all four instances the singular form is used in the sense of the plural. The meaning here is 'concerning the five aggregates seeking rebirth, while they have not ceased.' 'Of the ten' refers to the aggregates seeking rebirth and the functional aggregates. In the first question, he rejects it by stating that those aggregates are indeed five in terms of their characteristics and their function. In the second question, he affirms the diversity by considering the former and latter, and also in terms of the aggregates seeking rebirth and the functional aggregates. When asked about the conjunction of two contacts and consciousnesses, he rejects it due to the absence of a hint in the scriptures.

Kiriyā cattāroti rūpena vinā kusalā akusalā vā cattāro gahitā. Kiriyāñāṇanti paravādinā cakkhuviññāṇasamaṅgikkhaṇe arahato anuññātaṃ anārammaṇañāṇaṃ. Niruddhe maggo uppajjatīti pucchā paravādissa, aniruddhe anuppajjanato paṭiññā sakavādissa. Mato maggaṃ bhāvetīti [P 0.0122] chalena pucchā paravādissa. Yasmā pana paṭisandhito yāva cuticittā satto jīvatiyeva nāma, tasmā sakavādī na hevanti paṭikkhipati.

By 'four functional aggregates' is meant the four mental aggregates, apart from material form, which are taken as neither wholesome nor unwholesome. Functional knowledge is the non-objective knowledge acknowledged by the opponent at the moment an Arahant is endowed with eye-consciousness. The question from the opponent is: 'Does the path arise when it has ceased?' The affirmation from the proponent of his own doctrine is made because it does not arise while it has not ceased. The question, 'Does a dead person develop the path?' is a trick question from the opponent. Since a being is indeed said to be living from rebirth-linking up to the death-consciousness, the proponent of his own doctrine rejects it, saying, 'It is not so.'

Nirodhakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Cessation.

2. Rūpaṃmaggotikathāvaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Discourse 'Form is the Path'

573-575. Idāni [V 0.0216] rūpaṃ maggotikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “sammāvācākammantājīvā rūpa”nti laddhi, seyyathāpi mahisāsakasammitiyamahāsaṃghikānaṃ; te sandhāya maggasamaṅgissāti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi te sammāvācādayo rūpaṃ, na viratiyo, yathā sammādiṭṭhādimaggo sārammaṇādisabhāvo, evaṃ tampi rūpaṃ siyā”ti codetuṃ sārammaṇotiādimāha. Tattha paṭikkhepo ca paṭiññā ca paravādino laddhianurūpena veditabbā. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

573-575. Now is the discourse called 'Form is the Path'. Herein, for those who hold the view that 'right speech, right action, and right livelihood are form,' such as the Mahīśāsakas, Sammitīyas, and Mahāsaṅghikas—with reference to them, the question 'Is one endowed with the path?' is from the proponent of his own doctrine, while the other affirms it. Then, to challenge them, saying: 'If right speech and the like are form, and not abstinences, then just as right view and the rest of the path have the nature of being with an object and so on, so too should that form be,' he states 'with an object' and so on. Here, the rejection and the affirmation should be understood in accordance with the other's established view. The rest here is clear in meaning.

Rūpaṃ maggotikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse 'Form is the Path'.

3. Pañcaviññāṇasamaṅgissa maggakathāvaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Discourse on the Path for One Endowed with the Five Consciousnesses

576. Idāni [M 0.0220] pañcaviññāṇasamaṅgissa maggakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā na nimittaggāhī hotī”ti suttaṃ nissāya “pañcaviññāṇasamaṅgissa atthi maggabhāvanā”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṃghikānaṃ, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “sace tassa maggabhāvanā atthi, pañcaviññāṇagatikena vā maggena, maggagatikehi vā pañcaviññāṇehi bhavitabbaṃ, na ca tāni maggagatikāni anibbānārammaṇattā alokuttarattā ca, na maggo pañcaviññāṇagatiko tesaṃ lakkhaṇena asaṅgahitattā”ti codetuṃ nanu pañcaviññāṇā uppannavatthukātiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ adhippāyo – yadi [P 0.0123] pañcaviññāṇasamaṅgissa maggabhāvanā siyā, yena manoviññāṇena maggo sampayutto, tampi pañcaviññāṇasamaṅgissa siyā. Evaṃ sante yadidaṃ “pañcaviññāṇā uppannavatthukā”tiādi lakkhaṇaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ evaṃ avatvā “cha viññāṇā”ti vattabbaṃ siyā. Tathā pana avatvā “pañcaviññāṇā”tveva vuttaṃ, tasmā na vatabbaṃ “pañcaviññāṇasamaṅgissa atthi maggabhāvanā”ti. Yasmā cettha ayameva adhippāyo, tasmā sakavādī taṃ lakkhaṇaṃ paravādiṃ sampaṭicchāpetvā no ca vata re vattabbe pañcaviññāṇasamaṅgissa atthi maggabhāvanāti āha.

576. Now there is the discourse called 'The Path for One Endowed with the Five Consciousnesses.' Here, concerning those who, based on the sutta 'having seen a form with the eye, one is not an apprehender of signs,' hold the view that 'there is path-development for one endowed with the five consciousnesses'—such as the Mahāsāṅghikas—with reference to them, the question is from the proponent of his own doctrine, and the affirmation is from the other. Then, to challenge them, saying, 'If there is path-development for such a person, then either the path must proceed by way of the five consciousnesses, or the five consciousnesses must be path-going. But those are not path-going because they do not have Nibbāna as their object, nor are they supramundane; and the path does not proceed by way of the five consciousnesses because it is not included in their characteristic,' he begins by saying, 'Are not the five consciousnesses based on an arisen physical basis?' etc. Herein, this is the intention: If there were path-development for one endowed with the five consciousnesses, then the mental consciousness with which the path is associated would also belong to one endowed with the five consciousnesses. If this were so, then instead of stating the characteristic 'the five consciousnesses are based on an arisen physical basis,' etc., one would have to say 'six consciousnesses.' But since it is not said thus, and only 'five consciousnesses' is stated, therefore one should not say 'there is path-development for one endowed with the five consciousnesses.' Because this is precisely the intention here, the proponent of his own doctrine, after having the opponent accept that characteristic, says: 'And indeed, it should not be said that there is path-development for one endowed with the five consciousnesses.'

Aparo [V 0.0217] nayo – pañcaviññāṇā uppannavatthukā, maggo avatthukopi hoti. Te ca uppannārammaṇā, maggo navattabbārammaṇo. Te purejātavatthukāva maggo avatthukopi. Te purejātārammaṇā, maggo apurejātārammaṇo. Te ajjhattikavatthukāva maggo avatthukopi hoti. Te ca rūpādivasena bāhirārammaṇā, maggo nibbānārammaṇo. Te aniruddhaṃ vatthuṃ nissayaṃ katvā pavattanato asambhinnavatthukā, maggo avatthukopi. Te aniruddhāneva rūpādīni ārabbha pavattanato asambhinnārammaṇā, maggo nibbānārammaṇo. Te nānāvatthukā, maggo avatthuko vā ekavatthuko vā. Te nānārammaṇā maggo ekārammaṇo. Te attano attanova rūpādigocare pavattanato na aññamaññassa gocaravisayaṃ paccanubhonti, maggo rūpādīsu ekampi gocaraṃ na karoti. Te kiriyamanodhātuṃ purecārikaṃ katvā uppajjanato na asamannāhārā na amanasikārā uppajjanti, maggo nirāvajjanova. Te sampaṭicchanādīhi vokiṇṇā uppajjanti, maggassa vokāroyeva natthi. Te aññamaññaṃ pubbacarimabhāvena [M 0.0221] uppajjanti, maggassa tehi saddhiṃ purimapacchimatāva natthi, tesaṃ anuppattikāle tikkhavipassanāsamaye, tesaṃ anuppattidese āruppepi ca uppajjanato. Te sampaṭicchanādīhi antaritattā na aññamaññassa samanantarā uppajjanti, maggassa sampaṭicchanādīhi antaritabhāvova natthi. Tesaṃ aññatra abhinipātā ābhogamattampi kiccaṃ natthi, maggassa kilesasamugghātanaṃ kiccanti. Yasmā cettha ayampi [P 0.0124] adhippāyo, tasmā sakavādī imehākārehi paravādiṃ maggassa apañcaviññāṇagatikabhāvaṃ sampaṭicchāpetvā no ca vata re vattabbe pañcaviññāṇasamaṅgissa atthi maggabhāvanāti āha.

Another method: The five sense-consciousnesses have arisen bases, while the path may also be without a base. And they have arisen objects, whereas the path has an object that is not describable as arisen. They have only pre-arisen bases, while the path may also be without a base. They have pre-arisen objects, whereas the path does not have a pre-arisen object. They have only internal bases, while the path may also be without a base. And they have external objects, such as forms, etc., whereas the path has Nibbāna as its object. Because they proceed by relying on an unceased base, they have an unbroken base, while the path may also be without a base. Because they proceed by taking unceased objects, such as forms, etc., they have an unbroken object, whereas the path has Nibbāna as its object. They have various bases, while the path has either no base or one base. They have various objects, whereas the path has a single object. Because they operate within their own respective spheres of forms, etc., they do not experience each other’s spheres of objects, whereas the path does not make even one of the forms, etc., its object. Because they arise by making the functional mind-element their forerunner, they do not arise without bringing to mind or without attention, whereas the path is without adverting. They arise interspersed with receiving consciousness, etc., whereas for the path there is no interspersion at all. They arise in a state of preceding and succeeding one another, whereas for the path there is no anteriority or posteriority with them, because it arises at the time of sharp insight when they have not arisen, and in the formless realms where they do not arise. Because they are interrupted by receiving consciousness, etc., they do not arise immediately after one another, whereas for the path there is no state of being interrupted by receiving consciousness, etc. Apart from their mere impact upon an object, they have no function, not even of mere adverting, whereas the function of the path is the eradication of defilements. Since this is also the intended meaning here, the proponent of his own doctrine, having made the opponent accept by these means that the path does not share the nature of the five consciousnesses, says: 'And indeed, it should not be said that there is path-development for one endowed with the five sense-consciousnesses.'

577. Suññataṃ ārabbhāti “yathā lokuttaramaggo suññataṃ nibbānaṃ ārabbha, lokiyo suddhasaṅkhārapuñjaṃ ārabbha uppajjati, kiṃ te evaṃ cakkhuviññāṇa”nti pucchati. Itaro “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe cā”ti vacanato paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho “na nimittaggāhī”ti vacanato yaṃ tattha animittaṃ, tadeva suññatanti sandhāya paṭijānāti. Cakkhuñca paṭiccāti pañhadvayepi eseva nayo.

577. 'Does it take emptiness as its object?'—This question asks: just as the supramundane path arises taking emptiness, Nibbāna, as its object, and the mundane path arises taking the mere aggregate of formations as its object, is it so with eye-consciousness? The other denies this, citing the statement, 'dependent on the eye and on forms.' When asked the second question, 'Is it not an apprehender of signs?', he affirms, with reference to the fact that what is signless therein is itself emptiness. The principle of 'dependent on the eye and on forms' applies to both questions.

578-579. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ atītānāgataṃ ārabbhāti ettha ayamadhippāyo – manoviññāṇasamaṅgissa atthi maggabhāvanā, manoviññāṇañca atītānāgatampi ārabbha uppajjati, kiṃ te evaṃ cakkhuviññāṇampīti. Phassaṃ ārabbhātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Cakkhunā [V 0.0218] rūpaṃ disvā na nimittaggāhīti ettha javanakkhaṇe na nimittaggāhitā vuttā, na cakkhuviññāṇakkhaṇe. Tasmā lokiyamaggampi sandhāyetaṃ asādhakanti.

578-579. 'Does eye-consciousness take the past and future as its object?' Herein, this is the intended meaning: for one endowed with mind-consciousness there is path-development, and mind-consciousness arises taking even the past and future as its object; is it so for eye-consciousness too? The same principle applies to the questions beginning with, 'Does it take contact as its object?' In the statement, 'Having seen a form with the eye, one is not an apprehender of signs,' the non-apprehension of signs is spoken of for the javana-moment, not for the moment of eye-consciousness. Therefore, this is not conclusive even with reference to the mundane path.

Pañcaviññāṇasamaṅgissa maggakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Path for One Endowed with the Five Consciousnesses.

4. Pañcaviññāṇā kusalāpītikathāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Discourse: Are the Five Sense-Consciousnesses Wholesome and Accompanied by Joy?

580-583. Idāni pañcaviññāṇā kusalāpītikathā nāma hoti. Sā heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva atthato veditabbāti.

580-583. Now there is the discourse named, 'Are the Five Sense-Consciousnesses Wholesome and Accompanied by Joy?' Its meaning should be understood according to the method stated previously.

Pañcaviññāṇā kusalāpītikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discourse: Are the Five Sense-Consciousnesses Wholesome and Accompanied by Joy?

5. Pañcaviññāṇā sābhogātikathāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Discourse: Are the Five Sense-Consciousnesses Accompanied by Deliberation?

584-586. Idāni [M 0.0222] pañcaviññāṇā sābhogātikathā nāma hoti. Tattha ābhogo nāma kusalākusalavasena hoti satthārā [P 0.0125] ca “cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā nimittaggāhī hoti, na nimittaggāhī hotī”tiādi vuttaṃ, taṃ ayoniso gahetvā “pañcaviññāṇā sābhogā”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṃghikānaṃ, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha purimakathāsadisamevāti.

584-586. Now there is the discourse named, 'Are the Five Sense-Consciousnesses Accompanied by Deliberation?' Herein, deliberation occurs by way of the wholesome and unwholesome. And because the Teacher has said, 'Having seen a form with the eye, one becomes an apprehender of signs, or one does not become an apprehender of signs,' etc., the question by the proponent of his own doctrine is posed with reference to those—such as the Mahāsāṅghikas—who, having improperly grasped this, hold the doctrine that 'the five sense-consciousnesses are accompanied by deliberation'; the acknowledgement is by the other. The rest here is just like the previous discourse.

Pañcaviññāṇā sābhogātikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discourse: Are the Five Sense-Consciousnesses Accompanied by Deliberation?

6. Dvīhi sīlehītikathāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Discourse Concerning Two Kinds of Virtue.

587-589. Idāni [V 0.0219] dvīhi sīlehītikathā nāma hoti. Tattha “sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño”tiādivacanato (saṃ. ni. 1.23) yasmā lokiyena sīlena sīlavā lokuttaraṃ maggaṃ bhāveti, tasmā “purimena ca lokiyena maggakkhaṇe lokuttarena cāti dvīhi sīlehi samannāgato nāma hotī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṃghikānaṃyeva, te sandhāya maggasamaṅgīti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi so ekakkhaṇe lokiyalokuttarehi dvīhi sīlehi samannāgato, dvīhi phassādīhipi tena samannāgatena bhavitabba”nti codetuṃ dvīhi phassehītiādimāha. Itaro tathārūpaṃ nayaṃ apassanto paṭikkhipati. Lokiyena ca lokuttarena cāti pañhe pubbe samādinnañca maggakkhaṇe uppannasammāvācādīni ca sandhāya paṭijānāti.

587-589. Now there is the discourse named, 'With Two Kinds of Virtue.' Herein, from the saying, 'A wise person, established in virtue...' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.23), since a virtuous person cultivates the supramundane path by means of mundane virtue, the question about one endowed with the path is posed by the proponent of his own doctrine with reference to those—such as the Mahāsāṅghikas—whose doctrine is that 'one is endowed with two kinds of virtue, namely, the previous mundane virtue and the supramundane virtue at the moment of the path'; the acknowledgement is by the other. Then, to challenge him, he says, 'If at one moment he is endowed with two kinds of virtue, mundane and supramundane, then he must also be endowed with two kinds of contact,' and so on. The other, not seeing such a principle, rejects it. To the question, 'With mundane and with supramundane?', he acknowledges, with reference both to the virtue previously undertaken and to right speech, etc., arisen at the moment of the path.

Lokiye sīle niruddheti pucchā paravādissa, khaṇabhaṅganirodhaṃ sandhāya paṭiññā sakavādissa. Itaro pana taṃ vītikkamaṃ viya sallakkhento dussīlotiādimāha. Laddhipatiṭṭhāpanaṃ panassa pubbe abhinnasīlataṃyeva dīpeti, na dvīhi samannāgatataṃ. Tasmā appatiṭṭhitāva laddhīti.

The question, 'Is mundane virtue ceased?' is from the opponent; the acknowledgement, with reference to cessation by momentary dissolution, is from the proponent of his own doctrine. The other, however, regarding that as a transgression, says, 'He is immoral,' and so on. But the establishment of his doctrine only indicates the previous state of unbroken virtue, not the state of being endowed with two. Therefore, the doctrine is unestablished.

Dvīhi sīlehītikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discourse Concerning Two Kinds of Virtue.

7. Sīlaṃ acetasikantikathāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Discourse: Is Virtue Non-Mental?

590-594. Idāni [P 0.0126][M 0.0223] sīlaṃ acetasikantikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā sīle uppajjitvā niruddhepi samādānahetuko sīlopacayo nāma atthi, yena so sīlavāyeva nāma hoti, tasmā “sīlaṃ acetasika”nti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṃghikānaṃ, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha “dānaṃ acetasika”ntikathāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Laddhipatiṭṭhāpanampi ayoniso gahitattā appatiṭṭhāpanamevāti.

590-594. Now there is the discourse entitled 'Virtue is Non-Mental.' Herein, because even after virtue has arisen and ceased, there exists an accumulation of virtue due to the undertaking, by which one is indeed called virtuous, therefore, with reference to those whose doctrine is that 'virtue is non-mental'—such as the Mahāsaṅghikas—the question is from the proponent of his own view, and the acknowledgement is from the other. The rest here should be understood in the same way as stated in the discourse on 'Giving is Non-Mental.' And the establishment of the doctrine, being improperly grasped, is indeed a non-establishment.

Sīlaṃ acetasikantikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discourse 'Virtue is Non-Mental'.

8. Sīlaṃ na cittānuparivattītikathāvaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Discourse 'Virtue is Not Consequent Upon Consciousness'.

595-597. Idāni [V 0.0220] sīlaṃ na cittānuparivattītikathā nāma hoti. Tattha na cittānuparivattīti bhāsantarameva nānaṃ, sesaṃ purimakathāsadisamevāti.

595-597. Now there is the discourse entitled 'Virtue is Not Consequent Upon Consciousness.' Herein, 'not consequent upon consciousness' is merely a different expression; the rest is indeed similar to the previous discourse.

Sīlaṃ na cittānuparivattītikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discourse 'Virtue is Not Consequent Upon Consciousness'.

9. Samādānahetukathāvaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Discourse 'Undertaking as a Cause'.

598-600. Idāni samādānahetukathā nāma hoti. Tattha “ārāmaropā”ti gāthāya atthaṃ ayoniso gahetvā “sadā puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatī”ti vacanato “samādānahetukaṃ sīlaṃ vaḍḍhatī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṃghikānaññeva, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, cittavippayuttaṃ sīlopacayaṃ sandhāya paṭiññā paravādissa. Sesaṃ purimakathāsadisamevāti.

598-600. Now there is the discourse entitled 'Undertaking as a Cause.' Herein, having improperly grasped the meaning of the verse beginning 'Planters of parks,' and from the saying 'merit always increases,' there are those whose doctrine is that 'virtue which has undertaking as its cause grows'—such as the Mahāsaṅghikas. With reference to them, the question is from the proponent of his own view, and with reference to the accumulation of virtue dissociated from consciousness, the acknowledgement is from the opponent. The rest is indeed similar to the previous discourse.

Samādānahetukathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discourse 'Undertaking as a Cause'.

10. Viññatti sīlantikathāvaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Discourse 'Intimation is Virtue'.

601-602. Idāni [P 0.0127] viññatti sīlantikathā nāma hoti. Tattha kāyaviññatti kāyakammaṃ, vacīviññatti vacīkammanti gahitattā “viññatti sīla”nti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṃghikānañceva sammitiyānañca; te sandhāya viññattīti [M 0.0224] pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ yasmā sīlaṃ nāma virati, na rūpadhammo, tasmā tenatthena codetuṃ pāṇātipātā veramaṇītiādimāha. Abhivādanaṃ sīlantiādi yathārūpaṃ viññattiṃ so “sīla”nti maññati taṃ uddharitvā dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana sā virati na hoti, tasmā puna pāṇātipātātiādimāha. Laddhi panassa chalena patiṭṭhitattā appatiṭṭhitāyevāti.

601-602. Now there is the discourse entitled 'Intimation is Virtue.' Herein, because bodily intimation is taken as bodily action and verbal intimation as verbal action, there are those whose doctrine is that 'intimation is virtue'—such as the Mahāsaṅghikas and the Sammitīyas. With reference to them, the question 'Is it intimation?' is from the proponent of his own view, and the acknowledgement is from the other. Then, because virtue is abstention, not a material phenomenon, he says, 'Abstention from taking life,' and so forth, in order to challenge him with that meaning. The statement 'Greeting is virtue,' and so forth, is said in order to bring up and show that he considers such an intimation to be 'virtue.' But since that is not abstention, he again says, 'Taking life,' and so forth. His doctrine, however, being established by pretext, is indeed not established.

Viññatti sīlantikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discourse 'Intimation is Virtue'.

11. Aviññatti dussīlyantikathāvaṇṇanā

11. The Commentary on the Discourse 'Non-Intimation is Immorality'.

603-604. Idāni [V 0.0221] aviññatti dussīlyantikathā nāma hoti. Tattha cittavippayuttaṃ apuññūpacayañceva āṇattiyā ca pāṇātipātādīsu aṅgapāripūriṃ sandhāya “aviññatti dussīlya”nti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṃghikānaṃ, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “sace sā dussīlyaṃ, pāṇātipātādīsu aññatarā siyā”ti codetuṃ pāṇātipātotiādimāha. Pāpakammaṃ samādiyitvāti “asukaṃ nāma ghātessāmi, asukaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ avaharissāmī”ti evaṃ pāpasamādānaṃ katvā. Ubho vaḍḍhantīti puṭṭho dānakkhaṇe pāpassa anuppattiṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho cittavippayuttaṃ pāpūpacayaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Sesamettha paribhogamayakathāyaṃ vuttanayeneva [P 0.0128] veditabbaṃ. Laddhipatiṭṭhāpanampissa pāpasamādinnapubbabhāgameva sādheti; na aviññattiyā dussīlabhāvanti.

603-604. Now there is the discourse entitled 'Non-Intimation is Immorality.' Herein, with reference to the accumulation of demerit dissociated from consciousness and the fulfillment of the factors by command in acts such as taking life, there are those whose doctrine is that 'non-intimation is immorality'—such as the Mahāsaṅghikas. With reference to them, the question is from the proponent of his own view, and the acknowledgement is from the other. Then, to challenge him, he says, 'If that is immorality, it should be one of the acts such as taking life,' and so forth. 'Having undertaken an evil action' means having made an evil undertaking thus: 'I will kill so-and-so, I will steal such-and-such goods.' When asked, 'Do both increase?' he rejects it, with reference to the non-arising of evil at the moment of giving. When asked a second time, he acknowledges it, with reference to the accumulation of evil dissociated from consciousness. The rest here should be understood in the same way as stated in the discourse concerning use. And the establishment of his doctrine proves only the preliminary part of the evil that was undertaken, not the state of immorality of the non-intimation.

Aviññatti dussīlyantikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discourse 'Non-Intimation is Immorality'.

Dasamo vaggo.

The Tenth Chapter.

Dutiyapaṇṇāsako samatto.

The Second Fifty is concluded.

11. Ekādasamavaggo

11. The Eleventh Chapter.

1-3. Tissopi anusayakathāvaṇṇanā

1–3. The Commentary on the Three Discourses on Latent Tendencies.

605-613. Idāni [P 0.0129][M 0.0225] anusayā abyākatā, ahetukā, cittavippayuttāti tissopi anusayakathā nāma honti. Tattha yasmā puthujjano kusalābyākate citte vattamāne “sānusayo”ti vattabbo, yo cassa tasmiṃ khaṇe hetu, na tena hetunā anusayā sahetukā, na tena cittena sampayuttā, tasmā “te abyākatā, ahetukā, cittavippayuttā”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṃghikānañceva sammitiyānañca; te sandhāya tīsupi kathāsu pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā sakkā pāḷimaggeneva jānitunti, tasmā na vitthāritanti.

605–613. Now there are the three discourses on latent tendencies: that they are indeterminate, rootless, and dissociated from consciousness. Herein, because an ordinary person is to be called 'one with latent tendencies' even when a wholesome or indeterminate consciousness is occurring, and because the root present at that moment does not make the latent tendencies rooted, nor are they associated with that consciousness, therefore, there are those whose doctrine is that 'they are indeterminate, rootless, and dissociated from consciousness'—such as the Mahāsaṅghikas and the Sammitīyas. With reference to them, in all three discourses the question is from the proponent of his own view, and the acknowledgement is from the other. The rest, following the method stated previously, can be known through the Pāli text itself; therefore, it is not elaborated upon.

Tissopi anusayakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Three Discourses on Latent Tendencies.

4. Ñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Discourse on Knowledge.

614-615. Idāni [V 0.0222] ñāṇakathā nāma hoti. Tattha maggañāṇena aññāṇe vigatepi puna cakkhuviññāṇādivasena ñāṇavippayuttacitte vattamāne yasmā taṃ maggacittaṃ na pavattati, tasmā “na vattabbaṃ ñāṇī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṃghikānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi aññāṇe vigate ‘ñāṇī’ti paññatti na siyā, rāgādīsu vigatesu vītarāgādipaññattipi na siyāti puggalapaññattiyaṃ akovidosī”ti codetuṃ rāge vigatetiādimāha. Itaro tesu vigatesu sarāgādibhāve yuttiṃ [P 0.0130] apassanto paṭikkhipati. Pariyosāne yasmā ñāṇapaṭilābhena so ñāṇīti vattabbataṃ arahati, tasmā na hevanti paṭikkhepo sakavādissāti.

614–615. Now there is the discourse on knowledge. Herein, even though ignorance is removed by path-knowledge, when a consciousness dissociated from knowledge subsequently occurs by way of eye-consciousness and so on, because that path-consciousness does not recur, there are those whose doctrine is that 'one should not be called knowledgeable'—such as the Mahāsaṅghikas. With reference to them, the question is from the proponent of his own view, and the acknowledgement is from the other. Then, to challenge him, saying, 'If, when ignorance is removed, the designation "knowledgeable" does not exist, then when lust and so on are removed, designations like "free from lust" should also not exist—thus you are unskilled in the concept of a person,' he says, 'When lust is removed,' and so forth. The other, not seeing the logic in the state of being 'with lust,' etc., when these are removed, rejects it. In conclusion, because through the attainment of knowledge one deserves to be called 'knowledgeable,' therefore the proponent's rejection is, 'It is not so.'

Ñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Knowledge.

5. Ñāṇaṃ cittavippayuttantikathāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Discourse 'Knowledge is Dissociated from Consciousness'.

616-617. Idāni [M 0.0226] ñāṇaṃ cittavippayuttantikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā arahā cakkhuviññāṇādisamaṅgī paṭiladdhaṃ maggañāṇaṃ sandhāya “ñāṇī”ti vuccati, na cassa taṃ tena cittena sampayuttaṃ, tasmā “ñāṇaṃ cittavippayutta”nti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi te ñāṇaṃ cittavippayuttaṃ cittavippayuttesu rūpādīsu aññataraṃ siyā”ti codetuṃ rūpantiādimāha. Itaro paṭikkhipati. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Pariyosāne pana paññavāti puṭṭho paṭilābhavasena taṃ pavattiṃ icchati, tasmā paṭijānātīti.

616–617. Now there is the discussion entitled 'Knowledge is Dissociated from Consciousness.' Herein, because an arahant endowed with eye-consciousness and so forth is called 'knowledgeable' with reference to the path-knowledge he has attained, and that knowledge is not associated with that consciousness, the view of some, such as the Pubbaseliyas, is that 'knowledge is dissociated from consciousness.' With reference to them, the question is from the proponent of his own view, and the admission is from the other. Then, to challenge him by saying, 'If your knowledge is dissociated from consciousness, it would have to be one among things dissociated from consciousness, such as material form,' he states, 'Is it material form?' and so on. The other denies this. The rest is in accordance with the method stated above. At the end, however, when asked, 'Is one endowed with wisdom?', he accepts its occurrence by way of attainment; therefore, he assents.

Ñāṇaṃ cittavippayuttantikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion entitled 'Knowledge is Dissociated from Consciousness.'

6. Idaṃ dukkhantikathāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Discussion entitled 'This is Suffering.'

618-820. Idāni [V 0.0223] idaṃ dukkhantikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe yogāvacaro idaṃ dukkhanti vācaṃ bhāsati, evamassa idaṃ dukkhanti vācaṃ bhāsato ca idaṃ dukkhanti ñāṇaṃ pavattatī”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, maggakkhaṇe tathā vācābhāsanaṃ ñāṇappavattiñca sandhāya paṭiññā itarassa. Yasmā pana so sesasaccapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ vācaṃ puthujjanova bhāsati[P 0.0131], na ca tassa tathā ñāṇappavattīti icchati, tasmā samudayādipañhesu paṭikkhipati. Rūpaṃ aniccantiādi dukkhapariyāyadassanavasena vuttaṃ. Itaro pana sakasamaye tādisaṃ vohāraṃ apassanto paṭikkhipati. Iti ca danti cātiādi yadi tassa dukkhe ñāṇaṃ pavattati, i-kāra daṃ-kāra du-kāra kha-kāresu paṭipāṭiyā catūhi ñāṇehi pavattitabbanti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Itaro pana tathā na icchati, tasmā paṭikkhipati.

618–820. Now there is the discussion entitled 'This is Suffering.' Herein, the view of some, such as the Andhakas, is that 'at the moment of the supramundane path, the yogin utters the words, "This is suffering," and as he utters the words, "This is suffering," the knowledge, "This is suffering," arises.' With reference to them, the question is from the proponent of his own view, and the admission by the other is with reference to such utterance of words and the arising of knowledge at the moment of the path. But since he holds that only an ordinary person speaks words connected with the remaining truths, and he does not accept that knowledge arises in that way for him, he therefore rejects the questions about the origin and so on. 'Form is impermanent,' etc., is stated from the perspective of seeing the aspects of suffering. The other, however, not seeing such usage in his own system, rejects it. The passage beginning 'And "i," and "daṃ,"' is said to show that if knowledge of suffering arises for him, it would have to arise sequentially with four knowledges regarding the letters 'i,' 'daṃ,' 'du,' and 'kha.' The other, however, does not accept it thus; therefore, he rejects it.

Idaṃ dukkhantikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion entitled 'This is Suffering.'

7. Iddhibalakathāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Discussion of Psychic Powers.

621-624. Idāni [M 0.0227] iddhibalakathā nāma hoti. Tattha iddhipādabhāvanānisaṃsassa atthaṃ ayoniso gahetvā “iddhibalena samannāgato kappaṃ tiṭṭheyyā”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṃghikānaṃ; te sandhāya iddhibalena samannāgato kappaṃ tiṭṭheyyāti pucchā sakavādissa. Tattha kappo nāma mahākappo, kappekadeso, āyukappoti tividho. “Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, kappassa asaṅkhyeyyānī”ti (a. ni. 4.156) ettha hi mahākappova kappoti vutto. “Brahmakāyikānaṃ devānaṃ kappo āyuppamāṇa”nti (a. ni. 4.123) ettha kappekadesā. “Kappaṃ nirayamhi paccati, kappaṃ saggamhi modatī”ti (cūḷava. 354) ettha āyukappo. Āyukappanaṃ āyuvidhānaṃ kammassa vipākavasena vā vassagaṇanāya vā āyuparicchedoti attho. Tesu mahākappaṃ sandhāya pucchati, itaro paṭijānāti.

621–624. Now there is the discussion on psychic powers. Herein, some, such as the Mahāsaṅghikas, having wrongly grasped the meaning of the benefit of developing the bases of psychic power, hold the view that 'one endowed with psychic power could remain for an eon.' With reference to them, the question, 'Could one endowed with psychic power remain for an eon?' is from the proponent of his own view. Here, an 'eon' is of three kinds: a great eon, a fraction of an eon, and a lifespan-eon. In the passage, 'Bhikkhus, these are the four incalculables of an eon' (AN 4.156), the great eon is called 'eon.' In 'For the Brahmakāyika devas, an eon is the measure of their lifespan' (AN 4.123), it refers to fractions of an eon. In 'For an eon one is tormented in hell, for an eon one rejoices in heaven' (Cv. VII.3.5), it refers to a lifespan-eon. A lifespan-eon means the determination of a lifespan, that is, the delimitation of a life either by way of the result of kamma or by a number of years. Among these, he asks with reference to the great eon, and the other admits it.

Atha naṃ sakavādī “sace te iddhibalena samannāgato, ‘yo ciraṃ jīvati, so vassasataṃ appaṃ [V 0.0224] vā bhiyyo’ti (saṃ. ni. 2.143) evaṃ paricchinnā āyukappā uddhaṃ mahākappaṃ vā mahākappekadesaṃ vā jīveyya iddhimayikenassa āyunā bhavitabba”nti codetuṃ iddhimayiko so āyūtiādimāha. Itaro “jīvitindriyaṃ nāma iddhimayikaṃ natthi, kammasamuṭṭhānamevā”ti vuttattā paṭikkhipati. Ko panettha iddhimato viseso, nanu aniddhimāpi āyukappaṃ [P 0.0132] tiṭṭheyyāti? Ayaṃ viseso – iddhimā hi yāvatāyukaṃ jīvitappavattiyā antarāyakare dhamme iddhibalena paṭibāhitvā antarā akālamaraṇaṃ nivāretuṃ sakkoti, aniddhimato etaṃ balaṃ natthi. Ayametesaṃ viseso.

Then the proponent of his own view, in order to challenge him, began by saying, 'Is that lifespan created by psychic power?' The challenge is: 'If one endowed with psychic power could live beyond the lifespan-eon, which is defined thus, "One who lives long lives for a hundred years or a little more" (SN 2.143), up to a great eon or a fraction of a great eon, his life would have to be one created by psychic power.' The other rejects this, because it is said, 'There is no life faculty created by psychic power; it is originated solely from kamma.' What, then, is the distinction for one with psychic power? Could not one without psychic power also remain for a full lifespan? This is the distinction: one with psychic power is able, by means of psychic power, to ward off conditions that obstruct the continuation of life for as long as the lifespan lasts, and thus can prevent an untimely death in the interim. One without psychic power does not have this ability. This is the distinction between them.

Atītaṃ anāgatanti idaṃ avisesena kappaṃ tiṭṭheyyāti paṭiññātattā codeti. Dve kappetiādi “yadi iddhimā jīvitaparicchedaṃ atikkamituṃ sakkoti, na kevalaṃ ekaṃ anekepi kappe tiṭṭheyyā”ti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Uppanno phassotiādi na sabbaṃ iddhiyā labbhati, iddhiyā avisayopi atthīti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

The question about 'the past' and 'the future' is raised because it was admitted without specification that one could remain for an eon. The passage beginning 'Two eons' is stated for the purpose of the challenge: 'If one with psychic power is able to surpass the limit of life, one could remain not just for one but for many eons.' The passage beginning 'Contact has arisen' is stated to show that not everything is obtained through psychic power; there are also matters beyond the scope of psychic power. The rest here is of plain meaning.

Iddhibalakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion of Psychic Powers.

8. Samādhikathāvaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Discussion of Concentration.

625-626. Idāni [M 0.0228] samādhikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ ekacittakkhaṇe uppannāpi ekaggatā samādhānaṭṭhena samādhīti aggahetvā “satta rattindivāni ekantasukhapaṭisaṃvedī viharitu”ntiādivacanaṃ (ma. ni. 1.180) nissāya “cittasantati samādhī”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi sabbatthivādānañceva uttarāpathakānañca; te sandhāya cittasantatīti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi cittasantati samādhi, cittasantati nāma atītāpi atthi, anāgatāpi atthi. Na hi ekaṃ paccuppannacittameva cittasantati nāma hoti, kiṃ te sabbāpi sā samādhī”ti codetuṃ atītātiādimāha, itaro tathā anicchanto paṭikkhipati.

625–626. Now there is the discussion on concentration. Herein, some, not taking one-pointedness—even if arisen in a single mind-moment—as concentration in the sense of unification, but relying on statements such as, 'to dwell experiencing exclusive happiness for seven days and nights' (MN 1.180), hold the view that 'continuity of consciousness is concentration.' This is the doctrine of the Sarvāstivādins and the Uttarāpathakas. With reference to them, the question, 'Is the continuity of consciousness concentration?' is from the proponent of his own view, and the admission is from the other. Then, to challenge him by saying, 'If the continuity of consciousness is concentration, then continuity of consciousness exists in the past and also in the future—for it is not just a single present consciousness that is called "continuity of consciousness"—is all of that concentration for you?', he says, 'Is it past?' and so on. The other, not accepting this, rejects it.

Nanu [V 0.0225] atītaṃ niruddhantiādi “cittasantatiyaṃ paccuppannameva cittaṃ kiccakaraṃ, atītānāgataṃ niruddhattā anuppannattā ca natthi, kathaṃ taṃ samādhi nāma hotī”ti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Ekacittakkhaṇikoti pucchā paravādissa. Tato yā sakasamaye “samādhiṃ, bhikkhave, bhāvethā”tiādīsu paccuppannakusalacittasampayuttā ekaggatā samādhīti vuttā, taṃ sandhāya paṭiññā sakavādissa. Cakkhuviññāṇasamaṅgītiādi “ekacittakkhaṇiko”ti vacanamattaṃ gahetvā chalena vuttaṃ, teneva sakavādinā paṭikkhittaṃ. Nanu vuttaṃ bhagavatāti suttaṃ purimapacchimavasena pavattamānassa [P 0.0133] samādhissa abbokiṇṇataṃ sādheti, na santatiyā samādhibhāvaṃ, tasmā asādhakanti.

Is it not so that 'the past has ceased,' etc., was said to show that 'in the continuity of consciousness, only the present mind performs a function; the past and future do not exist because they have ceased and have not arisen, so how can that be called concentration?' The question, 'Is it of a single mind-moment?' is the opponent's. Then, with reference to what is stated in one's own doctrine, such as, 'Monks, develop concentration,' that one-pointedness associated with a present wholesome mind is called concentration—this is the proponent's affirmation. The statement 'endowed with eye-consciousness,' etc., was uttered deceitfully by merely taking the phrase 'of a single mind-moment,' and for that very reason it was refuted by the proponent. The sutta beginning 'Has it not been said by the Blessed One?' establishes the uninterrupted nature of concentration as it proceeds in its earlier and later phases, not the nature of concentration as a continuity. Therefore, it is not a valid proof.

Samādhikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discussion on Concentration.

9. Dhammaṭṭhitatākathāvaṇṇanā

9. The Exposition of the Discussion on the Fixedness of Phenomena.

627. Idāni dhammaṭṭhitatākathā nāma hoti. Tattha “ṭhitāva sā dhātū”ti vacanaṃ nissāya “paṭiccasamuppādasaṅkhātā dhammaṭṭhitatā nāma ekā atthi, sā ca parinipphannā”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi parinipphannānaṃ avijjādīnaṃ aññā [M 0.0229] dhammaṭṭhitatā nāma parinipphannā atthi, tāyapi ca te dhammaṭṭhitatāya aññā ṭhitatā parinipphannā āpajjatī”ti codetuṃ tāya ṭhitatātiādimāha. Paravādī evarūpāya laddhiyā abhāvena paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho anantarapaccayatañceva aññamaññapaccayatañca sandhāya paṭijānāti. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthamevāti.

627. Now there is the discussion on the fixedness of phenomena. Here, based on the statement 'that element remains fixed,' with reference to those whose doctrine is that 'there exists a certain fixed state of phenomena, designated as dependent origination, and it is perfected'—such as the Andhakas—the question is the proponent's, and the affirmation is the other's. Then, in order to challenge him by saying, 'If there exists another perfected fixed state of phenomena called dhammaṭṭhitatā, distinct from perfected phenomena such as ignorance, then from that fixed state of phenomena, another perfected fixed state would result,' he says, 'by that fixed state,' etc. The opponent rejects this due to the absence of such a doctrine. Asked a second time, he affirms with reference to both immediate conditionality and mutual conditionality. The rest is clear in meaning, being in accordance with the method stated previously.

Dhammaṭṭhitatākathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discussion on the Fixedness of Phenomena.

10. Aniccatākathāvaṇṇanā

10. The Exposition of the Discussion on Impermanence.

628. Idāni [V 0.0226] aniccatākathā nāma hoti. Tattha “aniccānaṃ rūpādīnaṃ aniccatāpi rūpādayo viya parinipphannā”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi te rūpādayo viya aniccatā parinipphannā, tassāpi aññāya parinipphannāya aniccatāya bhavitabba”nti codetuṃ tāya aniccatāyātiādimāha. Itaro dvinnaṃ aniccatāya ekato abhāvena paṭikkhipitvā puna yasmā sā aniccatā niccā na hoti, teneva aniccena saddhiṃ antaradhāyati, tasmā paṭijānāti. Athassa sakavādī lesokāsaṃ adatvā yā tena dutiyā aniccatā paṭiññātā[P 0.0134], tāyapi tato parāyapīti paramparavasena anupacchedadosaṃ āropento tāya tāyevātiādimāha. Jarā parinipphannātiādi yasmā uppannassa jarāmaraṇato aññā aniccatā nāma natthi, tasmā aniccatāvibhāgānuyuñjanavasena vuttaṃ. Tatrāpi paravādino purimanayeneva paṭiññā ca paṭikkhepo ca veditabbo.

628. Now there is the discussion on impermanence. Here, with reference to those whose doctrine is that 'the impermanence of impermanent things like form, etc., is itself perfected like form and so on'—such as the Andhakas—the question is the proponent's, and the affirmation is the other's. Then, in order to challenge him by saying, 'If impermanence is perfected for you like form and so on, then it must have another perfected impermanence,' he says, 'with that impermanence,' etc. The other, having rejected this due to the non-existence of two impermanences as one, then affirms it because that impermanence is not permanent, and for that very reason it disappears along with the impermanent thing itself. Then the proponent, giving him no opportunity for evasion, imputes the fault of non-cessation in a successive manner, saying 'with that, and with that too,' etc., because of the second impermanence affirmed by him. 'Aging is perfected,' etc., is said by way of an inquiry into the divisions of impermanence, because for that which has arisen, there is no other thing called impermanence apart from aging and death. There too, the opponent's affirmation and rejection should be understood in the same way as before.

629. Rūpaṃ parinipphannantiādi yesaṃ sā aniccatā, tehi saddhiṃ saṃsandanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha “yathā parinipphannānaṃ rūpādīnaṃ aniccatājarāmaraṇāni atthi, evaṃ parinipphannānaṃ aniccatādīnaṃ tāni natthī”ti maññamāno ekantena paṭikkhipatiyevāti.

629. 'Form is perfected,' etc., is said for the purpose of comparison with those for whom that impermanence exists. Here, one who thinks, 'Just as there is impermanence, aging, and death for perfected things like form, etc., so those things do not exist for perfected things like impermanence, etc.,' rejects it absolutely.

Aniccatākathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discussion on Impermanence.

Ekādasamo vaggo.

The Eleventh Chapter.

12. Dvādasamavaggo

12. The Twelfth Chapter.

1. Saṃvaro kammantikathāvaṇṇanā

1. The Exposition of the Discussion on 'Restraint is Action'.

630-632. Idāni [M 0.0230][P 0.0135] saṃvaro kammantikathā nāma hoti. Tattha “cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā nimittaggāhī [V 0.0227] hoti, na nimittaggāhī hotī”ti suttaṃ nissāya “saṃvaropi asaṃvaropi kamma”nti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṃghikānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa.

630-632. Now there is the discussion on 'Restraint is Action.' Here, based on the sutta, 'Having seen a form with the eye, one becomes a grasper of signs, or one does not become a grasper of signs,' with reference to those whose doctrine is that 'both restraint and non-restraint are action'—such as the Mahāsaṅghikas—the question is the proponent's, and the affirmation is the other's.

Atha naṃ yā sakasamaye cetanā “kamma”nti vuttā yathā sā kāyavacīmanodvāresu pavattamānā kāyakammādināmaṃ labhati, tathā “yadi te saṃvaro kammaṃ, sopi cakkhundriyādīsu pavattamāno cakkhukammādināmaṃ labheyyā”ti codetuṃ cakkhundriyasaṃvaro cakkhukammantiādimāha. Itaro tādisaṃ suttapadaṃ apassanto catūsu dvāresu paṭikkhipitvā pañcame kāyadvāre pasādakāyaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati, viññattikāyaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. So hi pasādakāyampi viññattikāyampi kāyindriyantveva icchati. Manodvārepi vipākadvāraṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati, kammadvāraṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Asaṃvarepi eseva nayo. “Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā”ti suttaṃ tesu dvāresu saṃvarāsaṃvarameva dīpeti, na tassa kammabhāvaṃ, tasmā asādhakanti.

Then, in order to challenge him by saying, 'Just as volition, which in one's own doctrine is called "action," when proceeding through the doors of body, speech, and mind, receives the name of bodily action, etc., so too, if restraint is action for you, it too, when proceeding through the eye faculty, etc., should receive the name of eye action, etc.,' he says, 'eye-faculty restraint is eye action,' etc. The other, not seeing such a sutta passage, rejects it in the four doors; in the fifth, the body-door, he rejects it with reference to the sensitive body but affirms it with reference to bodily intimation. For he holds that both the sensitive body and bodily intimation are simply the body faculty. In the mind-door too, he rejects it with reference to the door of result but affirms it with reference to the door of action. This same method applies to non-restraint. The sutta, 'Having seen a form with the eye,' reveals only restraint and non-restraint in those doors, not their nature as action. Therefore, it is not a valid proof.

Saṃvaro kammantikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discussion on 'Restraint is Action'.

2. Kammakathāvaṇṇanā

2. The Exposition of the Discussion on Kamma.

633-635. Idāni kammakathā nāma hoti. Tattha “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sañcetanikānaṃ [P 0.0136] kammāna”nti (a. ni. 10.217) suttapadaṃ nissāya “sabbaṃ kammaṃ savipāka”nti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṃghikānaṃ; tesaṃ “cetanāhaṃ, bhikkhave, kammaṃ vadāmī”ti (a. ni. 6.63) satthārā avisesena cetanā “kamma”nti vuttā; sā ca kusalākusalāva savipākā, abyākatā avipākāti imaṃ vibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ sabbaṃ kammanti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Puna sabbā cetanāti pañhesu abyākataṃ sandhāya paṭikkhepo, kusalākusale sandhāya paṭiññā veditabbā[M 0.0231]. Vipākābyākatātiādi savipākāvipākacetanaṃ sarūpena dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Sesamettha uttānatthameva. “Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave”ti suttaṃ sati paccaye diṭṭhadhammādīsu vipākapaṭisaṃvedanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, tasmā asādhakanti.

633-635. Now there is the discussion on kamma. Here, based on the sutta passage, “Monks, of volitional actions that have been done and accumulated, I do not declare the termination without their result having been experienced” (AN 10.217), some, such as the Mahāsaṅghikas, hold the view that “all kamma is with result.” To them, in order to show this distinction—that although the Teacher has stated without distinction, “Volition, monks, I declare to be kamma” (AN 6.63), only wholesome and unwholesome volition is with result, while indeterminate volition is without result—the question, ‘Is all kamma with result?’ is posed by the proponent, and the admission is made by the other. Furthermore, in the questions, ‘Is all volition with result?’, the denial refers to indeterminate volition, while the affirmation should be understood as referring to wholesome and unwholesome volition. The phrase beginning “Resultant-indeterminate” is stated to show, by its own nature, volition that is with result and volition that is without result. The rest here is of clear meaning. The sutta passage, “Monks, I do not say…,” is stated with reference to experiencing the result in this very life and so on, when conditions are present; therefore, it is not probative.

Kammakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discussion on Kamma.

3. Saddo vipākotikathāvaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discussion that Sound is a Result.

636-637. Idāni [V 0.0228] saddo vipākotikathā nāma hoti. Tattha “so tassa kammassa katattā upacitattā ussannattā vipulattā brahmassaro hotī”tiādīni (dī. ni. 3.236) ayoniso gahetvā “saddo vipāko”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṃghikānaṃ; tesaṃ “kammasamuṭṭhānā arūpadhammāva vipākāti nāmaṃ labhanti. Rūpadhammesu panāyaṃ vohāro natthī”ti dassetuṃ pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sukhavedanīyotiādi “vipāko nāma evarūpo hotī”ti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. “So tassa kammassā”ti suttaṃ lakkhaṇapaṭilābhadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Mahāpuriso hi kammassa katattā suciparivāropi hoti, na ca parivāro vipāko, tasmā asādhakametanti.

636-637. Now there is the discussion that sound is a result. Here, some, such as the Mahāsaṅghikas, incorrectly grasp phrases like “Due to the doing, accumulation, abundance, and greatness of that kamma, he has a voice like Brahmā” (DN 3.236) and hold the view that “sound is a result.” To show them that “only formless phenomena arising from kamma receive the designation of ‘result,’ but this usage does not apply to material phenomena,” the question is posed by the proponent, and the admission is made by the other. The phrase beginning “To be felt as pleasant” is stated to illustrate that “a result is of such a nature.” The sutta statement “Due to that kamma of his…” is made to show the attainment of characteristics. For a great man, due to the doing of kamma, also has a pure retinue, yet the retinue is not the result; therefore, this is not probative.

Saddo vipākotikathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discussion that Sound is a Result.

4. Saḷāyatanakathāvaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discussion on the Six Sense Bases.

638-640. Idāni [P 0.0137] saḷāyatanakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā saḷāyatanaṃ kammassa katattā uppannaṃ, tasmā “vipāko”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṃghikānaṃ; te sandhāya cakkhāyatanaṃ vipākoti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Saḷāyatanaṃ vipākoti ettha manāyatanaṃ siyā vipāko. Sesāni kevalaṃ kammasamuṭṭhānāni, na vipāko. Tasmā asādhakametanti.

638-640. Now there is the discussion on the six sense bases. Herein, because the six sense bases arise due to the doing of kamma, some, such as the Mahāsaṅghikas, hold the view that they are a “result.” With reference to them, the question, “Is the eye sense base a result?” is posed by the proponent, and the admission is made by the other. The rest is in the same manner as stated above. In the statement, “The six sense bases are a result,” the mind sense base could be a result. The remaining ones are merely originated by kamma, not a result. Therefore, this is not probative.

Saḷāyatanakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discussion on the Six Sense Bases.

5. Sattakkhattuparamakathāvaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discussion on the Seven-Times-at-Most.

541-545. Idāni [M 0.0232] sattakkhattuparamakathā nāma hoti, tattha yasmā “sattakkhattuparamo”ti [V 0.0229] vuttaṃ, tasmā “sattakkhattuparamo puggalo sattakkhattuparamatāya niyato”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi uttarāpathakānaṃ; tesaṃ ṭhapetvā “ariyamaggaṃ añño tassa niyamo natthi, yena so sattakkhattuparamatāya niyato bhaveyyā”ti imaṃ vibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa.

541-545. Now there is the discussion on the seven-times-at-most. Here, because it is said “seven-times-at-most,” some, such as the Uttarāpathakas, hold the view that “a seven-times-at-most individual is fixed by the nature of being seven-times-at-most.” To them, in order to show this distinction—that apart from the Noble Path, there is no other fixed course for him by which he would be fixed in the state of being seven-times-at-most—the question is posed by the proponent, and the admission is made by the other.

Mātā jīvitātiādīsu ayamadhippāyo – dve niyāmā sammattaniyāmo ca micchattaniyāmo ca. Sammattaniyāmo ariyamaggo. So avinipātadhammatañceva phaluppattiñca niyameti. Micchattaniyāmo ānantariyakammaṃ. Taṃ anantarā nirayūpapattiṃ niyameti. Tattha sattakkhattuparamo sotāpattimaggena avinipātadhammatāya ca phaluppattiyā ca niyamito. Sesamagganiyāmo panassa natthi anadhigatattā, ānantariyampi kātuṃ so abhabbo. Tvaṃ panassa niyāmaṃ icchasi, tena taṃ vadāma – “kiṃ te so iminā micchattaniyāmena niyamito”ti.

In the phrases like “depriving mother of life,” this is the meaning: there are two fixed courses, the fixed course of rightness and the fixed course of wrongness. The fixed course of rightness is the Noble Path. It fixes both the state of not being subject to downfall and the arising of fruition. The fixed course of wrongness is an action with immediate result. It fixes rebirth in hell immediately thereafter. Here, the seven-times-at-most individual is fixed by the path of stream-entry with respect to not being subject to downfall and with respect to the arising of fruition. But there is no fixed course of the remaining paths for him, as they have not been attained; and he is incapable of performing an action with immediate result. But you desire a fixed course for him, so we say to you: “Is he, then, fixed by this fixed course of wrongness?”

Abhabbo antarāti pañhesu ānantariyābhāvaṃ [P 0.0138] sandhāya paṭikkhipati, sattakkhattuparamaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Atthi so niyāmoti pañhe sattakkhattuparamatāya niyāmaṃ apassanto paṭikkhipati. Atthi te satipaṭṭhānātiādi niyāmasaṅkhāte maggadhamme dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tassa pana puna paṭhamamaggānuppattito tepi natthi, tasmā paṭikkhipati. Sesamettha uttānatthameva. Nanu so sattakkhattuparamoti ettha bhagavā “ayaṃ puggalo ettake bhave sandhāvitvā parinibbāyissati, ayaṃ ettake”ti attano ñāṇabalena byākaroti, na bhavaniyāmaṃ nāma kiñci tena sattakkhattuparamo, kolaṃkolo, ekabījī vāti vuttaṃ, tasmā asādhakametanti.

In the questions, “Is he incapable…?” he denies with reference to the absence of an action with immediate result, but admits with reference to the seven-times-at-most state. In the question, “Is there that fixed course?” he denies, not seeing a fixed course in the state of being a seven-times-at-most. The phrase beginning, “Are there for you the foundations of mindfulness?” is stated to show the path-states designated as a fixed course. But for him, even those do not exist, since the first path does not arise again; therefore, he denies. The rest here is of clear meaning. Regarding the statement, “Surely, he is a seven-times-at-most,” here the Blessed One declares by the power of his knowledge: “This person, after wandering through so many existences, will attain final Nibbāna; this one, through so many.” He is not called a “seven-times-at-most,” a “family-to-family,” or a “single-seed” because of some so-called fixed course of existence. Thus, this is not probative.

Sattakkhattuparamakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discussion on the Seven-Times-at-Most.

646-647. Kolaṃkolaekabījikathāyopi imināvupāyena veditabbā.

646-647. The discussions on the Kolaṅkola and the Ekabījī should also be understood in this manner.

Kolaṃkolaekabījikathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discussion on the Kolaṅkola and the Ekabījī.

8. Jīvitāvoropanakathāvaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Discussion on Taking Life.

648-649. Idāni [M 0.0233][V 0.0230] jīvitāvoropanakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā dosasampayuttena cittena pāṇātipāto hoti, doso ca diṭṭhisampannassa appahīno, tasmā “diṭṭhisampanno sañcicca pāṇaṃ jīvitā voropeyyā”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyāparaseliyānaṃ; te sandhāya diṭṭhisampannoti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sañcicca mātarantiādipañhesu pana “aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso”ti suttabhayena paṭikkhipati. Satthari agāravotiādi satthārādīsu sagāravassa sikkhāpadassa vītikkamābhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Itaro pana akusalavasena tassa agāravo nāma [P 0.0139] natthīti paṭikkhipitvā sagāravabhāvañca sampaṭicchitvā puna agāravoti puṭṭho tesu tesu kiccesu pasutatāya vikkhittānaṃ asatiyā amanasikārena cetiye abhivādanapadakkhiṇakaraṇābhāvaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Puna ohadeyyātiādinā nayena puṭṭho tādisāya kiriyāya sañcicca akaraṇato paṭikkhipati. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

648-649. Now comes the discussion on taking life. Here, since the taking of life occurs with a mind associated with aversion, and aversion is not abandoned by one endowed with right view, therefore, with reference to those who hold the view that “one endowed with right view would intentionally take the life of a living being”—such as the Pubbaseliyas and Aparaseliyas—the question, “Is one endowed with right view?”, is the proponent's, and the admission is the other's. However, regarding questions such as, “Would one intentionally kill one’s mother?”, he rejects it by saying, “This is impossible, it cannot occur,” out of fear of the suttas. “Disrespect toward the Teacher,” and so forth, is stated to show the absence of transgression of the training rule concerning one who is respectful toward the Teacher and others. The other party, however, rejects this, saying that with regard to unwholesome states, there is no such thing as disrespect for him. Having accepted the state of being respectful, when asked again about “disrespect,” he acknowledges it by referring to the lack of paying homage or circumambulating shrines due to being preoccupied with various tasks, being distracted, unmindful, or inattentive. When asked further in the manner of, “Would he disparage?”, he rejects it by stating the intentional non-performance of such an action. The rest here is clear in meaning.

Jīvitāvoropanakathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discussion on Taking Life.

9. Duggatikathāvaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Discussion on States of Woe

650-652. Idāni duggatikathā nāma hoti. Tattha ye duggatiñca duggatisattānaṃ rūpādiārammaṇaṃ taṇhañcāti ubhayampi duggatīti gahetvā puna tathā avibhajitvā aviseseneva “diṭṭhisampannassa pahīnā duggatī”ti vadanti, seyyathāpi uttarāpathakā; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Āpāyike rūpe rajjeyyātiādi paravādino laddhiyā diṭṭhisampannassa duggati appahīnā, tassa vasena codetuṃ vuttaṃ. Sesamettha uttānatthameva. Nirayaṃ upapajjeyyātiādi duggatipahānameva duggatigāminitaṇhāpahānaṃ vā dīpeti, na duggatisattānaṃ rūpādiārammaṇāya taṇhāya pahānaṃ, tasmā asādhakanti.

650-652. Now comes the discussion on states of woe. Here, some—such as the Uttarāpathakas—taking both the woeful state itself and the craving of beings in a woeful state for objects such as form to be the “woeful state,” without making this distinction, declare undifferentiatedly, “For one endowed with right view, the woeful state is abandoned.” With reference to them, the question is the proponent's, and the admission is the other's. The statement, “One might be attached to forms in the lower realms,” and so on, is made in order to challenge the opponent based on his view that for one endowed with right view, the woeful state is not abandoned. The rest here is clear in meaning. Statements like, “He might be reborn in hell,” illustrate only the abandoning of the woeful state or the abandoning of craving that leads to a woeful state, not the abandoning of craving for objects such as form on the part of beings in a woeful state. Therefore, this is not a valid proof.

Duggatikathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discussion on States of Woe.

653. Sattamabhavikakathāyapi [M 0.0234][V 0.0231] eseva nayoti.

653. The same method applies also to the discussion on one who is to be reborn at most seven more times.

Dvādasamo vaggo.

The Twelfth Chapter.

13. Terasamavaggo

13. The Thirteenth Chapter.

1. Kappaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Discussion on Remaining for an Aeon

654-657. Idāni [P 0.0140] kappaṭṭhakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “saṅghaṃ samaggaṃ bhetvāna, kappaṃ nirayamhi paccatī”ti “sakalampi kappaṃ saṅghabhedako niraye tiṭṭhatī”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi rājagirikānaṃ; te sandhāya kappaṭṭhoti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Buddho ca loketi idaṃ vinā buddhuppādena saṅghabhedassa abhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Kappo ca saṇṭhāti saṅgho ca bhijjatītiādi “yadi so sakalaṃ kappaṃ tiṭṭhati, saṇṭhahanato paṭṭhāya taṃ kammaṃ katvā tattha uppajjitvā tiṭṭheyyā”ti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Atītantiādi heṭṭhā vuttādhippāyameva. Kappaṭṭho iddhimāti pañhe bhāvanāmayaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati, parasamaye panassa jātimayaṃ iddhiṃ icchanti, taṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Chandiddhipādotiādi “jātimayāya iddhiyā iddhimāti laddhimattametaṃ, kiṃ tena, yadi panassa iddhi atthi, iminā nayena iddhipādā bhāvitā bhaveyyu”nti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Āpāyiko nerayikoti suttaṃ yaṃ so ekaṃ kappaṃ asītibhāge katvā tato ekabhāgamattaṃ kālaṃ tiṭṭheyya, taṃ āyukappaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, tasmā asādhakanti.

654-657. Now comes the discussion on remaining for an aeon. Here, with reference to those who hold the view that, “Having divided a harmonious Saṅgha, one is cooked in hell for an aeon,” or, “A schismatic of the Saṅgha remains in hell for an entire aeon”—such as the Rājagirikās—the question, “Does one remain for an aeon?”, is the proponent's, and the admission is the other's. The phrase, “And a Buddha in the world,” is stated to show that without the arising of a Buddha, there can be no schism in the Saṅgha. The statement, “The aeon is established, and the Saṅgha is divided,” and so on, is made to illustrate that, “if one were to remain for the entire aeon, one would have to be reborn there and remain, having performed that deed, from the very establishment of the aeon.” The term “past,” and so on, has the same meaning as previously explained. Regarding the question, “Is one who remains for an aeon possessed of psychic power?”, the rejection is made with reference to power born of meditative development; but in the doctrine of others, they hold that such a one has innate psychic power, and the acknowledgment is made with reference to that.
