The phrase, “The basis of psychic power that is will,” and so on, is stated to challenge: “This view that one is ‘endowed with psychic power’ through innate ability is a mere view—what of that? But if one truly possesses psychic power, then the bases of psychic power must have been developed in this way.” The sutta stating, “Bound for the lower realms, for hell,” where one would remain for a period equivalent to one part of an aeon divided into eighty, is said with reference to a lifespan-aeon. Therefore, it is not a valid proof.

Kappaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discussion on Remaining for an Aeon.

2. Kusalapaṭilābhakathāvaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Discussion on the Acquisition of Wholesome States

658-659. Idāni [P 0.0141] kusalapaṭilābhakathā nāma hoti. Tattha kappaṭṭho sakasamaye kāmāvacarakusalameva [V 0.0232] paṭilabhati. Yena pana taṃ upapattiṃ paṭibāheyya, taṃ mahaggataṃ lokuttaraṃ vā na paṭilabhati. Yesaṃ pana imaṃ vibhāgaṃ akatvā aviseseneva “so kusalacittaṃ na paṭilabhatī”ti [M 0.0235] laddhi, seyyathāpi uttarāpathakānaṃ; tesaṃ vibhāgadassanena taṃ laddhiṃ bhindituṃ pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

658-659. Now comes the discussion on the acquisition of wholesome states. Therein, one who remains for an aeon, in his own time, acquires only sense-sphere wholesome states. But he does not acquire that which would prevent that rebirth, namely, the exalted or supramundane. But with reference to those who, without making this distinction, hold the view that 'he does not acquire wholesome consciousness' without differentiation—as is the case with the Uttarāpathakas—the question is the proponent's, in order to break that view by showing the distinction, and the admission is the other's. The rest here is clear in meaning.

Kusalapaṭilābhakathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discussion on the Acquisition of Wholesome States.

3. Anantarāpayuttakathāvaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Discussion on What is Immediately Consequential

660-662. Idāni anantarāpayuttakathā nāma hoti. Tattha anantarāpayutto nāma yena khandhabhedato anantarā vipākadāyakaṃ mātughātādi ānantariyakammaṃ āṇattaṃ. Tattha yassa niyatāya āṇattiyā āṇatto taṃ kammaṃ karissati, so atthasādhikāya cetanāya uppāditattā micchattaniyato hoti, abhabbo sammattaniyāmaṃ okkamituṃ. Yassa aniyatāya āṇattiyā āṇatto taṃ kammaṃ karissati, so atthasādhikāya cetanāya anuppāditattā na micchattaniyato, bhabbo sammattaniyāmaṃ okkamitunti idaṃ sakasamaye sanniṭṭhānaṃ. Yesaṃ pana “aniyatāyapi āṇattiyā abhabboyeva sammattaniyāmaṃ okkamitu”nti laddhi, seyyathāpi uttarāpathakānaṃ; tesaṃ taṃ laddhiṃ bhindituṃ sakavādī pubbapakkhaṃ datvā anantarāpayuttoti paravādinā attānaṃ pucchāpeti. Tenettha paṭhamapucchā paravādissa, atthasādhikacetanāya abhāvaṃ sandhāya paṭiññā sakavādissa. Tato paravādī mātughātādikammassa āṇattattāva “so micchattaniyato”ti maññati. Tasmā micchattaniyāmañcāti [P 0.0142] pañhaṃ pucchati. Sakavādī pana ekassa puggalassa dvinnaṃ niyāmānaṃ anokkantimattameva sandhāya na hevanti paṭikkhipati.

Now, there is the discussion called 'On One Incited to an Act with Immediate Result.' Therein, 'one incited to an act with immediate result' refers to one who has been commanded to perform an action with immediate result, such as matricide, which yields its result immediately after the breakup of the aggregates. In this regard, one who is commanded by a fixed command will perform that action; because it is produced by a purposeful intention, he is fixed in wrongness and incapable of entering the fixed course of rightness. One who is commanded by an unfixed command will perform that action; because it is not produced by a purposeful intention, he is not fixed in wrongness and is capable of entering the fixed course of rightness—this is the conclusion in one's own doctrine. However, for those who hold the view that 'even by an unfixed command, one is incapable of entering the fixed course of rightness'—as is the case with the Northerners—to break that view, the proponent of one's own doctrine, having presented the preliminary argument, has the opponent question him regarding 'one incited to an act with immediate result.' Therefore, here the first question is from the opponent, and the admission, referring to the absence of purposeful intention, is from the proponent of one's own doctrine. Then the opponent thinks that 'he is fixed in wrongness' simply because the action of matricide, etc., has been commanded. Therefore, he asks the question: 'And is he fixed in wrongness?' But the proponent of one's own doctrine rejects it, saying 'Not so,' referring merely to the non-entry of one individual into the two fixed courses.

Nanu taṃ kammanti mātughātādikammaṃ. Tattha aniyatāṇattiṃ sandhāya “āmantā”ti paṭiññā sakavādissa. Aniyatampi hi āṇattiṃ payojetvā ṭhitassa “ananucchavikaṃ mayā kata”nti kukkuccaṃ uppajjateva, vippaṭisāro jāyateva. Hañcītiādi kukkuccuppattimattaṃ gahetvā paravādinā laddhipatiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

'Is that not an action?'—namely, the action of matricide, etc. Therein, referring to the unfixed command, the admission 'Yes' is from the proponent of one's own doctrine. For even in one who has instigated an unfixed command, remorse (kukkucca) certainly arises, thinking, 'I have done something unsuitable,' and regret certainly arises. The phrase 'If so,' etc., is stated by the opponent to establish their doctrine, taking only the mere arising of remorse.

661. Idāni [V 0.0233] yassa aniyatāṇattikassāpi anantarāpayuttassa paravādinā sammattaniyāmokkamanaṃ paṭisiddhaṃ, tameva puggalaṃ gahetvā anantarāpayutto [M 0.0236] puggalo abhabboti pucchā sakavādissa, attano laddhivasena paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ sakavādī “abhabbo nāma mātughātādikammānaṃ kārako, kiṃ te tena tāni kammāni katānī”ti codetuṃ mātā jīvitā voropitātiādimāha. Itaro tesaṃ vatthūnaṃ arogatāya tathārūpaṃ kiriyaṃ apassanto “na heva”nti paṭikkhipati.

661. Now, taking that very person for whom, though he was incited to an act with immediate result by an unfixed command, the opponent has denied entry into the fixed course of rightness, the proponent of one's own doctrine asks the question: 'Is a person incited to an act with immediate result incapable?' and the admission, according to his own doctrine, is from the other. Then, to accuse him, the proponent of one's own doctrine says, 'An incapable person is one who performs actions such as matricide. Have those actions been done by you?' and so on, 'Was your mother deprived of life?' The other, not seeing such an action in those instances due to their being unharmed, rejects it, saying, 'Certainly not.'

Taṃ kammaṃ paṭisaṃharitvāti aniyatāṇattikammaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tañhi “mā kho mayā āṇattaṃ ākāsī”ti āṇattaṃ nivārentena paṭisaṃhaṭaṃ nāma hoti. Paṭisaṃhaṭattāyeva cettha kukkuccaṃ paṭivinoditaṃ, vippaṭisāro paṭivinīto nāma hoti. Evaṃ santepi panettha purimāṇattiyāyeva niyatabhāvaṃ maññamāno paravādī “āmantā”ti paṭijānāti. Atha naṃ sakavādī tassa kammassa paṭisaṃhaṭabhāvaṃ sampaṭicchāpetvā attano laddhiṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā hañcītiādimāha.

The phrase 'having withdrawn that action' is stated with reference to the action of an unfixed command. For it is called 'withdrawn' when one prevents the commanded action by saying, 'Do not do what was commanded by me!' And here, by the very fact of its being withdrawn, remorse is dispelled, and regret is said to be removed. Even so, the opponent, thinking that the previous command is fixed, admits by saying, 'Yes.' Then the proponent of one's own doctrine, having made him accept the fact that that action was withdrawn and having established his own doctrine, says, 'If so,' etc.

662. Puna anantarāpayuttoti pariyosānapañhe paṭhamapañhe viya pucchā paravādissa, paṭiññā sakavādissa. Nanu taṃ kammanti anuyogo paravādissa, paṭisaṃhaṭakālato pubbe payuttakālaṃ sandhāya paṭiññā sakavādissa. Payuttapubbatāmattaṃ gahetvā aniyatāṇattivasena hañcīti laddhipatiṭṭhāpanaṃ paravādissa. Ayaṃ pana laddhi ayoniso patiṭṭhitattā appatiṭṭhitāva hotīti.

662. Again, regarding 'one incited to an act with immediate result,' in the concluding question, as in the first question, the question is from the opponent, and the admission is from the proponent of one's own doctrine. 'Is that not an action?' is the retort from the opponent, and the admission from the proponent of one's own doctrine refers to the time of instigation before the time of withdrawal. By merely taking the fact of its prior instigation, the opponent establishes a doctrine by way of an unfixed command, saying 'If so.' But this doctrine, because it is improperly established, is simply unestablished.

Anantarāpayuttakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on One Incited to an Act with Immediate Result.

4. Niyatassa niyāmakathāvaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Discussion on the Fixed Course of One Who is Fixed.

663-664. Idāni [P 0.0143] niyatassa niyāmakathā nāma hoti. Tattha duvidho niyāmo – micchattaniyāmo ca ānantariyakammaṃ, sammattaniyāmo ca ariyamaggo. Ime dve niyāme ṭhapetvā añño niyāmo nāma natthi. Sabbepi hi sesā tebhūmakadhammā aniyatā nāma. Tehi samannāgatopi [V 0.0234] aniyatoyeva. Buddhehi pana attano ñāṇabalena “ayaṃ satto anāgate bodhiṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti byākato bodhisatto puññussadattā niyatoti vuccati. Iti imaṃ vohāramattaṃ gahetvā “pacchimabhaviko bodhisatto [M 0.0237] tāya jātiyā bhabbo dhammaṃ abhisametu”nti adhippāyena “niyato niyāmaṃ okkamatī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyāparaseliyānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Micchattaniyatotiādi aññena niyāmena niyatassa aññaniyāmābhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Pubbe maggaṃ bhāvetvātiādi niyāmappabhedadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Satipaṭṭhānantiādi ekasmimpi niyāme dhammappabhedadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Bhabbo bodhisattoti vacanaṃ kevalaṃ bodhisattassa bhabbataṃ dīpeti, na niyatassa niyāmokkamanaṃ, tasmā asādhakaṃ. So hi pubbe ekenapi niyatadhammena aniyato bodhimūle saccadassanena niyāmaṃ okkantoti.

Now there is the discussion called 'On the Fixed Course of One Who is Fixed.' Herein, there are two kinds of fixed courses: the fixed course of wrongness, which is an action with immediate result, and the fixed course of rightness, which is the noble path. Apart from these two fixed courses, there is no other fixed course. Indeed, all other phenomena of the three realms are called unfixed. Even one endowed with them remains unfixed. However, the Bodhisatta, declared by the Buddhas through their power of knowledge as, 'This being will attain enlightenment in the future,' is called 'fixed' due to the abundance of merit. Thus, taking this mere conventional expression, with reference to those whose tenet is that 'the Bodhisatta in his final existence is capable of realizing the Dhamma in that birth' and that 'the fixed one enters the fixed course'—such as the Pubbaseliyas and Aparaseliyas—the question is from the proponent of one's own doctrine, and the admission is from the other. The phrase 'fixed in wrongness' and so forth is stated to show the absence of another fixed course for one who is fixed by a particular fixed course. The phrase 'having previously developed the path' and so forth is stated to show the divisions of the fixed course. The phrase 'foundations of mindfulness' and so forth is stated to show the divisions of phenomena within a single fixed course. The statement 'the Bodhisatta is capable' merely indicates the Bodhisatta's capability, not the entry of the fixed one into the fixed course, and thus it is inconclusive. For he, though previously unfixed by even a single fixed phenomenon, enters the fixed course through the vision of truth at the root of enlightenment.

Niyatassa niyāmakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on the Fixed Course of One Who is Fixed.

5. Nivutakathāvaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Discussion on the Concealed.

665-667. Idāni nivutakathā nāma hoti. Tattha suddhassa suddhakiccābhāvato nīvaraṇehi nivuto ophuṭo pariyonaddho ca nīvaraṇaṃ jahatīti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi uttarāpathakānaṃ; te sandhāya nivutotipucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Ratto rāgantiādi nivutassa nīvaraṇajahane dosadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Parisuddhe pariyodātetiādi vikkhambhanavisuddhiyā visuddhassa [P 0.0144] samucchedavisuddhidassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tassa evaṃ jānatotiādi jānato passato āsavakkhayaṃ dīpeti, na nivutassa nīvaraṇajahanaṃ, tasmā asādhakanti.

Now there is the discussion on being covered. Herein, the question, 'Is one covered?', is for the proponent of his own view, and the admission is for the other, this being directed at those whose tenet is that one who is covered, enveloped, and bound by the hindrances abandons the hindrances, because for one who is pure there is no function of purification; such as the Uttarāpathakas. The phrase 'one is stained by lust' and so forth is stated to show the fault in the abandonment of hindrances by one who is covered. The phrase 'purified, cleansed' and so forth is stated to show the purity of eradication for one who is pure through the purity of suppression. The phrase 'for one who knows thus' and so forth indicates the destruction of the taints for one who knows and sees, not the abandonment of hindrances by one who is covered; therefore, it is not a valid proof.

Nivutakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discussion on Being Covered.

6. Sammukhībhūtakathāvaṇṇanā

6. The Exposition of the Discussion on Being Face-to-Face.

668-670. Idāni [V 0.0235] sammukhībhūtakathā nāma hoti. Tattha sammukhībhūtoti saṃyojanānaṃ sammukhībhāvaṃ tehi samaṅgībhāvaṃ upagato. Sesamettha nivutakathāsadisamevāti.

Now there is the discussion on being face-to-face. Herein, 'face-to-face' means one who has attained the state of being face-to-face with the fetters, the state of being endowed with them. The rest here is just like the discussion on being covered.

Sammukhībhūtakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discussion on Being Face-to-Face.

7. Samāpanno assādetītikathāvaṇṇanā

7. The Exposition of the Discussion on 'One Who Has Attained Relishes'.

671-673. Idāni [M 0.0238] samāpanno assādetītikathā nāma hoti. Tattha “paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, so tadassādetī”tiādivacanaṃ (a. ni. 4.123) nissāya “samāpanno assādeti, sā cassa jhānanikanti jhānārammaṇā hotī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ, te sandhāya samāpannoti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Taṃ jhānaṃ tassa jhānassa ārammaṇanti pañhesu tasseva tadārammaṇataṃ apassanto suttavirodhabhayena paṭikkhipati, “tadassādetī”tivacanamattena paṭijānāti. So tadassādetīti suttaṃ jhānalābhino jhānā vuṭṭhāya jhānassādaṃ sādheti, na antosamāpattiyaṃyeva jhānanikantiyā jhānārammaṇataṃ, tasmā asādhakanti.

Now there is the discussion on 'One Who Has Attained Relishes.' Herein, based on the statement, 'Having entered upon and abided in the first jhāna, he relishes that' (cf. A.N. 4.123), the question, 'Does one who has attained relish?', is for the proponent of his own view, and the admission is for the other, this being directed at those whose tenet is that 'one who has attained relishes, and that delight in jhāna has jhāna as its object'; such as the Andhakas. In the questions concerning that jhāna being the object of that jhāna, not seeing that it has itself as its object, he rejects this out of fear of contradicting the sutta, and affirms it merely on the basis of the statement 'he relishes that.' The sutta passage 'he relishes that' establishes that one who has obtained jhāna, having emerged from jhāna, enjoys the taste of jhāna, not that the delight in jhāna having jhāna as its object occurs within the attainment itself. Therefore, this is not a valid proof.

Samāpanno assādetītikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discussion on 'One Who Has Attained Relishes'.

8. Asātarāgakathāvaṇṇanā

8. The Exposition of the Discussion on Lust for the Unpleasant.

674. Idāni [P 0.0145] asātarāgakathā nāma hoti. Tattha “yaṃkiñci vedanaṃ vedeti sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā, so taṃ vedanaṃ abhinandati abhivadatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.409) sutte diṭṭhābhinandanavasena vuttaṃ. “Abhinandatī”tivacanaṃ nissāya “dukkhavedanāyapi rāgassādavasena [V 0.0236] abhinandanā hoti. Tasmā atthi asātarāgo”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi uttarāpathakānaṃ; te sandhāya atthi asātarāgoti pucchā sakavādissa. Tattha asātarāgoti asāte dukkhavedayite “aho vata me etadeva bhaveyyā”ti rajjanā. Āmantāti laddhivasena paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

674. Now there is the discussion on lust for the unpleasant. Herein, in the sutta, it is said: 'Whatever feeling one feels—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one delights in that feeling, welcomes it' (cf. M.N. 1.409). This is stated in terms of delighting in views. Based on the statement 'delights in,' the question, 'Is there lust for the unpleasant?', is for the proponent of his own view, this being directed at those whose tenet is that 'there is delighting in painful feeling too, due to the relish of lust. Therefore, there is lust for the unpleasant'; such as the Uttarāpathakas. Here, 'lust for the unpleasant' means being impassioned towards an unpleasant, painful feeling with the thought, 'Oh, that this very thing might be for me!' The admission 'Yes' is from the other, in accordance with his tenet. The rest of the meaning here is evident.

675. So taṃ vedanaṃ abhinandatīti sutte pana vinivaṭṭetvā dukkhavedanameva ārabbha rāguppatti nāma natthi, samūhaggahaṇena pana vedayitalakkhaṇaṃ dhammaṃ dukkhavedanameva vā attato samanupassanto diṭṭhimaññanāsaṅkhātāya diṭṭhābhinandanāya vedanaṃ abhinandati, dukkhāya vedanāya vipariṇāmaṃ abhinandati, dukkhāya vedanāya abhibhūto tassā paṭipakkhaṃ kāmasukhaṃ patthayantopi [M 0.0239] dukkhavedanaṃ abhinandati nāma. Evaṃ dukkhavedanāya abhinandanā hotīti adhippāyo. Tasmā asādhakametaṃ asātarāgassāti.

675. However, in the sutta passage 'he delights in that feeling,' if one sets aside the others, there is no such thing as an arising of lust that has only painful feeling as its object. Rather, by grasping the aggregate, one who regards the phenomenon characterized by feeling—or even just painful feeling—as self, delights in feeling through the delight in views, which is reckoned as the conceit of views. One delights in the change of painful feeling. And being overwhelmed by painful feeling, while longing for sensual pleasure as its opposite, one is said to 'delight in painful feeling' only by name. This is the intended meaning of how there is delight in painful feeling. Therefore, this is not a valid proof for lust for the unpleasant.

Asātarāgakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discussion on Lust for the Unpleasant.

9. Dhammataṇhāabyākatātikathāvaṇṇanā

9. The Exposition of the Discussion on 'Craving for Phenomena is Indeterminate'.

676-680. Idāni dhammataṇhā abyākatātikathā nāma hoti. Tattha rūpataṇhā…pe… dhammataṇhāti imāsu chasu taṇhāsu yasmā sabbapacchimā taṇhā dhammataṇhāti vuttā, tasmā sā abyākatāti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesapañhānaṃ [P 0.0146] pāḷiyā attho niyyāti. Kāmataṇhātiādīhi tīhi koṭṭhāsehi chapi taṇhā saṅkhipitvā dassitā. Rūpādīsu hi chasu ārammaṇesu kāmassādavasena pavattā taṇhā kāmataṇhā. “Bhavissati attā ca loko cā”ti sassatadiṭṭhisahagatā taṇhā bhavataṇhā. “Na bhavissatī”ti ucchedadiṭṭhisahagatā taṇhā vibhavataṇhāti. Nanu sā dhammataṇhāti padaṃ taṇhāya dhammārammaṇaṃ ārabbha pavattiṃ dīpeti, na abyākatabhāvaṃ tasmā asādhakanti.

Now there is the discussion on 'Craving for Phenomena is Indeterminate.' Herein, among the six cravings—craving for forms... and so forth... craving for phenomena—the question is for the proponent of his own view, and the admission is for the other, this being directed at those whose tenet is that since the very last craving is called 'craving for phenomena,' it is therefore indeterminate; such as the Pubbaseliyas. The meaning of the remaining questions is deduced from the Pāli text. The six cravings are shown summarized into three divisions: 'sensual craving,' and so forth. For, craving that proceeds by way of the relish of sensual pleasure in the six objects beginning with forms is 'sensual craving.' Craving accompanied by the eternalist view, 'the self and the world will exist,' is 'craving for existence.' Craving accompanied by the annihilationist view, 'it will not exist,' is 'craving for non-existence.' Surely, the term 'craving for phenomena' indicates the proceeding of craving in relation to a mental phenomenon as its object, not its indeterminate nature. Therefore, this is not a valid proof.

Dhammataṇhā abyākatātikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discussion on 'Craving for Phenomena is Indeterminate'.

10. Dhammataṇhānadukkhasamudayotikathāvaṇṇanā

10. The Exposition of the Discussion on 'Craving for Phenomena is Not the Origin of Suffering'.

681-685. Idāni [V 0.0237] dhammataṇhā nadukkhasamudayotikathā nāma hoti. Tatrāpi yasmā sā dhammataṇhāti vuttā, tasmā na dukkhasamudayoti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyānaṃyeva; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesaṃ purimakathāsadisamevāti.

Now there is the discussion on 'Craving for Phenomena is Not the Origin of Suffering.' Here too, the question is for the proponent of his own view, and the admission is for the other, this being directed at those whose tenet is that since it is called 'craving for phenomena,' it is therefore not the origin of suffering; such as the Pubbaseliyas. The rest is just like the previous discussion.

Dhammataṇhā nadukkhasamudayotikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discussion on 'Craving for Phenomena is Not the Origin of Suffering'.

Terasamo vaggo.

The Thirteenth Chapter.

14. Cuddasamavaggo

14. The Fourteenth Chapter.

1. Kusalākusalapaṭisandahanakathāvaṇṇanā

1. The Exposition of the Discussion on the Relinking of Wholesome and Unwholesome.

686-690. Idāni [P 0.0147][M 0.0240] kusalākusalapaṭisandahanakathā nāma hoti. Tattha kusalaṃ vā akusalassa, akusalaṃ vā kusalassa anantarā uppajjanakaṃ nāma natthīti tesaṃ aññamaññaṃ paṭisandhānaṃ na yujjati. Ye pana yasmā ekavatthusmiññeva rajjati virajjati ca, tasmā taṃ aññamaññaṃ paṭisandahatīti laddhiṃ gahetvā ṭhitā, seyyathāpi mahāsaṅghikā; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa; paṭiññā itarassa. Āvaṭṭanā paṇidhīti ubhayaṃ āvajjanasseva nāmaṃ. Tañhi bhavaṅgaṃ āvaṭṭetīti āvaṭṭanā. Bhavaṅgārammaṇato aññasmiṃ ārammaṇe cittaṃ paṇidahati ṭhapetīti paṇidhi. Kusalaṃ anāvaṭṭentassāti yaṃ taṃ akusalānantaraṃ paṭisandahantaṃ kusalaṃ uppajjati, taṃ anāvaṭṭentassa uppajjatīti pucchati. Itaro pana vinā āvajjanena kusalassa uppattiṃ apassanto paṭikkhipati. Kusalaṃ ayoniso manasikarototi idaṃ yadi akusalānantaraṃ kusalaṃ uppajjeyya, akusalasseva āvajjanena ayoniso manasikaroto uppajjeyyāti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ yathāpāḷimeva niyyāti. Nanu yasmiṃyeva vatthusminti vacanaṃ ekārammaṇe sarāgavirāguppattiṃ dīpeti, na kusalākusalānaṃ anantarataṃ, tasmā asādhakanti.

686-690. Now there is the discussion called 'The Relinking of Wholesome and Unwholesome'. Herein, there is no such thing as the wholesome arising immediately after the unwholesome, or the unwholesome immediately after the wholesome; thus their mutual relinking is not valid. However, with reference to those who hold the view that because one becomes attached to and detached from the very same object, therefore the one is relinked to the other—such as the Mahāsāṅghikas—the question is for the proponent of one's own view; the admission is from the other. 'Averting' (āvaṭṭanā) and 'directing' (paṇidhi) are both names for advertence (āvajjanā). For it averts the life-continuum, hence it is called 'averting.' It directs and establishes the mind on an object other than the object of the life-continuum, hence it is called 'directing.' 'For one for whom the wholesome does not avert' (kusalaṃ anāvaṭṭentassa)—this asks if that wholesome which, being relinked, arises immediately after the unwholesome, arises for one who does not avert. The other, not seeing the arising of the wholesome without advertence, rejects it. 'For one who attends unwisely to the wholesome' (kusalaṃ ayoniso manasikaroto)—this is said for the purpose of censure: if the wholesome were to arise immediately after the unwholesome, it would arise for one who attends unwisely, by the very advertence of the unwholesome. The rest proceeds just as in the Pāli. The statement, 'Is it not in the very same object?' reveals the arising of attachment and detachment in a single object, not the immediacy of the wholesome and unwholesome; therefore, it is inconclusive.

Kusalākusalapaṭisandahanakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on the Relinking of Wholesome and Unwholesome.

2. Saḷāyatanuppattikathāvaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Discussion on the Arising of the Six Sense Bases.

691-692. Idāni [P 0.0148][V 0.0238] saḷāyatanuppattikathā nāma hoti. Tattha upapattesiyena paṭisandhicittena saheva opapātikānaṃ saḷāyatanaṃ uppajjati. Gabbhaseyyakānaṃ ajjhattikāyatanesu manāyatanakāyāyatanāneva paṭisandhikkhaṇe uppajjanti. Sesāni cattāri sattasattatirattimhi. Tāni ca kho yena kammunā paṭisandhi gahitā, tasseva aññassa vā katattāti ayaṃ sakasamaye vādo. Yesaṃ pana ekakammasambhavattā sampannasākhāviṭapānaṃ rukkhādīnaṃ aṃkuro viya bījamattaṃ saḷāyatanaṃ mātukucchismiṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇeyeva uppajjatīti laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyānaṃ; te sandhāya saḷāyatananti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sabbaṅgapaccaṅgītiādi saḷāyatane [M 0.0241] sati evarūpo hutvā okkameyyāti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Mātukucchigatassāti pucchā paravādissa. Parato mātukucchigatassa pacchā kesāti pucchā sakavādissa. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

691-692. Now there is the discussion called 'The Arising of the Six Sense Bases'. Herein, for spontaneously born beings, the six sense bases arise together with the rebirth-linking consciousness. For womb-born beings, at the moment of rebirth-linking, only the mind base and the body base among the internal sense bases arise. The remaining four arise in seventy-seven nights. And that these arise due to the same kamma by which rebirth was taken, or due to the action of another—this is a doctrine in our own system. But some, such as the Pubbaseliyas, hold the view that, because they arise from a single kamma, the six sense bases arise as a mere seed in the mother's womb at the very moment of rebirth-linking, like the sprout of trees that are complete with branches and foliage. With reference to them, the question 'The six sense bases?' is for the proponent of one's own view; the admission is from the other. The words 'With all limbs and minor limbs complete,' etc., are said for the purpose of censure, implying: 'If the six sense bases were present, one would have to enter the womb having become of such a form.' The question 'For one who has entered the mother's womb?' is for the opponent. The question 'For one who has entered the mother's womb, does hair arise afterwards?' is for the proponent of one's own view. The rest here is clear in meaning.

Saḷāyatanuppattikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on the Arising of the Six Sense Bases.

3. Anantarapaccayakathāvaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Discussion on the Contiguity Condition.

693-697. Idāni anantarapaccayakathā nāma hoti. Tattha naccagītādīsu rūpadassanasaddasavanādīnaṃ lahuparivattitaṃ disvā “imāni viññāṇāni aññamaññassa anantarā uppajjantī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi uttarāpathakānaṃ; te sandhāya cakkhuviññāṇassāti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sotaviññāṇaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃyevāti yadi cakkhuviññāṇassa anantarā uppajjeyya, vipākamanodhātu viya rūpārammaṇaṃ siyāti codetuṃ vuttaṃ. Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati sotaviññāṇanti pañhesu suttābhāvena paṭikkhipitvā anantaruppattiṃ sallakkhento laddhivasena paṭijānāti. Taññeva cakkhuviññāṇaṃ [P 0.0149] taṃ sotaviññāṇanti yathā paṭhamajavanānantaraṃ dutiyajavanaṃ manoviññāṇabhāvena taññeva hoti, kiṃ te tathā etampi dvayaṃ ekamevāti pucchati. Iminā nayena sabbavāresu attho veditabbo. Naccati gāyatītiādivacanaṃ [V 0.0239] ārammaṇasamodhāne lahuparivattitāya vokiṇṇabhāvaṃ dīpeti, na anantarapaccayataṃ, tasmā asādhakanti.

693-697. Now there is the discussion called 'The Contiguity Condition'. Herein, some—such as the Uttarāpathakas—hold the view that 'these consciousnesses arise immediately after one another,' having seen the rapid succession in such things as dancing and singing, the seeing of forms, the hearing of sounds, and so on. With reference to them, the question concerning eye-consciousness is for the proponent of one's own view; the admission is from the other. The censure is stated thus: 'If ear-consciousness were to arise immediately after eye-consciousness, it would have form as its object, just like the resultant mind-element.' In the questions, having rejected the proposition 'ear-consciousness arises dependent on the eye and on forms' due to the absence of a sutta, he, considering the immediate arising in accordance with his view, admits it. He asks: 'Is that very eye-consciousness that ear-consciousness?' This is to ask: 'Just as the second impulsion following the first impulsion is the very same in being mind-consciousness, are these two also one and the same?' In this way, the meaning should be understood in all cases. The statement 'dances, sings,' and so on, illustrates the intermingled state due to the rapid succession when objects come together, not the contiguity condition. Therefore, it is inconclusive.

Anantarapaccayakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on the Contiguity Condition.

4. Ariyarūpakathāvaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Discussion on Noble Form.

698-699. Idāni ariyarūpakathā nāma hoti. Tattha sammāvācākammantā rūpaṃ, tañca kho “sabbaṃ rūpaṃ cattāri ca mahābhūtāni catunnañca mahābhūtānaṃ upādāyarūpa”nti (ma. ni. 3.67) vacanato upādāyarūpanti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi uttarāpathakānaṃ; te sandhāya ariyarūpaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāyāti pucchā [M 0.0242] sakavādissa. Tattha ariyānaṃ rūpaṃ, ariyaṃ vā rūpanti ariyarūpaṃ. Āmantāti laddhiyaṃ ṭhatvā paṭiññā itarassa. Kusalanti puṭṭho laddhivaseneva paṭijānāti. Anāsavapucchādīsupi eseva nayo. Yaṃ kiñci rūpanti suttaṃ ṭhapetvā bhūtāni sesarūpassa upādābhāvaṃ dīpeti, na sammāvācākammantānaṃ. Tesañhi rūpamattaññeva asiddhaṃ, kuto upādārūpatā; tasmā asādhakanti.

698-699. Now there is the discussion called 'Noble Form'. Herein, with reference to those—such as the Uttarāpathakas—whose view is that right speech and right action are form, and that this is derived form according to the statement, 'All form consists of the four great elements and form derived from the four great elements' (MN 3.67), the question is for the proponent of one's own view: 'Is noble form derived from the great elements?' Herein, 'noble form' means the form of the noble ones, or form that is noble. The other's admission, standing on his view, is 'Yes.' When asked, 'Is it wholesome?' he admits it on the basis of his view. The same method applies to the questions about the taintless, and so on. The sutta statement, 'Whatever form there is,' indicates the derived nature of the remaining form, apart from the elements, but not of right speech and right action. For these, their nature as mere form is itself unestablished, so how could they be derived form? Therefore, it is inconclusive.

Ariyarūpakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on Noble Form.

5. Añño anusayotikathāvaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Discussion 'Latent Tendency is Another Thing'.

700-701. Idāni añño anusayotikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā puthujjano kusalābyākate citte vattamāne sānusayoti vattabbo, na pariyuṭṭhitoti tasmā añño anusayo, aññaṃ pariyuṭṭhānanti [P 0.0150] yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya añño kāmarāgānusayoti pucchā sakavādissa paṭiññā itarassa. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā anusayakathāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Sānusayotiādi pana tasmiṃ samaye anusayassa appahīnattā sānusayoti [V 0.0240] vattabbataṃ, anuppannattā ca pariyuṭṭhitoti avattabbataṃ dīpeti, na anusayapariyuṭṭhānānaṃ aññattaṃ, tasmā asādhakanti.

Now there is what is called the discussion, 'Is the Latent Tendency Another Thing?' Here, because an ordinary person, when a wholesome or indeterminate mind is occurring, should be said to have latent tendencies but not to be obsessed, therefore some—such as the Andhakas—hold that the latent tendency is one thing and obsession another. With reference to them, the question, 'Is the latent tendency of sensual lust another thing?' is posed by the Sakavādin, and the admission is made by the other. The rest should be understood in the way stated in the discussion on latent tendencies above. However, the phrase 'has latent tendencies,' and so on, indicates that at that time one is said to have latent tendencies because the latent tendency has not been abandoned, and that one cannot be said to be obsessed because obsession has not arisen. This does not indicate that the latent tendency and obsession are different; therefore, it is not a valid proof.

Añño anusayotikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion, 'Is the Latent Tendency Another Thing?'

6. Pariyuṭṭhānaṃ cittavippayuttantikathāvaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Discussion: 'Are Obsessions Disassociated from Consciousness?'

702. Idāni pariyuṭṭhānaṃ cittavippayuttantikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā aniccādito manasikarotopi rāgādayo uppajjanti. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “appekadā, bho bhāradvāja, asubhato manasikarissāmīti subhatova manasikarotī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.127). Tasmā pariyuṭṭhānaṃ cittavippayuttanti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃyeva; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

702. Now comes the discussion called, 'Are Obsessions Disassociated from Consciousness?' Here, this is because even while attending to impermanence and so forth, lust and other defilements arise. And this was said: 'Sometimes, friend Bhāradvāja, intending to attend to the unattractive, one attends to the attractive.' Therefore, the doctrine of those who hold that obsessions are disassociated from consciousness is just that of the Andhakas. With reference to them, the question is posed by the Sakavādin, and the admission is made by the other. The remainder here is clear in meaning.

Pariyuṭṭhānaṃ cittavippayuttantikathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discussion: 'Are Obsessions Disassociated from Consciousness?'

7. Pariyāpannakathāvaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Discussion on What is Comprised.

703-705. Idāni [M 0.0243] pariyāpannakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā kāmarāgo kāmadhātuṃ anuseti, kāmadhātupariyāpannoti ca vuccati, tasmā rūparāgārūparāgāpi rūpadhātuarūpadhātuyo anusenti. Rūpadhātuarūpadhātupariyāpannāyeva ca nāma hontīti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānañceva sammitiyānañca; te sandhāya rūparāgoti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa[P 0.0151]. Tattha anusetīti yathā kāmarāgo kāmavitakkasaṅkhātaṃ kāmadhātuṃ sahajātavasena anuseti, kiṃ te evaṃ rūparāgo rūpadhātunti pucchati. Pariyāpannoti yathā ca so tividhāya kāmadhātuyā kilesakāmavasena pariyāpannattā kāmadhātupariyāpanno, kiṃ te evaṃ rūparāgopi rūpadhātupariyāpannoti pucchati. Itaro panassa adhippāyaṃ asallakkhento kevalaṃ laddhivasena āmantāti [V 0.0241] paṭijānāti. Atha naṃ tamatthaṃ sallakkhāpetuṃ kusalavipākakiriyasaṅkhātehi samāpattesiyādīhi saṃsanditvā pucchituṃ samāpattesiyotiādimāha. Sesamettha yathāpāḷimeva niyyāti. Nanu kāmarāgotiādivacanampi kāmarāgasseva kāmadhātuyaṃ anusayabhāvaṃ pariyāpannatañca dīpeti, na itaresaṃ itaradhātūsūti.

703-705. Now comes the discussion called 'What is Comprised'. Here, since sensual desire underlies the sense-sphere realm and is called 'comprised in the sense-sphere realm,' similarly, desire for form and desire for the formless underlie the form and formless realms. Thus, they are called 'comprised in the form and formless realms'—this is the doctrine of those, such as the Andhakas and the Sammatiyas. It is with reference to them that the question concerning desire for form is posed by the proponent of one's own doctrine, and the admission is by the other. Here, 'underlies' means: just as sensual desire underlies the sense-sphere realm, which is characterized by sense-sphere thoughts, through co-nascence, does desire for form similarly underlie the form realm for you? —this is what is asked. 'Comprised' means: just as that sensual desire is comprised in the threefold sense-sphere realm by way of defilement-sensuality, is desire for form similarly comprised in the form realm for you? —this is what is asked. The other party, however, not discerning his intention, merely affirms based on their own doctrine. Then, to make him discern that meaning, he speaks of attainments and so forth, beginning with 'Is it an attainment?', connecting them with what is skillful, resultant, and functional, in order to question him. The remainder here should be understood just as it is in the text. Indeed, the statement 'sensual desire' and so forth indicates that sensual desire alone underlies and is comprised in the sense-sphere realm, not other desires in other realms.

Pariyāpannakathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discussion on What is Comprised.

8. Abyākatakathāvaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Discussion on the Indeterminate.

706-708. Idāni abyākatakathā nāma hoti. Tattha vipākakiriyarūpanibbānasaṅkhātaṃ catubbidhaṃ abyākataṃ avipākattā abyākatanti vuttaṃ. Diṭṭhigataṃ “sassato lokoti kho, vaccha, abyākatameta”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.416 thokaṃ visadisaṃ) sassatādibhāvena akathitattā. Yesaṃ pana imaṃ vibhāgaṃ aggahetvā purimābyākataṃ viya diṭṭhigatampi abyākatanti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānañceva uttarāpathakānañca; tesaṃ taṃ vibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ diṭṭhigataṃ abyākatanti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha yathāpāḷimeva niyyātīti.

706-708. Now comes the discussion called 'The Indeterminate'. Here, the fourfold indeterminate—namely, resultant, functional, material form, and Nibbāna—is said to be indeterminate because it is not a result. A dogmatic view is indeterminate because it is not stated in terms of eternalism and so forth, as in the phrase: 'Vaccha, that the world is eternal, that is indeterminate' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.416, slightly different). But for those whose doctrine, without grasping this distinction, holds a dogmatic view to be indeterminate like the former indeterminate—such as the Andhakas and the Uttarāpathakas; to show them this distinction, the question 'Is a dogmatic view indeterminate?' is posed by the proponent of one's own doctrine, and the admission is by the other. The remainder here should be understood just as it is in the text.

Abyākatakathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discussion on the Indeterminate.

9. Apariyāpannakathāvaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Discussion on What is Not Comprised.

709-710. Idāni [M 0.0244] apariyāpannakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā puthujjano jhānalābhī kāmesu vītarāgoti vattabbo hoti, na pana vigatadiṭṭhikoti[P 0.0152], tasmā diṭṭhigataṃ apariyāpannanti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha yathāpāḷimeva niyyātīti.

709-710. Now comes the discussion on what is not comprised. Here, since an ordinary person who has attained jhāna can be said to be free from lust for sensual pleasures but not free from wrong view, the doctrine of some—such as the Pubbaseliyas—is that a dogmatic view is not comprised. With reference to them, the question is posed by the Sakavādin, and the admission is made by the other. The remainder here proceeds just as in the Pāḷi text.

Apariyāpannakathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discussion on What is Not Comprised.

Cuddasamo vaggo.

The Fourteenth Section.

15. Pannarasamavaggo

15. The Fifteenth Section.

1. Paccayatākathāvaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Discussion on Conditionality.

711-717. Idāni [P 0.0153][V 0.0242] paccayatākathā nāma hoti. Tattha yo dhammo hetupaccayena paccayo, so yesaṃ hetupaccayena paccayo, tesaññeva yasmā ārammaṇānantarasamanantarapaccayena paccayo na hoti, yo vā ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo, so yasmā tesaṃyeva anantarasamanantarapaccayena paccayo na hoti, tasmā paccayatā vavatthitāti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṅghikānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha yathāpāḷimeva niyyātīti.

711-717. Now comes the discussion on conditionality. Here, since whatever state is a condition by way of root condition, for those very states for which it is a root condition, it is not a condition by way of object, contiguity, or immediacy condition; or whatever is a condition by way of object condition, for those very states, it is not a condition by way of contiguity or immediacy condition; therefore, 'conditionality is demarcated'—this is the doctrine of those such as the Mahāsaṅghikas. With reference to them, the question is posed by the Sakavādin, and the admission is made by the other. The remainder here proceeds just as in the Pāḷi text.

Paccayatākathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discussion on Conditionality.

2. Aññamaññapaccayakathāvaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Discussion on Mutual Conditionality.

718-719. Idāni aññamaññapaccayakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ samaye “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti ayameva tanti, “saṅkhārapaccayāpi avijjā”ti ayaṃ natthi, tasmā avijjāva saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo, na pana saṅkhārā avijjāyāti laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṅghikānaṃ; te sandhāya avijjāsaṅkhārādīnaṃ aññamaññapaccayatāpi atthīti dassetuṃ pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa[M 0.0245]. Avijjā saṅkhārenāti ettha apuññābhisaṅkhārova gahito. Tasmā saṅkhārapaccayāpi avijjāti ettha sahajātaaññamaññaatthiavigatasampayuttavasena paccayatā veditabbā. Upādānapaccayāpi taṇhāti ettha ṭhapetvā kāmupādānaṃ sesāni tīṇi upādānāni avijjāya saṅkhārā viya taṇhāya paccayā hontīti veditabbāni. Sesaṃ [P 0.0154] yathāpāḷimeva niyyāti. Jarāmaraṇapaccayāti pucchā paravādissa, nāmarūpaṃ viññāṇapaccayāti sakavādissāti.

718-719. Now comes the discussion on mutual conditionality. Here, for those whose doctrine is that 'with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise' is the only teaching, and 'with volitional formations as condition, ignorance arises' does not exist, therefore, their doctrine is that ignorance is a condition for volitional formations, but volitional formations are not a condition for ignorance, as with the Mahāsāṅghikas. With reference to them, to show that there is also mutual conditionality between ignorance, volitional formations, and so forth, the question is posed by the proponent of one's own view, and the affirmation is given by the other. Here, by 'ignorance with volitional formations,' only the unwholesome volitional formation is taken. Therefore, in 'with volitional formations as condition, ignorance,' the conditionality should be understood by way of co-nascence, mutuality, presence, non-disappearance, and association. Here, in 'with clinging as condition, craving,' excluding sensual clinging, the other three clingings should be understood to be conditions for craving, just as volitional formations are for ignorance. The rest proceeds just as in the Pāli text. The question 'with aging-and-death as condition?' is for the proponent of the opposing view, and 'name-and-form as condition for consciousness?' is for the proponent of one's own view.

Aññamaññapaccayakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on Mutual Conditionality.

3. Addhākathāvaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Discussion on Time.

720-721. Idāni [V 0.0243] addhākathā nāma hoti. Tattha “tīṇimāni, bhikkhave, kathāvatthūnī”ti (a. ni. 3.68) suttaṃ nissāya kālasaṅkhāto addhā nāma parinipphanno atthīti yesaṃ laddhi; tesaṃ “addhā nāma koci parinipphanno natthi aññatra kālapaññattimattā. Rūpādayo pana khandhāva parinipphannā”ti vibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ addhā parinipphannoti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “sace so parinipphanno, rūpādīsu anena aññatarena bhavitabba”nti codetuṃ rūpantiādimāha. Itaro paṭikkhipati. Sesaṃ yathāpāḷimeva niyyātīti.

720-721. Now comes the discussion on time. Here, the doctrine of some is that, based on the sutta 'There are, monks, these three grounds for discussion' (AN 3.68), time, reckoned as a period, is something that is an ultimate reality. To show them the distinction that 'time is not anything that is an ultimate reality apart from being a mere designation, but the aggregates such as form are ultimate realities,' the question 'Is time an ultimate reality?' is posed by the proponent of one's own view, and the affirmation is given by the other. Then, to challenge him by saying, 'If it is an ultimate reality, it must be one of form and so forth,' one says 'form,' and so forth. The other denies it. The rest proceeds just as in the Pāli text.

Addhākathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on Time.

4. Khaṇalayamuhuttakathāvaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Discussion on Moments, Instants, and Muhuttas.

722-723. Khaṇalayamuhuttakathāsupi eseva nayo. Sabbepi hete khaṇādayo addhāpariyāyā evāti.

722-723. The same method applies to the discussions on moments, instants, and muhuttas. For all these—moments and so forth—are simply terms for time.

Khaṇalayamuhuttakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on Moments, Instants, and Muhuttas.

5. Āsavakathāvaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Discussion on Taints.

724-725. Idāni āsavakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā catūhi āsavehi uttari añño āsavo nāma natthi, yena cattāro āsavā [M 0.0246] sāsavā siyuṃ, tasmā [P 0.0155] cattāro āsavā anāsavāti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi hetuvādānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi te āsavā anāsavā, evaṃ sante tehi maggādilakkhaṇappattehi bhavitabba”nti codetuṃ maggotiādimāha. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

724-725. Now comes the discussion on taints. Here, because there is no other taint beyond the four taints by which the four taints would be tainted, some hold the view that the four taints are untainted, such as the Hetuvādins. With reference to them, the question is posed by the proponent of one's own view, and the affirmation is given by the other. Then, to challenge them by saying, "If those taints are untainted, then they must possess the characteristics of the path and so forth," he says 'path,' and so forth. The rest here is of clear meaning.

Āsavakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on Taints.

6. Jarāmaraṇakathāvaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Discussion on Aging-and-Death.

726-727. Idāni [V 0.0244] jarāmaraṇakathā nāma hoti. Tattha jarāmaraṇaṃ nāma aparinipphannattā lokiyanti vā lokuttaranti vā na vattabbaṃ. “Lokiyā dhammā lokuttarā dhammā”ti hi duke jarāmaraṇaṃ neva lokiyapade, na lokuttarapade niddiṭṭhaṃ. Tattha yesaṃ imaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ anādiyitvā lokuttarānaṃ dhammānaṃ jarāmaraṇaṃ lokuttaranti laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṅghikānaṃ, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha yathāpāḷimeva niyyātīti.

726-727. Now comes the discussion on aging-and-death. Herein, aging-and-death cannot be said to be either mundane or supramundane because it is not an ultimate reality. For in the pair 'mundane phenomena and supramundane phenomena,' aging-and-death is not designated in either the mundane category or the supramundane category. With reference to those who, disregarding this characteristic, hold the view that the aging-and-death of supramundane phenomena is supramundane—such as the Mahāsāṅghikas—the question is posed by the proponent of one's own view, and the affirmation is given by the other. The rest here proceeds just as in the Pāli text.

Jarāmaraṇakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on Aging-and-Death.

7. Saññāvedayitakathāvaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Discussion on Perception and Feeling.

728-729. Idāni saññāvedayitakathā nāma hoti. Tattha saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti nāma na koci dhammo, catunnaṃ pana khandhānaṃ nirodho. Iti sā neva lokiyā na lokuttarā. Yasmā pana lokiyā na hoti, tasmā lokuttarāti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi hetuvādānaṃyeva; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesaṃ purimakathāsadisamevāti.

728-729. Now comes the discussion on perception and feeling. Herein, the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling is not any particular phenomenon, but the cessation of the four mental aggregates. Thus, it is neither mundane nor supramundane. However, since it is not mundane, the view that it is supramundane is held by some—such as the Hetuvādins. With reference to them, the question is posed by the proponent of one's own view, and the affirmation is given by the other. The rest is similar to the previous discussion.

Saññāvedayitakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on Perception and Feeling.

8. Dutiyasaññāvedayitakathāvaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Second Discussion on Perception and Feeling.

730-731. Idāni [P 0.0156][M 0.0247] yasmā sā lokuttarā na hoti, tasmā lokiyāti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi hetuvādānaṃ, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesaṃ purimasadisamevāti.

730-731. Now, since that attainment is not supramundane, some hold the view that it is mundane—such as the Hetuvādins. With reference to them, the question is posed by the proponent of one's own view, and the affirmation is given by the other. The rest is similar to the previous discussion.

Dutiyasaññāvedayitakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Second Discussion on Perception and Feeling.

9. Tatiyasaññāvedayitakathāvaṇṇanā

9. The Explanation of the Third Discussion on Perception and Feeling.

732. Idāni [V 0.0245] yasmā “asuko maraṇadhammo, asuko na maraṇadhammo”ti sattānaṃ maraṇadhammatāya niyāmo natthīti saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpannopi kālaṃ kareyyāti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi rājagirikānaṃ; tesaṃ samāpannāyapi maraṇadhammatāya maraṇasamayañca amaraṇasamayañca dassetuṃ pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ yasmā kālaṃ karontassa nāma maraṇantikehi phassādīhi bhavitabbaṃ, tasmā tenākārena codetuṃ atthītiādimāha.

732. Now, since there is no fixed rule for beings that 'this one is subject to death, this one is not subject to death,' some hold the view that even one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling might pass away—such as the Rājagirikas. For them, to demonstrate the time of death and the time of non-death even for one who has attained it and is subject to death, the question is posed by the proponent of one's own view, and the affirmation is given by the other. Then, because one who is passing away must experience contact and so forth near the time of death, therefore, to challenge him in that manner, he says 'there is,' and so forth.

Aphassakassa kālakiriyātiādīni puṭṭho sesasatte sandhāya paṭikkhipati visaṃ kameyyātiādīni puṭṭho samāpattiānubhāvaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Dutiyavāre sarīrapakatiṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Evaṃ sante pana samāpattiānubhāvo nāma na hoti, teneva na nirodhasamāpannoti anuyuñjati.

When asked about the death of one without contact and so forth, he rejects it with reference to other beings. When asked about 'could one die by poison?' and so forth, he rejects it with reference to the power of the attainment. In the second turn, he acknowledges it with reference to the nature of the body. But if this is so, then there is no such thing as the power of the attainment, and thus he is interrogated: 'Then he is not one who has attained cessation?'

733-734. Na kālaṃ kareyyāti pucchā paravādissa. Atthi so niyāmoti paravādissa pañhe pana yasmā evarūpo niyāmo nāma natthi, tasmā paṭikkhipati. Cakkhuviññāṇasamaṅgītiādi sakavādinā “niyāme asantepi maraṇasamayeneva marati, nāsamayenā”ti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tatrāyamadhippāyo – yadi niyāmābhāvena kālakiriyā bhaveyya, cakkhuviññāṇasamaṅginopi bhaveyya. Tato “pañcahi viññāṇehi na cavati, na upapajjatī”ti [P 0.0157] suttavirodho siyā. Yathā pana cakkhuviññāṇasamaṅgissa kālakiriyā na hoti, tathā nirodhasamāpannassāpīti.

733-734. 'He would not die'—this is the question of the opponent. Regarding the opponent's question, 'Is there such a fixed rule?', since there is no such fixed rule, he rejects it. 'Endowed with eye-consciousness' and so forth is said by the proponent to show that even in the absence of a fixed rule, one dies only at the time of death, not at an untimely moment. Herein, this is the intention: if death were to occur due to the absence of a fixed rule, it would also occur for one endowed with eye-consciousness. Then there would be a contradiction with the sutta, which states, 'One does not pass away or reappear with the five consciousnesses.' Just as death does not occur for one endowed with eye-consciousness, so too it does not occur for one who has attained cessation.

Tatiyasaññāvedayitakathāvaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Third Discussion on Perception and Feeling.

10. Asaññasattupikākathāvaṇṇanā

10. Exposition of the Discussion Pertaining to Non-percipient Beings

735. Idāni [M 0.0248] asaññasattupikākathā nāma hoti. Tattha saññāvirāgavasena pavattabhāvanā asaññasamāpattipi nirodhasamāpattipi saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti nāma. Iti dve [V 0.0246] saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpattiyo lokiyā ca lokuttarā ca. Tattha lokiyā puthujjanassa asaññasattupikā hoti, lokuttarā ariyānaṃ, sā ca nāsaññasattupikā. Imaṃ pana vibhāgaṃ akatvā avisesena saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti asaññasattupikāti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi hetuvādānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ yasmā asaññasamāpattiṃ samāpannassa alobhādayo atthi, na nirodhasamāpattiṃ, tasmā tesaṃ vasena codetuṃ atthītiādimāha.

735. Now comes the discussion called 'Pertaining to Non-percipient Beings'. Herein, the meditative development that proceeds by way of dispassion towards perception—both the attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation—is called the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling. Thus, there are two attainments of the cessation of perception and feeling: mundane and supramundane. Of these, the mundane one, belonging to an ordinary person, pertains to the realm of non-percipient beings, while the supramundane one belongs to the noble ones, and that does not pertain to the realm of non-percipient beings. But for those who, without making this distinction, hold the undifferentiated view that the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling pertains to the realm of non-percipient beings—such as the Hetuvādins—the question is posed by the proponent, and the admission is made by the other. Then, since for one who has attained the attainment of non-perception, non-greed and other wholesome qualities exist, but not for one who has attained the attainment of cessation, he says, beginning with 'there is', in order to challenge them on that basis.

736. Idhāpi asaññīti pañhe idha saññāvirāgavasena samāpannattā asaññitā anuññātā, tatrāpi asaññasatteneva. Tasmā imaṃ paṭiññaṃ gahetvā laddhiṃ patiṭṭhapentena chalena patiṭṭhāpitā hoti. Idha vā nirodhasamāpattiṃ sandhāya asaññitā anuññātā. Tatrāpi ito cutassa anāgāmino nirodhasamāpattimeva tasmāpi imāya paṭiññāya patiṭṭhāpitā laddhi appatiṭṭhitāyevāti.

736. Here too, in the question 'Is one non-percipient?', non-percipience is acknowledged because one has attained it by way of dispassion towards perception; there too, it is only as a non-percipient being. Therefore, when one establishes a doctrine by taking this admission, it is established through a trick. Or here, non-percipience is acknowledged with reference to the attainment of cessation. There too, for a non-returner who has passed away from here, it is only the attainment of cessation. Therefore, the doctrine established by this admission is indeed unfounded.

Asaññasattupikākathāvaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Discussion Pertaining to Non-percipient Beings.

11. Kammūpacayakathāvaṇṇanā

11. Exposition of the Discussion on the Accumulation of Kamma

737. Idāni kammūpacayakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ kammūpacayo [P 0.0158] nāma kammato añño cittavippayutto abyākato anārammaṇoti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānañceva sammitiyānañca; te sandhāya aññaṃ kammanti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi kammato añño kammūpacayo, phassāditopi aññena phassūpacayādinā bhavitabba”nti codetuṃ añño phassotiādimāha. Itaro laddhiyā abhāvena paṭikkhipati.

737. Now comes the discussion called 'The Accumulation of Kamma'. Herein, for those who hold the view that the accumulation of kamma is something other than kamma, dissociated from consciousness, indeterminate, and without an object—such as the Andhakas and the Sammitiyas—with reference to them, the question, 'Is kamma one thing and its accumulation another?' is posed by the proponent, and the admission is made by the other. Then, to challenge them, he says, beginning with 'Is contact one thing...', arguing, 'If the accumulation of kamma is something other than kamma, then there must also be an accumulation of contact and so on, other than contact and so on.' The other rejects this, as he does not hold such a view.

738-739. Kammena [M 0.0249] sahajātoti pañhesu cittavippayuttaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati, cittasampayuttaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Kusaloti pañhesupi cittavippayuttaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Parato akusalotipañhesupi eseva nayo.

738-739. In the questions 'Is it conascent with kamma?', he rejects it with reference to what is dissociated from consciousness, but acknowledges it with reference to what is associated with consciousness. In the questions 'Is it wholesome?', he also acknowledges it with reference to what is dissociated from consciousness. The same method also applies to the subsequent questions, 'Is it unwholesome?'

740. Sārammaṇoti [V 0.0247] puṭṭho pana ekantaṃ anārammaṇameva icchati, tasmā paṭikkhipati. Cittaṃ bhijjamānanti yadā cittaṃ bhijjamānaṃ hoti, tadā kammaṃ bhijjatīti attho. Bhummatthe vā paccattaṃ, citte bhijjamāneti attho. Ayameva vā pāṭho. Tattha yasmā sampayutto bhijjati, vippayutto na bhijjati, tasmā paṭijānāti ceva paṭikkhipati ca.

740. When asked 'Is it with an object?', he insists that it is exclusively without an object; therefore, he rejects it. 'When the mind is breaking' means that when the mind is breaking, the kamma breaks. Or, the accusative is used in the sense of the locative, meaning 'when the mind is breaking'. Or, this latter is an alternative reading. Here, since the associated breaks, but the dissociated does not break, he therefore both acknowledges and denies.

741. Kammamhi kammūpacayoti kamme sati kammūpacayo, kamme vā patiṭṭhite kammūpacayo, kammūpacayatova vipāko nibbattati. Tasmiṃ pana kamme niruddhe yāva aṃkuruppādā bījaṃ viya yāva vipākuppādā kammūpacayo tiṭṭhatītissa laddhi, tasmā paṭijānāti. Taññeva kammaṃ, so kammūpacayo, so kammavipākoti yasmā kammamhi kammūpacayo, so ca yāva vipākuppādā tiṭṭhatītissa laddhi, tasmā naṃ tesaṃ tiṇṇampi ekattaṃ pucchati vipāko sārammaṇoti idaṃ vipāko viya vipākadhammadhammopi ārammaṇapaṭibaddhoyevāti codanatthaṃ pucchati. Itaro pana laddhivasenekaṃ paṭijānāti, ekaṃ paṭikkhipati. Paṭilomepi eseva nayo. Sesamettha yathāpāḷimeva niyyātīti.

741. 'The accumulation of kamma in kamma' means that when kamma exists, there is an accumulation of kamma, or when kamma is established, there is an accumulation of kamma; from that very accumulation of kamma, the result arises. However, it is his view that even when that kamma has ceased, the accumulation of kamma persists until the result arises, just like a seed remains until a sprout appears. Therefore, he acknowledges it. Because it is his view that the accumulation of kamma exists in kamma and persists until the result arises, he therefore asks him about the unity of these three: 'Is that very kamma the accumulation of kamma, and is that the result of kamma?' He asks the question, 'Is the result with an object?' for the purpose of challenging, meaning that just as the result is dependent on an object, so too are phenomena that have the nature of being results dependent on an object. The other, however, accepts one aspect based on his view and rejects another. The same method applies in the reverse section. The rest here is to be understood according to the Pāli text itself.

Kammūpacayakathāvaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Discussion on the Accumulation of Kamma.

Pannarasamo vaggo.

The Fifteenth Chapter.

Tatiyapaṇṇāsako samatto.

The Third Fifty is Concluded.

16. Soḷasamavaggo

16. The Sixteenth Chapter

1. Niggahakathāvaṇṇanā

1. Exposition of the Discussion on Refutation

743-744. Idāni [P 0.0159][M 0.0250] niggahakathā nāma hoti. Tattha ye loke balappattā vasībhūtā, te yadi parassa cittaṃ niggaṇhituṃ na sakkuṇeyyuṃ, kā tesaṃ balappatti, ko vasībhāvo. Balappattiyā pana vasībhāvena ca addhā te parassa cittaṃ niggaṇhantīti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṅghikānaṃ; te sandhāya paro parassāti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Tattha [V 0.0248] niggaṇhātīti saṃkilesāpattito nivāreti. Sesamettha yathāpāḷimeva niyyātīti. Paggahakathāyapi eseva nayo.

743-744. Now there is the discussion called 'Refutation.' Herein, if those in the world who have attained power and mastery could not restrain another's mind, what is their attainment of power, what is their mastery? But for those whose doctrine is that, assuredly through the attainment of power and through mastery, they can restrain another's mind—such as the Mahāsaṅghikas—concerning them, the question, 'Does one person restrain another's mind?' is from the proponent, the admission from the other. Herein, 'restrains' means prevents from the arising of defilements. The rest here is to be understood just as in the Pāli text. The same method applies to the discussion on upholding.

Niggahakathāvaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Discussion on Refutation.

3. Sukhānuppadānakathāvaṇṇanā

3. Exposition of the Discussion on the Bestowal of Happiness

747-748. Idāni sukhānuppadānakathā nāma hoti. Tattha “bahūnaṃ vata no bhagavā sukhadhammānaṃ upahattā”ti (ma. ni. 2.148) suttaṃ nissāya paro parassa sukhaṃ anuppadetīti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi hetuvādānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Dukkhaṃ anuppadetīti puṭṭho pana tādisaṃ suttapadaṃ apassanto paṭikkhipati. Attano sukhantiādipañhe yaṃ [P 0.0160] attano parassa vā, taṃ anuppadātuṃ na sakkā. Yaṃ tasseva, kiṃ tattha anuppadānaṃ nāmāti paṭikkhipati. Nevattanotiādipañhe pana yaṃ evarūpaṃ, na taṃ anuppadinnaṃ nāma bhavitumarahatīti laddhiyāpaṭijānāti. No ca vata retitādisassa sukhassa abhāvā vuttaṃ. Sukhadhammānaṃ upahattātivacanaṃ bhagavato paresaṃ sukhuppattiyā paccayabhāvaṃ dīpeti, na annādīnaṃ viya sukhassa anuppadānaṃ, tasmā asādhakanti.

747-748. Now there is the discourse called 'The Bestowal of Happiness.' Herein, based on the sutta passage, 'Truly, the Blessed One is a provider for us of many states of happiness' (MN 2.148), is the doctrine of those who believe that one can bestow happiness upon another—such as the Hetuvādins. Concerning them, the question is posed by the proponent, and the admission is made by the other. However, when asked whether one can bestow suffering, he rejects it, not finding such a sutta passage. In the questions beginning 'one's own happiness,' he rejects them, saying that what is one's own or another's cannot be bestowed. As for that which is one's very own, what is meant by 'bestowal'?—thus he rejects it. However, in the question beginning 'neither one's own,' he admits according to his doctrine that a thing of such a nature is not fit to be called 'bestowed.' But this is not said because of the absence of happiness of that sort. The statement 'a provider of states of happiness' indicates the Blessed One's role as a condition for the arising of others' happiness, not the bestowal of happiness as in the case of food and so on; therefore, it is not probative.

Sukhānuppadānakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Bestowal of Happiness.

4. Adhigayhamanasikārakathāvaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse on Attention by Grasping.

749-753. Idāni [M 0.0251] adhigayha manasikārakathā nāma hoti. Tattha duvidho manasikāro nayato ca ārammaṇato ca. Tattha ekasaṅkhārassāpi aniccatāya diṭṭhāya sabbe saṅkhārā aniccāti avasesesu nayato manasikāro hoti. Atīte pana saṅkhāre manasikaronto na anāgate manasikātuṃ sakkoti. Atītādīsu aññataraṃ manasikaroto ārammaṇato manasikāro hoti[V 0.0249]. Tattha paccuppanne manasikaronto yena cittena te manasikaroti, taṃ paccuppannakkhaṇe manasikātuṃ na sakkoti. Tattha yesaṃ “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”tiādivacanaṃ nissāya “manasikaronto nāma adhigayha adhigaṇhitvā saṅgaṇhitvā sabbe saṅkhāre ekato manasikarotī”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyāparaseliyānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa.

749-753. Now there is the discourse called 'Attention by Grasping.' Herein, attention is twofold: by way of principle and by way of object. Herein, when the impermanence of even a single formation is seen, attention by way of principle occurs regarding the remaining formations as being impermanent. But one who attends to a past formation is not able to attend to a future one. When one attends to any one among the past and so on, attention by way of object occurs. Herein, one who attends to the present is not able, in that present moment, to attend to the very mind with which one attends to them. Herein, regarding those who, relying on statements like 'all formations are impermanent,' hold the view that 'one who attends, having grasped, comprehended, and collected, attends to all formations together'—such as the Pubbaseliyas and Aparaseliyas—the question is posed by the proponent, and the admission is made by the other.

Atha naṃ yasmā sabbe ekato manasikarontena yena cittena te manasikaroti, tampi manasikātabbaṃ hoti. Tasmā taṃcittatāya codetuṃ tena cittenāti āha. Itaro ārammaṇaṃ katvā na sakkā jānitunti sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Evaṃlakkhaṇaṃ cittanti ñātattā pana tampi cittaṃ ñātameva hotīti sandhāya paṭijānāti. Atha vā taññeva tassa ārammaṇaṃ na hotīti paṭikkhipati. “Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā, yadā paññāya passatī”tiādīni nissāya uppannaladdhivasena [P 0.0161] paṭijānāti. Sesapañhadvayepi eseva nayo. Tena phassenātiādīsu pana tathārūpaṃ suttaṃ apassanto paṭikkhipateva. Atītādipañhesu heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva paṭikkhepapaṭiññā veditabbā. Sesaṃ yathāpāḷimeva niyyātīti. Sabbe saṅkhārātiādivacanaṃ nayato dassanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na ekakkhaṇe ārammaṇato, tasmā asādhakanti.

Then, since the mind with which one attends to all things together must also be attended to, therefore, to challenge him regarding that very state of mind, he says, 'with that mind.' The other rejects this, implying that it cannot be known by making it an object. However, he admits it, intending that since it is known that 'the mind has such a characteristic,' that mind is indeed known. Alternatively, he rejects it, saying that very thing is not its object. He admits it based on the doctrine that arises through reliance on statements like 'all formations are impermanent, when one sees with wisdom.' The same method applies to the remaining two questions. Regarding 'by that contact,' and so on, not finding such a sutta, he simply rejects it. In the questions about the past, and so on, the rejection and admission should be understood in the manner stated above. The rest is to be construed just as in the Pāli text. The statement 'all formations,' and so on, is spoken referring to seeing by way of principle, not as an object in a single moment; therefore, it is not probative.

Adhigayhamanasikārakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discourse on Attention by Grasping.

5. Rūpaṃ hetūtikathāvaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse: 'Is Form a Cause?'

754-756. Idāni rūpaṃ hetūti kathānāma hoti. Tattha hetūti kusalamūlādino hetuhetussāpi nāmaṃ, yassa kassaci paccayassāpi. Imaṃ [M 0.0252] pana vibhāgaṃ akatvā “cattāro mahābhūtā hetū”ti vacanamattaṃ nissāya aviseseneva rūpaṃ hetūti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi uttarāpathakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Alobho hetūti kiṃ te rūpaṃ alobhasaṅkhāto hetūti pucchati, itaro paṭikkhipati. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Mahābhūtā upādāyarūpānaṃ upādāyahetūti ettha paccayaṭṭhena hetubhāvo vutto, na mūlaṭṭhena, tasmā asādhakanti.

754-756. Now there is the discourse called 'Is Form a Cause?' Herein, 'cause' is a name for a root-cause, such as a wholesome root, and also for any condition whatsoever. But without making this distinction, some, like the Uttarāpathakas, hold the view that form is a cause without differentiation, simply based on the statement, 'The four great elements are causes.' Concerning them, the question is posed by the proponent, and the admission is made by the other. He asks, 'Is your form a cause designated as non-greed?' The other rejects it. The same method applies to the remaining cases. That the great elements are a cause for derived form by way of support is stated here in the sense of a condition, not in the sense of a root; therefore, it is not probative.

Rūpaṃ hetūtikathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discourse: 'Is Form a Cause?'

757-759. Sahetukakathāyampi [V 0.0250] imināva nayena attho veditabboti.

757-759. In the discourse on being with a cause, too, the meaning should be understood in this same way.

Rūpaṃ sahetukantikathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discourse: 'Is Form With a Cause?'

7. Rūpaṃ kusalākusalantikathāvaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Discourse: 'Is Form Wholesome or Unwholesome?'

760-764. Idāni rūpaṃ kusalākusalantikathā nāma hoti. Tattha “kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ kusalampi akusalampī”tivacanaṃ [P 0.0162] nissāya kāyavacīkammasaṅkhātaṃ kāyaviññattivacīviññattirūpaṃ kusalampi akusalampīti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi mahisāsakānañceva sammitiyānañca; te sandhāya rūpaṃ kusalanti pucchā sakavādissa paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi te rūpaṃ kusalaṃ, evaṃvidhena anena bhavitabba”nti codetuṃ sārammaṇanti ādimāha. Parato akusalapañhepi eseva nayo. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

760-764. Now there is the discourse called 'Is Form Wholesome or Unwholesome?' Here, relying on the statement, 'Bodily action and verbal action are both wholesome and unwholesome,' is the doctrine of those who hold that form designated as bodily and verbal action—namely, the form of bodily intimation and verbal intimation—is both wholesome and unwholesome, such as the Mahīsāsakas and the Sammatiyas. Concerning them, the question 'Is form wholesome?' is posed by the proponent, and the admission is made by the other. Then, to challenge him, he begins by saying, 'with an object,' in order to censure him thus: 'If form is wholesome for you, it must be of this nature.' The same method applies to the subsequent question on the unwholesome. The rest here is of plain meaning.

Rūpaṃ kusalākusalantikathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discourse: 'Is Form Wholesome or Unwholesome?'

8. Rūpaṃ vipākotikathāvaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Discourse: 'Is Form a Result?'

765-767. Idāni rūpaṃ vipākotikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yaṃ kammassa katattā uppannā cittacetasikā viya kammassa katattā uppannaṃ taṃ rūpampi vipākoti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānañceva sammitiyānañca; te [M 0.0253] sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi te rūpaṃ vipāko, evaṃvidhena anena bhavitabba”nti codetuṃ sukhavedanīyantiādimāha. Sesaṃ yathāpāḷimeva niyyātīti.

765-767. Now there is the discourse called 'Is Form a Result?' Herein, there is the doctrine of those—such as the Andhakas and the Sammatiyas—that just as mind and mental factors that have arisen because kamma has been done are results, so too form that has arisen because kamma has been done is also a result. Concerning them, the question is posed by the proponent, and the admission is made by the other. Then, to challenge him, he begins by saying, 'accompanied by pleasant feeling,' in order to censure him thus: 'If form is a result for you, it must be of this nature.' The rest is to be construed as in the Pāli text.

Rūpaṃ vipākotikathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discourse: 'Is Form a Result?'

9. Rūpaṃ rūpāvacarārūpāvacarantikathāvaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Discourse: 'Does Form Pertain to the Form Realm or the Formless Realm?'

768-770. Idāni [V 0.0251] rūpaṃ rūpāvacarārūpāvacarantikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yaṃ kāmāvacarakammassa katattā rūpaṃ, taṃ yasmā kāmāvacaraṃ, tasmā rūpāvacarārūpāvacarakammānampi katattā rūpena rūpāvacarārūpāvacarena bhavitabbanti [P 0.0163] yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya atthi rūpaṃ rūpāvacarārūpāvacaranti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha heṭṭhā vuttanayamevāti.

768-770. Now there is the discussion entitled 'Form is of the Form-Sphere or Formless-Sphere.' Herein, some—such as the Andhakas—hold the view that since form which is due to the performance of kamma pertaining to the sense-sphere is of the sense-sphere, therefore, due to the performance of kamma pertaining to the form-sphere and the formless-sphere, form must also be of the form-sphere and the formless-sphere. With reference to them, the question, 'Is form of the form-sphere and formless-sphere?' is the proponent's; the admission is the other's. The remainder here is just according to the method stated above.

Rūpaṃ rūpāvacarārūpāvacarantikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion 'Form is of the Form-Sphere or Formless-Sphere'.

10. Rūpārūpadhātupariyāpannakathāvaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Discussion of What is Included in the Form and Formless Realms.

771-775. Idāni rūparāgo rūpadhātupariyāpanno arūparāgo arūpadhātupariyāpannoti kathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā kāmarāgo kāmadhātupariyāpanno, tasmā rūparāgārūparāgehipi rūpadhātuarūpadhātupariyāpannehi bhavitabbanti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Kevalañhi tattha “rūpadhātuṃ anuseti, arūpadhātuṃ anusetī”ti padaṃ viseso. Sā ca laddhi andhakānañceva sammitiyānañca. Ayaṃ andhakānaṃyevāti.

771-775. Now there is the discussion entitled 'Lust for Form is Included in the Form Realm; Lust for the Formless is Included in the Formless Realm.' Herein, with reference to those who hold the view—such as the Andhakas—that since sensual lust is included in the sense-sphere realm, lust for form and lust for the formless must also be included in the form realm and the formless realm, the question is the proponent's; the admission is the other's. The remainder should be understood in the manner stated above. The only difference here is the phrase, 'it lies latent in the form realm, it lies latent in the formless realm.' And this view is held by both the Andhakas and the Sammitiyas. This one, however, is only of the Andhakas.

Rūparāgo rūpadhātupariyāpanno arūparāgo arūpadhātupariyāpannotikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion 'Lust for Form is Included in the Form Realm; Lust for the Formless is Included in the Formless Realm'.

Rūpārūpadhātupariyāpannakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion of What is Included in the Form and Formless Realms.

Soḷasamo vaggo.

The Sixteenth Chapter.

17. Sattarasamavaggo

17. The Seventeenth Chapter.

1. Atthi arahato puññūpacayakathāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Discussion 'There is Accumulation of Merit for an Arahant'.

776-779. Idāni [M 0.0254][P 0.0164][V 0.0252] atthi arahato puññūpacayotikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ arahato dānasaṃvibhāgacetiyavandanādīni kammāni disvā atthi arahato puññūpacayoti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “arahā nāma pahīnapuññapāpo, so yadi puññaṃ kareyya, pāpampi kareyyā”ti codetuṃ apuññūpacayoti āha. Itaro pāṇātipātādikiriyaṃ apassanto paṭikkhipati. Puññābhisaṅkhārantiādīsu bhavagāmikammaṃ arahato natthīti paṭikkhipati. Dānaṃ dadeyyātiādīsu kiriyacittena dānādipavattisabbhāvato sakavādī paṭijānāti. Itaro cittaṃ anādiyitvā kiriyāpavattimattadassaneneva laddhiṃ patiṭṭhapeti. Sā pana ayoniso patiṭṭhāpitattā appatiṭṭhāpitā hotīti.

776-779. Now there is the discussion entitled, 'There is Accumulation of Merit for an Arahant.' Herein, with reference to those—such as the Andhakas—who, upon seeing an Arahant's actions such as giving, sharing, and venerating shrines, hold the view that 'there is accumulation of merit for an Arahant,' the question is the proponent's; the admission is the other's. Then, in order to challenge him with the argument, 'An Arahant has abandoned both merit and demerit; if he were to accumulate merit, he would also accumulate demerit,' the proponent asks about the accumulation of demerit. The other, not seeing any action such as the taking of life, rejects this. In the section on 'meritorious formations,' etc., the proponent rejects that an Arahant has kamma that leads to becoming. In the section on 'he may give a gift,' etc., the proponent admits this, because the occurrence of giving and so on is with a functional consciousness. The other, not taking consciousness into account, establishes his view merely by seeing the occurrence of the action. But that view, being established without proper attention, is not truly established.

Atthi arahato puññūpacayotikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion 'There is Accumulation of Merit for an Arahant'.

2. Natthi arahato akālamaccūtikathāvaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Discussion 'There is No Untimely Death for an Arahant'.

780. Idāni natthi arahato akālamaccūtikathā nāma hoti. Tattha “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sañcetanikānaṃ kammānaṃ katānaṃ upacitānaṃ apaṭisaṃveditvā byantībhāvaṃ vadāmī”ti (a. ni. 10.217) suttassa atthaṃ ayoniso gahetvā “arahatā nāma [P 0.0165] sabbakammavipākaṃ paṭisaṃvedayitvāva parinibbāyitabbaṃ, tasmā natthi, arahato akālamaccū”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi rājagirikānañceva siddhatthikānañca; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “sace tassa natthi akālamaccu, arahantaghātakena nāma na bhavitabba”nti [V 0.0253] codetuṃ natthi arahantaghātakoti āha. Itaro ānantariyakammassa ceva tādisānañca puggalānaṃ sabbhāvato paṭikkhipati.

780. Now there is the discussion entitled 'There is no untimely death for an Arahant.' Herein, with reference to those—such as the Rājagirikas and the Siddhatthikas—who, having inappropriately grasped the meaning of the sutta, 'Monks, I do not declare the termination of intentional actions that have been done and accumulated without their result having been experienced' (AN 10.217), hold the view that 'an Arahant must indeed experience the result of all kamma before attaining final Nibbāna; therefore, there is no untimely death for an Arahant,' the question is the proponent's; the admission is the other's. Then, in order to challenge him with the argument, 'If there is no untimely death for an Arahant, then there can be no such thing as a slayer of an Arahant,' the proponent states, 'There is no slayer of an Arahant.' The other rejects this on account of the existence of immediately resultant kamma and of such individuals.

781. Visaṃ na kameyyāti pañhe “yāva pubbe katakammaṃ parikkhayaṃ na gacchati, tāva na kamatī”ti laddhiyā paṭikkhipati. Sesamettha yathāpāḷimeva niyyāti.

781. Regarding the question, 'Would poison not take effect?', he rejects this with the view that 'so long as previously performed kamma is not exhausted, it does not take effect.' The remainder here is to be inferred exactly as in the Pāḷi text.

782. Nāhaṃ, [M 0.0255] bhikkhaveti suttaṃ idaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – sañcetanikānaṃ kammānaṃ katānaṃ vipākaṃ apaṭisaṃveditvā avinditvā ananubhavitvā byantībhāvaṃ tesaṃ kammānaṃ parivaṭumaparicchinnabhāvaṃ na vadāmi, tañca kho diṭṭhadhammavedanīyānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme, na tato paraṃ, upapajjavedanīyānaṃ anantaraṃ upapattiṃ upapajjitvāva na tato paraṃ, aparāpariyavedanīyānaṃ yadā vipākokāsaṃ labhanti, tathārūpe aparāpare vā pariyāye. Evaṃ sabbathāpi saṃsārapavatte sati laddhavipākavāre kamme na vijjateso jagatippadeso, yatthaṭṭhito mucceyya pāpakammāti. Evaṃ sante yadetaṃ “aladdhavipākavārampi kammaṃ avassaṃ arahato paṭisaṃveditabba”nti kappanāvasena “natthi arahato akālamaccū”ti laddhipatiṭṭhāpanaṃ kataṃ, taṃ dukkaṭamevāti.

782. The sutta beginning 'Monks, I...' was spoken with reference to this: I do not declare the termination of intentional actions that have been done and accumulated without their result having been experienced, found, and undergone.
