And indeed, for those actions whose results are to be experienced in this very life, they are experienced in this very life, not beyond; for those whose results are to be experienced in the next rebirth, they are experienced immediately upon rebirth, not beyond; and for those whose results are to be experienced in subsequent existences, they are experienced whenever they find an opportunity for fruition, in this or that subsequent occasion. Thus, as long as the cycle of existence continues, for kamma that has received its opportunity for fruition, there is no place in this world where one can stand and be freed from evil kamma. This being so, the establishment of the doctrine that 'there is no untimely death for an Arahant' by way of the supposition that 'even kamma whose opportunity for fruition has not yet been received must inevitably be experienced by an Arahant' is indeed wrongly done.

Natthi arahato akālamaccūtikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion 'There is No Untimely Death for an Arahant'.

3. Sabbamidaṃ kammatotikathāvaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Discussion 'All This is from Kamma'.

783. Idāni sabbamidaṃ kammatotikathā nāma hoti. Tattha “kammunā vattati loko”ti suttaṃ nissāya “sabbamidaṃ kammakilesavipākavaṭṭaṃ kammatova hotī”ti yesaṃ laddhi[P 0.0166], seyyathāpi rājagirikānañceva siddhatthikānañca; te sandhāya sabbamidanti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “evaṃ sante kammampi kammato āpajjatī”ti codetuṃ kammampi kammatoti āha. Itaro yadi kammampi kammatova nāma taṃ kammaṃ vipākoyeva siyāti paṭikkhipati. Pubbekatahetūti “yadi sabbamidaṃ kammato, pubbekatahetunā tena bhavitabba”nti codetuṃ pucchati, itaro pubbekatahetuvādabhayena paṭikkhipati.

783. Now, this is called the discussion 'All This Is from Kamma.' Here, based on the sutta 'The world proceeds by kamma,' for those whose doctrine is 'all this cycle of kamma, defilements, and results arises from kamma alone,' such as the Rājagirikas and the Siddhatthikas; referring to them, the question 'Is all this from kamma?' is posed by the proponent of one's own doctrine, and the other affirms it. Then, to challenge him with 'If that is so, then kamma itself would arise from kamma,' he asks, 'Is kamma also from kamma?' The other rejects this, saying, 'If kamma itself is indeed from kamma, then that kamma would merely be a result.' The question 'Is it due to a past-made cause?' is asked to challenge him with 'If all this is from kamma, then it must be due to a past-made cause.' The other, fearing the doctrine of a past-made cause, rejects it.

784. Kammavipākatoti [V 0.0254] “yadi sabbamidaṃ kammato, yaṃ atītabhave pavattassa hetubhūtaṃ kammaṃ, tampi purimatare bhave kammatoti kammavipāko sampajjati, tena te sabbamidaṃ kammavipākato āpajjatī”ti codetuṃ pucchati. Itaro bījato aṃkurasseva paccuppannapavattassa kammato nibbattiṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Dutiyaṃ puṭṭho tassāpi kammassa bījassa purimabījato viya [M 0.0256] purimakammato pavattattā paṭijānāti. Pāṇaṃ haneyyātiādi “yadi sabbaṃ kammavipākato, pāṇātipātādīni kammavipākeneva kareyyā”ti codetuṃ vuttaṃ. Itaro dussīlyacetanāpi purimakammanibbattā ekena pariyāyena vipākoyevāti laddhiyā paṭijānāti. Atha naṃ “yadi te pāṇātipāto kammavipākato nibbattati, pāṇātipāto viya vipākopi saphalo āpajjatī”ti codetuṃ saphaloti āha. Itaro pāṇātipātassa nirayasaṃvattanikādibhāvato saphalataṃ passanto paṭijānāti. Kammavipākassa pana idaṃ nāma phalanti vuttaṭṭhānaṃ apassanto paṭikkhipati. Adinnādānādīsupi eseva nayo. Gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāro saphaloti deyyadhammavasena dānaphalaṃ pucchati. Kammunā vattatīti suttaṃ “natthi kamma”nti akammavāditaṃ paṭikkhipitvā “atthi kamma”nti kammavāditaṃ kammassakataṃ dīpeti. Na sabbasseva kammato nibbattiṃ, tasmā asādhakanti.

784. ‘Is it from the result of kamma?’ The question is posed to challenge them: ‘If all this is from kamma, then the kamma that was the cause in a past existence must also be from kamma in a still earlier existence; thus, the result of kamma comes about, and thereby all this would arise for you from the result of kamma.’ The other rejects this, referring to the arising of presently occurring kamma from previous kamma, like a sprout from a seed. When asked a second time, they admit it, since that kamma-seed arises from a previous kamma, just as a seed arises from a previous seed. ‘Would one kill living beings, etc.?’ This is said to challenge them: ‘If everything is from the result of kamma, then killing living beings and so on would be done solely by the result of kamma.’ The other admits this, holding the view that even immoral volition, being produced by past kamma, is in a way a result. Then, to challenge them with ‘If killing living beings arises for you from the result of kamma, then, like killing living beings, the result would also be fruitful,’ he asks, ‘Is it fruitful?’ The other, seeing that killing living beings is fruitful in that it leads to hell and so on, admits it. But regarding the result of kamma, not seeing any instance where it is said, ‘This is the fruit,’ they reject it. The same method applies to stealing and so on. ‘Are the requisites of medicine for the sick fruitful?’ This asks about the fruit of giving in terms of things that can be given. The sutta ‘The world proceeds by kamma’ rejects the doctrine of no-kamma—the view that ‘there is no kamma’—and, affirming the doctrine of kamma—the view that ‘there is kamma’—it illustrates ownership of kamma. It does not show the arising of everything from kamma; hence, it is not a valid proof.

Sabbamidaṃ kammatotikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion 'All This Is from Kamma'.

4. Indriyabaddhakathāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Discourse on What Is Bound to the Faculties.

786-787. Idāni [P 0.0167] indriyabaddhakathā nāma hoti. Tattha duvidhaṃ dukkhaṃ – indriyabaddhaṃ, anindriyabaddhañca. Indriyabaddhaṃ dukkhavatthutāya dukkhaṃ, anindriyabaddhaṃ udayabbayapaṭipīḷanaṭṭhena “yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkha”nti saṅgahitattā dukkhaṃ. Imaṃ vibhāgaṃ aggahetvā “yassa pariññāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati, taṃ indriyabaddhameva dukkhaṃ, na itara”nti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi hetuvādānaṃ, tesaṃ itarassāpi dukkhabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ indriyabaddhaññevāti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yasmā bhagavatā ‘yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkha’nti vuttaṃ, tasmā indriyabaddheneva tena aniccena bhavitabba”nti codetuṃ indriyabaddhaññeva aniccantiādimāha. Nanu [V 0.0255] anindriyabaddhaṃ aniccanti nanu pathavīpabbatapāsāṇādi anindriyabaddhampi aniccanti attho.

786-787. Now, this is called the discourse on what is bound to the faculties. Herein, suffering is of two kinds: suffering bound to the faculties and suffering not bound to the faculties. Suffering bound to the faculties is suffering by way of being a basis for suffering, while suffering not bound to the faculties is suffering because it is included under the statement, 'Whatever is impermanent is suffering,' by way of oppression through rise and fall. Without grasping this distinction, some hold the view that 'Only suffering bound to the faculties is the suffering for the full understanding of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One, not the other kind'—such as the proponents of Hetuvāda. To show them that the other kind is also suffering, the question 'Is it only suffering bound to the faculties?' is posed by the proponent of one's own doctrine, and the other affirms it. Then, to challenge him with 'Since the Blessed One said, "Whatever is impermanent is suffering," therefore that which is impermanent must be only that which is bound to the faculties,' he asks, 'Is only that which is bound to the faculties impermanent?' and so on. The meaning of 'Is not that which is not bound to the faculties impermanent?' is 'Are not things not bound to the faculties, such as the earth, mountains, and rocks, also impermanent?'

788. Na vattabbaṃ indriyabaddhaññeva dukkhanti pañhe āmantāti paṭiññā sakavādissa. Anindriyabaddhañhi dukkhadomanassānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hoti. Uṇhakālasmiñhi aggi sītakāle ca vāto dukkhassa ārammaṇaṃ, niccampi [M 0.0257] bhogavināsādayo domanassassa. Tasmā vināpi aniccaṭṭhena anindriyabaddhaṃ dukkhanti vattabbaṃ. Kammakilesehi pana anibbattattā dukkhaṃ ariyasaccanti na vattabbaṃ, tathā maggena apariññeyyattā. Yasmā pana tiṇakaṭṭhādinirodho vā utubījādinirodho vā dukkhanirodhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ nāma na hoti, tasmā indriyabaddhaṃ dukkhañceva ariyasaccañca, itaraṃ pana dukkhamevāti idaṃ nānattaṃ dassetuṃ paṭijānāti. Yathā indriyabaddhassātiādivacanaṃ indriyabaddhassa pariññāya brahmacariyavāsaṃ pariññātassa puna anuppattiṃ dīpeti. Tenevettha sakavādinā paṭikkhepo kato. “Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkha”nti vacanena pana saṅgahitassa anindriyabaddhassa dukkhabhāvaṃ paṭisedhetuṃ na sakkāti, tasmā asādhakanti.

788. In response to the question 'It should not be said that only what is bound to the faculties is suffering,' the proponent of one's own doctrine affirms it. For what is not bound to the faculties is indeed a basis for suffering and distress. Indeed, in the hot season, fire, and in the cold season, wind, become a basis for suffering. Likewise, the destruction of wealth and so on are always a basis for distress. Therefore, even without the aspect of impermanence, what is not bound to the faculties should be called suffering. However, because it is not produced by kamma and defilements, it should not be called the Noble Truth of suffering, and similarly, because it is not to be fully understood by the path. But since the cessation of grass and sticks or the cessation of seasons and seeds is not called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, therefore, to show this difference, he admits that what is bound to the faculties is both suffering and a Noble Truth, while the other is merely suffering. The statement beginning 'As for what is bound to the faculties...' shows that the holy life is lived for the full understanding of what is bound to the faculties, and that for one who has fully understood it, there is no further arising. For this reason, the rejection is made here by the proponent of one's own doctrine. But it is impossible to deny the suffering nature of what is not bound to the faculties, as it is included by the statement, 'Whatever is impermanent is suffering.' Therefore, this is not a valid proof.

Indriyabaddhakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on What Is Bound to the Faculties.

5. Ṭhapetvā ariyamaggantikathāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Discussion 'Except for the Noble Path'.

789-790. Idāni [P 0.0168] ṭhapetvā ariyamaggantikathā nāma hoti. Tattha “yasmā ariyamaggo ‘dukkhanirodhagāminipaṭipadā’ti vutto, tasmā ṭhapetvā ariyamaggaṃ avasesā saṅkhārā dukkhā”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi hetuvādānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi evaṃ samudayassāpi dukkhabhāvo āpajjatī”ti codetuṃ dukkhasamudayopīti āha. Itaro hetulakkhaṇaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Puna puṭṭho pavattapariyāpannabhāvaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Tīṇevāti pañhesu suttavirodhabhayena paṭikkhipati, laddhivasena paṭijānāti. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

789-790. Now, there is a discussion called 'Excluding the Noble Path'. Here, regarding those who hold the view—such as the Hetuvādins—that 'since the Noble Path is called "the path leading to the cessation of suffering," therefore, excluding the Noble Path, all remaining conditioned things are suffering'—with reference to them, the question is posed by the proponent of one's own doctrine, and the admission is by the other. Then, in order to challenge him with 'if that is so, then the origin of suffering would also be suffering,' he says, 'also the origin of suffering.' The other rejects this by referring to the characteristic of a cause. When questioned again, he affirms by referring to the state of being included in the ongoing process. In the questions about 'only three,' he rejects this due to fear of contradicting the Suttas, but affirms it based on his own view. The rest here is clear in meaning.

Ṭhapetvā ariyamaggantikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion 'Excluding the Noble Path'.

6. Na vattabbaṃ saṅgho dakkhiṇaṃ paṭiggaṇhātītikathāvaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Discussion 'It Should Not Be Said That the Saṅgha Receives an Offering'.

791-792. Idāni [V 0.0256] na vattabbaṃ saṅgho dakkhiṇaṃ paṭiggaṇhātītikathā nāma hoti. Tattha “paramatthato maggaphalāneva saṅgho, maggaphalehi añño [M 0.0258] saṅgho nāma natthi, maggaphalāni ca na kiñci paṭiggaṇhanti, tasmā na vattabbaṃ saṅgho dakkhiṇaṃ paṭiggaṇhātī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi mahāpuññavādīsaṅkhātānaṃ vetullakānaṃ; te sandhāya na vattabbanti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi saṅgho na paṭiggaṇheyya, na naṃ satthā āhuneyyātiādīhi thomeyyā”ti codetuṃ nanu saṅgho āhuneyyotiādimāha. Saṅghassa dānaṃ dentīti “ye te saṅghassa denti, te paṭiggāhakesu asati kassa dadeyyu”nti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Āhutiṃ jātavedo vāti suttaṃ parasamayato āgataṃ. Tattha mahāmeghanti meghavuṭṭhiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Vuṭṭhiñhi medanī paṭiggaṇhāti, na meghameva. Maggo paṭiggaṇhātīti “maggaphalāni saṅgho”ti laddhiyā [P 0.0169] vadati, na ca maggaphalāneva saṅgho. Maggaphalapātubhāvaparisuddhe pana khandhe upādāya paññattā aṭṭha puggalā saṅgho, tasmā asādhakametanti.

791-792. Now, there is a discussion called 'It Should Not Be Said That the Saṅgha Receives an Offering'. Here, regarding those who hold the view—such as the present-day Vetullakas, known as the Mahāpuññavādins—that 'in the ultimate sense, the Saṅgha is only the path and fruits, and there is no Saṅgha apart from the path and fruits, and the path and fruits do not receive anything, therefore it should not be said that the Saṅgha receives an offering'—with reference to them, the question 'it should not be said' is posed by the proponent of one's own doctrine, and the admission is by the other. Then, in order to challenge him with 'if the Saṅgha did not receive, the Teacher would not praise them with such terms as “worthy of offerings,”' he says, 'Is not the Saṅgha worthy of offerings, etc.?' The statement 'They give a gift to the Saṅgha' is said with the intention to challenge: 'If there were no recipients, to whom would those who give to the Saṅgha give?' The sutta 'The fire god accepts the oblation' comes from another school. There, 'great cloud' is said with reference to rainfall. For the earth receives the rain, not the cloud itself. The statement 'The path receives' is spoken according to the view that 'the Saṅgha is the path and fruits,' but the Saṅgha is not merely the path and fruits. Rather, the Saṅgha is the eight individuals designated in dependence on the aggregates purified by the manifestation of the path and fruits. Therefore, this is not a valid proof.

Na vattabbaṃ saṅgho dakkhiṇaṃ paṭiggaṇhātītikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion 'It Should Not Be Said That the Saṅgha Receives an Offering'.

7. Na vattabbaṃ saṅgho dakkhiṇaṃ visodhetītikathāvaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Discussion 'It Should Not Be Said That the Saṅgha Purifies an Offering'.

793-794. Idāni na vattabbaṃ saṅgho dakkhiṇaṃ visodhetītikathā nāma hoti. Tattha “maggaphalāneva saṅgho nāma, na ca tāni dakkhiṇaṃ visodhetuṃ sakkonti, tasmā na vattabbaṃ saṅgho dakkhiṇaṃ visodhetī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi tesaññeva; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Āhuneyyotiādi “yadi saṅgho dakkhiṇaṃ visodhetuṃ na sakkuṇeyya, na naṃ satthā evaṃ thomeyyā”ti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Visodhetīti mahapphalaṃ karoti. Saṅghasmiñhi appaṃ dinnaṃ bahu hoti, bahu dinnaṃ bahutaraṃ. Dakkhiṇeyyāti dakkhiṇārahā dakkhiṇāya anucchavikā, dakkhiṇaṃ visodhetuṃ samatthāti attho. Dakkhiṇaṃ ārādhentīti sampādenti, appamattikāyapi dakkhiṇāya mahantaṃ phalaṃ pāpuṇantīti attho. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayamevāti.

793-794. Now, there is a discussion called 'It Should Not Be Said That the Saṅgha Purifies an Offering'. Here, regarding those who hold the view—such as those very same ones—that 'the Saṅgha is only the path and fruits, and these cannot purify an offering, therefore it should not be said that the Saṅgha purifies an offering'—with reference to them, the question is posed by the proponent of one's own doctrine, and the admission is by the other. The phrase beginning 'Worthy of offerings' is said to show: 'If the Saṅgha were incapable of purifying an offering, the Teacher would not praise them thus.' 'Purifies' means 'makes it of great fruit.' For a little given to the Saṅgha becomes much, and much given becomes even more. 'Worthy of offerings' means worthy of an offering, suitable for an offering, capable of purifying an offering. 'They fulfill an offering' means they accomplish it; the meaning is that they attain a great fruit even from a small offering. The rest is as explained above.

Na vattabbaṃ saṅgho dakkhiṇaṃ visodhetītikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion 'It Should Not Be Said That the Saṅgha Purifies an Offering'.

8. Na vattabbaṃ saṅgho bhuñjatītikathāvaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Discussion 'It Should Not Be Said That the Saṅgha Eats'.

795-796. Idāni [M 0.0259][V 0.0257] na vattabbaṃ saṅgho bhuñjatītikathā nāma hoti. Tatrāpi “maggaphalāneva saṅgho nāma, na ca tāni kiñci bhuñjanti, tasmā na vattabbaṃ saṅgho bhuñjati, pivati, khādati, sāyatī”ti [P 0.0170] yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi tesaṃyeva; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi saṅgho na bhuñjeyya, saṅghabhattādikaraṇaṃ niratthakaṃ bhaveyyā”ti codetuṃ nanu atthi keci saṅghabhattāni karontītiādimāha. Gaṇabhojanantiādi “yadi saṅgho na bhuñjeyya, kassa gaṇabhojanādīni siyu”nti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Aṭṭha pānānīti idampi “yadi saṅgho na piveyya, kassetāni pānāni satthā anujāneyyā”ti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Sesamidhāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

795-796. Now, there is a discussion called 'It Should Not Be Said That the Saṅgha Eats.' Here too, regarding those whose doctrine is that 'the Saṅgha is only the paths and fruits, and these do not consume anything; therefore, it should not be said that the Saṅgha eats, drinks, chews, or tastes'—just as for those very ones; with reference to them, the question is posed by the proponent of one's own doctrine, and the admission is by the other. Then, in order to challenge them with 'if the Saṅgha does not eat, the preparation of meals for the Saṅgha would be meaningless,' he states, beginning with: 'Surely, there are some who prepare meals for the Saṅgha?' The phrase beginning 'a meal for a group' is stated for the purpose of challenging: 'If the Saṅgha does not eat, for whom would there be group meals and the like?' This, too, 'the eight drinks,' is stated for the purpose of challenging: 'If the Saṅgha does not drink, for whom would the Teacher have allowed these drinks?' The rest here, too, should be understood in the same way as stated above.

Na vattabbaṃ saṅgho bhuñjatītikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion 'It Should Not Be Said That the Saṅgha Eats'.

9. Na vattabbaṃ saṅghassa dinnaṃ mahapphalantikathāvaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Discussion 'It Should Not Be Said That What Is Given to the Saṅgha Is of Great Fruit'.

797-798. Idāni na vattabbaṃ saṅghassa dinnaṃ mahapphalantikathā nāma hoti. Tatrāpi “maggaphalāneva saṅgho nāma, na ca sakkā tesaṃ kiñci dātuṃ, na ca tehi paṭiggaṇhituṃ, nāpi tesaṃ dānena koci upakāro ijjhati, tasmā na vattabbaṃ saṅghassa dinnaṃ mahapphala”nti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi tesaṃyeva; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Āhuneyyotiādi “yadi saṅghassa dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ na bhaveyya, na naṃ satthā evaṃ thomeyyā”ti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ yathāpāḷimeva niyyātīti.

797-798. Now, there is a discussion called 'It Should Not Be Said That What Is Given to the Saṅgha Is of Great Fruit.' Here too, regarding those whose doctrine is that 'the Saṅgha is only the paths and fruits, and it is not possible to give anything to them, nor for them to receive it, nor is any benefit accomplished by giving to them; therefore, it should not be said that what is given to the Saṅgha is of great fruit'—just as for those very ones; with reference to them, the question is posed by the proponent of one's own doctrine, and the admission is by the other. The phrase beginning 'worthy of offerings' is stated to show: 'If what is given to the Saṅgha were not of great fruit, the Teacher would not praise them thus.' The rest proceeds just as in the Pāḷi.

Na vattabbaṃ saṅghassa dinnaṃ mahapphalantikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion 'It Should Not Be Said That What Is Given to the Saṅgha Is of Great Fruit'.

10. Na vattabbaṃ buddhassa dinnaṃ mahapphalantikathāvaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Discussion 'It Should Not Be Said That What Is Given to the Buddha Is of Great Fruit'.

799. Idāni [V 0.0258] na vattabbaṃ buddhassa dinnaṃ mahapphalantikathā nāma hoti. Tattha “buddho bhagavā na kiñci paribhuñjati, lokānuvattanatthaṃ pana paribhuñjamānaṃ viya [P 0.0171] attānaṃ dasseti, tasmā nirupakārattā na vattabbaṃ tasmiṃ dinnaṃ mahapphala”nti yesaṃ [M 0.0260] laddhi, seyyathāpi tesaṃyeva; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Dvipadānaṃ aggotiādi “manussadussīlepi dānaṃ sahassaguṇaṃ hoti, kimaṅgaṃ pana evarūpe aggapuggale”ti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Sesamettha yathāpāḷimeva niyyātīti.

799. Now, there is a discussion called 'It should not be said that what is given to the Buddha is of great fruit.' Herein, concerning those whose doctrine is that 'the Blessed One, the Buddha, does not consume anything, but for the sake of conforming to the world, he displays himself as if consuming; therefore, since it is of no service to him, it should not be said that what is given to him is of great fruit'—as is the case with them; with reference to them, the question is for the proponent of his own view, the assertion for the other. The phrase beginning 'foremost of bipeds' is stated to show: 'Even a gift given to an immoral human is a thousandfold in fruit; how much more so when given to such a supreme individual?' The rest here is to be understood just as in the Pāḷi text.

Na vattabbaṃ buddhassa dinnaṃ mahapphalantikathāvaṇṇanā.

The commentary on the discussion that 'It should not be said that what is given to the Buddha is of great fruit.'

11. Dakkhiṇāvisuddhikathāvaṇṇanā

11. The Commentary on the Discussion on the Purification of Offerings.

800-801. Idāni dakkhiṇāvisuddhikathā nāma hoti. Tattha “yadi paṭiggāhakato dakkhiṇā visujjheyya, mahapphalā bhaveyya. Dāyakena dānaṃ dinnaṃ, paṭiggāhakena vipāko nibbattitoti añño aññassa kārako bhaveyya, paraṃkataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ āpajjeyya, añño kareyya, añño paṭisaṃvedeyya. Tasmā dāyakatova dānaṃ visujjhati, no paṭiggāhakato, dāyakasseva cittavisuddhi vipākadāyikā hotī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi uttarāpathakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Āhuneyyātiādi “yadi paṭiggāhakato dānaṃ na visujjheyya, kimassa āhuneyyādibhāvo kareyyā”ti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Añño aññassa kārakoti yadi dāyakassa dānacetanā paṭiggāhakena katā bhaveyya, yuttarūpaṃ siyā. Tassa pana dānacetanā parisuddhā paṭiggāhakasaṅkhātaṃ vatthuṃ paṭicca mahāvipākaṭṭhena visujjhati, tasmā acodanā esā “paṭiggāhakato dānaṃ visujjhatī”ti.

Now comes the discussion on the purification of offerings. Herein, concerning those whose doctrine is that 'if an offering were purified by the recipient, it would be of great fruit. The donor gives the gift, and the recipient generates the result—thus one would be the doer for another, happiness and suffering caused by another would be incurred, one would act, and another would experience. Therefore, a gift is purified by the donor, not by the recipient; it is the purity of the donor’s mind that yields the result'—as is the case with the Uttarāpathakas; with reference to them, the question is for the proponent of his own view, the assertion for the other. The phrase beginning 'worthy of offerings' is stated to show: 'If a gift were not purified by the recipient, what purpose would their status as worthy of offerings and so on serve?' The charge 'one is the doer for another' would be appropriate if the donor's intention to give were created by the recipient. However, the donor's pure intention to give, in dependence on the object designated as the recipient, is purified in the sense of yielding a great result. Therefore, this is not a valid objection to the statement, 'An offering is purified by the recipient.'

Dakkhiṇāvisuddhikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion on the Purification of Offerings.

Sattarasamo vaggo.

The Seventeenth Chapter.

18. Aṭṭhārasamavaggo

18. The Eighteenth Chapter.

1. Manussalokakathāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Discussion on the Human World.

802-803. Idāni [P 0.0172][V 0.0259] manussalokakathā nāma hoti. Tattha “tathāgato loke, jāto loke saṃvaḍḍho, lokaṃ abhibhuyya viharati [M 0.0261] anupalitto lokenā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.94) suttaṃ ayoniso gahetvā “bhagavā tusitabhavane nibbatto tattheva vasati, na manussalokaṃ āgacchati, nimmitarūpamattakaṃ panettha dassetī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi etarahi vetullakānaṃyeva, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ puṭṭhokāsena ceva suttasādhanena ca saññāpetuṃ nanu atthītiādimāha. Loke jātoti paravādī tusitapuraṃ sandhāya vadati. Satthārā panetaṃ manussalokaññeva sandhāya lokaṃ vuttaṃ. Lokaṃ abhibhuyyāti paravādī manussalokaṃ abhibhavitvāti diṭṭhiyā vadati, satthā pana ārammaṇalokaṃ abhibhavitvā vihāsi. Anupalitto lokenāti paravādī manussalokena anupalittataṃva sandhāya vadati, satthā pana lokadhammesu kilesehi anupalitto vihāsi. Tasmā asādhakametanti.

Now comes the discussion on the human world. Herein, some, having improperly grasped the sutta that states, 'The Tathāgata is in the world, born in the world, grown up in the world, having overcome the world, he dwells unstained by the world' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.94), hold the view that 'the Blessed One was born in the Tusita heaven and dwells there, not coming to the human world, but only displays a mere created form here'—as is the case with the Vetullakas nowadays. With reference to them, the question is for the proponent of his own view, the assertion for the other. Then, to convince him by the opportunity for questioning and by proof from the suttas, he says, beginning with 'Is there not...?' 'Born in the world'—the opponent says this with reference to the Tusita realm. But the Teacher spoke of 'the world' with reference to this very human world. 'Having overcome the world'—the opponent speaks from his view of having conquered the human world, but the Teacher dwelt having overcome the world of sense objects. 'Unstained by the world'—the opponent speaks with reference to being unstained by the human world, but the Teacher dwelt unstained by defilements in regard to worldly conditions. Therefore, this is not proof.

Manussalokakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion on the Human World.

2. Dhammadesanākathāvaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Discussion on the Teaching of the Dhamma.

804-806. Idāni dhammadesanākathā nāma hoti. Tattha “tusitapure ṭhito bhagavā dhammadesanatthāya abhinimmitaṃ pesesi, tena ceva tassa ca desanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā āyasmatā ānandena dhammo [P 0.0173] desito, na buddhena bhagavatā”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi vetullakānaññeva; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi tena dhammo desito, sveva satthā bhaveyyā”ti codetuṃ abhinimmito jinotiādimāha. Itaro tathā asampaṭicchanto paṭikkhipati. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

Now comes the discussion on the teaching of the Dhamma. Herein, concerning those whose doctrine is that 'the Blessed One, standing in the Tusita realm, sent forth a created being for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma, and having received the teaching from that created being, the Venerable Ānanda taught the Dhamma, not the Buddha, the Blessed One'—as is the case with the Vetullakas; with reference to them, the question is for the proponent of his own view, the assertion for the other. Then, to challenge him by saying, 'If the Dhamma was taught by that created being, he himself would be the Teacher,' he states the phrase beginning with 'the created conqueror.' The other, not accepting it thus, rejects it. The rest here is of clear meaning.

Dhammadesanākathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion on the Teaching of the Dhamma.

3. Karuṇākathāvaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Discussion on Compassion.

807-808. Idāni [V 0.0260] karuṇākathā nāma hoti. Tattha piyāyitānaṃ vatthūnaṃ vipattiyā sarāgānaṃ rāgavasena karuṇāpatirūpikaṃ pavattiṃ disvā “rāgova [M 0.0262] karuṇā nāma, so ca bhagavato natthi, tasmā natthi buddhassa bhagavato karuṇā”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi uttarāpathakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “karuṇā nāmesā nikkilesatāya ceva sattārammaṇatāya ca cetovimuttitāya ca ekādasānisaṃsatāya ca mettādīhi samānajātikā, tasmā yadi bhagavato karuṇā natthi, mettādayopissa na siyu”nti codanatthaṃ natthi buddhassa bhagavato mettātiādimāha. Ākāruṇikoti pañhe tathārūpaṃ vohāraṃ apassanto paṭikkhipati. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

Now comes the discussion on compassion. Herein, some, seeing that in those with attachment, a counterfeit of compassion arises through attachment due to the misfortune of beloved objects, hold the doctrine: 'What is called compassion is merely attachment, and the Blessed One is without that; therefore, the Buddha, the Blessed One, has no compassion'—as is the case with the Uttarāpathakas. With reference to them, the question is for the proponent of his own view, the assertion for the other. Then, for the purpose of challenging him, he says, beginning with 'The Buddha, the Blessed One, has no loving-kindness,' arguing: 'This which is called compassion is of the same nature as loving-kindness and so on, due to its being without defilement, having beings as its object, being a liberation of mind, and having eleven benefits. Therefore, if the Blessed One has no compassion, he would also not have loving-kindness and the like.' Regarding the question, 'Is he without compassion?', the opponent, not finding such a designation, rejects it. The rest here is of clear meaning.

Karuṇākathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion on Compassion.

4. Gandhajātakathāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Discussion on Fragrant Substances.

809. Idāni gandhajātakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ buddhe bhagavati ayoniso pemavasena “bhagavato uccārapassāvo aññe gandhajāte ativiya adhigaṇhāti, natthi tato ca sugandhataraṃ gandhajāta”nti laddhi, seyyathāpi ekaccānaṃ andhakānañceva [P 0.0174] uttarāpathakānañca; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha yathāpāḷimeva niyyātīti.

809. Now comes the discussion on fragrant substances. Herein, concerning those who, due to unwise affection for the Buddha, the Blessed One, held the doctrine that 'the Blessed One's excrement and urine greatly surpass other fragrant substances; there is no fragrant substance more fragrant than that'—as is the case with some of the Andhakas and the Uttarāpathakas; with reference to them, the question is for the proponent of his own view, the assertion for the other. The rest here is to be understood just as in the Pāḷi text.

Gandhajātakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion on Fragrant Substances.

5. Ekamaggakathāvaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Discussion on the Single Path.

810-811. Idāni ekamaggakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ buddhe bhagavati ayoniso pemavaseneva [V 0.0261] “bhagavā sotāpanno hutvā sakadāgāmī, sakadāgāmī hutvā anāgāmī, anāgāmī hutvā arahattaṃ sacchākāsi, ekeneva pana ariyamaggena cattāri phalāni sacchākāsī”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi tesaññeva; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ catūhi phalehi saddhiṃ uppannānaṃ catunnaṃ phassādīnaṃ ekato [M 0.0263] samodhānavasena codetuṃ catunnaṃ phassānantiādimāha. Sotāpattimaggenātiādi “kataramaggena sacchikarotī”ti pucchanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Arahattamaggenāti ca vutte tena sakkāyadiṭṭhiādīnaṃ pahānābhāvavasena codeti. Bhagavā sotāpannoti buddhabhūtassa sotāpannabhāvo natthīti paṭikkhipati. Parato pañhadvayepi eseva nayo. Sesamettha yathāpāḷimeva niyyātīti.

Now is the discussion on the single path. Here, some, due to unwise affection for the Blessed One, hold the view: 'The Blessed One, having become a stream-enterer, then a once-returner, then a non-returner, and then realized Arahantship, realized the four fruits with a single noble path.' This is the view of those very ones. With reference to them, the question is for the proponent of his own view, and the admission is for the other. Then, to challenge them by way of the simultaneous conjunction of the four contacts and other states that have arisen together with the four fruits, it is said: 'The four contacts,' and so on. 'With the stream-entry path,' and so on, is said for the purpose of asking, 'By which path does he realize it?' And when it is said, 'With the Arahant path,' it challenges them by way of the non-abandonment of personality-view and other defilements. The statement 'The Blessed One is a stream-enterer' is rejected because there is no state of a stream-enterer for one who has become a Buddha. The same method applies to the two subsequent questions as well. The rest here is to be understood exactly as in the Pāli.

Ekamaggakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion on the Single Path.

6. Jhānasaṅkantikathāvaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Discussion on Jhāna Transition.

813-816. Idāni jhānasaṅkantikathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ, tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ, catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.923-934) imaṃ paṭipāṭidesanaṃ [P 0.0175] nissāya “tassa tassa jhānassa upacārappavattiṃ vināva jhānā jhānaṃ saṅkamatī”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi mahisāsakānañceva ekaccānañca andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi te dutiyajjhānūpacāraṃ appatvā uppaṭipāṭiyā paṭhamajjhānā dutiyajjhānameva saṅkamati, paṭhamato tatiyaṃ, dutiyato catutthampi saṅkameyyā”ti codetuṃ paṭhamā jhānātiādimāha. Yā paṭhamassātiādi “yadi paṭhamato anantaraṃ dutiyaṃ, dutiyādīhi vā tatiyādīni samāpajjati, ekāvajjanena samāpajjeyyā”ti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Kāme ādīnavatoti paṭhamaṃ kāme ādīnavato manasi karoto pacchā uppajjati. Jhānakkhaṇe panesa nimittameva manasi karoti. Taññeva paṭhamanti “yadi purimajavanato pacchimajavanaṃ viya anantaraṃ uppajjeyya, ṭhapetvā purimapacchimabhāvaṃ lakkhaṇato taññeva taṃ bhaveyyā”ti codetuṃ pucchati. Iminā upāyena [V 0.0262] sabbattha attho veditabbo. Vivicceva kāmehītiādīhi paṭipāṭiyā jhānānaṃ desitabhāvaṃ dīpeti, na anantaruppattiṃ, tasmā asādhakanti.

Now is the discussion called the Discussion on Jhāna Transition. Here, some hold the thesis that 'a meditator transitions from jhāna to jhāna without the occurrence of the access concentration of that jhāna,' based on the sequential exposition: 'Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, enters and dwells in the first jhāna; with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, the third jhāna, and the fourth jhāna' (Saṃ. Ni. 5.923-934). This is the thesis of the Mahīśāsakas and some of the Andhakas. With reference to them, the question is for the proponent of his own view, and the admission is for the other. Then, to challenge him, he says, 'If, without attaining the access concentration of the second jhāna, you transition from the first jhāna directly to the second jhāna in an irregular sequence, then you should also be able to transition from the first to the third, and from the second to the fourth.' The phrase 'from the first,' etc., is stated for the purpose of challenging the opponent: 'If one attains the second immediately after the first, or the third and so on after the second and so on, then one should attain them with a single act of advertence.' As for 'seeing the danger in sensual pleasures,' it means that first, one attends to the danger in sensual pleasures, and only afterward does the jhāna arise. But at the moment of jhāna, one attends solely to the sign. As for 'just that first one,' he asks to challenge the opponent: 'If it were to arise immediately after the preceding impulsion, like a subsequent impulsion after a preceding one, then, setting aside the prior and subsequent nature, would it not be identical in characteristic?' The meaning should be understood in this way throughout. By 'secluded from sensual pleasures,' etc., it is shown that the jhānas are taught in sequence, not as arising immediately one after another. Therefore, this is not a valid proof.

Jhānasaṅkantikathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discussion on Jhāna Transition.

7. Jhānantarikakathāvaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Discussion on the Intermediate Jhāna.

817-818. Idāni [M 0.0264] jhānantarikakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ samaye “pañcakanaye pañca jhānāni vibhattāni, kevalaṃ tayo samādhī uddiṭṭhā”ti avitakkavicāramattassa samādhino okāsaṃ ajānantānaṃ “paṭhamassa ca dutiyassa ca jhānassa antare jhānantarikā nāma esā”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi sammitiyānañceva ekaccānañca andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “jhānampi cetasikā dhammā, phassādayopi, tasmā yadi jhānantarikā nāma bhaveyya, phassantarikādīhipi bhavitabba”nti codanatthaṃ atthi phassantarikātiādimāha[P 0.0176].

Now is the discussion called the Discussion on the Intermediate Jhāna. Here, for those in whose system 'in the fivefold method, five jhānas are distinguished, but only three concentrations are designated,' not recognizing the scope of a concentration that is merely without applied thought but with sustained thought, they hold the thesis that 'this is called the intermediate jhāna between the first and second jhāna,' like the Sammitiyas and some of the Andhakas. With reference to them, the question is for the proponent of his own view, and the admission is for the other. Then, to challenge him, he says, 'Jhāna is a mental factor, and so are contact and so on. Therefore, if there were something called an intermediate jhāna, there would also have to be an intermediate contact, etc.' He says 'is there an intermediate contact?' and so on, for the purpose of challenging the opponent.

Dutiyassa ca jhānassāti “yadi jhānantarikā nāma bhaveyya, dutiyatatiyādīnipi jhānāneva, tesampi antarikāya bhavitabba”nti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. So kevalaṃ laddhiyā abhāvena paṭikkhipati ceva paṭijānāti ca. Paṭhamassa cāti puṭṭho laddhivasena paṭijānāti.

As for 'and of the second jhāna,' it is stated for the purpose of challenging the opponent: 'If there were something called an intermediate jhāna, then since the second, third, and so on, are also jhānas, they too must have an intermediate state.' He denies this simply because he has no such thesis, while acknowledging his own position. And as for 'of the first,' when asked, he acknowledges it in accordance with his thesis.

819. Savitakko savicārotiādi “tiṇṇampi samādhīnaṃ samādhibhāve samāne avitakko vicāramattova samādhi jhānantariko, na itaroti ko ettha visesahetū”ti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

819. As for 'with applied thought and sustained thought,' etc., it is stated for the purpose of challenging the opponent: 'Even though the three concentrations are the same in respect of being concentration, the concentration that is merely without applied thought but with sustained thought is an intermediate jhāna, and not the others—what is the reason for this distinction here?'

820-822. Dvinnaṃ jhānānaṃ paṭuppannānanti paṭhamadutiyāni sandhāya pucchati. Itaro “tesaṃ paccuppannānaṃyeva antare avitakko vicāramatto samādhi jhānantariko nāma hotī”ti laddhiyā paṭijānāti. Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ niruddhanti puṭṭho tiṇṇaṃ ekakkhaṇe pavatti na yuttāti paṭijānāti[V 0.0263]. Avitakko vicāramatto samādhi paṭhamaṃ jhānanti catukkanayavasena pucchati. Sakavādī tasmiṃ naye tassa abhāvā paṭikkhipati. Nanu tayo samādhīti etthāyamadhippāyo – yathā tesu tīsu samādhīsu dve samādhī jhānāneva, na jhānantarikā, evaṃ itarenapi jhāneneva bhavitabbaṃ, na jhānantarikāyāti.

As for 'of the two jhānas that are present,' he asks referring to the first and second. The other acknowledges, according to his thesis, that 'the concentration that is merely without applied thought but with sustained thought, which is between those present jhānas, is called the intermediate jhāna.' When asked 'has the first jhāna ceased?', he acknowledges that it is not proper for three states to occur in a single moment. He asks, according to the fourfold system, 'Is the concentration that is merely without applied thought but with sustained thought the first jhāna?' The proponent of his own view denies this because of its absence in that system. Now, as for 'are there not three concentrations?', the intention here is this: just as among those three concentrations, two concentrations are indeed jhānas, not intermediate jhānas, so also the other should be a jhāna, not an intermediate jhāna.

Jhānantarikakathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discussion on the Intermediate Jhāna.

8. Samāpanno saddaṃ suṇātītikathāvaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Discussion on Whether One in Attainment Hears Sound.

823-825. Idāni [M 0.0265] samāpanno saddaṃ suṇātītikathā nāma hoti. Tattha “yasmā paṭhamassa jhānassa saddo kaṇḍako vutto bhagavatā, yadi ca samāpanno taṃ na suṇeyya, kathaṃ kaṇḍako siyā. Tasmā samāpanno saddaṃ, suṇātī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Cakkhunā rūpaṃ passatītiādi “samāpannassa tāva pañcadvārappavattaṃ natthi, tasmiṃ asati [P 0.0177] yadi so saddaṃ suṇeyya, rūpampi passeyyā”ti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Saddo kaṇḍakoti vikkhepakarattā vuttaṃ. Oḷārikena hi saddena sote ghaṭṭite paṭhamajjhānato vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, tenetaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā asādhakaṃ. Dutiyassa jhānassātiādi “yathā aññopi kaṇḍako antosamāpattiyaṃ natthi, evaṃ saddassavanampī”ti bodhanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

823-825. Now comes the discussion entitled, 'One in Attainment Hears Sound.' Herein, 'Because sound is called a thorn for the first jhāna by the Blessed One, if one in attainment did not hear it, how could it be a thorn? Therefore, one in attainment hears sound'—this is the view of some, such as the Pubbaseliyas. With reference to them, the question is from the proponent of the orthodox view, and the admission is from the other party. 'One sees form with the eye,' and so forth, is said for the purpose of challenging: 'For one in attainment, there is no activity of the five sense doors. In the absence of that, if one were to hear sound, one would also see form.' 'Sound is a thorn' is said because it is a cause of distraction. For when a gross sound strikes the ear, emergence from the first jhāna occurs—for this reason it is said. Therefore, this is not a valid proof. 'For the second jhāna,' and so forth, is said for the purpose of explaining that 'just as no other thorn exists within the attainment, so too does the hearing of sound not exist.' All this is of clear meaning.

Samāpanno saddaṃ suṇātītikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion: 'One in Attainment Hears Sound'.

9. Cakkhunārūpaṃpassatītikathāvaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Discussion: 'One Sees Form with the Eye'.

826-827. Idāni cakkhunā rūpaṃ passatītikathā nāma hoti. Tattha “cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā”ti vacanaṃ nissāya “pasādacakkhumeva rūpaṃ passatī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṅghikānaṃ[V 0.0264], te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi cakkhunā rūpaṃ passeyya, rūpena rūpaṃ passeyyātī”ti codetuṃ rūpena rūpaṃ passatīti āha. Itaro rūpāyatanaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipitvā puna puṭṭho cakkhumeva sandhāya paṭijānāti. Paṭivijānātīti ettha ayamadhippāyo – passatīti hi mayaṃ paṭijānanaṃ sandhāya pucchāma, na cakkhūpasaṃhāramattaṃ. Tasmā vadehi tāva “kiṃ te cakkhumā rūpena rūpaṃ paṭivijānātī”ti. Itaro purimanayeneva paṭikkhipati ceva paṭijānāti ca. Atha naṃ “evaṃ sante rūpaṃ manoviññāṇaṃ āpajjati, tañhi paṭivijānāti nāmā”ti codetuṃ rūpaṃ manoviññāṇanti āha. Itaro lesaṃ alabhanto paṭikkhipateva. Atthi cakkhussa āvaṭṭanātiādi “yadi cakkhu paṭivijānanaṭṭhena passati, cakkhuviññāṇassa viya tassāpi āvajjanāya [M 0.0266] bhavitabba”nti codetuṃ pucchati. Itaro yasmā na āvajjanapaṭibaddhaṃ cakkhu, na taṃ āvajjanānantaraṃ uppajjati, tasmā na hevanti paṭikkhipati. Sotena saddantiādīsupi [P 0.0178] eseva nayo. Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ passatīti sasambhārakathānayena vuttaṃ. Yathā hi usunā vijjhantopi “dhanunā vijjhatī”ti vuccati, evaṃ cakkhuviññāṇena passantopi “cakkhunā passatī”ti vutto, tasmā asādhakametaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayopi.

826-827. Now comes the discussion entitled, 'One Sees Form with the Eye.' Herein, based on the expression 'having seen form with the eye,' some, such as the Mahāsaṅghikas, hold the view that 'the sensitive eye itself sees form.' With reference to them, the question is from the proponent of the orthodox view, and the admission is from the other party. Then, to challenge them with, 'If one were to see form with the eye, one would see form with form,' he says, 'Does one see form with form?' The other party, referring to the form-base, denies this, but when questioned again, admits it with reference to the eye itself. Herein, the intention of 'perceives' is this: we ask with reference to the admission 'sees,' not merely with reference to the eye. Therefore, you should say, 'Does your eye perceive form with form?' The other party denies and admits in the same way as before. Then, to challenge them with, 'This being so, form would become mind-consciousness, for that is what is called 'perceiving',' he says, 'Is form mind-consciousness?' The other party, finding no way of evasion, simply denies. 'Is there adverting of the eye?' and so forth, is asked to challenge: 'If the eye sees in the sense of perceiving, then like eye-consciousness, it too must have adverting.' The other party denies with 'not so,' because the eye is not connected with adverting, nor does it arise immediately after adverting. The same method applies to 'sound with the ear,' and so on. Here, monks, the statement 'a monk sees form with the eye' is spoken by way of a statement including its components. Just as one who pierces with an arrow is said to 'pierce with a bow,' so too, one who sees with eye-consciousness is said to 'see with the eye.' Therefore, this is not a valid proof. The same method applies to the remaining cases as well.

Cakkhunā rūpaṃ passatītikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion: 'One Sees Form with the Eye'.

Aṭṭhārasamo vaggo.

The Eighteenth Chapter.

19. Ekūnavīsatimavaggo

19. The Nineteenth Chapter.

1. Kilesapajahanakathāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Discussion of Abandoning Defilements.

828-831. Idāni [P 0.0179] kilesapajahanakathā nāma hoti. Tattha “yasmā kilesapahānaṃ nāma atthi, pahīnakilesassa ca atītāpi kilesā pahīnāva honti, anāgatāpi, paccuppannāpi, tasmā atītepi kilese pajahati, anāgatepi, paccuppannepī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi ekaccānaṃ uttarāpathakānaṃ; te sandhāya atītetiādipucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa[V 0.0265]. Sesaṃ yathāpāḷimeva niyyāti. Natthi kilese jahatīti imasmiṃ pana paravādissa pañhe yasmā kacavaraṃ pajahantassa kacavare chaḍḍanavāyāmo viya kilese pajahantassa na atītādibhedesu kilesesu vāyāmo atthi, nibbānārammaṇe pana ariyamagge pavattite kilesā anuppannāyeva nuppajjantīti pahīnā nāma honti, tasmā na hevanti paṭikkhipati. Tena hi atīte kilese pajahatītiādi pana yasmā “natthi kilesapajahanā”ti na vattabbaṃ, tasmā atītādibhede pajahatīti chalena vuttaṃ.

828-831. Now comes the discussion entitled, 'The Abandoning of Defilements.' Herein, some, such as certain Uttarāpathakas, hold the view that 'since the abandoning of defilements exists, and for one who has abandoned defilements, past defilements are indeed abandoned, as are future and present ones, therefore one abandons defilements of the past, future, and present.' With reference to them, the question concerning the past, and so forth, is from the proponent of the orthodox view, and the admission is from the other party. The rest proceeds just as in the Pāli text. However, regarding the opponent's question, 'Does one not abandon defilements?', it is refuted for this reason: just as for one abandoning rubbish there is an effort in discarding the rubbish, for one abandoning defilements there is no such effort regarding defilements in the categories of past, and so on. Rather, when the noble path, which has Nibbāna as its object, proceeds, defilements that have not yet arisen simply do not arise—thus they are called 'abandoned.' Therefore, he refutes with 'not so.' Then, regarding the statement 'one abandons past defilements,' and so on, since it should not be said that 'there is no abandoning of defilements,' it is therefore stated by way of a pretext that one abandons them in the categories of past, and so forth.

Kilesapajahanakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion of Abandoning Defilements.

2. Suññatakathāvaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Discussion of Emptiness.

832. Idāni [M 0.0267] suññatakathā nāma hoti. Tattha suññatāti dve suññatā khandhānañca anattalakkhaṇaṃ nibbānañca. Tesu anattalakkhaṇaṃ [P 0.0180] tāva ekaccaṃ ekena pariyāyena siyā saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpannaṃ, nibbānaṃ, apariyāpannameva. Imaṃ pana vibhāgaṃ aggahetvā “suññatā saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpannā”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Animittanti sabbanimittarahitaṃ nibbānaṃ. “Appaṇihito”tipi tasseva nāmaṃ. Kasmā panetaṃ ābhatanti? Avibhajjavādīvāde dosāropanatthaṃ. Yassa hi avibhajitvā “ekadeseneva suññatā saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpannā”ti laddhi, tassa nibbānampi saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpannanti āpajjati. Imassa dosassāropanatthaṃ “animittaṃ appaṇihita”nti ābhataṃ. Itaro tassa pariyāpannabhāvaṃ anicchanto paṭikkhipati. Saṅkhārakkhandho na aniccotiādi nibbānasaṅkhātāya suññatāya aniccabhāvāpattidosadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

832. Now comes the discussion entitled, 'Emptiness.' Herein, 'emptiness' refers to two kinds: the characteristic of not-self of the aggregates, and Nibbāna. Among these, the characteristic of not-self may, in a certain way, be included in the aggregate of formations; Nibbāna, however, is never included. But without grasping this distinction, some, such as the Andhakas, hold the view that 'emptiness is included in the aggregate of formations.' With reference to them, the question is from the proponent of the orthodox view, and the admission is from the other party. 'The Signless' refers to Nibbāna, which is devoid of all signs. 'The Undirected' is also a name for it. Why then is this introduced? For the purpose of imputing a fault in the argument of one who does not make distinctions. For one who holds the view, without making a distinction, that 'emptiness is in one part included in the aggregate of formations,' for him it would follow that Nibbāna too is included in the aggregate of formations. For the purpose of imputing this fault, 'the Signless' and 'the Undirected' are introduced. The other party, not wishing for it to be included, rejects this. The statement 'The aggregate of formations is not impermanent,' and so forth, is said for the purpose of showing the fault that would follow of emptiness, designated as Nibbāna, having the state of being impermanent.

833. Saṅkhārakkhandhassa suññatāti “yadi aññassa khandhassa suññatā aññakkhandhapariyāpannā, saṅkhārakkhandhasuññatāyapi sesakkhandhapariyāpannāya bhavitabba”nti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Saṅkhārakkhandhassa suññatā na vattabbātiādi “yadi saṅkhārakkhandhasuññatā sesakkhandhapariyāpannā [V 0.0266] na hoti, sesakkhandhasuññatāpi saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpannā na hotī”ti paṭilomadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

833. The statement "the emptiness of the aggregate of formations" is stated for the purpose of a challenge: "If the emptiness of one aggregate is included in another aggregate, then the emptiness of the aggregate of formations should also be included in the remaining aggregates." The assertion that "the emptiness of the aggregate of formations cannot be stated" and so on is stated to show the converse: "If the emptiness of the aggregate of formations is not included in the remaining aggregates, then the emptiness of the remaining aggregates is also not included in the aggregate of formations."

834. Suññamidaṃ, bhikkhave, saṅkhārāti suttaṃ parasamayato ābhataṃ. Tattha saṅkhārāti “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”ti āgataṭṭhāne viya pañcakkhandhā, te ca attattaniyasuññattā suññatāti sāsanāvacaraṃ hoti, na virujjhati, tasmā anuññātaṃ. Yasmā panetaṃ na suññatāya saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpannabhāvaṃ dīpeti, tasmā asādhakanti.

834. The sutta passage, "Monks, these formations are empty," is cited from another school. Here, "formations" refers to the five aggregates, as in the passage, "All formations are impermanent." And since they are empty of self and what belongs to self, this is within the scope of the teaching and is not contradictory; therefore, it is permitted. However, because this does not demonstrate that emptiness is included in the aggregate of formations, it is not a valid proof.

Suññatakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Emptiness.

3. Sāmaññaphalakathāvaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Discourse on the Fruits of Recluseship

835-836. Idāni sāmaññaphalakathā nāma hoti. Tattha maggavīthiyampi phalasamāpattivīthiyampi ariyamaggassa vipākacittaṃ [P 0.0181] sāmaññaphalaṃ nāmāti [M 0.0268] sakasamaye sanniṭṭhānaṃ. Yesaṃ pana tathā aggahetvā “kilesapahānañceva phaluppatti ca sāmaññaphalaṃ, tasmā asaṅkhata”nti laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha heṭṭhā vuttanayattā yathā pāḷimeva niyyātīti.

835-836. Now there is the discourse called the discourse on the fruits of recluseship. Herein, the resultant consciousness of the noble path, whether in the path-process or the fruition-attainment process, is called the fruit of recluseship; this is the established conclusion in one's own system. But for those who, not having grasped it thus, hold the view that “the abandoning of defilements and the arising of the fruit is the fruit of recluseship, therefore it is unconditioned”—as is the doctrine of the Pubbaseliyas—with reference to them, the question is for the proponent of his own doctrine, and the affirmation is for the opponent. The rest here, because it follows the method stated earlier, is to be derived directly from the Pāḷi text.

Sāmaññaphalakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Fruits of Recluseship.

4. Pattikathāvaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Discourse on Attainment

837-840. Idāni pattikathā nāma hoti. Tattha “yaṃ yaṃ paṭilabbhati, tassa tassa paṭilābho patti nāma. Sā ca asaṅkhatā”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyānaññeva; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamidhāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayattā yathāpāḷimeva niyyātīti[V 0.0267]. Na vattabbantiādi yāya laddhiyā patti asaṅkhatāti maññati, taṃ pakāsetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha sakavādī “na hevaṃ vattabbe”ti paṭikkhipanto kevalaṃ pattiyā rūpādibhāvaṃ na sampaṭicchati. Na hi patti nāma koci dhammo atthi, na pana asaṅkhatabhāvaṃ anujānāti. Itaro pana paṭikkhepamatteneva asaṅkhatāti laddhiṃ patiṭṭhapeti, sā ayoniso patiṭṭhāpitattā appatiṭṭhitāyevāti.

837-840. Now there is the discourse called the discourse on attainment. Herein, concerning those whose doctrine is that “whatever is obtained, the obtaining of that is called attainment, and that is unconditioned”—as is the doctrine of the Pubbaseliyas themselves—with reference to them, the question is for the proponent of his own doctrine, and the affirmation is for the opponent. The rest here, because it follows the method stated earlier, is to be derived directly from the Pāḷi text. “It should not be said,” etc., is stated to clarify the doctrine by which one considers attainment to be unconditioned. Here, the proponent of his own doctrine, rejecting by saying, “It should not be said thus,” does not accept that attainment has the nature of form, etc. For there is no such phenomenon as attainment, nor does he concede its unconditioned nature. The other, however, merely by the rejection, establishes the doctrine that it is unconditioned. But because this is established unwisely, it is not firmly established.

Pattikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Attainment.

5. Tathatākathāvaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Discourse on Suchness

841-843. Idāni tathatākathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “rūpādīnaṃ sabbadhammānaṃ rūpādisabhāvatāsaṅkhātā tathatā nāma atthi, sā ca saṅkhatesu rūpādīsu apariyāpannattā asaṅkhatā”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi ekaccānaṃ uttarāpathakānaṃ, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa[P 0.0182], paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamidhāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayattā pākaṭamevāti.

841-843. Now there is the discourse called the discourse on suchness. Herein, concerning those whose doctrine is that “there exists what is called suchness, defined as the inherent nature of all phenomena such as form, etc., and since it is not included among conditioned phenomena such as form, etc., it is unconditioned”—as is the doctrine of some Northerners—with reference to them, the question is for the proponent of his own doctrine, and the affirmation is for the opponent. The rest here, because it follows the method stated earlier, is evident.

Tathatākathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Suchness.

6. Kusalakathāvaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Discourse on Wholesome States

844-846. Idāni [M 0.0269] kusalakathā nāma hoti. Tattha anavajjampi kusalaṃ iṭṭhapākampi. Anavajjaṃ nāma kilesavippayuttaṃ. Ayaṃ nayo ṭhapetvā akusalaṃ sabbadhamme bhajati. Iṭṭhavipākaṃ nāma āyatiṃ upapattipavattesu iṭṭhaphalanipphādakaṃ puññaṃ. Ayaṃ nayo kusalattike ādipadameva bhajati. Yesaṃ pana imaṃ vibhāgaṃ aggahetvā anavajjabhāvamatteneva nibbānaṃ kusalanti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ, tesaṃ iṭṭhavipākaṭṭhena nibbānassa kusalatābhāvaṃ dīpetuṃ [V 0.0268] pucchā sakavādissa, attano laddhivasena paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamidhāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthamevāti.

844-846. Now there is the discourse called the discourse on wholesome states. Herein, what is blameless is wholesome, and what has a desirable result is wholesome. Blameless means dissociated from defilements. This principle applies to all phenomena except the unwholesome. What has a desirable result refers to merit that produces desirable fruits in future existences and continuities. This principle applies only to the first term of the wholesome triad. But for those who, not having grasped this distinction, hold the view that Nibbāna is wholesome merely because of its blameless nature—as is the doctrine of the Andhakas—the question is for the proponent of his own doctrine to demonstrate to them the absence of Nibbāna’s wholesomeness in the sense of having a desirable result, and the affirmation is for the opponent according to his own doctrine. The rest here, because it follows the method stated earlier, is of evident meaning.

Kusalakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Wholesome States.

7. Accantaniyāmakathāvaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Discourse on the Absolutely Fixed Course

847. Idāni accantaniyāmakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “sakiṃ nimuggo nimuggova hotī”ti (a. ni. 7.15) suttaṃ nissāya “atthi puthujjanassa accantaniyāmatā”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi ekaccānaṃ uttarāpathakānaṃ, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Mātughātakotiādi “niyatamicchādiṭṭhikassa ca mātughātakādīnañca samāne micchattaniyāme mātughātakādīhipi te accantaniyatehi bhavitabba”nti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Itaro “niyatamicchādiṭṭhiko saṃsārakhāṇuko bhavantarepi niyatova ime pana ekasmiññeva attabhāve”ti laddhiyā na hevanti paṭikkhipati[P 0.0183].

847. Now there is the discourse called the discourse on the absolutely fixed course. Herein, concerning those who, relying on the sutta, "Once submerged, one remains submerged" (AN 7.15), hold the view that "there is an absolutely fixed course for an ordinary person," such as some Northerners—with reference to them, the question is for the proponent of his own doctrine, and the affirmation is for the opponent. The mention of "matricide, etc." is stated for the purpose of objection: "Since there is a sameness of fixed wrongness for one with fixed wrong view and for matricides, etc., it must be that these matricides, etc., are also on an absolutely fixed course." The other, holding the view that "one with fixed wrong view is a post in saṃsāra, fixed even in a future existence, but these others are so only in a single lifetime," rejects this by saying, "Not so."

848. Vicikicchā uppajjeyyāti “ayaṃ niyato vā no vā”ti evaṃ uppajjeyyāti pucchati. Itaro anuppattikāraṇaṃ apassanto paṭijānāti. Nuppajjeyyāti puṭṭho pana yaṃ diṭṭhiṃ āsevanto niyāmaṃ okkanto, tattha anuppattiṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Tato pahīnāti puṭṭho maggena appahīnattā paṭikkhipati, taṃ diṭṭhiṃ ārabbha asamudācārato paṭijānāti. Atha naṃ yasmā pahānaṃ nāma vinā ariyamaggena natthi, tasmā tassa vasena codetuṃ sotāpattimaggenātiādimāha. So ekamaggenāpi appahīnattā [M 0.0270] paṭikkhipati. Puna katamenāti puṭṭho micchāmaggaṃ sandhāya akusalenātiādimāha.

848. One asks if doubt would arise in this way: 'Is this person on a fixed course or not?' The other, not seeing a reason for its non-arising, acknowledges that it would. But when asked if it would not arise, referring to the view he cultivates, having entered the fixed course, he acknowledges its non-arising with reference to that. When asked whether it is abandoned, he denies it, since it has not been abandoned by the path; but he affirms that it is, on account of not acting in accordance with that view. Then, since abandonment does not exist without the noble path, to challenge him on that basis, one says, "by the stream-entry path," etc. He denies it because it has not been abandoned even by a single path. When further asked, "By which?", he refers to the wrong path, saying, "by the unwholesome," etc.

849. Ucchedadiṭṭhi uppajjeyyāti dutiyaniyāmuppattiṃ pucchati. Itaro yasmā “yepi te okkalā vayabhiññā natthikavādā akiriyavādā ahetukavādā”ti (ma. ni. 3.143) vacanato tissopi niyatamicchādiṭṭhiyo ekassa uppajjanti, tasmā paṭijānāti.

849. If an annihilationist view were to arise—this asks about the arising of the second fixed course. The other party acknowledges it because, as it is said, 'Those Okkalas who are annihilationists, proponents of nihilism, proponents of inaction, proponents of causelessness' (MN 3.143), thus even three fixed wrong views arise in one person.

850. Atha [V 0.0269] naṃ “na ca nāma so accantaniyāmo”ti codetuṃ hañcītiādimāha. Accantaniyatassa hi dutiyaniyāmo niratthako. Nuppajjeyyāti pañhe yaṃ sassatadiṭṭhiyā sassatanti gahitaṃ, tadeva ucchijjissatīti gahetvā anuppattiṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Pahīnāti puṭṭho maggena appahīnattā paṭikkhipati, vuttanayena anuppajjanato paṭijānāti. Sassatadiṭṭhi uppajjeyyātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Sesaṃ vicikicchāvāre vuttanayameva.

850. Then, to challenge him with 'But surely, that is not an absolute certainty,' he says 'if so,' and so on. For one who is absolutely fixed, a second fixed course is meaningless. In the question, 'Would it not arise?', taking that which is grasped as 'eternal' by the eternalist view as 'it will be cut off,' he acknowledges its non-arising. When asked, 'Is it abandoned?', he denies it because it has not been abandoned by the path, but acknowledges it on account of its non-arising in the way explained. The same method applies to questions such as, 'Would an eternalist view arise?'. The rest is as explained in the section on doubt.

851-852. Na vattabbanti pucchā paravādissa, suttassa atthitāya paṭiññā sakavādissa. Na pana so bhavantarepi nimuggova. Imasmiññeva hi bhave abhabbo so taṃ diṭṭhiṃ pajahitunti ayamettha adhippāyo, tasmā asādhakametanti. Sabbakālaṃ ummujjitvā nimujjatītiādi vacanamatte abhinivesaṃ akatvā attho pariyesitabboti dassanatthaṃ vuttanti.

851-852. The question, 'Should it not be said?' is the opponent's; the proponent's assertion is due to the existence of the sutta. But he is not submerged even in another existence. The meaning here is that in this very existence he is incapable of abandoning that view; therefore, this is inconclusive. This is said to show that the meaning should be sought without adhering to mere statements such as 'at all times emerging and submerging'.

Accantaniyāmakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discussion of Absolute Certainty.

8. Indriyakathāvaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Discussion of the Faculties

853-856. Idāni indriyakathā nāma hoti. Tattha lokiyā saddhā saddhā [P 0.0184] eva nāma, na saddhindriyaṃ. Tathā lokiyaṃ vīriyaṃ…pe… sati… samādhi… paññā paññāyeva nāma, na paññindriyanti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi hetuvādānañceva mahisāsakānañca; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa[M 0.0271]. Natthi lokiyā saddhātiādi yasmā lokiyāpi saddhādayova dhammā adhipatiyaṭṭhena indriyaṃ, na saddhādīhi aññaṃ saddhindriyādi nāma atthi, tasmā lokiyānampi saddhādīnaññeva saddhindriyādibhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Atthi lokiyo manotiādi yathā te lokiyāpi manādayo dhammā manindriyādīni, evaṃ lokiyā saddhādayopi saddhindriyānīti upamāya tassatthassa vibhāvanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Sesamettha yathāpāḷimeva niyyātīti.

853-856. Now there is the discussion on the faculties. Herein, 'Mundane faith is merely called faith, not the faculty of faith. Similarly, mundane energy… mindfulness… concentration… wisdom is merely called wisdom, not the faculty of wisdom'—this is the doctrine of some, such as the Hetuvādins and the Mahīsāsakas. With reference to them, the question is the proponent's, the assertion is the other's. As to 'There is no mundane faith,' etc.: because even mundane states such as faith are faculties in the sense of sovereignty, and there is nothing called the faculty of faith, etc., apart from faith, etc., themselves, this is said to show that even mundane states such as faith have the status of being the faculties of faith. As to 'There is a mundane mind,' etc.: this is said to clarify that meaning by way of analogy: just as those mundane states such as mind are the faculties of mind, so too are mundane states such as faith the faculties of faith. The rest here proceeds just as in the Pāli text.

Indriyakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discussion of the Faculties.

Ekūnavīsatimo vaggo.

The Nineteenth Section.

20. Vīsatimavaggo

20. The Twentieth Section

1. Asañciccakathāvaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discussion of Unintentionality

857-862. Idāni [P 0.0185][V 0.0270] asañciccakathā nāma hoti. Tattha “ānantariyavatthūni nāma garūni bhāriyāni, tasmā asañciccāpi tesu vatthūsu vikopitesu ānantariko hotī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi ekaccānaṃ uttarāpathakānaṃ; te sandhāya asañciccāti pucchā sakavādissa, laddhivasena paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yasmā ānantariyakammaṃ nāma kammapathappattaṃ. Yadi ca asañcicca kammapathabhedo siyā, avasesā pāṇātipātādayopi asañcicca bhaveyyu”nti codanatthaṃ asañciccapāṇaṃ hantvātiādimāha. Itaro tathārūpāya laddhiyā abhāvena paṭikkhipati. Sesaṃ yathāpāḷimeva niyyāti. Na vattabbaṃ mātughātakoti pucchā paravādissa, rogapaṭikārādikāle asañcicca ghātaṃ sandhāya paṭiññā sakavādissa. Nanu mātā jīvitā voropitāti pañhepi asañcicca voropitaṃ sandhāya paṭiññā sakavādisseva. Evaṃ adhippāyaṃ pana aggahetvā hañcīti laddhipatiṭṭhāpanaṃ itarassa. Taṃ ayoniso patiṭṭhāpitattā appatiṭṭhitameva. Pitughātakādīsupi eseva nayo. Saṅghabhedake pana dhammasaññiṃ sandhāya saṅghabhedo ānantarikoti pucchā sakavādissa, “saṅghaṃ samaggaṃ bhetvāna, kappaṃ [M 0.0272] nirayamhi paccatī”ti vacanaṃ ayoniso gahetvā paṭiññā paravādissa. Puna sabbeti puṭṭho sakapakkhe dhammasaññiṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati, parapakkhe dhammasaññiṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Dhammasaññīti [P 0.0186] pañhadvayepi eseva nayo. Nanu vuttaṃ bhagavatāti suttaṃ ekanteneva dhammavādissa ānantarikabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Āpāyiko nerayikoti gāthāyapi adhammavādīyeva adhippeto. Itaro pana adhippāyaṃ aggahetvā laddhiṃ patiṭṭhapeti. Sā ayoniso patiṭṭhāpitattā appatiṭṭhitāyevāti.

857-862. Now there is the discussion on unintentionality. Herein, 'The bases for acts with immediate consequence are grave and weighty; therefore, even if one violates those bases unintentionally, one commits an act with immediate consequence'—this is the doctrine of some, such as certain Uttarāpathakas. With reference to them, the question about unintentionality is the proponent's, and the assertion, according to their doctrine, is the other's. Then, to challenge them, it is said, 'having unintentionally killed a living being,' etc., for this reason: 'Because an act with immediate consequence is one that has attained to a course of action. If there could be an unintentional breach of a course of action, the remaining acts, such as killing living beings, could also be unintentional.' The other party rejects this, as they do not hold such a doctrine. The rest proceeds just as in the Pāli text. The question, 'Should one not say “a matricide”?' is the opponent's; the proponent's assertion is with reference to an unintentional killing at a time such as treating an illness. Indeed, even in the question, 'Was the mother deprived of life?', the assertion is the proponent's, with reference to an unintentional deprivation. However, without grasping this intention, the other party establishes their doctrine with 'if so.' But because it is established improperly, it remains unestablished. The same method applies to patricide and the rest. Regarding a schismatic, however, the question, 'Is creating a schism an act with immediate consequence?' is the proponent's, with reference to one who perceives his action as Dhamma. The opponent asserts this by improperly taking the statement, 'Having split a united Saṅgha, one is cooked in hell for an eon.' When asked again, 'All of them?', the proponent rejects it, with reference to one on his own side who perceives his action as Dhamma, but acknowledges it, with reference to one on the other side who perceives his action as Dhamma. In both questions regarding one who perceives his action as Dhamma, the method is the same. The sutta, 'Was it not said by the Blessed One?', was spoken to show that one who speaks according to the Dhamma is absolutely subject to the immediate consequence. In the verse, 'Bound for the plane of misery, for hell,' it is one who speaks not according to the Dhamma who is intended. The other party, however, without grasping the intended meaning, establishes their doctrine. Because it is established improperly, it remains unestablished.

Asañciccakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discussion of Unintentionality.

2. Ñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge

863-865. Idāni [V 0.0271] ñāṇakathā nāma hoti. Tattha duvidhaṃ ñāṇaṃ – lokiyañca lokuttarañca. Lokiyaṃ samāpattiñāṇampi hoti dānādivasena pavattaṃ kammassakatañāṇampi; lokuttaraṃ saccaparicchedakaṃ maggañāṇampi phalañāṇampi. Imaṃ pana vibhāgaṃ akatvā “saccaparicchedakameva ñāṇaṃ na itaraṃ, tasmā natthi puthujjanassa ñāṇa”nti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi hetuvādānaṃ, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Paññātiādi ñāṇavevacanadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tenetaṃ dīpeti – yadi tassa ñāṇaṃ natthi, paññādayopi natthi. Atha paññādayo atthi, ñāṇampi atthi. Kasmā? Paññādīnaṃ ñāṇato anaññattāti. Paṭhamaṃ jhānantiādi samāpattiñāṇassa dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Dānaṃ dadeyyātiādi kammassakatañāṇassa. Dukkhaṃ parijānātīti lokuttaramaggañāṇameva dīpeti, na ca lokuttarameva ñāṇanti.

863-865. Now comes the discussion on knowledge. Herein, knowledge is twofold: mundane and supramundane. Mundane knowledge includes both knowledge of attainment in concentration and knowledge of the ownership of kamma operative in acts like giving. Supramundane knowledge includes the path knowledge that discerns the truths and fruition knowledge. However, without making this distinction, some, such as the Hetuvādins, hold the view that 'only the knowledge that discerns the truths is knowledge, not the other kinds; therefore, an ordinary person has no knowledge.' With reference to them, the question is for the proponent of our own school, while the affirmation is for the other. The terms 'wisdom' and so forth are mentioned to show synonyms of knowledge. This is explained thus: If that person has no knowledge, then there is also no wisdom and the like. But if wisdom and the like exist, then knowledge also exists. Why? Because wisdom and the like are not different from knowledge. The phrase 'the first jhāna' and so on is stated to show knowledge of attainment in concentration. 'One should give gifts' and so on refers to the knowledge of the ownership of kamma. 'One fully understands suffering' points specifically to supramundane path knowledge, not that knowledge is solely supramundane.

Ñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discussion on Knowledge.

3. Nirayapālakathāvaṇṇanā

3. The Exposition of the Discussion on the Hell-Wardens.

866. Idāni [P 0.0187] nirayapālakathā nāma hoti. Tattha “niraye nerayikakammāneva nirayapālarūpavasena vadhenti, natthi nirayapālā nāma sattā”ti [M 0.0273] yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi tattha nirayapālā na siyuṃ, kammakāraṇāpi na bhaveyyuṃ. Kāraṇikesu hi sati kāraṇā”ti codetuṃ natthi nirayesūtiādimāha.

866. Now comes the discussion on the Hell-Wardens. Herein, with reference to those who hold the view that 'in hell, it is the kamma of the hell-beings themselves that torments them in the form of hell-wardens, and there are no beings called hell-wardens'—such as the Andhakas—the question is for the proponent of our own school, and the affirmation is for the other. Then, to challenge them by saying, 'If there were no hell-wardens there, there would also be no acts of torment. For where there are tormentors, there is torment,' he stated, 'there are in hells,' and so on.

867-868. Atthi manussesūti paccakkhena ñāpanatthaṃ. Yathā hi manussesu sati kāraṇikesu kāraṇā, evaṃ tatthāpīti ayamettha adhippāyo. Atthi nirayesūti pucchā paravādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Na vessabhū nopi ca pettirājāti paravādinā sakasamayato suttaṃ ābhataṃ. Taṃ pana sāsanāvacarikanti sakavādinā anuññātaṃ. Tattha vessabhūti eko devo. Pettirājāti pettivisaye petamahiddhiko. Somādayo pākaṭā eva. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – attano kammehi ito paṇunnaṃ [V 0.0272] paralokaṃ pattaṃ purisaṃ na ete vessabhūādayo hananti. Yehi pana so kammehi tattha paṇunno, tāni sakāni kammāniyeva naṃ tattha hanantīti kammassakataṃ dīpeti, na nirayapālānaṃ abhāvaṃ. Sakavādinā pana tamenaṃ, bhikkhaveti ābhatāni suttapadāni nītatthānevāti.

867-868. 'There are among humans' is stated to make it known through direct experience. Just as among humans, where there are agents of punishment, there are acts of punishment, so too is it there—this is the intended meaning here. 'There are in hells' is the question for the opponent, and the affirmation for the proponent of our own school. 'Not Vessabhū nor the King of the Petas' is a citation brought by the opponent from their own tradition. But this is acknowledged by the proponent of our own school as something within the scope of the teaching. Here, 'Vessabhū' is a certain deva. 'King of the Petas' refers to one with great power among the departed in the realm of the departed. Soma and others are well-known. This is said to mean—Vessabhū and others do not kill a person who, having been driven from here by their own kamma, has gone to the other world. Rather, it is their own kamma that kills them there—thus illustrating the ownership of kamma, not the absence of hell-wardens. The proponent of our own school, however, considers that the sutta passages beginning with 'monks' are of definitive meaning.

Nirayapālakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discussion on the Hell-Wardens.

4. Tiracchānakathāvaṇṇanā

4. The Exposition of the Discussion on Animals.

869-871. Idāni tiracchānakathā nāma hoti. Tattha devesu erāvaṇādayo devaputtā hatthivaṇṇaṃ assavaṇṇaṃ vikubbanti, natthi tattha tiracchānagatā. Yesaṃ pana tiracchānavaṇṇino devaputte disvā “atthi devesu tiracchānagatā”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ[P 0.0188]; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi devayoniyaṃ tiracchānagatā siyuṃ, tiracchānayoniyampi devā siyu”nti codetuṃ atthi tiracchānagatesūtiādimāha. Kīṭātiādi yesaṃ so abhāvaṃ icchati, te dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Erāvaṇoti pañhe tassa atthitāya paṭiññā sakavādissa[M 0.0274], na tiracchānagatassa. Hatthibandhātiādi “yadi tattha hatthiādayo siyuṃ, hatthibandhādayopi siyu”nti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha yāvasikāti yavassa dāyakā. Kāraṇikāti hatthācariyādayo, yehi te nānāvidhaṃ kāraṇaṃ kareyyuṃ. Bhattakārakāti hatthiādīnaṃ bhattarandhakā. Na hevanti tathā anicchanto paṭikkhipatīti.

869-871. Now is the discussion on animals. Herein, among the devas, deva-sons like Erāvaṇa perform transformations into the appearance of elephants and horses; there are no creatures of the animal realm there. But with reference to those who, seeing deva-sons with animal forms, hold the view that 'there are creatures of the animal realm among the devas'—such as the Andhakas—the question is for the proponent of our own school, and the affirmation is for the other. Then, to challenge him by saying, 'If there were creatures of the animal realm in the deva world, there would also be devas in the animal realm,' he said, 'Are there devas among the animals,' and so on. 'Insects,' and so on, are mentioned to show those whose non-existence he wishes to establish. Regarding 'Erāvaṇa' in the question, the proponent of our own school affirms its existence, but not as a creature of the animal realm. 'Elephant keepers,' and so on, are stated for the purpose of challenging by saying, 'If there were elephants and the like there, there would also be elephant keepers and the like.' Here, 'yāvasikā' means givers of barley. 'Kāraṇikā' refers to elephant trainers and the like, by whom they would be made to perform various actions. 'Bhattakārakā' means cooks for elephants and the like. 'Not indeed' is said by him, rejecting it as he does not wish it to be so.

Tiracchānakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discussion on Animals.

5. Maggakathāvaṇṇanā

5. The Exposition of the Discussion on the Path.

872-875. Idāni maggakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yesaṃ “pubbeva kho panassa kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ ājīvo suparisuddho hotī”ti (a. ni. 3.431) idañceva suttaṃ sammāvācākammantājīvānañca [V 0.0273] cittavippayuttataṃ nissāya “nippariyāyena pañcaṅgikova maggo”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi mahisāsakānaṃ, te sandhāya pañcaṅgikoti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sammāvācā maggaṅgaṃ, sā ca na maggotiādi parasamayavasena vuttaṃ. Parasamayasmiñhi sammāvācādayo maggaṅganti āgatā. Rūpattā pana maggo na hotīti vaṇṇitā. Sammādiṭṭhi maggaṅgantiādi maggaṅgassa amaggatā nāma natthīti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Pubbeva kho panassāti sutte parisuddhasīlassa maggabhāvanā nāma hoti, na itarassāti āgamaniyapaṭipadāya visuddhibhāvadassanatthaṃ “kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ ājīvo suparisuddho hotī”ti vuttaṃ, na imehi vinā pañcaṅgikabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Tenevāha [P 0.0189] “evamassāyaṃ ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchatī”ti. Sakavādinā ābhatasuttaṃ nītatthamevāti.

872-875. Now is the discussion on the path. Herein, with reference to those who hold the view that 'the path is unconditionally fivefold,' such as the Mahīśāsakas—basing this on the sutta, 'beforehand, his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood were already well-purified' (AN 3.431), and on the fact that right speech, right action, and right livelihood are disassociated from consciousness—the question 'Is the path fivefold?' is for the proponent of our own school, and the affirmation is for the other. That right speech is a path factor, but it is not the path—this and so on is stated according to another school’s doctrine. For in another school, right speech and the like are presented as path factors. However, because they are of the nature of form, they are not the path—this has been explained.
