That 'right view is a path factor,' and so on, is stated to show that there is no such thing as a path factor not being the path. In the sutta, the phrase 'beforehand, his…' indicates that the development of the path occurs for one whose virtue is already purified, not for others. To demonstrate the arising of purification through the proper preliminary practice, it is said, 'his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood were well-purified'—not to show the fivefold nature of the path in the absence of these. Therefore, it is said: 'Thus, this Noble Eightfold Path goes to the fulfillment of development.' The sutta cited by the proponent of our own school is of definitive meaning.

Maggakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Discussion on the Path.

6. Ñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

6. The Exposition of the Discussion on Knowledge.

876-877. Idāni ñāṇakathā nāma hoti. Tattha dhammacakkappavattane dvādasākārañāṇaṃ sandhāya “dvādasavatthukaṃ ñāṇaṃ lokuttara”nti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi [M 0.0275] pubbaseliyānaṃ, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “sace taṃ dvādasavatthukaṃ, dvādasahi maggañāṇehi bhavitabba”nti codetuṃ dvādasātiādimāha. Itaro maggassa ekattaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati, ekekasmiṃ sacce saccañāṇakiccañāṇakatañāṇānaṃ vasena ñāṇanānattaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Dvādasa sotāpattimaggātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Nanu vuttaṃ bhagavatāti suttaṃ saddhiṃ pubbabhāgaparabhāgehi ñāṇanānattaṃ dīpeti, na ariyamaggassa dvādasa ñāṇataṃ. Tasmā asādhakanti.

876-877. Now is the discussion on knowledge. Here, regarding the twelve aspects of knowledge in the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, for those whose view is that “the twelve-based knowledge is supramundane,” such as the Pubbaseliyas—the question is for the proponent of one’s own school, the affirmation for the other. Then, to challenge him by saying, “if that is twelve-based, there must be twelve path knowledges,” he said “twelve,” and so on. The other party denies this by referring to the oneness of the path, and affirms the diversity of knowledge based on truth-knowledge, function-knowledge, and accomplished-knowledge in each truth. The same method applies even to “twelve stream-entry paths,” and so on. But has it not been said by the Blessed One? The sutta, together with its preliminary and concluding parts, reveals the diversity of knowledges, not that the Noble Path consists of twelve knowledges. Therefore, it is not a valid proof.

Ñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Discourse on Knowledge.

Vīsatimo vaggo.

The Twentieth Chapter.

Catutthapaṇṇāsako samatto.

The Fourth Fifty is concluded.

21. Ekavīsatimavaggo

21. The Twenty-First Section.

1. Sāsanakathāvaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Dispensation.

878. Idāni [P 0.0190][V 0.0274] sāsanakathā nāma hoti. Tattha tisso saṅgītiyo sandhāya “sāsanaṃ navaṃ kata”nti ca “atthi koci tathāgatassa sāsanaṃ navaṃ karotī”ti ca “labbhā tathāgatassa sāsanaṃ navaṃ kātu”nti ca yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi ekaccānaṃ uttarāpathakānaṃ; te sandhāya tīsupi kathāsu pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Satipaṭṭhānātiādi sāsanaṃ nāma satipaṭṭhānādayo ceva ariyadhammā, kusalādīnañca desanā. Tattha yesaṃ bhagavatā desitā satipaṭṭhānādayo, ṭhapetvā te aññesaṃ vā satipaṭṭhānādīnaṃ karaṇena akusalādīnaṃ vā kusalādibhāvakaraṇena sāsanaṃ navaṃkataṃ nāma bhaveyya, kiṃ taṃ evaṃ kataṃ kenaci, atthi vā koci evaṃ karoti, labbhā vā evaṃ kātunti tīsupi pucchāsu codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha yathāpāḷimeva niyyātīti.

878. Now is the discussion on the Dispensation. Here, referring to the three Councils, for those whose view is that “the Dispensation has been renewed,” or “there is someone who renews the Tathāgata’s Dispensation,” or “it is possible to renew the Tathāgata’s Dispensation”—such as certain Northern Sectarians—regarding them, in all three discussions, the question is from the proponent of one’s own school, and the affirmation is from the other. The Dispensation is the name for the foundations of mindfulness and the like, and the noble doctrines, as well as the teaching of wholesome qualities and so on. Here, if—setting aside the foundations of mindfulness and other teachings proclaimed by the Blessed One—the Dispensation would be called renewed by the making of other foundations of mindfulness and the like, or by transforming unwholesome qualities into wholesome qualities and so on, then has such a thing ever been done by anyone? Or is there anyone who does so? Or is it possible to do so? In all three questions, this is stated for the purpose of censure. The remainder is to be understood everywhere according to the Pāli text itself.

Sāsanakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Dispensation.

2. Avivittakathāvaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Discourse on Non-Separation.

879-880. Idāni [M 0.0276] avivittakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yassa puggalassa yo dhammo paccuppanno, so tena avivitto nāmāti idaṃ sakasamaye sanniṭṭhānaṃ. Yasmā pana puthujjanena tedhātukā dhammā apariññātā, tasmā so ekakkhaṇeyeva sabbehipi tedhātukehi dhammehi avivittoti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi tesaññeva, te [P 0.0191] sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Phassehītiādi sabbesaṃ phassādīnaṃ ekakkhaṇe pavattidosadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

879-880. Now is the discussion on non-separation. Here, whatever phenomenon is present for a person, he is said to be not separate from it—this is the established conclusion in their own system. However, because the phenomena of the three realms have not been fully understood by an ordinary person, they are therefore not separate from all phenomena of the three realms in a single moment—this is the view of some, such as those very ones. With reference to them, the question is from the proponent of one’s own school, the affirmation from the other. “By contact,” and so on, is said to show the fault of all contacts and so on occurring in a single moment. The rest is clear in meaning everywhere.

Avivittakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discourse on Non-Separation.

3. Saññojanakathāvaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on the Fetters.

881-882. Idāni [V 0.0275] saññojanakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā arahā sabbaṃ buddhavisayaṃ na jānāti, tasmā tassa tattha avijjāvicikicchāhi appahīnāhi bhavitabbanti saññāya “atthi kiñci saññojanaṃ appahāya arahattappattī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṅghikānaṃ, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atthi kiñci sakkāyadiṭṭhītiādi arahato sabbasaṃyojanappahānadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Sabbaṃ buddhavisayanti pañhadvaye arahato sabbaññutaññāṇābhāvena paṭisedho kato, na avijjāvicikicchānaṃ appahānena. Itaro pana tesaṃ appahīnataṃ sandhāya tena hīti laddhiṃ patiṭṭhapeti. Sā ayoniso patiṭṭhāpitattā appatiṭṭhitāva hotīti.

881-882. Now is the discussion on the fetters. Here, because an arahant does not know the entire domain of a Buddha, with the perception that ignorance and doubt concerning it must therefore not be abandoned in them, some hold the view, “There is attainment of arahantship without having abandoned some fetter”—such as the Mahāsaṅghikas. With reference to them, the question is from the proponent of one’s own school, the affirmation from the other. “Is there any identity-view?” and so on, is stated to demonstrate the arahant’s abandonment of all fetters. In the two questions concerning “the entire domain of a Buddha,” the denial is made due to the arahant’s lack of omniscient knowledge, not due to the non-abandonment of ignorance and doubt. The other, however, establishes their view with “in that case,” referring to the non-abandonment of these. Because it is improperly established, it remains unestablished.

Saññojanakathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Fetters.

4. Iddhikathāvaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse on Psychic Power.

883-884. Idāni iddhikathā nāma hoti. Tattha iddhi nāmesā katthaci ijjhati, katthaci na ijjhati, aniccādīnaṃ niccādikaraṇe ekanteneva na ijjhati. Sabhāgasantatiṃ pana parivattetvā visabhāgasantatikaraṇe vā sabhāgasantativaseneva [M 0.0277] ciratarappavattane vā yesaṃ atthāya kariyati, tesaṃ puññādīni kāraṇāni nissāya katthaci ijjhati, bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya pānīyassa sappikhīrādikaraṇe viya mahādhātunidhāne dīpādīnaṃ cirasantānappavattane viya cāti idaṃ sakasamaye sanniṭṭhānaṃ. Yaṃ [P 0.0192] pana āyasmā pilindavaccho rañño pāsādaṃ suvaṇṇantveva adhimucci, taṃ nissāya yesaṃ “atthi adhippāyaiddhī”ti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya atthi adhippāyaiddhīti pucchā sakavādissa. Tattha adhippāyaiddhīti adhippāyaiddhi, yathādhippāyaṃ ijjhanaiddhīti attho. Āmantāti laddhimatte ṭhatvā paṭiññā paravādissa. Atha naṃ aniccādīnaṃ niccāditāya anuyuñjituṃ niccapaṇṇā rukkhā hontūtiādimāha. Sesamettha uttānatthameva. Laddhipatiṭṭhāpane suvaṇṇo ca panāsīti rañño puññūpanissayena āsi, na kevalaṃ therassa adhippāyeneva. Tasmā asādhakametanti.

883-884. Now is the discourse on psychic power. Here, this psychic power succeeds in some cases, but in others it does not. It absolutely does not succeed in making the impermanent permanent, and so forth. However, when it is done for the sake of those beings—by transforming a homogeneous continuity into a heterogeneous continuity, or by prolonging a homogeneous continuity for a very long time—it succeeds in some cases, relying on causes such as their merit. This is like making water into ghee, milk, and so forth, for the sake of monks, or like prolonging the continuity of lamps and so on for a long time in the great relic chamber. This is the conclusion in one's own system. But based on the fact that the Venerable Pilindavaccha resolved upon the king’s palace as gold, some, such as the Andhakas, hold the view that there is ‘intentional psychic power.’ With reference to them, the question, ‘Is there intentional psychic power?’ is from the proponent of one’s own school. Here, ‘intentional psychic power’ means the psychic power of succeeding according to one’s intention. ‘Yes,’ is the affirmation of the opponent, standing merely on their doctrine. Then, to challenge him regarding making the impermanent permanent, and so forth, he says, ‘May the leaves of the trees be permanent,’ and so on. The rest here is clear in meaning. In establishing the doctrine, it became gold due to the king’s merit as a supporting condition, not solely due to the elder’s intention. Therefore, this is not a valid proof.

Iddhikathāvaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Discourse on Psychic Power.

5. Buddhakathāvaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Buddhas.

885. Idāni [V 0.0276] buddhakathā nāma hoti. Tattha ṭhapetvā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāle sarīravemattataṃ āyuvemattataṃ pabhāvemattatañca sesehi buddhadhammehi buddhānaṃ buddhehi hīnātirekatā nāma natthi. Yesaṃ pana aviseseneva atthīti laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya atthi buddhānanti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ buddhadhammehi anuyuñjituṃ satipaṭṭhānatotiādimāha. Itaro tesaṃ vasena hīnātirekataṃ apassanto paṭikkhipatiyevāti.

885. Now, this is the discourse on the Buddhas. Here, apart from the differences in bodily size, lifespan, and radiance at various times, there is no inferiority or superiority among the Buddhas in terms of the remaining Buddha-qualities. However, for those who hold the doctrine that there is absolutely no distinction, such as the Andhakas, the question 'Are there Buddhas?' is posed by the proponent of one's own school, and the opponent's assertion is 'Yes'. Then, to examine him regarding the Buddha-qualities, he says, 'starting with the foundations of mindfulness,' and so on. The other party, not seeing any inferiority or superiority in those qualities, simply rejects it.

Buddhakathāvaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Discourse on the Buddhas.

6. Sabbadisākathāvaṇṇanā

6. Exposition of the Discourse on All Directions

886. Idāni sabbadisākathā nāma hoti. Tattha catūsu disāsu heṭṭhā [P 0.0193] uparīti samantato lokadhātusannivāsaṃ, sabbalokadhātūsu ca [M 0.0278] buddhā atthīti attano vikappasippaṃ uppādetvā “sabbadisāsu buddhā tiṭṭhantī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi mahāsaṅghikānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Puratthimāyāti puṭṭho sakyamuniṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Puna puṭṭho laddhivasena aññalokadhātuyaṃ ṭhitaṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Kinnāmo so bhagavātiādi “sace tvaṃ jānāsi, nāmādivasena naṃ kathehī”ti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Iminā upāyena sabbattha attho veditabboti.

886. Now, this is the discourse on all directions. Here, the doctrine of those such as the Mahāsaṅghikas, who generate their own imaginative skill by conceiving of the assemblage of world-systems in the four directions—below, above, and all around—and that Buddhas exist in all world-systems, is that 'Buddhas stand in all directions'. The question is posed by the proponent of one's own school, and the opponent's assertion is 'Yes'. When asked about the eastern direction, he denies it with reference to Sakyamuni. When asked again, he affirms it based on the doctrine of a Buddha dwelling in another world-system. 'What is the name of that Blessed One?' and so on—this is stated for the purpose of challenging him, meaning, 'If you know, then state his name and so forth'. By this method, the meaning should be understood everywhere.

Sabbadisākathāvaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Discourse on All Directions.

7. Dhammakathāvaṇṇanā

7. Exposition of the Discourse on Phenomena

887-888. Idāni dhammakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā rūpādayo rūpādisabhāvena niyatā [V 0.0277] na taṃ sabhāvaṃ vijahanti, tasmā sabbadhammā niyatāti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānañceva ekaccānañca uttarāpathakānaṃ; te sandhāya sabbe dhammāti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “sace te niyatā, micchattaniyatā vā siyuṃ sammattaniyatā vā, ito añño niyāmo nāma natthī”ti codetuṃ micchattaniyatātiādimāha. Tattha paṭikkhepo ca paṭiññā ca paravādissa. Rūpaṃ rūpaṭṭhenātiādi yenatthena niyatāti vadati, tassa vasena codetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ adhippāyo – rūpañhi rūpaṭṭhena niyatanti rūpaṃ rūpameva, na vedanādisabhāvanti adhippāyena vattabbaṃ, ito aññathā na vattabbaṃ. Kasmā? Rūpaṭṭhato aññassa rūpassa abhāvā. Rūpasabhāvo hi rūpaṭṭho, rūpasabhāvo ca rūpameva, na rūpato añño. Vedanādīhi panassa nānattapaññāpanatthaṃ esa vohāro hotīti. Tasmā “rūpaṃ rūpaṭṭhena niyata”nti vadantena rūpaṃ niyatanti vuttaṃ hoti. Niyatañca nāma micchattaniyataṃ [P 0.0194] vā siyā sammattaniyataṃ vā, ito añño niyāmo nāma natthīti. Atha kasmā paṭijānātīti? Atthantaravasena. Rūpaṃ rūpaṭṭhena niyatanti ettha hi rūpaṃ rūpameva, na vedanādisabhāvanti ayamattho. Tasmā paṭijānāti. Ito aññathā panassa niyatattaṃ natthīti puna teneva nayena codetuṃ micchattaniyatantiādimāha[M 0.0279]. Taṃ sabbaṃ uttānatthameva. Tena hi rūpanti laddhipi ayoniso patiṭṭhāpitattā appatiṭṭhitāva hotīti.

887-888. Now, this is the discourse on phenomena. Herein, because forms and so on are fixed by their own nature as forms and so forth, and do not abandon that nature, the tenet of those such as the Andhakas and some of the Northerners is that all phenomena are fixed. With reference to them, the question 'Are all phenomena fixed?' is posed by the proponent of one's own school, and the affirmation is given by the other. Then, to challenge him, it is said: 'If they are fixed, they would be fixed in wrongness or fixed in rightness; there is no other fixed principle besides these.' Thus he speaks, beginning with 'fixed in wrongness.' Herein, the rejection and the affirmation belong to the opponent. The statement 'Form is fixed by its nature as form' and so on is made to challenge him based on the meaning by which he says they are fixed. The intention here is this: when it is said 'form is fixed by its nature as form,' it means that form is merely form, not of the nature of feeling, etc. It should be stated with this intention; it should not be stated otherwise. Why? Because there is no form apart from the characteristic of form. For the nature of form is the characteristic of form, and the nature of form is form itself, not something else apart from form. However, this expression is used to distinguish it from feeling, etc. Therefore, by saying 'form is fixed by its nature as form,' it is said that form is fixed. And what is called 'fixed' is either fixed in wrongness or fixed in rightness; there is no other fixed principle besides these. Then why does he affirm it? Because of a different meaning. Here, the meaning of 'form is fixed by its nature as form' is that form is merely form, not of the nature of feeling, etc. Therefore, he affirms it. However, its fixedness is not otherwise than this. Thus, to challenge him again in the same way, he speaks, beginning with 'fixed in wrongness,' etc. All this is clear in meaning. Therefore, even the tenet 'form is...' is not firmly established because it is improperly established.

Dhammakathāvaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Discourse on Phenomena.

8. Kammakathāvaṇṇanā

8. Exposition of the Discourse on Kamma

889-891. Idāni kammakathā nāma hoti. Tattha “yasmā diṭṭhadhammavedanīyādīni diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṭṭhādīhi niyatāni, tasmā sabbe kammā niyatā”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi tesaññeva; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṭṭhena niyatanti ettha diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṭṭhameva. Sace diṭṭheva dhamme vipākaṃ dātuṃ sakkoti deti, no ce ahosikammaṃ nāma hotīti imamatthaṃ sandhāya paṭiññā sakavādissa. Micchattasammattaniyāmavasena panetaṃ aniyatamevāti sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

889-891. Now, this is the discourse on kamma. Here, with reference to those whose tenet is that 'since actions such as those ripening in this very life are fixed by their characteristic of ripening in this very life, etc., therefore all kamma is fixed'—as in the case of those same ones—the question is posed by the proponent of one's own school, and the affirmation is given by the other. In 'fixed by the characteristic of ripening in this very life,' here, 'ripening in this very life' is simply the characteristic of ripening in this very life. If it is able to give its result in this very life, it does; if not, it becomes defunct kamma—this meaning is implied by the affirmation of the proponent of one's own school. However, with respect to the fixed principles of wrongness and rightness, this is truly undetermined; everything should be understood in the same way as explained above.

Kammakathāvaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Discourse on Kamma.

Ekavīsatimo vaggo.

Twenty-first Chapter.

22. Bāvīsatimavaggo

22. Twenty-second Chapter

1. Parinibbānakathāvaṇṇanā

1. Exposition of the Discourse on Parinibbāna

892. Idāni [P 0.0195][V 0.0278] parinibbānakathā nāma hoti. Tattha “yasmā arahā sabbaññuvisaye appahīnasaṃyojanova parinibbāyati, tasmā atthi kiñci saṃyojanaṃ appahāya parinibbāna”nti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha heṭṭhā vuttanayamevāti.

892. Now, this is the discourse on Parinibbāna. Here, the question is posed by the proponent of one's own school to those whose tenet is that 'since an arahant attains Parinibbāna in the domain of the Omniscient One with fetters not yet abandoned, therefore there is Parinibbāna without having abandoned some fetter'—as is the case with the Andhakas; and the affirmation is from the other. The rest here is to be understood in the manner stated above.

Parinibbānakathāvaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Discourse on Parinibbāna.

2. Kusalacittakathāvaṇṇanā

2. Exposition of the Discourse on Wholesome Consciousness

894-895. Idāni [M 0.0280] kusalacittakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā arahā sativepullappatto parinibbāyantopi sato sampajānova parinibbāti, tasmā kusalacitto parinibbāyatīti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ yasmā kusalacitto nāma puññābhisaṅkhārābhisaṅkharaṇādivasena hoti, tasmā tenatthena codetuṃ arahā puññābhisaṅkhārantiādimāha. Sesamettha yathāpāḷimeva niyyāti. Sato sampajānoti idaṃ javanakkhaṇe kiriyasatisampajaññānaṃ vasena asammohamaraṇadīpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na kusalacittadīpanatthaṃ. Tasmā asādhakanti.

894-895. Now, this is the discourse on Wholesome Consciousness. Here, the question is posed by the proponent of one's own school to those whose tenet is that 'since an arahant, having attained the fullness of mindfulness, attains Parinibbāna mindfully and with clear comprehension, therefore one attains Parinibbāna with a wholesome consciousness'—as is the case with the Andhakas; and the affirmation is from the other. Then, since wholesome consciousness exists by way of forming meritorious volitional activities and so forth, to challenge him on that point, he says, 'Does an arahant form meritorious volitional activities?' and so forth. The rest here proceeds exactly according to the Pāli text. The phrase 'mindful and with clear comprehension' is stated with reference to the functional mindfulness and clear comprehension at the moment of impulsion, for the purpose of indicating death without delusion, not for the purpose of indicating wholesome consciousness. Therefore, it is not a valid proof.

Kusalacittakathāvaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Discourse on Wholesome Consciousness.

3. Āneñjakathāvaṇṇanā

3. Exposition of the Discourse on Imperturbability

896. Idāni [P 0.0196][V 0.0279] āneñjakathā nāma hoti. Tattha bhagavā catutthajjhāne ṭhito parinibbāyīti sallakkhetvā “arahā āneñje ṭhito parinibbāyatī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi ekaccānaṃ uttarāpathakānaṃ, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Pakaticitteti bhavaṅgacitte. Sabbe hi saññino sattā bhavaṅgacitte ṭhatvā bhavaṅgapariyosānena cuticittena kālaṃ karonti. Iti naṃ iminā atthena codetuṃ evamāha. Tattha kiñcāpi catuvokārabhave arahato pakaticittampi āneñjaṃ hoti, ayaṃ pana pañho pañcavokārabhavavasena uddhaṭo. Tasmā no ca vata re vattabbeti āha. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

896. Now comes the discussion on imperturbability. Here, reflecting that the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna while abiding in the fourth jhāna, the question is posed by the proponent of his own view to those whose tenet is that 'an arahant attains Parinibbāna while abiding in the imperturbable'—as is the case with some Northerners; the affirmation is from the other. By 'natural consciousness' is meant the life-continuum consciousness. For all sentient beings with perception, abiding in the life-continuum consciousness, pass away with a death-consciousness at the end of the life-continuum. Thus, to challenge him with this meaning, he said this. Although in a four-constituent existence even the natural consciousness of an arahant is imperturbable, this question, however, is raised concerning a five-constituent existence. Therefore, he said, 'Indeed, it should not be said thus!' The rest here is of plain meaning.

Āneñjakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion on the Imperturbable.

4. Dhammābhisamayakathāvaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Discussion on the Penetration of the Dhamma.

897. Idāni dhammābhisamayakathā nāma hoti. Tattha atītabhave sotāpannaṃ mātukucchiyaṃ vasitvā nikkhantaṃ disvā “atthi gabbhaseyyāya dhammābhisamayo”ti [M 0.0281] yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi ekaccānaṃ uttarāpathakānaṃ, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “yadi tattha dhammābhisamayo atthi, dhammābhisamayassa kāraṇehi dhammadesanādīhi bhavitabba”nti codetuṃ atthi gabbhaseyyāya dhammadesanātiādimāha. Suttassātiādi bhavaṅgavāraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Gabbhaseyyāya hi yebhuyyena bhavaṅgameva pavattati. Teneva satto kiriyamayappavattābhāvā sutto, bhāvanānuyogassa abhāvā pamatto, kammaṭṭhānapariggāhakānaṃ satisampajaññānaṃ abhāvā muṭṭhassati asampajāno nāma hoti, tathārūpassa kuto dhammābhisamayoti?

897. Now comes the discussion on the penetration of the Dhamma. Here, having seen one who, having become a stream-enterer in a past existence, dwelt in the mother's womb and then emerged, the question is posed by the proponent of his own view to those whose tenet is that 'there is penetration of the Dhamma in the womb'—as is the case with some Northerners; the affirmation is from the other. Then, to challenge him that 'if there is penetration of the Dhamma there, there must be causes for the penetration of the Dhamma, such as the teaching of the Dhamma,' he says, 'Is there teaching of the Dhamma in the womb?' and so forth. The phrase 'asleep,' and so on, is stated with reference to the life-continuum phase. For in the womb, it is mostly the life-continuum that proceeds. Therefore, the being is called 'asleep' due to the absence of active process, 'heedless' due to the absence of application to development, and 'unmindful and not clearly comprehending' due to the absence of mindfulness and clear comprehension that grasp a meditation subject. How could there be penetration of the Dhamma for such a one?

Dhammābhisamayakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion on the Penetration of the Dhamma.

5-7. Tissopikathāvaṇṇanā

5-7. The Commentary on the Discussion concerning Tissa.

898-900. Idāni [P 0.0197][V 0.0280] tissopikathā nāma honti. Tattha acirajātānaṃ pana sotāpannānaṃ arahattappattiṃ suppavāsāya ca upāsikāya sattavassikaṃ gabbhaṃ disvā “atthi gabbhaseyyāya arahattappattī”ti ca supine ākāsagamanādīni disvā “atthi dhammābhisamayo”ti ca “atthi tattha arahattappattī”ti ca idhāpi yesaṃ laddhiyo, seyyathāpi tesaññeva; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha purimakathā sadisamevāti.

Now, these are called the discussions concerning Tissa. Here, some hold the tenet that 'there is attainment of arahantship in the womb,' having seen the attainment of arahantship by recently born stream-enterers and the seven-year pregnancy of the laywoman Suppavāsā. And they hold the tenets that 'there is realization of the Dhamma' and 'there is attainment of arahantship there,' having seen in a dream things such as traveling through the sky. For those here whose views are such—as is the case with those same ones—the question is posed by the proponent of his own view, and the affirmation is from the other. The rest here is just like the previous discussion.

Tissopikathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion concerning Tissa.

8. Abyākatakathāvaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Discussion of the Undetermined.

901-902. Idāni abyākatakathā nāma hoti. Tattha “atthesā, bhikkhave, cetanā, sā ca kho abbohārikā”ti (pārā. 235) vacanato “sabbaṃ supinagatassa cittaṃ abyākata”nti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi ekaccānaṃ uttarāpathakānaññeva, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha yathā pāḷimeva niyyāti. Supinagatassa cittaṃ abbohārikanti idaṃ [M 0.0282] āpattiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Supinagatassa hi pāṇātipātādivasena kiñcāpi akusalacittaṃ pavattati, vatthuvikopanaṃ pana natthīti na sakkā tattha āpattiṃ paññapetuṃ. Iminā kāraṇena taṃ abbohārikaṃ, na abyākatattāti.

Now, this is the discussion of the undetermined. Here, because of the statement, “There is intention, bhikkhus, but it is non-actionable” (Pārā. 235), some hold the view that “All the consciousness of one who is dreaming is undetermined”—such as certain Northerners. Concerning them, the question is posed by the proponent of his own view, and the affirmation is from the other. The rest here proceeds just as in the Pāli text. The phrase, “The consciousness of one who is dreaming is non-actionable,” is stated with reference to an offense. For although an unwholesome consciousness arises in one who is dreaming by way of killing living beings and so on, there is no violation of the object, so it is not possible to lay down an offense in that case. For this reason, it is non-actionable, not because it is undetermined.

Abyākatakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion of the Undetermined.

9. Āsevanapaccayakathāvaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Discussion on the Repetition Condition.

903-905. Idāni āsevanapaccayakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā sabbe [P 0.0198] dhammā khaṇikā[V 0.0281], na koci muhuttampi ṭhatvā āsevanapaccayaṃ āsevati nāma. Tasmā natthi kiñci āsevanapaccayatā. Āsevanapaccayatāya uppannaṃ pana na kiñci atthīti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi tesaññeva; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ suttavaseneva paññāpetuṃ nanu vuttaṃ bhagavatā pāṇātipātotiādi ābhataṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

Now, this is the discussion on the repetition condition. Here, since all phenomena are momentary, nothing remains even for a moment to perform the function of a repetition condition. Therefore, there is no such thing as a repetition condition, and nothing whatsoever has arisen by way of a repetition condition. For those whose view is such—as is the case with those same ones—the question is posed by the proponent of his own view, and the affirmation is from the other. Then, to establish the point by means of the Sutta itself, the passage beginning, 'Has it not been stated by the Blessed One, "killing living beings..."' has been adduced. All of that is of plain meaning.

Āsevanapaccayakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion on the Repetition Condition.

10. Khaṇikakathāvaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Discussion of Momentariness.

906-907. Idāni khaṇikakathā nāma hoti. Tattha yasmā sabbasaṅkhatadhammā aniccā, tasmā ekacittakkhaṇikāyeva. Samānāya hi aniccatāya eko lahuṃ bhijjati, eko cirenāti ko ettha niyāmoti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi pubbaseliyāparaseliyānaṃ; te sandhāya ekacittakkhaṇikāti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Citte mahāpathavītiādīsu tesaṃ tathā saṇṭhānaṃ apassanto paṭikkhipati. Cakkhāyatanantiādi “yadi sabbe ekacittakkhaṇikā bhaveyyuṃ, cakkhāyatanādīni cakkhuviññāṇādīhi saddhiṃyeva uppajjitvā nirujjheyyu”nti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Itaro pana antomātukucchigatassa viññāṇuppattiṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati[M 0.0283], pavattaṃ sandhāya laddhivasena paṭijānāti. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti. Tena hi ekacittakkhaṇikāti yasmā niccā na honti, tasmā ekacittakkhaṇikāti attano ruciyā kāraṇaṃ vadati. Taṃ avuttasadisamevāti.

Now, this is the discussion of momentariness. Herein, some, such as the Pubbaseliyas and Aparaseliyas, hold the view: 'Since all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, they last only for a single mind-moment. For, given the shared characteristic of impermanence, what fixed rule is there that one thing perishes quickly and another after a long time?' Concerning them, the question, 'Do they last only for a single mind-moment?' is posed by the proponent of his own view, and the affirmation is from the other. Not seeing such a constitution in the case of consciousness, the great earth, and so on, he rejects it. The phrase 'the eye-base, etc.' is stated to raise the objection: 'If all things lasted only for a single mind-moment, then the eye-base and other sense-bases would arise and cease simultaneously with eye-consciousness, etc.' The other, however, denies this with reference to the arising of consciousness within the mother’s womb, but accepts it by way of his doctrine with reference to the ongoing process. The rest here is of plain meaning. Therefore, when he gives the reason, 'They last only for a single mind-moment because they are not permanent,' he speaks according to his own preference. But this is as good as saying nothing at all.

Khaṇikakathāvaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Discussion of Momentariness.

Bāvīsatimo vaggo.

The Twenty-second Chapter.

23. Tevīsatimavaggo

23. The Twenty-third Chapter.

1. Ekādhippāyakathāvaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Discussion on a Single Intention.

908. Idāni [P 0.0199][V 0.0282] ekādhippāyakathā nāma hoti. Tattha kāruññena vā ekena adhippāyena ekādhippāyo, saṃsāre vā ekato bhavissāmāti itthiyā saddhiṃ buddhapūjādīni katvā paṇidhivasena eko adhippāyo assāti ekādhippāyo. Evarūpo dvinnampi janānaṃ ekādhippāyo methuno dhammo paṭisevitabboti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānañceva vetullakānañca; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha yathāpāḷimeva niyyātīti.

908. Now comes the discussion on a single intention. Herein, 'single intention' means a single intention either through compassion, or a single intention by way of aspiration, having performed acts such as offerings to the Buddha together with a woman, with the thought, 'We will be together in saṃsāra.' The question is posed by the proponent of his own view to those whose tenet is that 'sexual intercourse is to be engaged in by two people with such a single intention'—as is the case with the Andhakas and the Vetullakas; the affirmation is from the other. The rest here proceeds exactly according to the Pāli text.

Ekādhippāyakathāvaṇṇanā.

The commentary on the discussion on a single intention.

2. Arahantavaṇṇakathāvaṇṇanā

2. The commentary on the discussion on the guise of arahants.

909. Idāni arahantavaṇṇakathā nāma hoti. Tattha iriyāpathasampanne ākappasampanne pāpabhikkhū disvā “arahantānaṃ vaṇṇena amanussā methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevantī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi ekaccānaṃ uttarāpathakānaṃ; te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

909. Now comes the discussion on the guise of arahants. Herein, the question is posed by the proponent of his own view to those whose tenet is that 'non-humans engage in sexual intercourse in the guise of arahants,' having seen wicked monks accomplished in deportment and appearance—as is the case with some Northerners; the affirmation is from the other. The rest here is of plain meaning.

Arahantavaṇṇakathāvaṇṇanā.

The commentary on the discussion on the guise of arahants.

3-7. Issariyakāmakārikākathāvaṇṇanā

3-7. The commentary on the discussion on exercising one's own will.

910-914. Idāni [M 0.0284] issariyakāmakārikākathā nāma hoti. Chaddantajātakādīni sandhāya [V 0.0283] “bodhisatto issariyakāmakārikāhetu vinipātaṃ [P 0.0200] gacchati, gabbhaseyyaṃ okkamati, dukkarakārikaṃ akāsi, aparantapaṃ akāsi, aññaṃ satthāraṃ uddisī”ti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ, te sandhāya pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Sesaṃ paṭhamakathāyaṃ uttānatthameva. Dutiyakathāyaṃ iddhimāti yadi issariyakāmakārikāhetu gaccheyya, iddhiyā gaccheyya, na kammavasenāti codanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Itaro pana paṭhamapañhe bhāvanāmayaṃ sandhāya paṭikkhipati. Dutiyapañhe puññiddhiṃ sandhāya paṭijānāti. Tatiyakathāyaṃ issariyakāmakārikāhetu nāma dukkarakārikā micchādiṭṭhiyā kariyati. Yadi ca so taṃ kareyya, sassatādīnipi gaṇheyyāti codanatthaṃ sassato lokotiādi vuttaṃ. Catutthakathāyampi eseva nayoti.

910-914. Now comes the discussion on exercising one's own will. With reference to the Chaddanta Jātaka and others, the question is posed by the proponent of his own thesis to those, such as the Andhakas, who hold the view that 'the Bodhisatta, because of exercising his own will, goes to a state of woe, takes conception in a womb, performed difficult practices, inflicted self-torment, and designated another teacher'; the admission is from the other. The rest is of clear meaning as in the first discussion. In the second discussion, the statement 'if one were to go due to exercising one's own will, he would go by psychic power, not by the force of kamma,' is said for the purpose of challenging. But the other rejects this in the first question, with reference to what is born of development. In the second question, he accepts it, with reference to the power of merit. In the third discussion, the point is that difficult practices, for the sake of exercising one's own will, are performed with wrong view. And if he were to do that, he would also grasp at eternalism and so on. Hence, 'the world is eternal,' and so on, is said for the purpose of challenging. The same method applies in the fourth discussion.

Issariyakāmakārikākathāvaṇṇanā.

The commentary on the discussion on exercising one's own will.

8. Patirūpakathāvaṇṇanā

8. The commentary on the discussion on counterparts.

915-916. Idāni rāgapatirūpakathā nāma hoti. Tattha mettākaruṇāmuditāyo sandhāya “na rāgo rāgapatirūpako”ti ca issāmacchariyakukkuccāni sandhāya “na doso dosapatirūpako”ti ca hasituppādaṃ sandhāya “na moho mohapatirūpako”ti ca dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahaṃ pesalānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anuggahaṃ pāpagarahitaṃ kalyāṇapasaṃsaṃ āyasmato pilindavacchassa vasalavādaṃ bhagavato kheḷāsakavādaṃ moghapurisavādañca sandhāya “na kileso kilesapatirūpako”ti ca yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi andhakānaṃ; te sandhāya sabbakathāsu pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ yasmā phassādipatirūpakā naphassādayo nāma natthi, tasmā rāgādipatirūpakā narāgādayopi natthīti [M 0.0285] codetuṃ atthi na phassotiādimāha[P 0.0201]. Itaro tesaṃ abhāvā paṭikkhipati. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

915-916. Now comes the discussion on the counterpart of lust. Herein, with reference to loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy, it is said, 'Lust is not a counterpart of lust.' With reference to envy, stinginess, and remorse, it is said, 'Hatred is not a counterpart of hatred.' With reference to the arising of laughter, it is said, 'Delusion is not a counterpart of delusion.' And with reference to the censure of ill-behaved individuals, the support of amiable bhikkhus, the dispraise of evil, the praise of good—such as the Venerable Pilindavaccha's 'outcast' speech, the Blessed One's 'spittle-eater' speech, and the 'worthless man' speech—it is said, 'Defilement is not a counterpart of defilement.' This is the view of those like the Andhakas. Addressing them, the question in all discussions is from the proponent of his own thesis, and the admission is from the other. Then, since there is no such thing as a counterpart of contact, etc., that is not contact, etc., therefore, to challenge them that there is also no such thing as a counterpart of lust, etc., that is not lust, etc., he said, 'Is there not contact?' etc. The other rejects this due to their non-existence. The rest is of clear meaning everywhere.

Patirūpakathāvaṇṇanā.

The commentary on the discussion on counterparts.

9. Aparinipphannakathāvaṇṇanā

9. The commentary on the discussion on the unrealized.

917-918. Idāni [V 0.0284] aparinipphannakathā nāma hoti. Tattha –

917-918. Now comes the discussion on the unrealized. Herein—

“Dukkhameva hi sambhoti, dukkhaṃ tiṭṭhati veti ca;

Nāññatra dukkhā sambhoti, nāññaṃ dukkhā nirujjhatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.171) –

"Suffering alone comes into being, suffering persists and passes away; nothing other than suffering comes into being, nothing other than suffering ceases."

Vacanaṃ nissāya dukkhaññeva parinipphannaṃ, sesā khandhāyatanadhātuindriyadhammā aparinipphannāti yesaṃ laddhi, seyyathāpi ekaccānaṃ uttarapathakānañceva hetuvādānañca; te sandhāya rūpaṃ aparinipphannanti pucchā sakavādissa, paṭiññā itarassa. Atha naṃ “sace rūpaṃ aparinipphannaṃ, na aniccādisabhāvaṃ siyā”ti codetuṃ rūpaṃ na aniccantiādimāha. Itaro tathārūpaṃ rūpaṃ apassanto paṭikkhipati. Sakavādī nanu rūpaṃ aniccantiādi vacanena tassa ekaṃ laddhiṃ paṭisedhetvā dutiyaṃ pucchanto dukkhaññeva parinipphannantiādimāha. Athassa tampi laddhiṃ paṭisedhetuṃ na yadaniccantiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ adhippāyo – na kevalañhi paṭhamasaccameva dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ pana kiñci aniccaṃ, taṃ dukkhameva. Rūpañca aniccaṃ, tasmā tampi parinipphannaṃ. Iti yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi “rūpaṃ aparinipphannaṃ, dukkhaññeva parinipphanna”nti, taṃ no vata re vattabbe “dukkhaññeva parinipphanna”nti. Vedanādimūlikādīsupi yojanāsu eseva nayo. Dhammāyatanadhammadhātūsu pana ṭhapetvā nibbānaṃ sesadhammānaṃ vasena aniccatā veditabbā. Indriyāni aniccānevāti.

Relying on this statement, 'only suffering is fully realized; the remaining aggregates, sense bases, elements, faculties, and phenomena are unrealized'—this is the view held by some, such as certain Northerners and proponents of causation. Addressing them, the question, 'Is form unrealized?' is from the proponent of his own thesis, and the admission is from the other. Then, to challenge him by saying, 'If form were unrealized, it would not have the nature of impermanence, etc.,' he said, 'Form is not impermanent,' etc. The other, not seeing such a form, rejects it. The proponent of his own thesis, having refuted one of his views with the statement, 'Is not form impermanent?' etc., then asks a second question, saying, 'Is only suffering fully realized?' etc. Then, to refute that view as well, he said, 'Is not whatever is impermanent suffering?' Herein, this is the intention: it is not only the first truth that is suffering. But whatever is impermanent, that is suffering. And form is impermanent; therefore, it too is fully realized. Thus, what you say, 'Form is unrealized, only suffering is fully realized,' that indeed, friend, should not be said, 'Only suffering is fully realized.' The same method applies in the applications rooted in feeling, etc. However, regarding the sense base of phenomena and the element of phenomena, apart from Nibbāna, the impermanence of the remaining phenomena should be understood. The faculties are indeed impermanent.

Aparinipphannakathāvaṇṇanā.

The commentary on the discussion on the unrealized.

Tevīsatimo vaggo.

The twenty-third chapter.

Nigamanakathā

The concluding discussion.

Ettāvatā [M 0.0286][P 0.0202][V 0.0285] ca –

And thus far—

Paṇṇāsakehi catūhi, tīhi vaggehi ceva ca;

Saṅgahetvā kathā sabbā, ūnatisatabhedanā.

By four groups of fifty, and by three chapters as well, all the discussions are included, having one hundred and twenty-seven divisions.

Kathāvatthuppakaraṇaṃ, kathāmaggesu kovido;

Yaṃ jino desayi tassa, niṭṭhitā atthavaṇṇanā.

Of the Kathāvatthu treatise, expert in the paths of discussion, which the Conqueror taught, the explanation of the meaning is completed.

Imaṃ terasamattehi, bhāṇavārehi tantiyā;

Ciraṭṭhitatthaṃ dhammassa, saṅkharontena yaṃ mayā.

This work, which I have compiled in a text of about thirteen recitation sections, is for the long duration of the Dhamma.

Yaṃ pattaṃ kusalaṃ tena, lokoyaṃ sanarāmaro;

Dhammarājassa saddhamma-rasamevādhigacchatūti.

By the merit attained by this, may this world, together with humans and gods, attain the very taste of the True Dhamma of the Dhamma King.

Kathāvatthu-aṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Kathāvatthu Commentary is completed.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Abhidhammapiṭake

In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.

Yamakappakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā

The Commentary on the Book of Pairs

Saṅkhepeneva [M 0.0287][P 0.0052][V 0.0286] devānaṃ, devadevo surālaye;

Kathāvatthuppakaraṇaṃ, desayitvā raṇañjaho.

Briefly, the God of gods in the heavenly abode, the conqueror of defilements, having taught the Kathāvatthuppakaraṇa to the gods.

Yamassa visayātīto, nānāyamakamaṇḍitaṃ;

Abhidhammappakaraṇaṃ, chaṭṭhaṃ chaṭṭhāna desako.

Beyond Yama's realm, adorned with various pairs, the sixth treatise of the Abhidhamma, the expounder of the sixth.

Yamakaṃ ayamāvatta-nīlāmalatanūruho;

Yaṃ desayi anuppatto, tassa saṃvaṇṇanākkamo;

Idāni yasmā tasmāssa, hoti saṃvaṇṇanā ayanti.

The Yamaka, which he, whose body is adorned with spiraling, dark-blue, flawless hair, attained and taught; the order of its description—now, for that reason, this description arises.

1. Mūlayamakaṃ

1. The Root Pair

Uddesavāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Summary Section

1. Mūlayamakaṃ[V 0.0287], khandhayamakaṃ, āyatanayamakaṃ, dhātuyamakaṃ, saccayamakaṃ, saṅkhārayamakaṃ, anusayayamakaṃ, cittayamakaṃ, dhammayamakaṃ, indriyayamakanti imesaṃ dasannaṃ yamakānaṃ vasena idaṃ pakaraṇaṃ dasavidhena vibhattanti hi vuttaṃ. Tattha yesaṃ dasannaṃ yamakānaṃ vasena idaṃ pakaraṇaṃ dasavidhena vibhattaṃ, tesañceva imassa ca pakaraṇassa nāmattho tāva evaṃ veditabbo – kenaṭṭhena yamakanti? Yugaḷaṭṭhena. Yugaḷañhi yamakanti vuccati – ‘yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ, yamakasālā’tiādīsu viya. Iti yugaḷasaṅkhātānaṃ yamakānaṃ vasena desitattā imesu dasasu ekekaṃ yamakaṃ nāma. Imesaṃ pana yamakānaṃ samūhabhāvato sabbampetaṃ pakaraṇaṃ yamakanti veditabbaṃ.

1. It is said that this treatise is divided in ten ways by means of these ten pairs: the Root Pair, the Aggregate Pair, the Sense-base Pair, the Element Pair, the Truth Pair, the Formation Pair, the Underlying Tendency Pair, the Mind Pair, the Dhamma Pair, and the Faculty Pair. Herein, regarding the ten pairs by means of which this treatise is divided in ten ways, and also the meaning of the name of this treatise, it should first be understood thus: In what sense is it called 'yamaka'? In the sense of 'pair.' For 'pair' is called 'yamaka'—as in the expressions 'the twin miracle,' 'the twin-hall,' and so on. Thus, because each of these ten is taught by means of yamakas, designated as pairs, each is called a 'yamaka.' Moreover, because this entire treatise is a collection of these yamakas, it should be understood as 'Yamaka.'

Tattha mūlavasena pucchāvissajjanaṃ katvā desitattā dasannaṃ tāva sabbapaṭhamaṃ mūlayamakanti vuttaṃ. Tassa uddesavāro, niddesavāroti dve vārā honti[M 0.0288]. Tesu uddiṭṭhānukkamena niddisitabbattā uddesavāro paṭhamo. Tassa ye keci kusalā dhammā, sabbe te kusalamūlā; ye vā pana kusalamūlā, sabbe te dhammā kusalāti idaṃ yamakaṃ ādi[P 0.0053]. Tassa kusalākusalamūlasaṅkhātānaṃ dvinnaṃ atthānaṃ vasena atthayamakanti vā, tesaññeva atthānaṃ vasena anulomapaṭilomato pavattapāḷidhammavasena dhammayamakanti vā, anulomapaṭilomato pavattapucchāvasena pucchāyamakanti vā tidhā yamakabhāvo veditabbo. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

Herein, because the questions and answers are given based on the root, therefore, first of all, it is called the Root Pair of the ten. It has two sections: the Summary Section and the Detailed Exposition Section. Among these, the Summary Section comes first because the exposition should follow the order of what is recited. Herein, the pair begins with: "Whatever states are wholesome, are they all rooted in the wholesome? Or whatever are rooted in the wholesome, are they all wholesome states?" The nature of this pair should be understood in three ways: as a pair of meanings by means of the two meanings designated as wholesome and unwholesome roots; or as a pair of phenomena by means of those same meanings, proceeding in forward and reverse order according to the text of the Dhamma; or as a pair of questions by means of questions proceeding in forward and reverse order. The same method applies to the remaining pairs.

Idāni imesaṃ yamakānaṃ vasena desite imasmiṃ mūlayamake uddesavārassa tāva nayayamakapucchāatthavārappabhedavasena pāḷivavatthānameva evaṃ veditabbaṃ – kusalattikamātikāya hi ‘kusalā dhammā’ti idaṃ ādipadaṃ nissāya mūlanayo, mūlamūlanayo, mūlakanayo, mūlamūlakanayoti ime cattāro nayā honti. Tesaṃ ekekasmiṃ naye mūlayamakaṃ, ekamūlayamakaṃ, aññamaññamūlayamakanti tīṇi tīṇi yamakāni. Evaṃ catūsu nayesu dvādasa yamakāni, ekekasmiṃ [V 0.0288] yamake anulomapaṭilomavasena dve dve pucchāti catuvīsati pucchā, ekekāya pucchāya sanniṭṭhānasaṃsayavasena dve dve atthāti aṭṭhacattālīsa atthāti.

Now, in this Root Pair, which is taught by means of these pairs, the arrangement of the Pali text in the Summary Section should be understood as follows, by way of the distinctions of method, pair, question, and meaning: Based on the initial phrase "wholesome states" from the wholesome triad matrix, there are four methods: the root method, the root-root method, the rooted method, and the root-rooted method. For each of these methods, there are three pairs: the root pair, the single-root pair, and the reciprocal-root pair. Thus, in the four methods, there are twelve pairs. In each pair, there are two questions by way of forward and reverse order, making twenty-four questions. For each question, there are two meanings—affirmation and doubt—making forty-eight meanings.

Tattha ye keci kusalā dhammāti kusalesu “kusalā nu kho, na kusalā nu kho”ti sandehābhāvato imasmiṃ pade sanniṭṭhānattho veditabbo. Sabbe te kusalamūlāti “sabbe te kusalā dhammā kusalamūlā nu kho, nanu kho”ti evaṃ vimativasena pucchitattā imasmiṃ pade saṃsayattho veditabbo. So ca kho veneyyānaṃ saṃsayaṭṭhāne saṃsayadīpanatthaṃ vutto, tathāgatassa pana saṃsayo nāma natthi. Ito paresupi pucchāpadesu eseva nayo.

Herein, in the phrase "whatever states are wholesome," because there is no doubt such as "are they wholesome or not?" the meaning in this phrase should be understood as affirmation. In the phrase "are they all rooted in the wholesome?" because it is asked with an attitude of inquiry, such as "are all those wholesome states rooted in the wholesome, or are they not?" the meaning in this phrase should be understood as doubt. This, however, was stated for the purpose of illuminating doubt where doubt exists for those who are to be guided, for the Tathāgata has no doubt whatsoever. The same method applies to the subsequent questions.

Yathā ca kusalapadaṃ nissāya ime cattāro nayā, ekekasmiṃ naye tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ yamakānaṃ vasena dvādasa yamakāni, ekekasmiṃ yamake dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ pucchānaṃ vasena catuvīsati pucchā; ekekāya pucchāya dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ atthānaṃ vasena aṭṭhacattālīsa atthā ca honti. Akusalapadaṃ nissāyapi tatheva. Abyākatapadaṃ nissāyapi tatheva. Tīṇipi padāni ekato katvā niddiṭṭhaṃ nāmapadaṃ nissāyapi tathevāti kusalattikamātikāya catūsu padesu sabbepi soḷasa nayā, aṭṭhacattālīsa yamakāni[M 0.0289], channavuti [P 0.0054] pucchā, dvenavutisataṃ atthā ca uddesavasena vuttāti veditabbā. Ettāvatā mūlavāro nāma paṭhamaṃ uddiṭṭho hoti.

Just as based on the wholesome term there are these four methods, and in each method three pairs, making twelve pairs; and in each pair two questions, making twenty-four questions; and for each question two meanings, making forty-eight meanings; so too it is when based on the unwholesome term, and so too when based on the indeterminate term. And so too it is when based on the nominal term, which is indicated by combining all three terms. Thus, it should be understood that in the wholesome triad matrix, across the four terms, there are in all sixteen methods, forty-eight pairs, ninety-six questions, and one hundred and ninety-two meanings stated by way of summary. With this, the first section, called the Root Section, has been set forth.

Tato paraṃ ye keci kusalā dhammā, sabbe te kusalahetūtiādayo tasseva mūlavārassa vevacanavasena nava vārā uddiṭṭhā. Iti mūlavāro, hetuvāro, nidānavāro, sambhavavāro, pabhavavāro, samuṭṭhānavāro, āhāravāro, ārammaṇavāro, paccayavāro, samudayavāroti sabbepi dasa vārā honti. Tattha mūlavāre āgataparicchedeneva sesesupi nayādayo veditabbāti sabbesupi dasasu vāresu saṭṭhisatanayā, asītiadhikāni cattāri yamakasatāni, saṭṭhiadhikāni navapucchāsatāni, vīsādhikāni ekūnavīsati atthasatāni ca uddiṭṭhānīti veditabbāni. Evaṃ tāva uddesavāre nayayamakapucchāatthavārappabhedavasena pāḷivavatthānameva veditabbaṃ.

Thereafter, nine further sections are pointed out by way of synonyms for that same Root Section, with questions such as, 'Whatever wholesome states there are, are they all wholesome causes?' Thus, there are ten sections in all: Root Section, Cause Section, Source Section, Generation Section, Origin Section, Arising Section, Nutriment Section, Object Section, Condition Section, and Collection Section. Herein, the method and so on that have come in the Root Section should be understood in the remaining sections as well. Thus, in all ten sections, it should be understood that one hundred and sixty methods, four hundred and eighty pairs, nine hundred and sixty questions, and one thousand nine hundred and twenty meanings have been pointed out. In this way, in the Summary Section, the arrangement of the Pali text should be understood simply in terms of the divisions of section, method, pair, question, and meaning.

Mūlaṃ hetu nidānañcāti gāthā dasannampi vārānaṃ uddānagāthā nāma. Tattha mūlādīni sabbānipi kāraṇavevacanāneva. Kāraṇañhi patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena mūlaṃ. Attano phalanipphādanatthaṃ hinoti pavattatīti hetu. ‘Handa, naṃ gaṇhāthā’ti dassentaṃ viya attano phalaṃ nidetīti nidānaṃ. Etasmā phalaṃ sambhotīti sambhavo. Pabhavatīti pabhavo. Samuṭṭhāti ettha phalaṃ, etena vā samuṭṭhātīti samuṭṭhānaṃ. Attano phalaṃ āharatīti āhāro. Appaṭikkhipitabbena attano phalena ālambiyatīti ālambaṇaṃ. Etaṃ paṭicca appaṭikkhipitvā phalaṃ eti pavattatīti paccayo. Etasmā phalaṃ samudetīti samudayo. Evametesaṃ padānaṃ vacanattho veditabbo.

“The root, the cause, and the origin,” etc., is the summary verse for all ten sections. Herein, “root” and the rest are all synonyms for “cause.” For a cause is called “root” in the sense of being a foundation. It is called “cause” (hetu) because it proceeds for the purpose of producing its own fruit. It is called “origin” (nidāna) because it indicates its own fruit, as if showing and saying, “Here, take this.” From this, a fruit comes into being—thus it is called “coming into being” (sambhavo). From this it originates—thus it is called “source” (pabhavo). A fruit arises from this, or arises by means of this—thus it is called “arising” (samuṭṭhāna). It brings its own fruit—thus it is called “nutriment” (āhāro). It is relied upon by its own fruit, in a way that cannot be rejected—thus it is called “support” (ālambaṇa). Dependent on this, not rejecting it, a fruit comes to be and proceeds—thus it is called “condition” (paccayo). From this, a fruit originates—thus it is called “origination” (samudayo). In this way, the meaning of these terms should be understood.

Uddesavāravaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Summary Section.

Niddesavāravaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition Section.

50. Idāni yekeci kusalā dhammātiādinā nayena niddesavāro āraddho. Tattha ye kecīti anavasesavacanaṃ. Kusalā dhammāti kusalattikassa padabhājane vuttalakkhaṇā anavajjasukhavipākā [P 0.0055] kusalasabhāvā. Sabbe te kusalamūlāti kiṃ te sabbeyeva kusalamūlāti pucchati. Tīṇeva [M 0.0290] kusalamūlānīti na te sabbe kusalamūlāni, alobhādīni pana tīṇi eva kusalamūlānīti attho. Avasesā kusalā dhammā na kusalamūlāti avasesā phassādayo kusalā dhammā kusalamūlāni nāma na honti. Atha vā avasesā phassādayo kusalā dhammāyeva nāma, na kusalamūlānītipi attho. Ye vā pana kusalamūlāti ye vā pana paṭhamapucchāya dutiyapadena kusalamūlāti tayo alobhādayo gahitā. Sabbe te dhammā kusalāti kiṃ te sabbe tayopi dhammā kusalāti pucchati. Āmantāti sabbesampi kusalamūlānaṃ kusalabhāvaṃ sampaṭicchanto āha. Ayaṃ tāva mūlanaye mūlayamakassa attho. Iminā upāyena sabbapucchāsu vissajjananayo veditabbo. Yaṃ pana yattha visesamattaṃ atthi, tadeva vaṇṇayissāma.

50. Now, the exposition section has been commenced with the phrase, “whatever wholesome states,” etc. Herein, “whatever” is an all-inclusive term. “Wholesome states” refers to those states described in the analysis of terms under the wholesome triplet, characterized as blameless, resulting in happiness, and being of a wholesome nature. “Are all these roots of the wholesome?”—this asks whether all of them are roots of the wholesome. “There are only three roots of the wholesome”—this means that not all of them are roots of the wholesome, but rather the three, namely non-greed and so on, are the roots of the wholesome. “The remaining wholesome states are not roots of the wholesome”—that is, the remaining wholesome states such as contact and so on are not called roots of the wholesome. Alternatively, the meaning is that the remaining wholesome states such as contact and so on are indeed called wholesome states, but not roots of the wholesome. “Or whatever are roots of the wholesome”—this refers to the three, non-greed and so on, which are taken up by the second part of the first question-pair. “Are all these states wholesome?”—this asks whether all three states are wholesome. “Yes”—this is said, affirming the wholesome nature of all the roots of the wholesome. This, for now, is the meaning of the root-pair in the root method. By this method, the way of answering all questions should be understood. Whatever distinctions exist in each case, only those will we explain.

51. Ekamūlayamake tāva sabbe te kusalamūlena ekamūlāti gaṇanaṭṭhena ekamūlakaṃ aggahetvā samānaṭṭhena gahetabbā. Ayañhettha attho – sabbe te kusalamūlena samānamūlā. Yaṃ phassassa mūlaṃ, tadeva vedanādīnanti. Atha nesaṃ tathābhāvaṃ sampaṭicchanto āmantāti āha. Kusalasamuṭṭhānanti kusalacittasamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ dassitaṃ. Ekamūlanti alobhādinā kusalamūlena samānamūlaṃ[V 0.0290]. Yatheva hi phassādīnaṃ alobhādayo hetupaccayattā mūlaṃ, tathā taṃ samuṭṭhānarūpassāpi, kusalalakkhaṇābhāvena pana taṃ na kusalaṃ.

51. In the single-root pair, firstly, the phrase “all these are of a single root with the wholesome root” should be understood not in the numerical sense of having one root, but in the sense of having a common root. The meaning here is this: all these have a common root with the wholesome root. The root of contact is the same as that of feeling and so on. Then, accepting that they are so, one says, “Yes.” By “arisen from the wholesome,” materiality arisen from wholesome consciousness is shown. “Of a single root” means having a common root with the wholesome root, that is, with non-greed and so on. For just as non-greed and so on are the root for contact and so on by being a root-condition, so too are they for the materiality arisen therefrom; but because it lacks the characteristic of the wholesome, that materiality is not wholesome.

52. Aññamaññayamake ‘yekeci kusalā’ti apucchitvā yekeci kusalamūlena ekamūlāti pucchā katā. Kasmā? Imināpi byañjanena tassevatthassa sambhavato. Kusalamūlānīti idaṃ purimassa visesanaṃ. ‘Mūlāni yāni ekato uppajjantī’ti hi vuttaṃ, tāni pana kusalamūlānipi honti akusalaabyākatamūlānipi, idha kusalamūlānīti visesadassanatthamidaṃ vuttaṃ. Aññamaññamūlāni cāti aññamaññaṃ hetupaccayena paccayā hontīti attho. Tasseva paṭilomapucchāya ‘sabbe te dhammā [P 0.0056] kusalamūlena ekamūlā’ti avatvā sabbe te dhammā kusalāti vuttaṃ. Kasmā? Atthavisesābhāvato. Kusalamūlena ekamūlāti hi pucchāya katāya ‘mūlāni yāni ekato uppajjantī’ti heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva vissajjanaṃ kātabbaṃ bhaveyya, evañca sati atthavisesābhāvo hoti. Tasmā tathā akatvā [M 0.0291] evaṃ pucchā katā. Iminā upāyena mūlamūlanayādīsupi aññamaññamūlayamake pucchāviseso veditabbo.

52. In the mutual-root pair, the question is asked not as, “whatever wholesome states,” but as, “whatever states are of a single root with the wholesome root.” Why? Because this phrasing also makes that same meaning possible. “Roots of the wholesome” is a qualification of the preceding. For it was said, “roots that arise together,” but those can be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate roots. Here, “roots of the wholesome” is stated to show the distinction. “And are mutually rooted” means they are conditions for each other by way of the root-condition. In the reverse question for this pair, instead of saying, “are all these states of a single root with the wholesome root,” it is said, “are all these states wholesome.” Why? Because there is no special meaning. For if the question had been asked as, “are of a single root with the wholesome root,” the answer would have had to be given in the same way as stated below, “roots that arise together,” and in that case there would be no special meaning. Therefore, the question was not asked in that way, but was asked thus. By this method, the distinction in the question in the mutual-root pair of the root-root method and others should be understood.

53-55. Mūlamūlanaye sabbe te kusalamūlamūlāti sabbe te kusalamūlasaṅkhātā mūlāti pucchati. Ekamūlamūlāti samānaṭṭhena ekameva mūlamūlaṃ etesanti ekamūlamūlā. Aññamaññamūlamūlāti aññamaññassa mūlaṃ aññamaññamūlaṃ, aññamaññamūlaṃ hetupaccayaṭṭhena mūlaṃ etesanti aññamaññamūlamūlā.

53-55. In the root-root method, “Are all these rooted in wholesome roots?” means one asks: “Are all those roots designated as wholesome roots?” “Rooted in a single root” means they have a single common root, in the sense of sameness. “Rooted in mutual roots” means that the root of one another is a mutual root, and they have that mutual root as their root in the sense of a root-condition.

56. Mūlakanaye kusalamūlakāti hetupaccayaṭṭhena kusalaṃ mūlaṃ etesanti kusalamūlakā.

56. In the rooted-method, “wholesome-rooted” means they have a wholesome root as their root in the sense of a root-condition.

57-61. Mūlamūlakanaye kusalamūlamūlakāti kusalānaṃ mūlaṃ kusalamūlaṃ. Hetupaccayaṭṭheneva kusalamūlaṃ mūlaṃ etesanti kusalamūlamūlakāti. Ayaṃ tāva kusalapadaṃ nissāya nayayamakapucchāsu visesattho.

57-61. In the root-rooted-method, “wholesome-root-rooted” means: the root of wholesome states is a wholesome root. Because a wholesome root is the root for these in the sense of a root-condition, they are “wholesome-root-rooted.” This, for now, is the special meaning in the questions of the method-pairs that relate to the wholesome term.

62-73. Akusalapadādīsupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ pana viseso, ahetukaṃ akusalanti vicikicchāya ceva uddhaccena ca sampayuttaṃ mohaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

62-73. The same method applies to the unwholesome terms and so on. This, however, is the distinction: “unwholesome without a root” is said in reference to the delusion associated with doubt and restlessness.

74-85. Ahetukaṃ [V 0.0291] abyākatanti aṭṭhārasa cittuppādā rūpaṃ, nibbānañca. Abyākatamūlena na ekamūlanti idha pana ṭhapetvā sahetukaabyākatasamuṭṭhānaṃ rūpaṃ, sesaṃ labbhati. Sahetukaabyākatasamuṭṭhānaṃ rūpaṃ abyākatamūlena ekamūlaṃ hoti, taṃ abbohārikaṃ katvā ekato labbhamānakavaseneva cetaṃ vissajjanaṃ kataṃ.

74-85. Rootless indeterminate states are the eighteen types of consciousness, materiality, and Nibbāna. Regarding “not of a single root with the indeterminate root,” here, excepting materiality arisen from a rooted-indeterminate state, the remainder is obtained. Materiality arisen from a rooted-indeterminate state is of a single root with the indeterminate root, but treating that as non-conventional, this answer is given only by way of what is obtained collectively.

86-97. Nāmā dhammāti nāmasaṅkhātā dhammā. Te atthato cattāro arūpino khandhā, nibbānañca. Naveva nāmamūlānīti kusalākusalaabyākatamūlavasena nava mūlāni. Ahetukaṃ nāmaṃ nāmamūlena na ekamūlanti ahetukaṃ sabbampi aṭṭhārasa cittuppādavicikicchuddhaccasampayuttamohanibbānasaṅkhātaṃ nāmaṃ nāmamūlena na ekamūlaṃ[P 0.0057]. Na hi taṃ tena saddhiṃ uppajjati. Sahetukaṃ [M 0.0292] nāmaṃ nāmamūlenāti padepi sahetukaṃ nāmaṃ nāmamūlenāti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

86-97. 'Name-states' are states designated as 'name.' In meaning, these are the four immaterial aggregates and Nibbāna. 'Nine roots of name' means there are nine roots by way of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate roots. 'Name without a root is not of a single root with the name-root' means that all rootless name—namely, the eighteen types of consciousness, the delusion associated with doubt and restlessness, and Nibbāna, designated as name—is not of a single root with the name-root. For it does not arise together with it. In the phrase 'name with a root by the name-root,' the meaning is 'name with a root by the name-root.' The rest is clear in meaning everywhere.

Mūlavāravaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Root Section.

98-99. Hetuvārādīsupi imināvupāyena attho veditabbo. Mūlaṃ hetu nidānañcātigāthā yathāniddiṭṭhānaṃ dasannampi vārānaṃ puna uddānavaseneva vuttāti.

98-99. In the sections beginning with conditions, the meaning should be understood by this same method. The verse "root, cause, origin," etc., is stated as an introductory verse again for all ten sections, just as was indicated.

Mūlayamakavaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Root Yamaka.

2. Khandhayamakaṃ

2. The Yamaka on the Aggregates

1. Paṇṇattiuddesavāravaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Recitation Section of the Designation Division.

1. Idāni mūlayamake desiteyeva kusalādidhamme khandhavasena saṅgaṇhitvā mūlayamakānantaraṃ desitassa khandhayamakassa vaṇṇanā hoti. Tattha pāḷivavatthānaṃ tāva evaṃ veditabbaṃ – imasmiñhi khandhayamake tayo mahāvārā honti – paṇṇattivāro, pavattivāro, pariññāvāroti. Tesu [V 0.0292] paṇṇattivāro khandhānaṃ nāmābhidhānasodhanavaseneva gatattā paṇṇattivāroti vuccati. Pavattivāro tena sodhitanāmābhidhānānaṃ khandhānaṃ uppādanirodhavasena pavattiṃ sodhayamāno gato, tasmā pavattivāroti vuccati. Pariññāvāro iminānukkamena pavattānaṃ khandhānaṃ saṅkhepeneva tisso pariññā dīpayamāno gato, tasmā pariññāvāroti vuccati. Tattha paṇṇattivāro uddesaniddesavasena dvīhākārehi vavatthito. Itaresu visuṃ uddesavāro natthi. Ādito paṭṭhāya pucchāvissajjanavasena ekadhā vavatthitā. Tattha pañcakkhandhātipadaṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva na khandhā, na saṅkhārāti padaṃ tāva paṇṇattivārassa uddesavāro veditabbo. Pucchāvārotipi tasseva nāmaṃ. Tattha pañcakkhandhāti ayaṃ yamakavasena pucchitabbānaṃ khandhānaṃ uddeso. Rūpakkhandho…pe… viññāṇakkhandhoti tesaññeva pabhedato nāmavavatthānaṃ.

1. Now, since the Root Yamaka has been taught, the commentary on the Aggregate Yamaka, which was taught after the Root Yamaka, is presented by grouping the wholesome and other phenomena by way of the aggregates. Herein, the Pāli arrangement should first be understood as follows: In this Aggregate Yamaka, there are three main divisions—the Designation Division, the Process Division, and the Full-Understanding Division. Among these, the Designation Division is so called because it is concerned with clarifying the naming and designation of the aggregates. The Process Division is so called because it clarifies the process, in terms of arising and cessation, of the aggregates whose names and designations have been clarified. The Full-Understanding Division is so called because it briefly illuminates the three kinds of full-understanding of the aggregates that proceed in this sequence. Herein, the Designation Division is established in two ways: by way of recitation and explanation. In the others, there is no separate recitation section. From the beginning, they are established in one way by way of question and answer. Herein, starting from the phrase “the five aggregates” up to the phrase “not aggregates, not formations,” this should be understood as the recitation section of the Designation Division. The Question Section is also just a name for that. Herein, “the five aggregates” is the recitation of the aggregates to be questioned in pairs. The detailed naming of them is as follows: “the form aggregate… the consciousness aggregate.”

2-3. Idāni [M 0.0293] imesaṃ khandhānaṃ [P 0.0058] vasena padasodhanavāro, padasodhanamūlacakkavāro, suddhakhandhavāro, suddhakhandhamūlacakkavāroti cattāro nayavārā honti. Tattha rūpaṃ rūpakkhandho, rūpakkhandho rūpantiādinā nayena padameva sodhetvā gato padasodhanavāro nāma. So anulomapaṭilomavasena duvidho hoti. Tattha anulomavāre ‘rūpaṃ rūpakkhandho, rūpakkhandho rūpa’ntiādīni pañca yamakāni. Paṭilomavārepi ‘na rūpaṃ, na rūpakkhandho; na rūpakkhandho na rūpa’ntiādīni pañceva. Tato paraṃ tesaññeva padasodhanavāre sodhitānaṃ khandhānaṃ ‘rūpaṃ rūpakkhandho, khandhā vedanākkhandho’tiādinā nayena ekekakhandhamūlakāni cattāri cattāri cakkāni bandhitvā gato padasodhanamūlakānaṃ cakkānaṃ atthitāya padasodhanamūlacakkavāro nāma. Sopi anulomapaṭilomavasena duvidho hoti. Tattha anulomavāre ‘rūpaṃ rūpakkhandho, khandhā vedanākkhandho’tiādīni ekekakhandhamūlakāni cattāri cattāri katvā vīsati yamakāni. Paṭilomavārepi ‘na rūpaṃ, na rūpakkhandho; na khandhā na vedanākkhandho’tiādīni vīsatimeva.

2-3. Now, with regard to these aggregates, there are four methodical divisions: the Word Clarification Division, the Word Clarification Root-Cycle Division, the Pure Aggregate Division, and the Pure Aggregate Root-Cycle Division. Here, the Word Clarification Division is so called because it proceeds by clarifying just the words themselves in the manner of "form is the form aggregate, the form aggregate is form," and so on. It is twofold: in forward and reverse order. Herein, in the forward order, there are five pairs, such as "form is the form aggregate, the form aggregate is form." In the reverse order, there are also just five pairs, such as "not form, not the form aggregate; not the form aggregate, not form." Thereafter, the Word Clarification Root-Cycle Division is so called because it proceeds by constructing four cycles, each based on a single aggregate, for those aggregates clarified in the Word Clarification Division—such as "form is the form aggregate, aggregates are the feeling aggregate," and so on—due to the presence of these cycles rooted in word clarification. This too is twofold: in forward and reverse order. Herein, in the forward order, there are twenty pairs, making four cycles each based on a single aggregate root, such as "form is the form aggregate, aggregates are the feeling aggregate." In the reverse order, there are also twenty pairs, such as "not form, not the form aggregate; not aggregates, not the feeling aggregate."

Tato paraṃ rūpaṃ khandho khandhā rūpantiādinā nayena suddhakhandhavaseneva gato suddhakhandhavāro nāma. Tattha khandhā rūpantiādīsu khandhā rūpakkhandho, khandhā vedanākkhandhoti attho gahetabbo. Kasmā? Niddesavāre evaṃ bhājitattā. Tattha hi ‘rūpaṃ khandhoti āmantā. Khandhā rūpakkhandhoti rūpakkhandho khandho ceva rūpakkhandho ca, avasesā khandhā na rūpakkhandho’ti evaṃ ‘khandhā rūpa’ntiādīnaṃ khandhā rūpakkhandhotiādinā nayena padaṃ uddharitvā attho vibhatto. Teneva ca kāraṇenese suddhakhandhavāroti vutto. Vacanasodhane viya hi ettha [V 0.0293] na vacanaṃ pamāṇaṃ. Yathā yathā pana suddhakhandhā labbhanti, tathā tathā atthova pamāṇaṃ. Parato āyatanayamakādīsupi eseva nayo. Esopi ca suddhakhandhavāro anulomapaṭilomavasena duvidho [P 0.0059] hoti. Tattha anulomavāre ‘rūpaṃ khandho khandhā rūpa’ntiādīni pañca yamakāni. Paṭilomavārepi ‘na rūpaṃ na khandho, na khandhā na rūpa’ntiādīni pañceva.

Then, the section proceeding by way of 'form is an aggregate, aggregates are form,' and so on, is called the Pure Aggregates Section because it proceeds solely by way of the pure aggregates. There, in phrases such as 'aggregates are form,' the meaning should be understood as 'aggregates are the form aggregate,' 'aggregates are the feeling aggregate,' and so on. Why? Because it is analyzed thus in the exposition section. For there, to the question 'Is form an aggregate?' the answer is 'Yes.' To the question 'Are aggregates the form aggregate?' the answer is: 'The form aggregate is both an aggregate and the form aggregate; the remaining aggregates are aggregates, but not the form aggregate.' In this way, for phrases such as 'aggregates are form,' the meaning is analyzed by specifying the term in the manner of 'aggregates are the form aggregate,' and so on. For this very reason, it is called the Pure Aggregates Section. For here, unlike in the clarification of wording, the wording is not the authority; rather, in whatever way the pure aggregates are found, in that way the meaning is the authority. This same method applies in the subsequent Yamakas, such as the Āyatana Yamaka. This Pure Aggregates Section is also twofold: in forward and reverse order. In the forward section, there are five pairs, such as 'form is an aggregate, aggregates are form,' and so on. In the reverse section, there are also just five pairs, such as 'not form, not an aggregate; not aggregates, not form,' and so on.

Tato paraṃ tesaññeva suddhakhandhānaṃ rūpaṃ khandho, khandhā vedanātiādinā nayena ekekakhandhamūlakāni cattāri cattāri cakkāni bandhitvā gato suddhakhandhamūlakānaṃ cakkānaṃ atthitāya suddhakhandhamūlacakkavāro nāma. Tattha [M 0.0294] khandhā vedanātiādīsu khandhā vedanākkhandhotiādinā nayena attho veditabbo. Itarathā niddesavārena saddhiṃ virodho hoti. Sopi anulomapaṭilomavasena duvidho hoti. Tattha anulomavāre ‘rūpaṃ khandho, khandhā vedanā’tiādīni ekekakhandhamūlakāni cattāri cattāri katvā vīsati yamakāni. Paṭilomavārepi ‘na rūpaṃ, na khandho, na khandhā na vedanā’tiādīni vīsatimeva. Evaṃ tāva ekena yamakasatena dvīhi pucchāsatehi ekekapucchāya sanniṭṭhānasaṃsayavasena dve dve atthe katvā catūhi ca atthasatehi paṭimaṇḍito paṇṇattivārassa uddesavāro veditabboti.

Next, based on those same pure aggregates, by way of 'form is an aggregate, aggregates are feeling,' and so on, four cycles each are constructed for each single aggregate as a root; thus, due to the presence of these cycles rooted in the pure aggregates, it is called the pure aggregate root-cycle division. There, in phrases like 'aggregates are feeling,' the meaning should be understood in the manner of 'aggregates are the aggregate of feeling,' and so on. Otherwise, there would be a conflict with the section on exposition. This too is twofold: in forward and reverse order. In the forward section, there are twenty pairs, made by taking each single aggregate as the root in sets of four, such as 'form is an aggregate, aggregates are feeling,' and so on. In the reverse section, there are also twenty pairs like 'not form, not an aggregate; not aggregates, not feeling,' and so on. Thus, adorned with one hundred pairs, two hundred questions, making two meanings for each question by way of conclusion and doubt, and thus four hundred meanings—this is how the recitation section of the designation division should be understood.

Paṇṇattiuddesavāravaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Recitation Section of the Designation Division.

1. Paṇṇattiniddesavāravaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Exposition Section of the Designation Division.

26. Idāni rūpaṃ rūpakkhandhotiādinā nayena niddesavāro āraddho. Tattha rūpaṃ rūpakkhandhoti yaṃkiñci rūpanti vuccati. Sabbaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ rūpakkhandhoti vacanasodhanatthaṃ pucchati. Piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, rūpaṃ, na rūpakkhandhoti yaṃ ‘piyarūpaṃ sātarūpa’nti ettha rūpanti vuttaṃ, taṃ rūpameva, na rūpakkhandhoti attho. Rūpakkhandho rūpañceva rūpakkhandho cāti yo pana rūpakkhandho, so rūpantipi rūpakkhandhotipi vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti attho. Rūpakkhandho rūpanti ettha pana yasmā rūpakkhandho niyameneva rūpanti vattabbo. Tasmā āmantāti āha. Iminā upāyena sabbavissajjanesu attho veditabbo. Yo pana yattha viseso bhavissati, tatheva taṃ vaṇṇayissāma[V 0.0294]. Saññāyamake tāva diṭṭhisaññāti ‘papañcasaññā’tiādīsu āgatā diṭṭhisaññā. Saṅkhārayamake avasesā saṅkhārāti ‘aniccā vata saṅkhārā’tiādīsu āgatā saṅkhārakkhandhato avasesā [P 0.0060] saṅkhatadhammā. Paṭilomavārepi eseva nayoti.

26. Now the section on exposition has been commenced by way of the method beginning with 'form is the aggregate of form,' and so on. Herein, 'form is the aggregate of form' refers to whatever is called form. 'Is all that form the aggregate of form?'—this is asked for the clarification of the statement. Regarding the statement, 'Pleasant form, delightful form is form, but not the aggregate of form,' the meaning is that what is called 'form' here, in 'pleasant form, delightful form,' is form itself, not the aggregate of form. As for 'the aggregate of form is both form and the aggregate of form,' the meaning is that whatever is the aggregate of form, it is fitting to call it both 'form' and 'the aggregate of form.' Here, however, regarding 'the aggregate of form is form,' since the aggregate of form must invariably be called form, therefore it is said 'yes.' By this method, the meaning in all replies should be understood. Wherever there will be a distinction, we shall explain it accordingly. First, in the section on perception, 'perception of views' refers to the perception of views that occurs in phrases like 'proliferated perceptions,' and so on. In the section on formations, 'the remaining formations' refers to the remaining conditioned phenomena apart from the aggregate of formations, as found in phrases like 'formations are indeed impermanent,' and so on. The same method applies in the reverse section.

Padasodhanavāro niṭṭhito.

The section on word clarification is concluded.

28. Padasodhanamūlacakkavāre khandhā vedanākkhandhoti yekeci khandhā, sabbe te vedanākkhandhoti pucchati. Sesapucchāsupi eseva nayo. Paṭilome na khandhā na vedanākkhandhoti ettha ye paññattinibbānasaṅkhātā dhammā [M 0.0295] khandhā na honti, te yasmā vedanākkhandhopi na honti, tasmā āmantāti āha. Sesavissajjanesupi eseva nayoti.

28. In the section on the root cycle of word clarification, regarding 'Are aggregates the feeling aggregate?', it is asked whether all aggregates, whatever aggregates there are, are the feeling aggregate. The same method applies in the remaining questions. In the reverse, regarding 'not aggregates, not the feeling aggregate,' since those phenomena designated as concepts and Nibbāna, which are not aggregates, are also not the feeling aggregate, therefore it is said 'yes.' The same method applies in the remaining answers.

Padasodhanamūlacakkavāro niṭṭhito.

The section on the root cycle of word clarification is concluded.

38. Suddhakhandhavāre rūpaṃ khandhoti yaṃkiñci rūpanti vuttaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ khandhoti pucchati. Tattha yasmā piyarūpasātarūpasaṅkhātaṃ vā rūpaṃ hotu, bhūtupādārūpaṃ vā, sabbaṃ pañcasu khandhesu saṅgahaṃ gacchateva. Tasmā āmantāti paṭijānāti. Dutiyapade ‘khandhā rūpa’nti pucchitabbe yasmā rūpantivacanena rūpakkhandhova adhippeto, tasmā vacanaṃ anādiyitvā atthavasena pucchanto khandhā rūpakkhandhoti āha. Iminā nayena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo. Parato āyatanayamakādīnaṃ niddesavārepi eseva nayo. Saññā khandhoti etthāpi diṭṭhisaññā vā hotu, saññā eva vā, sabbāyapi khandhabhāvato āmantāti vuttaṃ. Saṅkhārā khandhoti padepi eseva nayo. Khandhavinimuttako hi saṅkhāro nāma natthi.

38. In the section on the pure aggregates, regarding 'form is an aggregate,' it is asked whether all that is called form is an aggregate. Herein, since whether it is form designated as pleasant and delightful, or primary and derived matter, all are indeed included in the five aggregates, therefore it is affirmed 'yes.' In the second phrase, when 'aggregates are form' is to be asked, since by the word 'form' the aggregate of form itself is intended, therefore, disregarding the wording and asking based on the meaning, one says, 'aggregates are the aggregate of form.' By this method, the meaning in all phrases should be understood. The same method applies in the subsequent sections on the exposition of the sense bases, and so on. Regarding 'perception is an aggregate,' here too, whether it is perception of views or just perception, since all are of the nature of an aggregate, it is said 'yes.' The same method applies in the phrase 'formations are an aggregate' too. For there is no formation that is truly exempt from the aggregates.

39. Paṭilome na rūpaṃ na khandhoti yaṃ dhammajātaṃ rūpaṃ na hoti, taṃ khandhopi na hotīti pucchati. Vissajjane panassa rūpaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesā khandhā na rūpaṃ, khandhāti rūpato aññe vedanādayo khandhā rūpameva na honti, khandhā pana hontīti attho. Rūpañca khandhe ca ṭhapetvā avasesāti pañcakkhandhavinimuttaṃ nibbānañceva [P 0.0061] paññatti ca. Ito paresupi ‘avasesā’ti padesu eseva nayoti.

39. In the reverse, regarding 'not form, not an aggregate,' it is asked whether a phenomenon that is not form is also not an aggregate. In its reply, however, 'excluding form, the remaining aggregates are not form, but are aggregates' means that the aggregates other than form, such as feeling and so on, are indeed not form, but they are aggregates. And 'excluding form and the aggregates, the remainder' refers to Nibbāna and concepts, which are free from the five aggregates. In subsequent instances of the word 'remainder' too, the same method applies.

Suddhakhandhavāro niṭṭhito.

The section on the pure aggregates is concluded.

40-44. Suddhakhandhamūlacakkavāre [V 0.0295] rūpaṃ khandhotiādīnaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva attho veditabboti.

40-44. In the section on the root cycle of the pure aggregates, the meaning of 'form is an aggregate,' and so on, should be understood in the way explained previously.

Suddhakhandhamūlacakkavāro niṭṭhito.

The section on the root cycle of the pure aggregates is concluded.

Paṇṇattiniddesavāravaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Exposition Section of the Designation Division.

2. Pavattivāravaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Section on Occurrence.

50-205. Idāni [M 0.0296] yassa rūpakkhandhotiādinā nayena pavattivāro āraddho. Kasmā panettha uddesavāro na vuttoti? Heṭṭhā dassitanayattā. Paṇṇattivārasmiñhi uddesavāre nayo dassito.
