Now, having gathered a portion, according to availability, of the wholesome and other phenomena previously taught in those same Root Pairs, the exposition of the Pairs of Formations, taught immediately after the Pairs of Truths, takes place. Here too, the three major sections, such as the Section on Designations, as well as the remaining subdivisions, such as the intermediate sections, should be understood in the same way as stated before. However, this is the distinction here: In the Section on Designations, instead of starting thus with the section on the analysis of terms as before, where phenomena such as the aggregates were enumerated with 'Form is the form aggregate; the eye is the eye base; the eye is the eye element; suffering is the truth of suffering,' it first analyzes and presents the three formations with the phrase 'In-breath and out-breath are the bodily formation.'

Tattha [P 0.0080] kāyassa saṅkhāro kāyasaṅkhāro. “Assāsapassāsā kāyikā, ete dhammā kāyappaṭibaddhā”ti (ma. ni. 1.463; saṃ. ni. 4.348 atthato samānaṃ) hi vacanato kāraṇabhūtassa karajakāyassa phalabhūto eva saṅkhāroti kāyasaṅkhāro. Aparo nayo – saṅkhariyatīti saṅkhāro. Kena saṅkhariyatīti? Kāyena. Ayañhi vāto viya bhastāya karajakāyena [V 0.0313] saṅkhariyatīti. Evampi kāyassa saṅkhāroti kāyasaṅkhāro. Kāyena kato assāsapassāsavātoti attho. “Pubbeva kho, āvuso visākha, vitakketvā vicāretvā pacchā vācaṃ bhindati, tasmā vitakkavicārā vacīsaṅkhāro”ti (ma. ni. 1.463; saṃ. ni. 4.348) vacanato pana saṅkharotīti saṅkhāro. Kiṃ saṅkharoti? Vaciṃ. Vaciyā saṅkhāroti vacīsaṅkhāro. Vacībhedasamuṭṭhāpakassa vitakkavicāradvayassetaṃ nāmaṃ. “Saññā ca vedanā ca cetasikā ete dhammā cittapaṭibaddhā”ti (ma. ni. 1.463; saṃ. ni. 4.348) vacanatoyeva pana tatiyapadepi saṅkhariyatīti saṅkhāro. Kena saṅkhariyati? Cittena. Karaṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ katvā cittassa saṅkhāroti cittasaṅkhāro. Sabbesampi cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ cetasikadhammānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vitakkavicārānaṃ pana vacīsaṅkhārabhāvena visuṃ gahitattā “ṭhapetvā vitakkavicāre”ti vuttaṃ.

Here, the formation of the body is the bodily formation. 'In-breaths and out-breaths are bodily; these phenomena are bound up with the body' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.463; Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.348, the meaning being the same)—thus, because they are a result of the causal physical body, this formation is indeed the bodily formation. Another explanation: it is called a formation because it is formed. By what is it formed? By the body. For this, like wind in a bellows, is formed by the physical body. Thus, it is also called the bodily formation, meaning the in-breath and out-breath wind is made by the body. 'First, friend Visākha, one thinks and reflects, and afterward one breaks into speech; therefore, thought and examination are the verbal formation' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.463; Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.348)—thus, because it forms, it is called a formation. What does it form? Speech. The formation of speech is the verbal formation. This is a name for the pair of thought and examination, which give rise to the breaking into speech. However, from the very statement 'Perception and feeling are mental; these phenomena are bound up with the mind' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.463; Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.348), in the third term too, it is called a formation because it is formed. By what is it formed? By the mind. Taking the genitive case in the sense of instrumentality, it is called the mental formation, the formation of the mind. This is a designation for all mental phenomena that arise from the mind. However, because thought and examination are separately taken as the verbal formation, it is said, 'excluding thought and examination.'

2-7. Idāni [M 0.0314] kāyo kāyasaṅkhāroti padasodhanavāro āraddho. Tassa anulomanaye tīṇi, paṭilomanaye tīṇīti cha yamakāni. Padasodhanamūlacakkavāre ekekasaṅkhāramūlakāni dve dve katvā anulomanaye cha, paṭilomanaye chāti dvādasa yamakāni. Suddhasaṅkhāravāre pana yathā suddhakhandhavārādīsu “rūpaṃ khandho, khandhā rūpaṃ; cakkhu āyatanaṃ, āyatanā cakkhū”tiādinā nayena yamakāni vuttāni. Evaṃ “kāyo saṅkhāro, saṅkhārā kāyo”ti avatvā “kāyasaṅkhāro vacīsaṅkhāro, vacīsaṅkhāro kāyasaṅkhāro”tiādinā nayena kāyasaṅkhāramūlakāni dve, vacīsaṅkhāramūlakaṃ ekanti anulome tīṇi, paṭilome tīṇīti sabbānipi suddhikavāre cha yamakāni vuttāni. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Suddhikaekekapadavasena atthābhāvato. Yathā hi khandhayamakādīsu rūpādivisiṭṭhānaṃ khandhānaṃ cakkhādivisiṭṭhānañca āyatanādīnaṃ adhippetattā “rūpaṃ khandho[P 0.0081], khandhā rūpaṃ, cakkhu āyatanaṃ, āyatanā cakkhū”ti suddhikaekekapadavasena attho atthi. Evamidha “kāyo saṅkhāro, saṅkhārā kāyo”ti natthi. Kāyasaṅkhāroti pana dvīhipi padehi ekova attho labbhati. Assāso vā passāso vāti suddhikaekekapadavasena atthābhāvato “kāyo saṅkhāro, saṅkhārā kāyo”ti na vuttaṃ. “Kāyo kāyasaṅkhāro”tiādi pana vattabbaṃ siyā. Tampi kāyavacīcittapadehi idha adhippetānaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ aggahitattā na yujjati. Suddhasaṅkhāravāro hesa. Padasodhane pana vināpi atthena vacanaṃ yujjatīti tattha so nayo gahitova. Idha pana kāyasaṅkhārassa vacīsaṅkhārādīhi, vacīsaṅkhārassa ca cittasaṅkhārādīhi, cittasaṅkhārassa ca kāyasaṅkhārādīhi, aññattā “kāyasaṅkhāro vacīsaṅkhāro, vacīsaṅkhāro, kāyasaṅkhāro”ti [V 0.0314] ekekasaṅkhāramūlakāni dve dve katvā cha yamakāni yujjanti. Tesu aggahitaggahaṇena tīṇeva labbhanti. Tasmā tāneva dassetuṃ anulomanaye tīṇi, paṭilomanaye tīṇīti cha yamakāni vuttāni. Suddhasaṅkhāramūlacakkavāro panettha na gahitoti. Evaṃ paṇṇattivārassa uddesavāro veditabbo.

2-7. Now the section on the analysis of terms, 'the body is the bodily formation,' is begun. In its forward order, there are three pairs; in the reverse order, three pairs—thus six pairs. In the root round of the analysis of terms, taking each formation as a root to make two pairs, there are six pairs in the forward order and six in the reverse—thus twelve pairs. However, in the pure formations section, as in the pure aggregates section and so forth, pairs are stated in the manner of 'form is an aggregate, aggregates are form; the eye is a base, bases are the eye,' and so on. Thus, instead of saying 'the body is a formation, formations are the body,' it is stated in the manner of 'bodily formation is verbal formation, verbal formation is bodily formation,' and so on. Here, with two pairs rooted in bodily formation and one in verbal formation, there are three in the forward order and three in the reverse—making six pairs in the pure section. Why is this? Because there is no meaning by way of single pure terms. For just as in the aggregate pairs and so on, because the aggregates specified as form, etc., and the bases specified as the eye, etc., are intended, there is meaning by way of single pure terms—'form is an aggregate, aggregates are form; the eye is a base, bases are the eye.' So here, 'the body is a formation, formations are the body' does not apply. But 'bodily formation' obtains a single meaning from both terms. Since there is no meaning by way of single pure terms—'in-breath or out-breath'—the statement 'the body is a formation, formations are the body' is not made. One might say, 'the body is bodily formation,' and so on. But that too is unsuitable, because the formations intended here by the terms body, speech, and mind are not grasped. This is indeed the pure formations section. In the analysis of terms, however, an expression is suitable even without meaning, so that method is indeed adopted there. Here, however, since bodily formation is distinct from verbal formation and so on, verbal formation from mental formation and so on, and mental formation from bodily formation and so on, six pairs are suitable, such as 'bodily formation is verbal formation, verbal formation is bodily formation,' by making two pairs for each formation as a root. Among these, by the principle of taking up the un-taken, only three are obtained. Therefore, to show just these, three pairs are stated in the forward order and three in the reverse—six pairs in total. The root round of pure formations, however, is not included here. Thus, the enumeration section of the Section on Designations should be understood.

8-18. Niddesavāre panassa anulome tāva yasmā na kāyādayova kāyasaṅkhārādīnaṃ nāmaṃ, tasmā noti paṭisedho kato. Paṭilome na kāyo na kāyasaṅkhāroti yo na kāyo so kāyasaṅkhāropi na hotīti pucchati. Kāyasaṅkhāro na kāyo kāyasaṅkhāroti [M 0.0315] kāyasaṅkhāro kāyo na hoti, kāyasaṅkhāroyeva panesoti attho. Avasesanti na kevalaṃ sesasaṅkhāradvayameva. Kāyasaṅkhāravinimuttaṃ pana sesaṃ sabbampi saṅkhatāsaṅkhatapaṇṇattibhedaṃ dhammajātaṃ neva kāyo, na kāyasaṅkhāroti iminā upāyena sabbavissajjanesu attho veditabboti.

8-18. However, in the Exposition Section, first, in the forward order, since 'body' and so on are not the names for 'bodily formations' and so on, therefore the negation 'no' is made. In the reverse order, 'not the body, not bodily formation' asks whether that which is not the body is also not a bodily formation. 'A bodily formation is not the body, it is a bodily formation' means that a bodily formation is not the body, but it is indeed a bodily formation. 'The rest' means not only the remaining pair of formations. But all the remaining phenomena, classified as conditioned, unconditioned, and concept, apart from bodily formation, are neither the body nor a bodily formation. By this method, the meaning in all the answers is to be understood.

Paṇṇattivāravaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Section on Concepts.

2. Pavattivāravaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Section on Occurrence.

19. Pavattivāre panettha paccuppannakāle puggalavārassa anulomanaye “yassa kāyasaṅkhāro uppajjati, tassa vacīsaṅkhāro uppajjatī”ti kāyasaṅkhāramūlakāni dve, vacīsaṅkhāramūlakaṃ [P 0.0082] ekanti tīṇeva yamakāni labbhanti; tāni gahitāneva. Tassa paṭilomanayepi okāsavārādīsupi eseva nayo. Evamettha sabbavāresu tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ yamakānaṃ vasena yamakagaṇanā veditabbā.

19. Here in the Section on Occurrence, in the present time, in the forward method of the Section on Individuals, regarding the question, 'For one for whom a bodily formation arises, for them does a verbal formation arise?', two couplets are rooted in bodily formation and one is rooted in verbal formation—thus only three couplets are obtained; these have been taken up. This same method applies in its reverse method and also in the sections beginning with the Section on Location. Thus, here in all sections, the enumeration of couplets should be understood as being by way of three couplets each.

Atthavinicchaye panettha idaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ – imasmiñhi saṅkhārayamake “assāsapassāsānaṃ uppādakkhaṇe vitakkavicārānaṃ uppādakkhaṇe”tiādivacanato paccuppannādikālabhedo pavattivasenāpi gahetabbo, na cutipaṭisandhivaseneva. “Dutiyajjhāne tatiyajjhāne tattha kāyasaṅkhāro [V 0.0315] uppajjatī”tiādivacanato ca jhānampi okāsavasena gahitanti veditabbaṃ. Evamettha yaṃ yaṃ labbhati, tassa tassa vasena atthavinicchayo veditabbo.

Here, in the determination of meaning, this is the characteristic feature: For in this Formations-Yamaka, based on statements such as 'at the moment of arising of in-breaths and out-breaths, at the moment of arising of applied and sustained thought,' the distinction of time, such as the present, should be understood also by way of occurrence, not only by way of death and rebirth-linking. And from statements such as 'in the second jhāna, in the third jhāna, a bodily formation arises there,' it should be understood that jhāna is also taken by way of location. Thus, here, the determination of meaning should be understood by way of whatever is obtained.

Tatridaṃ nayamukhaṃ – vinā vitakkavicārehīti dutiyatatiyajjhānavasena vuttaṃ. Tesanti tesaṃ dutiyatatiyajjhānasamaṅgīnaṃ. Kāmāvacarānanti kāmāvacare uppannasattānaṃ. Rūpāvacaradevānaṃ pana assāsapassāsā natthi. Arūpāvacarānaṃ rūpameva natthi. Vinā assāsapassāsehīti rūpārūpabhavesu nibbattasattānaṃ vitakkavicāruppattiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

Herein, this is the introductory method: 'Without applied and sustained thought'—this is said by way of the second and third jhānas. 'For them' means for those endowed with the second and third jhānas. 'For those of the sense-sphere' means for beings arisen in the sense-sphere. However, for the devas of the form-sphere, there are no in-breaths and out-breaths. For those of the formless-sphere, there is no form at all. 'Without in-breaths and out-breaths'—this is said with reference to the arising of applied and sustained thought for beings reborn in the form and formless existences.

21. Paṭhamajjhāne kāmāvacareti kāmāvacarabhūmiyaṃ uppanne paṭhamajjhāne. Aṅgamattavasena cettha paṭhamajjhānaṃ gahetabbaṃ, na appanāvaseneva. Anappanāpattepi hi savitakkasavicāracitte idaṃ saṅkhāradvayaṃ uppajjateva.

21. 'In the first jhāna, in the sense-sphere'—this refers to the first jhāna that has arisen in the sense-sphere plane. Here, the first jhāna should be understood by way of its factors only, not by way of absorption. For even in a mind with applied and sustained thought that has not attained absorption, this pair of formations certainly arises.

24. Cittassa [M 0.0316] bhaṅgakkhaṇeti idaṃ kāyasaṅkhārassa ekantacittasamuṭṭhānattā vuttaṃ. Uppajjamānameva hi cittaṃ rūpaṃ vā arūpaṃ vā samuṭṭhāpeti, na bhijjamānaṃ.

24. 'At the dissolution-moment of consciousness'—this is said because a bodily formation is exclusively mind-originated. For consciousness, while arising, originates form or formless phenomena, not while dissolving.

37. Suddhāvāsānaṃ dutiye citte vattamāneti paṭisandhito dutiye bhavaṅgacitte. Kāmañcetaṃ paṭisandhicittepi vattamāne tesaṃ tattha nuppajjittheva. Yāva pana abbokiṇṇaṃ vipākacittaṃ vattati, tāva nuppajjittheva nāmāti dassanatthametaṃ vuttaṃ. Yassa vā jhānassa vipākacittena te nibbattā, taṃ satasopi sahassasopi uppajjamānaṃ paṭhamacittameva. Vipākacittena pana visadisaṃ bhavanikantiyā āvajjanacittaṃ dutiyacittaṃ nāma. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

37. 'For the Pure Abodes, while the second consciousness is occurring'—this refers to the second life-continuum consciousness after rebirth-linking. Although, even while the rebirth-linking consciousness is occurring, it certainly does not arise for them there. However, this is stated to show that as long as the uninterrupted resultant consciousness continues, it certainly does not arise. Or, by the resultant consciousness of whichever jhāna they are reborn, that consciousness, even if arising a hundred or a thousand times, is only the first consciousness. However, the adverting consciousness, which is dissimilar to the resultant consciousness due to craving for existence, is called the 'second consciousness'. It should be understood that this is said with reference to that.

44. Pacchimacittasamaṅgīnanti [P 0.0083] sabbapacchimena appaṭisandhikacittena samaṅgībhūtānaṃ khīṇāsavānaṃ. Avitakkaavicāraṃ pacchimacittanti rūpāvacarānaṃ dutiyajjhānikādicuticittavasena, arūpāvacarānañca catutthajjhānikacuticittavasenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tesanti tesaṃ pacchimacittasamaṅgīādīnaṃ.

44. 'For those endowed with the final consciousness' means for the destroyers of cankers who are endowed with the very last, non-rebirth-linking consciousness. 'The final consciousness is without applied and sustained thought'—this is said by way of the death-consciousness of those in the form-sphere, beginning with the second jhāna, and by way of the fourth-jhāna death-consciousness of those in the formless-sphere. 'For them' means for those endowed with the final consciousness, and so on.

79. Yassa kāyasaṅkhāro nirujjhati, tassa cittasaṅkhāro nirujjhatīti ettha niyamato kāyasaṅkhārassa cittasaṅkhārena saddhiṃ ekakkhaṇe nirujjhanato āmantāti paṭivacanaṃ dinnaṃ. Na cittasaṅkhārassa [V 0.0316] kāyasaṅkhārena saddhiṃ. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Cittasaṅkhāro hi kāyasaṅkhārena vināpi uppajjati ca nirujjhati ca. Kāyasaṅkhāro pana cittasamuṭṭhāno assāsapassāsavāto. Cittasamuṭṭhānarūpañca cittassa uppādakkhaṇe uppajjitvā yāva aññāni soḷasacittāni uppajjanti, tāva tiṭṭhati. Tesaṃ soḷasannaṃ sabbapacchimena saddhiṃ nirujjhatīti yena cittena saddhiṃ uppajjati, tato paṭṭhāya sattarasamena saddhiṃ nirujjhati. Na kassaci cittassa uppādakkhaṇe vā ṭhitikkhaṇe vā nirujjhati, nāpi ṭhitikkhaṇe vā bhaṅgakkhaṇe vā uppajjati. Esā cittasamuṭṭhānarūpassa dhammatāti niyamato cittasaṅkhārena saddhiṃ ekakkhaṇe nirujjhanato āmantāti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana vibhaṅgappakaraṇassa sīhaḷaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ rūpaṃ sattarasamassa cittassa uppādakkhaṇe nirujjhatī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ imāya pāḷiyā virūjjhati. Aṭṭhakathāto ca pāḷiyeva balavatarāti pāḷiyaṃ vuttameva pamāṇaṃ.

79. Regarding 'For one for whom a bodily formation ceases, for them does a mental formation cease?', here the reply 'Yes' is given because, as a rule, the bodily formation ceases in the same moment as the mental formation. But not the mental formation with the bodily formation. What is the reason? Because a mental formation can arise and cease even without a bodily formation. However, the bodily formation, being the wind of in-breaths and out-breaths, is mind-originated. And mind-originated matter arises at the arising-moment of a consciousness and persists until sixteen other consciousnesses have arisen. It ceases together with the last of those sixteen. That is, it ceases together with the seventeenth consciousness, counting from the one with which it arose. It does not cease at the arising-moment or presence-moment of any consciousness, nor does it arise at the presence-moment or dissolution-moment. This is the nature of mind-originated matter. Thus, it is said 'Yes' because, as a rule, it ceases in the same moment as the mental formation. However, what is stated in the Sinhalese commentary to the Vibhaṅga—'mind-originated matter ceases at the arising-moment of the seventeenth consciousness'—contradicts this Pāli text. And since the Pāli is more authoritative than the commentary, only what is stated in the Pāli should be taken as the authority.

128. Yassa kāyasaṅkhāro uppajjati, tassa vacīsaṅkhāro nirujjhatīti ettha yasmā kāyasaṅkhāro cittassa uppādakkhaṇe uppajjati, na ca tasmiṃ khaṇe [M 0.0317] vitakkavicārā nirujjhanti, tasmā noti paṭisedho katoti. Iminā nayamukhena sabbattha atthavinicchayo veditabbo. Pariññāvāro pākatikoyevāti.

128. For whom the bodily formation arises, for him does the verbal formation cease? Here, because the bodily formation arises at the moment of the arising of consciousness, and at that moment applied and sustained thought do not cease, therefore the denial 'no' is made. By this method, the determination of meaning should be understood in all cases. The chapter on full understanding is the natural one.

Pavattivāravaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Section on the Round of Existence.

Saṅkhārayamakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Saṅkhāra-Yamaka is concluded.

7. Anusayayamakaṃ

7. The Yamaka on Latent Tendencies

Paricchedaparicchinnuddesavāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on Delimitation and Enumerated Delimitation

1. Idāni [P 0.0084] tesaññeva mūlayamake desitānaṃ kusalādidhammānaṃ labbhamānavasena ekadesaṃ saṅgaṇhitvā saṅkhārayamakānantaraṃ desitassa anusayayamakassa atthavaṇṇanā hoti. Tattha pāḷivavatthānaṃ tāva veditabbaṃ – imasmiñhi anusayayamake khandhayamakādīsu viya desanaṃ akatvā [V 0.0317] aññena nayena pāḷidesanā katā. Kathaṃ? Paṭhamaṃ tāva paricchedato, uddesato, uppattiṭṭhānatoti tīhākārehi anusaye gahāpetuṃ paricchedavāro, paricchinnuddesavāro, uppattiṭṭhānavāroti, tayo vārā desitā. Tato sattannaṃ mahāvārānaṃ vasena anusaye yojetvā yamakadesanā katā. Tattha sattānusayāti ayaṃ “satteva, na tato uddhaṃ, na heṭṭhā”ti gaṇanaparicchedena paricchinditvā anusayānaṃ desitattā paricchedavāro nāma. Kāmarāgānusayo…pe… avijjānusayoti ayaṃ paricchedavārena paricchinnānaṃ nāmamattaṃ uddisitvā “ime nāma te”ti desitattā paricchinnuddesavāro nāma. Kattha kāmarāgānusayo anuseti…pe… ettha avijjānusayo anusetīti ayaṃ “imesu nāma ṭhānesu ime anusayā anusenti”ti evaṃ tesaṃyeva uppattiṭṭhānassa desitattā uppattiṭṭhānavāro nāma.

1. Now, having gathered a portion of those same wholesome and other states taught in the Mūla-Yamaka according to their obtainability, the explanation of the meaning of the Anusaya-Yamaka, which was taught after the Saṅkhāra-Yamaka, is given. Herein, first, the arrangement of the Pāli text should be understood—for in this Anusaya-Yamaka, the teaching is not presented as in the Khandha-Yamaka and others, but is given in a different manner. How? First, to grasp the latent tendencies in three ways—by delimitation, by enumeration, and by the place of arising—the sections on delimitation, enumerated delimitation, and the place of arising are taught. Then, the teaching of the pairs is given by applying the latent tendencies according to the seven great sections. Herein, "seven latent tendencies" is called the section on delimitation because the latent tendencies are taught by delimiting them through enumeration, stating, "Seven only, neither more nor less." "The latent tendency of sensual desire… the latent tendency of ignorance" is called the section on enumerated delimitation because, after delimiting them in the section on delimitation, their mere names are enumerated, teaching, "These are their names." "Where does the latent tendency of sensual desire lie latent… where the latent tendency of ignorance lies latent" is called the section on the place of arising because it teaches, "In these places these latent tendencies lie latent," thus indicating the very places where these latent tendencies arise.

Yesaṃ pana sattannaṃ mahāvārānaṃ vasena anusaye yojetvā yamakadesanā katā, tesaṃ imāni nāmāni – anusayavāro, sānusayavāro, pajahanavāro, pariññāvāro, pahīnavāro, uppajjanavāro dhātuvāroti. Tesu paṭhamo anusayavāro. So anulomapaṭilomanayavasena duvidho hoti.

Now, for those seven great sections according to which the Yamaka teaching is given by applying the latent tendencies, these are their names: the section on latent tendencies, the section with latent tendencies, the section on abandoning, the section on full understanding, the section on what has been abandoned, the section on arising, and the section on elements. Among these, the first is the section on latent tendencies. It is twofold by way of the direct and reverse method.

Tattha [M 0.0318] anulomanaye “yassa anuseti, yattha anuseti, yassa yattha anusetī”ti puggalokāsatadubhayavasena tayo antaravārā honti. Tesu paṭhame puggalavāre “yassa kāmarāgānusayo anuseti, tassa paṭighānusayo anuseti; yassa vā pana paṭighānusayo anuseti, tassa kāmarāgānusayo anuseti; yassa kāmarāgānusayo anuseti, tassa mānānusayo, diṭṭhānusayo, vicikicchānusayo, bhavarāgānusayo, avijjānusayo anuseti. Yassa vā pana avijjānusayo anuseti, tassa kāmarāgānusayo [P 0.0085] anusetī”ti kāmarāgānusayamūlakāni cha yamakāni. Puna agahitaggahaṇavasena paṭighānusayamūlakāni pañca, mānānusayamūlakāni cattāri, diṭṭhānusayamūlakāni tīṇi, vicikicchānusayamūlakāni dve, bhavarāgānusayamūlakaṃ ekanti evaṃ sabbānipi ekamūlakāni ekavīsati. Puna “yassa kāmarāgānusayo ca paṭighānusayo ca anusentī”ti evaṃ āgatāni dukamūlakāni pañca, tikamūlakāni cattāri, catukkamūlakāni tīṇi, pañcakamūlakāni dve, chakkamūlakaṃ ekanti aparānipi pannarasa honti. Tāni purimehi ekavīsatiyā saddhiṃ chattiṃsāti puggalavāre chattiṃsa yamakāni. Tathā okāsavāre, tathā puggalokāsavāreti sabbānipi anulomanaye aṭṭhasataṃ yamakāni. Tathā paṭilomanayeti anusayavāre soḷasādhikāni dve yamakasatāni, tato diguṇā [V 0.0318] pucchā, tato diguṇā atthā ca veditabbā. Yathā cettha, evaṃ sānusayavāro, pajahanavāro, pariññāvāro, pahīnavāro, uppajjanavāroti imesampi pañcannaṃ vārānaṃ, ekekasmiṃ yamakagaṇanā; yamakadiguṇā pucchā, pucchādiguṇā ca atthā veditabbā. Ayaṃ panettha purimesu tīsu vāresu viseso. Okāsavāre “yattha tatthā”ti avatvā yato tatoti nissakkavacanena desanā katā. Sesaṃ tādisameva.

Here, in the direct method, there are three intermediate sections based on the individual, the location, and both: "in whom it lies latent, where it lies latent, in whom and where it lies latent." Among these, in the first section concerning individuals: "In whom the latent tendency of sensual desire lies latent, in him does the latent tendency of aversion lie latent; or in whom the latent tendency of aversion lies latent, in him does the latent tendency of sensual desire lie latent. In whom the latent tendency of sensual desire lies latent, in him do the latent tendencies of conceit, wrong view, doubt, craving for existence, and ignorance lie latent. Or in whom the latent tendency of ignorance lies latent, in him does the latent tendency of sensual desire lie latent." Thus, there are six pairs rooted in the latent tendency of sensual desire. Again, by taking what has not been taken, there are five pairs rooted in the latent tendency of aversion, four rooted in the latent tendency of conceit, three rooted in the latent tendency of wrong view, two rooted in the latent tendency of doubt, and one rooted in the latent tendency of craving for existence. In this way, all twenty-one pairs are rooted in a single root. Further, "in whom both the latent tendency of sensual desire and the latent tendency of aversion lie latent," and so on, there are five pairs rooted in two roots, four in three roots, three in four roots, two in five roots, and one in six roots. Thus, there are another fifteen pairs. Together with the previous twenty-one, there are thirty-six pairs in the individual section. Similarly, in the location section, and likewise in the individual-location section, there are altogether one hundred and eight pairs in the direct method. Similarly in the reverse method. Thus, in the section on latent tendencies, there are two hundred and sixteen pairs. From that, the questions are double, and the meanings should be understood as double the questions. As it is here, so also in these five sections—with latent tendencies, abandoning, full understanding, what has been abandoned, and arising—in each one the calculation of pairs is the same; the questions are double the pairs, and the meanings are to be understood as double the questions. Here, however, there is a distinction in the first three sections. In the location section, instead of saying "where, there," the teaching is given with the expression "from where, there," using an expression in the ablative case. The rest is just the same.

Yo panāyaṃ sabbapacchimo dhātuvāro nāma, so pucchāvāro, vissajjanāvāroti dvidhā ṭhito. Tassa pucchāvāre kāmadhātuyā cutassa kāmadhātuṃ upapajjantassāti vatvā “kāmadhātuṃ vā pana upapajjantassa kāmadhātuyā cutassā”ti na vuttaṃ. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Atthavisesābhāvato. Dvepi hi etā pucchā ekatthāyeva, tasmā ekekasmā yamakā ekekameva pucchaṃ pucchitvā sabbapucchāvasāne pucchānukkameneva “kāmadhātuyā [M 0.0319] cutassa kāmadhātuṃ upapajjantassa kassaci satta anusayā anusentī”tiādinā nayena vissajjanaṃ kataṃ.

Now, this last section, called the section on elements, stands as twofold: the question section and the answer section. In its question section, having stated "Of one who has deceased in the sense-sphere and is being reborn in the sense-sphere," it is not stated "or of one who is being reborn in the sense-sphere and has deceased in the sense-sphere." What is the reason? Because there is no difference in meaning. For both these questions have the same meaning. Therefore, from each pair, only one question is asked, and at the end of all the questions, according to the order of the questions, the answer is given in this way: "Of one who has deceased in the sense-sphere and is being reborn in the sense-sphere, do the seven latent tendencies lie latent in anyone?" and so on.

Tattha “kāmadhātuyā cutassa kāmadhātuṃ upapajjantassa, rūpadhātuṃ, arūpadhātuṃ, nakāmadhātuṃ, narūpadhātuṃ naarūpadhātuṃ[P 0.0086], upapajjantassā”ti cha suddhikapucchā; “nakāmadhātuṃ, naarūpadhātuṃ, narūpadhātuṃ; naarūpadhātuṃ, nakāmadhātuṃ, narūpadhātuṃ, upapajjantassā”ti tisso missakā pucchā cāti kāmadhātumūlakā nava anulomapucchā honti. Tathā rūpadhātumūlakā nava, arūpadhātumūlakā navāti sattavīsati anulomapucchā honti. Tathā nakāmadhātunarūpadhātunaarūpadhātumūlakā sattavīsati paṭilomapucchā. Puna “nakāmadhātuyā, naarūpadhātuyā, narūpadhātuyā, naarūpadhātuyā, nakāmadhātuyā, naarūpadhātuyā”ti sattavīsati dukamūlakā pucchāti sabbāpi sampiṇḍitā ekāsīti pucchā honti. Tāsaṃ vasenettha vissajjanaṃ katanti idaṃ dhātuvāre pāḷivavatthānaṃ. Evaṃ tāva sakalepi anusayayamake pāḷivavatthānametaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Herein, “for one who has passed away from the sensual realm and is being reborn in the sensual realm, the form realm, the formless realm, not the sensual realm, not the form realm, not the formless realm”—these are six pure questions. “For one being reborn not in the sensual realm, not in the formless realm, not in the form realm; not in the formless realm, not in the sensual realm, not in the form realm”—these are three mixed questions. Thus, there are nine direct questions rooted in the sensual realm. Similarly, there are nine rooted in the form realm and nine rooted in the formless realm, making twenty-seven direct questions. Likewise, there are twenty-seven reverse questions rooted in not the sensual realm, not the form realm, and not the formless realm. Again, from “not in the sensual realm, not in the formless realm, not in the form realm; not in the formless realm, not in the sensual realm, not in the form realm,” there are twenty-seven questions rooted in dyads. Altogether, when combined, there are eighty-one questions. The answers herein are given in accordance with them. This is the arrangement of the Pāli text in the section on the elements. Thus, this arrangement of the Pāli text in the entire Yamaka on Latent Tendencies should be understood.

Ādito paṭṭhāya panettha yaṃ yaṃ anuttānaṃ, tattha tattha ayaṃ vinicchayakathā – anusayāti kenaṭṭhena anusayā? Anusayanaṭṭhena. Ko esa anusayanaṭṭho nāmāti? Appahīnaṭṭho. Ete hi appahīnaṭṭhena tassa tassa santāne anusenti nāma, tasmā anusayāti vuccanti. Anusentīti anurūpaṃ kāraṇaṃ labhitvā uppajjantīti attho. Athāpi siyā – anusayanaṭṭho nāma appahīnākāro. Appahīnākāro ca uppajjatīti vattuṃ na yujjati, tasmā na anusayā uppajjantīti[V 0.0319]. Tatridaṃ paṭivacanaṃ – appahīnākāro anusayo, anusayoti pana appahīnaṭṭhena thāmagatakileso vuccati. So cittasampayutto sārammaṇo sappaccayaṭṭhena sahetuko ekantākusalo atītopi hoti anāgatopi paccuppannopi, tasmā uppajjatīti vattuṃ yujjati.

From the beginning, wherever anything herein is unclear, this is the definitive discussion: ‘Latent tendencies’—in what sense are they latent tendencies? In the sense of lying latent. What is this sense of lying latent? It is the sense of not being abandoned. For these, because they lie latent in the mental continuum of this or that being in the sense of not being abandoned, are called ‘latent tendencies.’ ‘They lie latent’ means they arise upon obtaining a suitable condition. Or it might be said: the sense of lying latent is the state of not being abandoned. And it is not fitting to say that the state of not being abandoned arises; therefore, latent tendencies do not arise. To this, the reply is: the state of not being abandoned is the latent tendency, but by ‘latent tendency’ is meant a defilement that has gained strength in the sense of not being abandoned. It is associated with consciousness, has an object, is with its condition and with its cause, is exclusively unwholesome, and can be past, future, or present. Therefore, it is fitting to say that it arises.

Tatridaṃ pamāṇaṃ – abhidhamme tāva kathāvatthusmiṃ (kathā. 554 ādayo) “anusayā abyākatā, anusayā ahetukā, anusayā cittavippayuttā”ti sabbe vādā paṭisedhitā. Paṭisambhidāmagge (paṭi. ma. 3.21) “paccuppanne kilese pajahatī”ti pucchaṃ katvā anusayānaṃ paccuppannabhāvassa atthitāya “thāmagatānusayaṃ pajahatī”ti [M 0.0320] vuttaṃ. Dhammasaṅgahe pana mohassa padabhājane “avijjānusayo avijjāpariyuṭṭhānaṃ avijjālaṅgī moho akusalamūlaṃ, ayaṃ tasmiṃ samaye moho hotī”ti [P 0.0087] (dha. sa. 390) akusalacittena saddhiṃ avijjānusayassa uppannabhāvo vutto. Imasmiṃyeva anusayayamake sattannaṃ mahāvārānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ uppajjanavāre “yassa kāmarāgānusayo uppajjati, tassa paṭighānusayo uppajjatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tasmā “anusentīti anurūpaṃ kāraṇaṃ labhitvā uppajjantī”ti yaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ iminā tantippamāṇena suvuttanti veditabbaṃ. Yampi “cittasampayutto sārammaṇo”tiādi vuttaṃ, tampi suvuttameva. Anusayo hi nāmesa parinipphanno cittasampayutto akusaladhammoti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ. Kāmarāgānusayotiādīsu kāmarāgo ca so appahīnaṭṭhena anusayo cāti kāmarāgānusayo. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

Herein, this is the authority: first, in the Abhidhamma, in the Kathāvatthu (Kv 554ff.), all the views that “latent tendencies are indeterminate,” “latent tendencies are rootless,” and “latent tendencies are dissociated from consciousness” are refuted. In the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. M. 3.21), after the question, “Does one abandon defilements in the present?” is posed, it is said, “one abandons a latent tendency that has gained strength,” because of the existence of latent tendencies in the present. In the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, in the exposition of terms for delusion, it is said: “The latent tendency of ignorance, the obsession of ignorance, the fetter of ignorance, delusion, the unwholesome root—this is the delusion at that time” (Dhs §390), thus stating the arising of the latent tendency of ignorance together with unwholesome consciousness. In this very Yamaka on Latent Tendencies, in one of the seven great sections, in the section on arising, it is said: “For whomever the latent tendency of sensual lust arises, for him the latent tendency of aversion arises,” and so on. Therefore, what was stated—“‘They lie latent’ means they arise upon obtaining a suitable condition”—should be understood as well-spoken in accordance with this scriptural authority. And what was stated—“associated with consciousness, has an object,” etc.—is also well-spoken. For it should be concluded here that a latent tendency is indeed a fully developed, unwholesome state associated with consciousness. In expressions such as ‘the latent tendency of sensual lust,’ it is sensual lust and it is a latent tendency in the sense of not being abandoned; hence, ‘the latent tendency of sensual lust.’ This same method applies to the remaining terms.

Paricchedaparicchinnuddesavāravaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Section of Delimitation and the Statement of the Delimited.

Uppattiṭṭhānavāravaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section of the Place of Arising.

2. Idāni tesaṃ uppattiṭṭhānaṃ pakāsetuṃ kattha kāmarāgānusayo anusetītiādimāha. Tattha kāmadhātuyā dvīsu vedanāsūti kāmāvacarabhūmiyaṃ sukhāya ca upekkhāya cāti dvīsu vedanāsu. Ettha kāmarāgānusayo anusetīti imāsu dvīsu vedanāsu uppajjati. So panesa akusalavedanāsu sahajātavasena ārammaṇavasena cāti dvīhākārehi anuseti. Akusalāya sukhāya [V 0.0320] vedanāya ceva upekkhāya vedanāya ca sahajātopi hutvā uppajjati. Tā vedanā ārammaṇaṃ katvāpi uppajjatīti attho. Avasesā pana kāmāvacarakusalavipākakiriyavedanā ārammaṇameva katvā uppajjati. Kāmadhātuyā dvīsu vedanāsu anusayamāno cesa tāhi vedanāhi sampayuttesu saññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇesupi anusetiyeva. Na hi sakkā vedanāsu anusayamānena taṃsampayuttehi saññādīhi saddhiṃ asahajātena vā bhavituṃ, taṃsampayutte vā saññādayo ārammaṇaṃ akatvā uppajjituṃ. Evaṃ santepi [M 0.0321] pana yasmā imā dve vedanāva sātasantasukhattā assādaṭṭhena kāmarāgānusayassa uppattiyā sesasampayuttadhammesu padhānā, tasmā “dvīsu vedanāsu ettha kāmarāgānusayo anusetī”ti vuttaṃ, oḷārikavasena hi bodhaneyye sukhaṃ bodhetunti.

2. Now, to show their place of arising, he begins with, “Where does the latent tendency of sensual lust lie latent?” Herein, “in the two feelings in the sensual realm” means in the sensual-sphere plane, in pleasant feeling and in neutral feeling. The latent tendency of sensual lust lies latent, that is, it arises, in these two feelings. It lies latent in two ways: by way of co-nascence and by way of object. It arises having co-arisen with unwholesome pleasant feeling and with unwholesome neutral feeling. It also arises by taking those feelings as its object—this is the meaning. But as for the remaining sensual-sphere feelings—wholesome, resultant, and functional—it arises only by taking them as its object. And while this latent tendency lies latent in the two feelings of the sensual realm, it also lies latent in the perception, formations, and consciousness associated with those feelings. For it is impossible for that which lies latent in feelings not to be co-nascent with the associated perception and so on, or to arise without taking the associated perception and so on as its object. Even so, because these two feelings alone, being agreeable, peaceful, and pleasant, are primary among the other associated states for the arising of the latent tendency of sensual lust in the sense of gratification, it is therefore said, “the latent tendency of sensual lust lies latent herein in two feelings.” For by means of the gross, what is to be understood is easily explained.

Nanu cesa ārammaṇavasena anusayamāno na kevalaṃ [P 0.0088] imāsu dvīsu vedanāsu ceva vedanāsampayuttadhammesu ca anuseti, iṭṭhesu pana rūpādīsupi anusetiyeva. Vuttampi cetaṃ vibhaṅgappakaraṇe (vibha. 816) “yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, ettha sattānaṃ kāmarāgānusayo anusetī”ti imasmimpi pakaraṇe anusayavārassa paṭilomanaye vuttaṃ. “Yattha kāmarāgānusayo nānuseti tattha diṭṭhānusayo nānusetīti dukkhāya vedanāya rūpadhātuyā arūpadhātuyā ettha kāmarāgānusayo nānuseti, no ca tattha diṭṭhānusayo nānuseti. Apariyāpanne ettha kāmarāgānusayo ca nānuseti, diṭṭhānusayo ca nānusetī”ti. Ettha hi dukkhavedanāya ceva rūpadhātuādīsu ca nānusetīti vuttattā sasampayuttadhammaṃ dukkhavedanaṃ saokāse rūpārūpāvacaradhamme nava ca, lokuttaradhamme ṭhapetvā avasesesu rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbesu anusetīti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ idha kasmā na vuttanti? Anoḷārikattā. Heṭṭhā vuttanayena hi vedanānaññeva oḷārikattā imesaṃ pana anoḷārikattā etesu rūpādīsu anusetīti na vuttaṃ, atthato pana labbhati. Tasmā etesupi kāmarāgānusayo anusetiyevāti veditabbo. Na hi satthā sabbaṃ sabbattha katheti. Bodhaneyyasattānaṃ pana vasena katthaci yaṃ labbhati, taṃ sabbaṃ katheti, katthaci na katheti. Tathā hi anena katthaci diṭṭhānusayo anusetīti pucchitvā “sabbasakkāyapariyāpannesu dhammesu ettha diṭṭhānusayo anusetī”ti yaṃ labbhati taṃ sabbaṃ kathitaṃ. Aparasmiṃ ṭhāne vissajjantena “rūpadhātuyā arūpadhātuyā ettha vicikicchānusayo ca mānānusayo ca diṭṭhānusayo ca anusenti, kāmadhātuyā dvīsu vedanāsu ettha vicikicchānusayo ca kāmarāgānusayo ca mānānusayo ca diṭṭhānusayo ca anusenti, dukkhāya [V 0.0321] vedanāya ettha vicikicchānusayo ca paṭighānusayo ca diṭṭhānusayo ca avijjānusayo [M 0.0322] ca anusentī”ti yaṃ labbhati taṃ sabbaṃ akathetvā rūpadhātuarūpadhātūhi saddhiṃ tisso vedanāva kathitā. Vedanāsampayuttā pana arūpadhammā, sabbañca rūpaṃ na [P 0.0089] kathitaṃ. Kiñcāpi na kathitaṃ, diṭṭhānusayo panettha anusetiyeva. Evameva kiñcāpi idha rūpādiiṭṭhārammaṇaṃ na kathitaṃ, kāmarāgānusayo panettha anusetiyevāti. Evaṃ tāva kāmarāgānusayassa anusayanaṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Does not this latent tendency, lying latent by way of the object, lie latent not only in these two feelings and the states associated with feeling, but also in agreeable forms and so on? And this has been stated in the Vibhaṅga (Vibh. 816): 'Whatever in the world is pleasing and agreeable, here the latent tendency of sensual lust lies latent in beings.' Moreover, in the reverse method of the section on latent tendencies in this same treatise, it is said: 'Is it that where the latent tendency of sensual lust does not lie latent, the latent tendency of wrong view does not lie latent there? In painful feeling, the form realm, and the formless realm, the latent tendency of sensual lust does not lie latent, but the latent tendency of wrong view does lie latent there. In the unincluded, neither the latent tendency of sensual lust nor the latent tendency of wrong view lies latent.' Here, since it is said that it does not lie latent in painful feeling and in the form realm, etc., it is implied that, having excluded painful feeling with its associated states, the nine form-sphere and formless-sphere states with their bases, and the supramundane states, it does lie latent in the remaining forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles. So why is this not mentioned here? Because of their non-grossness. For by the method explained previously, due to the grossness of feelings alone, it was not stated that it lies latent in these forms, etc., which are non-gross; but the meaning is obtained. Therefore, it should be understood that the latent tendency of sensual lust indeed lies latent in these as well. For the Teacher does not explain everything in every context. Rather, according to the beings to be awakened, in some places he explains everything that is relevant, and in other places he does not. For example, in one place, when asked where the latent tendency of wrong view lies latent, he explains fully: 'It lies latent in all states encompassed by identity view.' But in another place, when answering, he says: 'In the form realm and the formless realm, the latent tendencies of doubt, conceit, and wrong view lie latent. In the sensual realm, in the two feelings, the latent tendencies of doubt, sensual lust, conceit, and wrong view lie latent. In painful feeling, the latent tendencies of doubt, aversion, wrong view, and ignorance lie latent.' Here, he mentions only the three feelings along with the form and formless realms, but does not mention the immaterial states associated with feeling or all material form. Although these are not mentioned, the latent tendency of wrong view still lies latent there. Similarly, although agreeable objects such as form are not mentioned here, the latent tendency of sensual lust still lies latent in them. Thus, the sphere of the latent tendency of sensual lust should be understood.

Paṭighānusayassa pana “dukkhāya vedanāyā”ti vacanato dve domanassavedanā kāyaviññāṇasampayuttā dukkhavedanāti tisso vedanā anusayanaṭṭhānaṃ. So panesa domanassavedanāsu sahajātavasena ārammaṇavasena cāti dvīhākārehi anuseti. Avasesadukkhavedanāya pana ārammaṇavaseneva anuseti. Tāsu vedanāsu anusayamāno cesa tāhi sampayuttesu saññākkhandhādīsupi anusetiyeva. Yāya hi vedanāya esa sahajāto, taṃsampayuttehi saññādīhipi sahajātova. Yā ca vedanā ārammaṇaṃ karoti, tāhi sampayutte saññādayopi karotiyeva. Evaṃ santepi pana yasmā dukkhavedanāva asātadukkhavedayitattā nirassādaṭṭhena paṭighānusayassa uppattiyā sesasampayuttadhammesu adhikā; tasmā “dukkhāya vedanāya ettha paṭighānusayo anusetī”ti vuttaṃ, oḷārikavasena hi bodhaneyye sukhaṃ bodhetunti.

Regarding the latent tendency of aversion, the phrase 'in painful feeling' indicates that two feelings of displeasure and the painful feeling associated with body-consciousness—making three feelings—serve as the sphere for the latent tendency. This latent tendency lies latent in feelings of displeasure in two ways: by co-arising and by taking as an object. In the remaining painful feeling, however, it lies latent only by taking as an object. When it lies latent in those feelings, it also lies latent in the associated perception aggregate and other factors. For with whatever feeling it co-arises, it also co-arises with the associated perceptions, etc. And whatever feeling it takes as its object, it also takes the associated perceptions, etc., as its object. Even so, because painful feeling—being an unpleasant, painful experience and devoid of savor—is more significant than the other associated phenomena for the arising of the latent tendency of aversion, it is therefore said, 'Here, the latent tendency of aversion lies latent in painful feeling.' For by means of what is gross, those who are to be taught are easily instructed.

Nanu cesa ārammaṇavasena anusayamāno na kevalaṃ dukkhavedanāya ceva taṃsampayuttadhammesu ca anuseti, aniṭṭhesu pana rūpādīsupi anusetiyeva? Vuttampi cetaṃ vibhaṅgappakaraṇe (vibha. 816) “yaṃ loke appiyarūpaṃ asātarūpaṃ, ettha sattānaṃ paṭighānusayo anusetī”ti imasmimpi pakaraṇe anusayavārassa paṭilomanaye vuttaṃ – “kāmadhātuyā dvīsu vedanāsu ettha paṭighānusayo nānuseti, no ca tattha kāmarāgānusayo nānuseti. Rūpadhātuyā arūpadhātuyā apariyāpanne ettha paṭighānusayo ca nānuseti, kāmarāgānusayo ca nānusetī”ti. Ettha hi dvīsu kāmāvacaravedanāsu ceva rūpadhātuādīsu ca nānusetīti vuttattā sasampayuttadhammā dve vedanā saokāse rūpārūpāvacaradhamme nava ca, lokuttaradhamme ṭhapetvā [P 0.0090] avasesesu rūpādīsu anusetīti vuttaṃ hoti[M 0.0323]. Taṃ idha kasmā na vuttanti? Anoḷārikattā. Heṭṭhā vuttanayena hi dukkhavedanāya eva oḷārikattā imesaṃ pana anoḷārikattā etesu rūpādīsu anusetīti na vuttaṃ. Atthato pana labbhati, tasmā etesupi paṭighānusayo anusetiyevāti veditabbo.

Does not this latent tendency, lying latent by way of its object, lie latent not only in painful feeling and the states associated with it, but also in disagreeable forms and so on? Indeed, this is stated in the Vibhaṅga (Vibh. 816): 'Whatever in the world is unpleasing and disagreeable, here the latent tendency of aversion lies latent in beings.' Moreover, in this very treatise, in the reverse method of the section on latent tendencies, it is said: 'In the two feelings in the sensual realm, the latent tendency of aversion does not lie latent, but the latent tendency of sensual lust does lie latent there. In the form realm, the formless realm, and the unincluded, neither the latent tendency of aversion nor the latent tendency of sensual lust lies latent.' Here, since it is said that it does not lie latent in the two sense-sphere feelings and in the form realm and so on, it is implied that, having excluded the two feelings with their associated states, the nine form-sphere and formless-sphere states with their bases, and the supramundane states, it does lie latent in the remaining forms, etc. So why is it not stated here? Because of their non-grossness. For by the method stated previously, due to the grossness of painful feeling alone, it was not stated that the latent tendency lies latent in these forms, etc., which are non-gross. But the meaning is obtained; therefore, it should be known that the latent tendency of aversion does indeed lie latent in these as well.

Kiṃ [V 0.0322] pana itarā dve vedanā iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ vā paṭighassa ārammaṇaṃ na hontīti? No na honti. Parihīnajjhānassa vippaṭisāravasena sasampayuttadhammā tā vedanā ārabbha domanassaṃ uppajjati. Iṭṭhārammaṇassa ca paṭiladdhassa vipariṇāmaṃ vā appaṭiladdhassa appaṭilābhaṃ vā samanussaratopi domanassaṃ uppajjati. Domanassamattameva pana taṃ hoti, na paṭighānusayo. Paṭighānusayo hi aniṭṭhārammaṇe paṭihaññanavasena uppanno thāmagato kileso, tasmā ettha domanassena saddhiṃ paṭigho uppannopi attano paṭighakiccaṃ akaraṇabhāvena eva paṭighānusayo na hoti abbohārikattaṃ gacchati. Yathā hi pāṇātipātacetanāya saddhiṃ uppannopi byāpādo manokammaṃ nāma na hoti abbohārikattaṃ gacchati, evaṃ paṭighānusayo na hoti, abbohārikattaṃ gacchati. Vuttampi cetaṃ ekaccaṃ iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ nekkhammasitampi vā domanassaṃ sandhāya “yaṃ evarūpaṃ domanassaṃ paṭighaṃ tena pajahati na tattha paṭighānusayo anusetī”ti (ma. ni. 1.465). Evaṃ paṭighānusayassa anusayanaṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

But do the other two feelings not become an object for aversion? It is not that they do not. For one whose jhāna has declined, sorrow arises by way of regret concerning those feelings and their associated states. Also, when one reflects on the change of a desirable object that was obtained or the non-obtainment of what was not obtained, sorrow arises. However, this is merely sorrow, not the latent tendency to aversion. The latent tendency to aversion is a defilement that has become firm, arisen by way of being repelled by an undesirable object. Therefore, even if aversion arises here along with sorrow, because it does not perform its function of aversion, it does not become the latent tendency to aversion; it becomes inoperative. Just as ill-will, even if it arises along with the intention to kill, is not called mental action and becomes inoperative, so too it does not become the latent tendency to aversion; it becomes inoperative. And this has been stated with reference to sorrow concerning a certain desirable object or even sorrow based on renunciation: 'One abandons that aversion, which is sorrow of such a kind, by means of that [path], but the latent tendency to aversion does not lie latent there' (cf. MN 1.465). Thus, the place where the latent tendency to aversion lies latent should be understood.

Mānānusayassa pana “kāmadhātuyā dvīsu vedanāsū”tiādivacanato dve kāmāvacaravedanā rūpārūpadhātuyo cāti idaṃ tividhaṃ anusayanaṭṭhānaṃ. Tassa akusalāsu vedanāsu kāmarāgānusayassa viya sahajātānusayatā veditabbā. Sasampayuttadhammāsu pana sabbāsupi kāmāvacarāsu sukhaadukkhamasukhavedanāsu rūpārūpadhātūsu ca ārammaṇavaseneva anuseti. Anusayavārassa pana paṭilomanaye “dukkhāya vedanāya apariyāpanne ettha kāmarāgānusayo ca nānuseti, mānānusayo ca nānusetī”ti vuttattā ṭhapetvā dukkhavedanañceva navavidhaṃ lokuttaradhammañca sesarūpārūpadhammesupi [P 0.0091] ayaṃ anusetiyevāti. Evaṃ mānānusayassa anusayanaṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Regarding the latent tendency to conceit, from the statement 'in the sensuous realm, in two feelings,' etc., it is understood that these two sensuous-sphere feelings and the form and formless spheres constitute the threefold basis for its lying latent. Its co-arising as a latent tendency should be understood to occur in unwholesome feelings, like that of the latent tendency to sensual desire. However, in its associated states, and in all sensuous-sphere pleasant and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings, and in the form and formless spheres, it lies latent only by way of the object. But in the reverse order of the Anusaya section, because it is said: 'In that which is not comprised in painful feeling, here the latent tendency to sensual desire does not lie latent, nor does the latent tendency to conceit,' therefore, excluding painful feeling and the nine kinds of supramundane phenomena, this [tendency] also lies latent in the remaining phenomena of the form and formless spheres. Thus, the basis for the latent tendency to conceit should be understood.

Diṭṭhānusayavicikicchānusayā [M 0.0324] pana kevalaṃ lokuttaradhammesveva nānusenti. Tebhūmakesu pana sabbesupi anusentiyeva. Tena vuttaṃ – “sabbasakkāyapariyāpannesu dhammesu ettha diṭṭhānusayo anuseti, ettha vicikicchānusayo anusetī”ti. Tattha sabbasakkāyapariyāpannesūti saṃsāravaṭṭanissitaṭṭhena sakkāyapariyāpannesu sabbadhammesūti attho. Tattha panete pañcasu cittuppādesu sahajātānusayanavasena anusenti. Te vā pana pañca cittuppāde aññe vā tebhūmakadhamme ārabbha pavattikāle ārammaṇānusayanavasena anusentīti. Evaṃ diṭṭhānusayavicikicchānusayānaṃ anusayanaṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

The latent tendencies of wrong view and doubt, however, do not lie latent in supramundane phenomena at all. But in all phenomena of the three planes, they certainly do lie latent. Therefore it is said: 'Here, the latent tendency of wrong view lies latent in all phenomena comprised in the existing body; here, the latent tendency of doubt lies latent.' Here, 'in all phenomena comprised in the existing body' means in all phenomena comprised therein in the sense of being dependent on the cycle of existence. Here, these lie latent in five types of consciousness by way of co-arising as a latent tendency. Or, by way of being an object-based latent tendency, they lie latent at the time of their occurrence in relation to those five types of consciousness or other phenomena of the three planes. Thus, the basis for the latent tendencies of wrong view and doubt should be understood.

Bhavarāgānusayo [V 0.0323] pana kiñcāpi diṭṭhivippayuttesu catūsu cittesu uppajjanato sahajātānusayanavasena “kāmadhātuyā dvīsu vedanāsu anusetī”ti vattabbo bhaveyya. Kāmadhātuyaṃ panesa dvīhi vedanāhi saddhiṃ uppajjamānopi rūpārūpāvacaradhammameva paṭilabhati. Kāmadhātuyā pariyāpannaṃ ekadhammampi ārammaṇaṃ na karoti, tasmā ārammaṇānusayanavasena niyamaṃ katvā “rūpadhātuyā arūpadhātuyā ettha bhavarāgānusayo anusetī”ti vuttaṃ. Apica rāgo nāmesa kāmarāgabhavarāgavasena duvidho. Tattha kāmarāgo kāmadhātuyā dvīsu vedanāsu anusetīti vutto. Sace pana bhavarāgopi kāmarāgo viya evaṃ vucceyya, kāmarāgena saddhiṃ desanā saṃkiṇṇā viya bhaveyyāti rāgakilesaṃ dvidhā bhinditvā kāmarāgato bhavarāgassa visesadassanatthampi evaṃ desanā katāti. Evaṃ bhavarāgānusayassa anusayanaṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

However, although the latent tendency to craving for existence arises in the four consciousnesses dissociated from views, it could be said that it lies latent in two feelings in the sensuous realm by way of co-arising as a latent tendency. But even though it arises together with two feelings in the sensuous realm, it only takes form-sphere and formless-sphere phenomena as its object. It does not make even a single phenomenon comprised in the sensuous realm its object. Therefore, having made a restriction by way of the object-based latent tendency, it is said: 'Here, the latent tendency to craving for existence lies latent in the form realm and the formless realm.' Furthermore, craving is of two kinds: sensual craving and craving for existence. Herein, sensual craving is said to lie latent in two feelings in the sensuous realm. But if craving for existence were also to be stated in this way, like sensual craving, the teaching would seem to be confused with that of sensual craving. Thus, in order to show the distinction of craving for existence from sensual craving by dividing the defilement of craving into two, the teaching has been given in this way. In this way, the basis for the latent tendency to craving for existence should be understood.

Avijjānusayo pana sabbesupi tebhūmakadhammesu anuseti. Tena vuttaṃ “sabbasakkāyapariyāpannesu dhammesu ettha avijjānusayo anusetī”ti. Tassa dvādasasu cittuppādesu sahajātānusayatā veditabbā. Ārammaṇakaraṇavasena pana na kiñci tebhūmakadhammaṃ ārabbha na pavattatīti. Evaṃ avijjānusayassa anusayanaṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ [P 0.0092] tāva paricchedavāraparicchinnuddesavārauppattiṭṭhānavāresu vinicchayakathā.

The latent tendency of ignorance, however, lies latent in all phenomena of the three planes. Therefore it is said: 'Here, the latent tendency of ignorance lies latent in all phenomena comprised in the existing body.' Its co-arising as a latent tendency should be understood to occur in the twelve types of unwholesome consciousness. However, by way of taking an object, there is no phenomenon of the three planes in relation to which it does not occur. Thus, the basis for the latent tendency of ignorance should be understood. This, then, is the definitive discourse on the Section on Delimitation, the Section on the Summary of the Delimited, and the Section on the Basis of Arising.

Uppattiṭṭhānavāravaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Section on the Basis of Arising.

Mahāvāro

The Great Section

1. Anusayavāravaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Section on Latent Tendencies

3. Sattannaṃ [M 0.0325] pana mahāvārānaṃ paṭhame anusayavāre yassa kāmarāgānusayo anuseti, tassa paṭighānusayo anusetīti ettha yadetaṃ “āmantā”ti paṭivacanaṃ dinnaṃ, taṃ duddinnaṃ viya khāyati. Kasmā? Kāmarāgapaṭighānaṃ ekakkhaṇe anuppattito. Yathā hi “yassa manāyatanaṃ uppajjati, tassa dhammāyatanaṃ uppajjatīti ‘āmantā’, assāsapassāsānaṃ uppādakkhaṇe tesaṃ kāyasaṅkhāro [V 0.0324] ca uppajjati, vacīsaṅkhāro ca uppajjatī”tiādīsu manāyatanadhammāyatanāni kāyasaṅkhāravacīsaṅkhārā ca ekakkhaṇe uppajjanti, na tathā kāmarāgapaṭighā. Kāmarāgo hi aṭṭhasu lobhasahagatacittuppādesu uppajjati. Paṭigho dvīsu domanassasahagatesūti, natthi nesaṃ ekakkhaṇe uppatti; tasmā ettha ‘no’ti paṭisedho kattabbo siyā. Taṃ akatvā pana ‘āmantā’ti paṭivacanassa dinnattā heṭṭhāyamakesu viya ettha khaṇapaccuppannavasena vattamānavohāraṃ aggahetvā aññathā gahetabbo.

3. However, in the first section, the Anusaya Section, of the seven great sections, regarding the question, 'For whom does the latent tendency for sensual desire lie dormant, for him does the latent tendency for aversion lie dormant?', the reply 'Yes' that was given seems to have been ill-given. Why? Because sensual desire and aversion do not arise in the same moment. For just as in cases such as, 'For whom the mind-base arises, for him the mental-object base arises? Yes,' and 'At the moment of the arising of in-breaths and out-breaths, both the bodily formation and the verbal formation arise,' the mind-base and mental-object base, and the bodily and verbal formations, arise in the same moment. But this is not so with sensual desire and aversion. For sensual desire arises in the eight consciousnesses accompanied by greed, and aversion in the two accompanied by displeasure; there is no arising of them in the same moment. Therefore, a denial, 'No,' should have been made here. But since the reply 'Yes' was given without doing so, the present usage here should not be taken as referring to a momentary presence, as in the preceding Yamakas; instead, it should be understood differently.

Kathaṃ? Appahīnavasena. Appahīnatañhi sandhāya ayaṃ “anusetī”ti vattamānavohāro vutto, na khaṇapaccuppannataṃ. Yasmā ca appahīnataṃ sandhāya vutto, tasmā “yassa kāmarāgānusayo anuseti, tassa paṭighānusayo anusetī”ti pucchāya yassa kāmarāgānusayo appahīno, na anuppattidhammataṃ āpādito, tassa paṭighānusayopi appahīnoti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Yasmā ca tesu yasseko appahīno, tassa itaropi appahīnova hoti, tasmā “āmantā”ti vuttaṃ. Yadi evaṃ, yaṃ upari uppajjanavāre ‘yassa kāmarāgānusayo uppajjati, tassa paṭighānusayo uppajjatī’ti pucchitvā ‘āmantā’ti vuttaṃ; tattha kathaṃ attho gahetabboti? Tatthāpi appahīnavaseneva uppattipaccaye sati uppattiyā anivāritavasena vā. Yathā hi cittakammādīni ārabhitvā apariniṭṭhitakammantā cittakārādayo tesaṃ kammantānaṃ akaraṇakkhaṇepi mittasuhajjādīhi diṭṭhadiṭṭhaṭṭhāne “imesu divasesu kiṃ karothā”ti vuttā, “cittakammaṃ karoma, kaṭṭhakammaṃ karomā”ti vadanti. Te kiñcāpi tasmiṃ khaṇe na karonti avicchinnakammantattā pana katakhaṇañca kattabbakhaṇañca upādāya [P 0.0093] karontiyeva nāma honti. Evameva yamhi santāne anusayā appahīnā, yamhi vā pana nesaṃ santāne uppattipaccaye sati uppatti anivāritā, tattha anuppajjanakkhaṇepi [M 0.0326] uppannapubbañceva kālantare uppajjanakañca upādāya yassa kāmarāgānusayo uppajjati, tassa paṭighānusayo uppajjatiyeva nāmāti evamattho veditabbo. Ito paresupi evarūpesu vissajjanesu eseva nayo. No ca tassāti idaṃ anāgāmissa kāmarāgabyāpādānaṃ anavasesato pahīnattā vuttaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ puggalānanti puthujjanasotāpannasakadāgāmīnaṃ. Dvinnaṃ puggalānanti sotāpannasakadāgāmīnaṃ. Paratopi evarūpesu ṭhānesu eseva nayo.

How? By way of non-abandonment. For this present usage 'lies dormant' is stated with reference to non-abandonment, not to momentary presence. And because it is stated with reference to non-abandonment, therefore, in the question 'For whom does the latent tendency for sensual desire lie dormant, for him does the latent tendency for aversion lie dormant?', the meaning should be understood thus: for whom the latent tendency for sensual desire is not abandoned, not brought to a state of non-arising, for him the latent tendency for aversion is also not abandoned. And because for such a one, if one is not abandoned, the other is also not abandoned, therefore 'Yes' is said. If so, then regarding what was said above in the section on arising, when it was asked 'For whom does the latent tendency for sensual desire arise, for him does the latent tendency for aversion arise?' and 'Yes' was said, how should the meaning be understood there? There too, it is by way of non-abandonment, or by way of the non-prevention of arising when the conditions for arising are present. For just as painters and others, having undertaken painting and other crafts, whose work is not yet finished, even at a moment when they are not doing that work, when asked by friends and companions wherever they are seen, 'What are you doing these days?', reply, 'We are doing painting work, we are doing carpentry work.' Although they are not doing it at that moment, because their work is uninterrupted, by taking into account the moments when they have done it and the moments when they will do it, they are indeed said to be doing it. Just so, in a continuum in which the latent tendencies are not abandoned, or in which, when the conditions for their arising are present, their arising is not prevented, even at a moment when they are not arising, by taking into account what has arisen previously and what will arise at another time, it should be understood that for whom the latent tendency for sensual desire arises, for him the latent tendency for aversion indeed arises. In similar answers beyond this, the same method applies. 'But not for him'—this is said because for the non-returner, sensual desire and ill-will have been completely abandoned without remainder. 'Of three persons'—meaning the ordinary person, the stream-enterer, and the once-returner. 'Of two persons'—meaning the stream-enterer and the once-returner. In similar cases beyond this, the same method applies.

14. Okāsavārassa paṭhamadutiyapucchāsu yasmā kāmarāgānusayo kāmadhātuyā dvīsu vedanāsu [V 0.0325] anuseti, paṭighānusayo dukkhavedanāya; tasmā ‘no’ti paṭisedho kato. Tatiyapucchāyaṃ ubhinnampi kāmadhātuyā dvīsu vedanāsu anusayanato ‘āmantā’ti paṭivacanaṃ dinnaṃ. Rūpadhātuarūpadhātuyā pana mānānusayassa kāmarāgānusayena saddhiṃ asādhāraṇaṃ uppattiṭṭhānaṃ. Tasmā no ca tattha kāmarāgānusayoti vuttaṃ. Iminā nayena sabbesaṃ uppattiṭṭhānavāraṃ oloketvā sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇaṃ uppattiṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

14. In the first and second questions of the Okāsa Section, because the latent tendency for sensual desire lies dormant in two feelings in the sense-sphere realm, and the latent tendency for aversion in painful feeling, the denial 'No' is made. In the third question, since both lie dormant in two feelings in the sense-sphere realm, the reply 'Yes' is given. However, in the form realm and the formless realm, the basis of arising for the latent tendency for conceit is not shared with the latent tendency for sensual desire. Therefore it is said: 'And the latent tendency for sensual desire is not there.' By this method, having examined the section on the basis of arising for all latent tendencies, one should understand the shared and unshared bases of arising.

20. Dukamūlakapucchāyaṃ yasmā kāmarāgapaṭighānusayā nāpi ekasmiṃ ṭhāne uppajjanti, na ekaṃ dhammaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karonti, tasmā natthīti paṭikkhepo kato. Ayañhettha adhippāyo. Yasmiṃ ime dve anusayā anusayeyyuṃ, taṃ ṭhānameva natthi. Tasmā “kattha mānānusayo anusetī”ti ayaṃ pucchā apucchāyevāti. Aññesupi evarūpesu eseva nayo.

20. In the question of the Dyad Root, since the latent tendencies for sensual desire and aversion neither arise in one and the same basis, nor take a single phenomenon as their object, the denial 'there is none' is made. This is the intended meaning here. There is no basis whatsoever where these two latent tendencies could lie dormant. Therefore, the question 'Where does the latent tendency for conceit lie dormant?' is indeed a non-question. The same principle applies in other similar cases.

27. Puggalokāsavāre catunnanti puthujjanasotāpannasakadāgāmianāgāmīnaṃ.

27. In the Section on Individuals and Bases, 'of four' means of the ordinary person, the stream-enterer, the once-returner, and the non-returner.

36. Paṭilomanaye yassa kāmarāgānusayo nānusetīti ayaṃ pucchā anāgāmiṃ gahetvā pucchati.

36. In the reverse method, the question, 'For whom does the latent tendency for sensual desire not lie dormant?', is asked with reference to the non-returner.

56. Dvinnaṃ [M 0.0327] puggalānaṃ sabbattha kāmarāgānusayo [P 0.0094] nānusetīti anāgāmiarahantānaṃ. Kāmadhātuyā tīsu vedanāsūti ca vedanāggahaṇena vedanāsampayuttakānampi tesaṃ vatthārammaṇānampīti sabbesampi kāmāvacaradhammānaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ anusayavāre vinicchayakathā.

56. For two individuals, the latent tendency for sensual desire does not lie dormant anywhere—namely, for the non-returner and the arahant. And regarding 'in the three feelings in the sense-sphere realm,' by the term 'feelings,' it should be understood that this includes all sense-sphere phenomena: those associated with feelings, as well as their bases and objects. This is the analytical discussion on the Anusaya Section.

Anusayavāravaṇṇanā.

Commentary on the Section on Latent Tendencies.

2. Sānusayavāravaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Section on (States) with Latent Tendencies.

66-131. Sānusayavāre pana yo kāmarāgānusayena sānusayoti yathā ekantarikajarādirogena ābādhiko yāva tamhā rogā na muccati, tāva tassa rogassa anuppattikkhaṇepi [V 0.0326] sarogoyeva nāma hoti. Evaṃ sasaṃkilesassa vaṭṭagāmisattassa yāva ariyamaggena anusayā samugghātaṃ na gacchanti, tāva tesaṃ anusayānaṃ anuppattikkhaṇepi sānusayoyeva nāma hoti. Evarūpaṃ sānusayataṃ sandhāya ‘āmantā’ti vuttaṃ. Sesamettha anusayavārasadisameva.

In the section on being with underlying tendencies, one who has the underlying tendency of sensual desire is with an underlying tendency. Just as a person afflicted by an intermittent disease like a fever is considered diseased until freed from that disease—even at a moment when the disease is not manifest—so too, for a being bound to the cycle of existence and still tainted by defilements, as long as the underlying tendencies are not uprooted by the noble path, they are called 'one with underlying tendencies'—even at a moment when these are not manifest. It is with reference to such a state of being with underlying tendencies that 'yes' was said. The rest here is similar to the section on underlying tendencies.

Okāsavāre pana “rūpadhātuyā arūpadhātuyā ettha mānānusayena sānusayo”ti vutte tāsu dhātūsu puggalassa sānusayatā paññāyeyya, anusayassa uppattiṭṭhānaṃ na paññāyeyya. Anusayassa ca uppattiṭṭhānadassanatthaṃ ayaṃ vāro āraddho, tasmā tato mānānusayena sānusayoti vuttaṃ. Evañhi sati tato dhātudvayato uppannena mānānusayena sānusayoti anusayassa uppattiṭṭhānaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Imassa pana pañhassa atthe avutte ādipañhassa attho pākaṭo na hotīti paṭhamaṃ na vutto, tasmā so evaṃ veditabbo. Yato kāmarāgānusayenāti yato uppannena kāmarāgānusayena sānusayo, kiṃ so tato uppannena paṭighānusayenapi sānusayoti? Yasmā panete dve ekasmā ṭhānā nuppajjanti; tasmā “no”ti paṭisedho kato. Arahā sabbatthāti arahā sabbadhammesu uppajjanakena kenaci anusayena nirānusayoti. Iminā atthavasena nippadesaṭṭhānesu bhummavacanameva katanti. Iminā upāyena sabbattha atthavinicchayo veditabboti.

Now, in the section on opportunity, when it is said, 'In the form realm and the formless realm, here one is with the underlying tendency of conceit,' a person's state of being with underlying tendencies in those realms would be evident, but the place of arising of the underlying tendency would not be evident. This section has been introduced to show the place of arising of the underlying tendency. Therefore, it is said, 'with the underlying tendency of conceit from there.' For in this way, when one is with the underlying tendency of conceit that has arisen from those two realms, the place of arising of the underlying tendency is indicated. However, since the meaning of the initial question would not be clear if the meaning of this question were not stated, it was not stated at first. Therefore, it should be understood thus: 'From which one is with the underlying tendency of sensual desire' means, from which arisen underlying tendency of sensual desire one is with an underlying tendency, is one also with the underlying tendency of aversion that has arisen from there? But since these two do not arise from the same place, the denial 'no' is made. 'The Arahant everywhere' means the Arahant is without underlying tendencies with respect to all phenomena, through any underlying tendency that could arise. By this reasoning, in cases where no specific location is mentioned, only the locative case is used. By this method, the analytical determination of the meaning should be understood everywhere.

Sānusayavāravaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Section on Being with Underlying Tendencies.

3. Pajahanavāravaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Section on Abandoning.

132-197. Pajahanavāre [P 0.0095][M 0.0328] pajahatīti tena tena maggena pahānapariññāvasena pajahati, āyatiṃ anuppattidhammataṃ āpādeti. Āmantāti anāgāmīmaggaṭṭhaṃ sandhāya paṭivacanaṃ. Tadekaṭṭhaṃ pajahatīti pahānekaṭṭhataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Noti arahattamaggaṭṭhaṃ sandhāya paṭisedho.

In the section on abandoning, 'abandons' means one abandons by means of the respective path, through the full understanding that is abandonment, and brings about the state of not being subject to future arising. 'Yes' is a reply referring to one established in the path of the non-returner. 'Abandons that which has the same object' is said with reference to the oneness of abandoning. 'No' is a denial referring to one established in the path of Arahantship.

Yato kāmarāgānusayaṃ pajahatīti yato uppajjanakaṃ kāmarāgānusayaṃ pajahatīti attho. Aṭṭhamakoti arahattaphalaṭṭhato paṭṭhāya paccorohanagaṇanāya gaṇiyamāno sotāpattimaggaṭṭho aṭṭhamako [V 0.0327] nāma. Dakkhiṇeyyagaṇanāya hi arahā aggadakkhiṇeyyattā paṭhamo, arahattamaggaṭṭho dutiyo, anāgāmī tatiyo…pe… sotāpattimaggaṭṭho aṭṭhamo. So idha “aṭṭhamako”ti vutto. Nāmasaññāyeva vā esā tassāti. Anāgāmimaggasamaṅgiñca aṭṭhamakañca ṭhapetvā avasesāti saddhiṃ puthujjanena sekkhāsekkhā. Tesu hi puthujjano pahānapariññāya abhāvena nappajahati. Sesā tesaṃ anusayānaṃ pahīnattā. Dvinnaṃ maggasamaṅgīnanti dve maggasamaṅgino ṭhapetvāti attho. Iminā nayena sabbattha vinicchayo veditabboti.

The meaning of 'from which one abandons the underlying tendency of sensual desire' is 'from which one abandons the underlying tendency of sensual desire that is prone to arising.' The eighth person: Counting in descending order from one established in the fruit of Arahantship, the one established in the path of stream-entry is called the eighth. For in the enumeration of those worthy of offerings, the Arahant is first as the foremost worthy of offerings, the one established in the path of Arahantship is second, the non-returner is third… and so on… the one established in the path of stream-entry is eighth. Here, that one is called 'the eighth.' Or, this is merely a designation for that person. Excluding the one endowed with the path of the non-returner and the eighth person, the remaining—together with the worldling—are trainees and those beyond training. Among them, the worldling does not abandon due to the absence of the full understanding that is abandonment. The rest do not abandon them, since for them those underlying tendencies have already been abandoned. 'Of the two endowed with the path' means excluding the two persons endowed with the path. In this way, the analytical determination should be understood in every instance.

Pajahanavāravaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Section on Abandoning.

4. Pariññāvāravaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Section on Full Understanding.

198-263. Pariññāvāre parijānātīti tīhi pariññāhi parijānāti. Sesamettha heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Ayampi hi vāro pajahanavāro viya maggaṭṭhānaññeva vasena vissajjitoti.

In the section on full understanding, 'fully understands' means one fully understands with the three kinds of full understanding. The rest here is to be understood in the same way as explained before. This section, like the section on abandoning, is explained solely by way of those established in the path.

Pariññāvāravaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Section on Full Understanding.

5. Pahīnavāravaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Section on What is Abandoned.

264-274. Pahīnavāre phalaṭṭhavaseneva desanā āraddhā. Anāgāmissa hi ubhopete anusayā pahīnā, tasmā “āmantā”ti vuttaṃ.

In the section on what is abandoned, the teaching was commenced solely with reference to those established in the fruit. For a non-returner, both these underlying tendencies are abandoned; therefore, 'yes' was said.

275-296. Okāsavāre [M 0.0329] yattha kāmarāgānusayo pahīno tattha paṭighānusayo pahīnoti pucchitvā na vattabbo pahīnoti vā appahīnoti vāti vuttaṃ taṃ kasmāti? Uppattiṭṭhānassa asādhāraṇattā. Aññaṃ hi kāmarāgānusayassa [P 0.0096] uppattiṭṭhānaṃ, aññaṃ paṭighānusayassa. Abhāvitamaggassa ca yattha anusayo uppajjati, magge bhāvite tattheva so pahīno nāma hoti[V 0.0328]. Tattha yasmā neva kāmarāgānusayaṭṭhāne paṭighānusayo uppajjati, na paṭighānusayaṭṭhāne kāmarāgānusayo, tasmā tattha so pahīnoti vā appahīnoti vā na vattabbo. So hi yasmiṃ attano uppattiṭṭhāne kāmarāgānusayo pahīno, tasmiṃ appahīnattā tattha pahīnoti na vattabbo. Yaṃ kāmarāgānusayassa uppattiṭṭhānaṃ, tasmiṃ aṭṭhitattā tattha appahīnoti na vattabbo.

In the section on opportunity, when asked whether, at the place where the underlying tendency of sensual desire is abandoned, the underlying tendency of aversion is also abandoned, it is said that it should not be stated that it is abandoned or not abandoned. Why is that? Because the place of their arising is not common. For the place of arising of the underlying tendency of sensual desire is one thing, and that of the underlying tendency of aversion is another. Moreover, for one who has not developed the path, wherever an underlying tendency arises, when the path is developed, it is right there that it is said to be abandoned. Since the underlying tendency of aversion never arises in the place of the underlying tendency of sensual desire, nor does the underlying tendency of sensual desire in the place of the underlying tendency of aversion, therefore it should not be said that it is abandoned or not abandoned there. For that tendency should not be said to be 'abandoned' there, since it is not abandoned in that place. Nor should it be said to be 'not abandoned' there, since it does not exist in the place where the tendency to sensual desire arises.

Yattha kāmarāgānusayo pahīno, tattha mānānusayo pahīnoti ettha pana sādhāraṇaṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya āmantāti vuttaṃ. Kāmarāgānusayo hi kāmadhātuyā dvīsu vedanāsu anuseti. Mānānusayo tāsu ceva rūpārūpadhātūsu ca. So ṭhapetvā asādhāraṇaṭṭhānaṃ sādhāraṇaṭṭhāne tena saddhiṃ pahīno nāma hoti. Tasmā ‘āmantā’ti vuttaṃ. Iminā nayena sabbasmimpi okāsavāre pahīnatā ca navattabbatā ca veditabbā. ‘Natthī’ti āgataṭṭhānesu pana heṭṭhā vuttasadisova vinicchayo. Puggalokāsavāro, okāsavāragatikoyeva.

Regarding the question, 'Where the underlying tendency of sensual desire is abandoned, is the underlying tendency of conceit abandoned there?', here 'yes' is stated with reference to a common location. For the underlying tendency of sensual desire lies latent in two feelings in the sense-sphere realm. The underlying tendency of conceit lies latent in those same feelings as well as in the form and formless realms. Therefore, setting aside the non-common location, in the common location it is said to be abandoned together with it. Thus, 'yes' was said. In this way, in the entire section on opportunity, abandonment and non-sayability should be understood. But in instances where 'there is not' appears, the analytical determination is just as was said before. The section on persons and opportunity is of the same nature as the section on opportunity.

297-307. Paṭilomanaye yassa kāmarāgānusayo appahīnoti puthujjanasotāpannasakadāgāmivasena pucchati. Kiñcāpi hi ime dve anusayā puthujjanato paṭṭhāya yāva anāgāmimaggaṭṭhā channaṃ puggalānaṃ appahīnā. Idha pana parato “tiṇṇaṃ puggalānaṃ dvinnaṃ puggalāna”ntiādivacanato maggaṭṭhā anadhippetā, tasmā puthujjanasotāpannasakadāgāminova sandhāya ‘āmantā’ti vuttaṃ. Dvinnaṃ puggalānanti sotāpannasakadāgāmīnaṃ. Iminā nayena puggalavāre vinicchayo veditabbo.

297-307. In the reverse method, the question asks, 'For whom is the underlying tendency of sensual desire not abandoned?' with reference to ordinary persons, stream-enterers, and once-returners. Although these two underlying tendencies are not abandoned by six types of individuals, from ordinary persons up to those standing on the path of non-returning, here, however, because the statement that follows, 'for three types of individuals, for two types of individuals,' and so on, does not refer to those standing on the path, therefore 'yes' was said only with reference to ordinary persons, stream-enterers, and once-returners. 'For two types of individuals' means for stream-enterers and once-returners. In this way, the determination in the section on individuals should be understood.

308-329. Okāsavārapuggalokāsavārā pana heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbāti.

308-329. However, the section on location and the section on persons and location should be understood in the same way as explained above.

Pahīnavāravaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Section on Abandonment.

6. Uppajjanavāravaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Section on Arising.

330. Uppajjanavāro [M 0.0330] anusayavārasadisoyeva.

330. The section on arising is similar to the section on underlying tendencies.

7. Dhātupucchāvāravaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Section of Questions about Elements.

332-340. Dhātuvārassa [V 0.0329] pucchāvāre tāva kati anusayā anusentīti kati [P 0.0097] anusayā santānaṃ anugatā hutvā sayanti. Kati anusayā nānusentīti kati anusayā santānaṃ na anugatā hutvā sayanti. Kati anusayā bhaṅgāti kati anusayā anusenti nānusentīti evaṃ vibhajitabbāti attho. Sesamettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ heṭṭhā pāḷivavatthāne vuttameva.

332-340. In the section of questions on the elements, first, 'How many underlying tendencies underlie?' means how many underlying tendencies lie dormant, having followed the mental continuum. 'How many underlying tendencies do not underlie?' means how many underlying tendencies do not lie dormant, not having followed the mental continuum. 'How many underlying tendencies are a matter of division?' means how many underlying tendencies are to be analyzed as 'they underlie' and 'they do not underlie'—this is the meaning. Whatever else needs to be said here has already been stated in the earlier delineation of the Pāli.

7. Dhātuvissajjanāvāravaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Section on the Elucidation of Elements.

341-349. Niddesavāre panassa kassaci satta anusayā anusentīti puthujjanavasena vuttaṃ. Kassaci pañcāti sotāpannasakadāgāmivasena vuttaṃ. Tesañhi diṭṭhānusayo ca vicikicchānusayo ca pahīnāti pañceva anusenti. Tattha yathā anusayavāre “anusentī”ti padassa uppajjantīti attho gahito, evamidha na gahetabbo. Kasmā? Tasmiṃ khaṇe anuppajjanato. Kāmadhātuṃ upapajjantassa hi vipākacittañceva kammasamuṭṭhānarūpañca uppajjati, akusalacittaṃ natthi. Anusayā ca akusalacittakkhaṇe uppajjanti, na vipākacittakkhaṇeti tasmiṃ khaṇe anuppajjanato tathā attho na gahetabbo. Kathaṃ pana gahetabboti? Yathā labbhati tathā gahetabbo. Kathañca labbhati? Appahīnaṭṭhena. Yathā hi rāgadosamohānaṃ appahīnattā. Kusalābyākatacittasamaṅgī puggalo “sarāgo sadoso samoho”ti vuccati, evaṃ maggabhāvanāya appahīnattā paṭisandhikkhaṇepi tassa tassa puggalassa te te anusayā anusentīti vuccanti. Na kevalañca vuccanti, appahīnattā pana te anusentiyeva nāmāti veditabbā.

341-349. In the exposition section, 'For some, seven underlying tendencies underlie' is stated with reference to ordinary persons. 'For some, five' is stated with reference to stream-enterers and once-returners. For them, the underlying tendencies of wrong view and doubt are abandoned, so only five underlie. Here, unlike in the section on underlying tendencies where the word 'underlie' was understood to mean 'arise,' that meaning should not be taken here. Why? Because they do not arise at that moment. For one being reborn in the sense-sphere realm, only resultant consciousness and kamma-originated matter arise; unwholesome consciousness is not present.
