Underlying tendencies arise only at the moment of unwholesome consciousness, not at the moment of resultant consciousness; hence, because they do not arise at that moment, that meaning should not be taken. How then should it be taken? It should be taken as it is available. And how is it available? In the sense of not being abandoned. Just as a person endowed with wholesome or indeterminate consciousness is called 'one with lust, hatred, and delusion' because lust, hatred, and delusion have not been abandoned, so too, because they have not been abandoned by path-development, even at the moment of rebirth-linking, those underlying tendencies are said to underlie that individual. And it should be understood that they not only are said to underlie, but they do indeed underlie because they are unabandoned.

Anusayā bhaṅgā natthīti yassa hi yo anuseti, so anusetiyeva; yo nānuseti, so nānusetiyeva. Ayaṃ anuseti ca nānuseti ca, ayaṃ siyā anuseti siyā nānusetīti, evaṃ vibhajitabbo anusayo nāma natthi. Rūpadhātuṃ upapajjantassa kassaci tayoti [M 0.0331] anāgāmivasena vuttaṃ. Tassa hi kāmarāgapaṭighadiṭṭhivicikicchānusayā cattāropi anavasesato pahīnā. Itare tayova appahīnā. Tena vuttaṃ – “kassaci tayo anusayā anusentī”ti.

'There are no underlying tendencies that are a matter of division' means that for whomever a certain tendency underlies, it simply underlies; for whomever it does not underlie, it simply does not underlie. There is no such thing as an underlying tendency that is to be analyzed as 'this one both underlies and does not underlie,' or 'this one may underlie and may not underlie.' 'For some being reborn in the form realm, three underlie' is stated with reference to non-returners. For them, the four underlying tendencies of sensual desire, aversion, wrong view, and doubt are all abandoned without remainder. The other three remain unabandoned. Hence, it is said, 'For some, three underlying tendencies underlie.'

Na [V 0.0330] kāmadhātunti kāmadhātuyā paṭisiddhattā sesā dve dhātuyo upapajjantassāti attho. Satte [P 0.0098] vāti yasmā ariyasāvakassa rūpadhātuyā cutassa kāmadhātuyaṃ upapatti nāma natthi, puthujjanasseva hoti, tasmā sattevāti niyametvā vuttaṃ. “Arūpadhātuyā cutassa kāmadhātuṃ upapajjantassa sattevā”ti etthāpi eseva nayo. Rūpadhātuyā upapatti natthīti kasmā natthi? Upapattinipphādakassa rūpāvacarajjhānassa abhāvā. So hi sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā taṃ dhātuṃ upapannoti nāssa tattha rūpāvacarajjhānaṃ atthi. Tadabhāvā rūpadhātuyaṃ upapatti natthīti veditabbā. Arūpadhātuyā cutassa na kāmadhātunti ettha arūpadhātuyeva adhippetā. Iminā nayena sabbavissajjanesu attho veditabboti.

'Not the sense-sphere realm' means for one who is being reborn in the remaining two realms, since the sense-sphere realm is excluded. 'Only seven' is stated with restriction because for a noble disciple who has passed away from the form realm, there is no such thing as rebirth in the sense-sphere realm—it happens only for an ordinary person. Similarly, in the phrase 'for one who has passed away from the formless realm and is being reborn in the sense-sphere realm, only seven,' the same principle applies. Why is there no rebirth in the form realm? Because the form-sphere jhāna, which produces rebirth, is absent. For one who has completely transcended all perceptions of form and is reborn in that realm, there is no form-sphere jhāna for him. Due to its absence, it should be understood that there is no rebirth in the form realm. In the phrase 'for one who has passed away from the formless realm, not the sense-sphere realm,' only the formless realm is meant. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all elucidations.

Dhātuvāravaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Section on Elements.

Anusayayamakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Yamaka on Underlying Tendencies is completed.

8. Cittayamakaṃ

8. The Yamaka on Consciousness.

Uddesavāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on the Summary.

1-62. Idāni tesaññeva mūlayamake desitānaṃ kusalādidhammānaṃ labbhamānavasena ekadesameva saṅgaṇhitvā anusayayamakānantaraṃ desitassa cittayamakassa atthavaṇṇanā hoti. Tattha pāḷivavatthānaṃ tāva veditabbaṃ. Imasmiñhi cittayamake mātikāṭhapanaṃ, ṭhapitamātikāya vissajjananti dve vārā honti. Tattha mātikāṭhapane puggalavāro, dhammavāro, puggaladhammavāroti āditova tayo suddhikamahāvārā honti.

1-62. Now, having collected just a part of those very wholesome and other states taught in the Mūlayamaka, by way of their obtainability, comes the explanation of the meaning of the Yamaka on Consciousness, which was taught after the Yamaka on Underlying Tendencies. Herein, first, the establishment of the Pāli text should be understood. In this Yamaka on Consciousness, there are two sections: the setting out of the matrix and the elucidation of the established matrix. Herein, in the setting out of the matrix, there are from the beginning three pure, great sections: the section on individuals, the section on phenomena, and the section on individuals and phenomena.

Tattha “yassa cittaṃ uppajjati, na nirujjhatī”ti evaṃ puggalavasena cittassa uppajjananirujjhanādibhedaṃ dīpento gato puggalavāro nāma. “Yaṃ cittaṃ uppajjati, na nirujjhatī”ti evaṃ dhammavaseneva cittassa uppajjananirujjhanādibhedaṃ dīpento gato dhammavāro nāma. “Yassa yaṃ cittaṃ uppajjati, na nirujjhatī”ti evaṃ ubhayavasena [M 0.0332] cittassa uppajjananirujjhanādibhedaṃ [V 0.0331] dīpento gato puggaladhammavāro nāma. Tato [P 0.0099] “yassa sarāgaṃ citta”nti soḷasannaṃ padānaṃ vasena apare sarāgādipadavisesitā soḷasa puggalavārā, soḷasa dhammavārā, soḷasa puggaladhammavārāti aṭṭhacattālīsaṃ missakavārā honti. Te sarāgādipadamattaṃ dassetvā saṅkhittā. Tato “yassa kusalaṃ citta”ntiādinā nayena chasaṭṭhidvisatasaṅkhānaṃ abhidhammamātikāpadānaṃ vasena apare kusalādipadavisesitā chasaṭṭhidvisatapuggalavārā, chasaṭṭhidvisatadhammavārā chasaṭṭhidvisatapuggaladhammavārāti aṭṭhanavutisattasatā missakavārā honti. Tepi kusalādipadamattaṃ dassetvā saṅkhittāyeva. Yānipettha sanidassanādīni padāni cittena saddhiṃ na yujjanti, tāni moghapucchāvasena ṭhapitāni.

Herein, the section called the 'Section on Individuals' proceeds by explaining the distinctions of arising, cessation, and so forth of consciousness in terms of an individual, thus: 'For whom consciousness arises, it does not cease.' The section called the 'Section on Phenomena' proceeds by explaining the distinctions of arising, cessation, and so forth of consciousness purely in terms of phenomena, thus: 'Whatever consciousness arises, it does not cease.' The section called the 'Section on Individuals and Phenomena' proceeds by explaining the distinctions of arising, cessation, and so forth of consciousness in terms of both, thus: 'For whom whatever consciousness arises, that does not cease.' Following this, by way of the sixteen terms, there are further sections specified by terms such as 'with lust'—sixteen Sections on Individuals, sixteen Sections on Phenomena, and sixteen Sections on Individuals and Phenomena—making forty-eight mixed sections. These are abbreviated, showing only terms like 'with lust.' Then, by the method beginning with 'For whom a wholesome consciousness,' by way of the two hundred and sixty-six terms of the Abhidhamma matrix, there are further sections specified by terms such as 'wholesome'—two hundred and sixty-six Sections on Individuals, two hundred and sixty-six Sections on Phenomena, and two hundred and sixty-six Sections on Individuals and Phenomena—making seven hundred and ninety-eight mixed sections. These too are abbreviated, showing only terms like 'wholesome.' Herein, terms such as 'with sight' that do not accord with consciousness are set aside as futile questions.

Tesu pana tīsu vāresu sabbapaṭhame suddhikapuggalamahāvāre uppādanirodhakālasambhedavāro, uppāduppannavāro, nirodhuppannavāro, uppādavāro, nirodhavāro, uppādanirodhavāro uppajjamānanirodhavāro, uppajjamānuppannavāro, nirujjhamānuppannavāro, uppannuppādavāro, atītānāgatavāro, uppannuppajjamānavāro, niruddhanirujjhamānavāro, atikkantakālavāroti cuddasa antaravārā. Tesu uppādavāro, nirodhavāro, uppādanirodhavāroti imesu tīsu vāresu anulomapaṭilomavasena cha cha katvā aṭṭhārasa yamakāni. Uppannuppādavāre atītānāgatakālavasena anulomato dve, paṭilomato dveti cattāri yamakāni. Sesesu ādito niddiṭṭhesu tīsu, anantare niddiṭṭhesu tīsu; avasāne niddiṭṭhesu catūsūti dasasu vāresu anulomato ekaṃ, paṭilomato ekanti dve dve katvā vīsati yamakāni. Evaṃ sabbesupi cuddasasu antaravāresu dvācattālīsa yamakāni, caturāsīti pucchā aṭṭhasaṭṭhiatthasataṃ hoti. Yathā ca ekasmiṃ suddhikapuggalamahāvāre, tathā suddhikadhammavārepi suddhikapuggaladhammavārepīti tīsu mahāvāresu chabbīsatiyamakasataṃ, tato diguṇā pucchā, tato diguṇā atthā ca veditabbā. Idaṃ pana vārattayaṃ sarāgādivasena soḷasaguṇaṃ, kusalādivasena chasaṭṭhidvisataguṇaṃ katvā imasmiṃ cittayamake anekāni yamakasahassāni, tato diguṇā pucchā, tato diguṇā atthā ca hontīti[P 0.0100]. Pāṭho pana saṃkhittoti. Evaṃ tāva imasmiṃ cittayamake pāḷivavatthānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Now, in these three sections, the very first great pure section on individuals includes fourteen intermediate sections: the section on the combination of the time of arising and cessation, the section on arising and what has arisen, the section on cessation and what has arisen, the section on arising, the section on cessation, the section on arising and cessation, the section on the cessation of what is arising, the section on what is arising and what has arisen, the section on what is ceasing and what has arisen, the section on what has arisen and arising, the section on past and future, the section on what has arisen and what is arising, the section on what has ceased and what is ceasing, and the section on elapsed time. Among these, in the three sections on arising, cessation, and arising and cessation, there are eighteen yamakas, being six each in forward and reverse order. In the section on what has arisen and arising, there are four yamakas: two in forward order and two in reverse, based on past and future time. In the remaining ten sections—three specified at the beginning, three specified immediately after, and four specified at the end—there are twenty yamakas, being two each with one in forward order and one in reverse. Thus, in all fourteen intermediate sections, there are forty-two yamakas, eighty-four questions, and one hundred and sixty-eight meanings. Just as in the one great pure section on individuals, so too in the great pure section on phenomena and the great pure section on individuals and phenomena, there are one hundred and twenty-six yamakas in the three great sections; the questions are double that, and the meanings are double that again. Furthermore, this threefold section, when multiplied sixteenfold by way of states such as lust, and two hundred and sixty-six-fold by way of states such as wholesome, results in many thousands of yamakas in this Yamaka on Consciousness; the questions are double that, and the meanings are double that again. The text, however, is concise. Thus far, the structure of the Pāli text in this Yamaka on Consciousness should be understood.

Mātikāṭhapanavaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Establishment of the Matrix.

Niddeso

Exposition

1. Puggalavāravaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Section on Individuals

63. Idāni [M 0.0333][V 0.0332] ṭhapitānukkamena mātikaṃ vissajjetuṃ yassa cittaṃ uppajjati na nirujjhatītiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha uppajjatīti uppādakkhaṇasamaṅgitāya uppajjati na nirujjhatīti nirodhakkhaṇaṃ appattatāya na nirujjhati. Tassa cittanti tassa puggalassa tato paṭṭhāya cittaṃ nirujjhissati nuppajjissatīti pucchati. Tesaṃ cittanti yesaṃ paricchinnavaṭṭadukkhānaṃ khīṇāsavānaṃ sabbapacchimassa cuticittassa uppādakkhaṇo vattati, etesaṃ tadeva cuticittaṃ uppādappattatāya uppajjati nāma, bhaṅgaṃ appattatāya na nirujjhati. Idāni pana bhaṅgaṃ patvā taṃ tesaṃ cittaṃ nirujjhissati, tato appaṭisandhikattā aññaṃ nuppajjissati. Itaresanti pacchimacittasamaṅgiṃ khīṇāsavaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesānaṃ sekkhāsekkhaputhujjanānaṃ nirujjhissati ceva uppajjissati cāti yaṃ taṃ uppādakkhaṇappattaṃ taṃ nirujjhissateva. Aññaṃ pana tasmiṃ vā aññasmiṃ vā attabhāve uppajjissati ceva nirujjhissati ca. Dutiyapucchāvissajjanepi tathārūpasseva khīṇāsavassa cittaṃ sandhāya ‘āmantā’ti vuttaṃ. Nuppajjati nirujjhatīti bhaṅgakkhaṇe arahato pacchimacittampi sesānaṃ bhijjamānacittampi. Tato paṭṭhāya pana arahato cittaṃ na nirujjhissatīti sakkā vattuṃ uppajjissatīti pana na sakkā. Sesānaṃ uppajjissatīti sakkā vattuṃ, na nirujjhissatīti na sakkā. Tasmā ‘no’ti paṭisedho kato. Dutiyapañhe yassa cittaṃ na nirujjhissati, uppajjissatīti so puggaloyeva natthi, tasmā natthīti paṭikkhepo kato.

63. Now, to explain the matrix in the established sequence, the text is introduced beginning, “For whom consciousness arises, it does not cease,” and so on. Herein, “arises” means it arises by being endowed with the moment of arising; “does not cease” means it does not cease because it has not reached the moment of cessation. The question is asked concerning that individual’s consciousness: from that point onward, will that consciousness cease or will it not arise? “For them, consciousness…” refers to those whose suffering in the round is fully comprehended, the Arahants, for whom the moment of arising of the very last death-consciousness is occurring. For them, that very death-consciousness is said to arise because it has reached the moment of arising, and it does not cease because it has not reached the moment of dissolution. But now, upon reaching dissolution, that consciousness of theirs will cease, and because there is no subsequent rebirth-linking, another will not arise. “For others” refers to all except the Arahant endowed with the final consciousness. For the remaining trainees, those beyond training, and ordinary people, that which has reached the moment of arising will indeed cease, and another will arise in this or another existence and will also cease. In the answer to the second question, with reference to the consciousness of such an Arahant, it is said, “Yes.” The phrase “does not arise, it ceases” refers to the final consciousness of an Arahant at the moment of dissolution and the disintegrating consciousness of others. From that point onward, however, it can be said that the Arahant’s consciousness will not cease, but it cannot be said that it will arise. For others, it can be said that it will arise, but it cannot be said that it will not cease. Therefore, the denial “No” is given. In the second question, 'for whom consciousness will not cease and will arise', no such individual exists; therefore, the rejection “there is not” is given.

65-82. Uppannanti uppādasamaṅginopetaṃ nāmaṃ. Uppādaṃ patvā aniruddhassāpi. Tattha uppādasamaṅgitaṃ sandhāya [P 0.0101] ‘āmantā’ti, uppādaṃ patvā aniruddhabhāvaṃ sandhāya “tesaṃ cittaṃ uppanna”nti vuttaṃ. Anuppannanti uppādaṃ appattaṃ. Tesaṃ cittaṃ uppajjitthāti etthāpi sabbesaṃ tāva cittaṃ khaṇapaccuppannameva hutvā uppādakkhaṇaṃ atītattā uppajjittha nāma, nirodhasamāpannānaṃ nirodhato pubbe uppannapubbattā, asaññasattānaṃ saññībhave uppannapubbattā. Uppajjittha ceva uppajjati cāti uppādaṃ pattattā uppajjittha, anatītattā uppajjati nāmāti attho.

65-82. 'Arisen' is a term for that which is endowed with the moment of arising, even for that which has reached arising but has not ceased. Herein, referring to being endowed with the moment of arising, 'Yes' is said; and referring to having reached arising but not yet having ceased, it is said, 'Their mind has arisen.' 'Not arisen' means not having reached arising. 'Their mind had arisen'—here, the mind of all of them, being momentarily present, is called 'had arisen' because it has passed the moment of arising; for those attained to cessation, because it had arisen previously before cessation; and for non-percipient beings, because it had arisen previously in a percipient existence. 'Had arisen and arises' means 'had arisen' because it has reached arising, and 'arises' because it has not passed—this is the meaning.

Uppādakkhaṇe [V 0.0333] anāgatañcāti uppādakkhaṇe ca cittaṃ anāgatañca cittanti attho.

'At the moment of arising and the future' means the mind at the moment of arising and the future mind—this is the meaning.

83. Atikkantakālavāre uppajjamānaṃ khaṇanti uppādakkhaṇaṃ. Tattha kiñcāpi uppādakkhaṇo uppajjamāno nāma na hoti, uppajjamānassa pana khaṇattā evaṃ [M 0.0334] vutto. Khaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ atikkantakālanti na ciraṃ vītikkantaṃ tameva pana uppādakkhaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ hutvā atikkantakālanti saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Nirujjhamānaṃ khaṇanti nirodhakkhaṇaṃ. Tattha kiñcāpi nirodhakkhaṇo nirujjhamāno nāma na hoti, nirujjhamānassa pana khaṇattā evaṃ vutto. Khaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ atikkantakālanti kiṃ tassa cittaṃ evaṃ nirodhakkhaṇampi vītikkantaṃ hutvā atikkantakālaṃ nāma hotīti pucchati. Tattha yasmā bhaṅgakkhaṇe cittaṃ uppādakkhaṇaṃ khaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ hutvā atikkantakālaṃ hoti, nirodhakkhaṇaṃ khaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ hutvā atikkantakālaṃ nāma na hoti. Atītaṃ pana cittaṃ ubhopi khaṇe khaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ hutvā atikkantakālaṃ nāma, tasmā “bhaṅgakkhaṇe cittaṃ uppādakkhaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ, bhaṅgakkhaṇaṃ avītikkantaṃ, atītaṃ cittaṃ uppādakkhaṇañca vītikkantaṃ bhaṅgakkhaṇañca vītikkantanti vissajjanamāha. Dutiyapañhassa vissajjane yasmā atītaṃ cittaṃ ubhopi khaṇe vītikkantaṃ hutvā atikkantakālaṃ nāma hoti, tasmā atītaṃ cittanti vuttaṃ. Paṭilomapañhassa vissajjane yasmā uppādakkhaṇe ca cittaṃ anāgatañca cittaṃ ubhopi khaṇe khaṇaṃ vītikkantaṃ hutvā atikkantakālaṃ nāma na hoti, tesaṃ khaṇānaṃ [P 0.0102] avītikkantattā. Tasmā “uppādakkhaṇe cittaṃ anāgataṃ citta”nti vuttaṃ. Dutiyavissajjanaṃ pākaṭameva.

83. In the section on past time, 'the arising moment' refers to the moment of arising. Although the moment of arising is not actually called 'arising,' it is referred to as such because it is the moment of that which is arising. A moment that has passed is called 'past time.' Though it has not passed for long, that very moment of arising, having passed, is reckoned as past time. 'The ceasing moment' refers to the moment of cessation. Although the moment of cessation is not actually called 'ceasing,' it is referred to as such because it is the moment of that which is ceasing. It is asked: 'Does that mind, having passed even the cessation moment, become past time?' In this regard, since at the moment of dissolution the mind becomes past time by having passed the moment of arising, but it does not become past time by having passed the moment of cessation. However, a past mind is called 'past time' by having passed both moments. Therefore, the answer states: 'At the moment of dissolution, the mind has passed the moment of arising, but has not passed the moment of dissolution. A past mind has passed both the moment of arising and the moment of dissolution.' In the answer to the second question, since a past mind is called 'past time' by having passed both moments, it is referred to as a 'past mind.' In the answer to the reverse question, since neither the mind at the moment of arising nor the future mind is called 'past time' by having passed the moment, because for them those moments have not passed. Therefore, it is stated: 'The mind at the moment of arising and the future mind.' The second answer is clear.

84-113. Dhammavārepi imināvupāyena sabbavissajjanesu attho veditabbo. Puggaladhammavāro dhammavāragatikoyeva.

84-113. Also in the chapter on phenomena, the meaning in all answers should be understood in this way. The chapter on individuals and phenomena follows the same course as the chapter on phenomena.

114-116. Sabbepi missakavārā yassa sarāgaṃ cittantiādinā nayena mukhamattaṃ dassetvā saṅkhittā. Vitthāro pana nesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Tesu pana “yassa sarāgaṃ cittaṃ uppajjati, na nirujjhati; tassa cittaṃ nirujjhissati, nuppajjissatī”ti evaṃ vitthāretabbatāya pucchāva sadisā hoti. Yasmā pana sarāgaṃ cittaṃ pacchimacittaṃ na hoti, tasmā “yassa sarāgaṃ cittaṃ uppajjati, na nirujjhati; tassa cittaṃ nirujjhissati, nuppajjissatīti [V 0.0334] no”ti evaṃ vissajjitabbattā vissajjanaṃ asadisaṃ hoti. Taṃ taṃ tassā tassā pucchāya anurūpavasena veditabbanti.

114-116. All the mixed sections are summarized, only showing the beginning, with the method 'for whom a lustful mind arises,' and so on. But their detailed explanation should be understood in the same way as stated above. Among these, the question to be elaborated thus, 'For whom a lustful mind arises, and does not cease; will that mind cease, but not arise?' is similar. But because a lustful mind is not a final mind, the answer, 'For whom a lustful mind arises, and does not cease; will that mind cease, but not arise? No,' should be given, thus the answer is dissimilar. This should be understood according to the appropriateness of each particular question.

Cittayamakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Cittayamaka is concluded.

9. Dhammayamakaṃ

9. The Dhammayamaka

1. Paṇṇattiuddesavāravaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Exposition Section on Designations

1-16. Idāni [M 0.0335] tesaññeva mūlayamake desitānaṃ kusalādidhammānaṃ mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā cittayamakānantaraṃ desitassa dhammayamakassa vaṇṇanā hoti. Tattha khandhayamake vuttanayeneva pāḷivavatthānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Yathā hi tattha paṇṇattivārādayo tayo mahāvārā, avasesā antaravārā ca honti, tathā idhāpi. “Yo kusalaṃ dhammaṃ bhāveti, so akusalaṃ dhammaṃ pajahatī”ti āgatattā panettha pariññāvāro, bhāvanāvāro nāmāti veditabbo. Tattha yasmā abyākato dhammo neva bhāvetabbo, na pahātabbo, tasmā taṃ padameva na uddhaṭaṃ. Paṇṇattivāre panettha tiṇṇaṃ kusalādidhammānaṃ vasena padasodhanavāro, padasodhanamūlacakkavāro, suddhadhammavāro, suddhadhammamūlacakkavāroti [P 0.0103] imesu catūsu vāresu yamakagaṇanā veditabbā.

1-16. Now, having established the matrix of wholesome states and the like, which were taught in the Mūlayamaka, the commentary on the Dhammayamaka, which was taught after the Cittayamaka, is given. Herein, the arrangement of the Pāli text should be understood in the same way as stated in the Khandhayamaka. Just as there are three great sections—the section on designations and so on—and the remaining intermediate sections, so too here. Since it is stated, "One who develops a wholesome state abandons an unwholesome state," it should be understood that this contains the section on full understanding and the section on development. Herein, because an indeterminate state is neither to be developed nor to be abandoned, that term itself is not taken up. In the section on designations here, the enumeration of pairs should be understood in these four sections—the section on term-purification, the section on the root-cycle of term-purification, the section on pure phenomena, and the section on the root-cycle of pure phenomena—by way of the three wholesome states and so on.

1. Paṇṇattiniddesavāravaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Explanation Section on Designations

17-32. Paṇṇattivāraniddese pana kusalā kusaladhammāti kusalānaṃ ekantena kusaladhammattā “āmantā”ti vuttaṃ. Sesavissajjanesupi eseva nayo. Avasesā dhammā na akusalā dhammāti avasesā dhammā akusalā na honti, dhammā pana hontīti attho. Iminā nayena sabbavissajjanāni veditabbāni.

17-32. In the Explanation of the Section on Designations, regarding "Are wholesome states wholesome phenomena?", since wholesome states are exclusively wholesome phenomena, it is said, "Yes." This same method applies to the remaining answers. Regarding "Are the remaining phenomena not unwholesome phenomena?", the meaning is that the remaining phenomena are not unwholesome, but they are phenomena. By this method, all the answers should be understood.

Paṇṇattivāravaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Section on Designations.

2. Pavattivāravaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Section on Occurrence

33-34. Pavattivāre [V 0.0335] panettha paccuppannakāle puggalavārassa anulomanaye “yassa kusalā dhammā uppajjanti, tassa akusalā dhammā uppajjanti; yassa vā pana akusalā dhammā uppajjanti, tassa kusalā dhammā uppajjantī”ti kusaladhammamūlakāni dve yamakāni, akusaladhammamūlakaṃ ekanti tīṇi yamakāni honti. Tassa paṭilomanayepi okāsavārādīsupi eseva nayo. Evamettha sabbavāresu tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ yamakānaṃ vasena yamakagaṇanā veditabbā. Atthavinicchaye panettha idaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ – imassa hi dhammayamakassa [M 0.0336] pavattimahāvāre “uppajjanti nirujjhantī”ti imesu uppādanirodhesu kusalākusaladhammā tāva ekantena pavattiyaṃyeva labbhanti, na cutipaṭisandhīsu. Abyākatadhammā pana pavatte ca cutipaṭisandhīsu cāti tīsupi kālesu labbhanti. Evamettha yaṃ yattha yattha labbhati, tassa vasena tattha tattha vinicchayo veditabbo.

33-34. Here, in the Section on Occurrence, in the present time, in the Section on Individuals, in the forward order: “For one for whom wholesome states arise, for that one do unwholesome states arise? Or again, for one for whom unwholesome states arise, for that one do wholesome states arise?” Thus, there are two couplets rooted in wholesome states and one couplet rooted in unwholesome states, making three couplets in total. This same method applies in the reverse order, and also in the sections beginning with the Opportunity Section. In this way, throughout all sections, the calculation of couplets should be understood as being three couplets each. Here, in the determination of meaning, this is the characteristic: in the Great Section on Occurrence of this Dhamma-yamaka, regarding “arising and ceasing,” wholesome and unwholesome states are obtained exclusively in the course of life, not at death and rebirth-linking. But indeterminate states are obtained in the course of life and at death and rebirth-linking, thus in all three times. Accordingly, wherever something is obtained, the determination should be understood based on that.

Tatridaṃ nayamukhaṃ – kusalākusalānaṃ tāva ekakkhaṇe anuppajjanato “no”ti paṭisedho kato. Abyākatā cāti cittasamuṭṭhānarūpavasena vuttaṃ.

Here is the method of approach: First, because wholesome and unwholesome states do not arise in a single moment, the negation "no" is made. And "indeterminate" is said in reference to mind-produced materiality.

35-36. Yattha kusalā dhammā nuppajjantīti asaññabhavaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tenevettha “āmantā”ti vissajjanaṃ kataṃ. Uppajjantīti idampi asaññabhavaṃyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Abyākatānaṃ pana anuppattiṭṭhānassa abhāvā “natthī”ti paṭikkhepo kato.

35-36. "Where wholesome states do not arise" refers to the realm of non-perception. Therefore, the answer "Yes" was given here. The statement 'they arise' is also said with reference to the realm of non-perception. However, since there is no place where indeterminate states do not arise, the denial "There is not" was made.

49. Dutiye akusaleti bhavaṃ assādetvā uppannesu nikantijavanesu dutiye javanacitte. Dutiye citte vattamāneti paṭisandhito dutiye bhavaṅgacitte vattamāne saha vā paṭisandhiyā bhavaṅgaṃ vipākavasena ekameva katvā bhavanikantiyā āvajjanacitte. Tañhi kiriyacittattā abyākatajātiyaṃ vipākato dutiyaṃ nāma hoti.

49. Regarding 'in the second unwholesome,' it refers to the second impulsion consciousness among those that have arisen with craving, having relished existence. When it says 'in the second consciousness occurring,' it refers to the second life-continuum consciousness occurring after rebirth-linking, or to the adverting consciousness that arises due to craving for existence, having made the life-continuum one with rebirth-linking as a single result. For that adverting consciousness, being a functional consciousness, is called the second in terms of result, belonging to the indeterminate class.

57. Yassa cittassa anantarā [P 0.0104] aggamagganti gotrabhucittaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kusalā dhammā uppajjissantīti te aggamaggadhammeyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ.

57. Regarding 'the consciousness immediately after which is the supreme path,' it is spoken with reference to the change-of-lineage consciousness. "Wholesome states will arise" is spoken with reference specifically to those states pertaining to the supreme path.

79. Yassa [V 0.0336] cittassa anantarā aggamaggaṃ paṭilabhissanti, tassa cittassa uppādakkhaṇeti idaṃ cittajātivasena vuttaṃ. Tajjātikassa hi ekāvajjanena uppannassa tato orimacittassa uppādakkhaṇepi etaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ labbhateva.

79. The phrase 'at the moment of arising of that consciousness'—referring to the consciousness immediately after which one will attain the supreme path—is stated in terms of the class of consciousness. For in the case of one of that same class that has arisen with a single adverting, this characteristic is certainly obtained even at the moment of arising of the consciousness prior to that.

99. Nirodhavārepi kusalākusalānaṃ ekato anirujjhanato “no”ti vuttaṃ. Iminā nayamukhena sabbattha vinicchayo veditabboti.

99. In the Section on Cessation, too, because wholesome and unwholesome states do not cease at once, it is said 'no.' Through this method of approach, the determination should be understood everywhere.

Dhammayamakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Dhammayamaka is concluded.

10. Indriyayamakaṃ

10. The Couplets on the Faculties

Idāni [M 0.0337] tesaññeva mūlayamake desitānaṃ kusalādidhammānaṃ labbhamānavasena ekadesaṃ saṃgaṇhitvā dhammayamakānantaraṃ desitassa indriyayamakassa vaṇṇanā hoti. Tattha khandhayamakādīsu vuttanayeneva pāḷivavatthānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Idhāpi hi paṇṇattivārādayo tayo mahāvārā avasesā antaravārā ca saddhiṃ kālappabhedādīhi khandhayamakādīsu āgatasadisāva. Indriyānaṃ pana bahutāya dhātuyamakatopi bahutarāni yamakāni honti. Yathā pana heṭṭhā puggalavārādīsu cakkhāyatanacakkhudhātumūlake naye cakkhāyatanacakkhudhātūhi saddhiṃ jivhāyatanakāyāyatanāni na yojitāni. Jivhāyatanakāyāyatanamūlakāni ca yamakāneva na gahitāni, tathā idhāpi cakkhundriyamūlake naye jivhindriyakāyindriyāni na yojitāni, jivhindriyakāyindriyamūlakāni ca yamakāneva na gahitāni. Tesaṃ aggahaṇe kāraṇaṃ tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Manindriyaṃ pana yathā cakkhundriyādimūlakehi tatheva itthindriyādimūlakehipi saddhiṃ yasmā yojanaṃ gacchati, tasmā nikkhittapaṭipāṭiyā ayojetvā sabbehipi cakkhundriyamūlakādīhi saddhiṃ pariyosāne yojitanti veditabbaṃ. Cakkhundriyena saddhiṃ itthindriyapurisindriyajīvitindriyāni [P 0.0105] yojitāni sukhindriyadukkhindriyadomanassindriyāni paṭisandhiyaṃ natthīti na gahitāni. Somanassindriyaupekkhindriyāni paṭisandhiyaṃ uppattisabbhāvato gahitāni. Tathā saddhindriyādīni pañca. Lokuttarāni tīṇi paṭisandhiyaṃ abhāveneva na gahitāni. Iti yāni gahitāni, tesaṃ [V 0.0337] vasenettha cakkhundriyamūlake naye yamakagaṇanā veditabbā. Yathā cettha, evaṃ sabbattha. Yāni pana na gahitāni, tesaṃ vasena yamakāni na gaṇetabbāni. Gaṇentena vā moghapucchāvasena gaṇetabbānīti evaṃ tāva sabbavāresu pāḷivavatthānameva veditabbaṃ.

Now, having gathered a portion of those very same wholesome states and so on, as they are obtainable, which were taught in the Mūla-yamaka, the exposition of the Indriya-yamaka, taught immediately after the Dhamma-yamaka, is now given. Here, the arrangement of the Pāli text should be understood in the same way as in the Khandha-yamaka and the other Yamakas. Indeed, here too, the three great sections beginning with the Designation Section, along with the remaining intermediate sections and the distinctions of time and so on, are similar to those found in the Khandha-yamaka and the other Yamakas. However, because the faculties are numerous, there are more couplets here than even in the Dhātu-yamaka. Just as below in the sections on individuals and so on, in the method based on the eye-sphere and eye-element, the tongue-sphere and body-sphere were not conjoined, and the couplets themselves based on the tongue-sphere and body-sphere were not taken, so too here in the method based on the eye-faculty, the tongue-faculty and body-faculty are not conjoined, and the couplets themselves based on the tongue-faculty and body-faculty are not taken. The reason for their non-inclusion should be understood in the same way as explained there. The mind-faculty, however, since it is conjoined with those rooted in the eye-faculty and so on, just as with those rooted in the femininity-faculty and so on, therefore, without being conjoined in the laid-down order, it should be understood that it is conjoined at the end with all, beginning with the eye-faculty. The femininity-faculty, masculinity-faculty, and life-faculty are conjoined with the eye-faculty; the pleasure-faculty, pain-faculty, and displeasure-faculty are not taken because they are not present at rebirth-linking. The joy-faculty and equanimity-faculty are taken because their arising is possible at rebirth-linking. Similarly, the five faculties beginning with the faith-faculty. The three supramundane faculties are not taken precisely because of their absence at rebirth-linking. Thus, the counting of couplets in the method based on the eye-faculty here should be understood by means of those that are taken. As it is here, so it is everywhere. However, those that are not taken should not be counted as couplets by means of them. Or, if one counts them, they should be counted by means of meaningless questions. Thus, for the time being, the arrangement of the Pāli text in all sections should be understood in this way.

Pavattivāravaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Section on Occurrence

1-86. Atthavinicchaye panettha idaṃ nayamukhaṃ – sacakkhukānaṃ na itthīnanti brahmapārisajjādīnañceva rūpīnaṃ purisanapuṃsakānañca vasena vuttaṃ. Tesañhi itthindriyaṃ nuppajjati. Sacakkhukānaṃ na purisānanti rūpībrahmānañceva itthinapuṃsakānañca vasena vuttaṃ. Tesañhi purisindriyaṃ nuppajjati. Acakkhukānaṃ upapajjantānaṃ tesaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ uppajjatīti ekavokāracatuvokārakāmadhātusatte sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sacakkhukānaṃ vinā somanassenāti upekkhāsahagatānaṃ [M 0.0338] catunnaṃ mahāvipākapaṭisandhīnaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Sacakkhukānaṃ vinā upekkhāyāti somanassasahagatapaṭisandhikānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Upekkhāya acakkhukānanti ahetukapaṭisandhivasena vuttaṃ. Ahetukānanti ahetukapaṭisandhicittena saddhiṃ saddhindriyādīnaṃ abhāvato vuttaṃ. Tattha hi ekanteneva saddhāsatipaññāyo natthi. Samādhivīriyāni pana indriyappattāni na honti. Sahetukānaṃ acakkhukānanti gabbhaseyyakavasena ceva arūpīvasena ca vuttaṃ. Añño hi sahetuko acakkhuko nāma natthi. Sacakkhukānaṃ ahetukānanti apāye opapātikavasena vuttaṃ. Sacakkhukānaṃ ñāṇavippayuttānanti kāmadhātuyaṃ duhetukapaṭisandhikānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Sacakkhukānaṃ ñāṇasampayuttānanti rūpībrahmāno ceva kāmāvacaradevamanusse ca sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ñāṇasampayuttānaṃ acakkhukānanti arūpino ca tihetukagabbhaseyyake ca sandhāya vuttaṃ.

1-86. In the determination of meaning here, this is the method of exposition: “For those with eyes, not females” is stated by way of the Brahmā’s Retinue and other fine-material beings who are male and neuter. For them, the female faculty does not arise. “For those with eyes, not males” is stated by way of the fine-material Brahmās and female and neuter beings. For them, the male faculty does not arise. “For those without eyes, when they are reborn, their life-faculty arises” is stated with reference to beings of the one-constituent and four-constituent planes, and beings of the sense-desire realm. “For those with eyes, without joy” is stated with reference to the four great resultant rebirth-linking consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity. “For those with eyes, without equanimity” is stated with reference to those whose rebirth-linking consciousness is accompanied by joy. “For those without eyes, with equanimity” is stated by way of the rootless rebirth-linking. “Rootless” is stated because of the absence of the faith-faculty and so on, together with the rootless rebirth-linking consciousness. For in that case, there is absolutely no faith, mindfulness, or wisdom. But concentration and energy, though present, do not attain the level of faculties. “For those with roots, without eyes” is stated by way of womb-born beings and formless beings. For there is no other being with roots who is without eyes. “For those with eyes, rootless” is stated by way of spontaneously arisen beings in the planes of misery. “For those with eyes, dissociated from knowledge” is stated with reference to those reborn with two roots in the sense-desire realm. “For those with eyes, associated with knowledge” is stated with reference to the fine-material Brahmās and the gods and humans of the sense-desire realm. “For those without eyes, associated with knowledge” is stated with reference to formless beings and womb-born beings with three roots.

190. Jīvitindriyamūlake vinā somanassena upapajjantānanti dvepi jīvitindriyāni sandhāya vuttaṃ. Pavatte [P 0.0106] somanassavippayuttacittassa uppādakkhaṇeti arūpajīvitindriyaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Iminā nayena sabbatthāpi paṭisandhipavattivasena jīvitindriyayojanā veditabbā. Somanassindriyādimūlakesupi paṭisandhipavattivasenevattho gahetabbo. Paṭilomanaye pana nirodhavāre ca etesañceva aññesañca dhammānaṃ yathālābhavasena cutipaṭisandhipavattesu tīsupi anuppādanirodhā veditabbā.

190. “For those reborn without joy, based on the life-faculty” is stated with reference to both life-faculties. “At the moment of arising of consciousness dissociated from joy in the course of existence” is stated with reference to the formless life-faculty. By this method, the conjoining of the life-faculty should be understood everywhere by way of rebirth-linking and the course of existence. The meaning should be taken similarly for those based on the joy-faculty and others, by way of rebirth-linking and the course of existence. However, in the reverse method and in the cessation section, the non-arising and cessation of these and other phenomena should be understood in all three occurrences—death, rebirth-linking, and the course of existence—according to their obtainability.

281. Anāgatavāre [V 0.0338] eteneva bhāvenāti etena purisabhāveneva, antarā itthibhāvaṃ anāpajjitvā purisapaṭisandhiggahaṇenevāti attho. Katici bhave dassetvā parinibbāyissantīti katici paṭisandhiyo gahetvā itthibhāvaṃ appatvāva parinibbāyissantīti attho. Dutiyapucchāyapi eseva nayo.

281. “In the future section, in this very state” means in this very male state, without undergoing a female state in between, by taking only a male rebirth-linking—this is the meaning. “After manifesting a few existences, they will attain final Nibbāna” means they will attain final Nibbāna after taking a few rebirth-linkings without attaining a female state—this is the meaning. The same method applies to the second question as well.

361. Paccuppannena atītavāre suddhāvāsānaṃ upapatticittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe manindriyañca nuppajjitthāti cittayamake viya uppādakkhaṇātikkamavasena atthaṃ aggahetvā tasmiṃ bhave anuppannapubbavasena gahetabboti. Iminā nayamukhena sabbasmimpi pavattivāre atthavinicchayo veditabbo.

361. In the present-past section, concerning the Pure Abodes, the statement that the mind-faculty also did not arise at the moment of dissolution of the rebirth-consciousness should be understood not by taking the meaning as the moment of arising having passed, as in the Citta Yamaka, but by taking it as not having arisen previously in that existence. By this method of exposition, the determination of meaning should be understood in the entire process section.

Pavattivāravaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Process Section.

Pariññāvāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on Full Understanding.

435-482. Pariññāvāre [M 0.0339] pana cakkhumūlakādīsu ekameva cakkhusotayamakaṃ dassitaṃ. Yasmā pana sesānipi lokiyaabyākatāni ceva lokiyaabyākatamissakāni ca pariññeyyāneva, tasmā tāni anupadiṭṭhānipi imināva dassitāni honti. Yasmā pana akusalaṃ ekantato pahātabbameva, ekantaṃ kusalaṃ bhāvetabbameva, lokuttarābyākataṃ sacchikātabbaṃ, tasmā “domanassindriyaṃ pajahatī”ti “anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ bhāvetī”ti “aññātāvindriyaṃ sacchikarotī”ti vuttaṃ. Aññindriyaṃ pana bhāvetabbampi atthi sacchikātabbampi, taṃ bhāvanāvaseneva gahitaṃ. Tattha dve puggalāti sakadāgāmimaggasamaṅgī ca, arahattamaggasamaṅgī ca. Tesu eko samucchindituṃ asamatthattā domanassindriyaṃ na pajahati nāma. Eko pahīnadosattā cakkhundriyaṃ na parijānātīti anuppādaṃ āpādetuṃ [P 0.0107] asamatthatāya na parijānāti. Iminā nayena sabbavissajjanesu attho veditabboti.

435-482. In the section on full understanding, among the sections beginning with the eye-base, only the eye-ear pair is shown. However, since the remaining mundane indeterminate states and those mixed with mundane indeterminate states are also to be fully understood, they are implicitly indicated by this, even though they are not explicitly stated. Furthermore, since the unwholesome must be entirely abandoned, the wholesome must be entirely developed, and the supramundane indeterminate must be realized, it is therefore said: “One abandons the faculty of displeasure,” “One develops the faculty of ‘I shall know the unknown’,” and “One realizes the faculty of one who has final knowledge.” The faculty of final knowledge (`aññindriya`), however, is both to be developed and to be realized; it is included here only by way of development. Here, “two persons” refers to one who is endowed with the path of the once-returner and one who is endowed with the path of arahantship. Among them, one, being unable to eradicate it, is said not to abandon the faculty of displeasure. The other, due to having abandoned aversion, does not fully understand the eye-faculty—that is, being unable to bring about its non-arising, one does not fully understand it. In this way, the meaning in all the answers should be understood.

Pariññāvāravaṇṇanā.

The Explanation of the Section on Full Understanding.

Indriyayamakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Indriya Yamaka is concluded.

Nigamanakathā

Concluding Verses

Ettāvatā [V 0.0339] ca –

And thus far:

Yassovāde ṭhatvā, niṭṭhitakiccassa kiccasampanno;

Yuvatijanopi atīto, suvihitaniyamo yamassāṇaṃ.

Standing in the instruction of him whose task is finished, one's own task is accomplished; He has gone beyond even the youthful, his discipline is well-ordered, his command is over Death.

Devaparisāya majjhe, devapure sabbadevadevena;

Yamakaṃ nāma pakāsitaṃ, yamāmalalomena yaṃ tena.

In the midst of the assembly of devas, in the city of devas, by the deva of all devas, the treatise called Yamaka was taught by him who is restrained, stainless, and without blemish.

Pāḷivavatthānavidhiṃ, pucchāvissajjane ca atthanayaṃ;

Dassetuṃ āraddhā, yamakaaṭṭhakathā mayā tassa.

I have begun this commentary on the Yamaka in order to show the method of establishing the Pāli text and the way of meaning in questions and answers.

Sā [M 0.0340] subahuantarāye, lokamhi yathā anantarāyena;

Ayamajja pañcamattehi, tantiyā bhāṇavārehi.

May she, in a world with many obstacles, be without obstacle; this day, by means of the text's five recitation measures.

Niṭṭhaṃ pattā evaṃ, niṭṭhānaṃ pāpuṇantu sabbepi;

Hitasukhanibbattikarā, manorathā sabbasattānanti.

Just as this work has reached completion, so may all beings attain the final goal; may the aspirations of all beings, which produce welfare and happiness, be fulfilled.

Yamakappakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Yamaka Treatise is concluded.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Abhidhammapiṭake

In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka

Paṭṭhānappakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā

The Commentary on the Paṭṭhāna Treatise

Devātidevo [M 0.0341][V 0.0340] devānaṃ, devadānavapūjito,

Desayitvā pakaraṇaṃ, yamakaṃ suddhasaṃyamo.

The deva above devas, honored by devas and dānavas, of pure restraint, having taught the Yamaka treatise.

Atthato dhammato ceva, gambhīrassātha tassa yaṃ,

Anantaraṃ mahāvīro, sattamaṃ isisattamo.

And that which is next to that profound treatise in meaning and in Dhamma, that seventh treatise, the Great Hero, the seventh and best of sages, taught.

Paṭṭhānaṃ nāma nāmena, nāmarūpanirodhano,

Desesi atigambhīra-nayamaṇḍitadesanaṃ.

He who brings about the cessation of name-and-form taught the Paṭṭhāna by name, a discourse adorned with extremely profound methods.

Idāni [V 0.0341] tassa sampatto, yasmā saṃvaṇṇanākkamo,

Tasmā naṃ vaṇṇayissāmi, taṃ suṇātha samāhitāti.

Now, since the time has come for its exposition, therefore I shall expound it; listen to it with a focused mind.

Paccayuddesavaṇṇanā

Description of the Exposition of Conditions

Sammāsambuddhena hi anulomapaṭṭhāne dvāvīsati tike nissāya tikapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma niddiṭṭhaṃ, sataṃ duke nissāya dukapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma niddiṭṭhaṃ. Tato paraṃ dvāvīsati tike gahetvā dukasate pakkhipitvā dukatikapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma dassitaṃ. Tato paraṃ dukasataṃ gahetvā dvāvīsatiyā tikesu pakkhipitvā tikadukapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma dassitaṃ. Tike pana tikesuyeva pakkhipitvā tikatikapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma dassitaṃ. Duke ca dukesuyeva pakkhipitvā dukadukapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma dassitaṃ. Evaṃ –

Indeed, by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, in the Anuloma Paṭṭhāna, relying on twenty-two triads, the Tikapaṭṭhāna was designated; relying on one hundred dyads, the Dukapaṭṭhāna was designated. Thereafter, taking the twenty-two triads and inserting them into the hundred dyads, the Dukatikapaṭṭhāna was shown. Then, taking the hundred dyads and inserting them into the twenty-two triads, the Tikadukapaṭṭhāna was shown. Moreover, inserting triads into triads themselves, the Tikatikapaṭṭhāna was shown. And inserting dyads into dyads themselves, the Dukadukapaṭṭhāna was shown. Thus—

Tikañca paṭṭhānavaraṃ dukuttamaṃ,

Dukaṃ tikañceva tikaṃ dukañca;

Tikaṃ tikañceva dukaṃ dukañca,

Cha anulomamhi nayā sugambhīrāti.

The supreme Paṭṭhāna of triads, and the excellent Paṭṭhāna of dyads; the dyad and the triad, and the triad and the dyad; the triad and the triad, and the dyad and the dyad—these six methods in the direct order are very profound.

Paccanīyapaṭṭhānepi [M 0.0342] dvāvīsati tike nissāya tikapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Dukasataṃ nissāya dukapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Dvāvīsati tike dukasate pakkhipitvā dukatikapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Dukasataṃ dvāvīsatiyā tikesu pakkhipitvā tikadukapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Tike tikesuyeva pakkhipitvā tikatikapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Duke dukesuyeva pakkhipitvā dukadukapaṭṭhānaṃ nāmāti evaṃ paccanīyepi chahi nayehi paṭṭhānaṃ niddiṭṭhaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ –

In the Paccanīya Paṭṭhāna also, relying on twenty-two triads, it is called Tikapaṭṭhāna. Relying on one hundred dyads, it is called Dukapaṭṭhāna. Taking the twenty-two triads and inserting them into the hundred dyads, it is called Dukatikapaṭṭhāna. Taking the hundred dyads and inserting them into the twenty-two triads, it is called Tikadukapaṭṭhāna. Inserting triads into triads themselves, it is called Tikatikapaṭṭhāna. Inserting dyads into dyads themselves, it is called Dukadukapaṭṭhāna. Thus, in the Paccanīya also, the Paṭṭhāna is designated by six methods. Therefore it is said:

“Tikañca paṭṭhānavaraṃ dukuttamaṃ,

Dukaṃ tikañceva tikaṃ dukañca;

Tikaṃ tikañceva dukaṃ dukañca,

Cha paccanīyamhi nayā sugambhīrā”ti.

“The supreme Paṭṭhāna of triads, and the excellent Paṭṭhāna of dyads; the dyad and the triad, and the triad and the dyad; the triad and the triad, and the dyad and the dyad—these six methods in the reverse order are very profound.”

Tato [V 0.0342] paraṃ anulomapaccanīyepi etenevupāyena cha nayā dassitā. Tenāha –

Thereafter, in the Anuloma-Paccanīya also, six methods are shown in the same way. Therefore it is said:

“Tikañca paṭṭhānavaraṃ dukuttamaṃ,

Dukaṃ tikañceva tikaṃ dukañca;

Tikaṃ tikañceva dukaṃ dukañca,

Cha anulomapaccanīyamhi nayā sugambhīrā”ti.

“The supreme Paṭṭhāna of triads, and the excellent Paṭṭhāna of dyads; the dyad and the triad, and the triad and the dyad; the triad and the triad, and the dyad and the dyad—these six methods in the direct-reverse order are very profound.”

Tadanantaraṃ paccanīyānulomamhi eteheva chahi nayehi niddiṭṭhaṃ. Tenāha –

Following that, in the Paccanīyānuloma, it is designated by these same six methods. Therefore it is said:

“Tikañca paṭṭhānavaraṃ dukuttamaṃ,

Dukaṃ tikañceva tikaṃ dukañca;

Tikaṃ tikañceva dukaṃ dukañca,

Cha paccanīyānulomamhi nayā sugambhīrā”ti.

“The supreme Paṭṭhāna of triads, and the excellent Paṭṭhāna of dyads; the dyad and the triad, and the triad and the dyad; the triad and the triad, and the dyad and the dyad—these six methods in the reverse-direct order are very profound.”

Evaṃ anulome cha paṭṭhānāni, paccanīye cha, anulomapaccanīye cha, paccanīyānulome cha paṭṭhānānīti idaṃ “catuvīsatisamantapaṭṭhānasamodhānapaṭṭhānamahāpakaraṇaṃ nāmā”ti hi vuttaṃ.

Thus, there are six Paṭṭhānas in the direct order, six in the reverse order, six in the direct-reverse order, and six in the reverse-direct order. Indeed, it has been said: 'This is called the Great Treatise of the Paṭṭhāna, the Compilation of the Twenty-Four Comprehensive Paṭṭhānas'.

Tattha yesaṃ catuvīsatiyā samantapaṭṭhānānaṃ samodhānavasenetaṃ catuvīsatisamantapaṭṭhānasamodhānaṃ paṭṭhānamahāpakaraṇaṃ nāmāti vuttaṃ, tesañceva imassa ca pakaraṇassa nāmattho tāva evaṃ veditabbo. Kenaṭṭhena [M 0.0343] paṭṭhānanti? Nānappakārapaccayaṭṭhena. ‘Pa-kāro’ hi nānappakāratthaṃ dīpeti, ṭhānasaddo paccayatthaṃ. Ṭhānāṭṭhānakusalatātiādīsu hi paccayo ṭhānanti vutto. Iti nānappakārānaṃ paccayānaṃ vasena desitattā imesu catuvīsatiyā paṭṭhānesu ekekaṃ paṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Imesaṃ pana paṭṭhānānaṃ samūhato sabbampetaṃ pakaraṇaṃ paṭṭhānanti veditabbaṃ.

Here, it has been said that this Great Treatise of the Paṭṭhāna, the Compilation of the Twenty-Four Comprehensive Paṭṭhānas, exists by way of synthesizing these twenty-four comprehensive Paṭṭhānas. First, the meaning of the name for both those and this treatise should be understood thus. In what sense is it “Paṭṭhāna”? In the sense of conditions of various kinds. For the prefix ‘pa’ indicates the meaning of variety, and the word ‘ṭhāna’ signifies the meaning of condition. For in phrases such as “skill in conditions and non-conditions,” ‘ṭhāna’ is said to be condition. Thus, because each of these twenty-four Paṭṭhānas is taught by way of various conditions, each is called a Paṭṭhāna. But, collectively, all of this treatise should be understood as Paṭṭhāna.

Aparo nayo – kenaṭṭhena paṭṭhānanti? Vibhajanaṭṭhena. “Paññāpanā paṭṭhapanā vivaraṇā vibhajanā uttānīkamma”nti (ma. ni. 1.371) āgataṭṭhānasmiñhi vibhajanaṭṭhena paṭṭhānaṃ paññāyati. Iti kusalādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ hetupaccayādivasena vibhattattā imesu catuvīsatiyā paṭṭhānesu [V 0.0343] ekekaṃ paṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Imesaṃ pana paṭṭhānānaṃ samūhato sabbampetaṃ pakaraṇaṃ paṭṭhānaṃ nāmāti veditabbaṃ.

Another method: In what sense is it called Paṭṭhāna? In the sense of analysis. For in the passage, “Explanation, establishing, revealing, analysis, making plain,” the term paṭṭhapana is understood in the sense of analysis. Thus, because wholesome and other phenomena are classified by way of root-condition and so on, each of these twenty-four Paṭṭhānas is called a Paṭṭhāna. Collectively, all of this treatise is to be understood as Paṭṭhāna.

Aparo nayo – kenaṭṭhena paṭṭhānanti? Paṭṭhitatthena. Gamanaṭṭhenāti attho. “Goṭṭhā paṭṭhitagāvo”ti (ma. ni. 1.156) āgataṭṭhānasmiñhi yena paṭṭhānena paṭṭhitagāvoti vutto, taṃ atthato gamanaṃ hoti. Iti nātivitthāritanayesu dhammasaṅgaṇīādīsu anissaṅgagamanassa sabbaññutaññāṇassa hetupaccayādibhedabhinnesu kusalādīsu vitthāritanayalābhato nissaṅgavasena pavattagamanattā imesu catuvīsatiyā paṭṭhānesu ekekaṃ paṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Imesaṃ pana paṭṭhānānaṃ samūhato sabbampetaṃ pakaraṇaṃ paṭṭhānaṃ nāmāti veditabbaṃ.

Another method: In what sense is it “Paṭṭhāna”? In the sense of “setting forth.” The meaning is “in the sense of going.” For in the passage “Cows set forth from the pen,” the setting forth by which they are called “cows set forth” is, in meaning, a going. Thus, because the all-knowing knowledge, which proceeds unhindered, obtains extensively elaborated methods in the wholesome and other states, which are divided into root-condition and so on—in contrast to the Dhammasaṅgaṇī and other methods that are not excessively detailed—each of these twenty-four Paṭṭhānas is called a Paṭṭhāna, due to its proceeding in an unhindered manner. However, the collection of these Paṭṭhānas, this entire treatise, should be understood as Paṭṭhāna.

Tattha anulomamhi tāva paṭhamaṃ tikavasena desitattā tikapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. Tassa padacchedo – tikānaṃ paṭṭhānaṃ ettha atthīti tikapaṭṭhānaṃ. Tikānaṃ nānappakārakā paccayā etissā desanāya atthīti attho. Dutiyavikappepi tikānaṃ paṭṭhānantveva tikapaṭṭhānaṃ. Hetupaccayādivasena tikānaṃ vibhajanāti attho. Tatiyavikappe hetupaccayādibhedabhinnatāya laddhavitthārā tikā eva paṭṭhānaṃ tikapaṭṭhānaṃ. Sabbaññutaññāṇassa nissaṅgagamanabhūmīti attho. Dukapaṭṭhānādīsupi eseva nayo. Evaṃ anulome chapaṭṭhānāni viditvā paccanīyādīsupi imināvupāyena veditabbāni.

Here, first, in the direct order, because it is taught by way of triads, it is called Tikapaṭṭhāna. Its word analysis is: “The Paṭṭhāna of triads exists here,” hence Tikapaṭṭhāna. The meaning is that the various kinds of conditions for the triads exist in this teaching. In the second alternative, too, “the Paṭṭhāna of triads” is simply Tikapaṭṭhāna. The meaning is the classification of triads by way of root-condition, etc. In the third alternative, because of the division into root-condition, etc., the triads themselves, having obtained elaboration, are the Paṭṭhāna, hence Tikapaṭṭhāna. The meaning is the sphere of unhindered movement of the all-knowing knowledge. The same method applies to Dukapaṭṭhāna, etc. Thus, having understood the six Paṭṭhānas in the direct order, those in the reverse order, etc., should also be understood by this method.

Yasmā panetāni anulome, paccanīye, anulomapaccanīye, paccanīyānulometi samantā cha cha hutvā catuvīsati honti; tasmā “catuvīsati samantapaṭṭhānānī”ti [M 0.0344] vuccanti. Iti imesaṃ catuvīsatiyā khuddakapaṭṭhānasaṅkhātānaṃ samantapaṭṭhānānaṃ samodhānavasenetaṃ catuvīsatisamantapaṭṭhānasamodhānaṃ paṭṭhānamahāpakaraṇaṃ nāma.

Since these, in the direct order, reverse order, direct-reverse order, and reverse-direct order, become six each on all sides, totaling twenty-four, they are therefore called “the twenty-four comprehensive Paṭṭhānas.” Thus, by way of a compilation of these twenty-four comprehensive Paṭṭhānas, reckoned as the minor Paṭṭhānas, this great treatise is called “Paṭṭhānamahāpakaraṇa,” the Compilation of the Twenty-Four Comprehensive Paṭṭhānas.

Taṃ panetaṃ ye tikādayo nissāya niddiṭṭhattā “tikapaṭṭhānaṃ dukapaṭṭhānaṃ…pe… dukadukapaṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ, te anāmasitvā yesaṃ paccayānaṃ vasena te tikādayo vibhattā te paccaye dassetuṃ ādito tāvassa mātikānikkhepavāro nāma vutto; paccayavibhaṅgavārotipi tasseva nāmaṃ. So uddesaniddesato duvidho. Tassa hetupaccayo…pe… avigatapaccayoti ayaṃ uddeso.

This treatise, because it is expounded based on triads, etc., and is specified as “Tikapaṭṭhāna,” “Dukapaṭṭhāna,”… up to “Dukadukapaṭṭhāna,” without referring to these, but to show the conditions by which these triads, etc., are distinguished, the section called “the laying down of the matrix” is first stated; the section on the analysis of conditions is also its name. It is twofold: by way of enunciation and exposition. Its enunciation is: “Root condition… non-disappearance condition.”

Tattha [V 0.0344] hetu ca so paccayo cāti hetupaccayo. Hetu hutvā paccayo, hetubhāvena paccayoti vuttaṃ hoti. Ārammaṇapaccayādīsupi eseva nayo. Tattha hetūti vacanāvayavakāraṇamūlānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. “Paṭiññā hetū”tiādīsu hi loke vacanāvayavo hetūti, vuccati. Sāsane pana “ye dhammā hetuppabhavā”tiādīsu (mahāva. 60) kāraṇaṃ. “Tayo kusalā hetū, tayo akusalā hetū”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 1059) mūlaṃ hetūti vuccati. Taṃ idha adhippetaṃ. Paccayoti ettha pana ayaṃ vacanattho – paṭicca etasmā etīti paccayo, appaccakkhāya naṃ vattatīti attho. Yo hi dhammo yaṃ dhammaṃ appaccakkhāya tiṭṭhati vā uppajjati vā, so tassa paccayoti vuttaṃ hoti.

Herein, “root condition” means that it is both a root and a condition. It is said to be a condition by being a root, a condition by way of its root-nature. The same method applies to the object condition, etc. Herein, the word “root” (hetu) is a designation for a part of speech, a cause, and a root. In the world, in statements like “acknowledgment is a root,” a part of speech is called a “root.” In the Dispensation, however, in statements like “those phenomena arising from a root,” it means a cause. In statements like “three wholesome roots, three unwholesome roots,” it means a root. That is what is intended here. As for “condition,” here it has this meaning: “that which comes to be in dependence on this” (paṭicca etasmā eti), meaning it proceeds without rejecting it. For whatever phenomenon exists or arises without rejecting another phenomenon, that is said to be its condition.

Lakkhaṇato pana upakārakalakkhaṇo paccayo, yo hi dhammo yassa dhammassa ṭhitiyā vā uppattiyā vā upakārako hoti, so tassa paccayoti vuccati. Paccayo, hetu; kāraṇaṃ nidānaṃ sambhavo, pabhavoti atthato ekaṃ, byañjanato nānaṃ. Iti mūlaṭṭhena hetu, upakārakaṭṭhena paccayoti saṅkhepato mūlaṭṭhena upakārako dhammo hetupaccayo. So hi sāliādīnaṃ sālibījādīni viya, maṇippabhādīnaṃ viya ca maṇivaṇṇādayo kusalādīnaṃ kusalādibhāvasādhakoti ācariyānaṃ adhippāyo. Evaṃ sante pana taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpesu hetupaccayatā na sampajjati. Na hi so tesaṃ kusalādibhāvaṃ sādheti, na ca paccayo na hotīti. Vuttañhetaṃ “hetū hetusampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca [M 0.0345] rūpānaṃ hetupaccayena paccayo”ti. Ahetukacittānañca vinā etena abyākatabhāvo siddho.

By way of characteristic, a condition has the characteristic of assisting. For whatever phenomenon assists in the stability or arising of another phenomenon, that is called its condition. Condition, root, cause, origin, source, and genesis—these are one in meaning, but different in expression. Thus, briefly, it is a root by way of its fundamental meaning, and a condition by way of its assisting meaning. A phenomenon that assists by way of its fundamental meaning is the root condition. For, according to the teachers' intention, just as rice seeds and so forth are for rice and so forth, and the color of a gem and so forth is for the gem's radiance and so forth, so it establishes the wholesome nature of wholesome states and so forth. However, if this is the case, the status of root condition does not apply to co-arisen material phenomena. For it does not establish their wholesome nature, and yet it is a condition. For it is said: “The roots are a condition by the root condition for the phenomena associated with the roots and for the material phenomena co-arisen with them.” Moreover, without this, the indeterminate nature of rootless consciousness is established.

Sahetukānampi ca yonisomanasikārādipaṭibaddho kusalādibhāvo na sampayuttahetupaṭibaddho. Yadi ca sampayuttahetūsu sabhāvatova kusalādibhāvo siyā, taṃsampayuttesu hetupaṭibaddho alobho kusalo vā siyā abyākato vā. Yasmā pana ubhayathāpi hoti, tasmā yathā sampayuttesu, evaṃ hetūsupi kusalāditā pariyesitabbā. Kusalādibhāvasādhanavasena pana hetūnaṃ mūlaṭṭhaṃ aggahetvā suppatiṭṭhitabhāvasādhanavasena gayhamāne na kiñci virujjhati. Laddhahetupaccayā hi dhammā viruḷhamūlā viya pādapā thirā honti suppatiṭṭhitā, ahetukā pana tilabījakādisevālā viya na suppatiṭṭhitā. Iti mūlaṭṭhena upakārakoti suppatiṭṭhitabhāvasādhanena upakārako dhammo hetupaccayoti veditabbo.

And for those with roots, the wholesome nature, etc., is connected with wise attention, etc., not dependent on the associated roots. And if the wholesome nature, etc., were naturally present in the associated roots, then non-greed, being connected with them, would be either wholesome or indeterminate. However, since it occurs in both ways, the wholesome nature, etc., must be sought in the roots just as it is in the associated factors. However, if the roots' fundamental meaning is not taken as establishing the wholesome nature, etc., but is taken as establishing firmness, then nothing is contradicted. For phenomena that have obtained the root condition, like trees with well-grown roots, become firm and well-established. Rootless phenomena, however, like moss or water plants on sesame seeds, are not well-established. Thus, it should be understood that a phenomenon that assists by way of its fundamental meaning, that is, by establishing firmness, is the root condition.

Tato [V 0.0345] paresu ārammaṇavasena upakārako dhammo ārammaṇapaccayo. So “rūpāyatanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā”ti ārabhitvāpi “yaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ ārabbha ye ye dhammā uppajjanti cittacetasikā dhammā, te te dhammā tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti osāpitattā na koci dhammo na hoti. Yathā hi dubbalo puriso daṇḍaṃ vā rajjuṃ vā ālambitvāva uṭṭhahati ceva tiṭṭhati ca, evaṃ cittacetasikā dhammā rūpādiārammaṇaṃ ārabbheva uppajjanti ceva tiṭṭhanti ca. Tasmā sabbepi cittacetasikānaṃ dhammānaṃ ārammaṇabhūtā dhammā ārammaṇapaccayoti veditabbā.

Next, a phenomenon that assists by way of an object is the object condition. And although it begins with “the form base is for the eye-consciousness element,” because it concludes with “Whatever mental states and mental factors arise in dependence on whatever phenomena as objects, those phenomena are a condition for those respective phenomena by way of the object condition,” no phenomenon is excluded. Just as a weak person rises and stands only by relying on a stick or a rope, so too do mental states and mental factors arise and persist only by relying on form and other objects. Therefore, all phenomena that serve as objects for mental states and mental factors should be understood as the object condition.

Jeṭṭhakaṭṭhena upakārako dhammo adhipatipaccayo. So sahajātārammaṇavasena duvidho. Tattha “chandādhipati chandasampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ adhipatipaccayena paccayo”tiādivacanato chandavīriyacittavīmaṃsasaṅkhātā cattāro dhammā sahajātādhipatipaccayoti veditabbā, no ca kho ekato. Yadā hi chandaṃ dhuraṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā cittaṃ pavattati, tadā chandova adhipati, na itare. Esa nayo sesesupi. Yaṃ pana dhammaṃ garuṃ katvā arūpadhammā pavattanti, so nesaṃ ārammaṇādhipati. Tena [M 0.0346] vuttaṃ – “yaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ garuṃ katvā ye ye dhammā uppajjanti cittacetasikā dhammā, te te dhammā tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ adhipatipaccayena paccayo”ti.

A phenomenon that assists by way of pre-eminence is the dominant condition. It is twofold: by way of co-nascence and by way of object. Herein, from the statement beginning “Desire as dominant condition is a condition by way of dominant condition for the phenomena associated with desire and for the material phenomena co-arisen with them,” it should be understood that the four phenomena—namely, desire, energy, consciousness, and investigation—are co-nascent dominant conditions, but not simultaneously. For when consciousness proceeds making desire the foremost and chief, then desire alone is the dominant condition, not the others. The same method applies to the rest. However, when immaterial phenomena proceed by taking a certain phenomenon as weighty, that is their object dominant condition. Hence it is said: “By taking whatever phenomena as weighty, whatever mental states and mental factors arise, those phenomena are a condition for those respective phenomena by way of dominant condition.”

Anantarabhāvena upakārako dhammo anantarapaccayo. Samanantarabhāvena upakārako dhammo samanantarapaccayo. Idañca paccayadvayaṃ bahudhā papañcayanti. Ayaṃ panettha sāro – yo hi esa cakkhuviññāṇānantarā manodhātu, manodhātuanantarā manoviññāṇadhātūtiādi cittaniyamo, so yasmā purimacittavaseneva ijjhati, na aññathā. Tasmā attano attano anantaraṃ anurūpassa cittuppādassa uppādanasamatthova dhammo anantarapaccayo. Tenevāha – “anantarapaccayoti cakkhuviññāṇadhātu taṃsampayuttakā ca dhammā manodhātuyā taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ anantarapaccayena paccayo”tiādi.

A phenomenon that assists by way of contiguity is the contiguous condition. A phenomenon that assists by way of immediate contiguity is the immediate contiguous condition. These two conditions are elaborated in many ways. But here is the essence: The sequence of consciousness, such as the mind-element immediately following eye-consciousness, and the mind-consciousness-element immediately following the mind-element, etc., succeeds only through the preceding consciousness, and not otherwise. Therefore, a phenomenon capable of producing the arising of a suitable consciousness immediately after itself is the contiguous condition. Hence it is said: 'The eye-consciousness-element and its associated phenomena are a condition for the mind-element and its associated phenomena by way of the contiguous condition,' and so on.

Yo anantarapaccayo, sveva samanantarapaccayo. Byañjanamattameva hettha nānaṃ, upacayasantatiādīsu viya, adhivacananiruttidukādīsu viya ca, atthato pana nānaṃ natthi. Yampi “addhānantaratāya anantarapaccayo, kālānantaratāya samanantarapaccayo”ti ācariyānaṃ mataṃ[V 0.0346], taṃ “nirodhā vuṭṭhahantassa nevasaññānāsaññāyatanakusalaṃ phalasamāpattiyā samanantarapaccayena paccayo”tiādīhi virujjhati. Yampi tattha vadanti – “dhammānaṃ samuṭṭhāpanasamatthatā na parihāyati, bhāvanābalena pana vāritattā dhammā samanantaraṃ nuppajjantī”ti, tampi kālānantaratāya abhāvameva sādheti. Bhāvanābalena hi tattha kālānantaratā natthīti, mayampi etadeva vadāma. Yasmā ca kālānantaratā natthi, tasmā samanantarapaccayatā na yujjati. Kālānantaratāya hi tesaṃ samanantarapaccayo hotīti laddhi. Tasmā abhinivesaṃ akatvā byañjanamattatovettha nānākaraṇaṃ paccetabbaṃ, na atthato. Kathaṃ? Natthi etesaṃ antaranti hi anantarā. Saṇṭhānābhāvato suṭṭhu anantarāti samanantarā.

What is the contiguous condition is precisely the immediate contiguous condition. Here, the difference is merely in expression, as in the cases of accumulation and continuity, etc., or designation and expression, etc., but there is no difference in meaning. Even the teachers' view that 'the contiguous condition is due to uninterruptedness in time, and the immediate contiguous condition is due to temporal contiguity' is contradicted by statements such as 'for one emerging from cessation, the wholesome state of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a condition for fruition attainment by way of the immediate contiguous condition,' and so on. Even what they say there—'the capacity to produce phenomena does not diminish, but because they are prevented by the power of development, phenomena do not arise immediately contiguously'—this too only proves the absence of temporal contiguity. For there, due to the power of development, temporal contiguity does not exist—this is what we also say. And since temporal contiguity does not exist, the status of an immediate contiguous condition is untenable. For the doctrine is that their immediate contiguous condition is due to temporal contiguity. Therefore, without insisting on this, the distinction here should be accepted as merely terminological, not substantial. How so? 'There is nothing between them'—thus they are contiguous. 'Being thoroughly contiguous due to the absence of any interval'—thus they are immediate contiguous.

Uppajjamāno saha uppajjamānabhāvena upakārako dhammo sahajātapaccayo, pakāsassa padīpo viya. So arūpakkhandhādivasena chabbidho hoti. Yathāha – cattāro khandhā arūpino aññamaññaṃ sahajātapaccayena paccayo. Cattāro mahābhūtā aññamaññaṃ…pe… okkantikkhaṇe nāmarūpaṃ [M 0.0347] aññamaññaṃ…pe… cittacetasikā dhammā cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ rūpānaṃ…pe… mahābhūtā upādārūpānaṃ…pe… rūpino dhammā arūpīnaṃ dhammānaṃ kiñcikāle sahajātapaccayena paccayo; kiñci kāle na sahajātapaccayena paccayoti. Idaṃ hadayavatthumeva sandhāya vuttaṃ.

A phenomenon that assists by way of arising together is the co-nascence condition, like a lamp for light. It is sixfold by way of the immaterial aggregates, etc. As it is said: 'The four immaterial aggregates are a condition for each other by way of the co-nascence condition. The four great elements are a condition for each other… At the moment of conception, name-and-form are a condition for each other… Consciousness and mental factors are a condition for mind-originated material phenomena… The great elements are a condition for derived material phenomena… Material phenomena are sometimes a condition for immaterial phenomena by way of the co-nascence condition; sometimes they are not a condition by way of the co-nascence condition.' This is said with reference to the heart-base.

Aññamaññaṃ uppādanupatthambhanabhāvena upakārako dhammo aññamaññapaccayo. Aññamaññupatthambhakaṃ tidaṇḍaṃ viya. So arūpakkhandhādivasena tividho hoti. Yathāha – cattāro khandhā arūpino aññamaññapaccayena paccayo. Cattāro mahābhūtā…pe… okkantikkhaṇe nāmarūpaṃ aññamaññapaccayena paccayoti.

A phenomenon that assists by way of mutually producing and supporting is the mutuality condition. Like three sticks mutually supporting each other. It is threefold by way of the immaterial aggregates, etc. As it is said: 'The four immaterial aggregates are a condition for each other by way of the mutuality condition. The four great elements… At the moment of conception, name-and-form are a condition for each other by way of the mutuality condition.'

Adhiṭṭhānākārena nissayākārena ca upakārako dhammo nissayapaccayo, tarucittakammādīnaṃ pathavīpaṭādayo viya. So “cattāro khandhā arūpino aññamaññaṃ nissayapaccayena paccayo”ti evaṃ sahajāte vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Chaṭṭho panettha koṭṭhāso “cakkhāyatanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā, sotaghānajivhākāyāyatanaṃ kāyaviññāṇadhātuyā taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ nissayapaccayena paccayo. Yaṃ rūpaṃ nissāya manodhātu ca manoviññāṇadhātu ca vattanti[V 0.0347], taṃ rūpaṃ manodhātuyā ca manoviññāṇadhātuyā ca taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ nissayapaccayena paccayo”ti evaṃ vibhatto.

A phenomenon that is helpful by way of being a foundation and a basis is the dependence condition, like the earth and so on for trees, paintings, etc. It should be understood in the same way as explained in the conascence condition: “The four immaterial aggregates are a condition for each other by dependence condition.” The sixth section here is distinguished thus: “The eye-base is a condition for the eye-consciousness element by dependence condition. The ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, and body-base are a condition for the body-consciousness element and its associated phenomena by dependence condition. That material form on which the mind-element and mind-consciousness element depend is a condition for the mind-element, the mind-consciousness element, and their associated phenomena by dependence condition.”

Upanissayapaccayoti idha pana ayaṃ tāva vacanattho – tadadhīnavuttitāya attano phalena nissito, na paṭikkhittoti nissayo. Yathā pana bhuso āyāso upāyāso, evaṃ bhuso nissayo upanissayo. Balavakāraṇassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tasmā balavakāraṇabhāvena upakārako dhammo upanissayapaccayoti veditabbo. So ārammaṇūpanissayo, anantarūpanissayo pakatūpanissayoti tividho hoti. Tattha “dānaṃ datvā sīlaṃ samādiyitvā uposathakammaṃ katvā taṃ garuṃ katvā paccavekkhati, pubbe suciṇṇāni garuṃ katvā paccavekkhati, jhānā vuṭṭhahitvā jhānaṃ garuṃ katvā paccavekkhati, sekkhā gotrabhuṃ garuṃ katvā paccavekkhanti, vodānaṃ garuṃ katvā paccavekkhanti, sekkhā maggā vuṭṭhahitvā maggaṃ garuṃ katvā paccavekkhantī”ti evamādinā nayena ārammaṇūpanissayo tāva ārammaṇādhipatinā saddhiṃ nānattaṃ akatvā vibhatto. Tattha yaṃ ārammaṇaṃ garuṃ katvā cittacetasikā uppajjanti, taṃ niyamato tesaṃ ārammaṇesu balavārammaṇaṃ hoti[M 0.0348]. Iti garukātabbamattaṭṭhena ārammaṇādhipati, balavakāraṇaṭṭhena ārammaṇūpanissayoti evametesaṃ nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

As for the decisive support condition, first, its meaning here is this: because its occurrence is dependent on that, it is depended upon by its own result, not rejected—thus it is a support (nissaya). Just as intense effort is extreme effort, so intense support is decisive support. This is a designation for a strong cause. Therefore, a phenomenon that is helpful by way of being a strong cause should be understood as a decisive support condition. It is of three kinds: object decisive support, immediately contiguous decisive support, and natural decisive support. Here, object decisive support is distinguished without making a difference from the object-dominance condition, in such ways as: “Having given a gift, undertaken virtue, performed the Uposatha observance, one reviews that, making it important. Having previously done good deeds, one reviews them, making them important. Having arisen from jhāna, one reviews the jhāna, making it important. Disciples review the change-of-lineage, making it important. They review purification, making it important. Disciples, having arisen from the path, review the path, making it important.” Herein, whatever object is made important, and upon which consciousness and mental factors arise, that is invariably a strong object for them. Thus, the distinction between these should be understood as: object-dominance condition by way of being something to be made important, and object decisive support by way of being a strong cause.

Anantarūpanissayopi “purimā purimā kusalā khandhā pacchimānaṃ pacchimānaṃ kusalānaṃ khandhānaṃ upanissayapaccayena paccayo”tiādinā nayena anantarapaccayena saddhiṃ nānattaṃ akatvāva vibhatto. Mātikānikkhepe pana nesaṃ “cakkhuviññāṇadhātu taṃsampayuttakā ca dhammā manodhātuyā taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ anantarapaccayena paccayo”tiādinā nayena anantarassa ca “purimā purimā kusalā dhammā pacchimānaṃ pacchimānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upanissayapaccayena paccayo”tiādinā nayena upanissayassa ca āgatattā nikkhepaviseso atthi, sopi atthato ekībhāvameva gacchati. Evaṃ santepi attano attano anantaraṃ anurūpassa cittuppādassa pavattanasamatthatāya anantaratā purimacittassa ca pacchimacittuppādane balavatāya anantarūpanissayatā veditabbā. Yathā hi hetupaccayādīsu kañci dhammaṃ vināpi cittaṃ uppajjati, na evaṃ anantaracittaṃ, vinā cittassa uppatti nāma atthi, tasmā balavapaccayo hoti. Iti attano attano anantaraṃ anurūpacittuppādavasena anantarapaccayo, balavakāraṇavasena anantarūpanissayoti evametesaṃ nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

The immediate decisive support condition is also explained without making a distinction from the contiguity condition, as in the phrase: “The preceding wholesome aggregates are a condition for the succeeding wholesome aggregates by way of the decisive support condition,” and so on. However, in the exposition of the matrix, since both the contiguity condition, as in “The eye-consciousness element and its associated phenomena are a condition for the mind-element and its associated phenomena by way of the contiguity condition,” and so on, and the decisive support condition, as in “The preceding wholesome phenomena are a condition for the succeeding wholesome phenomena by way of the decisive support condition,” and so on, are presented, there is a specific exposition, but in meaning, it amounts to the same thing. Even so, contiguity is to be understood by way of the ability to bring about the arising of a suitable mind immediately after itself, and the immediate decisive support by way of the strength of the preceding mind in producing the subsequent mind. For just as a mind arises even without some phenomena in the case of root conditions, etc., it is not so without an immediately preceding mind; there is no such thing as the arising of a mind without a [preceding] mind. Therefore, it is a strong condition. Thus, the contiguity condition is by way of the arising of a suitable mind immediately after itself, and the immediate decisive support by way of being a strong cause. In this way, their distinction should be understood.

Pakatūpanissayo [V 0.0348] pana pakato upanissayo pakatūpanissayo. Pakato nāma attano santāne nipphādito vā saddhāsīlādi; upasevito vā utubhojanādi. Pakatiyāyeva vā upanissayo pakatūpanissayo, ārammaṇānantarehi asammissoti attho. Tassa “pakatūpanissayo – saddhaṃ upanissāya dānaṃ deti, sīlaṃ samādiyati, uposathakammaṃ karoti, jhānaṃ uppādeti, vipassanaṃ uppādeti, maggaṃ uppādeti, abhiññaṃ uppādeti, samāpattiṃ uppādeti, sīlaṃ… sutaṃ… cāgaṃ… paññaṃ upanissāya dānaṃ deti…pe… samāpattiṃ uppādeti. Saddhā… sīlaṃ… sutaṃ… cāgo… paññā saddhāya… sīlassa… sutassa… cāgassa… paññāya upanissayapaccayena paccayo”tiādinā nayena anekappakārako pabhedo veditabbo. Iti ime saddhādayo pakatā ceva balavakāraṇaṭṭhena upanissayā cāti pakatūpanissayoti.

Natural decisive support, however, is a decisive support that is natural. ‘Natural’ means something produced in one’s own continuum, such as faith, virtue, etc.; or something made use of, such as climate, food, etc. Alternatively, it is natural decisive support because it is a decisive support by its very nature, meaning it is not mixed with object or contiguity conditions. Its manifold divisions should be understood by way of such phrases as: “Having taken faith as decisive support, one gives a gift, undertakes virtue, observes the Uposatha, develops jhāna, develops insight, develops the path, develops supernormal knowledge, attains meditative attainments. Having taken virtue… learning… generosity… wisdom as decisive support, one gives a gift…pe… attains meditative attainments. Faith… virtue… learning… generosity… wisdom are a condition for faith… virtue… learning… generosity… wisdom by way of the decisive support condition.” Thus, these things such as faith are both natural and decisive supports in the sense of being strong causal factors; therefore, they are called natural decisive supports.

Paṭhamataraṃ uppajjitvā vattamānabhāvena upakārako dhammo purejātapaccayo. So pañcadvāre vatthārammaṇahadayavatthuvasena ekādasavidho hoti[M 0.0349]. Yathāha – cakkhāyatanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ purejātapaccayena paccayo. Sota… ghāna… jivhā… kāyāyatanaṃ, rūpāyatanaṃ, sadda… gandha… rasa… phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ, kāyaviññāṇadhātuyā taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ purejātapaccayena paccayo. Rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ manodhātuyā taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ purejātapaccayena paccayo. Yaṃ rūpaṃ nissāya manodhātu ca manoviññāṇadhātu ca vattanti, taṃ rūpaṃ manodhātuyā taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ purejātapaccayena paccayo, manoviññāṇadhātuyā taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ kiñci kāle purejātapaccayena paccayo, kiñci kāle na purejātapaccayena paccayoti.

The phenomenon that is helpful by having arisen earlier and being present is the pre-nascence condition. It is of eleven kinds by way of the five sense-bases, the five sense-objects, and the heart-base. As it is said: “The eye-base is a condition for the eye-consciousness element and its associated phenomena by way of the pre-nascence condition. The ear-base… nose-base… tongue-base… body-base; the visible form base, sound base… odor base… taste base… tangible base are a condition for the body-consciousness element and its associated phenomena by way of the pre-nascence condition. The visible-form base, sound base, odor base, taste base, and tangible base are a condition for the mind-element and its associated phenomena by way of the pre-nascence condition. That material form on which the mind-element and the mind-consciousness element function is a condition for the mind-element and its associated phenomena by way of the pre-nascence condition; and for the mind-consciousness element and its associated phenomena, at some times it is a pre-nascence condition, and at other times it is not a pre-nascence condition.”

Purejātānaṃ rūpadhammānaṃ upatthambhakaṭṭhena upakārako arūpadhammo pacchājātapaccayo, gijjhapotakasarīrānaṃ āhārāsācetanā viya. Tena vuttaṃ – “pacchājātā cittacetasikā dhammā purejātassa imassa kāyassa pacchājātapaccayena paccayo”ti.

The immaterial phenomenon that is helpful by way of supporting pre-nascent material phenomena is the post-nascence condition, like the volition of desire for food supporting the bodies of vulture chicks. Therefore, it is said: “Post-nascent consciousness and mental factors are a condition for this pre-nascent body by way of the post-nascence condition.”
