Vīsatimūlake paṭhamaekūnavīsatikena saddhiṃ vippayuttapaccayādīsu pañcasu paccayesu ekamekassa yojanāvasena pañcavīsatikā honti. Tesu ekamekasmiṃ ekūnapaññāsaṃ katvā –

In the twenty-root method, together with the first novendecuplet, five sets of twenty are formed by combining each of the five conditions beginning with the dissociation condition. In each of these, forty-nine are made—

Dve satā honti pucchānaṃ, cattālīsā ca pañca ca;

Pucchā gaṇanato honti, naye vīsatimūlake.

Two hundred and forty-five questions are counted in the twenty-root method.

Ekavīsatimūlake paṭhamavīsatikena saddhiṃ atthipaccayādīsu catūsu paccayesu ekamekassa yojanāvasena cattāro ekavīsatikā honti. Tesu ekamekasmiṃ ekūnapaññāsaṃ katvā –

In the twenty-one-root method, together with the first vicenuplet, four sets of twenty-one are formed by combining each of the four conditions beginning with the presence condition. In each of these, forty-nine are made—

Sataṃ chanavuti ceva, pucchā honti sampiṇḍitā;

Gaṇitā lakkhaṇaññūhi, ekavīsatike naye.

One hundred and ninety-six questions are thus compiled, reckoned by those skilled in reckoning, in the twenty-one-root method.

Dvāvīsatimūlake paṭhamaekavīsatikena saddhiṃ natthipaccayādīsu tīsu paccayesu ekamekassa yojanāvasena tayo dvāvīsatikā honti. Tesu ekamekasmiṃ ekūnapaññāsaṃ katvā –

In the twenty-two-root method, together with the first unvicenuplet, three sets of twenty-two are formed by combining each of the three conditions beginning with the absence condition. In each of these, forty-nine are made—

Cattālīsādhikaṃ sataṃ, satta ceva punāparā;

Pucchā gaṇanato honti, naye dvāvīsatimūlake.

One hundred and forty-seven questions are counted in the twenty-two-root method.

Tevīsatimūlake [M 0.0402] paṭhamadvāvīsatikena saddhiṃ dvīsu vigatāvigatapaccayesu ekamekassa yojanāvasena dve tevīsatikā honti. Tesu ekamekasmiṃ ekūnapaññāsaṃ katvā –

In the twenty-three-root method, together with the first duovicenuplet, two sets of twenty-three are formed by combining each of the two conditions, disappearance and non-disappearance. In each of these, forty-nine are made—

Aṭṭhanavutimevidha, pucchā gaṇanato matā;

Nayamhi tevīsatime, tevīsatikamūlake.

Ninety-eight questions are considered in this way in the twenty-three-root method.

Catuvīsatimūlako [V 0.0400] pana sabbapaccayānaṃ samodhānavasena veditabbo, teneva sabbamūlakoti vutto. Tattha ekūnapaññāsameva pucchā hontīti sabbāpetā hetupaccayapadameva gahetvā ekamūlakādīnaṃ sabbamūlakapariyosānānaṃ vasena satthārā devaparisati vitthārato vibhattā pucchā idha saṅkhepena dassitā.

The method with twenty-four roots, however, is to be understood as the combination of all conditions; hence, it is called the all-root. In that, there are indeed forty-nine questions. All these questions, taking only the root-condition term, were explained in detail by the Teacher in the assembly of devas, in the manner of the single-root and so on, up to the all-root conclusion, but here they are shown briefly.

Tāsaṃ pana sabbāsampi ayaṃ gaṇanapiṇḍo – ekamūlakanayasmiñhi ekādasa satāni chasattati ca pucchā āgatā. Hetupaccayanaye teneva mūlakena ekūnapaññāsaṃ katvā imasmiṃ hetupaccayamūlake gahetabbā, sesā sesapaccayamūlakesu pakkhipitabbā. Dumūlake sattavīsāni ekādasa satāni, timūlake sahassaṃ aṭṭhasattati ca, catumūlake sahassaṃ ekūnatiṃsañca, pañcamūlake asītādhikāni nava satāni, chamūlake ekatiṃsāni nava satāni, sattamūlake dvāsītāni aṭṭha satāni, aṭṭhamūlake tettiṃsāni aṭṭha satāni, navamūlake caturāsītāni satta satāni, dasamūlake pañcatiṃsāni satta satāni, ekādasamūlake chāsītāni cha satāni, dvādasamūlake sattatiṃsāni cha satāni, terasamūlake aṭṭhāsītāni pañca satāni, cuddasamūlake ekūnacattālīsāni pañca satāni, pannarasamūlake navutāni cattāri satāni, soḷasamūlake ekacattālīsāni cattāri sattāni, sattarasamūlake dvānavutāni tīṇi satāni, aṭṭhārasamūlake tecattālīsāni tīṇi satāni, ekūnavīsatimūlake catunavutāni dve satāni, vīsatimūlake pañcacattālīsāni dve satāni, ekavīsatimūlake chanavutisataṃ, dvāvīsatimūlake sattacattālīsasataṃ, tevīsatimūlake aṭṭhanavuti, sabbamūlake ekūnapaññāsāti evaṃ hetupadaṃ ādiṃ katvā vibhattesu ekamūlakādīsu –

Among all of these, this is the summary count: In the single-root method, there are eleven hundred and seventy-six questions. In the root condition method, forty-nine questions should be taken for this root condition root itself, and the rest should be placed in the remaining condition-roots. In the two-root method, there are eleven hundred and twenty-seven. In the three-root method, one thousand and seventy-eight. In the four-root method, one thousand and twenty-nine. In the five-root method, nine hundred and eighty. In the six-root method, nine hundred and thirty-one. In the seven-root method, eight hundred and eighty-two. In the eight-root method, eight hundred and thirty-three. In the nine-root method, seven hundred and eighty-four. In the ten-root method, seven hundred and thirty-five. In the eleven-root method, six hundred and eighty-six. In the twelve-root method, six hundred and thirty-seven. In the thirteen-root method, five hundred and eighty-eight. In the fourteen-root method, five hundred and thirty-nine. In the fifteen-root method, four hundred and ninety. In the sixteen-root method, four hundred and forty-one. In the seventeen-root method, three hundred and ninety-two. In the eighteen-root method, three hundred and forty-three. In the nineteen-root method, two hundred and ninety-four. In the twenty-root method, two hundred and forty-five. In the twenty-one-root method, one hundred and ninety-six. In the twenty-two-root method, one hundred and forty-seven. In the twenty-three-root method, ninety-eight. In the all-root method, forty-nine. Thus, having distinguished beginning with the root-condition term, in the single-root and so on...

Cuddaseva sahassāni, puna satta satāni ca;

Pucchā hetupadasseva, ekamūlādibhedatoti.

Fourteen thousand, and again seven hundred; these are the questions of the root-condition term, by way of the divisions beginning with the single-root.

39-40. Evaṃ [M 0.0403] hetupaccayaṃ ādiṃ katvā ekamūlakato paṭṭhāya yāva sabbamūlakanayā pucchābhedaṃ dassetvā idāni ārammaṇapaccayaṃ ādiṃ katvā dassetuṃ siyā kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca kusalo dhammo uppajjeyya ārammaṇapaccayā hetupaccayātiādimāha. Tattha ārammaṇapaccayā hetupaccayāti ettāvatā ārammaṇapaccayaṃ ādiṃ katvā hetupaccayapariyosāno ekamūlakanayo dassito. Tato paraṃ ārammaṇapaccayā adhipatipaccayāti dukamūlakaṃ āraddhaṃ. Tattha imaṃ paṭhamadukañceva [V 0.0401] ārammaṇāvigatadukañca dassetvā sesaṃ saṅkhittaṃ. Ārammaṇapaccayā hetupaccayāti ayaṃ osānadukopi na dassito. Sace pana katthaci vācanāmagge sandissati, sveva vācanāmaggo gahetabbo. Tato paraṃ ārammaṇapaccayavasena tikamūlakādayo adassetvāva adhipatipaccayaṃ ādiṃ katvā ekakādayo dassetuṃ adhipatipaccayā, anantarapaccayā, samanantarapaccayā, sahajātapaccayā, aññamaññapaccayāti ettakameva vuttaṃ, taṃ ekamūlakavasena vā sabbamūlakavasena vā veditabbaṃ.

39-40. Having thus shown the divisions of questions, beginning with the root condition and extending from the single-root method up to the all-root method, now, to show them beginning with the object condition, he said, beginning with: 'A wholesome state arises dependent on a wholesome state by way of object condition and root condition,' and so on. Herein, by 'by way of object condition and root condition,' the single-root method is shown, beginning with the object condition and ending with the root condition. Thereafter, the two-root method is commenced with 'by way of object condition and predominance condition.' Herein, this first dyad and the object-non-disappearance dyad are shown, while the rest are condensed. The concluding dyad, 'by way of object condition and root condition,' is also not shown here. But if it appears somewhere in the course of the reading, that very course of reading should be adopted. After that, without showing the three-root method and so forth by way of object condition, to show the single-root and so on, beginning with the predominance condition, only this much is said: 'by way of predominance condition, immediately preceding condition, contiguity condition, conascent condition, and mutuality condition.' This should be understood either by way of the single-root or the all-root method.

41. Tato paraṃ avigatapaccayaṃ ādiṃ katvā dumūlakameva dassetuṃ – avigatapaccayā hetupaccayātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha avigatahetuduko, avigatārammaṇaduko, avigatādhipatidukoti paṭipāṭiyā tayo duke vatvā pariyosāne ca avigatavigataduko eko duko dassito. Tato avigatapaccayavaseneva timūlakaṃ dassetuṃ – “avigatapaccayā hetupaccayā ārammaṇapaccayā, avigatapaccayā hetupaccayā adhipatipaccayā, avigatapaccayā hetupaccayā anantarapaccayā”ti evaṃ paṭipāṭiyā tayo tike vatvā “avigatapaccayā hetupaccayā vigatapaccayā”ti pariyosānattiko vutto. Tato avigatapaccayavaseneva catumūlakaṃ dassetuṃ “avigatapaccayā hetupaccayā ārammaṇapaccayā adhipatipaccayā, avigatapaccayā hetupaccayā ārammaṇapaccayā anantarapaccayā”ti dve catukke vatvā “vigatapaccayā”ti padaṃ uddharitvā ṭhapitaṃ, sesaṃ sabbaṃ saṅkhittaṃ. Tassa saṅkhittabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “ekekassa padassa ekamūlakaṃ, dumūlakaṃ, timūlakaṃ, sabbamūlakaṃ asammuyhantena vitthāretabba”nti vuttaṃ. Tasmā yathā hetupaccayaṃ ādiṃ katvā hetuādipadavasena ekamūlake ekādasa pucchāsatāni chasattati ca pucchā…pe… sabbamūlake ekūnapaññāsaṃ, evaṃ ārammaṇapaccayādīsupi ekamekaṃ ādiṃ katvā ārammaṇādipadavasena ekamekassa [M 0.0404] padassa ekamūlake ekādasa pucchāsatāni chasattati ca pucchā…pe… sabbamūlake ekūnapaññāsāti ekekassa padassa ekamūlakādibhede sattasatādhikāni cuddasa pucchā sahassāni honti. Tāsaṃ sabbesupi catuvīsatiyā paccayesu ayaṃ gaṇanaparicchedo –

41. Then, to show only the two-rooted method, beginning with the non-disappearance condition, the section beginning with 'by way of non-disappearance condition, root condition,' and so on, is commenced. Herein, three dyads are stated in sequence: the non-disappearance-root dyad, the non-disappearance-object dyad, and the non-disappearance-predominance dyad. And at the end, the non-disappearance-disappearance dyad is shown as one dyad. Next, to show the three-rooted method by way of the non-disappearance condition: 'by way of non-disappearance condition, root condition, object condition; by way of non-disappearance condition, root condition, predominance condition; by way of non-disappearance condition, root condition, contiguity condition'—thus, three triplets are stated in sequence, and at the end, the concluding triplet 'by way of non-disappearance condition, root condition, disappearance condition' is stated. Then, to show the four-rooted method by way of the non-disappearance condition: 'by way of non-disappearance condition, root condition, object condition, predominance condition; by way of non-disappearance condition, root condition, object condition, contiguity condition'—two quadruples are stated, and the term 'disappearance condition' is extracted and set aside. The rest is all condensed. To explain its condensed nature, it is said: 'For each term, the single-rooted, two-rooted, three-rooted, and all-rooted should be expanded without confusion.' Therefore, just as beginning with the root condition, in the single-rooted, by way of the root-and-so-on term, there are 1,176 questions... up to 49 in the all-rooted, so too for the object condition and others—each taken as the beginning—by way of the object-and-so-on term, for each term, in the single-rooted, there are 1,176 questions... up to 49 in the all-rooted. Thus, for each term, in the divisions of single-rooted and so on, there are fourteen thousand seven hundred questions. For all these, across the twenty-four conditions, this is the calculation section—

Dvāpaññāsasahassāna-ṭṭhasatāni tīṇi satasahassāni;

Kusalattikassa pucchā, anulomanayamhi suvibhattā.

Three hundred fifty-two thousand eight hundred questions; these are the questions of the wholesome triad, well distinguished in the direct order method.

Yathā [V 0.0402] ca kusalattikassa, evaṃ vedanāttikādīnampīti sabbesupi dvāvīsatiyā tikesu –

Just as with the wholesome triad, so too with the feeling triad and others; thus, in all twenty-two triads—

Ekasaṭṭhisahassāni, cha satāni sattasattati;

Satasahassāni pucchānaṃ, tikabhede pabhedato.

One hundred sixty-one thousand six hundred seventy-seven questions; these are distinguished by way of division in the divisions of triads.

Saṅkhittā vācanāmagge.

Abridged in the course of recitation.

Dukesu pana “siyā hetuṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca hetudhammo uppajjeyya hetupaccayā”ti evaṃ hetuṃ paṭicca hetu, hetuṃ paṭicca nahetu, hetuṃ paṭicca hetu ca nahetu ca, nahetuṃ paṭicca nahetu, nahetuṃ paṭicca hetu, nahetuṃ paṭicca hetu ca nahetu ca, hetuñca nahetuñca paṭicca hetu, hetuñca nahetuñca paṭicca nahetu, hetuñca nahetuñca paṭicca hetu ca nahetu cāti ekamekasmiṃ duke hetupaccayādīsu ekamekasmiṃ paccaye nava pucchā honti. Tāsu hetupaccayaṃ ādiṃ katvā ekamūlake dvesatāni soḷasa ca pucchā honti. Tāsu hetupaccayasseva aññena asammissā nava pucchā gahetabbā, sesā aṭṭha vārena gahitā.

Now, in the dyads, (beginning with the example) 'Dependent on a root state, might a root state arise by way of root condition?'—thus, dependent on a root state: a root state; dependent on a root state: a non-root state; dependent on a root state: both a root state and a non-root state; dependent on a non-root state: a non-root state; dependent on a non-root state: a root state; dependent on a non-root state: both a root state and a non-root state; dependent on both a root state and a non-root state: a root state; dependent on both a root state and a non-root state: a non-root state; dependent on both a root state and a non-root state: both a root state and a non-root state—in each dyad, among the root condition and so on, in each condition, there are nine questions. Among these, taking the root condition as the starting point, in the single-root method, there are two hundred and sixteen questions. Of these, nine questions should be taken for the root condition alone, unmixed with others; the remaining are taken in eight turns.

Tāsaṃ dukamūlakādīsu tevīsatiyā vāresu ekekaṃ navakaṃ apanetvā yāva sabbamūlakā ayaṃ gaṇanaparicchedo – dukamūlake tāva ekamūlake dassitesu dvīsu soḷasādhikesu pucchāsatesu nava apanetvā dvesatāni satta ca pucchā honti, tato nava apanetvā timūlake aṭṭhanavutisataṃ. Evaṃ purimapurimato nava nava apanetvā catumūlake ekūnanavutisataṃ, pañcamūlake asītisataṃ, chamūlake ekasattatisataṃ, sattamūlake dvāsaṭṭhisataṃ, aṭṭhamūlake tepaṇṇāsasataṃ, navamūlake [M 0.0405] catucattālīsasataṃ, dasamūlake pañcatiṃsasataṃ, ekādasamūlake chabbīsasataṃ, dvādasamūlake sattarasādhikasataṃ, terasamūlake aṭṭhādhikasataṃ, cuddasamūlake navanavuti, pannarasamūlake navuti, soḷasamūlake ekāsīti, sattarasamūlake dvāsattati, aṭṭhārasamūlake tesaṭṭhi, ekūnavīsatimūlake catupaññāsaṃ, vīsatimūlake pañcacattālīsaṃ, ekavīsatimūlake chattiṃsaṃ, dvāvīsatimūlake sattavīsa, tevīsatimūlake aṭṭhārasa, sabbamūlake navāti. Yathā panetāni hetupaccayavasena ekamūlake soḷasādhikāni dve pucchāsatāni…pe… sabbamūlake nava, evaṃ ārammaṇapaccayādīsupi ekamekaṃ ādiṃ katvā ārammaṇādipadavasena ekekassa padassa [V 0.0403] ekamūlake soḷasādhikāni dve pucchāsatāni…pe… sabbamūlake navāti ekekassa padassa ekamūlakādibhede dve pucchā sahassāni sattasatāni ca pucchā honti. Tāsaṃ sabbesupi catuvīsatiyā paccayesu ayaṃ gaṇanaparicchedo –

Among these, in the twenty-three turns of the two-root method and so on, by removing one set of nine each time up to the all-root method, this is the calculation section: First, in the two-root method, from the two hundred and sixteen questions shown in the single-root method, by removing nine, there are two hundred and seven questions. Then, by removing nine again, in the three-root method, there are one hundred ninety-eight. Thus, by removing nine each time from the previous ones: in the four-root method, one hundred eighty-nine; in the five-root method, one hundred eighty; in the six-root method, one hundred seventy-one; in the seven-root method, one hundred sixty-two; in the eight-root method, one hundred fifty-three; in the nine-root method, one hundred forty-four; in the ten-root method, one hundred thirty-five; in the eleven-root method, one hundred twenty-six; in the twelve-root method, one hundred seventeen; in the thirteen-root method, one hundred eight; in the fourteen-root method, ninety-nine; in the fifteen-root method, ninety; in the sixteen-root method, eighty-one; in the seventeen-root method, seventy-two; in the eighteen-root method, sixty-three; in the nineteen-root method, fifty-four; in the twenty-root method, forty-five; in the twenty-one-root method, thirty-six; in the twenty-two-root method, twenty-seven; in the twenty-three-root method, eighteen; and in the all-root method, nine. Just as these, by way of the root condition, in the single-root method, are two hundred and sixteen questions... and in the all-root method, nine; so too for the object condition and others—each taken as the beginning—by way of the object-and-so-on term, for each term, in the single-root method, there are two hundred and sixteen questions... and in the all-root method, nine. Thus, for each term, in the divisions of single-root and so on, there are two thousand seven hundred questions. For all these, across the twenty-four conditions, this is the calculation section:

Catusaṭṭhisahassāni, puna aṭṭhasatāni ca;

Pucchā hetudukasseva, anulomanaye matā.

Sixty-four thousand, and again eight hundred; these questions of the root dyad alone are considered to be in the direct order method.

Yathā ca hetudukassa, evaṃ sahetukadukādīnampīti sabbasmimpi dukasate –

Just as with the root dyad, so too with the dyad of 'with roots' and so forth—that is, in all one hundred dyads—

Saṭṭhi satasahassāni, cattāri ca tatoparaṃ;

Asīti ca sahassāni, pucchā dukasate vidū.

Six million, four hundred and eighty thousand questions are known by the wise in the hundred dyads.

Ayaṃ tāva suddhike tikapaṭṭhāne ceva dukapaṭṭhāne ca pucchānaṃ gaṇanaparicchedo.

This, firstly, is the enumeration of questions in the Suddhika, in both the Tikapaṭṭhāna and the Dukapaṭṭhāna.

Yaṃ pana tato paraṃ dvāvīsati tike gahetvā dukasate pakkhipitvā dukatikapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma desitaṃ, tattha “siyā hetuṃ kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca hetu kusalo dhammo uppajjeyya hetupaccayā”ti evaṃ dvāvīsatiyā tikesu ekekaṃ tikaṃ dukānaṃ satena satena saddhiṃ yojetvā dassetabbānaṃ pucchānaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayena sabbesaṃ ekamūlakādīnaṃ vasena gahetvā paricchedo veditabbo.

Moreover, taking the twenty-two triads and inserting them into the hundred dyads, the exposition called the Dukatikapaṭṭhāna was taught. Therein, the delimitation of the questions to be shown should be understood by taking all of them according to the method stated below, by way of having a single root and so forth. This is exemplified by combining each of the twenty-two triads with each of the hundred dyads, as in the question: 'Might a wholesome phenomenon that is a root arise dependent on a wholesome phenomenon that is a root by way of root condition?'

Yampi tato paraṃ dukasataṃ gahetvā dvāvīsatiyā tikesu pakkhipitvā tikadukapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma desitaṃ, tatthāpi “siyā kusalaṃ hetuṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca kusalo hetudhammo uppajjeyya hetupaccayā”ti evaṃ dukasate ekekaṃ [M 0.0406] dukaṃ dvāvīsatiyā tikehi saddhiṃ yojetvā dassetabbānaṃ pucchānaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayena sabbesaṃ ekamūlakādīnaṃ vasena gahetvā paricchedo veditabbo.

Moreover, having taken the hundred dyads and inserting them into the twenty-two triads, the exposition called the Tikadukapaṭṭhāna was taught. Therein, too, the delimitation of the questions to be shown should be understood by taking all of them according to the method stated below, by way of having a single root and so forth. This is exemplified by combining each dyad in the hundred dyads with the twenty-two triads, as in the question: 'Might a wholesome root-phenomenon arise dependent on a wholesome root-phenomenon by way of root condition?'

Yampi tato paraṃ tike tikesuyeva pakkhipitvā tikatikapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma desitaṃ, tatthāpi “siyā kusalaṃ sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca kusalo sukhāya vedanāya sampayutto dhammo uppajjeyya hetupaccayā”ti evaṃ dvāvīsatiyā tikesu ekekaṃ tikaṃ sesehi ekavīsatiyā [V 0.0404] tikehi saddhiṃ yojetvā dassetabbānaṃ pucchānaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayena sabbesaṃ ekamūlakādīnaṃ vasena gahetvā paricchedo veditabbo.

Moreover, inserting triads into triads alone, the exposition called the Tikatikapaṭṭhāna was taught. Therein, too, the delimitation of the questions to be shown should be understood by taking all of them according to the method stated below, by way of having a single root and so forth. This is exemplified by combining each triad in the twenty-two triads with the remaining twenty-one triads, as in the question: 'Might a wholesome phenomenon associated with pleasant feeling arise dependent on a wholesome phenomenon associated with pleasant feeling by way of root condition?'

Yampi tato paraṃ duke dukesuyeva pakkhipitvā dukadukapaṭṭhānaṃ nāma desitaṃ, tatthāpi “siyā hetuṃ sahetukaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca hetu sahetuko dhammo uppajjeyya hetupaccayā”ti evaṃ dukasate ekekaṃ dukaṃ sesehi navanavutiyā dukehi saddhiṃ yojetvā dassetabbānaṃ pucchānaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayena sabbesaṃ ekamūlakādīnaṃ vasena gahetvā paricchedo veditabbo. Tathāgatena hi sabbampetaṃ pabhedaṃ dassetvāva devaparisāya dhammo desito, dhammasenāpatissa pana tena “ajja idañcidañca desita”nti saṅkhipitvā nayadassanamatteneva desanā akkhātā. Therenāpi saṅkhipitvāva vācanāmaggo pavattito, so therena pavattitanayeneva saṅgītikāle saṅgahaṃ āropito.

Moreover, inserting dyads into dyads alone, the exposition called the Dukadukapaṭṭhāna was taught. Therein, too, the delimitation of the questions to be shown should be understood by taking all of them according to the method stated below, by way of having a single root and so forth. This is exemplified by combining each dyad in the hundred dyads with the remaining ninety-nine dyads, as in the question: 'Might a phenomenon that is a root and is with a root arise dependent on a phenomenon that is a root and is with a root by way of root condition?' Indeed, after showing all these distinctions, the Tathāgata taught the Dhamma to the assembly of devas. However, to the General of the Dhamma, the teaching was explained only by briefly indicating the method, saying, 'Today, this and that was taught.' The Elder, too, established the path of recitation in a summarized form, and it was included in the compilation at the time of the council according to the method established by that Elder.

Taṃ panassa saṅkhepanayaṃ dassetuṃ tikañca paṭṭhānavaranti ayaṃ gāthā ṭhapitā. Tassattho – tikañca paṭṭhānavaranti pavaraṃ tikapaṭṭhānañca. Dukuttamanti uttamaṃ seṭṭhaṃ dukapaṭṭhānañca. Dukatikañcevāti dukatikapaṭṭhānañca. Tikadukañcāti tikadukapaṭṭhānañca. Tikatikañcevāti tikatikapaṭṭhānañca. Dukadukañcāti dukadukapaṭṭhānañca. Cha anulomamhi nayā sugambhīrāti ete tikapaṭṭhānādayo suṭṭhu gambhīrā cha nayā anulomamhi veditabbāti. Tattha dve anulomāni – dhammānulomañca paccayānulomañca. Tattha “kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca kusalo dhammo”ti evaṃ abhidhammamātikāpadehi saṅgahitānaṃ dhammānaṃ [M 0.0407] anulomadesanāvasena pavattaṃ dhammānulomaṃ nāma. “Hetupaccayā ārammaṇapaccayā”ti evaṃ catuvīsatiyā paccayānaṃ anulomadesanāvasena pavattaṃ paccayānulomaṃ nāma.

To show that summarized method, this verse was established: 'The triad and the excellent Paṭṭhāna...' Its meaning is: 'The triad and the excellent Paṭṭhāna' refers to the excellent Tikapaṭṭhāna. 'The supreme dyad' refers to the supreme Dukapaṭṭhāna. 'And the dyad-triad indeed' refers to the Dukatikapaṭṭhāna. 'And the triad-dyad' refers to the Tikadukapaṭṭhāna. 'And the triad-triad indeed' refers to the Tikatikapaṭṭhāna. 'And the dyad-dyad' refers to the Dukadukapaṭṭhāna. 'The six methods in forward order are profoundly deep'—these Tikapaṭṭhāna and others are to be understood as six exceedingly deep methods in forward order. Herein, there are two forward orders: the forward order of phenomena and the forward order of conditions. Herein, 'dhammānuloma' is the name of that which proceeds by way of teaching the forward order of phenomena included in the Abhidhamma matrix categories, such as 'a wholesome phenomenon dependent on a wholesome phenomenon.' 'Paccayānuloma' is the name of that which proceeds by way of teaching the forward order of the twenty-four conditions, such as 'root condition, object condition.'

Tattha heṭṭhā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “tikañca paṭṭhānavaraṃ…pe… cha anulomamhi nayā sugambhīrā”ti ayaṃ gāthā dhammānulomaṃ sandhāya vuttā. Idha pana ayaṃ gāthā tasmiṃ dhammānulome paccayānulomaṃ sandhāya vuttā. Tasmā “cha anulomamhi nayā sugambhīrā”ti aṭṭhakathāgāthāya dhammānulome tikapaṭṭhānādayo cha nayā sugambhīrāti evamattho veditabbo. Imasmiṃ panokāse “hetupaccayā ārammaṇapaccayā”ti evaṃ pavatte paccayānulome ete dhammānulome tikapaṭṭhānādayo “cha nayā sugambhīrā”ti evamattho veditabbo. Tesu anulome tikapaṭṭhāne kusalattikamattasseva [V 0.0405] vasena ayaṃ imasmiṃ paṭiccavārassa paṇṇattivāre saṅkhipitvā pucchāpabhedo dassito. Sesesu pana tikesu sesapaṭṭhānesu ca ekāpi pucchā na dassitā. Tato paresu pana sahajātavārādīsu kusalattikassāpi vasena pucchaṃ anuddharitvā labbhamānakavasena vissajjanameva dassitaṃ. “Cha anulomamhi nayā sugambhīrā”ti vacanato pana imasmiṃ paccayānulome chapi ete paṭṭhānanayā pucchāvasena uddharitvā dassetabbā. Paṭṭhānaṃ vaṇṇayantānañhi ācariyānaṃ bhāro esoti.

In the commentary below, the verse 'The triad and the excellent Paṭṭhāna... the six methods in forward order are profoundly deep' was stated with reference to the forward order of phenomena (dhammānuloma). Here, however, this verse is stated with reference to the forward order of conditions (paccayānuloma) within that forward order of phenomena. Therefore, the meaning of the commentary verse 'The six methods in forward order are profoundly deep' should be understood as: the six methods, such as the Tikapaṭṭhāna, are exceedingly deep in the forward order of phenomena. In this context, however, when the forward order of conditions proceeds as 'root condition, object condition,' the meaning should be understood as: these Tikapaṭṭhāna and other methods, which belong to the forward order of phenomena, are 'six exceedingly deep methods.' Among these, in the Tikapaṭṭhāna of the forward order, the division of questions is briefly shown in the Paṇṇattivāra of this Paṭiccavāra, only with regard to the wholesome triad. However, in the remaining triads and other Paṭṭhānas, not a single question is shown. Furthermore, in subsequent sections like the sahajātavāra, even for the wholesome triad, no question is explicitly raised, but only the answers are given based on what is obtainable. Yet, because of the statement 'The six methods in forward order are profoundly deep,' in this forward order of conditions, all six of these Paṭṭhāna methods should be shown by raising questions. For the teachers who expound the Paṭṭhāna, this is their responsibility.

2. Paccayapaccanīyavaṇṇanā

2. Exposition of the Counter-Conditions

42-44. Idāni paccanīyaṃ hoti. Taṃ dassetuṃ siyā kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca kusalo dhammo uppajjeyya na hetupaccayātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha anulomapucchāhi samappamāṇova pucchāparicchedo. Tenevettha “yathā anulome hetupaccayo vitthārito, evaṃ paccanīyepi nahetupaccayo vitthāretabbo”ti vatvā puna pariyosāne “yathā anulome ekekassa padassa ekamūlakaṃ, dumūlakaṃ, timūlakaṃ, catumūlakaṃ yāva tevīsatimūlakaṃ, evaṃ paccanīyepi vitthāretabba”nti vuttaṃ. Tevīsatimūlakanti idañcettha dumūlakaṃyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Pariyosāne pana sabbamūlakaṃ catuvīsatimūlakampi hotiyeva. Taṃ sabbaṃ saṅkhittamevāti.

42-44. Now comes the antithesis. To demonstrate this, the statement, "A wholesome state may arise dependent on a wholesome state, not by way of root condition," and so forth, is commenced. Here, the scope of inquiry is commensurate with the direct questions. Therefore, it is said here, "Just as the root condition is elaborated in the direct order, so also should the non-root condition be elaborated in the antithesis." Then, at the conclusion, it is said, "Just as in the direct order, for each term there is a single-rooted, two-rooted, three-rooted, four-rooted, up to a twenty-three-rooted case, so also in the antithesis it should be elaborated." This "twenty-three-rooted" is said here with reference to the two-rooted case. However, at the conclusion, all roots, even the twenty-four-rooted case, are indeed present. All this is in brief.

Tikañca [M 0.0408] paṭṭhānavaraṃ…pe… cha paccanīyamhi nayā sugambhīrāti etthāpi dve paccanīyāni – dhammapaccanīyañca paccayapaccanīyañca. Tattha “kusalā dhammā”ti evaṃ abhidhammamātikāpadehi saṅgahitānaṃ dhammānaṃ “na kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca na kusalo dhammo”ti paccanīyadesanāvasena pavattaṃ dhammapaccanīyaṃ nāma. “Nahetupaccayā nārammaṇapaccayā”ti evaṃ catuvīsatiyā paccayānaṃ paccanīyadesanāvasena pavattaṃ paccayapaccanīyaṃ nāma. Tattha heṭṭhā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “tikañca paṭṭhānavaraṃ…pe… cha paccanīyamhi nayā sugambhīrā”ti ayaṃ gāthā dhammapaccanīyaṃ sandhāya vuttā. Idha pana ayaṃ gāthā dhammānulomeyeva paccayapaccanīyaṃ sandhāya vuttā. Tasmā “cha paccanīyamhi nayā sugambhīrā”ti aṭṭhakathāgāthāya dhammapaccanīye tikapaṭṭhānādayo cha nayā sugambhīrāti evamattho veditabbo. Imasmiṃ panokāse na hetupaccayā nārammaṇapaccayāti evaṃ pavatte paccayapaccanīye ete dhammānulomeyeva tikapaṭṭhānādayo cha nayā sugambhīrāti evamattho veditabbo.

"And the Tika-Paṭṭhāna is supreme... up to... the six methods in the antithesis are very profound." Here too, there are two antitheses: the antithesis of phenomena and the antithesis of conditions. Herein, concerning "wholesome phenomena"—thus, among the phenomena comprised by the Abhidhamma matrix terms—the teaching that proceeds by way of antithetical exposition, such as "dependent on a non-wholesome phenomenon, a non-wholesome phenomenon arises," is called the antithesis of phenomena. Concerning "Not by root condition, not by object condition"—thus, the teaching that proceeds by way of antithetical exposition among the twenty-four conditions is called the antithesis of conditions. Herein, in the earlier commentary, the verse "the Tika-Paṭṭhāna is supreme... up to... the six methods in the antithesis are very profound" was spoken with reference to the antithesis of phenomena. Here, however, this verse is spoken with reference to the antithesis of conditions within the direct order of phenomena itself. Therefore, in the commentary verse "the six methods in the antithesis are very profound," the meaning should be understood thus: the Tika-Paṭṭhāna and so on—the six methods—are very profound in the antithesis of phenomena. In this case, however, when the antithesis of conditions proceeds as "not by root condition, not by object condition," the meaning should be understood thus: these same Tika-Paṭṭhāna and so on—the six methods—are very profound within the direct order of phenomena itself.

Tesu [V 0.0406] anulomatikapaṭṭhāneyeva kusalattikamattassa vasena ayaṃ imasmiṃ paṭiccavārassa paṇṇattivāre saṅkhipitvā pucchāpabhedo dassito. Sesesu pana tikesu sesapaṭṭhānesu ca ekāpi pucchā na dassitā. Tato paresu pana sahajātavārādīsu kusalattikassāpi vasena pucchaṃ anuddharitvā labbhamānakavasena vissajjanameva dassitaṃ. “Cha paccanīyamhi nayā sugambhīrā”ti vacanato pana imasmiṃ paccayapaccanīye chapi ete paṭṭhānanayā pucchāvasena uddharitvā dassetabbā. Paṭṭhānaṃ vaṇṇayantānañhi ācariyānaṃ bhāro esoti.

Among these, in the direct Tika-Paṭṭhāna itself, by way of the wholesome triad alone, this division of questions is shown concisely in the designation chapter of this conditional chapter. But in the remaining triads and remaining Paṭṭhānas, not even one question is shown. Then, in subsequent chapters such as the conascence chapter, without extracting questions even by way of the wholesome triad, only the answers are shown by way of what is obtainable. However, due to the statement, "the six methods in the antithesis are very profound," in this antithesis of conditions, all six of these Paṭṭhāna methods should also be extracted and shown by way of questions. For the teachers who explain the Paṭṭhāna, this is indeed their burden.

3. Anulomapaccanīyavaṇṇanā

3. Exposition of the Affirmative-Negative

45-48. Idāni anulomapaccanīyaṃ hoti. Taṃ dassetuṃ siyā kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca kusalo dhammo uppajjeyya hetupaccayā naārammaṇapaccayātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha “hetupaccayā naārammaṇapaccayā…pe… hetupaccayā naavigatapaccayā”ti hetupadassa sesesu tevīsatiyā paccayesu ekekena saddhiṃ yojanāvasena hetupadādike ekamūlake tevīsati anulomapaccanīyāni. Tesu ekekasmiṃ ekūnapaññāsaṃ katvā sattavīsādhikāni ekādasa pucchāsatāni honti. Dumūlake pana hetārammaṇapadānaṃ sesesu dvāvīsatiyā paccayesu ekekena saddhiṃ [M 0.0409] yojanāvasena dvāvīsati anulomapaccanīyānīti evaṃ anulome vuttesu sabbesu ekamūlakādīsu ekekaṃ padaṃ parihāpetvā avasesānaṃ vasena pucchāgaṇanā veditabbā. Ekamūlakādīsu cettha yā pucchā pāḷiyaṃ āgatā, yā ca na āgatā, tā sabbā heṭṭhā vuttanayānusāreneva veditabbā.

45-48. Now comes the affirmative-negative. To demonstrate this, the statement, "A wholesome state may arise dependent on a wholesome state by way of root condition, but not by way of object condition," and so forth, is commenced. Here, concerning "by way of root condition, but not by way of object condition... up to... by way of root condition, but not by way of non-disappearance condition"—by combining the root term with each of the remaining twenty-three conditions, there are twenty-three affirmative-negatives in the single-rooted case beginning with the root term. In each of these, making forty-nine, there are one thousand one hundred and twenty-seven questions. In the two-rooted case, however, by combining the root and object terms with each of the remaining twenty-two conditions, there are twenty-two affirmative-negatives. Thus, in all the single-rooted and other cases mentioned in the direct order, the counting of questions should be understood by way of the remaining terms, having excluded one term at a time. Here, among the single-rooted and other cases, whichever questions appear in the Pāḷi text and whichever do not, all should be understood according to the method stated earlier.

Tikañca paṭṭhānavaraṃ…pe… cha anulomapaccanīyamhi nayā sugambhīrāti ettha pana heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva dve anulomapaccanīyāni – dhammānulomapaccanīyaṃ paccayānulomapaccanīyañca. Tattha “kusalā dhammā”ti evaṃ abhidhammamātikāpadehi saṅgahitānaṃ dhammānaṃ “kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca na kusalo dhammo”ti anulomapaccanīyadesanāvasena pavattaṃ dhammānulomapaccanīyaṃ nāma. “Hetupaccayā naārammaṇapaccayā”ti evaṃ catuvīsatiyā paccayesu labbhamānapadānaṃ anulomapaccanīyadesanāvasena pavattaṃ paccayānulomapaccanīyaṃ nāma. Tattha heṭṭhā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “tikañca paṭṭhānavaraṃ…pe… cha anulomapaccanīyamhi nayā sugambhīrā”ti ayaṃ gāthā dhammānulomapaccanīyaṃ sandhāya vuttā. Idha pana ayaṃ gāthā dhammānulomeyeva paccayānulomapaccanīyaṃ [V 0.0407] sandhāya vuttā. Tasmā “cha anulomapaccanīyamhi nayā sugambhīrā”ti aṭṭhakathāgāthāya dhammānulomapaccanīye tikapaṭṭhānādayo cha nayā sugambhīrāti evamattho veditabbo. Imasmiṃ panokāse hetupaccayā nārammaṇapaccayāti evaṃ pavatte paccayānulomapaccanīye ete dhammānulomeyeva tikapaṭṭhānādayo cha nayā sugambhīrāti evamattho veditabbo.

Here, "The Tika-Paṭṭhāna is supreme... and so on... the six methods in the affirmative-negative are very profound." In this context, by the method stated earlier, there are two affirmative-negatives: the affirmative-negative of phenomena and the affirmative-negative of conditions. Herein, concerning "wholesome phenomena"—thus, among the phenomena comprised by the Abhidhamma matrix terms—the teaching that proceeds by way of affirmative-negative exposition, such as "dependent on a wholesome phenomenon, a non-wholesome phenomenon arises," is called the affirmative-negative of phenomena. The teaching that proceeds by way of affirmative-negative exposition among the obtainable terms in the twenty-four conditions, such as "by root condition, not by object condition," is called the affirmative-negative of conditions. Herein, in the earlier commentary, the verse "The Tika-Paṭṭhāna is supreme... and so on... the six methods in the affirmative-negative are very profound" was spoken with reference to the affirmative-negative of phenomena. But in this context, this verse is spoken with reference to the affirmative-negative of conditions within the direct order of phenomena itself. Therefore, the meaning of the commentary verse, "the six methods in the affirmative-negative are very profound," should be understood thus: the Tika-Paṭṭhāna and so on—these six methods—are very profound in the affirmative-negative of phenomena. However, in this passage, when the affirmative-negative of conditions proceeds as "by root condition, not by object condition," the meaning should be understood thus: these same Tika-Paṭṭhāna and so on—the six methods—are very profound within the direct order of phenomena itself.

Tesu anulome tikapaṭṭhāneyeva kusalattikamattassa vasena ayaṃ imasmiṃ paṭiccavārassa paṇṇattivāre saṅkhipitvā pucchāpabhedo dassito. Sesesu pana tikesu sesapaṭṭhānesu ca ekāpi pucchā na dassitā. Tato paresu pana sahajātavārādīsu kusalattikassāpi vasena pucchaṃ anuddharitvā labbhamānakavasena vissajjanameva dassitaṃ. “Cha anulomapaccanīyamhi nayā sugambhīrā”ti vacanato pana imasmiṃ paccayānulomapaccanīye chapi ete paṭṭhānanayā pucchāvasena uddharitvā dassetabbā. Paṭṭhānaṃ vaṇṇayantānañhi ācariyānaṃ bhāro esoti.

Among these, in the direct-order Triad-Paṭṭhāna itself, by way of the wholesome triad alone, this division of questions is shown concisely in the Designation Section of this Conditional Section. But in the remaining triads and remaining Paṭṭhānas, not even one question is shown. Then, in subsequent sections such as the Co-nascence Section, without extracting questions even by way of the wholesome triad, only the answers are shown by way of what is obtainable. However, due to the statement, “The six methods in the affirmative-negative are very profound,” in this affirmative-negative of conditions, all six of these Paṭṭhāna methods should also be extracted and shown by way of questions. For this is indeed the burden of the teachers who expound the Paṭṭhāna.

4. Paccanīyānulomavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Negative-Affirmative

49-52. Idāni [M 0.0410] paccanīyānulomaṃ hoti. Taṃ dassetuṃ siyā kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca kusalo dhammo uppajjeyya nahetupaccayā ārammaṇapaccayātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha anulomapaccanīyapucchāhi samappamāṇo eva pucchāparicchedo. Ekamūlakādīsu cettha yā pucchā pāḷiyaṃ āgatā, yā ca na āgatā, tā sabbā heṭṭhā vuttanayānusāreneva veditabbā.

Now there is the negative-affirmative. To show this, it begins with [the question]: “Might a wholesome phenomenon arise dependent on a wholesome phenomenon by way of non-root condition, by way of object condition?” and so on. Here, the scope of the questions is exactly equal to the questions in the affirmative-negative. And here, in the sections beginning with the single root, all the questions that appear in the Pāli text, and those that do not appear, should be understood according to the method stated previously.

Tikañca paṭṭhānavaraṃ…pe… cha paccanīyānulomamhi nayā sugambhīrāti etthāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva dve paccayānulomāni – dhammapaccanīyānulomaṃ paccayapaccanīyānulomañca. Tattha “kusalā dhammā”ti evaṃ abhidhammamātikāpadehi saṅgahitānaṃ dhammānaṃ “nakusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca kusalo dhammo”ti paccanīyānulomadesanāvasena pavattaṃ dhammapaccanīyānulomaṃ nāma. “Nahetupaccayā ārammaṇapaccayā”ti evaṃ catuvīsatiyā paccayesu labbhamānapadānaṃ paccayapaccanīyānulomadesanāvasena pavattaṃ paccayapaccanīyānulomaṃ nāma. Tattha heṭṭhā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “tikañca paṭṭhānavaraṃ…pe… cha paccanīyānulomamhi nayā sugambhīrā”ti ayaṃ gāthā dhammapaccanīyānulomaṃ sandhāya vuttā. Idha pana ayaṃ gāthā dhammānulomeyeva paccayapaccanīyānulomaṃ sandhāya vuttā. Tasmā “cha paccanīyānulomamhi nayā sugambhīrā”ti aṭṭhakathāya [V 0.0408] dhammapaccanīyānulome tikapaṭṭhānādayo cha nayā sugambhīrāti evamattho veditabbo. Imasmiṃ panokāse nahetupaccayā ārammaṇapaccayāti evaṃ pavatte paccayapaccanīyānulome ete dhammānulomeyeva tikapaṭṭhānādayo cha nayā sugambhīrāti evamattho veditabbo.

And the supreme Paṭṭhāna of the Triads… [up to]… “the six methods in the negative-affirmative are very profound.” Here too, according to the method stated previously, there are two negative-affirmative [methods]: the negative-affirmative of phenomena and the negative-affirmative of conditions. Therein, the negative-affirmative of phenomena is that which proceeds by way of the negative-affirmative declaration, “A wholesome phenomenon [arises] dependent on a non-wholesome phenomenon,” concerning phenomena included by the Abhidhamma matrix headings such as “wholesome phenomena.” The negative-affirmative of conditions is that which proceeds by way of the negative-affirmative declaration of the terms obtainable in the twenty-four conditions, such as “by way of non-root condition, by way of object condition.” Here, the verse previously stated in the commentary—“And the supreme Paṭṭhāna of the Triads… [up to]… the six methods in the negative-affirmative are very profound”—was spoken with reference to the negative-affirmative of phenomena. But here, this verse was spoken with reference to the negative-affirmative of conditions within the affirmative of phenomena itself. Therefore, the meaning of “the six methods in the negative-affirmative are very profound” in the commentary should be understood thus: in the negative-affirmative of phenomena, the six methods, such as the Triad-Paṭṭhāna, are very profound. However, in this instance, in the negative-affirmative of conditions that proceeds as “by way of non-root condition, by way of object condition,” the meaning should be understood thus: even in this affirmative of phenomena, these six methods, such as the Triad-Paṭṭhāna, are very profound.

Tesu anulomatikapaṭṭhāneyeva kusalattikamattassapi vasena ayaṃ imasmiṃ paṭiccavārassa paṇṇattivāre saṅkhipitvā pucchāpabhedo dassito. Sesesu pana tikesu sesapaṭṭhānesu ca ekāpi pucchā na dassitā. Tato paresu pana sahajātavārādīsu kusalattikassapi vasena pucchaṃ anuddharitvā labbhamānakavasena vissajjanameva dassitaṃ. “Cha paccanīyānulomamhi nayā sugambhīrā”ti vacanato pana imasmiṃ paccayapaccanīyānulome chapi ete paṭṭhānanayā pucchāvasena uddharitvā dassetabbā. Paṭṭhānaṃ vaṇṇayantānañhi ācariyānaṃ bhāro esoti.

Among these, in the direct-order Triad-Paṭṭhāna itself, this division of questions has been shown concisely in the Designation Section of the Conditional Section, even by way of the wholesome triad alone. However, in the remaining triads and remaining Paṭṭhāna sections, not even a single question has been shown. But in the subsequent sections, such as the Co-nascence Section, even regarding the wholesome triad, the answers have been shown by way of what is obtainable, without extracting the questions. However, according to the statement, “The six methods in the negative-affirmative are very profound,” in this negative-affirmative of conditions, all six of these Paṭṭhāna methods should be extracted and shown by way of questions. For this is indeed the burden of the teachers who expound the Paṭṭhāna.

Pucchāvāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Section on Questions is concluded.

1. Kusalattikavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Wholesome Triad

1. Paṭiccavāravaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Conditionality Section

1. Paccayānulomaṃ

1. The Affirmative of Conditions

(1.) Vibhaṅgavāro

The Section on Analysis

53. Idāni [M 0.0411] yā etā paṇṇattivāre kusalattikaṃ nissāya hetupaccayādivasena ekūnapaññāsaṃ ādiṃ katvā nayamattaṃ dassentena aparimāṇā pucchā dassitā. Tattha kusalākusalādīnaṃ sahuppattiyā abhāvato yā pucchā “kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca akusalo dhammo uppajjati hetupaccayā”ti evaṃ vissajjanaṃ na labhanti. Tā pahāya yā vissajjanaṃ labhanti, tāyeva [V 0.0409] vissajjetuṃ ayaṃ kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca kusalo dhammo uppajjati hetupaccayātiādinā nayena paṭiccavārassa niddesavāro āraddho.

53. Now, in the Designation Section, countless questions were shown, starting with the forty-nine [types of questions] by way of root condition and so on, by showing just the method, based on the wholesome triad. Therein, because of the absence of simultaneous arising of wholesome, unwholesome, and so on, those questions—such as, “Does an unwholesome phenomenon arise dependent on a wholesome phenomenon by way of root condition?”—do not receive an answer. Setting those aside, in order to answer only those that do receive an answer, this Exposition Section of the Conditional Section has been commenced with the method beginning, “A wholesome phenomenon arises dependent on a wholesome phenomenon by way of root condition,” and so on.

Tattha siyā – sace imā hetupaccayādivasena ekūnapaññāsaṃ pucchā sabbaso vissajjanaṃ na labhanti, atha kasmā dassitā? Nanu yā labhanti, tāyeva dassetabbāti? Āma, dassetabbā siyuṃ. Tathā dassiyamānā pana sabbesu tikadukapaṭṭhānādīsu ekekasmiṃ tike, duke, dukatike, tikaduke, tikatike, dukaduke ca saṅkhepaṃ akatvā dassetabbāyeva bhaveyyuṃ. Kasmā? Yasmā yā kusalattike labhanti, na tāyeva vedanāttikādīsu. Dhammānulomapaccanīye ca tikapaṭṭhāne vitakkattikapītittikānaṃ vissajjane sabbāpetā vissajjanaṃ labhanti, tasmā ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena ekekasmiṃ tike yattakāhi pucchāhi bhavitabbaṃ sabbā kusalattike dassitā. Evaṃ dassitāsu hi yā tattha vissajjanaṃ na labhanti, tā pahāya yā labhanti, tā vuccamānā sakkā sukhena vijānitunti sukhena vijānanatthaṃ sabbāpi kusalattike dassitā. Yā panettha vissajjanaṃ na labhanti, tā pahāya yā labhanti, tāyeva vissajjitāti veditabbā.

Here, one might ask: “If these forty-nine questions by way of root condition and so on do not receive answers at all, then why are they shown? Should not only those that do receive answers be shown?” Yes, they should be shown. However, if they were shown in that way, then in all the Paṭṭhāna sections of triads, dyads, and so on—in each triad, dyad, dyad-triad, triad-dyad, triad-triad, and dyad-dyad—they would have to be shown without abbreviation. Why? Because those that receive answers in the wholesome triad do not necessarily receive them in the feeling triad and so on. And in the affirmative-negative of phenomena, in the Triad-Paṭṭhāna, all these receive answers in the answers for the thought triad and the joy triad. Therefore, by way of the highest enumeration, all the questions that should be in each triad are shown in the wholesome triad. Indeed, when they are shown in this way, setting aside those that do not receive answers there, those that do receive answers can, when stated, be easily understood. Thus, for the sake of easy understanding, all questions are shown in the wholesome triad. It should be understood that, setting aside those here that do not receive answers, only those that do receive answers are answered.

Tattha kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiccāti catubhūmakakusaladhammesu vedanākkhandhādibhedaṃ ekaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca paṭigantvā sahuppattisaṅkhātena sadisabhāvena patvā, tena saddhiṃ ekato uppattibhāvaṃ upagantvāti attho. Kusalo dhammoti catubhūmakakusaladhammesuyeva saññākkhandhādibhedo eko dhammo. Uppajjatīti uppādato yāva nirodhagamanā uddhaṃ pajjati, nibbattatītipi attho[M 0.0412]. Attānaṃ labhati, uppādādayo tayopi khaṇe pāpuṇātīti vuttaṃ hoti. Hetupaccayāti kusalahetunā hetupaccayabhāvaṃ sādhentena.

Here, “dependent on a wholesome phenomenon” means: having taken one phenomenon among the wholesome phenomena of the four planes, distinguished as the feeling aggregate and so on, having attained a similar state by way of what is designated as co-arising, that is, having reached a state of arising together with it—this is the meaning. “Wholesome phenomenon” refers to one phenomenon among the wholesome phenomena of the four planes, distinguished as the perception aggregate and so on. “Arises” means it proceeds upwards from arising until reaching cessation, or it is produced—this is also the meaning. It obtains itself, that is to say, it reaches all three moments beginning with arising—this is stated. “By way of root condition” means by the wholesome root, bringing about the state of being a root condition.

Evaṃ “uppajjeyyā”ti pucchāya “uppajjatī”ti vissajjanaṃ vatvā idāni yaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca yo dhammo uppajjati, taṃ dhammaṃ khandhavasena dassetuṃ kusalaṃ ekaṃ khandhantiādimāha. Tattha ekanti vedanādīsu catūsu yaṃkiñci ekaṃ. Tayo khandhāti yo yo paccayabhāvena gahito, taṃ taṃ ṭhapetvā avasesā tayo khandhā. Tayo khandheti vedanādīsu yo eko khandho uppajjatīti gahito, taṃ ṭhapetvā sese tayo. Dve khandheti vedanāsaññādukādīsu chasu dukesu yekeci [V 0.0410] dve khandhe paṭicca. Dve khandhāti ye ye paccayabhāvena gahitā, te te ṭhapetvā avasesā dve khandhā kusalahetunā hetupaccayabhāvaṃ sādhentena uppajjantīti attho.

Thus, having stated the answer “It arises” to the question “Might it arise?”, now, in order to show, by way of aggregates, which phenomenon arises dependent on which phenomenon, it is said, beginning with “one wholesome aggregate.” Here, “one” refers to any one of the four, such as feeling. “Three aggregates” means the remaining three aggregates, excluding whichever one is taken as the condition. “Three aggregates” also refers to the remaining three, excluding whichever single aggregate, such as feeling, is taken as arising. “Two aggregates” means ‘dependent on any two aggregates among the six dyads, such as the dyad of feeling and perception.’ “Two aggregates” means the remaining two aggregates, excluding whichever ones are taken as conditions; the meaning is that they arise, with the wholesome root establishing the state of root-condition.

Yasmā pana eko khandho ekasseva dvinnaṃyeva vā, dve vā pana ekasseva paccayo nāma natthi, tasmā “ekaṃ khandhaṃ paṭicca eko khandho, ekaṃ khandhaṃ paṭicca dve khandhā, dve khandhe paṭicca eko khandho”ti na vuttaṃ. Kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca abyākato dhammo uppajjatītiādīsupi vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ rūpanti idaṃ paṭiccatthassa sahajātatthattā yaṃ kusalena sahajātañceva hetupaccayañca labhati, taṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Paratopi evarūpesu ṭhānesu ayameva nayo.

However, since there is no such thing as one aggregate being a condition for just one or for two, or two aggregates being a condition for just one, therefore it is not said, “one aggregate dependent on one aggregate, one aggregate dependent on two aggregates, or two aggregates dependent on one aggregate.” The meaning should be understood in the same way as stated in cases like “an indeterminate phenomenon arises dependent on a wholesome phenomenon,” and so on. The phrase “mind-originated form” is stated to show that which obtains both co-arising with the wholesome and the root condition, because the meaning of “dependent” here is “co-arising.” And elsewhere in such places, this same method applies.

Vipākābyākataṃ kiriyābyākatanti ettha hetupaccayābhāvato ahetukaṃ, rūpena saddhiṃ anuppattito āruppavipākañca na gahetabbaṃ. Paṭisandhikkhaṇeti kaṭattārūpasaṅkhātassa abyākatassa abyākataṃ paṭicca uppattidassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Vipākābyākatanti tasmiṃ khaṇe vijjamānābyākatavasena vuttaṃ. Khandhe paṭicca vatthu, vatthuṃ paṭicca khandhāti idaṃ kaṭattārūpaggahaṇena vatthumhi gahitepi vatthuṃ paṭicca khandhānaṃ uppattidassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

Here, regarding ‘resultant indeterminate’ and ‘functional indeterminate’: the rootless [consciousness] should not be included, due to the absence of a root condition; and the formless resultant [consciousness] should not be included, because it does not arise together with form. “At the moment of rebirth-linking” is stated to show the arising of an indeterminate phenomenon dependent on the indeterminate phenomenon designated as kamma-produced form. “Resultant indeterminate” is stated by way of the indeterminate states existing at that moment. “The aggregates dependent on the physical base, the physical base dependent on the aggregates”—this is stated to show the arising of the aggregates dependent on the physical base, even though the physical base is included by the mention of kamma-produced form.

Ekaṃ mahābhūtantiādi rūpābyākataṃ paṭicca rūpābyākatassa uppattidassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Ekaṃ khandhantiādīsu vuttanayeneva panettha atthayojanā veditabbā. Evaṃ rūpābyākatamhi bhūte paṭicca bhūtānaṃ uppattiṃ vatvā idāni bhūte [M 0.0413] paṭicca upādārūpānaṃ uppattiṃ dassetuṃ mahābhūte [V 0.0411] paṭicca cittasamuṭṭhānantiādi vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sante upādārūpanti ettakameva vattabbaṃ, itaradvayaṃ kasmā vuttanti? Mahābhūtepi paṭicca uppattidassanatthaṃ. Yañhi heṭṭhā “cittasamuṭṭhānañca rūpaṃ kaṭattā ca rūpa”nti dassitaṃ, taṃ na kevalaṃ khandheyeva ca paṭicca uppajjati, mahābhūtepi pana paṭicca uppajjatīti dassanatthamidaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Tattha cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ pavatteyeva, kaṭattārūpaṃ paṭisandhiyampi. Upādārūpanti tasseva ubhayassa visesanaṃ.

“One great element,” etc., is stated to show the arising of indeterminate materiality dependent on indeterminate materiality. The meaning here should be understood in the same way as explained in the sections on “one aggregate,” etc. Having thus stated the arising of the primary elements dependent on an indeterminate primary element, now, to show the arising of derived materiality dependent on the primary elements, it is stated, “dependent on the great elements, mind-originated,” etc. If this is the case, only “derived materiality” should be stated. Why then are the other two stated? To show their arising dependent on even the great elements. For what was indicated earlier as “mind-originated materiality and kamma-originated materiality” does not arise solely dependent on the aggregates, but also arises dependent on the great elements—this is the purpose of this statement. Here, mind-originated materiality occurs only in the course of existence, while kamma-originated materiality occurs also at rebirth-linking. “Derived materiality” is a qualification of both.

Kusale khandhe ca mahābhūte ca paṭiccāti ettha cittasamuṭṭhānāva mahābhūtā gahitā. Cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ rūpanti ettha pana bhūtarūpampi upādārūpampi gahitaṃ. “Ekaṃ mahābhūtaṃ paṭicca tayo mahābhūtā”tiādinā nayena hi bhūtarūpampi khandhe ca mahābhūte ca paṭicca uppajjati. Mahābhūte paṭicca upādārūpanti vuttanayena upādārūpampi. Akusalañca abyākatañcāti pañhāvissajjanesupi eseva nayo. Evaṃ hetupaccaye nava pucchā vissajjitā. Etāyeva hi ettha labbhanti, sesā cattālīsa moghapucchāti na vissajjitā. Iminā upāyena ārammaṇapaccayādīsupi pucchāvissajjanānaṃ attho veditabbo. Tattha tattha pana vicāretabbayuttakameva vicārayissāma.

In the phrase “dependent on the wholesome aggregates and the great elements,” here only mind-originated great elements are taken. In the phrase “mind-originated materiality,” however, both primary materiality and derived materiality are taken. For indeed, primary materiality also arises dependent on the aggregates and the great elements, in the manner stated in the phrase “dependent on one great element, the three other great elements,” and so on. Derived materiality also arises in the manner stated in “derived materiality dependent on the great elements.” This same method also applies in the answers to the questions on “unwholesome and indeterminate.” Thus, under the root-condition, nine questions have been answered. Only these are obtainable here; the remaining forty are futile questions and thus not answered. By this method, the meaning of questions and answers regarding the object-condition and the others should also be understood. There, however, we will examine only what is fitting to examine.

54. Ārammaṇapaccaye tāva rūpassa ārammaṇapaccayavasena anuppattito tāsu navasu rūpamissakā pahāya tissova pucchā vissajjitā. Teneva ca kāraṇena “vatthuṃ paṭicca khandhā”ti vatvā “khandhe paṭicca vatthū”ti na vuttaṃ. Na hi taṃ ārammaṇapaccayena uppajjati.

54. Regarding the object-condition, first, since materiality does not arise by way of the object-condition, having set aside from those nine questions the ones mixed with materiality, only three questions are answered. For the same reason, it is said, “aggregates dependent on a base,” but it is not said, “a base dependent on aggregates.” For that does not arise by way of the object-condition.

55. Adhipatipaccaye vipākābyākatanti lokuttarameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tenevettha “paṭisandhikkhaṇe”ti na gahitaṃ. Sesaṃ hetupaccayasadisameva.

55. Regarding the dominance-condition, “resultant-indeterminate” is stated only in reference to the supramundane states. Therefore, “at the moment of rebirth-linking” is not included here. The rest is similar to the root-condition.

56. Anantarasamantaresupi rūpaṃ na labbhatīti ārammaṇapaccaye viya tissova pucchā.

56. In the contiguity and immediate contiguity conditions, too, materiality is not found; therefore, just as in the case of the object-condition, there are only three questions.

57. Sahajātapaccaye paṭisandhikkhaṇeti pañcavokāre paṭisandhivasena vuttaṃ. Heṭṭhā pana paccayavibhaṅge “okkantikkhaṇe”ti āgataṃ tampi iminā saddhiṃ atthato ekaṃ, byañjanamattameva hettha nānanti. Apica “tiṇṇaṃ sannipātā gabbhassa [M 0.0414] avakkanti hotī”ti (ma. ni. 1.408) vacanato okkantīti pañcavokārapaṭisandhiyāvetaṃ nāmaṃ. Paṭisandhīti sabbabhavasādhāraṇaṃ. Idha pana “kaṭattā ca rūpa”ntiādivacanato pañcavokārapaṭisandhiyeva adhippetā. Sā hi rūpassapi arūpassapi paccayabhāvañceva paccayuppannabhāvañca saṅgaṇhāti, tasmā paripuṇṇavissajjanā hotīti gahitā. Bāhiraṃ ekaṃ mahābhūtanti anindriyabaddhesu pathavīpāsāṇādīsu mahābhūtaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Paccayavibhaṅgavārasmiñhi cattāro mahābhūtāti ajjhattikañca bāhirañca ekato katvā gahitaṃ. Saṅkhepadesanā hi sā. Ayaṃ pana vitthāradesanā, tasmā sabbaṃ vibhajitvā dassento “bāhiraṃ ekaṃ mahābhūta”ntiādimāha. Asaññasattānaṃ ekaṃ mahābhūtaṃ paṭiccāti dvisantatisamuṭṭhānabhūtavasena vuttaṃ. Mahābhūte paṭicca kaṭattārūpanti idaṃ pana kammasamuṭṭhānavaseneva vuttaṃ. Upādārūpanti utusamuṭṭhānavaseneva.

57. In the co-nascence condition, “at the moment of relinking” is stated with reference to relinking in the five-constituent existence. However, in the Analysis of Conditions previously, the term “moment of descent” (okkantikkhaṇa) also appears; that too is one in meaning with this, only the expression differs here. Furthermore, according to the statement, “The descent of an embryo occurs through the union of three factors” (MN 1.408), the term “descent” is a name for relinking in the five-constituent existence. “Relinking” is common to all existences. Here, however, based on statements such as “and kamma-originated materiality,” only relinking in the five-constituent existence is intended. For it encompasses being a condition and being a conditioned state for both materiality and immateriality; thus it is taken because it provides a complete answer. “An external great element” is stated with reference to the great elements in things not bound to faculties, such as earth and stones. In the section on the Analysis of Conditions, “the four great elements” are taken by combining the internal and the external. For that is a concise exposition. This, however, is a detailed exposition; therefore, showing everything by distinguishing them, it states, “an external great element,” etc. For non-percipient beings, “dependent on one great element” is stated with reference to the primary elements arising from two continuities. However, “kamma-originated materiality dependent on the great elements” is stated only in terms of that which is kamma-originated. “Derived materiality” is stated only in terms of that which is temperature-originated.

58. Aññamaññapaccaye [V 0.0412] khandhe paṭicca vatthu, vatthuṃ paṭicca khandhāti catunnampi khandhānaṃ ekato vatthunā aññamaññapaccayataṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ.

58. In the mutuality condition, “the aggregates are dependent on the base, and the base is dependent on the aggregates” is stated to show the mutuality-conditionality of the four immaterial aggregates together with the base.

59. Nissayapaccaye yasmā paṭiccattho nāma sahajātattho, tasmā yā heṭṭhā paccayavibhaṅgavāre cakkhāyatanādīnaṃ nissayapaccayatā dassitā, na sā gahitā. Cakkhāyatanādīni hi purejātāni hutvā paccayā honti, idha sahajātameva labbhati. Teneva vuttaṃ – “nissayapaccayo sahajātapaccayasadiso”ti.

59. In the support condition, since the meaning of “dependent on” is the meaning of co-nascent, the support-conditionality of the eye-base, etc., shown in the previous section on the Analysis of Conditions, is not included here. For the eye-base, etc., arise prior and serve as conditions, whereas here only co-nascent phenomena are obtained. Hence it is said, “The support condition is similar to the co-nascence condition.”

60. Upanissayapaccaye rūpassa upanissayapaccayābhāvā tīṇeva vissajjanāni labbhanti, tena vuttaṃ “ārammaṇapaccayasadisa”nti. Tattha kiñcāpi na sabbe kusalākusalābyākatā ārammaṇūpanissayaṃ labhanti, ye pana labhanti, tesaṃ vasenetaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

60. In the decisive support condition, because materiality lacks a decisive support condition, only three answers are obtained. Therefore, it is said, “similar to the object-condition.” Here, although not all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states obtain objective decisive support, it should be understood that this is stated with reference to those that do.

61. Purejātapaccaye vatthuṃ purejātapaccayāti vatthuṃ paṭicca vatthunā purejātapaccayataṃ sādhentena uppajjantīti attho. Vipākābyākataṃ ekaṃ khandhanti ettha yaṃ vipākābyākatassa vatthu okkantikkhaṇe sahajātapaccayo hoti, taṃ purejātapaccayabhājaniyattā idha na gahetabbaṃ. Yepi kusalādayo [M 0.0415] āruppe purejātapaccayaṃ na labhanti, tepi purejātapaccayabhājaniyatoyeva idha na gahetabbā. Ārammaṇaṃ pana niyamato purejātapaccayabhāvaṃ na labhati. Rūpāyatanādīni hi cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃyeva purejātapaccayataṃ sādhenti, manoviññāṇadhātuyā atītānāgatānipi ārammaṇaṃ hontiyeva. Tasmā idha na gahitaṃ. Khandhavasena hi ayaṃ desanā, na viññāṇadhātuvasena. “Vipākābyākataṃ ekaṃ khandha”nti desanāya ca sabbāpi viññāṇadhātuyo gahitā, na cakkhuviññāṇadhātuādayo evāti.

61. In the prenascence condition, the meaning of 'the base as a prenascence condition' is that states arise dependent on the base, which establishes its prenascence-conditionality. Here, regarding 'one resultant-indeterminate aggregate,' that base of the resultant-indeterminate consciousness which is a co-nascence condition at the moment of descent should not be taken here, because it is to be classified under the prenascence condition. Those wholesome states, etc., in the immaterial realms that do not obtain a prenascence condition are also not to be included here, precisely because they are to be classified under the prenascence condition. An object, however, does not necessarily obtain the state of a prenascence condition. For the form-base, etc., establish prenascence-conditionality only for eye-consciousness, etc., whereas even past and future phenomena can be objects for the mind-consciousness element. Therefore, it is not included here. For this teaching is in terms of aggregates, not in terms of consciousness elements. And by the teaching, 'one resultant-indeterminate aggregate,' all consciousness elements are included, not just the eye-consciousness element, etc.

Pacchājāto kusalākusalānaṃ paccayo na hoti, abyākatassapi upatthambhakova na janako, tasmā “uppajjati pacchājātapaccayā”ti evaṃ vattabbo ekadhammopi natthīti pacchājātapaccayavasena vissajjanaṃ na kataṃ.

The post-nascence condition is not a condition for wholesome and unwholesome states; and for indeterminate states, it is only a supporter, not a producer. Therefore, since there is not even a single phenomenon that can be described as 'arising by the post-nascence condition,' an answer has not been given in terms of the post-nascence condition.

62. Āsevanapaccaye kāmaṃ sabbā kiriyā āsevanapaccayaṃ na labhanti, labbhamānavasena pana “kiriyābyākata”nti vuttaṃ. Tasmā javanakiriyāvettha gahitāti veditabbā.

62. In the repetition condition, indeed, not all functional states obtain the repetition condition, but, in terms of what can be obtained, it is called “functional-indeterminate.” Therefore, it should be understood that here only impulsive functional states are included.

63. Kammapaccaye [V 0.0413] kusalākusalesu ekakkhaṇiko kammapaccayo veditabbo, tathā kiriyābyākate. Vipākābyākate pana nānākkhaṇikopi, tathā paṭisandhikkhaṇe mahābhūtānaṃ. Cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ pana ekakkhaṇiko. Kaṭattārūpānaṃ nānākkhaṇikova tathā asaññasattarūpānaṃ. Kaṭattārūpaṃ panettha jīvitindriyaṃ. Sesaṃ na ekantato kammasamuṭṭhānattā upādārūpanti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ santepi idha kammasamuṭṭhānameva adhippetaṃ.

63. In the kamma condition, for wholesome and unwholesome kamma, the kamma condition should be understood as single-momentary. Similarly, for functional-indeterminate states. However, for resultant-indeterminate states, it can be multi-momentary, as also at the moment of relinking for the great elements. But for mind-originated materiality, it is single-momentary. For kamma-originated materiality, it is multi-momentary, as also for the materiality of non-percipient beings. Here, the kamma-originated materiality referred to is the life faculty. The rest are not exclusively kamma-originated, hence they are called derived materiality. Even so, here only kamma-originated materiality is intended.

64. Vipākapaccaye kusalākusalaṃ kiriyañca na labbhatīti abyākatavaseneva vissajjanaṃ kataṃ. Cittasamuṭṭhānanti vipākacittasamuṭṭhānameva. Kaṭattārūpanti yathālābhavasena indriyarūpañca vatthurūpañca. Upādārūpanti tadavasesaṃ tasmiṃ samaye vijjamānakaṃ upādārūpaṃ.

64. In the result condition, wholesome, unwholesome, and functional states are not obtained, so the answer is given only in terms of the indeterminate states. “Mind-originated materiality” means only resultant mind-originated materiality. “Kamma-originated materiality” means sense-faculty materiality and base materiality, according to what is obtained. “Derived materiality” means the remaining derived materiality existing at that time.

65. Āhārapaccaye sabbesampi kusalādīnaṃ khandhānaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānarūpassa ca arūpāhāravasena uppatti veditabbā, tathā paṭisandhikkhaṇe mahābhūtānaṃ. Cittasamuṭṭhānanti bhavaṅgādicittasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Āhārasamuṭṭhānanti kabaḷīkārāhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ[M 0.0416]. Cittasamuṭṭhānanti kusalākusalacittasamuṭṭhānameva. Paccayavibhaṅgavāre āhārapaṭipāṭiyā paṭhamaṃ kabaḷīkāro āhāro dassito, idha pana kusalaṃ dhammanti pucchāvasena paṭhamaṃ arūpāhārā dassitāti veditabbā.

65. In the nutriment condition, it should be understood that the arising of all aggregates of wholesome states, etc., and of mind-originated materiality is due to immaterial nutriment, as is the arising of the great elements at the moment of relinking. 'Mind-originated' refers to that originated by states of consciousness such as the life-continuum. 'Nutriment-originated' refers to that originated by physical nutriment. 'Mind-originated' refers only to that originated by wholesome and unwholesome states of consciousness. In the section on the Analysis of Conditions, physical nutriment is shown first in the sequence of nutriments, but it should be understood that here, due to the question 'a wholesome phenomenon...,' immaterial nutriments are shown first.

66. Indriyapaccaye paccayavibhaṅge indriyapaṭipāṭiyā paṭhamaṃ cakkhundriyādīni dassitāni, idha pana kusalādipucchāvasena paṭhamaṃ arūpindriyānaṃ paccayatā dassitā. Tattha kusalādīsu yathālābhavasena arūpindriyā gahetabbā. Asaññasattānaṃ bhūtarūpesupi jīvitindriyanti.

66. In the faculty condition, in the analysis of conditions, the eye faculty and so forth are presented first in the sequence of faculties, but here, by way of the question concerning the wholesome and so forth, the conditionality of the immaterial faculties is presented first. There, in regard to the wholesome and so forth, the immaterial faculties should be understood according to their availability. For non-percipient beings, the life faculty exists even among the primary material elements.

67. Jhānamaggapaccayesu hetupaccayasadisameva vissajjanaṃ, tenevettha “hetupaccayasadisa”nti vuttaṃ.

67. In the jhāna and path conditions, the exposition is similar to that of the root condition; therefore it is said here, 'similar to the root condition.'

68. Sampayuttapaccaye vissajjanaṃ ārammaṇapaccayagatikaṃ, tenevettha “ārammaṇapaccayasadisa”nti vuttaṃ.

68. In the associated condition, the exposition follows the course of the object condition; therefore it is said here, 'similar to the object condition.'

69. Vippayuttapaccaye [V 0.0414] vatthuṃ vippayuttapaccayāti vatthuṃ paṭicca vippayuttapaccayā, vatthunā vippayuttapaccayataṃ sādhentena uppajjantīti attho. Khandhe vippayuttapaccayāti khandhe paṭicca vippayuttapaccayā, khandhehi vippayuttapaccayataṃ sādhentehi uppajjatīti attho. Khandhā vatthuṃ vippayuttapaccayāti vatthuṃ paṭicca khandhā vippayuttapaccayā. Vatthunā vippayuttapaccayataṃ sādhentena uppajjantīti attho. Cittasamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ khandhe vippayuttapaccayāti khandhe paṭicca vippayuttapaccayā cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ rūpaṃ khandhehi vippayuttapaccayataṃ sādhentehi uppajjatīti attho. Sesavissajjanesupi vatthuṃ vippayuttapaccayātiādīsupi vuttanayenevattho veditabbo. Vipākābyākate cettha vatthuggahaṇena cakkhādīni saṅgahitabbāni. Ekaṃ mahābhūtantiādi rūpābyākatassa paccayabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Cittasamuṭṭhānanti abyākatacittasamuṭṭhānampi kusalākusalacittasamuṭṭhānampi.

69. In the dissociated condition, the statement 'the base is a dissociated condition' means that in dependence on the base, there are dissociated conditions, and the meaning is that they arise establishing the state of being a dissociated condition through the base. The statement 'the aggregates are a dissociated condition' means that in dependence on the aggregates, there are dissociated conditions, and the meaning is that they arise establishing the state of being a dissociated condition through the aggregates. The statement 'the aggregates are a dissociated condition for the base' means that in dependence on the base, the aggregates are dissociated conditions, and the meaning is that they arise establishing the state of being a dissociated condition through the base. The statement 'mind-originated form is a dissociated condition for the aggregates' means that in dependence on the aggregates, mind-originated form is a dissociated condition, and the meaning is that it arises establishing the state of being a dissociated condition through the aggregates. In the remaining expositions as well, such as 'the base is a dissociated condition' and so forth, the meaning should be understood in the same way as stated. Here, in the resultant-indeterminate, by the inclusion of 'base,' the eye and so forth should be understood. The statement 'one great element' and so forth is said to show the conditionality of indeterminate materiality. 'Mind-originated' refers to that which is originated by indeterminate consciousness as well as that originated by wholesome and unwholesome consciousness.

70. Atthipaccaye sabbaṃ sahajātapaccayagatikaṃ. Tenevettha “sahajātapaccayasadisa”nti vuttaṃ.

70. In the presence condition, everything follows the course of the co-nascence condition. Therefore it is said here, 'similar to the co-nascence condition.'

71-72. Natthivigatā ārammaṇapaccayagatikā, avigataṃ sahajātagatikaṃ. Tenevettha “ārammaṇapaccayasadisaṃ, sahajātapaccayasadisa”nti vuttaṃ[M 0.0417]. Ime tevīsati paccayāti saṅkhipitvā dassitānaṃ vasenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Vitthāretabbāti yā pucchā vissajjanaṃ labhanti, tāsaṃ vasena vitthāretabbā. Ayaṃ hetupaccayaṃ ādiṃ katvā ekamūlake paccayānulome paṭiccavārassa kusalattikavissajjane atthavaṇṇanā.

71-72. The absence and disappearance conditions follow the course of the object condition, while the non-disappearance condition follows the course of the co-nascence condition. Therefore it is said here, 'similar to the object condition' and 'similar to the co-nascence condition.' This is stated by way of the twenty-three conditions that have been shown in brief. The meaning of 'should be elaborated' is that they should be elaborated by way of the questions that obtain an exposition. This is the explanation of the meaning in the exposition of the wholesome triad of the Dependent Section in the forward order of conditions, beginning with the root condition, in the single-root section.

(2.) Saṅkhyāvāro

(2.) The Enumeration Section

73. Idāni ye ettha hetupaccayādīsu ekekasmiṃ paccaye vissajjanavārā laddhā, te gaṇanavasena dassetuṃ hetuyā navātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha hetuyā navāti hetupaccaye nava pucchāvissajjanavārā honti. Seyyathidaṃ – kusalena kusalaṃ, kusalena abyākataṃ, kusalena kusalābyākataṃ; akusalena akusalaṃ, akusalena abyākataṃ, akusalena akusalābyākataṃ, abyākatena abyākataṃ, kusalābyākatena abyākataṃ, akusalābyākatena abyākatanti.

73. Now, to present by way of enumeration the occasions for exposition that are obtained in each of the conditions, beginning with the root condition and so forth, the text 'Nine by root' and so forth is commenced. Herein, 'Nine by root' means there are nine occasions for question and exposition in the root condition. Namely: (1) the wholesome by the wholesome, (2) the indeterminate by the wholesome, (3) the wholesome and the indeterminate by the wholesome; (4) the unwholesome by the unwholesome, (5) the indeterminate by the unwholesome, (6) the unwholesome and the indeterminate by the unwholesome; (7) the indeterminate by the indeterminate, (8) the indeterminate by the wholesome and the indeterminate, and (9) the indeterminate by the unwholesome and the indeterminate.

Ārammaṇe [V 0.0415] tīṇīti kusalena kusalaṃ, akusalena akusalaṃ, abyākatena abyākataṃ. Adhipatiyā navāti hetuyā vuttasadisāva. Dvādasasu hi paccayesu nava navāti vuttaṃ. Sabbesupi pucchāvissajjanāni hetupaccayasadisāneva. Vibhaṅge pana atthi viseso. Dasasu paccayesu tīṇi tīṇīti vuttaṃ. Sabbesupi pucchāvissajjanāni ārammaṇasadisāneva. Vibhaṅge pana atthi viseso. Aññamaññapaccayasmiñhi abyākatapadassa vissajjane rūpampi labbhati, tathā purejātapaccaye. Āsevanapaccaye vipākāni ceva vīthicittāni ca na labbhanti. Vipāke ekanti abyākatameva. Evamettha saṅkhepato nava tīṇi ekanti, tividhova vāraparicchedo. Vitthārato dvādasa navakā, dasa tikā, ekaṃ ekakanti sabbesupi tevīsatiyā paccayesu ekūnacattālīsādhikaṃ vārasataṃ hoti, ekūnacattālīsādhikañca pucchāsataṃ. Ekūnacattālīsādhikaṃ pucchāvissajjanasatantipi tasseva nāmaṃ.

In the object condition, 'three' means the wholesome by the wholesome, the unwholesome by the unwholesome, and the indeterminate by the indeterminate. In the dominance condition, 'nine' means just as stated for the root condition. Indeed, for twelve conditions, it is stated 'nine each.' In all of these, the questions and expositions are similar to those of the root condition. However, there is a distinction in the analysis. For ten conditions, it is stated 'three each.' In all of these, the questions and expositions are similar to those of the object condition. However, there is a distinction in the analysis. Indeed, in the mutuality condition, materiality is also obtained in the exposition of the indeterminate term, and similarly in the pre-nascence condition. In the repetition condition, neither resultants nor process-consciousnesses are obtained. In the resultant condition, 'one' means only the indeterminate. Thus, here in brief, 'nine, three, one' means the division of occasions is threefold. In detail, there are twelve groups of nine, ten groups of three, and one group of one; in all twenty-three conditions, there are one hundred and thirty-nine occasions, and one hundred and thirty-nine questions. The one hundred and thirty-nine questions and expositions are also known by that same name.

74. Evaṃ hetupaccayādike ekamūlake gaṇanaṃ dassetvā ito paresu dumūlakādīsu vitthāradesanaṃ saṅkhipitvā ekamūlake dassitāya desanāya labbhamānagaṇanaññeva ādāya vāraparicchedaṃ dassetuṃ dumūlake tāva hetupaccayā ārammaṇe tīṇītiādimāha. Tatridaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ [M 0.0418] – bahugaṇanopi paccayo abahugaṇanena saddhiṃ yutto tena samānagaṇanova hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “hetupaccayā ārammaṇe tīṇī”ti. Hetuārammaṇaduke ārammaṇe vuttāni tīṇeva vissajjanāni labbhantīti attho. Samānagaṇano pana samānagaṇanena saddhiṃ yutto aparihīnagaṇanova hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “hetupaccayā adhipatiyā navā”ti. Hetādhipatiduke naveva vissajjanāni labbhantīti attho. Vipāke ekanti hetuvipākaduke vipāke vuttaṃ ekameva vissajjanaṃ labbhatīti evaṃ tāva dumūlake vāraparicchedo veditabbo.

74. Having thus shown the calculation in the single-root section, beginning with the root condition and so forth, summarizing the detailed exposition in the subsequent two-root sections and so forth, and taking only the calculation obtainable from the exposition shown in the single-root section, to present the division of occasions, he first says in the two-root section, 'Regarding root condition and object condition, three' and so forth. Here is the characteristic: Even a condition with a large number, when combined with one with a small number, becomes of the same number as that. Therefore it is said, 'Regarding root condition and object condition, three.' The meaning is that in the root-object dyad, only the three expositions stated regarding the object condition are obtained. However, one with the same number, when combined with one with the same number, does not have a reduced number. Therefore it is said, 'Regarding root condition and dominance condition, nine.' The meaning is that in the root-dominance dyad, only nine expositions are obtained. Regarding result, 'one' means that in the root-result dyad, only the one exposition stated regarding the result condition is obtained. Thus, the division of occasions for the two-root case should be understood in this way.

75. Timūlakādīsupi idameva lakkhaṇaṃ. Tenevāha – hetupaccayā ārammaṇapaccayā adhipatiyā tīṇīti. Hetārammaṇādhipati tike ārammaṇe vuttāni tīṇeva vissajjanāni labbhantīti attho. Evaṃ sabbattha nayo netabbo.

75. The same characteristic applies in the three-root sections and so forth. Therefore he says, 'Root condition, object condition, and dominance condition—three.' The meaning is that in the triad of root, object, and dominance, only the three expositions stated regarding the object condition are obtained. This method should be applied everywhere.

76-79. Dvādasamūlake pana vipākapaccayo na labbhati, tasmā āsevanapaccayā kamme tīṇīti vatvā vipākaṃ aparāmasitvā āhāre tīṇīti vuttaṃ. Terasamūlakādīsupi eseva nayo. Te pana saṅkhipitvā tevīsatimūlakovettha dassito. So duvidho hoti – sāsevano vā savipāko [V 0.0416] vā. Tattha paṭhamaṃ sāsevano dassito, so tīṇeva vissajjanāni labhati. Tena vuttaṃ “āsevanapaccayā avigate tīṇī”ti. Savipāko pana āsevanaṃ na labhati, tasmā taṃ pahāya vipākavasena gaṇanāya dassanatthaṃ anantarāyeva “hetupaccayā…pe… vipākapaccayā āhāre eka”nti ekaṃ nayaṃ dassetvā pacchā tevīsatimūlakova dassito. Etesu pana dvīsu tevīsatimūlakesu kiñcāpi ekasmiṃ vipākapaccayo natthi, ekasmiṃ āsevanapaccayo, pacchājātapaccayo pana ubhayatthāpi. Ruḷhīsaddena panete tevīsatimūlakātveva veditabbā. Tesu sāsevane āsevanassa vasena sabbattha tīṇeva vissajjanāni, savipāke vipākapaccayassa vasena ekamevāti ayaṃ hetupaccayaṃ ādiṃ katvā ekamūlakādīsu gaṇanā.

76-79. In the twelve-root section, however, the resultant condition is not obtained. Therefore, having said 'three in action due to the repetition condition,' and without referring to the resultant, 'three in nutriment' is stated.
