The same method applies in the thirteen-root sections and so forth. These, when summarized, are shown here as the twenty-three-root section. It is of two kinds: either with repetition or with resultant. Among them, the first is shown as with repetition, and it obtains only three expositions. Therefore it is said, 'Due to the repetition condition, three in the non-absence condition.' However, the one with resultant does not obtain repetition. Therefore, setting that aside, to show the counting by way of resultant, immediately after, 'Due to the root condition... up to the resultant condition, one in nutriment'—one method is shown. Afterwards, the twenty-three-root section alone is shown. However, among these two twenty-three-root sections, although in one the resultant condition is absent, and in one the repetition condition is absent, the post-nascence condition is present in both. However, by the conventional term, these should be understood as just twenty-three-root sections. Among them, in the one with repetition, by way of the repetition condition, there are always only three expositions. In the one with resultant, by way of the resultant condition, there is only one. This is the counting beginning with the root condition in the single-root sections and so forth.

Yaṃ panetaṃ hetumūlakānantaraṃ “ārammaṇe ṭhitena sabbattha tīṇeva pañhā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ ārammaṇapaccayaṃ ādiṃ katvā ekamūlakepi dumūlakādīsupi sabbattha [M 0.0419] ārammaṇapade ceva ārammaṇena saddhiṃ sesapaccayayojanāsu ca yattha navahi bhavitabbaṃ, tattha tayova pañhā hontīti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Vipākapade pana vipākapadena saddhiṃ sesapaccayayojanāsu ca ekova pañho hotīti. Iti yaṃ heṭṭhā avocumha “bahugaṇanopi paccayo abahugaṇanena saddhiṃ yutto tena samānagaṇano hotī”ti, taṃ suvuttameva.

And what was said immediately after the root-root section, 'In all cases where the object is fixed, there are only three questions,' that is stated to show that, taking the object condition as primary, even in the single-root section and in the two-root sections and so forth, everywhere in the object term and in the combinations of other conditions with the object, where there should be nine, there are only three questions. However, in the resultant term, and in the combinations of other conditions with the resultant term, there is only one question. Thus, what we said below, 'Even a condition with a large number, when combined with one with a small number, becomes of the same number as that,' is indeed well-stated.

80-85. Idāni ye ārammaṇādīnaṃ paccayānaṃ vasena ekamūlakādayo dassetabbā, tesu ekamūlako tāva hetuekamūlakeneva sadisoti ekasmimpi paccaye na dassito. Ārammaṇapaccayavasena pana dumūlake gaṇanaṃ dassetuṃ ārammaṇapaccayā hetuyā tīṇi, adhipatiyā tīṇi…pe… avigate tīṇīti vuttaṃ. Ettha ca “ārammaṇapaccayā adhipatiyā tīṇi…pe… avigate tīṇī”ti vattabbe ye hetupaccayādayo paccayā bahugaṇanā, tesaṃ ūnataragaṇanehi ca samānagaṇanehi ca saddhiṃ saṃsandane yā gaṇanā labbhati, taṃ dassetuṃ ārammaṇapaccayassa purimabhāge ṭhitampi hetupaccayaṃ pacchimabhāgeva ṭhapetvā “ārammaṇapaccayā hetuyā tīṇī”ti vuttaṃ. Tenetaṃ āvi karoti – ārammaṇapaccayo yena yena bahutaragaṇanena vā samānagaṇanena vā paccayena saddhiṃ dukatikādibhedaṃ gacchati, sabbattha tīṇeva pañhāvissajjanāni veditabbāni. Vipākapaccayena pana saddhiṃ saṃsandane ekameva labbhati, taṃ vipākapaccayādikāya gaṇanāya āvi bhavissatīti idha na dassitaṃ. Yā cesā dumūlake gaṇanā [V 0.0417] dassitā, timūlakādīsupi esāva gaṇanāti ārammaṇapaccayavasena timūlakādayo na vitthāritā.

80-85. Now, regarding those single-root sections, etc., which are to be shown by way of conditions such as the object-condition, etc.: the single-root section is similar to the single-root section by the root-condition alone, and so it is not shown even in a single condition. However, to show the enumeration of the double-root section by way of the object-condition, it is said: "By the object-condition, three by the root-condition, three by the dominance-condition… up to three by the non-disappearance-condition." Here, although it should have been said, "By the object-condition, three by the dominance-condition… up to three by the non-disappearance-condition," to show the enumeration obtained by comparing the root-condition, etc. (which are conditions of higher enumeration), with those of lesser or equal enumeration, the root-condition, though placed earlier, is placed in the latter part, saying, "By the object-condition, three by the root-condition." This makes it clear that wherever the object-condition, when combined with any condition having a more numerous or equal enumeration, gives rise to divisions such as dualities and triads, the answers to the questions should always be understood as three. However, when compared with the resultant-condition, only one is obtained; this will become clear in the enumeration beginning with the resultant-condition, etc., and so it is not shown here. And this enumeration shown in the double-root section is the same in the triple-root sections, etc.; therefore, the triple-root sections, etc., by way of the object-condition, are not elaborated.

Idāni adhipatipaccayādivasena dumūlakādīsu gaṇanaṃ dassetuṃ adhipatipaccayā hetuyā navātiādi vuttaṃ. Tatthāpi vuttanayeneva paccayasanniveso veditabbo. Yathā ca adhipatipaccayā hetuyā nava, evaṃ sesesupi hetunā samānagaṇanāsu naveva. Iti yo yo paccayo ādimhi tiṭṭhati, tena tena saddhiṃ samānagaṇanānaṃ saṃsandane ādimhi ṭhitassa vasena gaṇanā hoti. Tena pana saddhiṃ ūnataragaṇanānaṃ saṃsandane ūnataragaṇanānaṃyeva vasena gaṇanā hotīti veditabbo. Yathā ca ārammaṇapaccayavasena evaṃ adhipatipaccayavasenāpi tato paresaṃ anantarādīnaṃ vasenāpi timūlakādayo na vitthāritā. Tasmā dumūlake [M 0.0420] dassitagaṇanāvaseneva sabbattha sādhetabbā. Teneva vuttaṃ “ekekaṃ paccayaṃ mūlakaṃ kātuna sajjhāyamaggena gaṇetabbā”ti.

Now, to show the enumeration in the double-root sections, etc., by way of the dominance-condition, etc., it is said: "By the dominance-condition, with the root-condition, nine," and so on. Herein too, the arrangement of the conditions should be understood in the same way as explained. Just as there are nine by the dominance-condition with the root-condition, so too with the remaining conditions of equal enumeration with the root-condition, there are nine. Thus, whichever condition stands first, the enumeration is done based on that first condition when combining with those of equal enumeration. However, when combining with those of lesser enumeration, the enumeration is done based on the lesser enumeration. And just as with the object-condition, so too with the dominance-condition, and thereafter with the remaining conditions such as the contiguity-condition, etc., the triple-root sections, etc., are not elaborated. Therefore, everywhere the enumeration should be accomplished according to the method shown in the double-root section. Therefore, it is said: "Taking each condition as a root, one should enumerate by way of the recitation method."

Paccayānulomavaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Conditional Concordance.

Paṭiccavāro

The Section on Dependence

Paccayapaccanīyavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Conditional Opposition

86-87. Paccayapaccanīyaṃ pana yasmā kusalapade na labbhati kusaladhammassa hetupaccayena vinā anuppattito, tasmā akusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiccātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha nahetupaccayāti hetupaccayapaṭikkhepo hetupaccayaṃ vinā aññena paccayena uppajjatīti attho. Vicikicchāsahagato uddhaccasahagato mohoti ayañhi sampayuttadhammānañceva cittasamuṭṭhānarūpassa ca sayaṃ hetupaccayo hoti, aññassa pana sampayuttahetuno abhāvā na hetupaccayā uppajjatīti ṭhapetvā hetupaccayaṃ sesehi attano anurūpapaccayehi uppajjati. Iminā nayena sabbapaccayapaṭikkhepesu attho veditabbo. Ahetukaṃ vipākābyākatanti idaṃ rūpasamuṭṭhāpakavaseneva veditabbaṃ. Aññesupi evarūpesu eseva nayo.

86-87. However, since the conditional opposition is not obtained in the wholesome category because a wholesome phenomenon cannot arise without the root-condition, therefore the phrase "dependent on an unwholesome phenomenon," etc., is begun. Herein, "not by root-condition" means the negation of the root-condition; it signifies that a phenomenon arises by another condition, not by the root-condition. For instance, delusion accompanied by doubt and restlessness—this indeed is a root-condition for its associated phenomena and for mind-originated materiality, but because of the absence of another associated root-condition, it does not arise by the root-condition. Excluding the root-condition, it arises by the remaining conditions suitable to it. In this way, the meaning should be understood in the negations of all the conditions. "Rootless, resultant, indeterminate" should be understood only with reference to the origination of materiality. In other such cases, the same method applies.

88. Naadhipatipaccaye kāmaṃ adhipatipi attanā saddhiṃ dutiyassa adhipatino abhāvā [V 0.0418] naadhipatipaccayaṃ labhati, yathā pana vicikicchuddhaccasahagato moho ahetuko, na tathā adhipatayo eva nirādhipati. Chandādīsu pana aññataraṃ adhipatiṃ akatvā kusalādīnaṃ uppattikāle sabbepi kusalādayo nirādhipatino. Tasmā mohaṃ viya visuṃ adhipatimattameva anuddharitvā sabbasaṅgāhikavasena esā “ekaṃ khandhaṃ paṭicca tayo khandhā”tiādikā desanā katāti veditabbā.

88. In the non-dominance condition, desire, though a dominance factor itself, does not obtain the non-dominance condition because of the absence of a second dominance factor alongside it. Just as delusion accompanied by doubt and restlessness is rootless, dominance factors are not in that way without dominance. However, when any one of the dominance factors such as desire is not made a dominance at the time of the arising of wholesome states, etc., all wholesome and other states are without dominance. Therefore, it should be understood that this teaching—'one aggregate conditions three aggregates,' etc.—is stated in an all-inclusive way, without singling out merely the dominance factor, just as with delusion.

89. Nānantaranasamanantaresu nārammaṇe viya rūpameva paccayuppannaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “nārammaṇapaccayasadisa”nti. Sahajātapaccayo parihīno. Yathā cesa, tathā nissayaatthiavigatapaccayāpi. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Etehi vinā kassaci anuppattito. Sahajātanissayaatthiavigatapaccayepi hi paccakkhāya ekopi rūpārūpadhammo nuppajjati, tasmā te parihīnā.

89. In the non-contiguity and non-proximity conditions, as in the non-object condition, only materiality is the conditioned phenomenon. Therefore, it is said, 'it is similar to the non-object condition.' The non-co-nascence condition is excluded. As with this, so too are the non-dependence, non-presence, and non-disappearance conditions. What is the reason? Because without these, nothing arises. Indeed, without the co-nascence, dependence, presence, and non-disappearance conditions, not even a single material or immaterial phenomenon arises; therefore, they are excluded.

90. Naaññamaññapaccayavibhaṅge [M 0.0421] paṭisandhikkhaṇe vipākābyākate khandhe paṭicca kaṭattārūpanti hadayavatthuvajjaṃ veditabbaṃ.

90. In the analysis of the non-mutuality condition, at the moment of rebirth-linking, kamma-born materiality should be understood as conditioned by the resultant-indeterminate aggregates, with the exception of the heart-basis.

91. Naupanissayapaccayavibhaṅge rūpameva paccayuppannaṃ, tañhi upanissayaṃ na labhati. Arūpaṃ pana kiñcāpi ārammaṇūpanissayapakatūpanissaye na labheyya, anantarūpanissayamuttakaṃ pana natthi. Tena vuttaṃ “nārammaṇapaccayasadisa”nti.

91. In the analysis of the non-strong-dependence condition, only materiality is the conditioned phenomenon, for it does not obtain strong-dependence. However, the immaterial, though it may not obtain object-strong-dependence or natural strong-dependence, is not without contiguity-strong-dependence. Therefore, it is said, 'It is similar to the non-object condition.'

92. Napurejāte cittasamuṭṭhānarūpanti pañcavokāravasena vuttaṃ.

92. In the analysis of the non-pre-nascence condition, the term 'mind-originated materiality' is stated with reference to the five-constituent existence.

93. Napacchājātapaccayāti ettha sahajātapurejātapaccayā saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Tasmā sahajātapaccayasadisā ettha pāḷi, sā naadhipatipaccaye vitthāritāti idha saṅkhittā. Nāsevanapaccaye kusalākusalā paṭhamajavanavasena veditabbā, tathā kiriyābyākataṃ. Pāḷi pana idhāpi naadhipatipaccaye vitthāritavasena veditabbā. Tenevāha – “napacchājātapaccayampi nāsevanapaccayampi nādhipatipaccayasadisa”nti.

93. In the non-post-nascence condition, the co-nascence and pre-nascence conditions are included. Therefore, the text here is similar to that for the co-nascence condition, and it is abbreviated here because it is elaborated in the non-dominance condition. In the non-repetition condition, wholesome and unwholesome states should be understood by way of the first impulsion, and similarly for functional-indeterminate states. The text here, however, should also be understood by way of the elaboration in the non-dominance condition. Therefore, it is said: 'The non-post-nascence condition and the non-repetition condition are similar to the non-dominance condition.'

94-97. Nakammapaccaye [V 0.0419] vipākacetanā nānākkhaṇikakammapaccayaṃ labhatīti na gahitā. Nāhārapaccaye ekaccaṃ rūpameva paccayuppannaṃ, tathā naindriyapaccaye.

94-97. In the non-kamma condition, resultant volition is not included because it obtains the different-moment kamma condition. In the non-nutriment condition, only some materiality is the conditioned phenomenon; and similarly in the non-faculty condition.

98. Najhānapaccaye pañcaviññāṇadhammā ceva ekaccañca rūpaṃ paccayuppannaṃ. Pañcaviññāṇasmiñhi vedanā ca cittekaggatā ca dubbalattā upanijjhānalakkhaṇaṃ na pāpuṇantīti jhānapaccaye na gahitā.

98. In the non-jhāna condition, the states of the five sense-consciousnesses and also some materiality are the conditioned phenomena. For in the five sense-consciousnesses, feeling and one-pointedness, being weak, do not attain the characteristic of close contemplation; hence, they are not included in the jhāna condition.

99-102. Namaggapaccaye ahetukavipākakiriyañceva ekaccañca rūpaṃ paccayuppannaṃ. Nasampayuttanonatthinovigatesu rūpameva paccayuppannaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “nārammaṇapaccayasadisa”nti.

99-102. In the non-path condition, rootless resultant and functional states and some materiality are the conditioned phenomena. In the non-association, non-presence, and non-disappearance conditions, only materiality is the conditioned phenomenon. Therefore, it is said, 'It is similar to the non-object condition.'

103. Nahetuyā dveti ekamūlakagaṇanāya yathāpāḷimeva niyyāti.

103. The phrase 'two by the non-root condition' proceeds according to the enumeration of the single-root, just as in the Pāli text.

104. Dumūlake nahetupaccayā nārammaṇe ekanti ettha kiñcāpi bahugaṇanena saddhiṃ ūnataragaṇanassa saṃsandane ūnataragaṇanavasena nahetuyā viya dvīhi bhavitabbaṃ. Nārammaṇavasena pana arūpadhammānaṃ parihīnattā abyākataṃ paṭicca rūpābyākatassa uppattiṃ sandhāya “eka”nti vuttaṃ[M 0.0422]. Sabbesu ekakesupi eseva nayo. Dveti vuttaṭṭhāne pana nahetuyā laddhavasena vāradvayaṃ veditabbaṃ.

104. In the double-root, regarding the phrase 'in the non-object condition, one by the non-root condition': here, although in comparing the lesser enumeration with the more numerous enumeration, it should be two by way of the lesser enumeration, as in the non-root condition, yet by way of the non-object condition, because immaterial phenomena are excluded, 'one' is said with reference to the arising of indeterminate materiality conditioned by the indeterminate. The same method applies in all single cases. But where 'two' is said, two occurrences should be understood as obtained by way of the non-root condition.

105-106. Timūlakādīsu pana sabbesu nārammaṇapaccayassa aparihīnattā ekameva vissajjananti ayaṃ paccanīye nahetupaccayaṃ ādiṃ katvā ekamūlakādīsu gaṇanā.

105-106. However, in all the triple-root, etc., since the non-object condition is not excluded, there is only one solution. This is the enumeration in the negative section, beginning with the non-root condition, in the single-root, etc.

107-130. Nārammaṇapaccayādayo pana ekamūlake tāva purimena sadisattā idhāpi na dassitāyeva. Nārammaṇapaccayavasena dumūlake nārammaṇapaccayā, nahetuyā ekanti nahetudumūlake vuttameva. Nādhipatiyā pañcāti nārammaṇapaccaye laddhavasena veditabbāti evaṃ sabbasaṃsandanesu ūnataragaṇanasseva paccayassa vasena gaṇanā veditabbā. Yattha yattha ca nārammaṇapaccayo pavisati, tattha tattha rūpameva paccayuppannaṃ. Nānantaranasamanantaranaaññamaññanaupanissayanāhāranaindriyanasampayuttanonatthinovigatapaccayānaṃ paviṭṭhaṭṭhānepi eseva nayo. Nāhāranaindriyanajhānanamaggapaccayā sabbattha sadisavissajjanā. Nasahajātādicatukkaṃ idhāpi parihīnamevāti [V 0.0420] idamettha lakkhaṇaṃ. Iminā pana lakkhaṇena sabbesu dumūlakādīsu “ayaṃ paccayo mūlaṃ, ayamettha dumūlako, ayaṃ timūlako, ayaṃ sabbamūlako”ti sallakkhetvā ūnataragaṇanassa paccayassa vasena gaṇanā veditabbāti.

107-130. However, the non-object condition, etc., being similar to the preceding in the single-root, are not shown here either. By way of the non-object condition in the double-root, the phrase 'by non-object condition, one by non-root condition' is already stated in the non-root double-root. 'Five by the non-dominance condition' should be understood as obtained by way of the non-object condition. Thus, in all combinations, the enumeration should be understood based on the condition with the lesser enumeration. And wherever the non-object condition enters, there only materiality is the conditioned phenomenon. The same method applies even in the places where the non-contiguity, non-proximity, non-mutuality, non-strong-dependence, non-nutriment, non-faculty, non-association, non-presence, and non-disappearance conditions have entered. The non-nutriment, non-faculty, non-jhāna, and non-path conditions have the same solutions everywhere. The four beginning with non-co-nascence are also excluded here. This is the characteristic in this case. But by this characteristic, in all the double-root, etc., having discerned 'this condition is a root, this here is a double-root, this is a triple-root, this is an all-root,' the enumeration should be understood based on the condition with the lesser enumeration.

Paccayapaccanīyavaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Conditional Negative.

Paccayānulomapaccanīyavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Conditional Positive-Negative.

131-189. Idāni anulomapaccanīye gaṇanaṃ dassetuṃ hetupaccayā nārammaṇe pañcātiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha hetādhipatimaggapaccayesu anulomato ṭhitesu sahajātādayo cattāro sabbaṭṭhānikapaccayā, āhārindriyajhānamaggapaccayā cattāroti ime aṭṭha paccanīyato na labbhanti. Hetupaccayādivasena hi uppajjamāno dhammo ime aṭṭha paccaye alabhanto nāma natthi. Ārammaṇaanantarasamanantaraupanissayasampayuttanatthivigatapaccayesu pana anulomato ṭhitesu arūpaṭṭhānikā paccanīkato [M 0.0423] na labbhanti. Na hi ārammaṇapaccayādīhi uppajjamānā anantarasamanantarapaccayādayo na labhanti. Sahajātaaññamaññanissayakammāhārindriyaatthiavigatapaccayesu pana anulomato ṭhitesu cattāro sabbaṭṭhānikāyeva, paccanīkato na labbhanti. Etesañhi paccayānaṃ vasena uppajjamāno sabbaṭṭhānike alabhanto nāma natthi. Pacchājātapaccayassa anulomato ṭhānaṃ nāma natthi. Evaṃ sesesu anulomato ṭhitesu ye ca labbhanti, ye ca na labbhanti, te sallakkhetvā sabbesupi dumūlakādīsu nayesu tesaṃ tesaṃ paccayānaṃ saṃsandane ūnataragaṇanānaṃyeva vasena gaṇanā veditabbāti.

131-189. Now, to show the calculation in the direct-reverse mode, the section beginning with 'by way of root condition, five in non-object' is commenced. Here, when the root, dominance, and path conditions are established in the direct order, the four universally applicable conditions—co-nascence and the others—and the four conditions—nutriment, faculty, jhāna, and path—these eight are not obtainable in the reverse order. For there is no phenomenon arising by way of the root condition and the others which lacks these eight conditions. However, when the object, contiguity, immediate, support, association, absence, and disappearance conditions are established in the direct order, the conditions pertaining to the immaterial sphere are not obtainable in the reverse order. For phenomena arising by way of the object condition and the others do not lack the contiguity, immediate, and other conditions. When the co-nascence, reciprocity, dependence, kamma, nutriment, faculty, presence, and non-disappearance conditions are established in the direct order, only the four universally applicable conditions are not obtainable in the reverse order. For there is no phenomenon arising by way of these conditions which lacks the universally applicable conditions. There is no establishment in the direct order for the post-nascence condition. Thus, in the remaining cases, when established in the direct order, having discerned which are obtainable and which are not, in all the methods of the dyads and so forth, the calculation should be understood based on the lesser count in their respective combinations.

Paccayānulomapaccanīyavaṇṇanā.

Exposition of the Direct-Reverse of Conditions.

Paccayapaccanīyānulomavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Reverse-Direct of Conditions

190. Idāni paccanīyānulome gaṇanaṃ dassetuṃ nahetupaccayā ārammaṇe dvetiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha hetumhi paccanīkato ṭhite ṭhapetvā adhipatiṃ avasesā anulomato labbhanti. Pacchājāto [V 0.0421] pana anulomato sabbattheva na labbhati, ye nava paccayā “arūpānaññevā”ti vuttā, tesu purejātañca āsevanañca ṭhapetvā avasesesu sattasu paccanīkato ṭhitesu sesā arūpaṭṭhānikā anulomato na labbhanti. Yo hi ārammaṇādīhi nuppajjati, na so anantarādayo labhati. Paṭisandhivipāko pana purejātato, sabbavipāko ca saddhiṃ kiriyamanodhātuyā āsevanato anuppajjamānopi anantarādayo labhati, tasmā “purejātañca āsevanañca ṭhapetvā”ti vuttaṃ.

190. Now, to show the calculation in the reverse-direct mode, the section beginning with 'by way of non-root condition, two in object' is commenced. Here, when the root condition is established in the reverse order, excluding dominance, the remaining conditions are obtained in the direct order. However, the post-nascence condition is never obtained at all in the direct order. Among the nine conditions stated as 'only for the immaterial,' excluding pre-nascence and habitual recurrence, when the remaining seven conditions are established in the reverse order, the remaining conditions pertaining to the immaterial sphere are not obtained in the direct order. For what does not arise through the object condition, etc., does not obtain the contiguity condition, etc. But the rebirth-linking resultant, though not arising from pre-nascence, and all resultants, along with the functional mind-element, though not arising from habitual recurrence, do obtain the contiguity condition, etc. Therefore, it is said, 'excluding pre-nascence and habitual recurrence.'

Purejātapacchājātaāsevanavipākavippayuttesu paccanīkato ṭhitesu ekaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesā anulomato labbhanti. Kammapaccaye paccanīkato ṭhite ṭhapetvā vipākapaccayaṃ avasesā anulomato labbhanti. Āhārindriyesu paccanīkato ṭhitesu ṭhapetvā sabbaṭṭhānike ceva aññamaññakammāhārindriyapaccaye ca avasesā anulomato na labbhanti, itare yujjamānakavasena labbhanti. Jhānapaccaye paccanīkato ṭhite. Hetādhipatiāsevanamaggapaccayā [M 0.0424] anulomato na labbhanti. Maggapaccaye paccanīkato ṭhite hetādhipatipaccayā anulomato na labbhanti. Vippayuttapaccaye paccanīkato ṭhite purejātapaccayaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesā anulomato labbhanti. Evaṃ tesu tesu paccayesu paccanīkato ṭhitesu ye ye anulomato na labbhanti, te te ñatvā tesaṃ tesaṃ paccayānaṃ saṃsandane ūnataragaṇanānaṃ vasena gaṇanā veditabbā.

When pre-nascence, post-nascence, habitual recurrence, resultant, and dissociation conditions are established in the reverse order, excluding one, the remaining are obtained in the direct order. When the kamma condition is established in the reverse order, excluding the resultant condition, the remaining are obtained in the direct order. When the nutriment and faculty conditions are established in the reverse order, excluding the universally applicable conditions and the reciprocity, kamma, nutriment, and faculty conditions, the remaining are not obtained in the direct order; the others are obtained as applicable. When the jhāna condition is established in the reverse order, the root, dominance, habitual recurrence, and path conditions are not obtained in the direct order. When the path condition is established in the reverse order, the root and dominance conditions are not obtained in the direct order. When the dissociation condition is established in the reverse order, excluding the pre-nascence condition, the remaining are obtained in the direct order. Thus, concerning these various conditions established in the reverse order, having known which ones are not obtained in the direct order, the calculation in the combination of those respective conditions should be understood based on the lesser count.

191-195. Dumūlakādīsu ca nayesu yaṃ yaṃ paccayaṃ ādiṃ katvā ye ye dukādayo dassitā, te te labbhamānālabbhamānapaccayavasena yathā yathā dassitā, tathā tathā sādhukaṃ sallakkhetabbā. Tattha yaṃ nahetuvasena dumūlakādayo naye dassentena nahetupaccayā nārammaṇapaccayā…pe… nāsevanapaccayāti vatvā “yāva āsevanā sabbaṃ sadisa”nti vuttaṃ. Tassa, “naaññamaññapaccayā sahajāte eka”ntiādīhi sadisatā veditabbā. Yaṃ pana “nakamme gaṇite pañca gaṇhātī”ti sīhaḷabhāsāya likhitaṃ, tassattho – nahetupaccayaṃ ādiṃ katvā nakammapaccayāti evaṃ nakammapaccayena ghaṭite sahajāte ekanti evaṃ dassitā pañceva paccayā anulomato labbhanti, na aññeti. Evaṃ aññesupi evarūpesu ṭhānesu byañjanaṃ anādiyitvā adhippetatthoyeva gahetabbo. Evarūpañhi byañjanaṃ attano saññānibandhanatthaṃ porāṇehi sakasakabhāsāya likhitaṃ.

191-195. In the methods of the dyads and so forth, whichever condition is taken as the beginning and whichever dyads, etc., are shown, they should be carefully noted according to whether the conditions are obtainable or unobtainable. There, when showing the methods of the dyads and so forth by way of the non-root condition, it is said, 'not the root condition, not the object condition... up to... not the habitual recurrence condition,' and then, 'up to habitual recurrence, all is the same.' Its similarity should be understood by statements like, 'in the co-nascent, the non-reciprocity condition is one,' etc. However, what is written in the Sinhalese language as, 'when non-kamma is reckoned, it takes five,' its meaning is: starting with the non-root condition, up to the non-kamma condition, thus, when connected with the non-kamma condition, in co-nascence, one—thus, only five conditions are obtained in the direct order, not others. Similarly, in other such instances, the wording should not be adhered to, but only the intended meaning should be grasped. For such wording was written by the ancients in their own language for the sake of their own conventions.

Apica [V 0.0422] imasmiṃ paccanīyānulome paccayuppannadhammesupi atthi dhammo kammapaccayaṃ labhati, na indriyapaccayaṃ. So asaññesu ceva pañcavokāre pavatte ca rūpajīvitindriyavasena veditabbo. Atthi dhammo maggapaccayaṃ labhati, nahetupaccayaṃ. So vicikicchuddhaccasahajātamohavasena veditabbo. Atthi dhammo jhānapaccayaṃ labhati, namaggapaccayaṃ. So manodhātuahetukamanoviññāṇadhātuvasena veditabbo. Yattha kaṭattārūpāni nānākkhaṇikakammavaseneva kammapaccayaṃ labhanti, tattha rūpadhammā hetādhipativipākindriyajhānamaggapaccaye na labhanti, sabbaṭṭhānikā paccanīyā na honti. Ahetuke adhipatipaccayo natthīti imesampi pakiṇṇakānaṃ vasenettha gaṇanavāro asammohato veditabbo.

Moreover, in this reverse-direct mode concerning conditioned phenomena, there is a phenomenon that receives the kamma condition but not the faculty condition. This should be understood by way of the material life-faculty in non-percipient beings and in the course of five-aggregate existence. There is a phenomenon that receives the path condition but not the root condition. This should be understood by way of delusion co-arisen with doubt and agitation. There is a phenomenon that receives the jhāna condition but not the path condition. This should be understood by way of the mind-element and the rootless mind-consciousness-element. Where material forms produced by kamma receive the kamma condition only by way of kamma of diverse moments, there material phenomena do not receive the root, dominance, resultant, faculty, jhāna, or path conditions. The universally applicable conditions are not negated. In the rootless, there is no dominance condition. Thus, by way of these miscellaneous cases, the section on calculation here should be understood without confusion.

Tatrāyaṃ [M 0.0425] nayo – nahetupaccayā ārammaṇe dveti ettha tāva ahetukamoho ceva ahetukavipākakiriyā ca paccayuppannaṃ, tasmā akusalenākusalaṃ, abyākatena abyākataṃ sandhāyettha dveti vuttaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Āsevane pana vipākaṃ na labbhati, tathā kiriyamanodhātu. Tasmā kiriyāhetumanoviññāṇadhātuvasenettha abyākatena abyākataṃ veditabbaṃ. Vipāke ekanti abyākatena abyākatameva. Magge ekanti akusalena akusalameva.

Here is the method: Regarding 'in non-root condition, two in object'—here, to begin with, rootless delusion and rootless resultant-and-functional states are the conditioned phenomena. Therefore, it is said 'two' in this connection, with reference to the unwholesome conditioning the unwholesome, and the indeterminate conditioning the indeterminate. The same method applies to the rest. However, in repetition, a resultant is not obtained, and likewise with the functional mind-element. Therefore, here, the indeterminate conditioning the indeterminate should be understood by way of the functional rootless mind-consciousness-element. In resultant, 'one' means only the indeterminate conditioning the indeterminate. In path, 'one' means only the unwholesome conditioning the unwholesome.

196-197. Nārammaṇamūlake hetuyā pañcāti rūpameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tañhi kusalaṃ akusalaṃ abyākataṃ kusalābyākataṃ akusalābyākatañcāti pañca koṭṭhāse paṭicca uppajjati. Sabbapañcakesu eseva nayo. Aññamaññe ekanti bhūtarūpāni ceva vatthuñca sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tāni hi nārammaṇapaccayā aññamaññapaccayā uppajjanti. Timūlakepi eseva nayo.

196-197. Regarding 'in the non-object-rooted section, five in root,' this is said with reference only to material form. For it arises dependent on five categories: wholesome, unwholesome, indeterminate, wholesome-and-indeterminate, and unwholesome-and-indeterminate. The same method applies to all the sets of five. Regarding 'one in mutual condition,' this is said with reference to the primary elements and the physical basis. For these arise by way of mutual condition, not by way of object condition. The same method applies also in the three-rooted section.

198-202. Nādhipatimūlake hetuyā navāti anulome hetumhi vuttāneva. Tīṇītiādīnipi heṭṭhā anulome vuttasadisāneva. Timūlake dveti heṭṭhā nahetupaccayā ārammaṇe vuttasadisāneva.

198-202. Regarding 'in the non-dominance-rooted section, nine in root,' they are just as stated in the root section in the positive series. The 'three,' etc., are also similar to what was said below in the positive series. 'Two in the three-rooted section' is similar to what was said below regarding 'in non-root condition, in object'.

203-233. Napurejātamūlake hetuyā sattāti heṭṭhā “āruppe kusalaṃ ekaṃ khandhaṃ paṭiccā”tiādinā nayena purejāte dassitāneva. Sabbasattakesu eseva nayo. Nakammamūlake hetuyā tīṇītiādīsu cetanāva paccayuppannā. Tasmā kusalaṃ akusalaṃ abyākatañca paṭicca uppattiṃ [V 0.0423] sandhāya tīṇīti vuttaṃ. Iminā nayena “ekaṃ dve tīṇi pañca satta navā”ti āgataṭṭhānesu gaṇanā veditabbā. “Cattāri cha aṭṭhā”ti imā pana tisso gaṇanā natthevāti.

203-233. Regarding 'in the non-prenascence-rooted section, seven in root,' they are just as shown below in the prenascence section by the method beginning with 'in the immaterial sphere, a wholesome aggregate dependent on one aggregate…' This same method applies to all the sets of seven. In the non-kamma-rooted section, in 'three in root,' etc., volition itself is the conditioned phenomenon. Therefore, 'three' is said with reference to arising in dependence on wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. By this method, the enumeration should be understood in the places where 'one, two, three, five, seven, nine' occur. But these three enumerations, 'four, six, eight,' do not exist at all.

Paccayapaccanīyānulomavaṇṇanā.

Explanation of the Positive of the Negative of Conditions.

Niṭṭhitā ca paṭiccavārassa atthavaṇṇanā.

The explanation of the meaning of the Dependence Section is concluded.

2. Sahajātavāravaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Conascence Section

234-242. Sahajātavāre [M 0.0426] kusalaṃ dhammaṃ sahajātoti kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca tena sahajāto hutvāti attho. Sesamettha paṭiccavāre vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Avasāne panassa “paṭiccattaṃ nāma sahajātattaṃ, sahajātattaṃ nāma paṭiccatta”nti idaṃ ubhinnampi etesaṃ vārānaṃ atthato ninnānākaraṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Atthato hi ete dvepi ninnānākaraṇā. Evaṃ santepi aññamaññassa atthaniyamanatthaṃ vuttā. “Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe cā”tiādīsu hi asahajātampi paṭicca uppajjatīti vuccati. Sahajātampi ca upādārūpaṃ bhūtarūpassa paccayo na hoti. Iti paṭiccavārena sahajātapaccayabhāvaṃ, sahajātavārena ca paṭiccāti vuttassa sahajātabhāvaṃ niyametuṃ ubhopete vuttā. Apica tathā bujjhanakānaṃ ajjhāsayavasena desanāvilāsena niruttipaṭisambhidāppabhedajānanavasena cāpi ete ubhopi vuttāti.

234–242. In the Conascence Section, “a wholesome phenomenon is a condition through conascence” means that having arisen dependently on that wholesome phenomenon, it is conascent with it. The rest here should be understood in the same way as explained in the Dependence Section. At its end, it is stated: “Dependence is called conascence, and conascence is called dependence.” This is said to show that these two sections are not different in meaning, that they do not have a different nature. For in meaning, these two are indeed not different. Even so, they are stated to delimit the meaning of each other. For in statements like “dependent on the eye and on forms,” it is said that even a non-conascent phenomenon arises dependently. And conascent derived materiality is not a condition for primary materiality. Thus, both are stated: the Dependence Section to delimit the state of being a conascent condition, and the Conascence Section to delimit the conascent nature of what is called “dependent.” Moreover, both are stated for the sake of those who understand accordingly, according to their disposition, through the elegance of the teaching, and by way of the knowledge of the distinctions in the analytical knowledge of language.

Sahajātavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Conascence Section is concluded.

3. Paccayavāravaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Condition Section

243. Paccayavāre kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paccayāti kusaladhamme patiṭṭhito hutvā kusalaṃ dhammaṃ nissayaṭṭhena paccayaṃ katvāti attho. Kusalaṃ ekaṃ khandhaṃ paccayāti kusalaṃ ekaṃ khandhaṃ nissayapaccayaṃ [V 0.0424] katvā tayo khandhā uppajjanti hetupaccayāti vuttaṃ hoti. Imināvupāyena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo. Vatthuṃ paccayā vipākābyākatā kiriyābyākatā khandhāti idaṃ pañcavokāre pavattivasena vuttaṃ. Pañcavokāre pavattiyañhi khandhānaṃ purejātaṃ vatthu nissayapaccayo hoti. Paṭiccaṭṭhassa pana sahajātaṭṭhattā paṭiccavāre esa nayo na labbhatīti paṭisandhiyaṃ sahajātameva vatthuṃ sandhāya “vatthuṃ paṭicca khandhā”ti vuttaṃ. Kusalaṃ ekaṃ khandhañca vatthuñca paccayā tayo khandhātiādīsupi imināva nayena attho veditabbo.

243. In the Condition Section, 'a wholesome phenomenon is a condition' means: having been established in a wholesome phenomenon, one makes that wholesome phenomenon a condition in the sense of support. 'One wholesome aggregate is a condition' means: having made one wholesome aggregate a support condition, three aggregates arise; this is said to be by root condition. The meaning in all instances should be understood by this method. 'The physical basis is a condition for resultant-indeterminate and functional-indeterminate aggregates'—this is said with reference to occurrence in the five-constituent existence. For in occurrence in the five-constituent existence, the prenascent physical basis is a support condition for the aggregates. But since the meaning of 'dependence' is 'conascence,' this method is not found in the Dependence Section. Therefore, with reference to the conascent physical basis at rebirth-linking, it is said, 'dependent on the physical basis, the aggregates arise.' The meaning in instances such as 'one wholesome aggregate and the physical basis are conditions for three aggregates' should also be understood by this same method.

Abyākataṃ [M 0.0427] dhammaṃ paccayā kusalo ca abyākato cāti kusalābyākatānaṃ hetupaccayavasena ekato uppattiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kusaluppattikkhaṇasmiñhi vatthuṃ nissāya kusalā khandhā, cittasamuṭṭhāne ca mahābhūte nissāya cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ upādārūpaṃ hetupaccayavasena ekato uppajjati. Iti paccayabhūtassa abyākatassa nānattepi paccayuppannānaṃ hetupaccayavasena ekato uppattiṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Aññesupi evarūpesu ṭhānesu eseva nayo. Evaṃ imasmiṃ hetupaccaye sahajātañca purejātañca nissayaṭṭhena paccayaṃ katvā sattarasa pañhā vissajjitā. Tattha khandhā ceva bhūtā ca sahajātavasena, vatthu sahajātapurejātavasena gahitaṃ. Paṭiccavāre pana sahajātavasena paccayo labbhati, tasmā tattha naveva pañhā vissajjitā. Ye panete ettha sattarasa pañhā vissajjitā, tesu ekādike ekāvasāne vissajjane kusalādīsu ekapaccayato eko paccayuppanno. Ekādike dukāvasāne ekapaccayato nānāpaccayuppanno. Dukādike ekāvasāne nānāpaccayato eko paccayuppanno. Dukādike dukāvasāne nānāpaccayato nānāpaccayuppanno.

'By condition of an indeterminate phenomenon, a wholesome and an indeterminate phenomenon arise'—this is said with reference to the simultaneous arising of the wholesome and the indeterminate by way of root condition. For at the moment of the arising of the wholesome, the wholesome aggregates arise in dependence on the physical basis, and mind-originated derived materiality arises in dependence on the mind-originated primary elements, simultaneously by way of root condition. Thus, it should be understood that this is said with reference to the simultaneous arising of the conditioned phenomena by way of root condition, even though the indeterminate phenomenon that has become a condition is diverse. This same method applies in other similar instances. In this way, in this root condition, seventeen questions have been answered by taking both the conascent and the prenascent as a condition in the sense of support. Here, the aggregates and the primary elements are taken as conascent, while the physical basis is taken as both conascent and prenascent. In the Dependence Section, however, the condition is obtained only as conascent; therefore, only nine questions are answered there. Now, regarding these seventeen questions that are answered here: in the answer with a single beginning and a single ending, from one condition, one conditioned phenomenon arises in the wholesome, etc.; in the answer with a single beginning and a double ending, from one condition, diverse conditioned phenomena arise; in the answer with a double beginning and a single ending, from diverse conditions, one conditioned phenomenon arises; in the answer with a double beginning and a double ending, from diverse conditions, diverse conditioned phenomena arise.

248-252. Ārammaṇapaccayādīsupi imināvupāyena pañhāvissajjanappabhedo veditabbo. Yaṃ panetaṃ ārammaṇapaccaye vatthuṃ paccayā khandhāti vuttaṃ, taṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe vipākakkhandheyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Cakkhuviññāṇādīni abyākataṃ nissāya ārammaṇapaccayena uppajjantānaṃ pabhedadassanatthaṃ vuttāni. Puna vatthuṃ paccayāti pavatte vipākakiriyābyākatānaṃ uppattidassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ imasmiṃ ārammaṇapaccaye sahajātañca purejātañca paccayaṃ katvā satta pañhā vissajjitā. Tattha khandhā sahajātavasena, vatthu sahajātapurejātavasena, cakkhāyatanādīni purejātavaseneva gahitāni. Paṭiccavāre pana sahajātavaseneva paccayo labbhati. Tasmā tattha tayova pañhā vissajjitā.

In the object condition and others, the distinction of questions and answers should be understood by this same method. What was said regarding 'the base as condition for the aggregates' refers specifically to the resultant aggregates at the moment of rebirth-linking. Eye-consciousness and so on, arising dependent on the indeterminate by way of the object condition, are stated for the purpose of showing the distinction. Again, 'the base as condition' is stated to indicate the arising of resultant, functional, and indeterminate phenomena in the course of existence. The rest should be understood in the same way as before. Thus, in this object condition, seven questions have been answered by treating both the co-arisen and the pre-arisen as conditions. Therein, the aggregates are taken by way of co-arising, the base by way of both co-arising and pre-arising, and the eye-base and so on solely by way of pre-arising. However, in the Dependence Section, the condition is obtained only by way of co-arising. Therefore, there, only three questions have been answered.

253-254. Adhipatipaccaye [V 0.0425] vipākābyākataṃ lokuttarameva veditabbaṃ. Anantarasamanantarā rūpābhāvena ārammaṇasadisā. Parato āsevananatthivigatesupi eseva nayo.

In the Dominance Condition, the resultant-indeterminate should be understood as only supramundane. The contiguity and proximity conditions are similar to the object condition due to the absence of materiality. Further, this same method applies also in the repetition, absence, and disappearance conditions.

255. Sahajātapaccaye [M 0.0428] kaṭattārūpaṃ upādārūpanti upādārūpasaṅkhātaṃ kaṭattārūpaṃ. Idaṃ asaññasattānaññeva rūpaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Cakkhāyatanādīni pañcavokāravasena vuttāni.

255. In the Co-arising Condition, 'kamma-born materiality is derived materiality' means kamma-born materiality designated as derived materiality. This is stated with reference only to the materiality of non-percipient beings. The eye-base and so on are stated by way of the five-aggregate existence.

256-257. Aññamaññapaccaye ca yathā ārammaṇapaccayā evanti vissajjanasamataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Paccayuppannesu pana nānattaṃ atthi.

And in the Mutual Condition, the statement that it is 'just as in the object condition' is said with reference to the similarity of the answer. However, there is diversity among the conditioned phenomena.

258. Upanissayapaccaye ārammaṇapaccayasadisanti rūpābhāvatopi vissajjanasamatāyapi vuttaṃ.

258. In the Strong Dependence Condition, the statement that it is 'similar to the object condition' is said both due to the absence of materiality and due to the similarity of the answer.

259-260. Vatthuṃ purejātapaccayātiādīnaṃ paṭiccavāre vuttanayenevattho gahetabbo.

The meaning of “the base as a pre-arisen condition” and so on should be understood in the way stated in the Dependence Section.

261-266. Kammapaccaye tīṇīti kusalaṃ paccayā kusalo abyākato kusalābyākato cāti evaṃ tīṇi veditabbāni. Akusalepi eseva nayo.

In the Kamma Condition, 'three' should be understood thus: the wholesome as condition for the wholesome, the wholesome as condition for the indeterminate, and the wholesome as condition for the wholesome-indeterminate. This same method applies also to the unwholesome.

267-268. Vippayuttapaccaye khandhe vippayuttapaccayāti khandhe nissāya vippayuttapaccayā uppajjantīti attho. Khandhā vatthuṃ vippayuttapaccayāti khandhā vatthuṃ nissāya vippayuttapaccayā uppajjantīti attho. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

In the Dissociation Condition, 'aggregates are a condition through dissociation' means that phenomena arise dependent on aggregates by way of dissociation condition. 'Aggregates and the base are a condition through dissociation' means that phenomena arise dependent on aggregates and the base by way of dissociation condition. The rest should be understood in the manner previously stated.

269-276. Idāni yathāladdhāni vissajjanāni gaṇanavasena dassetuṃ hetuyā sattarasātiādimāha. Tattha hetuyā sattarasāti kusalena kusalaṃ, kusalena abyākataṃ, kusalena kusalābyākatanti evaṃ kusalavasena ekādikāni ekāvasānāni dve, dukāvasānaṃ ekanti tīṇi vuttāni honti, tathā akusalavasena. Abyākatena abyākataṃ, teneva kusalaṃ, akusalaṃ, kusalābyākataṃ akusalābyākatañca; kusalābyākatehi kusalaṃ, abyākataṃ, kusalābyākataṃ; akusalābyākatehi akusalaṃ, abyākataṃ, akusalābyākatanti evaṃ sattarasa veditabbāni.

Now, to present the answers as obtained by way of calculation, it is said, beginning with 'seventeen in the root condition.' Herein, 'seventeen in the root condition' are: by the wholesome, the wholesome; by the wholesome, the indeterminate; and by the wholesome, the wholesome-indeterminate—thus, with respect to the wholesome, three are stated: two beginning with one and ending with one, and one ending with two. Similarly with respect to the unwholesome. By the indeterminate, the indeterminate; by that same condition, the wholesome, the unwholesome, the wholesome-indeterminate, and the unwholesome-indeterminate. By the wholesome-indeterminate, the wholesome, the indeterminate, and the wholesome-indeterminate. By the unwholesome-indeterminate, the unwholesome, the indeterminate, and the unwholesome-indeterminate. Thus, seventeen should be understood.

Ārammaṇe [V 0.0426] sattāti kusalena kusalaṃ; akusalena akusalaṃ, abyākatena abyākataṃ, kusalaṃ, akusalaṃ; kusalābyākatena kusalaṃ; akusalābyākatena akusalanti evaṃ satta.

“Seven in the object condition” are: by the wholesome, the wholesome; by the unwholesome, the unwholesome; by the indeterminate, the indeterminate, the wholesome, and the unwholesome; by the wholesome-indeterminate, the wholesome; by the unwholesome-indeterminate, the unwholesome—thus, seven.

Vipāke [M 0.0429] ekanti abyākatena abyākatameva. Evamettha sattarasa, satta, ekanti tayo vāraparicchedā honti. Tesu dvādasa sattarasakā, dasa sattakā, ekaṃ ekakanti te sabbe sādhukaṃ sallakkhetvā parato dukatikādivasena paccayasaṃsandane ūnataragaṇanassa vasena gaṇanā veditabbā. Sakkā hi imāya gaṇanāya dukamūlādīsu vāraparicchede jānitunti puna “kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paccayā kusalo dhammo”ti anāmasitvā gaṇanavaseneva vāraparicchedaṃ dassetuṃ hetupaccayā ārammaṇe sattātiādi āraddhaṃ.

“One in the resultant condition” is only the indeterminate by the indeterminate. Thus, here there are three section divisions: seventeen, seven, and one. Among these conditions, twelve belong to the seventeen-group, ten to the seven-group, and one to the one-group. All these should be carefully noted, and then, in the subsequent sections of dyads, triads, and so on, the calculation in the connection of conditions should be understood by way of the lesser count. For by this calculation it is possible to know the section divisions in the Dyad-group and so on. Hence, without repeating 'a wholesome phenomenon is a condition for a wholesome phenomenon,' the exposition beginning with 'seventeen in the root condition, seven in the object condition,' etc., was undertaken to show the section divisions merely by enumeration.

Tattha kusalaṃ dhammaṃ paccayā kusalo dhammo uppajjati hetupaccayā ārammaṇapaccayā. Kusalaṃ ekaṃ khandhaṃ paccayā tayo khandhāti iminā nayena ārammaṇe laddhavissajjanāni vitthāretabbāni. Ayaṃ tāva anulome nayo.

Herein, 'a wholesome phenomenon arises conditioned by a wholesome phenomenon by way of root condition and object condition.' 'One wholesome aggregate is a condition for three aggregates'—by this method, the answers obtained in the object condition should be elaborated. This, for now, is the method in the positive order.

277-285. Paccanīye pana kusalaṃ na labbhatīti akusalaṃ dhammaṃ paccayāti akusalameva ādiṃ katvā vissajjanaṃ āraddhaṃ. Taṃ yathāpāḷimeva niyyāti. Yañhettha vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ paṭiccavārassa paccanīye vuttameva.

In the negative order, however, since the wholesome is not found, the answer is begun starting with 'an unwholesome phenomenon as condition.' This proceeds just according to the text. Whatever should be stated here has already been stated in the negative part of the Dependence Section.

286-287. Yaṃ panetaṃ paccanīye laddhavissajjanaparicchedaṃ gaṇanato dassetuṃ nahetuyā cattārītiādi vuttaṃ, tattha cattāri, sattarasa, satta, pañca, tīṇi, ekanti cha paricchedā. Tesaṃ vasena dukatikādīsu paccayasaṃsandane gaṇanā veditabbā. Yo hi paccayo sattarasa vissajjanāni labhati, tena saddhiṃ sadisasaṃsandane sattarasa, ūnatarasaṃsandane sesā chapi paricchedā labbhanti. Evaṃ sesesupi adhikaparicchedaṃ ṭhapetvā samasamā ūnatarā ca labbhantīti.

Now, what was said, beginning with 'four in the no-root condition,' was to show by enumeration the divisions of the answers obtained in the negative order. Herein, there are six divisions: four, seventeen, seven, five, three, and one. According to these, the enumeration in the connection of conditions in the dyads, triads, and so forth should be understood. For whichever condition obtains seventeen answers, with it, in a similar connection, seventeen are obtained; in a connection with a lesser number, the other divisions are also obtained. Similarly, in the remaining cases, having set aside the higher division, the equal and the lesser ones are obtained.

Ettha ca adhikatarā na labbhantīti ayamettha niyamo. Samasamā pana ūnatarā ca atthā virodhe sati labbhanti. Tenettha “nahetupaccayā nārammaṇe eka”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Ettha hi nahetuyā catunnaṃ, nārammaṇe pañcannaṃ āgatattā nahetuvasena cattārīti vattabbaṃ siyā, nārammaṇena [V 0.0427] saddhiṃ ghaṭitattā pana ārammaṇadhammo virujjhatīti akusalaṃ dhammaṃ paccayā akusalo dhammo, abyākataṃ dhammaṃ paccayā akusalo, akusalañca [M 0.0430] abyākatañca dhammaṃ paccayā akusaloti tīṇi vissajjanāni parihīnāni. Abyākataṃ dhammaṃ paccayā abyākatoti rūpavasena ekameva vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sabbattha viruddhāviruddhaṃ ñatvā labbhamānaparicchedo veditabbo. Apicettha idaṃ nayamattadassanaṃ. Nādhipatiyā cattārīti nahetuyā laddhāneva. Sesacatukkesupi eseva nayo.

Here, moreover, the more numerous are not obtainable; this is the rule here. However, the equal and the lesser cases are obtainable when there is opposition. Therefore, here it is said, “one in no-root condition, in no-object condition,” and so forth. Here, indeed, because four have come by way of the no-root condition and five by way of the no-object condition, it should be said that four are obtainable by way of the no-root condition. But because it is connected with the no-object condition, the object-phenomenon is opposed, and therefore, “an unwholesome phenomenon as condition for an unwholesome phenomenon, an indeterminate phenomenon as condition for an unwholesome phenomenon, and both an unwholesome and an indeterminate phenomenon as condition for an unwholesome phenomenon”—these three answers are omitted. “An indeterminate phenomenon as condition for an indeterminate phenomenon” is stated only once, in terms of material form. Thus, everywhere, knowing what is opposed and unopposed, the obtainable division should be understood. Moreover, here this is merely a glimpse of the method. For the no-predominance condition, four are just those obtained with the no-root condition. The same method applies to the remaining fourfold sets.

Nānantare ekanti ahetukacittasamuṭṭhānassa ceva sesarūpassa ca vasena abyākatena abyākataṃ. Evaṃ sabbesu ekakesu yujjamānakarūpaṃ jānitabbaṃ. Napurejāte dveti idhāpi nahetuvasena cattārīti vattabbaṃ siyā, napurejātena saddhiṃ ghaṭitattā pana abyākataṃ dhammaṃ paccayā akusalo, akusalañca abyākatañca dhammaṃ paccayā akusaloti vatthupurejātavasena dve vissajjanāni parihīnāni. Āruppe pana ahetukamohassa ahetukakiriyassa ca vasena dve vuttāni. Navippayutte dveti āruppe ahetukākusalakiriyavasena dve. Nonatthi novigatesu ekanti sabbassa rūpassa vasena abyākatena abyākataṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tikādīsu apubbaṃ natthi.

In no-immediacy condition, one: this is the indeterminate conditioned by the indeterminate, in terms of rootless-consciousness-originated matter and the remaining matter. Thus, in all single cases, the applicable form should be known. In no-prenascence condition, two: here also, it should be said that four are obtainable by way of the no-root condition. However, because of its connection with the no-prenascence condition, “an indeterminate phenomenon as condition for an unwholesome phenomenon” and “both an unwholesome and an indeterminate phenomenon as condition for an unwholesome phenomenon”—these two answers are omitted by way of the base-prenascence. But in the formless sphere, two are stated by way of rootless delusion and rootless functional consciousness. In no-dissociation condition, two: in the formless sphere, two are stated by way of rootless unwholesome and functional consciousness. In no-absence and no-disappearance conditions, one: this is to be seen as the indeterminate conditioned by the indeterminate in terms of all matter. In the triads and so forth, there is nothing new.

288. Nārammaṇamūlake pana naadhipatiyā pañcāti nārammaṇe laddhāneva. Nakamme ekanti ettha cittasamuṭṭhānañca kaṭattārūpañca aggahetvā sesarūpavasena abyākatena abyākataṃ veditabbaṃ.

288. However, in the no-object-condition root, five in no-predominance condition are just those obtained in the no-object condition. In no-kamma condition, one: here, not taking consciousness-originated matter and kamma-born matter, it should be understood as the indeterminate conditioned by the indeterminate in terms of the remaining matter.

289-296. Nādhipatimūlake napurejāte sattāti napurejāte laddhāneva. Napacchājāte sattarasāti imānipi tattha laddhāni sattaraseva. Nānantaranasamanantaranaaññamaññanaupanissayanasampayuttanonatthinovigatamūlakāni nārammaṇamūlakasadisāneva. Imināva nayamattadassanena sabbattha āgatānāgataṃ labbhamānālabbhamānañca veditabbanti.

289-296. In the no-predominance-condition root, seven in no-prenascence condition are just those obtained in the no-prenascence condition. In no-postnascence condition, seventeen: these too are just those seventeen obtained there. The roots of no-immediacy, no-contiguity, no-mutuality, no-decisive support, no-association, no-absence, and no-disappearance conditions are similar to the no-object-condition root. By this mere glimpse of the method, what has been stated and what has not been stated, and what is obtainable and what is not obtainable, should be understood everywhere.

Paccanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the negative conditions is completed.

297-328. Imināyeva pana lakkhaṇena anulomaṃ purato katvā anulomapaccanīye paccanīyaṃ [V 0.0428] purato katvā paccanīyānulome ca gaṇanaparicchedo āgatānāgataṃ labbhamānālabbhamānañca veditabbanti.

297-328. Moreover, by this very characteristic, having placed the positive first in the positive-negative, and having placed the negative first in the negative-positive, the delimitation of the count, what has been stated and what has not been stated, and what is obtainable and what is not obtainable, should be understood.

Paccayavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the Section on Conditions is completed.

4. Nissayavāravaṇṇanā

4. Exposition of the Section on Dependence

329-337. Nissayavāre [M 0.0431] kusalaṃ dhammaṃ nissāyāti kusalaṃ dhammaṃ patiṭṭhaṭṭhena nissayaṃ katvāti attho. Sesamettha paccayavāre vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Avasāne panassa “paccayattaṃ nāma nissayattaṃ, nissayattaṃ nāma paccayatta”nti idaṃ ubhinnampi etesaṃ vārānaṃ atthato ninnānākaraṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Atthato hi etepi paṭiccasahajātā viya ninnānākaraṇā. Evaṃ santepi aññamaññassa atthaniyamanatthaṃ vuttā. Avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārātiādīsu hi anissāya vattamānaṃ nānākkhaṇikampi “paccayā uppajjatī”ti vuttaṃ. Aññamaññaṃ allīyitvā ṭhitakaṭṭhādīsu ca ekaṃ ekassa nissayapaccayo na hoti, tathā upādārūpaṃ mahābhūtassa nissayapaccayo na hotiyeva. Iti paccayavārena nissayapaccayabhāvaṃ nissayavārena ca paccayāti vuttassa sahajātapurejātabhāvaṃ niyametuṃ ubhopete vuttā. Apica tathā bujjhanakānaṃ ajjhāsayavasena desanāvilāsena niruttipaṭisambhidāpabhedajānanavasena cāpi ete ubhopi vuttāti.

329-337. In the Section on Dependence, ‘depending on a wholesome phenomenon’ means making a wholesome phenomenon a dependence in the sense of a foundation. The rest here should be understood in the same way as explained in the Section on Conditions. At its end, however, it is said, ‘Condition-ness is dependence-ness, and dependence-ness is condition-ness,’ in order to show that these two sections are not different in meaning. For in meaning, these too are not different, like things that are dependently co-arisen. Even so, they are stated to define the meaning for each other. For instance, in ‘dependent on ignorance, formations arise,’ and so forth, it is said that even a non-simultaneous phenomenon, which occurs without dependence, ‘arises from a condition.’ And in cases like pieces of wood leaning against each other, one is not a dependence-condition for another; similarly, derived matter is not a dependence-condition for the great elements. Thus, both these sections are stated in order to define, by means of the Section on Conditions, the nature of the dependence-condition, and by means of the Section on Dependence, the co-arisen and prenascent nature of what is called a ‘condition.’ Moreover, these two are also stated according to the disposition of those who understand in such a way, through the elegance of the teaching, and through the knowledge of the varieties of the analytical knowledge of language.

Nissayavāravaṇṇanā.

The Exposition of the Section on Dependence.

5. Saṃsaṭṭhavāravaṇṇanā

5. Exposition of the Intermingled Section.

338-346. Saṃsaṭṭhavāre kusalaṃ dhammaṃ saṃsaṭṭhoti kusalaṃ dhammaṃ ekuppādādilakkhaṇena sampayogaṭṭhena paccayaṃ katvāti attho. Kusalaṃ ekaṃ khandhaṃ saṃsaṭṭhoti kusalaṃ ekaṃ khandhaṃ sampayuttapaccayaṃ katvā tayo khandhā uppajjanti hetupaccayāti vuttaṃ hoti. Iminā upāyena sabbapadesu [V 0.0429] attho veditabbo. Imasmiṃ pana hetupaccaye arūpadhammasseva sampayogaṭṭhena paccayaṃ katvā tayo pañhā vissajjitā. Yathā ca hetupaccaye, tathā ārammaṇapaccayādīsupi, kevalaṃ vipākapaccaye ekameva vissajjanaṃ.

338-346. In the Section on the Intermingled, ‘a wholesome phenomenon is intermingled’ means making a wholesome phenomenon a condition in the sense of association, characterized by single arising and so forth. ‘One wholesome aggregate is intermingled’ means that, having made one wholesome aggregate an association-condition, three aggregates arise by root-condition—this is what is stated. By this method, the meaning should be understood in all instances. Here, however, in the root-condition, with only formless phenomena having been made a condition in the sense of association, three questions are answered. And just as in the root-condition, so too in the object-condition and so forth, except that in the resultant-condition, there is only one answer.

347-350. Idāni yathāladdhāni vissajjanāni gaṇanavasena dassetuṃ hetuyā tīṇītiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sabbatikesu kusalena kusalaṃ, akusalena [M 0.0432] akusalaṃ, abyākatena abyākatanti ayameva niyamo. Ekake pana abyākatena abyākatameva labbhatīti evamettha bāvīsatiyā paccayesu tīṇi, vipāke ekanti dve paricchedā. Pacchājāte anulomaṃ natthi. Tasmā tīṇi ekanti imesaññeva vasena dukatikādīsu paccayasaṃsandane yattha vipākapaccayo pavisati; tattha ekaṃ, sesesu tīṇīti evaṃ gaṇanā veditabbā. Sesamettha anulome uttānatthameva.

347-350. Now, to show the answers as obtained by way of enumeration, it is stated, 'three by way of root condition,' and so forth. Here, in all the triads, 'wholesome with wholesome, unwholesome with unwholesome, and indeterminate with indeterminate'—this is indeed the rule. But in the single-item groups, only 'indeterminate with indeterminate' is obtained. Thus, here, among the twenty-two conditions, there are two divisions: three, and one in the resultant condition. In the post-nascence condition, there is no positive application. Therefore, based only on these three and one, in the combination of conditions in the dyads, triads, and so forth, wherever the resultant condition enters, there it is one; in the rest, it is three. Thus the enumeration should be understood. The remainder here, in the positive application, is indeed clear in meaning.

351-354. Paccanīye pana kusalaṃ na labbhatīti akusalameva ādiṃ katvā vissajjanaṃ kataṃ, taṃ uttānatthameva.

351-354. But in the negative, since the wholesome is not obtained, the answer is given beginning only with the unwholesome; that is indeed clear in meaning.

359. Yaṃ panettha paccanīye vissajjanaparicchedaṃ gaṇanato dassetuṃ nahetuyā dvetiādi vuttaṃ, tattha dve tīṇi ekanti tayo paricchedā. Tesaṃ vasena dukatikādīsu paccayasaṃsandane gaṇanā veditabbā. Idhāpi adhikataragaṇanānaṃ ūnataragaṇanena saddhiṃ saṃsandane ūnataragaṇanameva labbhati, samagaṇanena saddhiṃ samagaṇanaṃ. Yasmā cettha arūpadhammāyeva paccayuppannā, tasmā nahetunādhipatinapurejātanapacchājātanāsevananakammanavipākanajhānanamagganavippayuttavasena daseva paccayā paccanīkato dassitā, sesā cuddasa na labbhanti. Yepi labbhanti, tesupi vipāke paccayuppanne nakammanavipākā na labbhanti.

359. Here, in the negative, in order to show the division of answers by way of enumeration, it is stated, 'two by way of non-root condition,' and so forth. In that context, there are two, three, and one—thus there are three divisions. Based on these, the enumeration should be understood in the combination of conditions in the dyads, triads, and so forth. Here too, when combining greater enumerations with lesser enumerations, only the lesser enumeration is obtained; with equal enumerations, an equal enumeration is obtained. Because here only immaterial phenomena are the conditionally arisen, therefore, only ten conditions are shown from the negative perspective: non-root, non-dominance, non-pre-nascence, non-post-nascence, non-repetition, non-kamma, non-resultant, non-jhāna, non-path, and non-dissociation. The remaining fourteen are not obtained. Even among those that are obtained, when the conditionally arisen is a resultant, non-kamma and non-resultant are not obtained.

360-368. Nahetupaccayā nādhipatiyā dveti nahetuyā laddhaṃ dvayameva. Sesadvayesupi eseva nayo. Nakamme ekanti ahetukakiriyacetanaṃ paccayuppannaṃ katvā abyākatena abyākataṃ. Navipāke dveti ahetukamohakiriyavasena dve. Najhāne ekanti ahetukapañcaviññāṇavasena abyākatavissajjanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Namagge ekanti ahetukavipākakiriyavasena abyākatavissajjanaṃ. Imināvupāyena sabbasaṃsandanesu attho veditabboti.

360-368. 'By non-root condition, by non-dominance condition—two' means that the two obtained by non-root condition are meant. The same method applies to the remaining two pairs. 'By non-kamma—one' means that, making rootless functional volition the conditionally arisen, the indeterminate is with the indeterminate. 'By non-resultant—two' means two by way of rootless delusion and functional consciousness. 'By non-jhāna—one' means that the indeterminate answer should be understood by way of the rootless fivefold consciousness. 'By non-path—one' means the indeterminate answer by way of rootless resultant and functional consciousness. By this method, the meaning should be understood in all combinations.

369-383. Anulomapaccanīye [V 0.0430] heṭṭhā vuttā nahetuādayo daseva paccanīyato labbhanti, na sesā. Yepi labbhanti, tesu hetumhi anulomato ṭhite jhānamaggā paccanīyato na labbhantīti sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

369-383. In the positive-negative, only the ten conditions stated previously—beginning with the non-root condition—are obtained from the negative side, not the rest. And among those that are obtained, when the root condition stands in the positive application, jhāna and path are not obtained from the negative side. All should be understood according to the method stated previously.

384-391. Paccanīyānulome [M 0.0433] nahetupaccayuppannesu ahetukamohova jhānamaggapaccayaṃ labhati, sesā na labhanti. Najhānapaccaye aṭṭhāhetukacittānipi. Nakammapaccayā nahetupaccayā nādhipatipaccayā napurejātapaccayā ārammaṇe ekanti āruppe ahetukakiriyacetanāvasena abyākatena abyākataṃ. Iminā upāyena yaṃ labbhati, yañca na labbhati, tassa vasena sabbattha gaṇanā veditabbāti.

384-391. In the negative-positive, among those arisen by non-root condition, only rootless delusion obtains the jhāna and path conditions; the rest do not. In the non-jhāna condition, the eight rootless consciousnesses also obtain them. 'By non-kamma condition, by non-root condition, by non-dominance condition, by non-pre-nascence condition—one in the object condition' means that in the formless realm, by way of rootless functional volition, the indeterminate is with the indeterminate. By this method, the enumeration everywhere should be understood based on what is obtained and what is not obtained.

Saṃsaṭṭhavāravaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Intermingled Section.

6. Sampayuttavāravaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Associated Section.

392-400. Sampayuttavāre kusalaṃ dhammaṃ sampayuttoti kusalaṃ dhammaṃ sampayuttapaccayaṃ katvāti attho. Sesamettha saṃsaṭṭhavāre vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Avasāne panassa “saṃsaṭṭhattaṃ nāma sampayuttattaṃ, sampayuttattaṃ nāma saṃsaṭṭhatta”nti idaṃ ubhinnampi etesaṃ vārānaṃ atthato ninnānākaraṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Atthato hi etepi paṭiccasahajātā viya paccayanissayā viya ca ninnānākaraṇā. Evaṃ santepi aññamaññassa atthaniyamanatthaṃ vuttā. “Saṃsaṭṭhā yojitā hayā”tiādīsu (jā. 2.22.70) hi asampayuttampi saṃsaṭṭhanti vuccati. “Yā sā vīmaṃsā kosajjasahagatā kosajjasampayuttā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.832) asaṃsaṭṭhaṃ vokiṇṇampi sampayuttanti. Iti saṃsaṭṭhavārena ekuppādalakkhaṇassa sampayuttassa saṃsaṭṭhabhāvaṃ sampayuttavārena ca saṃsaṭṭhassa ekuppādādilakkhaṇassa sampayuttabhāvaṃ niyametuṃ ubhopete vuttā. Apica tathā bujjhanakānaṃ ajjhāsayavasena desanāvilāsena niruttipaṭisambhidāpabhedajānanavasena cāpi ete ubhopi vuttāti.

392-400. In the section on association, 'associated with a wholesome phenomenon' means 'having made a wholesome phenomenon a condition by way of association.' The rest here should be understood in the same way as explained in the section on intermingling. But at its end, 'intermingling is association, and association is intermingling'—this is stated to show that these two sections are, in meaning, undifferentiated. For in meaning, these too, like co-nascence and dependence, are undifferentiated. Even so, they are stated for the purpose of defining the meaning for each other. For in phrases like 'horses yoked together are intermingled' (Jā. 2.22.70), even what is not associated is called intermingled. And in phrases like 'that investigation accompanied by laziness, associated with laziness' (Saṃ. Ni. 5.832), even what is un-intermingled and scattered is called associated. Thus, the section on intermingling is stated to define the intermingled nature of what is associated and has the characteristic of single arising; and the section on association is stated to define the associated nature of what is intermingled and has the characteristic of single arising, and so forth. Moreover, both of these are stated according to the disposition of those who are to be enlightened, by the elegance of the teaching, and also by the knowledge of the distinctions of the analytical knowledge of language.

Sampayuttavāravaṇṇanā.

The Commentary on the Associated Section.

Etesu [V 0.0431] pana chasu vāresu atthi koci paccayo ekantaṃ anulomato na tiṭṭhati, paccanīkatova tiṭṭhati; atthi ekantaṃ paccanīkato na tiṭṭhati, anulomatova tiṭṭhati; atthi anekantaṃ anulomato ceva tiṭṭhati, paccanīkato cāti idaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tattha paṭhamo pañho [M 0.0434] pacchājātassa, dutiyo mahācatukkassa, tatiyo yujjamānakānaṃ sesānaṃ vasena veditabboti.

But among these six sections, is there any condition that does not stand exclusively in the positive application, but stands only in the negative? Is there any that does not stand exclusively in the negative, but stands only in the positive application? Is there any that stands non-exclusively in both the positive application and the negative? This should be understood as miscellaneous. Herein, the first question pertains to the post-nascence condition, the second to the great tetrad, and the third should be understood by way of the remaining paired ones.

7. Pañhāvāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Exposition of the Section on Questions.

401-403. Pañhāvāre “siyā kusalo dhammo kusalassa dhammassa hetupaccayena paccayo”tiādinā kusalattike uddharitabbapucchānaṃ labbhamānavasena vissajjanaṃ dassetuṃ kusalo dhammo kusalassa dhammassa hetupaccayena paccayotiādi vuttaṃ. Kusalo ca nāmesa sayaṃ uppajjanto ṭhapetvā pacchājātañca vipākañca sesehi dvāvīsatiyā paccayehi uppajjati. Kusalassa paccayo honto ṭhapetvā purejātapacchājātavipākavippayutte sesehi vīsatiyā paccayehi paccayo hoti. Tasmā yehi paccayehi kusalo kusalassa paccayo hoti, te paccaye paṭipāṭiyā dassetuṃ hetupaccayenātiādi āraddhaṃ.

401-403. In the Section on Questions, in order to show the answers, according to what is obtainable, to the questions to be raised concerning the wholesome triad, such as, 'Could a wholesome phenomenon be a condition for a wholesome phenomenon by way of root condition?', the statement, 'A wholesome phenomenon is a condition for a wholesome phenomenon by way of root condition,' and so on, was made. Now, a wholesome phenomenon, when it itself arises, arises by way of twenty-two conditions, excluding post-nascence and result. When it is a condition for a wholesome phenomenon, it is a condition by way of twenty conditions, excluding pre-nascence, post-nascence, result, and dissociation. Therefore, in order to show in sequence the conditions by which a wholesome phenomenon is a condition for a wholesome phenomenon, the passage beginning 'by way of root condition' was commenced.

Tattha yā esā paccayavibhaṅgavāre viya “hetusampayuttakānaṃ dhammāna”nti akatvā “hetū sampayuttakānaṃ khandhāna”nti desanā katā, tassā eva karaṇe idaṃ payojanaṃ – tattha hi suññaṭṭhaṃ dīpetuṃ dhammānanti vuttaṃ. Idha paccayato uppajjamānā dhammā rāsito uppajjanti, na ekekatoti rāsaṭṭhaṃ dīpetuṃ khandhānanti vuttaṃ. Paṭiccavārādīsu vā khandhavasena paccayuppannadesanā āruḷhāti tenevānukkamena idhāpi āruḷhāti. Kasmā panetesu evaṃ āruḷhāti? Asaṅkarato vibhāgadassanatthaṃ. “Ekaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca sesā dhammā”ti hi ādinā nayena vuccamāne asukadhammaṃ nāma nissāya asukadhammāti na sakkā asaṅkarato paccaye paccayuppanne ca jānituṃ, evaṃ sante uddesaniddesā nibbisesā siyuṃ. Tasmā asaṅkarato vibhāgadassanatthaṃ evaṃ āruḷhāti veditabbā. Cittasamuṭṭhānānanti idaṃ yassa abyākatassa kusalo hetupaccayena paccayo hoti, tameva dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Paccayavibhaṅge pana kusalādivasena vibhāgaṃ akatvā sāmaññato sabbesaṃ hetūnaṃ vasena uppannarūpadassanatthaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānānanti avatvā taṃsamuṭṭhānānanti vuttaṃ. Tasmā tattha abyākatahetusamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ, okkantikkhaṇe [V 0.0432] kaṭattārūpampi saṅgahaṃ gataṃ. Iminā upāyena sesesupi evarūpesu vissajjanesu attho veditabbo.

Here, the teaching was given as 'for the aggregates associated with the roots' instead of 'for the phenomena associated with the roots,' as in the Section on the Analysis of Conditions. The purpose for doing so is this: there, 'phenomena' was stated to indicate the aspect of emptiness. Here, however, phenomena arising from conditions arise as a mass, not individually; thus, 'aggregates' was stated to indicate the aspect of a mass. Alternatively, in the Dependent Origination Section and so forth, the teaching of conditionally arisen phenomena is established in terms of aggregates, and so it is established in the same sequence here too. But why is it established in this way in these sections? For the purpose of showing the distinction without confusion. For if it were stated according to the method beginning, 'Depending on one phenomenon, the remaining phenomena arise,' it would not be possible to know without confusion the conditions and the conditionally arisen phenomena, as in 'such-and-such a phenomenon depending on such-and-such a phenomenon.' In that case, the enumeration and the exposition would be undifferentiated. Therefore, it should be understood that it is established in this way for the purpose of showing the distinction without confusion. The phrase 'mind-originated' is stated to show that very indeterminate phenomenon for which a wholesome phenomenon is a condition by way of root condition. In the Analysis of Conditions, however, without making a distinction in terms of wholesome, etc., but generally, 'that-originated' was stated instead of 'mind-originated' to show the form that has arisen by way of all roots. Thus, there, form originated from indeterminate roots and kamma-born form at the moment of conception are also included. By this method, the meaning should be understood similarly in other such explanations.

404. Dānaṃ [M 0.0435] datvāti deyyadhammaṃ cajitvā. Yāya vā cetanāya so diyyati, sā cetanā dānaṃ. Datvāti taṃ cetanaṃ pariyodāpetvā visuddhaṃ katvā. Sīlaṃ samādiyitvāti pañcaṅgādivasena niccasīlaṃ gaṇhitvā. Iminā samādānaviratiyeva dassitā. Sampattaviratisamucchedaviratiyo pana loke sīlanti apākaṭattā na vuttā. Kiñcāpi na vuttā, ārammaṇapaccayā pana hontiyeva. Tattha samucchedavirati sekkhānaṃyeva kusalassa ārammaṇaṃ hoti, na itaresaṃ. Uposathakammaṃ katvāti “pāṇaṃ na hane, na cādinnamādiye”ti (a. ni. 3.71) evaṃ vuttaṃ uposathadivasesu aṭṭhaṅgauposathakiriyaṃ katvā. Taṃ paccavekkhatīti taṃ kusalaṃ sekkhopi puthujjanopi paccavekkhati, arahāpi paccavekkhateva. Arahatopi hi pubbe kataṃ kusalaṃ kusalameva, yena pana cittena paccavekkhati, taṃ kiriyacittaṃ nāma hoti. Tasmā “etaṃ kusalo dhammo kusalassa dhammassā”ti imasmiṃ adhikāre na labbhati. Pubbe suciṇṇānīti “datvā samādiyitvā katvā”ti hi āsanne katāni vuttāni, imāni na āsanne katānīti veditabbāni. Dānādīhi vā sesāni kāmāvacarakusalāni dassetuṃ idaṃ vuttaṃ. Jhānā vuṭṭhahitvāti jhānā vuṭṭhahitvā. Ayameva vā pāḷi. Sekkhā gotrabhunti sotāpannaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. So hi gotrabhuṃ paccavekkhati. Vodānanti idaṃ pana sakadāgāmianāgāmino sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tesañhi taṃ cittaṃ vodānaṃ nāma hoti. Sekkhāti sotāpannasakadāgāmianāgāmino. Maggā vuṭṭhahitvāti maggaphalabhavaṅgātikkamavasena attanā paṭiladdhā maggā vuṭṭhahitvā, suddhamaggatoyeva pana vuṭṭhāya paccavekkhaṇaṃ nāma natthi.

404. 'Having given a gift' means having relinquished a thing worthy of being given. Or, the volition by which it is given is the gift. 'Having given' means having purified and clarified that volition. 'Having undertaken virtue' means having undertaken the constant virtue, such as the five precepts. By this, only the restraint of undertaking is shown. The restraint on occasion and the restraint of eradication, however, are not stated because they are not well-known as virtue in the world. Although not stated, they do exist as object conditions. Among them, the restraint of eradication is an object for the wholesome consciousness of trainees only, not for others. 'Having performed the Uposatha observance' means having performed the eight-factored Uposatha practice on Uposatha days, as stated: 'One should not kill living beings, nor take what is not given,' etc. (AN 3.71). 'Reflecting on that' means that both the trainee and the ordinary person reflect on that wholesome deed, and even the Arahant reflects. For even for an Arahant, a wholesome deed done in the past is indeed wholesome; however, the mind with which one reflects is called functional consciousness. Therefore, in this context, the case of 'this wholesome phenomenon for a wholesome phenomenon' is not obtained. 'Previously well-practiced': the terms 'having given, having undertaken, having performed' refer to deeds done recently, whereas these should be understood as not done recently. Alternatively, this is stated to show the remaining wholesome deeds of the sense sphere, apart from giving, etc. 'Having emerged from jhāna': this is the Pāli text itself. The phrase 'trainees, on change-of-lineage' is stated with reference to the stream-enterer, for he reflects on the change-of-lineage consciousness. The phrase 'on purification' is stated with reference to the once-returner and non-returner, for their consciousness is called purification. 'Trainees' refers to stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners. 'Having emerged from the path' means having emerged from the paths attained by oneself, by way of transcending path, fruit, and life-continuum. However, there is no such thing as reflection having emerged from the mere path.

Kusalaṃ aniccatoti ettha vipassanūpagaṃ tebhūmakakusalameva veditabbaṃ, vipassanākusalaṃ pana kāmāvacarameva. Cetopariyañāṇenāti rūpāvacarakusalaṃ dasseti. Ākāsānañcāyatanantiādīhi arūpāvacarakusalārammaṇavasena uppajjamānaṃ arūpāvacarakusalameva. Kusalā khandhā iddhividhañāṇassātiādīhi puggalaṃ anāmasitvā dhammavasena dasseti. Tenevettha heṭṭhā gahitampi cetopariyañāṇaṃ puna vuttaṃ.

'Wholesome is impermanent'—here, only the mundane wholesome pertaining to the three planes, which is conducive to insight, should be understood; however, wholesome insight itself pertains only to the sense sphere. 'By the knowledge of others' minds'—this indicates form-realm wholesome consciousness. Through 'the base of infinite space,' etc.—this refers to formless-realm wholesome consciousness arising with a formless-realm wholesome state as its object. By 'the wholesome aggregates for the knowledge of the kinds of psychic power,' etc.—this shows the teaching in terms of phenomena, without referring to a person. For that reason, the knowledge of others' minds, which was previously taken up, is stated again here.

405. Assādetīti somanassasahagatalobhasampayuttacittehi anubhavati ceva rajjati ca[V 0.0433]. Abhinandatīti sappītikataṇhāvasena nandati haṭṭhapahaṭṭho [M 0.0436] hoti, diṭṭhābhinandanāya vā abhinandati. Rāgo uppajjatīti assādentassa rāgo uppajjati nāma. Idaṃ aṭṭhapi lobhasahagatāni gahetvā vuttaṃ. Diṭṭhi uppajjatīti abhinandantassa attā attaniyantiādivasena catūhipi cittehi sampayuttā diṭṭhi uppajjati. Asanniṭṭhānagatassa panettha vicikicchā uppajjati. Vikkhepagatassa uddhaccaṃ, akataṃ vata me kalyāṇanti vippaṭisārino domanassaṃ. Taṃ ārabbhāti tāni suciṇṇāni ārammaṇaṃ katvāti attho. Bahuvacanassa hesa ekavacanādeso, jātivasena vā ekavacanamevetaṃ.

405. 'He savors' (`Assādetīti`) means he experiences and is impassioned by means of minds accompanied by joy and associated with greed. 'He delights' (`Abhinandatīti`) means he delights by way of craving accompanied by joy, becomes elated and delighted, or he delights by way of delight in views. 'Lust arises' (`Rāgo uppajjatīti`) means lust arises in one who savors. This is stated by taking the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed. 'Wrong view arises' (`Diṭṭhi uppajjatīti`) means wrong view associated with the four types of minds arises in one who delights, by way of considering 'self' or 'what belongs to self,' and so on. For one who has not reached a firm conclusion, doubt arises herein. For one who is distracted, restlessness arises. For one who regrets, thinking, 'Alas, I have not done good,' grief arises. 'With reference to that' (`Taṃ ārabbhā`) means having taken those well-done deeds as the object. This is a substitution of the singular for the plural, or it is singular by way of its class.

406. Arahā maggā vuṭṭhahitvāti maggavīthiyaṃ phalānantarassa bhavaṅgassa atikkamavasena vuṭṭhahitvā. Paccavekkhaṇacittāni panassa kiriyābyākatāni.
